payload.title: Worklink #1490: tests: three ACP/worklink tests race a wall-clock budget against a scheduler stall; the ordering witness needs restructuring, not a bigger number

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Right fix, and it resists the obvious shortcut the issue warned against.

The two ordering witnesses are restructured rather than retuned: the 'after' case now schedules NO release, so the deadline must expire and there is nothing to race. That is the idiom already documented in this file on test_drain_deadline_before_and_after_witnesses, applied to its two siblings — consistent rather than invented.

Leaving a delay on the 'before' case is correct, not a missed half. The failure mode being fixed is close_writer overrunning its own deadline, which lands a late release early and inverts the 'after' assertion. That same slowness gives 'before' more headroom, so it is not the fragile direction.

The test_server.py change is a bigger number, but for a readline hang guard rather than an ordering witness, and the added comment says so explicitly. That is the right call for a bound that is not asserting timing behaviour.

13/13 green. Merging.

payload.title: Worklink #1492: Operator-approval alert omits the causal blocking source and dumps every accumulated source label

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Verified against the spec at head 2afb3aac:

- Causal source surfaced above the bulk material, and the certainty scope is honored honestly: causing_source is labelled as the cause, representative_source is explicitly 'not confirmed as the cause', and no_sources / unknown / classification_failed each say so plainly rather than guessing.
- Classification is best-effort — an exception is caught, logged, and the alert still sends, matching the audit path's 'diagnostics cannot affect authorization' contract.
- Grouping is by the intended tuple, with count, principals and bridge_instances aggregated per group.
- Untrusted active-ingest sources are still enumerated individually with resource_id, so the gate-relevant ones are never collapsed.
- Bounded at 20 groups with an explicit 'N additional source groups not shown'.
- Nice touch beyond the ask: extra_fields enumerates any SourceLabel field not in the known set and renders it per group, so adding a field to SourceLabel cannot silently widen a group. That was a review criterion and it's handled structurally rather than by comment.
- Every value still goes through _render_approval_metadata; only ids and provenance reach the channel, no atom content.
- Five tests covering cause, representative, unclassified, classification exception, and the group bound.

13/13 checks green. Merging.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1491: docs: ACP_TESTING Layer 2 cannot be followed as written, and one documented step revokes the saved key

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Good change overall — the Layer 2 route rewrite is right, and tabling all four
`/tmp/acp-h` hardcodes instead of only `SOCK` is exactly the gap that made the old
text unfollowable. The dated-snapshot framing is the correct way to handle this file.

Requesting changes on one item that is measurably wrong, plus two additions from
live testing that post-date this build's claim.

## Blocking: the saved-key guidance cannot work against `mimir-acptest`

The new step 3 says to "use the existing output with its `acp-tester` key". That key
does not authenticate against this container. Verified by hashing it with the
codebase's own `hash_web_key` (`mimir/identities.py:96`, `webkey:` + sha256 hex) and
comparing against the container's stored aliases:

    saved acp-key.out key -> webkey:40d0be96...
    matches identity `jason`       : False
    matches identity `acp-tester`  : False

The saved `acp-key.out` belongs to the retired host-side `/tmp/acp-h` rig, not to this
container — at the time of the live run the container's roster held only `jason`.
So the section correctly warns against the README's reissue flow, then recommends a
fallback that also fails. A reader following it hits an authentication error whose
cause is not the step they just performed.

Please replace the recommendation: state that the saved `acp-key.out` is not valid
against `mimir-acptest`, and that the reader must issue a key for a principal in THIS
container and use it consistently. Keep the existing warning about principal
`acp-tester` vs `acptest` — that part is real and worth keeping.

## Please also fold in (found live after this issue was claimed, so the build could not have seen it)

1. **Issuing a key against a running daemon does not work without a restart.** A key
   issued while `mimir run` is up is never accepted on the ACP surface until the
   process restarts — DETERMINISTIC 6/6, then the same key passed first try after
   `s6-svc -r /run/service/mimir`. Filed as chainlink #1494. This matters here because
   the revised step 3 tells the reader to issue a replacement key, which will appear to
   fail for unrelated reasons. Until #1494 lands, the step needs the restart, or a
   pointer to it.

2. **`ACP_TESTING.md` finding B's marker string is stale.** It cites
   `ifc_label_blocked:shell_process`. Live at `02c71c57` the refusals are the
   budget-gate messages instead: `hands_edit permission was rejected before execution`
   (post-eligibility) and `shell_exec permission eligibility refused: capability-context
   wiring failed (profile_policy)` (eligibility). Anyone grepping for the documented
   marker will conclude the behaviour is gone when it is not. Filed as #1497.

Both are in a comment on chainlink #1491 with the frame-level detail.

## Non-blocking notes

- The relay pointer (`127.0.0.1:2222`, `acp-test-home/acp_smoke.py`) is correct, but be
  aware the relay was dead until tonight: the forced command in
  `acp-test-home/ssh/authorized_keys` still pointed at `/workspace/mimir/.venv/bin/mimir`,
  which the container rebuild replaced with `/workspace/.mimir-venv`. Fixed host-side and
  verified end to end with `StrictHostKeyChecking=yes`; `known_hosts` also needed
  refreshing after the rebuild regenerated the host key. Nothing to change in this PR —
  recording it so the claim stays true.
- Worth noting for scenario-5-style expectations: agent replies arrive as a SINGLE
  `agent_message_chunk` at end of turn, not streamed, so chunk counts are 1/turn and
  presence/absence is the usable signal.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
All three blocking items addressed at head 62498ca2, verified against the current file rather than the commit message:

1. Saved-key guidance now states the key belongs to the retired /tmp/acp-h rig and matches no identity in mimir-acptest — consistent with hashing it via hash_web_key against the container's stored aliases.
2. The #1494 restart requirement is present with the concrete command, so the reissue step no longer appears to fail for unrelated reasons.
3. Finding B carries both refusal strings actually emitted at this commit, and marks ifc_label_blocked:shell_process stale.

13/13 checks green. Merging.

payload.author: jasoncarreira

Added the version bump: **0.8.8**, at `0cbfec2b`.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Pushed `5b3b382b`. Every point in the review was correct — I verified each against the branch rather than taking them on trust.

**Finding A was recording a fixed defect as live.** `mimir/acp/agent.py:324` requires `structuredContent` and raises `Client provider result is missing structuredContent` without it, so the MCP-spec shape is what is accepted and the bare object is what is rejected — the reverse of what the section said. `tests/test_client_provider.py` exists with 40 references across the three Hands tools. The section now separates what the live harness measured from what the code does today. That distinction is the whole value of the document: a testing map that reports a fixed defect as current sends the next reader to "fix" working code, or teaches them to discount the map.

**The no-automated-coverage claim is narrowed to B and C.** A is covered now, which is the better story anyway: the harness found it, the suite keeps it fixed.

**The inventory was stale in nearly every row, not just missing a file.** Measured with `--collect-only` at this head:

| | doc said | actual |
|---|---:|---:|
| tests | 323 | **472** |
| files | 20 | **21** |

Individual rows had drifted too — `test_acp_sdk_contract.py` is 83 rather than 50, `test_acp_bootstrap.py` 30 rather than 13. The whole table is rebuilt from measurement and now records how the numbers were obtained, so the next refresh is reproducible rather than another hand-count.

**Also folded in #1746** at the operator's request, so `ACP_HANDS_REPL_DESIGN.md` lands alongside this file — which removes this document's dangling "not yet on this branch" reference. One citation in the design note needed correcting on the way in: `_incomplete_protected_result` moved from `access_control.py:8295` to `:9444` as main grew today, verified against `origin/main`.

**On the red check.** Your run hit `test_abort_wait_deadline_before_and_after_witnesses[0.06-False]`; hosted CI hit `test_real_acp_failure_leaves_exact_bundle_and_unrelated_channel_turn_healthy`. With the parity test fixed earlier today that is three instances, so it is a pattern in this area rather than three coincidences. Out of scope for a docs PR; worth its own item.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Pushed `283e77f1`. Both findings were correct, and both were my error: I corrected finding A in `ACP_TESTING.md` and left it restated in two other places, so the PR contradicted itself.

2. **The gaps section** is narrowed to B and C, and states the real remaining gap for A: `tests/test_client_provider.py` pins the response shape, but nothing exercises it against a live client. That distinction is the one you asked for and it is worth keeping — a contract test and an interop test fail for different reasons.

On the red check: `pytest-macos (3.12)`. I agree it should not be attributed to a docs-only change. For evidence rather than assertion — the failures observed on this branch have been `test_real_acp_failure_leaves_exact_bundle_and_unrelated_channel_turn_healthy` (hosted) and `test_abort_wait_deadline_before_and_after_witnesses[0.06-False]` (your local run). Both assert absolute wall-clock budgets: a 1s socket read, a 1s drain poll, and a 20ms margin between two timers. A third test of the same shape, `test_contained_timeout_bounds_cancel_and_collection_independently`, failed the same way on an unrelated PR today and was fixed by widening its guard.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Approved at `17be3593641f542b9dcca30dbd82b2bc627f0a3c`.

The 0.8.7 release metadata and changelog are internally consistent, and the operator-action section clearly captures the coupled image rebuild, publishing-identity migration, and installed-skill refresh. payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Pushed `17be3593`, which widens a timeout in `tests/test_worklink_worker_parity.py`. Explaining why a release PR now carries a test change.

**The failure.** `pytest-macos (3.11)` failed on `test_contained_timeout_bounds_cancel_and_collection_independently[collection]` with a Timeout. This PR changes `CHANGELOG.md`, `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock` — and the lock diff is **four lines, only the `mimir-agent` version**. No dependency moved and no code changed, so the PR cannot have caused a test to time out.

**What the test actually asserts.** It monkeypatches the cancel and collection bounds to `0.01` and asserts the resulting `RuntimeError` names which layer was stuck. The outer `asyncio.wait_for(..., timeout=0.2)` is not part of that property — it is a hang guard, so a broken bound fails the test instead of blocking the suite.

At 0.2s that guard was a wall-clock budget on a shared runner. Under CI load the event loop can take longer than 200ms to schedule the timeout path, and `wait_for` then raises `TimeoutError` before the `RuntimeError` propagates: a false failure reporting the runner rather than the code. This is also the test that ran 8s on a host and hung past 800s in a container, so its timing already varies by orders of magnitude with the environment.

**The change** widens the guard to 10s. The assertion is untouched, and the guard still does its job — with the internal bound disabled the test fails in **10.3s** rather than hanging. Three orders of magnitude of scheduling headroom, and an unbounded wait is still caught promptly.

**Why here rather than a separate PR.** Re-running until green is what lets a fragile assertion survive indefinitely, and this one has now cost a red check on a PR that changes no code. Fixing it in place keeps the rule that no PR merges with a red check honest, rather than satisfying it by retrying. If you would rather this land separately, say so and I will split it — the release content itself is the three-line version bump and the changelog.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1489: web: the Factory Runs detail view rejects every run, because the endpoint validates run ids against a digits-only pattern the system never mints

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approved. 103 tests pass on the branch, all 12 checks green, and both guards are mutation-proven.

**It took the shared-definition route**, which was the preferred answer: `web_ui.py:62` imports the backend's own `_RUN_ID` rather than declaring a second pattern that has to agree. The defect was two patterns disagreeing, so removing the second pattern removes the failure mode rather than re-synchronising it.

**Tests hit the specific traps the spec called out:**

- `test_factory_runs_detail_loads_record_with_minted_run_id` builds its id from `epic_run_id(1337)` rather than a literal, and saves a real record first — so it exercises validate-then-load, not just the regex. A hardcoded `"chainlink-1337"` would have passed while the endpoint still rejected what the system mints.
- `test_factory_runs_detail_rejects_unsafe_run_ids` covers all six shapes: `..`, encoded slash and backslash, leading dot, absolute path, and empty.

**Mutation-tested both halves.** Restoring the digits-only pattern fails `..._loads_record_with_minted_run_id`; dropping the `".." in run_id` check fails `...rejects_unsafe_run_ids[dot-dot]`. Each was a single-line change confirmed with `git diff --numstat`.

**Checked the one property the widened pattern could have lost.** `_RUN_ID` has no length bound where the old pattern capped at 19 characters, and the id is a path component. A 5000-character id matches the pattern, reaches `load_factory_record`, and raises `FactoryRecordError` — which `factory_runs_detail_v1` already catches and returns as a 400. It fails closed with a proper error rather than an unhandled `ENAMETOOLONG`, so the missing bound is not a hole.

One observation, deliberately not a change request: importing `_RUN_ID` — a private name — across a module boundary couples `web_ui` to a backend internal. I considered blocking on it and decided not to, because the failure mode is loud: renaming `_RUN_ID` breaks the import at import time rather than silently reverting to a permissive or divergent pattern. If the coupling is ever formalised, promoting it to a public name in `feature_factory` is the tidier end state.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1488: worklink/factory: a late-gate status refusal discards a completed build, because the failure path archives the record but never preserves the work

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approved. All 12 checks green, and I verified each criterion against the branch rather than the diff summary.

**Ordering** — the part that actually mattered. `_preserve_failed_factory_run` is called inside the `except` block immediately after the supervision failure, before archival and before the lease is released, and it reloads the live record so it sees the merged slices rather than a stale snapshot. `test_post_merge_factory_failure_pushes_branch_before_record_becomes_failed` pins that ordering by name, which is the right shape: the defect being fixed was that the work was gone within minutes, so a fix that preserved after the checkout became sweep-eligible would not have fixed anything.

**Bounded correctly.** Skips when `pr_url` is already set (never preserved twice) and when no slice shows `:merged(` (no branch spam on early failures). Reuses `ControllerGitPublication` rather than shelling out. Zero mentions of retry or resume — it stayed out of the resumption question the spec put out of scope.

**Preservation cannot mask the refusal.** The `except` carries `# noqa: BLE001 - preservation must not replace the refusal`, and the reason string is built by APPENDING to `original_reason`, so the underlying failure survives whether preservation succeeds, fails, or is skipped. `preserved_ref` and `preservation_error` are recorded in both the escalated signal and the archived record, so an operator finds the branch without reading logs.

Mutation-tested: replacing the preservation call with `None, None` (one-line change, confirmed with `git diff --numstat`) fails both `test_post_merge_factory_failure_pushes_branch_before_record_becomes_failed` and `test_post_merge_factory_preservation_failure_keeps_original_refusal`. 296 tests pass on the branch.

Merge ordering note: this and #1787 sit on the same failure sequence — #1787 changes `parse_factory_status`, and this PR changes the `except` that catches the `FactoryContractError` it raises. They do not overlap textually and each is independently green, but I will verify the union before merging the second of the two rather than trusting two green CIs.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1487: worklink/factory: parse_factory_status refuses the documented validator verdict string, discarding a completed epic at gate:pre_pr

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The verdict handling is right and the tests are the ones the spec asked for: the recorded `gate:pre_pr` payload round-trips, all three documented verdicts parse, `null` still parses before the validator runs, an unknown verdict is refused, and `_opaque_dict` itself is untouched so the other status fields keep their object requirement. I mutation-tested it — restoring `_opaque_dict(..., nullable=True)` at the call site fails five tests including `test_status_rejects_unknown_validator_verdict`.

**Blocking: drop the object form.**

`_validator_verdict` falls through to `_opaque_dict(value, "validator")` for a non-string, justified as:

    # Older status projections exposed the validator report inline as an object.

Remove that branch and the `dict` half of the `str | dict[str, Any] | None` annotation. Reasons:

1. **The claim is unverified.** No status projection in this repository's history is cited, and I could not find one. A compatibility branch whose justification cannot be checked is worse than no branch — the next reader inherits it as settled fact.
2. **This is a pre-release surface with a single consumer.** The house rule is a clean remove rather than a shim; back-compat shims get flagged in review here, not added.
3. **The factory's own contract says string.** `WORKFLOW.md` specifies the validator returns `GO` / `GO-WITH-NITS` / `NO-GO` and writes the structured report to `reviews/implementation-validator.json`. The object never travels in the status field, so the branch is unreachable in practice — dead code at the exact gate where a refusal is unrecoverable, which is the worst place to carry something nobody exercises.

After the change the field is `str | None`, an object joins `[]`, `True` and `1` in `test_status_rejects_invalid_validator_types`, and the refusal message stays the one already asserted. Please extend that parametrisation to include a dict so the removal is pinned rather than merely done.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approved. All 12 checks green, and all four consumers moved together.

The object form is gone at the source — `FactoryStatus.validator` is `str | None` and `_validator_verdict` returns `str | None` — and the removal is **pinned** rather than merely done: `{}` joins `[]`, `True` and `1` in `test_status_rejects_invalid_validator_types`. Mutation-tested: re-admitting a dict fails `[value0]`.

The four consumers I listed:

1. `tests/test_web_ui.py` — fixture is `"validator": "GO"` and the assertion is `run["validator"] == "GO"`.
2. `tests/test_worklink_factory_state.py` — `validator="GO"`.
3. `mimir/web_contracts.py:1119` — `validator: string | null;`.
4. `frontend/src/api/generated/contracts.ts:938` — regenerated to match.

That last pair is the part worth noting: the declared REST contract now says what the factory actually emits. `frontend/src/fixtures/api.ts` already carried `validator_verdict: "GO"`, so the frontend had independently concluded this was a verdict rather than a report — the declared contract was the last place still describing it as an object.

Also confirmed `_opaque_dict` is untouched, so `terminal_result` and the other status fields keep their object requirement. That distinction is the whole point: `terminal_result` genuinely is an object — it carries `{status, reason}`, which is how attempt 9's park was read — while `validator` was a verdict string sitting in a group of structured fields, which is likely how it got typed by pattern-match in the first place.

Merge ordering: #1788 (preserve-before-discard) is already on main and touches the `except` that catches the `FactoryContractError` this PR raises. No textual overlap, but I will confirm the union after merging rather than trusting two independently-green CIs.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The object form is correctly gone from `_validator_verdict` — that part is done. But the removal stopped at the parser, and all six pytest jobs are now red on `13c31379`:

    FAILED tests/test_web_ui.py::test_factory_runs_detail
    FAILED tests/test_worklink_factory_state.py::test_factory_record_binds_status_run_id_to_durable_identity
    FactoryContractError: factory status validator must be a documented verdict

This is my request landing wider than I scoped it, so here is the full set. The field is typed as an object in four places and only the parser moved:

1. `tests/test_web_ui.py:492` builds `"validator": {"verdict": "GO"}` and `:518` asserts `run["validator"]["verdict"] == "GO"`. Both need the verdict string — `"validator": "GO"` and `run["validator"] == "GO"`.
2. `tests/test_worklink_factory_state.py:293` passes `validator={"status": "approved"}`. That value is incidental to what the test checks (record/status run_id binding), so a documented verdict or `None` both work.
3. `mimir/web_contracts.py:1119` declares `validator: Record<string, unknown> | null;`. After this change that is wrong and should read `validator: string | null;`.

So the frontend was already treating this as a verdict rather than a report, and item 3 brings the declared contract in line with what the factory actually emits and what the frontend already assumes.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.title: Worklink #1337: turn capability (operator arm) — make the untrusted-active-ingest refusal conditional on sink boundedness for server-authored argv

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Verdict: request changes

The overall Arm 2 shape is careful: it binds authorization and execution to a server-issued exact argv, preserves active-ingest provenance, separates hard refusal from pre-ingest fallback, and adds broad sync/async and audit-boundary coverage. The three directly affected test modules pass locally (1,929 tests), and the completed CI checks are green; several matrix jobs were still running when I reviewed.

### Blocking finding

- `mimir/access_control.py:4294` — pathless `wc` and `grep` are currently accepted as bounded direct executions. Their `effective_paths` and `canonical` collections are empty, so the original argv executes unchanged and these programs read inherited stdin. The direct `shell_exec` subprocess path does not set `stdin=DEVNULL`, making this an unbound input surface (and a possible timeout) after active ingest. I left an inline comment with the narrow remediation: reject operandless `wc`/`grep`, or otherwise introduce and test a server-owned stdin binding.

### Test coverage

The new tests are extensive and generally pin the right security properties: exact request/auth/call identity, pinning, cwd and operand confinement, Git hardening, live-taint transitions, monotonic provenance, sync/async parity, and value-free audit records. One test currently asserts the problematic operandless-reader behavior; please invert that expectation and add an execution-level regression proving inherited stdin cannot be consumed.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Verdict: approve

The blocking inherited-stdin finding is resolved at both relevant layers on `e7a56055`. The binding path now hard-refuses content readers with no canonical operand, while preserving cwd-default behavior for `ls` and `rg --files`; independently, `shell_exec` binds every child process to `subprocess.DEVNULL`, preventing future admitted argv from inheriting the agent process's stdin.

The regressions exercise the right boundaries: the previous operandless `wc`/`grep` acceptance cases are inverted with the specific value-free refusal rule asserted, and the execution-level test invokes `shell_exec` itself and inspects its actual subprocess call rather than testing `subprocess.run` in isolation. The mutation checks described in the remediation comment give useful evidence that each test fails when its corresponding one-line safeguard is removed.

All current CI checks are green, and the reported full-suite result on this head is 10,984 passed, 39 skipped, 0 failed. I found no remaining blocker in the remediation.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Full suite on this branch: **10983 passed, 38 skipped, 0 failed** (560s).

One local run showed `tests/test_root_dockerfile.py::test_built_image_provides_process_tools` failing, which was my verification worktree rather than the branch: the test resolves the image's git ref via `git symbolic-ref HEAD` and `git config --get branch.<name>.merge`, and my worktree was detached with no upstream. With a branch checked out and upstream set, `tests/test_root_dockerfile.py` passes 9/9 in 3m32s. CI checks out normally and that job is green here.

Recorded rather than omitted, since "green locally" has already meant less than it sounded once on this stack — a `/proc`-gated test skipped on macOS hid a real Linux failure earlier today.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Remediated at `e7a56055`. The finding was correct and I verified it in the code before fixing: `subprocess.run` at `mimir/tools/extra.py:514` passed no `stdin=`, while every other subprocess in this repository already binds `DEVNULL` — that call site was the outlier.

Fixed at **both** layers, because either alone leaves a gap:

- **Binding layer.** A content-reading argv that binds no operand is now refused (`OPERATOR_READ_OPERAND_POLICY`). A server-issued read always names what it reads. `ls` and `rg --files` are unaffected: they read no content and their operand defaults to the resolved cwd.
- **Execution boundary.** `shell_exec`'s subprocess call now passes `stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL`. The binding rule covers two programs today; this covers the boundary, so a future reader that binds no operand cannot silently regain the surface.

Tests, as requested: the parametrised reader test asserted the operandless argv was ACCEPTED and passed through verbatim — that expectation is inverted, and the refusal reason and rule are asserted. A new execution-level test drives `shell_exec` itself and asserts its call site binds stdin.

Two things worth recording rather than hiding:

1. My first version of that execution test called `subprocess.run` directly. **It passed with the fix reverted** — it exercised the standard library, not this code path. Rewritten to invoke `shell_exec`, with the reason in its docstring so it is not reintroduced.
2. Mutation-tested both halves, each a single-line change confirmed with `git diff --numstat`. Removing the stdin binding fails `test_operator_arm2_direct_execution_binds_stdin_away_from_the_agent`; removing the operandless refusal fails `test_operator_arm2_reader_defaults_multiple_missing_and_root[command2-False-False-False]`.

Full suite on the new head: **10984 passed, 39 skipped, 0 failed** (623s).

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1486: worklink/factory: migrate to feature-factory 0.8.0 -- environment-resolved publishing identity, declaration key removed, all 39 pins moved together

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approved. Verified every criterion against the head branch rather than the diff summary.

**Migration correctness**
- `publishing_identity` is gone from `.factory.json`; remaining keys are exactly `bootstrap, pr_draft, publish, resolve, verify, verify_timeout_ms`.
- `tests/test_factory_declaration.py` keeps the key-set assertion as an **equality** with the key removed, rather than loosening it to a subset check.
- `FACTORY_VERSION = "0.8.0"`, and the pins move together.
- `FACTORY_PUBLISHING_IDENTITY` is added to `worklink-ready-queue`'s `pass_env`, with a test asserting it. Without that entry the name is scrubbed before the dispatched build sees it, since it is not `MIMIR_`-prefixed and not in the builtin poller allowlist.
- `opencode_argv` still passes only `--autonomous`, `--max-retries` and the run id. No constructed identity flag, which under 0.8.0 could only ever be empty.

**The drift guard survives the consolidation**, which was the main risk. The check moved from "the registry pin appears literally in the Dockerfile" to "the registry pin equals the `ARG FACTORY_VERSION=` default". That is still two independently-maintained declarations compared against each other, not a value compared with itself, so it can still fail. `tool_pins.py` and `targets.json` correctly kept their own literals instead of importing `FACTORY_VERSION`.

`ARG FACTORY_VERSION=0.8.0` is declared at Dockerfile:71 and consumed at 80-81 within the same stage, so it is in scope and defaults correctly — an undeclared ARG would have expanded to empty and installed latest instead of the pin.

**One spec contradiction, resolved correctly.** My review criteria said no occurrence of `0.7.5` should remain, while an acceptance criterion said comments dating a behaviour to a release stay as written. Five occurrences remain, all the same sentence — "feature-factory 0.7.5 stages the workflow inside the run directory" — kept consistently across the three docs, the code comment and the test that asserts the doc text. That is the right reading; the fault was in how I wrote the spec.

**Operator follow-up, not a change request:** the deployment needs `FACTORY_PUBLISHING_IDENTITY=mimir-carreira` in `compose.env`. With the declaration key gone there is no fallback left, and factory control commands read that name from the process environment. mimir's own launch path is unaffected — it resolves `MIMIR_FACTORY_PUBLISHING_IDENTITY` and injects the value. Deploy is also being held until the #1337 factory run terminates, since the rebuild this pin requires would kill a build that is currently 5 of 7 slices in.

This correctly changes the repository's fallback factory publishing identity from `jasoncarreira` to `mimir-carreira`. The runtime already supports per-deployment overrides, so maintainer-local publication can continue to declare `jasoncarreira` through `MIMIR_FACTORY_PUBLISHING_IDENTITY` / `FACTORY_PUBLISHING_IDENTITY` while the tracked default matches mimirbot.

Please add an assertion that the declaration equals `mimir-carreira`; otherwise this exact policy change can be accidentally reverted while the declaration test remains green, and the error will surface only at factory publication preflight/Gate 1.

I left the blocking finding inline on `.factory.json:6`. The change itself is narrowly scoped and sound. Several CI jobs were still running when reviewed; the completed checks were green.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Verdict: approve

The requested regression guard is now present and pins the exact policy value: `data["publishing_identity"] == "mimir-carreira"`. That closes the only blocking finding and ensures a future reversal cannot leave the declaration test green.

I also accept the correction in the PR comment: `MIMIR_FACTORY_PUBLISHING_IDENTITY` is the functioning controller-side selector, while feature-factory's `FACTORY_PUBLISHING_IDENTITY` is only documented and is not reliably honored by the current driver. The tracked default is therefore intentionally optimized for unattended mimirbot publication; maintainer-local runs may still park loudly until the upstream override is implemented in code.

Validation at current head `84129914af39c86c744e34015edd2561ca375d57`: `uv run pytest -q tests/test_factory_declaration.py` passed all 18 tests, and `git diff origin/main...HEAD --check` passed. CI was still in progress and is not a reason to withhold this approval.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Added `assert data["publishing_identity"] == "mimir-carreira"` in `tests/test_factory_declaration.py`, alongside the existing `verify_timeout_ms` and `pr_draft` value assertions and with a comment recording why the tracked value is mimirbot's. Mutation-tested: restoring `jasoncarreira` in `.factory.json` fails that test.

One correction to the review, so the limitation is on record. It says maintainer-local publication "can continue to declare `jasoncarreira` through `MIMIR_FACTORY_PUBLISHING_IDENTITY` / `FACTORY_PUBLISHING_IDENTITY`". Those two are not interchangeable:

- `MIMIR_FACTORY_PUBLISHING_IDENTITY` is mimir's controller-side selector. It works — `_read_factory_publishing_identity` prefers it over the file, and #1781 forwards the resolved value into the launch environment.
- `FACTORY_PUBLISHING_IDENTITY` is feature-factory's own name, and it is the override that is **not** honored today. In the installed 0.7.5 package it appears in `README.md` and `WORKFLOW.md` and in no `.js` file, so acting on it is driver behavior. Attempt 8 of chainlink #1337 parked at Gate 1 with `declared "jasoncarreira", observed "mimir-carreira"` having probed no environment at all — no `printenv` and no mention of the variable anywhere in its transcript.

That is the whole reason this PR exists: the override could not carry the value, so the tracked file has to. A maintainer running the factory locally will therefore still park until the factory honors the override in code, and the operator is working on that. The failure is loud and names both identities rather than publishing under the wrong account, and it lands where a human is present to see it.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.title: worklink: own the ephemeral repo-test execution copy as the runner so a repository's own provisioning can chmod tracked files

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The ownership change itself matches the failure mechanism: the disposable execution copy is already worker-writable and is destroyed after the run, while making the runner its owner permits repository provisioning to change tracked-file modes without widening access to the issued controller-owned checkout.

One blocking regression remains in the test suite. The existing `test_uv_execution_copy_normalizes_for_runner_without_relaxing_source` deliberately uses a synthetic runner UID different from the current process. With the new owner passed into the real normalizer, an unprivileged contained test process now attempts `fchown` to that other UID and fails with `EPERM`. The new mock-based test verifies the argument selection but does not repair or replace that executable behavioral proof.

Validation: the bound repository test command ran with selectors for `tests/test_worklink_worker_exec.py` and `tests/test_repo_tools.py`; result was **1 failed, 175 passed, 3 skipped**. The failure is the test above at `worker_exec._execution_checkout_fd`, reaching `_normalize_checkout_fd` and then `os.fchown(... owner_uid=1003 ...)`. Fresh-head GitHub checks also currently show failures for `pytest (3.12)` and `pytest-worker-uid`.

Please adapt the existing test to the runner-owned contract (or add a suitable root-gated identity proof) while retaining its source-preservation and runner-access assertions.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The updated head resolves my blocking test concern. The executable normalization test now models the runner as the current unprivileged process and the controller/group-only identity as foreign, so it exercises the real normalization path without attempting an unauthorized cross-UID `fchown`; it retains the source-preservation and group-access assertions. The added parameterized test also pins runner ownership for both repo-test and Worklink checkout roots.

The implementation remains appropriately scoped to the disposable execution copy: the issued checkout stays controller-owned, while ownership of the private copy lets repository provisioning change tracked-file modes before that copy is destroyed. The bound full suite reached 67% without a failure before the repository runner's 5-minute timeout, and all 12 current-head GitHub checks are green, including both Python versions, both macOS jobs, `pytest-worker-uid`, `pytest-enforced`, and `worklink-image-identity`.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1483: place the factory-dispatch checkout on the target ref so pr_base matches the record

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The core of this is right, and one part is better than the spec asked for. Six of eight acceptance criteria are met; two are not, and both are ones the leaf argued for specifically.

## What's right

The placement change is exactly the decided shape, and it is **additive** rather than a replacement:

```python
-    branch = f"issue/{issue_id}-a{attempt}"
+    branch = checkout_branch or f"issue/{issue_id}-a{attempt}"
...
     checkout_branch=base if isinstance(backend, FeatureFactoryBackend) else None,
```

so leaves keep the attempt branch and only the factory path is repointed. That was the review criterion standing between a targeted fix and an outage, and it holds.

The three-way test does the right thing and picks the right fixture:

```python
assert status.pr_base == symbolic.stdout.strip() == record.base_ref
assert lease.branch == record.base_ref
```

read through `git symbolic-ref --quiet --short HEAD` — the same thing init reads — and with `base_ref="feature/acp"`. Choosing the non-default target with a `/` in it is the case that would have silently broken under the rejected `--pr-base` route, so this is the fixture that proves the point rather than one that merely passes.

`--base` and `--pr-base` are both asserted absent, so #1606 stays satisfied. Error messages now name observed and expected at all three sites. The `:merged(` slice requirement is in. No pin site was touched, as scoped.

**And a hazard the leaf did not name, caught here:**

```python
+        attempt_branch = f"issue/{lease.issue_id}-a{lease.attempt}"
+        if lease.branch == attempt_branch:
+            delete = runner([... "branch", "-D", lease.branch])
```

Cleanup previously ran `git branch -D lease.branch` unconditionally. Once the factory checkout sits on the target ref, that would have attempted **`git branch -D main` in the parent repository**. Guarding it is the difference between this change being safe and being destructive, and it was found rather than specified.

## Blocking: two acceptance criteria are unmet

**1. The detached-HEAD precondition is not pinned.** The diff contains no occurrence of "detach".

> *A test pins that placement leaves a real branch checked out, never a detached HEAD, since a detached HEAD makes init refuse and write no run.json.*

This matters because it is the failure mode that produces **no run.json at all** — init refuses with `could not observe a symbolic branch in PR base worktree ...` and there is no record to diagnose from. The whole change moves what placement does, so "placement always leaves a symbolic ref" is precisely the invariant that should not be left to inspection.

**2. The completion path still verifies only against the sandbox.**

> *The completion path verifies the recorded PR against GitHub — repository, base, and head sha — rather than only against the sandbox.*

`_verify_factory_checkout` operates on the sandbox via `git -C <sandbox> rev-parse …`; nothing in this diff consults GitHub. The existing `pr_url` / canonical-URL / repository checks are string checks against the recorded status, not confirmation that the PR exists with the expected base and head. That gap is why a run could claim a PR it had not opened — the thing that started this chainlink.

If GitHub verification is genuinely out of reach for the sandboxed build (no network), say so explicitly in the PR body and state what the controller must do instead — that is an acceptable answer, and better than the criterion silently going unmet. But it should not be dropped without a word.

CI is still running (6/12 green, none failing).

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving at `7791a877`. One of my two blocking items was addressed; the other I should not have raised.

## Correcting my second finding

I claimed the completion path "verifies only against the sandbox" and that nothing consulted GitHub. **That was wrong**, and your body was right that the verification already exists and was retained rather than duplicated:

```python
api = _fixed_command(..., ["gh", "api", f"repos/{record.repository}/pulls/{match.group(3)}"])
base_name = _require_pr_string(base_repo, "full_name")
base_ref   = _require_pr_string(base_data, "ref")
head_sha   = _require_pr_string(head_data, "sha")
if base_name.lower() != record.repository.lower(): ...
```

My mistake was grepping the *diff* for new GitHub calls, finding none, and concluding it was absent from the codebase — after reading only `_verify_factory_checkout` and generalising from that one function to the whole path. So I wrote an acceptance criterion for work that was already done, then blocked for not doing it twice. Duplicating it would have been the wrong outcome; not duplicating it was correct.

## The detached-HEAD item

Addressed, and correctly. `git symbolic-ref --quiet --short HEAD` exits non-zero on a detached HEAD, so `assert symbolic.returncode == 0` already pinned the invariant — renaming to `..._without_detached_head` and adding the message makes it explicit rather than incidental. Minimal, but it does pin the thing the criterion was about.

## What stands out in the original work

- **Placement is additive**: `branch = checkout_branch or f"issue/{issue_id}-a{attempt}"`, with `checkout_branch` supplied only for `FeatureFactoryBackend`. Leaves keep the attempt branch; only the factory path is repointed. That was the criterion between a targeted fix and breaking every leaf.
- **The fixture is `base_ref="feature/acp"`** — a non-default target containing `/`, which is precisely the case the rejected `--pr-base` route would have silently broken. That is the fixture that proves the point rather than one that merely passes.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. This is a faithful implementation of the leaf, including the two points the spec was most at risk of being read past.

## The root-cause fix is the right one

```python
-    exe = Path(sys.executable).resolve()
+    # Keep the lexical venv path: bin/python is commonly a symlink to the base
+    # interpreter, and resolving it would erase the venv identity.
+    exe = Path(sys.executable)
```

## It respected the distinction rather than collapsing it

`MIMIR_SOURCE_REPO` keeps meaning "the repo branches are pushed from", now documented as *"deliberately distinct from MIMIR_SOURCE_DIR"*, with `test_source_repo_hook_uses_pushed_from_repo_not_running_source` asserting the hook lands on the pushed-from repo when the two differ. That was easy to get wrong and it didn't.

- `REPO`/`SEED` in `scripts/worklink_image_identity.py` now come from `WORKLINK_REPO`, with the proof's own tests asserting the parameterisation — so the CI job exercises the real layout instead of a literal.

`MIMIR_SOURCE_REPO` is **not set** in mimirbot's `compose.env` today — it was relying on the `/workspace/mimir` default this PR removes. So on merge+deploy the pre-push staleness gate (chainlink #249) silently stops being installed until `MIMIR_SOURCE_REPO=/workspace/mimir` is added.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1482: worklink: the gate reports counts: None on a passing suite, so evidence carries no test totals and no failed test names

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The implementation is right, and it found the cause I could not — I filed chainlink #1482 having eliminated the JUnit size cap, command recognition, and the `PYTEST_ADDOPTS` merge order, and left "file absent or unparseable" as the open question. This answers it:

> Contained workers enter the checkout through an authorized fd and may not be able to traverse the controller's absolute parent path.

Passing the report path **relative to the checkout** is the fix. Three other things here are good:

- `report_error` distinguishes missing / parse-error / oversize instead of collapsing all three into `None` — that ambiguity was itself part of the defect.
- `_PYTEST_REPORT_MAX_BYTES` 2 MB → 20 MB. Worth knowing why that mattered: measured ~150 bytes/test against this suite, extrapolating to ~1.6 MB for 10,626 tests — **under** the old cap but at ~80% of it, so another ~25% of test growth would have silently reintroduced `counts: None` with no signal.
- `read_pytest_result` now returns early for a non-pytest command rather than probing paths that cannot exist.

**Blocking: `pytest-worker-uid` is red, and it is a real portability defect in the new tests — not a flake and not an artifact of that leg.**

The leg is green on `main` (`d6fbb709`) and green on the sibling PR #1777, so it fails only here. Three failures, one root cause:

```
FAILED tests/test_worklink_evidence.py::test_gate_records_counts_from_pytest_generated_junit
FAILED tests/test_worklink_evidence.py::test_gate_records_failed_node_ids_from_pytest_cache
FAILED tests/test_env_isolation.py::test_coding_state_tests_ignore_the_host_override

TestResult(cmd='pytest -q test_gate_sample.py', exit_code=127,
           summary='/bin/sh: 1: pytest: not found')
reasons=('gate_command_not_found',)
```

The two new tests build a gate command of bare `pytest -q …`. Run as the owner that resolves, because the suite is invoked through `uv run`, which puts `.venv/bin` on PATH. Run as a uid that owns neither the checkout nor `$HOME`, it does not — so the gate exits 127 and the assertions fail.

The third failure is downstream of the same cause: `_CODING_STATE_TESTS` in `tests/test_env_isolation.py:199` **includes `tests/test_worklink_evidence.py`**, and `test_coding_state_tests_ignore_the_host_override` runs that file in a child process. The child fails, so the parent fails and reports the child's output as its payload — which is why the log reads like an unrelated `MIMIR_CODING_ENABLED` leak. It is not; that string appears exactly once in the whole job log, inside that assertion message.

Please invoke pytest the way the code under test does — `sys.executable -m pytest`, as `test_env_isolation.py:250` already does, or an absolute interpreter path — rather than relying on `pytest` being on `PATH`. A test for gate evidence **under the worker uid** should not itself assume the owner's environment.

Everything else here is green: 11/12, and the fix is one I want to merge as soon as the leg passes.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Addressed in `790d351a`. Verified at the head rather than from the commit message.

The two tests that actually execute a gate now invoke pytest through the running interpreter:

```python
test_command = f"{shlex.quote(sys.executable)} -m pytest -q test_gate_sample.py"
```

`pytest-worker-uid` is green on this head, and so are the other 11. The remaining bare `"pytest -q"` strings in that file are never executed — they are inputs to `read_pytest_result` / `validate_evidence` exercising `_is_pytest_command`, so they are correct as literals.

Recapping why I want this merged, since it closes a question I could not:

- The cause was the report path being passed **absolute** into the contained worker's `PYTEST_ADDOPTS`. A contained worker enters the checkout through an authorized fd and cannot traverse the controller's absolute parent path, so `junit.xml` never landed and every build reported `counts: None` on a passing suite. Passing it relative to the checkout is the fix.
- `report_error` stops missing / parse-error / oversize collapsing into one indistinguishable `None`. That ambiguity is what made the defect hard to localise — I eliminated three candidate causes from the outside and still could not tell which of the remaining two it was.
- The 2 MB → 20 MB cap raise removes a latent version of the same failure: measured ~150 bytes/test on this suite, ~1.6 MB extrapolated for 10,626 tests — under the old cap, but at ~80% of it, so ordinary test growth would have silently reintroduced `counts: None`.

Closes chainlink #1482.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1465: worklink branches builds from the running agent own source tree, so a build contaminates the live controller and the whole arrangement has no equivalent under a PyPI install - worklink needs its own base repository

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The mimir-side change is right and, importantly, the PR is honest about what it does *not* accomplish on its own.

## Verified

- `_assert_base_separate_from_controller` refuses a base overlapping `MIMIR_SOURCE_DIR`, applied at both `create_worktree` and `create_isolated_checkout`.
- The CLI fails closed: `test_worklink_run_cli_requires_explicit_base_instead_of_using_cwd` asserts exit 1 and `"WORKLINK_REPO is required"`, with both `WORKLINK_REPO` and `MIMIR_WORKLINK_REPO` unset. No cwd fallback, and no path derived from `__file__` or site-packages.

- The deployment procedure is stated concretely, which the leaf explicitly required when provisioning is out of the sandbox's reach.

## Operational note for whoever deploys this

Merging changes nothing by itself, and I verified that rather than assuming it:

```
MIMIR_SOURCE_DIR = <UNSET>          in the live container
WORKLINK_REPO    = /workspace/mimir  i.e. the controller's own checkout
```

With `MIMIR_SOURCE_DIR` unset the guard returns early, so builds keep branching from `/workspace/mimir` exactly as today. **Nothing breaks on deploy** — but the defect is only closed once the base clone is provisioned per the procedure in the body (clone to `/var/lib/mimir-worklink/base/mimir`, repoint the inventory root and `WORKLINK_REPO`, retain `MIMIR_SOURCE_DIR=/workspace/mimir`, restart, prune the old attempt checkouts afterward). That is a heavier step than the usual pull-and-restart and touches the live build system, so it wants sequencing rather than folding into a routine redeploy.

The fail-open-when-unconfigured shape is a deliberate tradeoff rather than an oversight — a PyPI install genuinely has no controller checkout, and it is not distinguishable from an editable deployment that forgot to set the variable without exactly the path-guessing this change sets out to remove. Worth knowing that a future deployment which drops `MIMIR_SOURCE_DIR` becomes silently unguarded again.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1475: worklink: a build that fails at the timeout bound never releases its Chainlink lock, so a dead run holds one of two slots for the full 24h reaper TTL

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. This meets the chainlink's review criteria squarely, and the tests are the kind that would actually have caught the original defect.

## Verified against the acceptance criteria

| criterion | result |
|---|---|
| timeout-bound failure releases the lock without waiting for the reaper | met — `_TerminalClaimRelease` invoked on the exception path and in `finally` |
| every other terminal path releases too | met — applied at all five sites: the `run()` exception handler, the `run()` `finally`, `_finalize`, and both `reattach` branches |
| release **precedes** label routing | met — `if terminal_release():` gates `transition_issue` everywhere; on failure the transition is skipped with `"Chainlink did not confirm lock release"` |
| release failure retains run state + emits a failure event | met — `_log_terminal_recovery_failed`, and `_finalize` returns `"terminal recovery incomplete"` rather than proceeding |
| no double-release | met — `if self.attempted: return self.confirmed` memoises |

## The tests

`test_bounded_timeout_releases_lock_before_failure_routing` drives a **real** bounded timeout (`timeout_s: 1`, a compute backend that sleeps past it, asserting `result.timed_out is True`) rather than simulating the terminal state, and then asserts on lock **state**, not on a call:

```python
assert claims.active_worklink_lock_count() == 0
assert calls.index(release) < calls.index(route)
assert load_run_state(tmp_path, 441) is None
```

That ordering assertion is the one that matters — it is what distinguishes this from a release that happens after the label has already been routed, which was the failure mode. The release-failure cases additionally pin `lock_released: False`, `label_transition_applied: False`, `state_retained: True`, so the partial-recovery contract is covered rather than assumed.

All 12 checks green on `8d43fa4b8`.

## One non-blocking nit for whenever this file is next touched

In `reattach`, the closing paren of the `_log_event("worklink_reattach_branch_mismatch", ...)` call was dedented from column 20 to 16, leaving it misaligned with the call it closes. I checked the block membership at the head — `restored_review` sits at the same level it did before, so there is no semantic change and I am not holding the PR for it.

## Context worth carrying

This build's own evidence recorded `counts: None` — the gate passed but produced no structured totals. That is **not** caused by this PR, and it is no longer the report-directory permission defect either (#1481 is fixed and verified live). Filed as chainlink #1482 with three candidate causes already eliminated. Related note recorded there: the JUnit size cap sits at roughly 80% of the current suite size, so it will start biting on its own before long.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.title: worklink: give the executor's pytest report directory to the worker group

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The successful path is narrowly scoped: it retains controller ownership, grants only the Worklink group, and the new focused tests pass. All 12 hosted checks are also green.

I’m requesting changes because the best-effort fallback is unsafe for the worker execution mode. If identity lookup, `chown`, or `chmod` fails, the function returns the original controller-owned 0700 directory and the orchestrator still injects report paths beneath it into the worker’s `PYTEST_ADDOPTS`. That recreates the exact post-suite `PermissionError` this PR is intended to eliminate, only later and with less direct diagnostics. The inline comment has the concrete fix: use the caller’s already-known `worker_uid_drop` decision, require successful sharing before launching a worker (and clean up on failure), and keep controller-mode reports private at 0700 rather than granting the worker group unconditionally.

Test coverage should add explicit `chown`-failure and `chmod`-failure cases for worker mode and assert failure occurs before backend launch; replace the current missing-account fallback expectation with a controller-mode test proving no sharing call is needed.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Re-reviewed at `de143de4` and the blocker is resolved. Worker-mode report-directory sharing is now a required pre-launch condition: `worker_uid_drop` is passed explicitly, sharing failures clean up and raise `WorklinkError`, and controller mode retains the private 0700 directory without touching identities or group ownership.

The added coverage pins the worker group grant, retained controller ownership, lack of world access, private controller mode, and both `chown`/`chmod` failure paths. The current head is unchanged from the inspected SHA, and all 12 hosted checks are green, including `pytest-worker-uid` and both enforced/full pytest jobs.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Addressed in `de143de4`. You were right, and the irony is not lost on me — I flagged exactly this shape in #1770 (silent degradation instead of loud failure) and then shipped it here.

## What changed

Worker-path sharing is now a **precondition**, not a best effort:

```python
if not worker_uid_drop:
    return path                      # controller mode: 0700, private, no group granted
try:
    os.chown(path, -1, get_identities().worklink_gid)
    os.chmod(path, 0o770)
except Exception as exc:
    rmtree_missing_ok(path)          # leave nothing behind
    raise WorklinkError(...) from exc  # fail BEFORE the backend launches
```

It takes the caller's already-known `worker_uid_drop` (defined at `orchestrator.py:547`, same `run()` scope) rather than re-deriving anything, exactly as you suggested. Controller mode keeps 0700 and grants no group — there is no worker uid to accommodate.

## The root cause of the bad fallback

The `AttributeError` that pushed me to best-effort came from a test double: `SimpleNamespace(worklink_uid=worker_uid)` with no `worklink_gid`. I have completed that stub to match the real `WorklinkIdentities` dataclass instead of degrading production code to accommodate an under-specified double. Two further doubles still took `(issue, attempt)` positionally and rejected the new keyword; both updated.

## Tests, per your list

| test | covers |
|---|---|
| `..._is_shared_with_the_worker_group` | group granted, ownership retained by controller, no world access |
| `test_controller_mode_report_dir_stays_private` | **no sharing call at all**, 0700 holds — `get_identities` and `os.chown` are patched to raise if touched |
| `..._failure_aborts_before_the_backend_launches[chown]` | raises `WorklinkError`, directory removed |
| `..._failure_aborts_before_the_backend_launches[chmod]` | raises `WorklinkError`, directory removed |

The failure tests assert the raise happens inside `_make_executor_report_dir`, which the caller invokes before `with_worker_environment`/backend launch, so the abort is necessarily pre-launch.

### Mutation results

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| `chmod 0o770` → `0o700` | `..._is_shared_with_the_worker_group` fails |
| delete the `os.chown` line | `..._aborts_before_the_backend_launches[chown]` fails |
| `return path` instead of cleanup+raise (the old fallback) | `..._aborts_before_the_backend_launches[chmod]` fails |

Clean restore after each, confirmed via `git diff --numstat`.

## Validation

- Full suite on the **integrated** tree (with #1770 merged in): `10626 passed, 38 skipped` (0:11:04)
- All 12 hosted checks green on `de143de4`, `pytest-worker-uid` included

Note the earlier `10620 passed` figure in this PR's history was against a pre-merge base; the number above is the one that counts.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1467: poller relevance is checked only when replaying a failed turn, so an event queued while its PR was open still spawns a turn after that PR merges - the check must also run at delivery

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The delivery-time check is well placed and the tests are real — they drive an actual `Dispatcher` and assert on whether the turn was *delivered*, not on mock calls, which is what makes them worth having. I verified the acceptance criteria against the code rather than the description:

| criterion | result |
|---|---|
| relevance evaluated at delivery, not only replay | met — `_worker_loop` pops and awaits the predicate before running the turn |
| indeterminate fails **open** | met — `except` sets `relevant = None`, and only `is False` drops |
| pollers with no predicate unaffected | met — `_enqueue_with_relevance` short-circuits on `None` |
| drop distinguishable from a replay drop | met — delivery emits `poller_delivery_stale_dropped`; replay counts `summary["stale_dropped"]` |
| no failure-flavoured signal on drop | met — plain `continue`, no `poller_turn_gave_up` |
| relevance resolved once per cycle | met — one closure now built per `run_poller` call and shared with the replay path |

I also chased two things I suspected were defects and **confirmed neither is**, recorded so they don't get re-raised:

- **`id(event)` keying with no reference held.** I looked for a path that strands an entry so a later object could reuse the address and inherit a stale check. `drain_startup_user_messages` re-inserts any non-`user_message` event, so poller events never leave the queue there; `drain()` only abandons entries after `_closed`, when the dispatcher is not reused. Not reachable.
- **Registering the check *after* `await queue.put(event)`.** `_ChannelQueue` inherits `asyncio.Queue.put`, which does not await when the queue is not full, and when it is full the event is not yet queued during the wait. `put_nowait` only *schedules* a waiting getter. No suspension point, so no window.

## Blocking: `_enqueue_with_relevance` silently drops the check on a signature mismatch

```python
supports_relevance = any(...)
if not supports_relevance:
    return await enqueue(event)          # check discarded, no signal
```

Every production `enqueue` callable already accepts the parameter after this PR — `dispatcher.enqueue` (`server.py:1208/1224/1245/1268/1519`) and `enqueue_with_turn_budget` (`scheduler.py:2476`). So the sniffing guards nothing that exists, while adding a path where the feature stops working **silently**: a future enqueue boundary that omits the keyword disables stale-turn suppression with no event, no log, and a green suite. That is the same shape as the defect this leaf exists to fix — work quietly not happening — and it is the one thing the acceptance criteria are most insistent about being observable.

Please pass `relevance_check` explicitly. If the shim must stay for a caller I have not found, then name that caller in the PR body and make the fallback emit an event, so "the check did not run" is visible rather than inferred.

Two smaller things to fold into the same change:

- `scheduler.py` imports the private `_enqueue_with_relevance` across module boundaries. If it is a real cross-module contract, give it a public name; if the explicit-passing fix above lands, it disappears.
- That import is inserted out of order in the `from .pollers import (...)` list (between `forget_circuit_breakers_except` and `run_poller`).

Nothing else blocking. CI is 12/12 green on `2bcdec59`.

One note not about this PR: its own evidence records `counts: None`, so the gate could not read its JUnit report — chainlink #1481, fixed in #1771. Worth knowing that the green gate here was not backed by structured results.

| private cross-module import | gone — `scheduler.py` takes its own `relevance_check=None` parameter |
| import ordering | moot, the import no longer exists |
| dangling references repo-wide | none |
| the three delivery tests | intact |

Forwarding is now explicit in both modules:

```python

    return await enqueue(event)
return await enqueue(event, relevance_check=relevance_check)
```

That is the substance of it: a callable that cannot accept the keyword now raises `TypeError` instead of silently discarding the check, so "the relevance check did not run" is a loud failure rather than an invisible one.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The fix preserves Git’s URL scoping instead of flattening credential helpers, while retaining helper/reset ordering in the controller-owned publication config. The scoped-host and cross-host tests exercise the important success and isolation properties, and the askpass change removes the misleading `/dev/null` exec failure without re-enabling prompts.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Additional evidence: ran both the old and new capture against a **second, independently configured host** (a developer macOS checkout with `gh auth setup-git` applied), not just the container and the synthetic fixtures.

```
OLD behaviour (unscoped only): ['osxkeychain']
NEW behaviour (verbatim capture):
    credential.helper                        = 'osxkeychain'
    credential.https://github.com.helper     = ''
    credential.https://github.com.helper     = '!<...>/gh auth git-credential'
    credential.https://gist.github.com.helper = ''
    credential.https://gist.github.com.helper = '!<...>/gh auth git-credential'
```

Two things this shows that the container evidence does not:

1. **The old failure mode is not always "empty".** Here it captured `osxkeychain` — a non-empty but wrong helper that cannot authenticate a push inside the sanitized publication environment. So the defect would not have looked like "no helper captured" on this host; it would have looked like a working capture. That is part of why it survived since #1426.

2. **Reset entries are preserved.** The two `''` values are Git's list-reset directives, captured in configured order. `--get-urlmatch` discards them along with the chain — another reason the verbatim copy is the faithful choice.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:

The test currently proves only that both fetch commands exist and that the SHA fetch appears first. It would still pass if `||` were changed to `&&` (or if the ref fetch otherwise ran unconditionally afterward). In that mutation, the moving-ref fetch overwrites `FETCH_HEAD`, reintroducing the exact merge race this PR fixes, while all new assertions remain green.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The blocker is resolved on `9029934e`. The contract test now pins all three load-bearing parts of the fetch flow: the immutable SHA fetch exists and precedes the ref fetch, the text between those commands starts with `||` so the ref is a fallback rather than an unconditional overwrite of `FETCH_HEAD`, and the existing SHA-authority assertions remain in place.

This directly catches the `||` → `&&` / unconditional-ref-fetch mutation from the previous review while preserving formatting flexibility through continuation joining and whitespace normalization. The Dockerfile implementation itself remains sound: try the immutable commit first, fall back only for reachability, then fail closed unless `FETCH_HEAD` equals `MIMIR_EXECUTOR_COMMIT`.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:

Matching runs on text with shell line-continuations joined and whitespace collapsed, so the

payload.title: worklink: escalate a failure AND dispatch in the same tick (chainlink #1471)

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The barrier-based handoff is sound: the framework now durably logs and receipts a failure alert while the subprocess is still alive, and the Worklink poller waits for that receipt before proceeding to continuation handling and a same-tick ready scan. The preserved failure path is important: an unacknowledged barrier or insufficient remaining budget still prevents dispatch, while acknowledged failures remain backed off and other eligible work can use free slots.

The implementation also avoids double-emitting accepted barrier records during the normal post-exit parse and accounts for them in `signals_emitted`. The tick deadline derives from the framework-exported effective timeout and reserves shutdown margin; per-dispatch budget checks bound the detached-launch phase.

Validation:
- Focused barrier/order tests: 4 passed.
- Full `tests/test_pollers.py tests/test_worklink_autonomy.py`: 346 passed.
- Repository-wide local run reached 67% before the bounded 5-minute runner timeout; no failure was reported before timeout.
- All 11 GitHub checks are successful, including Linux/macOS pytest matrices and pytest-enforced.

No blocking findings.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The overall sequencing is sensible: the Worklink poller emits a failure alert, waits for a framework receipt, and only then spends the remaining tick budget on scanning and dispatch. The new tests cover the intended alert-before-dispatch ordering, and all hosted checks are green.

There is one blocking durability gap in `mimir/pollers.py:2368`. `_accept_delivery_barrier()` calls ordinary `log_event()` before fsyncing the receipt, but that event path is explicitly best-effort: its append is not fsynced and `EventLogger.log()` catches write failures internally. The receipt can therefore become durable even though the alert was never written—or was only present in volatile cache. The child then marks that failure notified and begins detached dispatch, recreating the permanent-loss window this barrier is intended to close.

Please use the existing failure-propagating durable event append before writing the receipt, and add a regression where the event append fails or cannot become durable, asserting that no receipt is created and dispatch does not begin.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The durability blocker is resolved at `90d29efa`. Both receipt-producing signal paths now perform a failure-propagating `log_durable_sync()` append before `_write_delivery_receipt()`, so neither a mid-run barrier nor the normal process-exit parser can durably acknowledge an alert that was never durably recorded. The enqueue path remains correctly distinct: its receipt follows the accepted enqueue/stash handoff rather than an event-log-only handoff.

The regression is well targeted: forcing `log_durable_sync()` to fail proves that no receipt is created and the child never enters dispatch. Because the same barrier record is parsed again after process exit, the test also prevents either receipt-producing signal path from falling back to best-effort logging. The existing successful-barrier test still proves the intended alert-before-dispatch behavior.

Validation on the new head:
- Focused durability regressions: 2 passed.
- Full affected suites (`tests/test_pollers.py` and `tests/test_worklink_autonomy.py`): 347 passed.
- All 11 hosted checks are successful across Linux/macOS, packaging, frontend, skill conformance, and Worklink image identity.

No blocking findings.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Fixed in `90d29efa`. The finding was correct and the reasoning held up exactly — thank you.

**Root cause, as you described it**: `_accept_delivery_barrier` wrote the receipt after an ordinary
`log_event()`. That path is best-effort — not fsynced, and `EventLogger.log()` swallows write
failures internally — so a receipt could become durable while the alert it acknowledges was never
written. The child then treats the failure as notified and begins detached dispatch, reopening the
permanent-loss window the barrier exists to close.

Both call sites now use `log_durable_sync`, whose docstring is precisely this contract:

> *"failures propagate so the caller can refuse the state transition that depends on this audit
> record."*

## Your review named one site; writing the regression found a second

With the barrier fixed and the append forced to fail, **a receipt was still created**. The same
ordering exists on the **process-exit signal path** — best-effort `log_event()`, then durable
receipt. Both are now durable.

I deliberately left the **enqueue path** (`_write_delivery_receipt` after
`stash_enqueued_event`) unchanged: it writes receipts after a successful enqueue and stash, which is
an actual handoff rather than an unverified one. If you disagree that the distinction holds, say so
and I'll change it.

## Regression

`test_delivery_barrier_refuses_receipt_when_alert_append_fails` — with `log_durable_sync` raising,
asserts **no receipt is written** and **dispatch never begins**.

- Mutating both call sites back to a best-effort append fails that test
- **345 passed, 2 skipped** across the poller and autonomy suites
- Host full suite re-running; CI below

Re-requesting review on the new head.

payload.title: Worklink #1454: worklink: startup reconciliation clears a dead run state but not its chainlink lock or label, so an unclean restart permanently consumes a build slot and orphans finished work

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes — two issues, both in the bundled reaper changes rather than the core
reconciliation, which is well built.

## Blocking — the new fail-closed epic guard is silent, so a degraded tracker stalls the reaper invisibly

`reap_home` flips the epic check to `default_on_unavailable=True`:

```python
if self._issue_has_label(issue_id, WORKLINK_EPIC_LABEL, default_on_unavailable=True):
    continue
```

`_issue_has_label` returns that default on **any** failure — non-zero exit, invalid JSON, or
a missing `labels` key — and it returns it *silently*. So if `chainlink issue show --json`
is degraded, every issue is treated as an epic, every one is skipped, and the reaper does
nothing at all. No event, no counter, no log line.

That is a regression in precisely the failure domain this chainlink exists to fix. Before
the flip, an unreadable label meant "not an epic" and reaping proceeded (protection came
from the TTL floor). After it, a tracker hiccup silently converts the reaper into a no-op
and stale locks accumulate — which is the "permanently consumes a build slot" symptom in
the title, reached by a different route and with less evidence than before.

I hit exactly this class earlier today: the queue read `active: 2, slots: 0` for ~50 minutes
and nothing in the logs said why.

**The fix is small and the mechanism already exists.** `reap_home` builds
`discovery_skipped`, which is already merged into the result at
`claims.py:1213` (`skipped={**discovery_skipped, **result.skipped}`), alongside
`issue_discovery_failed` and `lock_discovery_failed`. Have `_issue_has_label` distinguish
"label absent" from "label unreadable" for this caller, and record e.g.
`discovery_skipped["epic_label_unavailable"] = n`. Then the skip is still fail-closed, but
observable — and "the reaper skipped everything" becomes diagnosable in one query instead of
50 minutes of guessing.

## Blocking — `_issue_has_label`'s docstring now contradicts its only exclusion caller

`claims.py:951-952` still reads:

> in-progress race guards preserve prior behavior with the default True; **exclusion
> predicates such as the epic guard use False**.

The epic guard is the exclusion predicate, and this PR changes it to `True`. The docstring
now documents the opposite of what the code does, on the exact parameter whose direction is
the safety property. Please update it to state the new rule and why (skip rather than risk
applying the leaf TTL to a factory lock).

## Verified, not objections

Recording these so the next reviewer doesn't redo them:

- **The TTL floor reduction is sound.** Dropping `minimum_reaper_ttl_s` to `2 * timeout_s`
  removes a label-independent guarantee, so I checked whether the epic label could be applied
  after a factory run takes its lock — it cannot. Per `chainlink-orchestrator/SKILL.md:131` an
  epic issue "must carry both `worklink:ready` and `worklink:epic`", and
  `orchestrator.py:410/443` read it off `issue.labels` at selection time. It is a static
  pre-dispatch property, not a claim-time race, so the exclusion holds whenever the read
  succeeds. That is what makes issue 1 the whole of the residual risk.
- **Both flips are genuinely tested.** I mutation-tested the fail-closed guard: reverting
  `default_on_unavailable` to `False` fails
  `test_reap_home_skips_stale_claim_when_leaf_vs_factory_is_unknown`
  (`test_worklink_autonomy.py:290`), with `git diff --numstat` confirming the mutation applied.
- **`_checkout_has_unpublished_commits` is correctly conservative.** Every failure path —
  missing checkout, unavailable HEAD, failed base comparison, failed remote lookup — returns
  "unpublished", which parks at `worklink:blocked` and preserves the work. That is the right
  direction for a function whose wrong answer either overwrites finished work or wedges a slot.

## What is good here

The core design is right and addresses a real recurring failure: releasing the Chainlink lock
**before** touching labels or local state, retaining the
