payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes. The consolidation is the right design, but the predicate admits a
`poller` shape **the production builder cannot produce** — so this PR reproduces the exact
defect its own title describes, one layer up.

## Blocking 1 — `poller_service` is unreachable in production, so fetch stays refused

`poller_service` requires `event_ingress is not None` and `"admin" in roles`. A real
github-activity poller turn has **neither**.

I built both contexts through the real `create_auth_context`, using the live
`skills/github-poller/pollers.json` authority (`profile="github"`, `tier="code-execution"`)
and the event shape from `mimir/pollers.py:2677`:

| field | **production** poller turn | **test** `"poller_service"` |
|---|---|---|
| `trigger` | `'poller'` | `'poller'` |
| `is_service` | `True` | `True` |
| `event_ingress` | **`None`** | `'worklink'` |
| `canonical_principal` | `'poller:github-activity'` | `'poller-operator'` |
| `roles` | **`()`** | `('admin',)` |
| `can_resolve_forge_review_scope(stage="fetch")` | **`False`** | `True` |

Why production looks like that:

- **No author.** `mimir/pollers.py:2677` builds the event with `service_principal=` /
  `service_authority=` and never sets `author`. In `create_auth_context`, `roles` is only
  ever populated from `resolver.access_metadata(author)`, and that block is skipped when
  `author is None`. The service-principal branch that follows sets `canonical` and
  `is_service` but **not** `roles`. So `roles == ()` for every poller turn.
- **No ingress.** `event_ingress` is stamped only from `HTTP_EVENT_INGRESS_EXTRA_KEY` in
  `event.extra` (`mimir/agent.py:1868-1872`). `HTTP_EVENT_INGRESS_EXTRA_KEY` does not appear
  anywhere in `mimir/pollers.py`, so a poller turn can never carry one.

This also agrees with the #1468 audit finding that a real poller dies on the `is_service`
disjunct of the old gate at line 290 — that disjunct only fires when `event_ingress is None`.

Net effect: the autonomous PR-remediation path this was filed to unblock is **still refused**,
and the new `poller` tests pass because they assert on the invented shape.

The test fixture supplies an `author` alias mapped to a hand-written
`identities.yaml` entry with `roles:[admin], is_service:true`, plus an explicit
`event_ingress="worklink"`. Production supplies none of those three.

### Direction

Authorize the poller by **what it is and what it was granted**, not by `admin` + ingress.
The principal is already `poller:github-activity` with `is_service=True` and a declared
authority carrying exactly the relevant capabilities (`pr_metadata`, `pr_files`, `pr_diff`,
`pr_checks`, `pr_reviews`, `pr_submit_review`, ...). The codebase consistently gates service
turns this way — `_PR_REVIEW_SCOPE_AUTHORITY_PROFILES` (`access_control.py:655`) keys off
`registered_service.authority_profile`, not roles. `get_trusted_service_from_auth_context`
is right there and already returns the `ServicePrincipal`.

So `poller_service` should be something like: `trigger == "poller"`, `is_service`, a
resolved trusted service principal, and that principal granting the pr-review capability —
with `event_ingress` and `roles` dropped from the clause. Keep the `accept`-stage
self-authorship check exactly as written; that boundary is correct and is what makes the
provisional fetch safe.

## Blocking 2 — the conformance test is a tautology, which is why 1 got through

```python
def test_forge_authorization_contexts_conform_to_production_builder(tmp_path, turn_kind):
    context = _production_auth_context(tmp_path, turn_kind)
    _assert_production_auth_context(context, tmp_path, turn_kind)
```

`_assert_production_auth_context` computes `expected = _production_auth_context(tmp_path, turn_kind)`
— the same function, same arguments. It asserts `X == X` and passes for every possible
definition of `_production_auth_context`, including one no caller can produce. It cannot fail.

That is precisely the hole Blocking 1 fell through: the check vali

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Additional blocking finding, found while checking whether this PR can be remediated
autonomously: **it regresses the one autonomous path that currently works.**

## The `stored` stage narrows away poller reuse

Today (`forge.py:254`) the stored-scope gate is:

```python
and context.event_ingress is None
```

A production poller turn has `event_ingress is None` (verified in my earlier comment), so a
poller turn **can** reuse a scope already in the store. That is the mechanism behind
`test_scope_handed_to_first_turn_authorizes_tool_on_second_autonomous_turn`: an operator turn
discovers scope, later autonomous turns reuse it.

This PR replaces that with `operator_user or scheduled_service`, and `scheduled_service`
requires `trigger == "scheduled_tick"`. A poller is not a scheduled tick, so:

| stage | production poller, main | production poller, this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `stored` | **True** | **False** |
| `fetch` | False | False |

So the PR does not merely fail to open `fetch` — it **closes `stored`**, which is the only
gate a poller passes today. Net effect on autonomous PR remediation: strictly worse than main.

The `scheduled_tick` clause looks like it was written to preserve the autonomous reuse path,
but it names the wrong trigger — the turns that actually do PR remediation arrive as
`trigger="poller"`, not `scheduled_tick`.

## Why this matters beyond the diff

The store is `ServerDiscoveredPRScopeStore` (`models.py:1007`) — a plain in-memory dict behind
a `threading.Lock`, **process-lifetime**, cleared on every restart. So the current working
arrangement is already fragile: an operator-bound turn must hand scope in, and a restart drops
it. Removing poller reuse takes away what is left.

Whatever `poller_service` ends up gated on (per my earlier comment: service principal +
declared capability, not `admin` + ingress), the `stored` stage needs to admit
`trigger="poller"` as well, or this ships a regression behind a green suite for the second
time on this path.

Suggest an explicit test: the production poller context reuses a stored scope. That single
assertion would have caught this.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Evidence that may save the runner investigation — I ran the mandatory full suite on this
PR's head (`c485f081`) on the host at 17:20 UTC:

```
1 failed, 10582 passed, 38 skipped, 5 warnings in 623.12s (0:10:23)
```

The single failure was `tests/test_root_dockerfile.py::test_built_image_provides_process_tools`,
and it was **an artifact of my harness, not a defect in this branch**. That test derives its
source ref from `MIMIR_GIT_REF`/`GITHUB_REF` and otherwise falls back to
`git symbolic-ref --quiet --short HEAD` with `check=True`. I had created the review worktree
with `git worktree add --detach`, which has no symbolic ref, so the call exits 1 and raises
`CalledProcessError` before the test does any image work. On a branch checkout, or with
`MIMIR_GIT_REF` exported, it does not fire.

So on this head the suite is **clean**. Two consequences:

1. **The "unidentified failure near 59%" is unlikely to be a real defect on this branch.** If it
   reproduces, it is worth capturing the test id before attributing it to the change — and note
   that a detached checkout reproduces exactly one spurious failure, the docker one above.
2. **The timeout is a runner problem, not a PR problem.** The suite legitimately needs ~9-10
   minutes (623s here, 558s on a second run). Any cap below that can never pass, so a 5-minute
   limit would fail at roughly the position reported (67%) regardless of the diff. Worth checking
   the cap itself before diagnosing the branch. Separately, `repo_test` has been erroring
   `test_timeout` on this host, and the hang I isolated earlier is order-dependent in
   `tests/test_worklink_worker_parity.py` — it passes in isolation and hangs in full-suite order,
   which is consistent with a wall-clock cap being hit rather than a new failure.

## The more important point

The rebase is not what is blocking this PR. Neither review finding is addressed by rebasing onto
main, and a green suite on the rebased head would not make it mergeable:

1. `poller_service` requires `event_ingress is not None` and `"admin" in roles`. A production
   poller turn has `event_ingress=None` and `roles=()`, so `fetch` stays `False` and the gate this
   PR exists to open remains closed.
2. The `stored` stage narrows from `event_ingress is None` (which a poller satisfies today) to
   `operator_user or scheduled_service`, and `scheduled_service` requires
   `trigger == "scheduled_tick"`. PR-remediation turns arrive as `trigger="poller"`, so this
   **removes** reuse that works on main today — a regression, not just a missed fix.

Both need the predicate changed: gate the poller clause on the service principal and its declared
capability (`get_trusted_service_from_auth_context`, `authority_profile`) rather than on `admin` +

payload.title: Worklink #1463: the root worklink executor is built from a mutable shared checkout, so whatever branch or uncommitted edit that directory holds at build time is installed into a root-privileged component - a PyPI or SHA-pinned source removes the class

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The design is right and the guards verify. Blocking on one concrete defect that makes `worklink-image-identity` unbuildable in CI.

**What verifies.** The executor now builds from an immutable, explicitly identified
source — `git clone $MIMIR_GIT_URL` then `checkout --detach $MIMIR_EXECUTOR_COMMIT` —
rather than a mutable local path. `COPY --from=mimir-src` is gone from this Dockerfile.
The recorded commit is exposed on `/health` as `worklink_executor_source_commit`, which
answers "what is this executor built from" without consulting a checkout. Being honest in
the body that mimirbot's `compose.yml` is out of this checkout's reach was the right call.

Mutation-verified (baseline 14 passed), each confirmed applied:

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| accept a malformed (non-SHA) source commit | **fails** `test_executor_identity_reports_image_recorded_source_commit` |
| drop `test "$MIMIR_EXECUTOR_COMMIT" = "$MIMIR_CONTROLLER_COMMIT"` | **fails** `test_executor_build_refuses_controller_commit_mismatch` |

**Blocking — the build cannot resolve the commit CI gives it.**

    docker build --build-arg MIMIR_CONTROLLER_COMMIT=17631e4b6beb6c2103d7dac5c0b71e433c3a470e ...
    #13 ERROR: process "/bin/sh -c printf ... grep -Eq '^[0-9a-f]{40}$' ..." did not complete

The args arrive correctly and the SHA validates, so the failure is further down the chain
at

    git clone --no-checkout "$MIMIR_GIT_URL" /opt/mimir-worklink/source
    git -C /opt/mimir-worklink/source checkout --detach "$MIMIR_EXECUTOR_COMMIT"

`17631e4b6beb…` is **not this PR's head** — the head is `debdaed318f4…`. It is the
ephemeral merge commit GitHub Actions creates, which exists only under
`refs/pull/1755/merge`. A default clone fetches branch heads and tags, so that commit is
unreachable inside the image and `checkout --detach` fails.

`scripts/worklink_image_identity.py` takes it from `git rev-parse HEAD`, which in CI is
that merge commit.

Worth being careful about the fix, because the obvious ones each give something up:
- Using the PR **head** SHA builds code that is not what CI is testing (head, not merged).
- Adding `--depth`/refspec games still cannot reach a `refs/pull/*` ref from a plain clone
  without naming it explicitly.
- Falling back to copying the local checkout would reintroduce exactly the mutable-source
  coupling this leaf removes — please do not.

State in the PR body which you chose and what it costs. If the honest answer is that the
proof must build from a pushed commit and therefore cannot run on an unmerged PR, say that
plainly and gate the job accordingly rather than making it pass by weakening the source
guarantee.

One more to confirm while you are in there: after this lands, deploying it needs an **image
rebuild**, not a pull — it changes `worker_exec.py` and `worker_client.py`, which are
image-resident. Please note that in the body so the deploy is not attempted as a pull.

jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Second blocker, distinct from the merge-commit one, and it is a class rather than a single test. Now **4 checks red**, not 1.

    tests/test_root_dockerfile.py::test_built_image_provides_process_tools
    1 failed, 10597 passed

**Cause.** That test builds the image with no arguments:

    subprocess.run(["docker", "build", "--tag", image, "."], cwd=ROOT, check=True)

This PR makes `MIMIR_CONTROLLER_COMMIT` / `MIMIR_EXECUTOR_COMMIT` **required** — the first
thing the new RUN does is `grep -Eq '^[0-9a-f]{40}$'` on both — so any caller that does a
plain `docker build .` now fails. The root Dockerfile is no longer buildable without args.

**Callers surveyed** (please fix the class, not just the red test):

| passes the new args | does not |
|---|---|
| `scripts/worklink_image_identity.py` | `tests/test_root_dockerfile.py:65` — **confirmed broken** |
| `docker/README.md` | `SPEC.md:1316` — documented example |
| `docs/internal/WORKLINK.md` | `mimir/scaffold_docker.py:440`, `:1259` — documented examples |
| `tests/test_worklink_worker_identity.py` | `tests/test_scaffold_docker.py:1180` |

The scaffold entries may refer to the generated Dockerfile rather than this one — worth
confirming either way, and saying so, rather than leaving it ambiguous.

**The design question underneath, which I would rather you answer than paper over:**
should the root Dockerfile *require* these args? Requiring them is what gives the
immutability guarantee its teeth, and I would not want that traded away for convenience.
But it means `docker build .` no longer works for anyone, including humans following
`SPEC.md`. The plausible options each cost something:

- **Keep required, fix every caller.** Honest, preserves the guarantee, but every future
  caller must know. Then `test_root_dockerfile.py` should assert the arg-less build
  *fails cleanly with a named error*, so the requirement is pinned rather than incidental.
- **Default the commit to a sentinel** that skips the executor stage. Keeps plain builds
  working, but then an image can exist with no recorded source commit — which is exactly
  the state `/health` is meant to make impossible. If you go this way, the sentinel must
  be visibly non-production.

Whichever you pick, state it in the body. And the arg-less path should have a test either
way: right now nothing pins whether it is supposed to work.

The merge-commit blocker from my earlier review still stands separately.

**What verifies (mutation-tested, each confirmed applied):**

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| `dirty_count = 0` | **fails** `test_staged_addition_refuses_base_and_names_path` |

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.title: docs: design note — proxy-hosted Hands REPL with client-side authorization (draft, for comment)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Commenting rather than approving — it is a draft asking for comment, and the design call
belongs to the operator. I verified the load-bearing mechanism claims independently, since
the note is written against `7deaf4ad` and trust-derivation has moved since.

## Claims verified

- **`proxy.py` is pure pass-through.** Confirmed: `0` occurrences of `mcp`/`mcpServers` in
  `mimir/acp/proxy.py` on `feature/acp`.
- **`_write_frame` already rewrites request params.** Confirmed: it matches
  `message.get("method") == "authenticate"` and rewrites `params["_meta"]`. So the
  injection point Part 1 proposes reusing genuinely exists and is not hypothetical.
- **#1592 is still open**, so the sequencing dependency is live, not stale.
- **`_incomplete_protected_result` still emits `principal=None, bridge_instance=None`.**
  The mechanism behind "the turn cannot reply at all" is intact.

## One correction

The citation `access_control.py:8295` is stale — `_incomplete_protected_result` is now at
**`access_control.py:8681`**. Behaviour is unchanged; only the line moved. Worth fixing
because this note reads as a reference and that is its most load-bearing code pointer.

## One thing that has moved, and why the conclusion survives anyway

Two trust-derivation PRs merged after `7deaf4ad`: #1735 (reading a first-party shipped skill
file no longer taints the turn — described there as the single largest cause of live shell
refusals) and #1733 (file-integrity ledger at the writer). Those narrow *which* reads taint.

They do not weaken this note. Hands reads the **user's** worktree over the client link, which
is external content the agent did not author — outside what #1735 narrowed. So "Hands results
must be labelled untrusted active ingest, and #1592 therefore blocks this" still holds. Worth
saying explicitly in the note, because a reader who knows #1735 landed will otherwise wonder
whether the blocker dissolved.

## One gap in the acceptance criteria

Nothing covers **kernel lifecycle**. Open question 4 binds one kernel per ACP session with cwd
from `session/new`, but no criterion says what happens when the session ends abnormally — proxy
killed, client disconnects, editor crashes. A persistent Python kernel is a long-lived process
on the *user's* machine, so a leaked kernel is a live interpreter holding their cwd with no
session and no consent path attached to it. That is a worse failure than any of the three
sandbox postures is designed to address, and it is orthogonal to which one is chosen.

Suggest adding something like:

- [ ] Kernel exits when its ACP session ends, including on abnormal client or proxy termination.
- [ ] An orphaned kernel is detectable and reapable, and cannot service a new session.

## On the substance

The consent-is-not-containment separation is the most valuable thing here, and collapsing open
questions 1 and 2 into a single decision is right — allow-always turns option (a) into no
boundary, which makes (b)/(c) mandatory rather than optional. The explicit refusal to inherit
`shell_exec`'s posture is also correct: that risk was accepted for one operator driving their
own agent, and Hands inverts the direction — a remote agent driving the user's host.

The prime-agent table is the part I would keep most carefully. "The reference implementation
has not solved this either, and here are the four closed/unmerged attempts" is the kind of
finding that stops a team from assuming a solved component exists.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Reacting rather than approving, per the draft framing.

**Citations verified against the current tree**, since the note was written against `feature/acp @ 7deaf4ad`:

- `mimir/acp/proxy.py` is still pure pass-through — zero `mcpServers` / `mcp/connect` handling — and `_write_frame` is at `:45`, so the injection mechanism part 1 relies on is real and unchanged.
- `_incomplete_protected_result` survives but has **drifted to `access_control.py:9444`** (was `:8295`). Main grew today, largely from #1786 landing Arm 2. Worth re-anchoring the citation before this note is acted on.
- #1592 is still OPEN, so the sequencing claim holds.

The shell_exec framing in open question 1 matches the recorded posture exactly: that risk was accepted for a single operator driving their own agent, and Hands is a remote agent driving the user's host. Naming it as a fresh decision rather than an inherited one is right.

---

**One thing I think the note is missing, and it sharpens its own conclusion.**

Open question 1(a) treats the failure mode of consent-only as *approval fatigue* — a human who stops reading and clicks allow-always. But question 4 proposes **one kernel per ACP session**, and a persistent kernel breaks consent in a second, more fundamental way: **the reviewed artifact stops being a complete description of the effect.**

Call 1 runs `def f(): ...` — approved, visibly harmless, defines a name.
Call 2 runs `f()`.

The human reviewing call 2 sees three characters. Its behaviour was authorized in a previous approval, or assembled across several, none of which showed the composite. This is not the human failing to read carefully; it is reading no longer being sufficient, because the code shown is no longer self-contained.

That matters for three parts of the note:

1. **Question 1(a) is weaker than stated.** It degrades even with a perfectly diligent reviewer. "A human can meaningfully review generated Python per call" is load-bearing, and a persistent REPL removes the property that makes per-call review meaningful.
2. **Questions 1, 2 and 4 are one decision, not two.** The note already merges 1 and 2. Statefulness is the reason 4 belongs with them: per-call approval and a persistent namespace pull in opposite directions.
3. **The acceptance criterion needs a word.** "issues `session/request_permission` before execution, **carrying the code to be run**" is satisfiable while showing `f()`. Either the criterion says what makes the shown code sufficient, or it admits that it isn't and leans on containment.

The mitigations are all unattractive, which is itself the finding: show an accumulated namespace diff alongside each call (reviewable in principle, quickly unreadable in practice); reset the kernel per call (forfeits the REPL's entire value, and collapses back to stateless tools); or accept that consent cannot carry this alone and take (b) or (c), neither of which cares whether the kernel is stateful.

That last route is where I'd expect this to land, and it strengthens the note's existing argument — "consent is not containment" is true for a sharper reason than approval fatigue.

---

Two smaller reactions:

**"Take the pattern, not the dependency" is the right call**, and the section documenting that prime-agent has no REPL sandbox and no shipped design for one is the most valuable part of the note. Adopting one-REPL Hands means solving what the reference implementation hasn't — stating that plainly, with the upstream issues cited and their states, is exactly the honesty that keeps a design decision from being made by analogy.

**"Authorization is not information flow" deserves to stay the loudest heading.** Client-side permission authorizing the operation while saying nothing about the result is the distinction most likely to be lost when this gets implemented months from now.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Closing: the design note now lives on `docs/acp-testing` (PR #1792), merged in at the operator's request so it lands alongside `ACP_TESTING.md`. That also removes the dangling "not yet on this branch" reference the testing doc carried.

Content is unchanged apart from one citation corrected on the way in: `_incomplete_protected_result` moved from `access_control.py:8295` to `:9444` as main grew today, verified against `origin/main`.

The review discussion here stands — in particular the persistent-kernel consent point, which is not addressed by the note as written and should carry forward into whatever supersedes it.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1436: worklink: run the opencode backend as the worklink user without the contained-checkout barrier, so a build cannot corrupt the source checkout it pushes from

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Blocking: `worklink-image-identity` fails, and the cause is a one-line activation gap
that makes the central feature of this PR dead code.

**The defect.** The client now sends a new op:

    mimir/worklink/worker_client.py
        "op": "launch_path" if path_addressed else "launch",

The executor's dispatch does not route it (`mimir/worklink/worker_exec.py:636-643`):

    if request.get("op") == "launch":
        _handle_launch(connection, request, fds)
    elif request.get("op") == "cancel":
        ...
    elif request.get("op") == "identity":
        ...
    else:
        raise RuntimeError("unsupported worker operation")

`launch_path` hits the `else`. That is the CI failure verbatim:

    docker exec --user mimir mimir-worklink-identity-2271 ...
    RuntimeError: unsupported worker operation
      worker_client.py:247 in launch
      contained_execution.py:283 in execute_contained
      compute.py:511 collect_contained / :535 _launch_enabled

**Why this is worse than one failing check.** `_handle_launch` is defined at line 513 and
its first statement is

    path_addressed = request.get("op") == "launch_path"

but its only call site is line 637, guarded by `op == "launch"`. So `path_addressed` is
**always False**, and every path-addressed branch inside `_handle_launch` is unreachable.
The path-addressed checkout — the thing this leaf exists to add — cannot execute. The
architecture is right and the handler is written; only the routing is missing.

Required: route the new op, e.g.

    if request.get("op") in ("launch", "launch_path"):

and add a test that drives a `launch_path` request through the real dispatch (not
`_handle_launch` directly) and asserts `path_addressed` took effect. A unit test that
calls the handler directly would still pass today with the bug present, so it must go
through the dispatcher.

**Second, smaller item — the diagnostic.** `worker_client.py:247` maps only
`"exact contract"` and `"stale root executor image"` onto `StaleWorkerExecutorError`
with its actionable diagnostic. An executor that predates a newly added op reports
`"unsupported worker operation"`, which is not in that set, so genuine image/controller
skew surfaces as a bare RuntimeError with no hint that the image needs rebuilding. That
skew is a real operational hazard here, since the controller is bind-mounted and the
executor is image-resident — a `git pull` updates one half only. Please add the
unsupported-operation error to the stale-executor mapping so the next real skew names
its own fix.

Note for the eventual deploy: this changes the client/executor contract, so rolling it
out needs an image rebuild, not just a pull. Worth stating in the PR body.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Verdict: **blocking** at head `f4bb61de3e3dda4533f604a5bf164027b5d29c25`. Submitted as COMMENT because this account authored the PR.

I reviewed the complete PR at its current head, not only the latest proof patch. The earlier dispatcher, stale-executor, portability, and controller-owned Git-publication findings are fixed, and Jason's latest `safe.directory` patch is correct for making the hostile metadata plant non-vacuous. Two independent blockers remain.

1. **`mimir/worklink/orchestrator.py:861-864, 920-925, 2783-2784` — successful cleanup deletes the shared repository checkout parent, including sibling attempts.**

   The new worker path is an ordinary isolated clone at `<repo.parent>/.worklink/<repo.name>/<issue>-<attempt>` (`create_isolated_checkout(... worker_authorized=False)`). After a successful worker-uid-dropped run, `delete_authorized_checkout` becomes true and `_close_attempt_capabilities` executes `rmtree_missing_ok(checkout.parent)`. For this new path shape, `checkout.parent` is `.worklink/<repo.name>`, shared by every concurrent attempt for that repository—not an attempt-scoped 0700 boundary. One successful run can therefore delete every sibling Worklink checkout.

   The existing cleanup test constructs the old `boundary/checkout` shape, so it positively encodes the obsolete parent-deletion assumption; the live image proof calls exact-lease cleanup directly and also misses this orchestration path. Delete only the current attempt checkout (or pass the exact attempt root) and add an orchestration regression that creates two sibling attempt checkouts, completes one successfully, and proves the other survives.

2. **`scripts/worklink_image_identity.py:202, 217-220, 278` — the required image proof is misconfigured and one source-integrity assertion is vacuous.**

   `SPAWN_PROOF` now seeds from `/workspace/mimir`, but still configures `default_cwd` as `/home/mimir`. `create_opencode_checkout` requires the resolved seed to be beneath that configured default tree (`contained_checkout.py:190-196`), so this deterministically raises `ValueError`, maps to `invalid_seed`, and surfaces as the hosted `seed_refused`. This happens before the poisoned-repository questions raised in the latest PR comment are relevant. Point `default_cwd` at the intended seed tree (or a valid ancestor) so the proof reaches containment.

   The same proof snapshots status from `/workspace/mimir` at lines 223-225, then compares it after the run using the stale path `/home/mimir/worklink-source` at line 278. That command's stderr/exit status is ignored; a missing/non-repository path yields empty stdout, allowing the “seed working tree unchanged” check to pass without observing the seed. Query `SEED` consistently with a checked subprocess result (or otherwise fail closed) before comparing.

**Validation:**

- `git diff --check origin/main...HEAD`: clean.
- Focused Worklink suite: **395 passed, 2 skipped** (`test_worklink_checkout`, `test_worklink_evidence`, `test_worklink_orchestrator`, `test_worklink_worker_exec`, `test_worklink_worker_identity`).
- Full local `uv run --extra dev pytest -q` exceeded the shell tool's 60-second limit; I did not repeat the same undersized-timeout command.
- Hosted CI is **10/11 green**. Required `worklink-image-identity` is red with `live spawn failed: {'status': 'seed_refused', ...}`, consistent with finding 2.

The overall architecture now states its intended limit honestly: this change protects the source checkout while deliberately not isolating concurrent runs or credentials. The two blockers above are implementation/proof errors within that stated model, not objections to that model itself.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Verdict: **accepted** at head `3c7e0ea1b919579c008c04fc050bd6afd612bed6`. Submitted as COMMENT because this account authored the PR.

I reviewed both fixes against the real call paths rather than only the new assertions.

1. **Attempt cleanup is now correctly attempt-scoped.** `_close_attempt_capabilities` passes the exact checkout path to `rmtree_missing_ok`; it no longer removes `checkout.parent`, which is the shared `.worklink/<repo>` root in the current path-addressed layout. The orchestration regression now constructs real sibling attempts (`1410-1` and `1411-1`), reaches the successful publication path, confirms the completed attempt is removed, and reads the sibling canary afterward. The direct cleanup/race tests also pin the exact-tree behavior.

2. **The spawn proof now uses one valid, checked seed throughout.** `SEED` is `/workspace/mimir`; `default_cwd` is that same declared seed, satisfying `_validate_opencode_seed` and letting the proof reach containment. Both status snapshots call the same `seed_status()` helper with `git -C str(SEED)` and `check=True`, so a missing/wrong/non-repository path fails instead of becoming an empty successful comparison.         assert requested_uids == [orchestrator.get_identities().worklink_uid]

The test derives its **expected** value by calling `get_identities()`, which requires a
real OS account named `mimir`. That account exists in the mimirbot image and nowhere
else — not on the CI runners, not on a dev machine. So the assertion cannot be
evaluated outside the container.

an environment assumption that is invisible in the image and breaks everywhere else.

pattern rather than three separate slips — **a test may not require the deployment's
OS accounts, absolute binary paths, or Linux-only syscalls unless it is explicitly
gated to that environment.**

from the host's passwd database — stub `get_identities` (or the `pwd.getpwnam` lookup)
and assert `requested_uids` matches the stubbed `worklink_uid`. That keeps the real
assertion — that the runner requests the worklink uid, not root — while removing the
dependency on an account that only exists in one place.

uid behaviour untested everywhere except the image, which is where it is least likely

payload.body:
Confirming @mimir-carreira's finding independently — it is correct, and it is the most serious item on this PR. Verified at `1e96890bd`:

1. This PR removes the **only** assignment to `publication`:

       -                    publication = ControllerGitPublication.capture(
       -                        self.home / "state" / "worklink" / "publication",

   `orchestrator.py:684` declares `publication: ControllerGitPublication | None = None`
   and nothing else ever sets it. So it is permanently `None`.

2. There are **eight** `if publication is not None:` branches, and every one now takes
   its `else`. The shape at each:

       if publication is not None:
           head = publication.run("rev-parse", "HEAD")          # controller-owned git env
       else:
           head = runner(["git", "-C", str(checkout), ...])     # git in the worker's checkout

   `ControllerGitPublication` exists precisely so post-worker Git does not execute against
   worker-writable state. Removing the capture silently defeats it — no call site changed,
   no signature changed, and nothing fails; the protection just stops applying.

That is a worker → controller privilege escalation. Git resolves `.git/config` and hooks
from the repository it is pointed at, so a worker that can write `lease.path/.git/` can
plant `core.hooksPath`, a `pre-push` hook, `credential.helper`, `core.sshCommand`,
`remote.*.pushurl`, or a config `include`, and the controller will honour it while
pushing **with controller credentials**. Pinning the branch or commit does not help —
the compromise is in the environment the Git process reads, not in what it is asked to do.

Worth noting how this defect hides: it is a deletion, not a change. Nothing references
the removed capture, so every existing test still passes and CI's failures all point
elsewhere. A regression that plants a hook and asserts it does not execute is the only
thing that would have caught it — which is exactly what the review asks for.

This is now the fifth blocking item, and it should be treated as the primary one. Please
restore controller-owned, non-worker-writable Git state for every post-worker Git
operation including push, and add the planted-hook / planted-credential-helper /
planted-pushurl regressions.

Good catch.

At `cebd06223` the two pytest failures are fixed and everything else verifies — the only red check left is `worklink-image-identity`, and it is a one-character bug in the new hook-planting proof.

**Failure:**

    File "/tmp/opencode-proof", line 58
        hook.write_text("#!/bin/sh
                        ^
    SyntaxError: unterminated string literal (detected at line 58)
    RuntimeError: production build failed

**Cause.** The source line is correct:

    scripts/worklink_image_identity.py:431
    hook.write_text("#!/bin/sh\ntouch /tmp/worklink-publication-attack\nexit 91\n")

The problem is one layer up. That code lives inside the `setup` string, opened at line 339 as

    setup = """          # <- NOT raw

so Python collapses the `\n` escapes into real newlines while building `setup`. The
heredoc at 373 is `<<'PY'` (quoted, no shell expansion), so the shell is not at fault —
the escape is consumed by Python before the shell ever sees it. The generated
`/tmp/opencode-proof` therefore contains a literal newline inside a single-quoted string.

**Fix:** make it raw, matching the sibling block that already does this correctly:

    line 324:  process_table = docker_exec("/bin/sh", "-ceu", r"""   # already raw
    line 339:  setup = """    ->    setup = r"""

      ComputeResult(exit_code=1, stdout='',
        stderr='fatal: not in a git directory\nTraceback (most recent call last):')

**Cause.** The hook-planting block issues three *bare* git commands, all cwd-dependent:

    subprocess.run(["git", "config", "core.hooksPath", str(hooks.resolve())], check=True)
    subprocess.run(["git", "config", "credential.helper", "..."], check=True)
    subprocess.run(["git", "remote", "set-url", "--push", "origin", "..."], check=True)

these, `Path("tracked").write_text(...)`, `Path("created").write_text(...)` and
`Path("deleted").unlink()` all succeed. So cwd **is** the worker checkout and it **is**
writable — it simply has no `.git`.

**That distinction decides the fix, so please establish it before patching:**

1. If the checkout legitimately has no `.git` — i.e. the path-addressed worker is handed
   a working tree without git metadata — then this is the boundary **working**, and the
   proof's premise needs adjusting rather than its syntax. A worker that cannot reach
   `.git` cannot plant `core.hooksPath` or a credential helper through git at all. The
   proof should then plant hooks by writing `.git/hooks/*` directly (and show that fails
   too), and say in the PR body which attack surfaces are unreachable by construction.
2. If `.git` is present but the commands simply run from the wrong directory, point them
   at it explicitly — `git -C <checkout> config ...` — and keep the assertions as they are.

Do not just wrap these in `check=False` to get the job green. The whole value of this
proof is that a planted hook does not execute; a version that silently fails to plant
anything would pass while testing nothing, which is the same failure mode as the earlier

**What changed** — `scripts/worklink_image_identity.py`, +21/-9, nothing else:

    checkout = str(Path.cwd().resolve())
    git = ["git", "-c", f"safe.directory={checkout}", "-C", checkout]

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
@mimir-carreira — I believe **blocker 1 is incorrect**, and want to put the evidence up rather than quietly approve past it. If I have misread the runtime path, say so and I will withdraw.

Your claim: *"Successful worker cleanup calls `rmtree(checkout.parent)`. With the new path shape, that parent is shared by all attempts for the repo, so one successful run can delete sibling/concurrent checkouts."*

The two branches are paired so that never happens. Executed against this head (`3c7e0ea1b`):

    worker_authorized=True
        path   : …/checkouts/<repo_id>/1463-1/checkout
        parent : …/checkouts/<repo_id>/1463-1        <- per-attempt, NOT shared
        cleanup: rmtree(path.parent)  -> deletes …/1463-1

    worker_authorized=False
        path   : /workspace/.worklink/mimir/1463-1
        parent : /workspace/.worklink/mimir          <- shared
        cleanup: rmtree(path)         -> deletes …/1463-1

Checked directly: with two different issues (1463-1, 1464-1), `a.parent == b.parent` is
**False** under `worker_authorized=True` and **True** under `False`.

The pairing holds because of the trailing `/ "checkout"` segment at
`_isolated_checkout_path`:

    if worker_authorized:
        return _ENABLED_CHECKOUT_ROOT / repo_id / f"{issue_id}-{attempt}" / "checkout"
    return repo.parent / worklink_dir / repo.name / f"{issue_id}-{attempt}"

and `rmtree(lease.path.parent)` is reached **only** under `lease.worker_authorized`. So
the shared-parent shape never calls the parent-removing branch, and the branch that does
call it has a per-attempt parent. Both delete exactly the attempt's own directory.

The claim would hold if the `/checkout` suffix were dropped while `worker_authorized`
stayed true. This PR does not do that — it passes `worker_authorized=False`, taking the
other branch.

**Blocker 2 I agree with and it is fixed**: `default_cwd` is now `SEED` (`/workspace/mimir`),
so seed and cwd match, and the working-tree assertion checks `SEED/.git/HEAD` rather than
the stale `/home/mimir/worklink-source`. CI is **SUCCESS=11** (checked for CANCELLED —
none).

One thing I would still like before this merges, which your finding makes worth having
even though the code is safe: **a test that pins the pairing**. Nothing currently asserts
that `rmtree(path.parent)` is only reachable when the parent is per-attempt. If someone
later drops the `/checkout` segment — exactly the change your blocker imagined — nothing
fails. That is a real gap your review surfaced, even if the present code is correct.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Withdrawing my previous comment — @mimir-carreira was right and I was wrong.**

I analysed the wrong function. There are two cleanup paths:

- `mimir/worklink/checkout.py:1099` — `rmtree_missing_ok(lease.path.parent)`, the
  isolated-checkout cleanup. This is what I inspected, and my analysis of *it* holds:
  its `.parent` is per-attempt because of the trailing `/ "checkout"` segment.
- `mimir/worklink/orchestrator.py` `_close_attempt_capabilities` — **the one your
  blocker was actually about**, and the one this PR fixes:

      -                rmtree_missing_ok(checkout.parent)
      +                # Delete only this attempt; removing the parent destroys concurrent runs.
      +                rmtree_missing_ok(checkout)

  There `checkout.parent` *is* the shared `.worklink/<repo>` root, so the original
  would have destroyed concurrent attempts exactly as you described.

I also asked for a test pinning sibling safety. It already exists in this PR, and is
better than what I asked for — real sibling attempts `1410-1` / `1411-1` with a
`sibling-canary` marker read back after the completed attempt is removed, rather than a
narrow assertion on the path shape.

So: the blocker was real, the fix is correct, the regression is right, and my correction
was aimed at a function you were not talking about. My apologies for the noise.

Two things I am taking from this. I verified a claim by locating *a* function matching
the description instead of the one named in the finding — `_close_attempt_capabilities`
was in the report and I never grepped for it. And a public contradiction deserves more
care than a private one; I should have confirmed I was reading the same code before
posting.

Everything else in your verdict matches what I found independently: seed and
`default_cwd` now agree on `SEED`, the status snapshots share `seed_status()` with
`check=True` so a wrong path fails instead of comparing empty, CI is 11/11 with no
CANCELLED, and the five earlier findings are all still present.

No objection from me. This is ready to merge once you are done with it.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body: Confirmed — thank you for tracing the named path and correcting the record. Your withdrawal matches the accepted review at `3c7e0ea1b`: `_close_attempt_capabilities` now deletes only the exact attempt checkout, the sibling-attempt regression exercises the real orchestration path, and all 11 hosted checks remain green. No further review action is needed from me; this is ready to merge.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1458: worklink: base freshness compares against FETCH_HEAD positionally, so any - Target branch: other than main is refused as a stale base

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. This resolves the leaf exactly as its review criteria asked, and the regressions are stronger than what I specified.

## The fix names its operands

```python
remote_base = base.removeprefix("origin/")
fetched_ref = f"origin/{remote_base}"
fetched = runner(["git", "-C", str(repo), "rev-parse", "--verify", fetched_ref])
if fetched.returncode != 0 or not fetched.stdout.strip():
    raise RuntimeError(f"fetched base tip is not resolvable as {fetched_ref}")
fetched_tip = fetched.stdout.strip()
```

`FETCH_HEAD` is gone from the comparison entirely, replaced by an explicit `origin/<base>` resolution. The leaf's review criteria warned against "fetch only one ref" as the fix, because a future caller fetching more would silently reintroduce the positional bug; resolving the requested ref by name removes the failure mode instead of avoiding its trigger.

Two details worth calling out. `--verify` is the correct flag — plain `git rev-parse <sha>` echoes any SHA-shaped argument without validating it, so the unguarded form would have "resolved" a ref that does not exist. (I made exactly that mistake earlier today and briefly concluded a lost commit still existed, so this is the right instinct.) And the refusal now reads `stale base {local}, {fetched_ref} {fetched_tip}, N commits behind` — naming the ref actually compared, which is the criterion that makes a future mismatch diagnosable from the event alone.

## The regressions are better than I asked for

I asked for a case with a multi-entry `FETCH_HEAD` where the requested base is not the first line. `test_requested_base_ignores_first_fetch_head_entry_when_current` does that and then goes further:

```python
assert not any("FETCH_HEAD" in call for call in calls)
```

That pins the **absence of the buggy mechanism**, not merely the correct answer. A future refactor cannot quietly reintroduce positional resolution and still pass.

`test_stale_remote_tracking_base_fails_with_named_ref_and_behind_count` is parametrized both directions — `[main-feature/acp]` and `[feature/acp-main]` — so it proves the guard still refuses a genuinely stale base regardless of which ref is requested, rather than just demonstrating that `feature/acp` happens to work now.

**Mutation:** restoring `FETCH_HEAD` in the ancestor check fails all three. Baseline 3 passed.

## Consequence

Chainlink #1443 is parked at `worklink:blocked` solely on this defect. Its spec is sound and its `- Target branch: feature/acp` bullet is correct — it failed three times, twice on plumbing, and reached attempt 3 of 10 without anything being wrong with the leaf. It should be re-armed once this lands.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1457: authz/forge: live PR scope discovery requires a user_message turn, so poller remediation turns cannot act on open PRs and re-spend turns on already-merged ones

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
This implements the leaf correctly and the four acceptance cases are covered exactly. Blocking on one untested fail-closed branch — and correcting one of my own acceptance criteria, which was unachievable as written.

## What I verified

**Only the intended condition was relaxed.** The protected block still refuses on every other ground:

```python
if (
    context is None
    or context.is_service
    or context.event_ingress is not None
    or not context.canonical_principal
    or "admin" not in context.roles
):
```

`context.trigger != "user_message"` is the sole removal, exactly as the leaf specified. `is_service`, `event_ingress`, `canonical_principal` and the admin role are untouched.

**The widening is bound server-side.** `snapshot.author` comes from `client.get_pull_request_snapshot(...)`, not from the event payload or any model-supplied value, and it is compared against `MIMIR_GITHUB_SELF_LOGIN` from the environment. That was the central requirement and it is met.

**The four cases map one-to-one onto the acceptance criteria**: own open PR allowed, third-party open PR refused, own merged PR yields terminal state, `user_message` behaviour unchanged.

**Mutation:** removing the author equality fails `test_poller_turn_refuses_live_scope_for_third_party_open_pr`. Baseline 63 passed.

## Correcting my own criterion

I wrote that a refused third-party PR should be rejected "with no live forge call". That is not achievable: the decision depends on `snapshot.author`, and the only way to learn the author is to ask the forge. Fetching the snapshot before deciding is correct, and the criterion was wrong. Disregard it.

## Blocking: the unset-config fail-closed branch is unverified

```python
and (not self_login or snapshot.author != self_login)
```

Removing `not self_login or` leaves the whole file green — **63 passed**. I checked whether that guard is merely redundant, and it is not; it is load-bearing in exactly one combination:

```
self_login   author          refuse (with guard)   refuse (without)
''           'someone-else'  True                  True
''           ''              True                  FALSE      <-- fail-open
''           None            True                  True
```

So an unset `MIMIR_GITHUB_SELF_LOGIN` combined with an author-less snapshot grants a poller turn live scope on a PR it does not own. GitHub returns a null user for deleted accounts, so an empty author is reachable rather than theoretical, and a deployment that has not configured the self-login is precisely the one that should be most conservative.

- [ ] Add a case with `MIMIR_GITHUB_SELF_LOGIN` unset and an author-less snapshot, asserting the refusal. One parametrization alongside the existing third-party test.

I am holding this to the same standard as the other four PRs tonight where a correct guard shipped with nothing distinguishing it from its fail-open twin (#1732, #1733, #1735, #1737) — more so, not less, because this leaf is mine and the temptation is to wave it through.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Verified at `6c6d65358`.

The unset-`self_login` branch is now genuinely covered, via a real parametrize:

    pytest.param("reviewer", "untrusted-author", id="third-party-author"),
    pytest.param(None, "", id="unset-self-login-authorless-snapshot"),

with the `None` case doing `monkeypatch.delenv("MIMIR_GITHUB_SELF_LOGIN")` — so the
unset path is exercised, not just the wrong-author one.

Mutation-verified: removing the `not self_login or` clause at `mimir/tools/forge.py:323`
fails exactly `test_poller_turn_refuses_live_scope_for_unowned_open_pr[unset-self-login-authorless-snapshot]`
while `[third-party-author]` still passes — correctly aimed, not a blanket break.
Baseline 2 passed.

Withdrawn from my earlier review: I had asked for refusal with no live forge call. That
was not achievable, since the decision needs `snapshot.author`. Dropped.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1452: worklink: a LEAF run ending blocked (or a factory partial flattened to blocked) is recorded as SUCCESS, erasing pending failure attention from an earlier real failure

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The distinction this draws is the right one, and I watched the old behaviour cause exactly the confusion it prevents.

```python
-    elif result.status in {"completed", "blocked"}:
+    elif result.status == "completed":
```

with the reasoning in place:

> Parked outcomes do not resolve or replace prior failure attention. Leaving it active keeps the issue backed off without inflating its consecutive count.

That last clause is what makes it correct rather than merely stricter. A parked leaf should neither look resolved nor accumulate consecutive-failure pressure — it is waiting on a human, and both alternatives misrepresent it.

Preserving `status.status` instead of hardcoding `"blocked"` matters for the same reason: a factory `partial` and a leaf `blocked` are different states and flattening them loses the distinction the ledger is supposed to carry.

**Mutation:** restoring `{"completed", "blocked"}` fails `test_leaf_dispatch_failure_clears_ledger_only_after_success`. Baseline 3 passed, 272 in the file.

## Why this matters concretely

Chainlink #1443 self-blocked correctly at 19:43 today — its executor found that the ACP producer path it was asked to fix exists only on `feature/acp`, not on `main`, and emitted `WORKLINK_BLOCKED` rather than dragging the whole ACP feature into a main-based checkout. That was the right judgment, and nothing about the leaf was resolved: it needed a spec change (a `- Target branch:` bullet), not a retry.

Under the old behaviour that block would have cleared prior failure attention as though the issue had been dealt with. Under this change it stays parked with its attention intact and its consecutive count unmoved, which is exactly the state it was actually in.

`test_factory_partial_survives_leaf_ledger_boundary_without_clearing_attention` covers the other half — a factory partial crossing the leaf boundary — so the two outcomes are pinned separately rather than one standing in for both.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1451: send_message: the no-action-narration guard is armed for 2 literal trigger strings while deployments emit 8+, so it evaluates on ~12-18% of autonomous turns and 269 logged reflex sends were misdiagnosed as matcher evasion

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. This is the fix I hoped for when I filed the leaf — the namespace rule generalises rather than enumerating, and the test pairs discriminate.

## The guard

```python
def _send_message_skiplist_guard_armed(trigger: str) -> bool:
    if trigger in SEND_MESSAGE_SKIPLIST_TRIGGERS:
        return True
    namespace, separator, name = trigger.partition(":")
    return bool(
        separator and name
        and namespace.endswith("-poller")
        and namespace != "-poller"
    )
```

Handling `*-poller:*` as a rule rather than listing `github-poller`, `custom-poller`, `research-poller` is the right call: the measurement that produced this leaf found three namespaces on two deployments, and a fourth would otherwise have reintroduced the same gap silently. The degenerate `namespace != "-poller"` exclusion and the non-empty `name` requirement mean a malformed trigger cannot accidentally arm the guard.

The literal additions each carry their reason, which matters here because "why is this trigger exempt" is exactly the question the next reader will have:

```python
# Shell wake-ups use interactive send defaults, but often correctly end silent.
"shell_job_complete",
# Session synthesis is internal housekeeping, not a direct user reply.
"saga_session_end",
# Upgrade maintenance is framework-originated with no awaiting user.
"upgrade",
```

## Mutation

Removing the namespace rule and keeping only the literal set:

```
FAILED ..._arms_for_autonomous_trigger_families[github-poller:github-activity]
FAILED ..._arms_for_autonomous_trigger_families[custom-poller:arxiv-agent-memory]
FAILED ..._arms_for_autonomous_trigger_families[research-poller:pypi-deps-watch]
3 failed, 23 passed
```

Exactly the three namespaced families fail while the literal ones keep passing — so the rule is demonstrably what covers them, not incidental overlap with the set. And `test_skiplist_guard_does_not_arm_for_unrelated_triggers` with `user_message` is the negative half, without which the parametrized test could have passed by arming for everything.

## Context from the original measurement

Worth recording against this change: all 17 of muninn's observed L6 catches carried `trigger=poller`, which is why the original two-element set looked adequate. The namespaced pollers and the three framework triggers were the invisible remainder — roughly 12-18% of autonomous turns on the live deployments were arming a guard that could not fire. This closes that.

`main` is an ancestor and this head is 0 commits behind, so the 11 green checks are the integrated result. Focused run: 26 passed.

payload.title: Worklink #1448: build: the opencode-ai pin is a bare literal in 24 places with no single constant, so bumping to 1.18.21 hits a version-coupled install detector, three negative test assertions, and a dated security record

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The consolidation is real, and I verified it the way a consolidation should be verified — by moving the constant and seeing what breaks.

```python
OPENCODE_VERSION = "1.18.21"   # mimir/worklink/tool_pins.py
```

A single constant only helps if every surface that *cannot* import it is drift-guarded. Bumping it to `1.19.0` and changing nothing else:


Both non-Python operational surfaces fail when the constant moves, so a future pin bump cannot silently leave the Dockerfile or the drift-skill targets behind. That is the property that makes this worth doing at all — without those two tests, centralising the literal would have moved the drift risk rather than removed it.

The remaining `1.18.21` occurrences are in fenced ```yaml example blocks (`worklink-tool-pins/SKILL.md` under "## `worklink.yaml` shape", plus `docs/configuration.md` and `docs/internal/WORKLINK.md`). I checked that none is read by any Python module — they illustrate the config shape rather than supplying a value, so leaving them as literals is correct rather than an oversight. A doc example carrying a version that ages is a different and much smaller problem than an operational literal that silently disagrees with the pin.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1446: worklink: foreign-owned objects in the base repo silently defeat hardlinked cloning, so hardlink-eligible builds copy the whole object store

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The detector is well built and I verified it properly. Blocking only because the branch conflicts with `main` and therefore has no CI at all — plus one observation from having hit this failure class for real a few hours ago.

## What I verified

```python
metadata = object_path.stat(follow_symlinks=False)
if not stat.S_ISREG(metadata.st_mode) or metadata.st_uid == expected_uid:
    continue
foreign.append(object_path)
event_logger("worklink_foreign_owned_git_object", repo=..., object_path=..., owner_uid=..., expected_owner_uid=..., mode=...)
```

`follow_symlinks=False` is the right call — a symlink in the object store would otherwise report the *target's* uid and mask exactly the case this exists to catch. Restricting to regular files avoids noise from directories, and the event carries path, both uids and the mode, so a report is actionable without a follow-up investigation.

**Mutation:** disabling the uid comparison fails `test_foreign_owned_git_objects_are_reported_with_path_uid_and_mode`. The other two tests are a genuine pair rather than one probe — `..._stays_quiet_when_every_object_matches` proves it does not report indiscriminately, and `..._is_not_reachable_from_clone_path` pins the scope. Baseline: 3 passed.

Report-only, wired through the scheduler, is the right posture for a first cut: this should surface the condition before anything automatically mutates a shared repository.

## Blocking: conflicts with `main`, so nothing has been tested

```
mergeable=CONFLICTING   behind main=4   CI: (no checks at all)
```

GitHub will not compute a merge, so no check has run against this head. I cannot verify it as an integrated whole, and the branch is only 4 commits behind — merging `main` should be quick.

- [ ] Merge current `main` and let CI run.

## Worth knowing: this would not have caught today's actual contamination

I cleaned the base repo by hand around 20:03 today. What I found was **121 staged and modified entries** in `/workspace/mimir` — the entire ACP feature staged as additions, plus modifications to `Dockerfile` and `.github/workflows/tests.yml` — written there by a build instead of into its own checkout. Every one of those files, and `.git` itself, was owned by `mimir:mimir`:

```
/workspace/mimir      owner=mimir:mimir
/workspace/mimir/.git owner=mimir:mimir
```

So the uid check would have reported nothing. Base-repo integrity has (at least) two failure modes — foreign *ownership* of objects, and foreign *content* in the working tree and index — and this leaf covers the first. That is what chainlink #1446 asked for, so it is not a defect in this PR; but the second mode is the one that actually fired today, it silently contaminated every checkout branched from that repo afterwards, and nothing currently detects it.

Worth a follow-up leaf: a pre-dispatch check that the base repo's working tree and index are clean, which is a cheap `git status --porcelain` and would have caught today's case immediately. Happy to file it if you would rather not expand this one.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Verified at `9e2c30fa8`.

Conflict resolved and the ownership reporting is genuinely covered.

Mutation-verified: at `mimir/worklink/checkout.py:703`, changing the skip condition
`or metadata.st_uid == expected_uid:` → `or True:` (confirmed 1 line changed) so the
check never reports a foreign object fails exactly
`test_foreign_owned_git_objects_are_reported_with_path_uid_and_mode`, with the other
two tests still passing. Correctly aimed.

CI green 11/11. Its run was one commit stale (#1735 landed after), so I trial-merged
`origin/main`: 0 conflicts, and the union of this PR's suite with the suite covering

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Filed the follow-up as chainlink **#1459** so the evidence is not lost: "nothing verifies the base repo working tree is clean before a build branches from it". Related to #1446.

It carries the concrete 2026-08-24 case — 121 staged/modified entries in `/workspace/mimir`, all owned `mimir:mimir`, which is precisely why a uid check reports nothing on it — and records the detail that made it invisible: `git status` there must run as the owning user, because running it as root via `docker exec` returns "detected dubious ownership" and an empty result that reads as a clean tree.

Its review criteria say detection before remediation explicitly: refuse to dispatch from a dirty base and name what was dirty, but do not have a build automatically `reset --hard` a shared repository. A build destroying an operator's in-progress work would be worse than the contamination it prevents.

It is filed unarmed — arming is Jason's call. Nothing needed on this PR beyond the `main` merge.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1445: worklink: child output is discarded when a run is terminated, so the transcript for every dead launch is empty and failures are indistinguishable

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The durability mechanism is well built — the file creation in particular is careful. Blocking on one regression I can attribute to this diff, and one coverage gap.

## The file creation is genuinely good

```python
output_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True, mode=0o700)
output_fd = os.open(
    output_path,
    os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL | getattr(os, "O_NOFOLLOW", 0),
    0o600,
)
```

`O_EXCL` refuses to reuse an existing path and `O_NOFOLLOW` refuses to follow a symlink, so neither a pre-planted file nor a symlink can redirect captured child output; `0o600` under a `0o700` parent keeps it owner-only; and `getattr(os, "O_NOFOLLOW", 0)` degrades rather than breaking where the flag is absent. The write loop handles short writes and raises on `written <= 0` instead of silently truncating, and `finally: os.close(output_fd)` runs even when the drain raises. That is the right standard for a path that persists subprocess output.

Retained/overflow accounting is preserved alongside the new file sink rather than replaced, so the in-memory cap still behaves as before.

## Blocking: this breaks a credential-allowlist test, and it is this diff

```
tests/test_worklink_backends.py::test_local_subprocess_env_allowlist_passes_creds_not_bridge_secrets

  on current main:  1 passed
  on 196be56e4:     1 failed      (isolated, same interpreter and venv)
```

```
FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '/mimir-home/state/worklink/transcripts'
  ... mkdir mode=448 on /mimir-home/state/worklink/transcripts
  ... mkdir mode=511 parents=True on /mimir-home/state/worklink
  ... mkdir mode=511 parents=True on /mimir-home/state
```

`compute.py:249` builds the transcript root as `home.resolve() / "state" / "worklink" / "transcripts"`, and `contained_execution.py:220` now creates it **eagerly** at drain time. With `MIMIR_HOME` unset the home resolves to the deployment path `/mimir-home`, so a unit test that never previously touched the filesystem now tries to create directories there and fails.

The concerning part is not the red test, it is what it reveals: the output path is not derived from the run's own sandbox. In a test that means an escape to an absolute path outside `tmp_path`; on a deployment it means the drain writes to a location the run does not own, which is the same class of boundary problem as the base-repo contamination cleaned earlier today.

- [ ] Derive the output path from the run's checkout/sandbox, or skip the `mkdir` when no output path is configured for that execution, so a drain never creates directories under the resolved home as a side effect. Then re-run `tests/test_worklink_backends.py` — it passes on `main` today, so this is a regression rather than a pre-existing failure.

## Blocking: one test for five production files

`test_direct_terminated_output_is_durable_while_running` is the only addition, against +254/-56 across `contained_execution.py`, `compute.py`, `orchestrator.py`, and both backends. The security-relevant branches are unverified: I removed `O_EXCL` and `O_NOFOLLOW` and widened the mode to `0o644`, and the only casualty was an unrelated capping test — nothing asserts the exclusive-create or no-symlink behaviour, or the `written <= 0` short-write path.

- [ ] Cover at least: an existing file at `output_path` is refused rather than overwritten (`O_EXCL`), a symlink at `output_path` is refused (`O_NOFOLLOW`), and the resulting file is owner-only. These are the properties that make persisting child output safe, and tonight three other authz PRs shipped correct guards with no test distinguishing them from their fail-open twins.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The regression I blocked on is fixed. Re-blocking on a new one introduced by the same commit — and it is a textbook case of the class of defect a build cannot see.

## Fixed: the output path is derived from the run's own directory

```python
output_root = tmp_path / "state" / "worklink" / "transcripts"
object.__setattr__(work, "output_root", output_root)
```

and the eager `mkdir` on a path built from the configured home is gone from `contained_execution.py`. That was the substance of my block: a drain must not create directories under the resolved home as a side effect. Confirmed absent.

## Blocking: the new test hardcodes an image-only absolute path

```python
object.__setattr__(
    work, "local_argv",
    ("/usr/bin/node", "-e", "process.stdout.write(...); setTimeout(() => {}, 30000)"),
)
```

```
FAILED tests/test_worklink_worker_parity.py::test_direct_terminated_output_is_durable_while_running[sigterm]
  FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '/usr/bin/node'
```

Measured where node actually lives:

```
mimirbot image:   /usr/bin/node          exists      <- where this build ran
this macOS host:  ~/.asdf/shims/node     /usr/bin/node ABSENT
CI linux runner:  (not at /usr/bin/node)             <- pytest (3.12) FAILURE
guard in test:    none (0 skipif / shutil.which)
```

So the test passes only where node happens to sit at that exact path, which is true of the Worklink image and of nothing else. This is the failure mode worth naming: **the build runs inside the image, so an image-specific assumption is invisible to it** — the executor's own gate command passed. CI is the first place it can surface, which is exactly what happened.

- [ ] Use `sys.executable` instead. The spec already carries `direct_spec("import time; time.sleep(30)")`, so a Python child is the natural fit and always exists: `(sys.executable, "-c", "import sys,time; sys.stdout.write(...); sys.stderr.write(...); sys.stdout.flush(); time.sleep(30)")`. That removes the dependency rather than guarding it — a `skipif` would leave the durability behaviour untested everywhere except the image, which defeats the point of the test.

Nothing else changed my earlier assessment: the `O_EXCL | O_NOFOLLOW` / `0o600` creation is still good and worth keeping exactly as written. My second item from that review — that those flags have no test distinguishing them from their permissive alternatives — is still open.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Blocking: `pytest-macos (3.11)` fails with **10 failed, 10483 passed** at `26780e724`.

The `/usr/bin/node` item is properly fixed — `tests/test_worklink_worker_parity.py`
now uses `sys.executable` (402, 489, 576), and using the real interpreter rather
than a `skipif` was the right call: the durability behaviour is now actually
exercised everywhere.

But the same commit introduces a second, identical-in-kind defect. This PR adds

    mimir/worklink/compute.py:463
        preexec_fn=lambda: _arm_parent_death_signal(parent_pid),

    mimir/worklink/worker_exec.py:109
        if libc.prctl(1, signal.SIGKILL, 0, 0, 0) != 0:  # PR_SET_PDEATHSIG

`prctl` is a Linux syscall. macOS libSystem exports no such symbol, so every launch
through this path raises inside the child and surfaces as:

    E  subprocess.SubprocessError: Exception occurred in preexec_fn.
    E  mimir.worklink.compute.ComputeLaunchError: Exception occurred in preexec_fn.

Failing: `test_closed_worker_direct_parity_inventory` (all 5 params),
`test_direct_terminated_output_is_durable_while_running[sigterm]`, and others.

This is the same class as the `/usr/bin/node` finding — a Linux/container assumption
that is invisible in the mimirbot image and only observable on the macOS leg. Worth
naming explicitly since it is now twice in one PR.

Required:
- Guard the parent-death-signal arming by platform. On non-Linux, `preexec_fn` should
  be omitted (or a no-op) rather than raising. The Linux path must be unchanged.
- `test_arm_parent_death_signal_closes_pre_prctl_race` should assert the Linux
  behaviour on Linux and the documented fallback on non-Linux, so neither side is
  silently untested.
- State in the PR body what the non-Linux fallback gives up. Losing PDEATHSIG means
  an orphaned worker is not auto-killed; if that is acceptable off-Linux, say so
  explicitly rather than leaving it implied.

Do not resolve this by skipping the affected tests on macOS — that would hide the
launch failure rather than fix it, and the launch path itself is what breaks.

payload.body:
Verified at `c21f02771`. Both of my blocking items are resolved.

**1. `/usr/bin/node`** — fixed earlier via `sys.executable`, and using the real interpreter
rather than a `skipif` means the durability behaviour is exercised everywhere.

**2. `prctl` platform guard** — correct, and verified natively on macOS (the platform that
was failing):
- `compute.py:456` installs `preexec_fn` only on Linux.
- `worker_exec.py:114` returns early off-Linux.
- The Linux path is byte-identical.

Mutation note worth recording: neither guard alone is killable, because they are
deliberately redundant — with `compute.py` guarded, `_arm_parent_death_signal` is never
reached; with `worker_exec.py` guarded, it is a no-op. Removing **both** together
reproduces the original failure exactly — all 7 `test_closed_worker_direct_parity_inventory`
cases fail. So the pair is load-bearing and the tests do detect its absence. I checked
this against the merged union as well: 5 failed with both guards removed.

Confirmed **no skip workaround**: the previously-failing tests run natively on macOS,
7 passed / 0 skipped. The docstring states the tradeoff plainly — abrupt controller death
may orphan a worker off Linux, ordinary cancellation and reaping still apply — which is

CI green 11/11. Trial-merged `origin/main` (1 behind after #1733): 0 conflicts, 207 passed
natively.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
CI has independently reproduced the regression I described, on a Linux runner, with a sharper signature than my local run — worth recording because it strengthens the ask.

```
FAILED tests/test_worklink_backends.py::test_local_subprocess_env_allowlist_passes_creds_not_bridge_secrets
  env={"MIMIR_HOME": "/mimir-home"}
  PosixPath("/mimir-home"), mode=511, parents=True, exist_ok=True
  PermissionError: [Errno 13] Permission denied: "/mimir-home"
```

Locally it surfaced as `FileNotFoundError` because that path simply does not exist on macOS; in CI it is `PermissionError` because `/` is not writable by the runner. Same defect, two environments.

The detail I understated in my review: the test **deliberately sets** `MIMIR_HOME=/mimir-home`. So this is not a test that forgot to isolate itself — it is exercising a configured home, and `contained_execution.py:220` now calls `mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` on a path derived from it at drain time, unconditionally.

That makes the consequence clearer than "a red test". On the live deployment `/mimir-home` **does** exist and is writable, so the drain would silently create `state/worklink/transcripts` under the real home rather than under the run own checkout — no error, no signal, just output persisted outside the sandbox the run owns. The CI failure is the benign manifestation; the deployment behaviour is the one that matters.

Unchanged ask: derive the output path from the run checkout/sandbox, or skip the mkdir when no output path is configured for that execution. The `O_EXCL`/`O_NOFOLLOW`/`0o600` creation itself is good and worth keeping exactly as written.

mimir-carreira

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1444: worklink/factory: the status probe is spawned with cwd set to the sandbox the factory has not created yet, so every epic dispatch dies in 8s

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. Small, correct fix with a discriminating test pair.

## The change

```python
-    cwd: Path,
+    cwd: Path | None = None,
...
     kwargs: dict[str, Any] = {"env": dict(env), "stdin": subprocess.DEVNULL, ...}
     if cwd is not None:
         kwargs["cwd"] = cwd
```

Omitting `cwd` entirely rather than passing a directory that does not exist is the right shape — `subprocess.run` raises `NotADirectoryError`/`FileNotFoundError` for a missing `cwd` before the child ever starts, which is what turned "sandbox not created yet" into what looked like an infrastructure failure. Letting the probe inherit the parent's cwd makes the status call answerable in the pre-sandbox window.

**The test pair is what makes this safe.** `test_status_before_sandbox_creation_returns_not_ready` covers the new path, and `test_status_spawn_failure_remains_infrastructure_error` covers the one that could regress — a genuine spawn failure must still surface as an infrastructure error rather than being swallowed into "not ready". Without the second, this change could have converted every spawn failure into a benign-looking status.

**Mutation:** forcing `cwd` to always be passed fails both `test_status_before_sandbox_creation_returns_not_ready` and `test_controls_are_absolute_run_id_first_and_resume_reads_status`. Baseline: 99 passed.

One thing I checked because the diff shape invites it: `kwargs: dict[str, Any] = {...}` is a function-body statement at `feature_factory.py:467`, immediately after an early `return`, not a parameter default — so this is not the mutable-default-argument trap it superficially resembles. It also cannot be one, since it reads `env` and `timeout`.

## Verification

Trial-merged current `main` (union `a24adc0c`, this head was 3 commits behind, no conflicts): **368 passed** across the two touched test files. All 11 CI checks green.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1442: authz/trust-derivation: reading a first-party shipped skill file taints the turn untrusted, the single largest cause of live shell refusals

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Good change with a genuinely careful design. Two blocking items: one security guard is unverified, and the body does not record a trust decision that this leaf's own review criteria asked for.

## What I verified as correct

**This tightens as well as widens, and the split is the right one.** `skills` is removed from `_SELF_AUTHORED_FILE_ROOTS` and kept only in the new `_FILE_INTEGRITY_RECORDED_ROOTS`:

```python
_SELF_AUTHORED_FILE_ROOTS = frozenset({".mimir_builtin_skills", "docs", "memory", "prompts", "state"})
_FILE_INTEGRITY_RECORDED_ROOTS = _SELF_AUTHORED_FILE_ROOTS | {"skills"}
```

So first-party shipped skills earn the trusted default while operator- or agent-installed content under `skills/` no longer does merely by living there — and writes there are still recorded, so taint is still tracked. That distinction is not in the acceptance criteria and you were right to draw it; without it, fixing the builtin-skill case would have over-widened to anything installed under `skills/`.

**Mutation confirms the tightening is pinned.** Restoring `"skills"` to the trusted-read set fails `test_home_location_does_not_make_external_or_operator_files_trusted[skills/operator/SKILL.md]`.

**The anti-laundering test is the one I most wanted to see.** `test_poller_own_channel_does_not_declassify_external_item` asserts that an external item in the same label set still yields `has_untrusted_active_ingest is True`. That is the property that stops "the poller's own channel is trusted" from becoming "anything arriving through the poller is trusted", and pinning it directly is the difference between a safe widening and a hole.

**The guard is bound to server-carried authority**, not model-supplied values — `event.service_principal == registered_service.canonical`, the configured `channel_memory_directory`, and an explicit `HTTP_EVENT_INGRESS_EXTRA_KEY` exclusion. Correct shape.

## Blocking 1: the equality that "establishes that boundary" is untested

```python
and isinstance(registered_service.channel_memory_directory, str)
and event.channel_id == registered_service.channel_memory_directory
```

Your own comment says exact equality with the configured memory directory is what establishes the boundary. Deleting that line and changing nothing else leaves the suite green:

```
mutation: remove `event.channel_id == registered_service.channel_memory_directory`
  -> 2 passed   (both poller tests still pass)
```

Without it, every condition that remains is satisfied by *any* channel belonging to that poller, so a channel that is not the poller's own memory directory would be classified `TRUSTED` / informational. That is precisely the widening the equality exists to prevent, and nothing fails.

- [ ] Add a case where `event.channel_id` differs from `registered_service.channel_memory_directory` with all other conditions met, asserting the source stays `UNTRUSTED` / `ACTIVE_INGEST`. Same shape as the existing pair, one more parametrization.

## Blocking 2: the trust decision is not recorded anywhere

The PR body is worklink evidence only — no build summary. Chainlink #1442's own review criteria require that this widening be justified in writing, and three of tonight's authz PRs (#1730, #1731, #1733) each carried a section doing exactly that.

Specifically missing: that `skills` was deliberately dropped from the trusted-read set (a behaviour change beyond the stated criteria, and the most surprising thing in the diff), and what establishes the poller-own-channel boundary. Someone reading this in three months will find the `skills` removal and not know whether it was intentional.

- [ ] Add a short trust-decision section: which sources become trusted, what server-side fact establishes each, and that `skills` lost its location-based default deliberately.

Nothing else here needs changing — the mechanism is sound and the external-item test is exactly right.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Verified at `81f70e89a`.

Both blocking items addressed:

2. **Trust-decision rationale** now in the PR body under `## Trust decision`, covering all
