payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: test: synchronize Worklink grandchild termination setup

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. This replaces a timing assumption with a synchronization primitive, which is the right shape for the class of flake it targets.

```python
-  "subprocess.Popen([... 'signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM,signal.SIG_IGN); time.sleep(30)']); "
-  "time.sleep(.1); "
+  "ready_r,ready_w=os.pipe(); "
+  child_source = "... signal.signal(SIGTERM,SIG_IGN); os.write({ready_w},b'1'); ..."
+  "subprocess.Popen([...], pass_fds=(ready_w,)); os.close(ready_w); "
+  "assert os.read(ready_r,1)==b'1'; "
```

The ordering is the part that matters: the grandchild signals readiness **after** installing the handler, so the parent cannot proceed into the termination assertion while the grandchild would still die on SIGTERM. That is precisely the window the old fixed 100ms sleep left open.

It also fails safe rather than hanging. The parent closes its own copy of `ready_w` before reading, so if the grandchild dies before writing, the read returns EOF and the assertion fails — instead of blocking forever on a pipe nothing will ever write to.

**Verification**

- 15 consecutive runs of the two-case regression on this head: **0 failures**.
- Whole file on a trial-merge with current `main` (union `b6289848`): **91 passed**.
- `main` is 1 commit behind this head, and that commit does not touch `tests/test_worklink_worker_parity.py`, so the merged result for the changed file is identical to what CI tested. All 11 checks green.

**One honest gap in my verification.** I tried to reproduce the original failure on the old sleep-based version and could not — 12 runs under synthetic CPU load, 0 failures. So my mutation is inconclusive rather than confirming. I do not read that as evidence against the fix: I observed this test fail exactly once tonight, in #1731's full-suite run, while a Docker image build and two Worklink builds were saturating disk IO — and CPU pressure is not the same pressure. Your 40-run figure plus the full suite is better evidence than my 12.

Either way the change stands on its own: a handshake is strictly more deterministic than a sleep, and it is test-only.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1430: authz: the file-integrity ledger is opt-in at the writer, so any shell or subprocess write into a self-authored root reads back trusted - content nobody vouched for becomes self-authored

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Good mechanism — `ctime` is the right primitive and the discriminating test is real. Blocking on one thing: the two fail-closed branches that make this safe are untested, and flipping either to fail-open is currently invisible.

## What I verified as correct

**`st_ctime_ns`, not `st_mtime_ns`.** There is no syscall to set ctime arbitrarily, while `utimes` lets any writer backdate mtime — so an mtime-based epoch would be trivially defeated by the shell writes this exists to catch. Using ctime is the load-bearing choice here and it is the right one.

**Explicit entries still win.** `if value is not None: return ...` runs before the epoch path, so #1730's recorded-untrusted ratchet is preserved and this cannot launder a recorded taint.

**`isinstance(epoch_ns, bool)` is excluded.** `True` is an `int` and `True > 0`, so without that a ledger containing `{"__ledger_epoch_ns__": true}` would compare against `1` and trust essentially nothing — or worse, on a different comparison, everything. Catching it explicitly is careful work.

**Mutation confirms the core check bites.** Replacing the comparison with a bare `return "trusted"` — i.e. the pre-fix behaviour — fails `test_ledger_epoch_distinguishes_seeded_file_from_unrecorded_shell_write`. Baseline `2 passed`.

**The `timeout=10` -> `timeout=30` change is legitimate and I am not flagging it.** That is an outer `subprocess.run` guard around a nested pytest whose intentional sleep is three seconds; under contention the nested interpreter's *startup* can eat the remaining seven. The assertion's own faulthandler threshold is untouched, and this file is the only place it changed. I produced this exact failure class tonight by running four suites at once, so the diagnosis matches what I independently observed.

## I checked the operational cost and it is fine

I went looking for a regression here and did not find one, so recording it rather than making you chase it. My worry was that `refresh_builtin_skills` — whose docstring says it **always overwrites** — would re-stamp ctime on every boot while the epoch is written only once, making the agent's own skill documentation read untrusted from the second restart onward. Measured against the live home (container up 19h, so a 19h-old epoch as a stand-in):

```
.mimir_builtin_skills      0 /    61 files post-epoch
skills                     0 /   129
memory                     9 /   304
state                     97 / 41803
prompts / docs             0 /    25
```

So the refresh is not re-stamping those trees in practice, and the real churn is ~100 files a day — mostly `state/raw`, which the ledger already records as untrusted (115 of its 218 entries). The forward-looking taint is small and is the intended behaviour, not a regression.

## Blocking: both fail-closed branches are unverified

```python
if not isinstance(epoch_ns, int) or isinstance(epoch_ns, bool) or epoch_ns <= 0:
    return "untrusted"
...
except OSError:
    return "untrusted"
```

Flipping either one to `return "trusted"` and changing nothing else leaves the whole file green:

```
mutation B (malformed/negative epoch fails open):  285 passed
mutation C (stat failure fails open):              285 passed
```

These are the branches that decide behaviour when the ledger is corrupt or the file cannot be stat'd — exactly the states an attacker or a disk fault produces, and exactly where failing open would silently restore blanket trust. A fail-safe no test can distinguish from a fail-open is one refactor away from being one.

- [ ] Cover both: a ledger whose epoch is a non-int / bool / non-positive value, and an unstattable path under a self-authored root. Each should assert `untrusted`.

Noting for sequencing rather than as a change request: this is the third file-integrity change in flight tonight. #1730 (recorded-write ratchet) merged, and #1732 is blocked on trusting a lease root whose contents arrive by `git fetch` — this epoch check would classify those fetched files as post-

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Blocking. CI is green and the fix itself looks right, but the test named for the
fail-closed branches does not constrain two of the three clauses it names.

Mutation results at `601a6d4cd`, against
`test_malformed_nonpositive_and_bool_ledger_epochs_fail_closed`
(`mimir/access_control.py:8477`), each mutation confirmed applied via `git diff --numstat`:

| clause removed | result |
|---|---|
| `not isinstance(epoch_ns, int)` | **4 failed** (null, list, object, float) — constrained |
| `isinstance(epoch_ns, bool)` | 9 passed — **not constrained** |
| `epoch_ns <= 0` | 9 passed — **not constrained** |
| all three bool sites (8477, 8506, 8573) | 9 passed — **not constrained** |

Why: the test writes the target file at test time and asserts the verdict is
`("untrusted", "active_ingest")`. With the bool or nonpositive clause gone, the value
falls through to

    return "trusted" if file_ctime_ns <= epoch_ns else "untrusted"

and for `True` (== 1), `False` (== 0), `0`, `-1` the comparison `file_ctime_ns <= 1`
is False for any real file — so the verdict is `untrusted` anyway, by arithmetic
rather than by the guard. Five of the nine parameters pass whether or not their guard
clause exists.

This is not exploitable today: the accidental path yields the same safe answer. The
defect is that the guard is unpinned — a later refactor that drops or reorders these
clauses leaves the suite green, and the test's name reads as coverage that is not
there.

Suggested fix, small: make the fall-through produce the *unsafe* verdict so only the
guard can produce the safe one. Stub the stat so `file_ctime_ns` is 0 — then for
`epoch_ns=True` (1), `0 <= 1` is True and the fall-through would return `trusted`.
The assertion then fails unless the guard fires, which is what the test claims to
prove. Re-run the three mutations above and confirm each now fails.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Verified at `590e07c50`. My blocking item is genuinely resolved.

Previously the `bool` and `<= 0` clauses were unconstrained — malformed values fell
through to `file_ctime_ns <= epoch_ns`, which is False for any real file, so the safe
verdict arrived by arithmetic rather than by the guard. The fix makes the fall-through
*unsafe* so only the guard can produce the safe answer, which is the right shape.

I ran my own mutation matrix across all six clauses at all three sites (8480, 8509,
8576), each confirmed applied via `git diff --numstat`:

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| site1 `isinstance(epoch_ns, bool)` | killed (1 failed) |
| site1 `epoch_ns <= 0` | killed (2 failed) |
| site2 `not isinstance(epoch_ns, bool)` | killed (1 failed) |
| site2 `epoch_ns > 0` | killed (2 failed) |
| site3 `isinstance(epoch_ns, bool)` | killed (1 failed) |
| site3 `epoch_ns <= 0` | killed (2 failed) |

6/6 killed. Baseline coverage went 9 → 19 tests.

CI green 11/11, `behind_main=0`, trial-merged `origin/main` with 0 conflicts and
`tests/test_information_flow.py` passing 315.

payload.body:

The invalid-epoch tests now force the fall-through to produce the unsafe verdict, so each guard is independently load-bearing rather than passing accidentally because real ctime is large. Added equivalent guard tests for ledger initialization and write recording.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1427: authz: a server-owned root outside MIMIR_HOME can never be trusted on read, so reading its own PR lease taints the turn and costs it repo_test - throttling PR remediation now

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The mechanics here are careful — resolution order, symlink handling and the anti-laundering path are all right. I am blocking on the premise rather than the implementation: "server-owned root" does not establish "server-authored content" when the root holds a git checkout.

## What I verified as correct first

**No symlink escape on the read path.** `resource = Path(resource_id).resolve(strict=True)` (`access_control.py:7873`) happens before the containment test at `:7911`, so a symlink inside the lease root that points outside resolves outside and fails `relative_to(root)`. It then falls through to `untrusted`/`active_ingest`.

**The root itself is validated**: absolute, not a symlink, `resolve(strict=True)`, and `is_dir()`. `MIMIR_FILE_TOOL_ROOTS` is deliberately excluded, which is the right call — an access grant is not an integrity assertion, and conflating them is how `:ro`/`:rw` external data would have become trusted.

**Trust is not unconditional.** The branch returns `_persisted_file_integrity(home, resource)`, not a literal `"trusted"`, so a recorded model write downgrades the read. Mutation-confirmed: replacing it with `return "trusted", "informational"` fails `test_untrusted_model_write_cannot_launder_through_configured_lease_root`.

## Blocking: the lease root contains checked-out PR branches, not server-authored content

`MIMIR_PR_CHECKOUT_LEASE_ROOT` is `/workspace/pr-leases` on the live deployment, and each lease is a full working tree:

```
/workspace/pr-leases/57f7a924.../     28 entries: .git .github AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md ...
   .git/HEAD -> ref: refs/heads/issue/1403-a1
   .git/HEAD -> ref: refs/heads/issue/1388-a1
   .git/HEAD -> ref: refs/heads/issue/1379-a3
```

Those are PR branches (#1704, #1687, #1683). The *directory* is server-created; the *file contents* arrive by `git fetch` from a branch a worklink build wrote. Because fetched content is never a recorded model write, it has no entry in `file-integrity.json`, and `_persisted_file_integrity` returns `"trusted"` for a missing key (`:7977-7978`). So the default-trusted path applies to exactly the content whose provenance is least established.

This codebase already rejects this inference, three lines above the new branch:

> Poller subprocesses write this tree directly, outside the protected tool boundary, and may persist attacker-derived cursor/event fields. A path under `state/pollers` is therefore not proof of self-authorship.

A worklink build is the same shape: an opencode subprocess writing outside the protected tool boundary, whose inputs include chainlink text and PR review bodies. "It is our own branch" is not proof the content is untainted, for the same reason `state/pollers` is carved out.

**Why it is not exploitable today, and why that is the problem.** A lease requires a `RepoPRActionScope` granting `CHECKOUT` (`pr_checkout_lease.py:249-252`), and that scope only exists for an open PR whose author equals `MIMIR_GITHUB_SELF_LOGIN` (`forge.py:322`). So leases are self-authored today. But that invariant lives three modules from the trust decision, nothing at the trust site states or asserts it, and **chainlink #1457 — filed today — proposes changing exactly that gate.** A future relaxation there silently converts this into "reading a third-party PR's files is trusted," with no failing test.

- [ ] Bind the trust to provenance rather than to the directory. Two workable shapes: record an integrity entry for the checkout at lease-creation time, derived from the PR author's trust via the existing `_github_author_is_trusted` machinery (extended for more event types in #1731), so the missing-key default never decides a lease read; or assert the self-authorship precondition at the trust site so the invariant is enforced where it is relied upon rather than inherited.
- [ ] Either way, add a regression for a lease whose content is *not* self-authored, so the day `forge.py:322` changes, something fails.

payload.title: Worklink #1426: authz: 7 of the github-activity poller 11 event types cannot resolve an author, so they fail closed to untrusted and cost the poller its shell - the largest single cause of live taint refusals

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The trust decisions are server-anchored in the places where getting it wrong would be a real hole, and the conformance test makes the classification impossible to leave incomplete by accident.

## The two newly-resolved actors take the right field

**`pr_synchronize`** resolves from the compare response's newest commit via `commit.get("author") or commit.get("committer")`. That is the *top-level* `author` on the commit list entry — the GitHub user object the server resolved — not `commit["commit"]["author"]`, which is git metadata any pusher can set to arbitrary name/email. Taking the latter would have let anyone forge a trusted actor by setting a git config value, so this is the distinction the whole change rests on and it is on the correct side of it.

The endpoint interpolation is also guarded before use:

```python
7 <= len(value) <= 64 and all(character in "0123456789abcdefABCDEF" for character in value)
```

Both SHAs are validated hex-only and length-bounded before landing in `repos/{repo}/compare/{previous_head}...{new_head}`, so a malformed extras value cannot reshape the request path.

**`pr_review_requested`** filters the timeline to `event == "review_requested"` entries whose `requested_reviewer.login` matches exactly, then takes `actor` from the most recent match — the requester, server-side. Falling back to `None` when the payload is not a list, or when nothing matches, keeps the untrusted default.

**`pr_review`** matching on `html_url` identifies the specific review rather than guessing by position. Every branch returns `None` on a malformed or missing response, so a failed attestation stays untrusted active ingest rather than defaulting open.

## The conformance test is the durable part

`test_github_activity_integrity_classification_is_total` extracts the emitted event types from the poller source and asserts `emitted == _GITHUB_ACTIVITY_EVENT_TYPES`, plus disjointness of the actor and framework tables and non-empty rationale strings for every entry. So a future event type added to the poller cannot silently fall through to untrusted — which is the exact failure mode this chainlink is about.

**Mutation:** removing the `pr_synchronize` entry from `_GITHUB_ACTOR_EVENT_TYPES` fails it at `tests/test_pollers.py:1883`. Baseline `1 passed`.

## Suite

Full suite on a trial-merge with current `main` (union `98a304c0`): **10218 passed, 35 skipped, 2 failed** — and both failures are mine, not yours:

- `test_worklink_worker_parity.py::test_direct_termination_kills_pipe_holding_grandchild[timeout]` — passes on its own in **1.12s**.
- `test_root_dockerfile.py::test_built_image_provides_process_tools` — passes on its own in **145.85s**.

I had four full suites plus a Docker build running concurrently on this machine; a 145-second image build and a process-termination timing test are exactly what starves first. Neither has any causal path to `mimir/pollers.py`, which is all this PR touches. Your own CI is `SUCCESS=11` (checked by grouping on conclusion, not by counting failures — three `CANCELLED` legs on another PR tonight taught me that "0 failures" is not the same as green).

One note for the body rather than the code: the claim that live `ifc_label_blocked` re-attribution needs a post-deployment window is right, and worth keeping in mind when it lands — the 81 hard-boundary denials I measured today on `poller:github-activity` were `ToolPolicyRefusal` from `forge.py`'s scope gate, not taint refusals, so this change will not move that number. That is chainlink #1457, filed separately; I noted the split there so the two are not mistaken for duplicates.

payload.title: Worklink #1424: authz: reading a recorded-untrusted self-authored file disqualifies the rewrite that would repair it, so the agent cannot restore its own memory without a blind overwrite

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. This changes an integrity rule, so I went at the one line that widens trust rather than the surface area — and it holds up.

## The widening is consistent with the gate's own definition

```python
integrity = "trusted" if labels is not None and all(
    source.integrity == "trusted" for source in sources
) else "untrusted"
```

`all()` over an empty tuple is `True`, so the behavioural change is exactly: *non-None carrier with zero sources* goes from untrusted to trusted. That is the one case to scrutinise, and it is correct — `InformationFlowLabels.has_untrusted_active_ingest` is computed from `self.sources` too, so a turn with no sources genuinely has no untrusted active ingest by the system's own gate predicate. The new rule agrees with the predicate that guards the sinks rather than inventing a second notion of clean.

The `labels is not None` half is doing real work: absent provenance stays untrusted, unchanged from before. My concern was that `labels` (the `frozenset[str]` sensitivity axis) and `sources` could diverge and let a tainted turn through with an empty source tuple — they cannot, because integrity is source-derived on both paths.

## Verified

**Stickiness is load-bearing.** Replacing the guarded update with an unconditional `payload[key] = integrity` — i.e. letting an ordinary clean write clear an existing untrusted mark, which is the laundering vector — fails two tests:

```
FAILED test_digest_bound_repair_breaks_self_authored_integrity_ratchet
FAILED test_invalid_legacy_integrity_value_stays_fail_closed
```

**`repair_file_write_integrity` is bound tightly**: exact-SHA256 match against current bytes, `re.fullmatch(r"[0-9a-f]{64}")` on the input digest, strict resolve, symlink rejected, root restricted to `_SELF_AUTHORED_FILE_ROOTS` with excluded subtrees honoured, refuses when the key is absent or already trusted, and appends the prior verdict to a protected ledger. Trust comes from an operator attestation bound to inspected bytes, which is the distinction that makes this recovery rather than laundering.

**The test set carries a real discriminating pair** — `test_file_write_integrity_discriminates_clean_empty_from_tainted_ingest` is clean-vs-tainted rather than a single probe that would confirm either prior.

**The body's inventory claim is exact.** Live store: **71** entries under `memory/issues/`, matching the body. `state/` reads 133 now against the body's 123, consistent with growth between build and review — about 15 new untrusted records an hour, all currently `untrusted`, `__declassifications__` empty. So the ratchet the PR describes is real and actively accruing, which is the argument for landing this rather than deferring it.

**Full suite on a trial-merge with current `main`** (union `49303f8d`, and note `main` had moved — #1729 touched both of these files since your CI ran): **10208 passed, 35 skipped, 0 failed.** All 11 CI checks green.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1423: saga: migration v9 is the first statement to demand (content_hash, agent_id, owner_principal) uniqueness and has no dedup pre-pass, so a legacy store with duplicate content becomes permanently unopenable

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The migration is well-designed and I want to start with something I checked and cleared, because it reflects well on the runner and is worth knowing.

**A suspected serious defect that turned out to be a non-issue.** The unguarded `ALTER TABLE atoms ADD COLUMN tombstoned_at TEXT` looked like it would reproduce the exact failure this PR fixes: `mimir/saga/schema.sql:41` already declares `tombstoned_at` in the base `atoms` table, and the live store carries both lifecycle columns while its `schema_version` shows v9 applied on 2026-07-17 — so stores reaching v9 with those columns present demonstrably exist. Plain SQLite gives `duplicate column name: tombstoned_at`.

It is fine, because `_execute_migration_script` runs statement-by-statement and its `sqlite3.OperationalError` handler tolerates a duplicate-column error when `_column_exists` confirms the column is genuinely there. I verified it end to end rather than by reading:

```
v9 against a store that ALREADY has tombstoned_at / tombstoned_reason:
  succeeded
  rows: [('a', 0, None), ('b', 1, 'merged')]
```

Correct survivor, correct retraction, no error. Flagging it because the guard lives in the runner rather than at the call site, so the next reader will have the same reaction I did.

**The design choices are right.** Tombstoning rather than deleting keeps the data — the correct instinct for a migration, where a `DELETE` is unrecoverable. And the survivor rule is genuinely well-reasoned:

> The id is durable logical data, unlike rowid or insertion order, so replicas of the same store choose the same survivor.

That determinism matters and is easy to get wrong; picking `MIN(rowid)` would have produced different survivors on different replicas of the same logical store.

The `IntegrityError` handler is the other half of the fix and is what turns "permanently unopenable" into something diagnosable — it names the colliding `content_hash` / `agent_id` / `owner_principal` rather than surfacing a bare constraint error.

**Live-store check, for the record:** `/mimir-home/.mimir/saga.db` is at schema version 10 with 2263 atoms and **zero** duplicate `(content_hash, agent_id, owner_principal)` groups, so this deployment was never exposed. The fix protects legacy and replica stores, not this one. Worth stating so nobody treats it as an incident fix.

`tests/test_saga_migrations.py`: 51 passed on a clean merge with current `main`.

## One blocking item: `tombstoned_at` is added but never set

The migration adds the column and the `UPDATE` sets only `tombstoned` and `tombstoned_reason`, so every merged row ends with `tombstoned_at = NULL`. Confirmed in the run above.

Both ordinary tombstone paths set it — `forget.py:104` and `dedup.py:533` are `UPDATE atoms SET tombstoned = 1, tombstoned_at = ?, ...` — so merged rows are inconsistent with every other tombstone in the store, and there is no record of when the merge happened.

Nothing currently filters or sorts on `tombstoned_at`, so this is not a live functional bug. I am still asking for it because of where it sits: **this is a migration, it runs once, and it is irreversible.** A NULL written now can only be corrected by writing another migration later, whereas setting it costs one expression today. Data-affecting code that executes exactly once is the wrong place to leave a known inconsistency for later.

- [ ] Set `tombstoned_at` on the merged rows — the migration timestamp is the honest value, and it matches what `forget` and `dedup` record.

Nothing else. The dedup pre-pass, the survivor rule, and the error reporting are all right, and the comment explaining the id choice is the kind of reasoning I wish more migrations carried.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. `tombstoned_at` is set on the merged rows, and the addition beyond the ask is a good one.

```sql
UPDATE atoms AS duplicate
SET tombstoned = 1,
    tombstoned_at = strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%f+00:00', 'now'),
    tombstoned_reason = COALESCE(duplicate.tombstoned_reason, 'merged')
```

Adding `tombstoned_reason` was not requested and is right: a row tombstoned by the v9 dedup merge is a different thing from one tombstoned by `forget`, and without a reason the two are indistinguishable afterwards. The `COALESCE` preserving an existing reason rather than overwriting it is the careful version — a row that already carried a reason keeps it.

**Mutation:** removing the `tombstoned_at` assignment fails both parametrizations of `test_legacy_collision_is_deterministically_tombstoned`. Baseline 3 passed.

## One thing I checked and decided not to block on

The migration writes millisecond precision via SQL `strftime` (`2026-08-24T22:49:59.743+00:00`), while the runtime path writes microseconds via `datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()` (`...59.743216+00:00`). My original item said the value should match what `forget` and `dedup` record, so a literal reading would flag the difference.

I traced whether it matters: nothing in `mimir/saga/` orders, filters or compares `tombstoned_at` — it is written by `dedup.py:533`, `forget.py:104` and this migration, and read back only as a value. `schema.sql:41` documents the column as `ISO ts, nullable`, and both forms are valid ISO-8601 UTC that parse identically. Blocking on three digits of sub-second precision in a one-time migration would be pedantry rather than rigor, so I am noting it instead: if `tombstoned_at` ever becomes an ordering key, the two writers should be unified first.

**Verification:** trial-merged current `main` (union `1be0f452`, this head was 25 commits behind, no conflicts) and ran the full suite: **10478 passed, 35 skipped, 0 failed.** All 11 CI checks green.

payload.body:

payload.title: Worklink #1422: observability: three of Scheduler._fire early returns log.error and return with no log_event, so a shell_commands or authority misconfiguration makes a scheduled tick go dark forever with no event trace

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The fix is right and it closes the gap correctly. One blocking item — the same defect I blocked #1695 for, in the same file, three hours later.

**The gap is genuinely closed.** These three early returns were the ones I flagged when approving #1695: `EVENT_JOB_ERROR` only fires when a job body *raises*, and these are deliberate `return`s after a configuration fault, so the listener never saw them. A scheduled job could go dark forever through this path. Emitting `scheduled_tick_dropped` at each site with a distinct `reason` is exactly the right shape.

**And you registered the event, which is the half that usually gets missed.** Verified rather than read:

```
scheduled_tick_dropped      -> ('negative', 'tick_dropped')
```

payload.title: fix: preserve failed startup evidence

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Good to see this land as a PR — this is the work that was stranded in an orphaned checkout, and the fix itself is the right one. It has a real break though, reproduced locally on all three failing legs.

**Failing test:** `tests/test_server.py::test_notify_handoff_marker_failure_stays_retryable`

```
RuntimeError: failed to persist unclean-restart notification handoff
  mimir/server.py:2129 in _notify_and_record_handoff
  -> cancel_background_tasks -> _on_cleanup -> ExceptionGroup("server cleanup failed")
```

Reproduced on a clean tree at `3f319d11`, fully up to date with `main` (`behind main: 0`), so this is not a stale-base union effect. `1 failed, 193 passed` across the three touched test files. That matches CI: `pytest (3.11)`, `pytest (3.12)` and `pytest-enforced` all fail, which is a consistent break rather than the intermittent pattern.

**The cause** is the new raise:

```python
if not write_session_marker(config.home, current_marker):
    raise RuntimeError("failed to persist unclean-restart notification handoff")
```

That converts a retryable marker failure into a fatal one. Because it is raised inside a background task, it does not surface at the point of failure — it is re-raised by `cancel_background_tasks` and arrives as an `ExceptionGroup` from `_on_cleanup`, so a failed marker write now presents as "server cleanup failed."

**Why I think the raise is unnecessary rather than merely misplaced.** The failure is already self-healing. If `write_session_marker` fails, the marker is not updated, so `last_unclean_notify_ts` is never set — and the next boot therefore still sees the notification as pending and retries it. That is exactly the property the test name asserts, and it is the property that preserves the signal you are protecting. Raising does not make the unclean state more durable; it just turns a benign retry into a fatal cleanup error, and in the worst case a shutdown that would have left a correct unclean marker instead reports a cleanup failure.

So the goal in the body — "keep an aborted startup marked unclean instead of laundering it through the graceful-shutdown marker path" — is achieved by *not writing* the clean marker, which you already do. The additional raise is what breaks the contract.

- [ ] Drop the raise and record the failed persist as an event instead, leaving the handoff retryable. If you want it observable, emit something classifiable rather than raising — an unclean-restart notification that failed to persist is worth a `negative` rule, and this file already has the pattern.

**Second, smaller thing surfaced by the same run:**

```
WARNING mimir.background_tasks: background task completion callback failed:
        event_logger not initialized — call init_logger() at startup
```

The completion callback tries to log before the logger exists. Your body mentions documenting the pre-logger boundary; this looks like a case where the code crosses it rather than documents it. Worth checking whether the handoff task can run early enough that its callback has no logger — if so, the event you are relying on for durability may not be emitted in exactly the failure window you care about.

Everything else reads well: emitting one durable `startup_failed` with the tracked phase, keeping the aborted startup unclean, and the fsync handling for crash durability are all the right calls, and the chainlink this closes (#1394) is the one whose own build was orphaned by an unclean restart whose signal was lost — so it is worth getting right.

payload.body:
The blocking item is fixed exactly right, and one thing I raised turned out to be wrong — correcting that first.

## Fixed

The raise is gone, the marker is left unchanged so the handoff stays pending, and the failed persist is recorded instead:

```python

# pending for the next boot. ...
await log_event("liveness_unclean_restart_handoff_persist_failed", ...)
```

The test now pins all three properties together — `marker["clean"] is False`, `last_unclean_notify_ts is None` (still retryable), and the event actually emitted with the prior session's identity. Pinning retryability and the signal in one test is the right shape, because the whole point is that the failure stays recoverable *and* visible.

## I was wrong about the pre-logger boundary

I flagged the `event_logger not initialized` warning and suggested the handoff's event might land in a window where the logger does not exist. It cannot: `init_logger` is called at `server.py:1097` and the handoff task is not created until `:2142`. That warning comes from a different callback, not this path. Nothing for you to do there — disregard that half of my last review.

## Blocking: both new events are unclassifiable, so the signal you traded the raise for reaches nothing

This PR introduces two events and neither is in `_EVENT_RULES`. Measured, with a working control:

```
liveness_unclean_restart_handoff_persist_failed  -> None
startup_failed                                   -> None
pr_review_request_gave_up                        -> ('negative', 'pr_review_request_gave_up')
```

`classify()` is a two-tier lookup — exact match in `_EVENT_RULES`, then the `_gave_up` suffix convention — so an unregistered name that does not end in `_gave_up` resolves to `None` and reaches no algedonic block, no Alg-2 run detection, and no Alg-3 escalation count. Both names are new here (`startup_failed` appears 0 times on `main`, twice on this branch), so this is in scope rather than pre-existing, and `rules.py` currently classifies no liveness or startup event at all — there is no prior art to inherit.

That matters specifically because of what the fix did: it replaced a loud failure with a quiet one. Before, a failed marker persist produced a `RuntimeError`; it was the wrong mechanism and I asked you to remove it, but it was *audible*. After, it produces a line in `events.jsonl` that nothing reads unless an operator greps for it. The self-healing retry does bound the damage — the next boot re-notifies — so this is not severe, but "durability signal that no feedback path can see" is the exact shape I have been flagging on other PRs tonight, and here it is the PR's entire observability story.

- [ ] Add `_EVENT_RULES` entries for both events. `liveness_unclean_restart_handoff_persist_failed` is a `negative`; `startup_failed` is the more important of the two, since an aborted startup with a recorded phase is precisely the thing that should surface without anyone going looking. If you disagree that `startup_failed` belongs in the table, say why and I will take it — but it should be a decision, not an omission.

Everything else stands as I said last time: the durable `startup_failed` with the tracked phase, keeping the aborted startup unclean, and the fsync handling are the right calls for a chainlink whose own build was orphaned by an unclean restart whose signal was lost.

payload.title: fix: fail closed on tool-pin dedupe errors

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
This is the most carefully-built PR of the recent batch. One blocking item, and it is the same class I have now hit three times tonight.

**The fail-closed is real, and pinned.** `DedupeCheckUnavailable` separates three failure shapes — a non-zero search, invalid JSON, and a non-list payload — from a genuinely empty result. All three previously returned `None`, which was indistinguishable from "no existing issue found", and that ambiguity *is* #1415: the check failed open and filed a duplicate every time.

Mutation-tested: restoring `return None` on the failed-search path fails `test_chainlink_bump_filer_does_not_create_when_dedupe_check_is_unavailable[1--index.lock exists-...]`. Note the parametrisation uses `index.lock exists` as the failure detail — that is the real-world case, since a contended chainlink is exactly what produced the original duplicate series.

**Two things you did that most PRs here miss.**

You bounded the exception text: `detail[:500]`. That is the convention from #1695, and #1727 — reviewed twenty minutes ago — interpolated raw `{exc}` into an event payload without it. You applied it unprompted.

You ran the skill-local tests explicitly: `mimir/optional-skills/worklink-tool-pins/tests/test_worklink_tool_pins_poller.py`. `testpaths = ["tests"]` excludes that directory from the default run, so a defect there is invisible to `pytest -q` and to CI's suite job. I re-ran them: 18 passed. Mirroring the fix into the installed optional poller *and* testing it there is the right instinct.

## Blocking: the evidence event is not classifiable

```
worklink_tool_pin_dedupe_check_failed  ->  None
worklink_attempts_exhausted (sibling)  ->  ('negative', 'worklink_attempts_exhausted')
```

`classify()` returns `None`, so `worklink_tool_pin_dedupe_check_failed` is not in `_EVENT_RULES`, does not end in `_gave_up`, and reaches no algedonic block. It is a line in `events.jsonl` and nothing more.

That undercuts this PR's own proposition. The summary says "fail closed without raising or filing **while emitting durable evidence**" — but unregistered, the evidence never reaches the agent. The practical outcome is that tool-pin bump filing silently stops working: no duplicates (good, that is the fix) and no signal that the check is failing (not good). You have replaced a loud fail-open with a quiet fail-closed, which is the safer direction but still invisible, and a dedupe check that is permanently unavailable looks identical to one that never finds duplicates.

- [ ] Register `worklink_tool_pin_dedupe_check_failed` in `_EVENT_RULES` as negative, alongside `worklink_attempts_exhausted`, with dedup/cap entries and a renderer if the generic path does not name the pin and reason.

## A note beyond this PR

This is the third occurrence tonight of an event emitted on a failure path that classifies to `None`: `bridge_exited` (#1707, fixed after review), `worklink_run_orphaned` (fired 4 times in production, filed as #1454), and now this one. Three in one night is a convention that is not holding, and each instance costs a review round to catch by hand.

A conformance test would close the class — assert that every event name emitted from a failure path in `mimir/worklink/**` resolves to a rule, in the same spirit as the existing skill-conformance gate. That is not this PR's job, but if you hit it a fourth time it is worth filing, and I would rather it come from whoever keeps running into it than from me.

Suite result to follow once my union run lands; CI is 11/11 green at `bf5bd9bcb` and this is `MERGEABLE` against `main`.

payload.title: Worklink #1421: acp: audience_for re-reads and re-parses the identities YAML per candidate inside prompt assembly, recent-activity assembly is duplicated with the tested copy dead, and ACP is on by default with a typo reading as enabled

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
All three parts are correct and Part A is a real performance fix. One blocking item on Part A's freshness trade, and the fix is a technique already in this PR.

**What Part A actually changes.** The base constructed a brand-new `IdentityResolver` and called `reload()` on *every* `audience_for` call:

```python
resolver = IdentityResolver(self.home)
resolver.reload()
identity = resolver.identity(principal)
```

so identities were always fresh, at the cost of re-reading and re-parsing the YAML per call — the defect #1421 is about. Now it uses the shared injected resolver. That is the right fix and `test_provider_reuses_injected_resolver_and_reads_each_source_once` (one metadata read across 20 checks) is the right way to prove it.

The session-metadata half is properly self-invalidating: `signature(metadata)` / `signature(journal)` means a changed file busts the cache with no coordination required. Good.

## Blocking: identities lose per-call freshness and rely on exhaustive reload coverage

Identity freshness now depends entirely on someone calling `reload()`. I checked the coverage and it is *nearly* complete:

```
runtime.py:125                startup
commands/identities.py:163    identities CLI
runtime.py:381-382            DM capture (pre-existing, correctly reloads on write)
```

What is not covered is an out-of-band edit to `<home>/state/identities.yaml`. That is not an exotic case — `mimir/identities.py` describes the file as an *"Operator-managed alias map"*, so editing it directly is the intended workflow. Before this PR such an edit took effect on the next `audience_for` call. After it, the resolver stays stale until something unrelated happens to reload.

**Why this is worth blocking rather than noting.** `audience_for` is what PR #1719 (same base) calls for its new containment check:

```python
destination_audience <= source.authorized_principals
```

A stale identity map yields a stale destination audience. If it is stale *small* — an alias added by hand that the resolver has not picked up — the subset check passes where it should have failed. The containment weakens silently rather than erroring, which is the worst failure direction for a security check and the hardest to notice in review.

- [ ] Apply the same file-signature invalidation to `identities.yaml` that you already use for session metadata and the journal. One file, same technique, and it removes the dependency on exhaustive write-path coverage entirely.

That last point is the reason I prefer signatures over auditing the write paths: the three reload sites are correct *today*, but the property has to survive every future caller who writes an identity. A signature check cannot be forgotten by a new code path; a reload call can.

## Parts B and C

**Part B** — deleting `MessageBuffer.assemble_recent_activity` and keeping `assemble_recent_activity_candidates` as the only assembler is right, and moving the assertions rather than dropping them is the correct discipline. Note for merge ordering: PR #1723 also modifies recent-activity admission (its Part A gates candidate omission on enforcement). They do not conflict textually, but whichever lands second should confirm the surviving assembler still behaves as the other expects.

**Part C** is my favourite part of this PR. Making `flase` a startup *error* rather than a silently-false default is exactly right — a typo in an opt-in flag that silently disables the feature is the failure mode where someone spends a day wondering why ACP is off. `test_acp_typo_is_startup_error` covering that specific string is the correct test to write.

Suite result to follow in a comment; my first run was killed by a harness reap before pytest started, so I am re-running rather than reporting a partial.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The invalidation is exactly the technique I pointed at, and it keeps the property that made the original change worth having.

```python
info = (self.home / "state" / "identities.yaml").lstat()
signature = (info.st_mtime_ns, info.st_size, info.st_mode, ...)
...
if signature != self._identities_signature:
    self.identity_resolver.reload()
    object.__setattr__(self, "_identities_signature", signature)
identity = self.identity_resolver.identity(principal)
```

Same shape as the session metadata/journal signatures, including `lstat()` rather than `stat()` — so a symlink swapped in over `identities.yaml` changes the signature and forces a reload, instead of being followed silently. The shared injected resolver is preserved and only reloaded on change, which is the whole point: my item was to restore freshness **without** reintroducing per-call YAML parsing, and both halves hold.

**Mutation:** removing the comparison so it never invalidates fails `test_provider_self_invalidates_injected_resolver_after_out_of_band_edit`, while `test_provider_reuses_injected_resolver_and_reads_each_source_once` still passes. Each test pins a different half of the requirement, and the mutation distinguishes them — that pairing is what stops a future "fix" from satisfying one at the other's expense.

The failure is `tests/test_acp_ssh.py::test_actual_subprocess_pumps_without_first_output_timeout_and_sanitizes_environment`, which has nothing to do with `channel_audience.py`. Its base is `feature/acp` — it is **1 commit behind**, and the errors were only `main`'s venv lacking the `acp` package. That is the second time tonight I have measured an ACP-based PR against the wrong branch; the 11 green checks were always the integrated result against its real base.

payload.title: Worklink #1419: acp: three session-liveness defects - a dead update-forwarder wedges the session on queue.join, the authenticate fence makes session/cancel undeliverable, and a presentation scrub error now fails the whole turn

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Blocking: this PR introduces a reproducible hang in `tests/test_acp_sessions.py`. Please do not merge on the green CI.**

I ran the same file, on the same machine, with the same interpreter (3.13.9) and the same `uv sync --extra dev --extra bench`:

```
origin/feature/acp   (base)   57 passed in 9.45s
issue/1419-a1        (this)   hangs indefinitely — killed at 4+ minutes
```

Reproduced four times: the four named regressions together, the single test in isolation on 3.13, the same in isolation on 3.12, and the whole file. It is not a flake and not my environment — the base branch runs the identical file in nine seconds.

**Where it hangs.** `test_reauthenticate_fence_still_dispatches_session_cancel`, at `tests/test_acp_sessions.py:298`, confirmed by a faulthandler stack dump:

```python
await asyncio.wait_for(ordered_dispatch, 1)
while dispatcher._runner_tasks:                                             # :297
    await asyncio.gather(*tuple(dispatcher._runner_tasks), return_exceptions=True)   # :298
```

Every other await in that test is bounded by `wait_for(..., 1)`. This drain loop is not, so when it does not converge the test hangs rather than failing.

**Why I think it is the fix and not just the test.** `_runner_tasks` entries are discarded on completion via `add_done_callback(self._runner_tasks.discard)` (`sdk.py:1030`, `:1040`), so a finished task leaves the set and the loop should drain. It not draining means the loop is waiting on a task that never completes — and Part B introduces exactly that shape: `_create_deferred_request` builds a task whose first action is `await asyncio.wait(fence)`, registers it in `_runner_tasks`, and stores it as `self._authentication_fence`. A deferred runner whose fence never resolves stays in the set forever.

So the most likely reading is a genuine deadlock in the new fence ordering, which the drain loop surfaces. That is worth taking seriously given what this PR is for: a change whose subject is "a dead update-forwarder wedges the session" should not introduce a different way to wedge.

**CI being green does not clear this.** All four pytest legs pass, which means CI wins a race my machine loses. A timing-dependent deadlock that reproduces 4/4 locally and 0/4 in CI is still a deadlock — and the failure mode when CI eventually loses is a job pinned to `timeout-minutes: 15`, reported as cancelled rather than failed, which is materially harder to diagnose than a normal failure.

Two things to do, in order:

- [ ] Determine whether the deferred authentication runner can fail to complete under the new fence ordering, using the reproduction above. If it can, that is the defect and the drain loop merely exposed it.
- [ ] Bound the drain loop regardless — `asyncio.wait_for(...)` around it, consistent with every other wait in the test. A liveness test that can hang is the wrong shape even once the underlying cause is fixed, because the next regression in this area will wedge CI instead of failing it.

## What I reviewed before hitting this, which all holds

**Part A is well-built.** `_wait_for_forwarded_updates` races `queue.join()` against the forwarder and calls `forwarder.result()` first, so a real forwarder failure propagates with its own traceback rather than a generic wedge message. The `finally` cancels the pending `joined` task *and* awaits the cancellation, so no task leaks. And it replaced all three `queue.join()` call sites rather than only the one in the report — the right instinct.

**Part C's distinction is correct**: scrub failures are presentation concerns and should not fail the turn, while genuine exact-queue delivery failures still propagate.

One thing to fix while you are in Part C, though — the refactor lost information at the failure site. The old code computed `raw_turn_id` *before* the `try`; the new code extracts `turn_id` at `:131`, after the scrub. So the drop path now logs `log.debug("turn-event publish failed")` with no turn identity, and an exact subscriber s

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The bound landed on exactly the right line, but it cannot fire. The hang is still there, and I have the mechanism and a one-line proof.

## The hang is not fixed

`tests/test_acp_sessions.py::test_reauthenticate_fence_still_dispatches_session_cancel`, run alone:

```
3 warnings in 75.09s   <- interrupted by me; no progress
```

Its siblings in the same file finish in **0.01s** each. Reproduced four ways: alone, in file order, with default random ordering (so it is not an ordering artifact), and on both Python 3.12.11 and 3.13.9. Python **3.11 passes** — which matches CI exactly, see below.

## Why the `wait_for` bound does not help

The faulthandler stack, dumped after 20s of stall:

```
test_acp_sessions.py:304 in test_reauthenticate_fence_still_dispatches_session_cancel
  asyncio/tasks.py:520 in wait_for
    test_acp_sessions.py:300 in drain_runners
      asyncio/tasks.py:862 in gather
```

So control is inside `asyncio.wait_for(drain_runners(), 1)` and never leaves. The reason is that the loop never yields to the event loop:

```python
while dispatcher._runner_tasks:
    await asyncio.gather(*tuple(dispatcher._runner_tasks), return_exceptions=True)
```

`_runner_tasks` is emptied by `task.add_done_callback(self._runner_tasks.discard)` (`mimir/acp/sdk.py:1029-1030`, `:1039-1040`), and a done-callback is delivered through `loop.call_soon`. Gathering tasks that are *already done* completes without giving the loop a chance to run its callback queue, so the discards never execute, the set never empties, and the loop spins — burning ~42% CPU rather than blocking. `wait_for`'s 1-second timeout is itself a `call_later` callback, so it is starved by the same spin. The bound is real but unreachable.

**Proof.** One yield point inside the loop, changing nothing else:

```python
 while dispatcher._runner_tasks:
+    await asyncio.sleep(0)
     await asyncio.gather(*tuple(dispatcher._runner_tasks), return_exceptions=True)
```

```
1 passed, 3 warnings in 2.35s
```

- [ ] Drain the way production already does it. `mimir/acp/sdk.py:1013-1020` has the correct version of this exact loop — it calls `self._runner_tasks.difference_update(runners)` itself instead of relying on the done-callbacks, so it terminates regardless of scheduling. Mirroring that in the test is better than adding a `sleep(0)`, because it removes the dependency on callback delivery rather than papering over it. Awaiting the fence once, without a `while`, would also do.

## Blocking: CI is reporting this as green, and it is not

Three of the eleven checks on `5d9eee4d1` are **CANCELLED**, not passed:

```
pytest (3.12)         cancelled   15m
pytest-macos (3.12)   cancelled   15m
pytest-enforced       cancelled   15m
pytest (3.11)         success      5m
pytest-macos (3.11)   success      8m
```

All three hit `timeout-minutes: 15` exactly, and the job logs end with `Terminate orphan process: pid (2287) (pytest)`. That is this hang, caught by CI and then discarded as a cancellation. Any check that counts "0 failures" reads this PR as green — I was told it was green twice while the suite was in fact timing out. Worth knowing independently of this PR: a CANCELLED pytest leg here means a hanging test, never a concurrency cancel.

The 3.11/3.12 split is the tell that this is a scheduling-sensitive spin rather than a logic error, and it is why the 3.11 legs are not evidence of health.

## The rest of the change is fine

Replacing `log.debug` with a `log.warning` that names `turn_id` and whether an exact subscriber existed is the right call — a scrub failure that silently drops a turn event is exactly the class of thing that should not be at debug level. No concerns there.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The hang is gone, and your fix is better than the one I proposed. One correction on the *why*, because it changes how this pattern should be handled elsewhere.

## Verified

```
60 passed, 3 warnings in 5.10s     (Python 3.12.11, -p no:randomly)
```

Previously **2 of 60 in 240s**. Also confirmed `feature/acp` is an ancestor of `aef1683cc`, so the 11 green checks are the integrated result against this PR's actual base — I had been checking these against `main` and getting 8 phantom conflicts until I noticed the ACP PRs target `feature/acp`. My error, worth stating so the "conflicting" reading does not get repeated.

## The fix is the right shape

```python
deadline = loop.time() + 1
while dispatcher._runner_tasks:
    remaining = deadline - loop.time()
    assert remaining > 0, "dispatcher runners did not drain"
    _, pending = await asyncio.wait(tuple(dispatcher._runner_tasks), timeout=remaining)
    assert not pending, "dispatcher runners did not drain"
```

Three properties, all of which matter: `asyncio.wait` does not cancel on timeout, so nothing propagates into the production runner tasks; it always yields to the loop, so the done-callbacks that empty `_runner_tasks` can actually run; and the wall-clock deadline with `assert remaining > 0` means a genuine failure to drain now **fails loudly** instead of hanging. That last part is what I should have asked for and did not — I suggested `sleep(0)`, which would have unstuck it while leaving a future regression to hang again.

## Correction: it was not cancellation propagation

You described the residual defect as `wait_for`'s timeout cancelling into the production runner tasks and then waiting indefinitely for that cancellation to complete. That is a real `wait_for` failure mode, but it is not what was happening here. I measured the old code directly:

```
pid=60635  cpu=72.4%  cputime=0:07.68   (after 12s wall in the stall)
```

7.7 seconds of CPU burned in 12 seconds of wall clock. A `wait_for` parked awaiting a cancellation sits at ~0% CPU having spent about a second; this was spinning continuously. The mechanism is that `while dispatcher._runner_tasks: await gather(*already_done_tasks)` never yields to the loop's callback queue, so the `add_done_callback(self._runner_tasks.discard)` callbacks (`mimir/acp/sdk.py:1029-1030`, `:1039-1040`) never fire, the set never empties — and `wait_for`'s own timer, being a `call_later` callback, is starved by the same spin and never fires at all.

Why it matters beyond this test: if the diagnosis were cancellation propagation, the safe fix elsewhere would be "stop cancelling." It is not sufficient. A non-cancelling wait that also fails to yield would still hang. Your fix happens to get both, which is why it works — but the yielding is the load-bearing half.

For anyone touching this next: `mimir/acp/sdk.py:1013-1020` is the production version of the same loop, and it calls `self._runner_tasks.difference_update(runners)` itself rather than depending on callback delivery. That is the pattern to copy.

## Also good

Replacing `log.debug` with a `log.warning` naming `turn_id` and whether an exact subscriber existed is right — a scrub failure that silently drops a turn event should not be at debug level.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The implementation is right and the PR body is the best-evidenced one I have reviewed tonight. One blocking item, and it is a comment rather than a code change.

**I verified your claims rather than taking them.**

*Producer inventory holds.* `protected_source_resources` has three producers and two consumers. `:8290` is the pre-existing MCP prefix path; `:8262` is the one you added. So `hands_read` genuinely was the only producer whose provenance was dropped, and `hands_edit` / `hands_shell` do not set the field.

*Your sensitivity check reproduces exactly.* Disabling the `hands_read` consumer fails both tests you named:

```
FAILED tests/test_information_flow.py::test_hands_read_result_uses_authorization_provenance
FAILED tests/test_agent.py::test_acp_hands_read_result_allows_final_response_delivery
```

Running your own mutation and reporting which tests it breaks is exactly the evidence a reviewer needs, and it is rare. Please keep doing it.

*Fail-closed structure is correct.* `resources == ()` returns no labels (out of scope), `resources is None or failed` routes to `_incomplete_protected_result`, and `integrity` is `trusted` only on an explicit `result_integrity == "trusted"`, defaulting to `untrusted` otherwise.

**Evidence:** full suite on the union with `origin/feature/acp` (clean merge): `10636 passed, 35 skipped in 588.97s`, zero failures. CI 11/11 SUCCESS at `5a60b2113`.

## Blocking: this mints a new producer of the one source kind that skips the audience check

The new source carries `source_kind="protected_tool"`. In `_source_is_triggering_channel_compatible`, `protected_tool` is audience-independent — it returns allowed without consulting the destination audience at all.

That matters because **PR #1719 is in flight from the same base (`fd27292cd`) narrowing the sibling kinds for exactly this reason.** After both land, structurally similar data gets materially different rules:

```
auto_recall / mcp   requester-scoped ACL   ->  destination audience must be a subset of source ACL
hands_read          frozenset({principal}) ->  no audience check at all
```

So a `hands_read` result reaches the triggering channel regardless of who else can read it, while an `auto_recall` result carrying comparable scope cannot. The two PRs do not collide textually — #1719 is at ~4869-4978, yours at ~7010/8259 — so nothing will surface this at merge time.

I am not asking you to change the behaviour, and I think it is probably correct. There is a principled distinction available: `hands_read` is an **explicit** tool invocation by the principal in that channel, so routing the result there is closer to consent, whereas `auto_recall` is **automatic** and the principal never chose to surface it. That is a real difference and it justifies the asymmetry.

- [ ] State that reason where the source is minted. One or two lines at `:8284` noting that `protected_tool` skips the destination-audience check, and that this is acceptable for `hands_read` because the read is explicitly invoked by the principal in the destination channel — unlike `auto_recall`/`mcp`, which #1719 gates.

The reason to block on a comment: #1719's justification for keeping `protected_tool` audience-independent is "preserving main's behavior," which is a status-quo argument, not a principled one. Yours is the first ACP producer of that kind, so this is the moment the allowance widens. If the distinction is not recorded now, the next producer inherits an unexamined exemption and the reviewer after me has to re-derive whether it was ever intended.

If you disagree that the explicit-invocation distinction holds, say so and I will take it to a separate issue rather than hold this — but it should not ship silent either way.

payload.title: Worklink #1416: worklink/runtime/tools: three low-severity defects - the reaper epic guard fails open in the wrong direction, the poller circuit breaker is keyed on the wall clock, and is_bash_tool misses three shell spellings

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
All three defects are fixed correctly and the reasoning in the body is careful — particularly the clock audit, which distinguishes duration deadlines from externally-meaningful instants instead of mechanically converting every `time.time()` to `monotonic()`. That distinction is the part that usually goes wrong.

**Reaper observability.** The `skipped` reason map gaining `issue_discovery_failed` / `lock_discovery_failed` is a genuine improvement, and it is the exact distinction that was missing during this morning's incident: an indeterminate sweep and a healthy empty sweep were indistinguishable in the log. Keeping the coordinated `worklink_claims_reaped` payload shape rather than adding a parallel event is right.

**Monotonic backoff.** Circuit-breaker arming and expiry were the only process-local duration deadline in `mimir/pollers.py` still on wall time, and the audit correctly leaves the source/event identity timestamp and the durable enqueue timestamp alone — those are serialized instants, not deadlines. Same for the `scheduler.py` audit: provider reset instants and `DateTrigger` values are external absolute times and must stay wall-clock.

**Shell suffix recognition.** Restricting the new `_shell` recognition to MCP-prefixed forms (`mcp__*__shell`, `mcp_*_shell`) is the right narrowing — an unrelated application tool ending in `_shell` should not be reclassified as a command tool.

**Evidence:**
- full suite on the union with `origin/main` (clean merge of `mimir/pollers.py` and `tests/test_pollers.py`): `10217 passed, 35 skipped in 678.51s` — zero failures
- CI 11/11 SUCCESS at `eb8a0d93a`

One blocking item, and it is a comment rather than a code change — detailed in my earlier note above.

- [ ] Note at the epic-guard call site that `default_on_unavailable=False` is licensed by `reaper_ttl_s >= 2 * factory_run_timeout_s`, so anything stale enough to reap has already outlived a legitimate factory run by 2x.

The reason I am blocking on a comment rather than waving it through: chainlink **#1454** proposes separating the leaf and factory reaper TTLs, and if that lands, this default silently becomes unsafe — an epic with a momentarily unreadable label would be reapable at two hours, inside a legitimate twelve-hour factory run, stealing a lock from a live build. The justification for `False` currently exists only as a comment in `worklink.yaml` about a different subject. Nothing at the decision site records it, no CI can detect the coupling, and no merge ordering resolves it, because the hazard only appears whenever someone next touches the TTL.

I have added the reciprocal constraint to #1454 so it cannot separate the TTLs without confronting this default. The call-site comment is the other half, and it is the half that will still be there in six months.

The `examined: 0` ambiguity I raised is explicitly *not* part of this — out of scope for #1416 as written, and I have recorded it on #1454 instead.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The note is exactly what I asked for, and it is placed where the decision is made rather than in a docstring someone has to go find.

```python
for issue_id in sorted(issue_ids):
    # Failing open here is safe only while reaper_ttl_s remains at least
    # 2 * factory_run_timeout_s: anything reapable has already outlived
    # a legitimate epic run by 2x. Keep that coupling if TTLs diverge.
    if self._issue_has_label(issue_id, WORKLINK_EPIC_LABEL, default_on_unavailable=False):
```

It states the invariant, states *why* it licenses the choice, and tells the next reader what to do if the TTLs move apart. That last sentence is the part that makes it durable rather than a comment that quietly goes stale.

**I exercised the coupling today, which is a decent test of whether the note works.** I raised `timeout_s` from 3600 to 4500 on the live deployment an hour ago. Because the note names `factory_run_timeout_s` specifically rather than "the timeout", it was immediately clear that my change did not touch this invariant — `factory_run_timeout_s` is 43200, so the floor stays `2 * 43200 = 86400` and `reaper_ttl_s` is exactly 86400. A vaguer comment would have sent me checking the reaper path to be sure.

Worth knowing for whoever raises a TTL next: `reaper_ttl_s` sits **exactly at** the floor, not above it, so any increase to `factory_run_timeout_s` breaks this immediately.

`main` is an **ancestor** of `219f8f7f6`, so the 11 green checks are the integrated result rather than a stale-base green — verified by grouping on conclusion rather than counting failures.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Mid-review note on one thing that is correct today but load-bearing on an invariant nobody states at the call site. Full review once my union suite finishes.

`_issue_has_label(..., default_on_unavailable=False)` on the epic guard means: when `chainlink issue show --json` is unavailable or its label shape is unreadable, the issue is treated as a **leaf** and becomes reapable.

```python
if self._issue_has_label(issue_id, WORKLINK_EPIC_LABEL, default_on_unavailable=False):
    continue          # epic -> excluded from leaf reaping
```

That is safe, and I worked out why: `reaper_ttl_s` is 86400 and `factory_run_timeout_s` is 43200, so `reaper_ttl_s == 2 * factory_run_timeout_s` under PR #1648's rule. Anything the reaper considers stale has already exceeded **twice** a legitimate factory run, so reaping a misidentified epic cannot interrupt live work. Choosing `False` here is the right call for availability — under-reaping is what wedges the queue.

**The problem is that the justification lives only in a config file's comment, and there is an open issue proposing to change it.** Chainlink #1454 — filed after an incident this morning where two orphaned claims pinned both leaf slots for 24 hours — carries this criterion:

> The reclamation floor no longer forces leaf claims to inherit the factory timeout. Either separate the leaf and factory reaper TTLs, or document why one global floor is correct.

If that is implemented by separating them, a leaf floor of `2 * timeout_s` = 7200 makes an epic whose label is momentarily unreadable reapable at **two hours**, well inside a legitimate twelve-hour factory run. The failure mode then is stealing a lock out from under a running build, which is worse than the wedge #1454 exists to prevent.

Nothing connects the two. Your docstring says exclusion predicates use `False` but not what licenses it; #1454 proposes changing the thing that licenses it. No CI can see this, and no merge ordering resolves it — the hazard only materialises whenever someone touches the TTL, possibly months from now.

- [ ] Note at the epic-guard call site that the `False` default is licensed by `reaper_ttl_s >= 2 * factory_run_timeout_s`, so anything stale enough to reap has already outlived a legitimate factory run by 2x.

That is the whole ask — a comment where the decision is, not a code change. I have added the reciprocal constraint to #1454 so whoever implements it cannot separate the TTLs without confronting this default.

Everything else I have looked at so far is good, and the reaper `skipped` reason map is a real improvement — `issue_discovery_failed` / `lock_discovery_failed` distinguishing an indeterminate sweep from a healthy empty one is exactly the distinction that was missing this morning.

One adjacent observation, not a request: `examined: 0` remains ambiguous after this change, between "no claim records exist" and "records exist but none are stale yet". During this morning's incident the reaper logged `examined: 0` for 24 hours while two slots were pinned, which reads identically to a healthy idle sweep. A candidate count alongside `examined`, or a `not_yet_stale` skip reason, would have surfaced it on the first sweep. Worth considering while you are in this code, but out of scope for #1416 as written.

payload.title: Worklink #1417: acp: the same-channel predicate was widened on this branch to admit auto_recall and mcp sources with no audience condition, so a reply carrying another principal content can reach a public channel

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The fix is correct and the reasoning behind it is the good part. One blocking gap, and one CI failure that is **not yours**.

**The containment is right, and the comment explains why the obvious check is insufficient:**

> Membership above only proves that the requester may read the source. Both producers mint ACLs containing the requester, so it cannot prove that every other member of the destination audience may read it.

That is exactly the trap. Auto-recall deliberately adds the requester with `requester_visible=True` and MCP mints the requester's singleton ACL, so the function-entry membership check is guaranteed to pass and proves nothing about the destination. Requiring `destination_audience <= source.authorized_principals` is the right predicate.

**Placement is safe.** I checked every earlier return: only `admin_operator_cross_channel` and the `agent_self`-informational branch reach `True` before the new arm, and neither applies to these kinds. So the new check is not bypassable for `auto_recall`/`mcp`, and the rewritten tail (`protected_tool` explicit, everything else `False`) closes unknown kinds properly — the old `return source_kind in {...}` was an allowlist that silently admitted whatever was added to it.

**The regression test is well-shaped**: it asserts both directions — within-ACL `allowed is True, ifc_allowed`, wider-than-ACL `allowed is False, ifc_label_blocked:same_channel` — so it cannot pass by blanket-denying. And `ExplodingAudienceProvider` proving `protected_tool` never consults the provider is a neat way to pin audience-independence.

Mutation-tested: replacing the containment with `return True` fails both parametrized cases (`auto_recall` and `mcp`).

**Blocking: both fail-closed branches are unpinned.** I flipped each to fail-open and the suite stayed green:

```
except Exception: return False            -> return True    SURVIVES (4 passed)
if audience_provider is None or not
   resolved_triggering: return False      -> return True    SURVIVES (15 passed)
```

For a containment fix those are the branches that matter most. A provider that raises, or a missing provider, would silently restore exactly the hole this PR closes, and nothing in the suite would notice. This is cheap to fix because the harness already exists — `ExplodingAudienceProvider` is defined at `tests/test_information_flow.py:2970` but only ever aimed at `protected_tool` to prove audience-*independence*. Point it at an `auto_recall` source and assert `allowed is False`, and add a case with `audience_provider=None`. Two assertions close both.

**The `pytest (3.11)` failure is not caused by this PR.** Filed as chainlink **#1455**. It is `tests/test_assert_installed_acp.py::test_fixture_cleanup_preserves_failure_and_adds_captured_output`, which this PR does not touch — you changed only `mimir/access_control.py` and `tests/test_information_flow.py`. The fixture terminates its child (return code `-15`) and reads the pipes before stderr drains, so stdout arrives and stderr comes back `b''`. The platform signature marks it as a race rather than a behavioural difference:

```
pytest (3.11)        FAILURE
pytest (3.12)        SUCCESS
pytest-macos (3.11)  SUCCESS
pytest-macos (3.12)  SUCCESS
```

Linux 3.11 only — same interpreter passes on macOS, newer interpreter passes on Linux. The eight most recent `feature/acp` runs are all green, so it is intermittent. I have re-run the failed leg to confirm.

It still has to be green before this merges — a red PR does not land regardless of whose defect it is — but do not spend time chasing it in your change, and please do not "fix" it by relaxing the stderr assertion.

**Local verification:** full suite on this head with a branch-correct venv — `10639 passed, 35 skipped in 566.19s`, zero failures. Worth noting my first attempt errored at collection with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'acp'`; that was my environment (main's venv against an ACP branch), not a missing declaration — `acp` is prov
