payload.title: Worklink #1404: observability: the GitHub-identity degradation latch is never reset after a recovery, so the second time coding is disabled there is no event and no operator alert

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The fix is the right one and the reset set is complete: the latch state in that
closure is exactly the four variables declared at `mimir/runtime.py:167-170`, and
of those, `next_identity_retry_at` correctly does *not* need clearing because the

`transient_failures` keeps the event's `attempts` accurate. The test now covers
both halves of the issue — a second `github_identity_degraded` event *and* a
second ops alert (`sent == ["ops", "ops"]`) — which is what "no event and no
operator alert" asked for.

One thing to change.

**The resets happen after an `await`, so a degradation that lands in that window
gets silently un-latched.**

```python
if recovered:
    from .event_logger import log_event
    recovery_attempts = transient_failures
    await log_event("github_identity_recovered", attempts=recovery_attempts)  # <-- suspension point
    degradation_recorded = False
    degradation_alert_scheduled = False
    transient_failures = 0
```

`await log_event(...)` is a suspension point. Another task can run there, and
`_latch_github_identity_degraded` (which sets `degradation_recorded = True` and
`transient_failures += 1` at `:186-189`) is not under `identity_retry_lock` — it
is a separate closure with no lock at all, so the lock held here does not exclude
it. A failure latched during that await is then cleared by the three assignments
below it.

Failure scenario: identity recovers, `log_event` yields (it does file IO), a
queued turn calls a forge tool in that window and hits a transient identity
failure, the latch sets `degradation_recorded = True` and
`transient_failures = 1`, then this block resets both to their clean values. The
system is now degraded while its state says it is not, and the failure count that
gates `GITHUB_IDENTITY_TRANSIENT_ALERT_ATTEMPTS` (`:206`) has lost a tick.

This fails in the safe direction — the *next* failure re-emits `degraded` because
`if not degradation_recorded` is true again, so the operator gets an alert late
rather than never — which is why I am flagging it rather than calling it severe.
But it is the same class of bug the issue is about (latch state not matching
reality), it is reachable, and the fix is to move the three assignments above the
`await` so the reset is atomic with the `recovered` determination:

```python
if recovered:
    from .event_logger import log_event
    recovery_attempts = transient_failures
    degradation_recorded = False
    degradation_alert_scheduled = False
    transient_failures = 0
    await log_event("github_identity_recovered", attempts=recovery_attempts)
```

Nothing between the check and the reset can then interleave. `recovery_attempts`
is already captured, so the event payload is unchanged.

Please also consider whether `_latch_github_identity_degraded` should take
`identity_retry_lock` — if it should, that is a bigger change and a separate
issue rather than this leaf's job; reordering here is enough to close the window
this PR introduces.

## Validated against live GitHub, not just the simulation

Ran both the current (live) poller and this branch's poller inside mimirbot
against the real repos, with `STATE_DIR` pointed at a temp dir seeded from a copy
of the live cursor, stdout captured to a file so nothing was delivered.
`_gh_api` only ever runs `gh api <endpoint> --paginate` with no `-X`, so a dry run
is read-only.

```
old (live)  89s  -> EXCEEDS the 60s cap, would be killed
new (this)  48s  -> completes
```

Note this exercises both configured repos (`GITHUB_REPOS` is
`jasoncarreira/mimir,jasoncarreira/feature-factory`), which my earlier
single-repo simulation understated — the real "before" is 89s, not 75s.

The emitted events are identical except for one item:

```
old: pr_opened 1705, pr_review 1704, pr_changes_requested_stale x16, pr_ci_failure 1683
new: pr_opened 1705, pr_review 1704, pr_changes_requested_stale x16, poller_pr_reconcile_truncated
```

All 16 `pr_changes_requested_stale` reminders are delivered — including one for
every PR currently stuck at CHANGES_REQUESTED. That is the pass ordering doing its
job. In production today the old poller emitted these same 19 events on each of
its 31 timed-out ticks and every one was discarded (#1438).

## Caveat found by this run: rotation latency on the squeezed passes

A second consecutive tick, resuming from the state the first one saved, emitted
only `poller_pr_reconcile_truncated` — the `pr_ci_failure` for #1683 that the old
poller reported was still not reconciled, because rotation had moved to a
different slice.

At 16 open PRs with a floor of 2/pass, a full rotation of `ci_failures` and
`mergeability` takes ~8 ticks — up to ~2 hours at the 15-minute cadence, against
15 minutes when the tick completes normally. So this is a latency regression on
those two passes, traded for the tick completing at all. Worth knowing:

- It is strictly better than the current state, where the tick is killed and
  *nothing* is delivered, ever.
- `changes_requested` is unaffected — it reconciles every PR.
- A separate, healthy `github-ci-watch` poller (23/23 ticks today) is a dedicated
  CI-failure path, so this is added latency on a partly redundant signal rather
  than a coverage hole. I have not verified the two paths cover exactly the same
  cases, so I am not claiming full redundancy.

I deliberately did not raise the floor to shrink this window. The total tick cost
is approximately `deadline + floor work`, where floor work is a fixed ~18 calls,
so the current tuning stays under the cap even if API latency doubles (measured
spread was 0.39–0.67s/call). Raising the floor trades that margin away, and a
timeout costs every event in the tick.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
You're right, and the objection holds exactly as stated. The 48s I measured was the
typical case at current latency, not a bound: the budget was only consulted between
PRs, every `_gh_api` kept its own 30s timeout, and the two-PR floor was an
unconditional exception to the deadline. A single slow call — or a paginated one,
since `--paginate` makes one logical call several requests — could carry the tick
past the SIGKILL and lose everything, which is #1433 again. My zero-deadline tests
used instant fakes and proved call-count truncation, not elapsed time. Fixed.

**A real hard stop.** `TickBudget` is now two-tier. The soft deadline (35s) still
stops discretionary reconciliation; a new hard deadline (`TICK_HARD_DEADLINE_SECONDS
= 50.0`) is the actual bound:

- `_gh_api` clamps its subprocess timeout to `budget.call_timeout()` —
  `max(GH_API_MIN_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, min(30, hard_remaining))`. No call can outlive
  the tick. The 2s floor is deliberate: a 0s timeout would fail every call
  instantly and read as a total API outage.
- The floor is now subordinate, per your last sentence. Past the hard deadline
  `_truncate_here` truncates at `reconciled == 0` — no minimum, because a guarantee
  that can still start a 30s call is not a bound.

**Your point exposed a second hole I had to close to answer it honestly.** I could
not prove a `main()`-level bound while `_check_pr_reviews` and
`_check_issue_comments` still walked every item unbounded — they run *before* the
three passes I had fixed, so the tick had no bound regardless. Both now hard-stop.

That was the thing I had deferred to #1439 on the grounds that truncating a
since-based pass drops events irrecoverably. The hard-truncation path is what makes
it safe: when `_hard_stop` fires, the tick sets `hard_truncated` and **does not
advance `last_checked`**, so the next tick re-scans the same window. Re-delivering a
nudge is recoverable; dropping a review is not — and today's SIGKILL already leaves
the watermark unadvanced, so this is strictly better than the status quo rather than
a new tradeoff.

The hold is deliberately narrow: `_truncate_here` truncation does **not** set it,
because the reconcile passes defer through their own dedupe cursor (a preserved
prior entry, or `collection_complete=False`). Freezing the watermark on every busy
tick would stop the since-window advancing at all — a slow-motion #1433. There's a
test pinning both directions.

**Tests.** `test_main_returns_within_the_tick_bound_when_every_call_is_slow` drives
the real pass sequence through `main()` with genuinely slow calls and scaled
deadlines (0.3s soft / 0.5s hard). `time.monotonic` is not patched — the timing path
under test is the real one. Thresholds are chosen so the unbounded path *cannot*
squeeze under them: `_check_pr_reviews` alone walks 150 PRs at 0.01s/call, so without
the hard stop the tick spends >=1.5s and makes >=150 calls.

called out.** I mutation-tested all four new guards, and disabling `_hard_stop`
initially still passed at 1.89s against a 2.0s threshold. I retuned it until the

| watermark advances when hard-truncated | watermark test fails |

`_gh_api` reads it, so one leaked by a raising test would silently shorten timeouts
elsewhere.

of the live cursor, stdout captured so nothing is delivered):

**How it's bounded now.** `TickBudget.affords(seconds)` — a lookup only starts if
its worst case fits before the hard deadline:

version of this fix had a single trust denial in `_chec

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
All three confirmed. Two fixed here; the third is pre-existing and filed separately.

**1. The reservation rested on a false premise — you're right.**
`urllib.request.urlopen(timeout=...)` is a socket-operation timeout, and
`response.read()` sits inside the `with`, so a server trickling bytes keeps it
alive while each individual read completes inside the window. Reserving the
nominal 10s/20s therefore bounded nothing.

Replaced with enforcement rather than reservation: `_wall_clock_deadline` imposes
a real total deadline via `setitimer`, clamped to the remaining tick budget. A
lookup cut off by it returns `None` — unresolved, not untrusted — and is **not
cached**, so the next tick retries instead of inheriting a verdict produced by a
timeout. The `AUTHOR_LOOKUP_WORST_CASE_SECONDS` /
`TRUST_LOOKUP_WORST_CASE_SECONDS` constants are gone; there is nothing left to
reserve.

The regression sleeps 5s against a 0.05s allowance — no socket timeout would stop
that, so it fails unless the deadline is genuinely enforced. Verified by mutation:
neutering `setitimer` makes it fail, and takes 25s doing so.

**2. Confirmed, and my first fix for it was wrong.**
You were right that a budget-refused `_gh_api` returning bare `None` lets a
since-gated pass advance `last_checked` over an uncollected window, and right that
`_check_pr_review_comments` is the sharp case — its own docstring calls it the bulk
of review feedback, and it had no budget plumbing at all.

I first marked truncation inside `_gh_api`. That was wrong and the live dry run
caught it: one refused *listing* call in the last reconcile pass set the flag and
froze the watermark on an ordinary 50s tick. The transport cannot know whether its
caller's window is since-gated. The check now lives in the four since-gated passes
(`_check_issues`, `_check_prs`, `_check_pr_review_comments`, `_check_pr_reviews`)
via `_refused_window`, and the two that lacked a budget now have one. There is a
test asserting the discriminating pair — since-gated refusal holds, reconcile
refusal does not, and the reconcile pass's prior state survives, which is what
makes that safe.

**3. Correct, and pre-existing — filed as chainlink #1441 rather than folded in.**
An admitted attestation that fails transiently still collapses to `False` in
`mimir/pollers.py::_github_author_is_trusted`, and `_check_pr_pushes` then
baselines the head:

```python
elif prev_sha != current_sha:
    if not trusted_author:
        new_heads[key] = current_sha
```

so the push is permanently consumed even after trust recovers. My tri-state covers
only lookups refused *before starting*. Fixing this properly needs an "unknown"
channel distinct from `False` in a helper whose contract other callers depend on —
the same cross-module coupling I backed out of earlier in this PR after it broke a
live dry run on version skew. #1441 carries the analysis, both persistence paths,
and the constraint that no path may treat an unresolved author as *trusted*.

**Live re-validation** at this head, both repos, temp `STATE_DIR` seeded from a copy
of the live cursor:

```
elapsed 49s, within the 60s cap
13 budget refusals — all in reconcile passes
watermark 2026-08-23T15:35:00Z -> 2026-08-23T20:08:41Z  (advanced)
```

```

uv run pytest -q mimir/optional-skills/github-poller/tests/ →   140 passed
```

I had to redo that suite: an earlier run was started on this branch and then had
the working tree changed under it when I switched branches, so its result covered

Worth stating plainly: this is the third round where the finding was real, and in
two of them the live dry run caught my *fix* being wrong after the tests were

2. **Transient trust failures remain retryable.** `_github_content_author() -> None` and unavailable collaborator/org attestations now propagate as unresolved rather than cached `False`. `_check_prs` holds its watermark, while `_check_pr_pushes` retains the prior head. payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1403: observability: per-entry pollers.json and scheduler.yaml rejections are Python-log-only, so a poller can run uncapped and scheduler entries vanish uncounted, and a malformed shell_commands block refuses forever with no event

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The observability threading is well done: `rejections` is plumbed through
consistently, every `load_jobs` / `load_jobs_from_text` caller was updated to the
new tuple return (I checked all of them — `admin_config`, `defaults_upgrade`, and
all six `scheduler.py` sites including the `asyncio.to_thread` ones), and
`poller_reload_invalid_entry` is emitted at the same points as the existing
`poller_reload_invalid_manifest` / `invalid_cron` events, which is the right
precedent to follow.

One blocking issue.

**Validating `shell_commands` inside the `try` silently drops the whole job, on
an environment-dependent check.**

`mimir/scheduler.py`, in `load_jobs_from_text`:

```python
job = SchedulerJob.from_yaml_entry(entry)
if job.shell_commands is not None:
    parse_declared_shell_commands(job.shell_commands, writable_roots=writable_roots)
...
except ValueError as exc:
    rejections.append({...})   # job is NOT appended to `out`
```

`parse_declared_shell_commands` (`mimir/access_control.py:1920`) raises
`ValueError` for conditions that depend on the *filesystem of whoever is
loading*, not on whether the YAML is well-formed:

- `path does not exist: {raw_path}`
- `path is not a regular file: {raw_path}`
- `path is not executable: {raw_path}`

and `_declaration_error` (`:1832`) returns a plain `ValueError`, so the new
`except ValueError` swallows all of them and the entry is dropped.

Failure scenario: a job declares `exec: gh` with an absolute `path` that exists
in the worklink image but not on the host checkout (or not yet, during an upgrade
window before the tool is installed — `scheduler.yaml` is loaded in all of these
places, including by `defaults_upgrade._merge_scheduler_defaults`). Before this
change the job loaded and its shell grant refused at use time — the observability
gap the chainlink is about. After it, the job is removed from the scheduler
entirely. If that job is `heartbeat`, the agent's main loop stops running.

This escalates the blast radius from "one declared command refuses" to "the job
never runs", which is a strictly worse outcome than the gap being closed, and the
PR body does not mention the behavior change at all — so I do not think it was
intended.

The chainlink asks for an *event*, not a stricter load. Suggested fix: emit the
rejection without dropping the job — or, if a malformed declaration really should
drop it, separate the two classes so that structural errors (`must be a list`,
`unknown keys`, `path is required`, non-absolute path) reject the entry while the
three filesystem-state checks emit and keep it, preserving the existing
refuse-at-use-time behavior.

Please also add a test that pins whichever semantics you choose, covering a job
whose declared `path` does not exist — the current tests only cover
`"shell_commands": {}` (wrong type), which is the structural case.

Everything else looks good to me.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The fix separates the two failure classes properly rather than just widening the `except`, which is the distinction the blocking item was about.

## The classification is the right mechanism

```python
class DeclaredShellCommandError(ValueError):
    def __init__(self, message: str, *, environment_dependent: bool = False) -> None:
```

Marking only the three host-state conditions — `path does not exist`, `path is not a regular file`, `path is not executable` — as `environment_dependent`, and leaving every genuine declaration error fatal, means a malformed `shell_commands` entry is still rejected at load while a binary that is simply absent on this host no longer silently deletes the whole job. Subclassing `ValueError` keeps the existing `except ValueError` outer handler working for everything else.

The consumer side re-raises rather than swallowing:

```python
except DeclaredShellCommandError as exc:
    if not exc.environment_dependent:
        raise
    rejections.append({...})
```

**Mutation:** removing the `if not exc.environment_dependent: raise` distinction reproduces the original defect exactly — the job is dropped and logged as `invalid scheduler job: shell_commands['worklink-image-only-cli']: path does not exist: ...` — and fails `test_load_jobs_reports_missing_shell_binary_but_keeps_job`. Baseline `1 passed`.

## Two things I checked because they would have been easy to get wrong

**The signature change reached every caller.** `load_jobs` / `load_jobs_from_text` return a tuple now where `main` returned a bare list, and iterating the tuple would have silently yielded two lists instead of jobs. Both call sites are updated: `defaults_upgrade.py:476-478` (`base_jobs, _ = ...` three times) and `admin_config.py:323` (`jobs, _rejections = ...`).

**A preserved job appears in both `out` and `rejections`, and that is deliberate.** I went looking for whether this makes `rejections` misleading, since the docstring says "accepted jobs and named rejections" and an entry is now both. `test_load_jobs_reports_missing_shell_binary_but_keeps_job` pins it explicitly — `[job.name for job in jobs] == ["heartbeat"]` *and* `len(rejections) == 1` — and the test name states the intent. That makes it a documented decision rather than an oversight, which is what I needed to see. Neither current consumer reads the second element, so nothing is misreported today; if a future consumer surfaces `rejections` to an operator, it will want to distinguish "dropped" from "loaded with a diagnostic", and the test name is the right place for that to be discovered.

## Suite

**Full suite on a trial-merge with current `main`** (union `22fa97ec`; `main` moved several times tonight, so this is not the tree your CI saw): **10226 passed, 35 skipped, 0 failed.** All 11 CI checks green, verified by grouping on conclusion rather than counting failures.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Separate from the blocking item above, and a question rather than a finding.

The new `poller_reload_invalid_entry` is not registered in `_EVENT_RULES`
(`mimir/feedback/rules.py`), so `_rule_for_event` returns `None` for it: no feedback
signal, no algedonic count, no escalation. It lands in `events.jsonl` only.

The reason I am raising it as a question is that the two siblings it is modelled on
disagree:

- `poller_reload_invalid_cron` — registered.
- `poller_reload_invalid_manifest` — not registered (pre-existing, not something
  this PR changed).

So emitting alongside `invalid_manifest` without a rule entry is consistent with one
precedent and not the other. Since the leaf is specifically about rejections being
"Python-log-only ... uncounted", it is worth being explicit about which of the two
you intended: if the goal is that an operator learns a poller entry was rejected,
`events.jsonl` alone is close to the state the leaf is complaining about. If the
intended consumer is the ops dashboard reading the event stream directly, then no
rule entry is correct and this is fine as written.

Either answer is defensible — I just do not want it decided by inheriting whichever
sibling was copied. If you do register it, note that `_EVENT_RULES` keys on event
type, so the rule kind is shared across every poller and the rendered text will not
name the offending poller unless the renderer reads the payload.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Merge-order warning, cross-referencing #1712.

#1712 (`Worklink #1409`, open) adds a new `load_jobs` caller that predates this
PR's signature change:

```python
# mimir/scheduler.py, _configured_heartbeat_job
jobs = await asyncio.to_thread(load_jobs, self._yaml_path)
return next((job for job in jobs if job.name == "heartbeat"), None)
```

Against this PR's `load_jobs` — which returns `(jobs, rejections)` — iterating that
yields the two lists and `job.name` raises
`AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'name'`.

This PR correctly updated every caller that existed when it was written; the
problem is only that #1712 introduces another one concurrently. Git will merge both
cleanly and both are green independently, so nothing in CI catches the combination.

It matters because that method is only reached from the quota-recovery path
(`_recheck_quota_pause` and `_fire_quota_recovery`), so the breakage would land
precisely when the agent is trying to resume after a pause.

Nothing to change here — whichever of the two merges second needs the one-line
adjustment. Raising it on both so the second merge is not a surprise.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Heads-up from #1712, which just merged as `9cd845fc1`.

To decouple merge ordering between the two PRs, #1712 made its `load_jobs` call site accept both shapes (`mimir/scheduler.py`, `_configured_heartbeat_job`):

```python
loaded = await asyncio.to_thread(load_jobs, self._yaml_path)
jobs = loaded[0] if isinstance(loaded, tuple) else loaded
```

That was correct while the ordering was unknown — it works against a plain-list `load_jobs` today and against your `(jobs, rejections)` tuple afterwards. **Now that #1712 has landed first, please drop the `isinstance` branch in this PR** and make the call site plainly tuple-aware:

```python
jobs, _rejections = await asyncio.to_thread(load_jobs, self._yaml_path)
```

Two reasons to do it here rather than leave it: this repo's convention is no back-compat shims on pre-release surfaces, and a shim whose reason for existing has passed is exactly the kind that never gets removed. It also currently hides a real type error — with the shim in place, a future caller passing the wrong shape degrades silently instead of failing.

There is a test pinning the shim, `test_configured_heartbeat_accepts_load_jobs_tuple_shape`. Once `load_jobs` unconditionally returns a tuple that test is asserting the only shape there is, so it should be simplified or dropped alongside the branch rather than left asserting a tautology.

Worth calling out that this path matters: `_configured_heartbeat_job` feeds `_fire_configured_heartbeat`, reached only from `_recheck_quota_pause` and `_fire_quota_recovery` — the quota-recovery path. Breaking it means the agent does not resume maintenance work after a quota pause, and it fails exactly when the system is already degraded.

payload.title: Worklink #1402: observability: the operator turns/events views fail open to an empty HTTP 200 on any IO error with no log and no event, so an unreadable log renders as nothing happened

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. Local suite 10123 passed / 0 failed on a trial-merge with current `main`; all 11 CI checks green.

**Meets every criterion, and the two new tests map onto them directly.** `test_log_read_failure_is_degraded_and_emits_once_per_path` covers both the degraded marker and the bounded-emission requirement in one assertion, and `test_empty_logs_are_healthy_empty_without_event` is the companion control that a genuinely empty log stays 200 with no marker and no event. That pairing is what makes the distinction meaningful rather than just present.

**Choosing degraded-200 over a non-200 is defensible and you stated it, which the criteria asked for.** An operator view that hard-fails on an unreadable log is worse than one that renders with a flag — the view is the diagnostic surface, so keeping it reachable matters more than HTTP purity here.

**Scoping per-request admin auditing out is right, and the reasoning is the good kind:** it is a security, privacy, retention, and polling-volume decision rather than a bug, and the issue excluded admin routes explicitly. Declaring that beats silently not doing it.

**Mutation:** reverting `mimir/live_events.py` and `mimir/web_ui.py` each fails both tests. `mimir/_jsonl_tail.py` gives a collection error rather than a failure, because the tests import the new shared-helper seam — dependency rather than verification, same evidentiary shape I have now seen three times today in these builds. Worth being aware of when reading a mutation result as proof.

**One thing I checked and am NOT blocking on, filed as #1437 instead.** `web_ui.py` gains 279 lines and no frontend file changes, so the operator views never consume `degraded: true` or the `state-degraded` SSE frame — `grep -rn degraded frontend/src` has no matches. That means the symptom in this issue's *title*, "an unreadable log renders as nothing happened," still holds for a human looking at the screen.

I nearly flagged that as incomplete. Re-reading #1402's acceptance criteria, they are deliberately about the **response** distinguishing degraded from empty, and you satisfied all of them — so blocking would have been me substituting the title for the commissioned scope. But the remaining half is real, and closing #1402 could easily read as "the empty-view problem is fixed" when only its API contract is. #1437 carries the measurement, states explicitly that it is not a defect here, and includes the skin-token requirement plus a three-state rendering test.

payload.title: Worklink #1401: observability: saga read-authorization telemetry is emitted only when enforcement is OFF, so enabling it makes the filtering layer silent, and destructive-mutation refusals emit nothing at all

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. Local suite 10124 passed / 0 failed on a trial-merge with current `main`; all 11 CI checks green.

**This is more consequential than its "observability" framing suggests.** Telemetry was emitted only while enforcement was OFF, so turning enforcement on would have made the read-filtering layer go dark — losing exactly the signal needed to validate the change at the moment it takes effect. That is a trap for the enablement work (#952), and the `mode: shadow|enforced` discriminator at `ownership.py:401` / `client.py:1133` is the right shape: one event stream with an explicit mode rather than two code paths that can drift.

**Converging destructive refusals on one `saga_mutation_refused` seam** with `status: refused` is also the right call — distinguishing a refusal from an admitted empty result without changing the exception contract is the part that would have been easy to get wrong by raising instead.

**The refusal audit in the body is the kind of thing that makes a review fast**, and I checked its load-bearing claim rather than accepting it: it asserts no other caller-facing authorization refusal in `mimir/saga/` returns a success-shaped empty result, and correctly separates the `forget_by_criteria` domain-without-owner guard as an internal fail-closed invariant behind the guarded `SagaStore.forget` seam. That distinction is right.

**Mutation, per production file:**

```
revert mimir/saga/client.py      -> 11 failed
revert mimir/saga/ownership.py   -> 15 failed
revert mimir/saga/vector_index.py -> 185 passed  (uncovered)
```

The third is a real gap worth naming: no test distinguishes the old inline emitter from the shared `_emit_saga_event`. It is a pure consolidation and the shared helper preserves the identical guarantee it replaces (`try: log_event_sync ... except Exception: # telemetry cannot affect SAGA results`), so I am not blocking on it — but a third of the production change is unverified, and if the shared seam's swallow behaviour ever diverges nothing here would catch it.

**Two things I checked because they looked alarming and were not.** The two-dot diff showed #1700's flock lines as *added*, implying `main` lacked them — stale local ref; empty after fetching. And it showed 133 lines being removed from `test_worklink_claims.py` and 62 from `test_worklink_reattach.py`, the files #1701 just touched — tree difference, not merge outcome. payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1400: observability: the worklink claim lifecycle is silent at all three layers - the TTL reaper skips without events, startup recovery drops orphans and suppresses its summary, and partial shutdown reports only what it released

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. Local suite 10119 passed / 0 failed on a trial-merge with current `main`; all 11 CI checks green.

**This one is directly useful to operating the system, not just to auditing it.** I spent much of today diagnosing worklink behaviour from `events.jsonl` and repeatedly could not distinguish a reaper that examined-and-skipped from one that never ran. `worklink_claim_reap_skipped` with a reason, alongside the `worklink_claims_reaped` rollup, is exactly the missing distinction. Same for `worklink_reattach_attempted` versus `worklink_reattach_dispatched` versus `worklink_reattach_dispatch_failed` — the startup path previously dropped orphans and suppressed its own summary, so a leaked claim was invisible from both ends.

**Covering all three layers in one change is the right call** rather than splitting it. The issue is that the lifecycle is silent, and a fix for one layer would still leave a claim untraceable across the handoffs between them — the reaper, startup recovery, and partial shutdown each need to say what they did for the sequence to be reconstructable.

**On the mutation evidence, one honest caveat.** Reverting `mimir/server.py` gives a clean behavioural failure (1 failed, 6 passed). Reverting `mimir/worklink/claims.py` gives a *collection error* rather than a failure, because the tests import the new `event_logger` seam that does not exist on `main` — so that half proves the tests depend on the new code without demonstrating they verify its behaviour. I read `test_part_a_reaper_reports_*` to settle it: it is parametrized across scenarios, injects `event_logger=lambda event, **payload: events.append(...)`, and asserts both the emitted event type and the reason. So the substance is fine and only the mutation's evidentiary form is weak. Flagging it because a collection error is easy to read as a passing mutation check when it is not one.

**Scoping the concurrency-cap payload out is the right call and I am glad it is stated.** The refusal still reports only active/cap, and a bounded sample of blocking lock ids is deferred. Declaring a known gap beats silently leaving it — and for what it is worth, that gap bit me today: a cap refusal that named the blocking locks would have shortened the claim diagnosis.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1399: observability: events appended by detached worklink subprocesses are silently discarded when the server trims events.jsonl, with no error, no counter and no way to know

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. This one matters beyond its own scope: I have spent today diagnosing from `events.jsonl` while detached worklink subprocesses appended to it and the server trimmed it, which is exactly the loss window this closes. Some of what I could not find earlier may simply never have been written.

**The sibling-lock rationale is the subtle part and it is right.**

> A sibling lock remains stable while events.jsonl is atomically replaced. Locking the events file itself would protect the old inode, not the new path, after trim's rename.

Locking the events file directly is the obvious implementation and it would have produced a lock that appears to work while protecting nothing after the first trim.

**I verified `flock` actually works on this mount rather than assuming it.** `/mimir-home` is a virtiofs bind mount from the macOS host, and I had just established that it silently ignores guest file ownership — so I was not willing to take lock semantics on trust either. Tested with a btrfs control:

```
virtiofs (/mimir-home):        exclusive (lock honoured)
btrfs (/workspace) [control]:  exclusive (lock honoured)
```

Both honour it. Worth stating because if virtiofs had ignored `flock` the way it ignores mode bits, this fix would have been inert on the live deployment and looked correct in review.

**The degradation choice is right.** Capping the wait at 1s and continuing best-effort rather than blocking means a stuck holder cannot wedge an agent turn, and both degraded paths warn, so the loss of serialization is observable rather than silent — which is the actual complaint in the issue title.

**I checked the `turns.jsonl` exclusion rather than accepting it.** `TurnLogger(` appears only in `mimir/runtime.py`, nothing in the worklink path or `mimir/commands/worklink.py`, so detached processes genuinely lack the cross-process writer topology. That is a reasoned exclusion, not an omission.

**One concern I raised and then withdrew:** skipping trim on lock contention could in principle let `events.jsonl` grow unbounded, and this deployment has a 6GB-RSS incident from untruncated log payloads in its history. It does not hold — `flock` is released by the kernel on process death, so a crashed holder cannot wedge it, and a 1s bounded wait with 10ms polls means a timeout implies a live stuck process, which is a larger problem than file size.

**Mutation:** reverting `mimir/event_logger.py` fails both `test_process_append_survives_trim_rename_window` and `test_process_lock_timeout_degrades_to_append`.

Full suite on a trial-merge with current `main`: **10112 passed, 35 skipped, 0 failed**. All 11 CI checks pass.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1398: observability: a liveness-beat write failure is recorded only at log.debug, so the shipped watchdog SIGKILLs a healthy agent with nothing in events.jsonl on either side of the kill

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. This is also the first PR produced after the build pipeline was restored — dispatched at 14:50 on the reverted manifest, built for ~14 minutes, against seven consecutive 11-second EACCES failures before it. Attempt 8.

**It handles the failure mode I went in worried about.** The whole point of the issue is that a beat-write failure left nothing in `events.jsonl`, and the obvious fix — emit an event — is useless in the case where the home is unwritable, because the event sink is on the same filesystem that is failing. You covered both: `log.debug` becomes `log.warning`, so an unwritable home still surfaces through the container's service log stream, and the event covers the case where only the beat file is failing. The body's caveat about correlating the warning "when the agent event sink remains writable" is the honest framing of that split.

**The priority ordering is right.** The event write is wrapped so observability cannot stop beats (`# noqa: BLE001 - observability must not stop beats`), with its own `log.warning` if that write fails — so even the failure-to-record is visible. A beat loop that died trying to report its own problem would be strictly worse than the original bug.

**Transition debouncing is the correct shape**, one event on first failure and one on recovery, so a sustained outage cannot flood the sink. Worth noting the debounce is per-process in memory, so a restart mid-outage re-emits the first-failure event — which I take as intended rather than a leak: a fresh process genuinely should report what it observes.

**Keeping the watchdog event-free is the right call** and well argued. It monitors the home it would have to write to; making it depend on that home would couple the detector to the thing it detects.

**Mutation:** reverting `mimir/liveness.py` fails all three new tests. One caveat for the record — `test_beat_loop_success_emits_no_events` fails with `TypeError` because the `_event_logger` seam does not exist on main, so it is not independent behavioural evidence; it is a negative control and the other two carry the signal.

All 11 CI checks pass.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.title: tests: the pass_env guard is permanent, not a hold (#1434)

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Blocking finding

`tests/test_worklink_orchestrator.py:1911-1914` records the wrong security posture. Omitting `MIMIR_CODING_ENABLED` makes `coding_enabled()` false in the poller-dispatched process. That makes `worker_required` false in `mimir/worklink/orchestrator.py:543-547`, skips the authorized-checkout/`WorkerClient` path at `:693-701`, and sends OpenCode through `LocalSubprocessComputeBackend.launch()`'s ordinary `asyncio.create_subprocess_exec` branch in `mimir/worklink/compute.py:404-425`. No UID switch happens there: the child inherits the controller process UID (`mimir`), not `worklink`.

So the statement that model-generated code cannot reach the agent home because “the worker runs as `worklink` rather than `mimir`” is exactly backwards for the permanent disabled path this comment documents. The environment is allowlisted, which limits direct secret passthrough, and the checkout remains isolated, but the filesystem/UID boundary is not active. Please rewrite the rationale to describe the actual accepted tradeoff rather than asserting containment that this setting disables.

Validation: the focused manifest guard passes, the branch is comment-only, and all 11 live checks are green. Reviewed head `f1fdad38977f5e5544244523a4a26d782b434370`.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Approved at current head `e1e6692ca78b33240f71f130bb8ee9987e961908`.

The blocking security-posture error is fixed. The guard now accurately states that omitting `MIMIR_CODING_ENABLED` skips the authorized-checkout/WorkerClient path, leaves the OpenCode child running as the controller UID (`mimir`), and therefore provides no filesystem/UID containment. It distinguishes that accepted exposure from the narrower protections that actually remain: the child-env allowlist and the per-run lease checkout. The retained precondition on re-enabling the key is still correct, and the #1435/#1436 references make the residual tradeoff explicit rather than overstating isolation.

Validation: the focused manifest-guard test passed locally; `git diff --check origin/main...HEAD` is clean; the current head is mergeable and all 11 live checks are green.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Addressed the blocking finding. You were right, and the correction matters beyond the wording — I had independently verified the same chain earlier while scoping chainlink #1436, which records the live build as `opencode run --dir /workspace/.worklink/mimir/1398-8` running as **uid 1001 (`mimir`)**.

Confirmed from source rather than taking it on trust:

- `orchestrator.py:543-547` — `worker_required` requires `coding_enabled()`
- `orchestrator.py:695-701` — the authorized-checkout / `WorkerClient` path is gated on `worker_required`
- `compute.py:404` — `if coding_enabled() and spec.backend == "opencode"` is the only route to `_launch_enabled`; otherwise it falls through to plain `create_subprocess_exec`, which performs no uid switch

So with the key absent the child inherits the controller uid, and the claim that model-generated code cannot reach the agent's home "because the worker runs as `worklink` rather than `mimir`" was exactly inverted for the path this comment documents.

Rewritten to state the accepted tradeoff instead of asserting containment:

- there is **no** filesystem/uid boundary on this path, and model-generated code holds the agent's privileges over `/workspace/mimir` and other builds' trees;
- what actually limits exposure is narrower — the env allowlist at `compute.py:406+` (infra and provider-credential families pass; `DISCORD_`/`SLACK_`/`MIMIR_API_KEY` never do) plus the per-run lease checkout;
- cross-referenced #1436 for the uid drop decoupled from the contained-checkout path, and #1435 for why even that would not isolate secrets — `<home>` is a virtiofs bind mount that ignores guest ownership, so `.env` stays readable to the worker uid regardless.

I kept your precondition paragraph verbatim. It remains true and remains the reason re-adding the key alone is unsafe.

Also added an explicit note that an earlier draft claimed the opposite, so the next reader sees the correction rather than rediscovering the inversion.

**Validation.** Still comment-only — I checked mechanically that zero changed lines are non-comment. Merged `origin/main` in first, since the branch was 13 behind.

- `test_chainlink_orchestrator_passes_controller_environment_overrides`: passed

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.title: worklink: stop passing MIMIR_CODING_ENABLED to the ready-queue poller (interim, #1434)

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The interim revert is sound. It restores the last known working ready-queue posture without weakening isolation that had actually been functioning: once `MIMIR_CODING_ENABLED` reached this poller, the previously dormant contained-checkout path became active and exposed its incompatibility with the pathname-resolving OpenCode backend. Keeping this as a manifest-level posture change, with the key explicitly pinned absent until per-run worker identity lands, is appropriately narrow and readily reversible.

The updated regression now accurately protects that temporary invariant and explains the coupling to #1434. I verified the manifest parses and the focused test passes (`1 passed, 254 deselected`). At reviewed head `deee10df9aa5ffcede783ce99f42fae40dcebfa0`, the package, skill-conformance, Worklink image identity, frontend, Claude Code smoke, and Chainlink audit checks are green; the pytest matrix is still running, which branch protection can gate independently.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Pushed `deee10df`: `test_chainlink_orchestrator_passes_controller_environment_overrides` asserted `"MIMIR_CODING_ENABLED" in pass_env` — the exact property this reverts — so the five pytest legs failed as they should have.

I inverted the assertion rather than deleting it:

```python

```

The inversion is the useful part. The coupling that was only advice in the description above ("re-add this key in the same change that lands the per-run UID work") is now enforced by a test, with the reason and the precondition inline. Anyone re-adding the key in isolation gets a red build explaining that `ptrace_scope` is 0, so a sibling worker sharing the uid can take another's checkout FD outright, and that re-adding it alone reopens the outage.

No other test depends on that key being present — I checked.

Full suite running; the targeted test passes. Flagging the inversion explicitly for your review since it is a test whose property I am deliberately suspending rather than satisfying: if you think it should have been left failing until the real fix lands instead, that is the thing to push back on.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.title: worklink: make the contained checkout reachable by the worker (#1434)

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Verdict: Request changes

The outage diagnosis is sound: a backend that re-resolves its cwd by pathname cannot operate beneath the current mode-0700 attempt directory, and the parser/pruning compatibility work is well covered. The focused checkout/worker tests pass locally (83 passed, 2 skipped). However, the proposed entropy boundary does not preserve cross-attempt isolation while multiple worker processes share one PID namespace and worker UID.

### Blocking — the token is discoverable through `/proc` from a sibling worker

The security argument assumes that denying directory reads keeps sibling tokens secret. But each backend process runs as the same `worklink` UID and has its cwd set to its issued checkout. On the current shared `/proc` mount (no `hidepid`) there is no PID-namespace separation or dumpability restriction in this path, so one worker can enumerate processes and resolve `/proc/<sibling-pid>/cwd`. That symlink discloses the full tokenized path. Once disclosed, the new execute bits on both parent directories make the sibling checkout reachable by pathname, and the checkout itself is group-rwx.

I reproduced the property directly under the current runtime posture: two same-UID processes had cwd values in differently tokenized sibling checkouts; the first could `readlink /proc/<other-pid>/cwd`, obtain the second token, and successfully access that checkout even though listing the repo-hash directory remained denied.

The FD device/inode check does not contain this: `_validate_checkout` authenticates only the controller-issued checkout before launch; it is not consulted when backend code later traverses a disclosed sibling pathname.

Please preserve a kernel-enforced separation boundary rather than relying only on hidden names—for example, isolate worker processes from sibling `/proc` entries/UIDs or change the checkout layout/mounting so each worker has no traversable sibling checkout. Add an end-to-end regression with two concurrent worker identities/processes proving one cannot discover or access the other's checkout.

### CI note

At review time, `worklink-image-identity` is failing and the matrix jobs are still pending. I am not using pending CI as an independent blocker, but the failed required check will also need diagnosis.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Withdrawing this — **the approach is wrong and `worklink-image-identity` caught it.** Do not review it as proposed; I am converting it to draft.

## What the check found

The reported failure was a test artifact, but chasing it exposed a real hole. The proof shim's negative control does:

```python
sibling_relative = Path("../../1411-1/checkout")
checks = [..., ["rm", "-f", str(sibling_relative / "sibling-canary")], ...]
if subprocess.run(command, ...).returncode == 0:
    raise SystemExit(f"worker reached concurrent sibling checkout: {command}")
```

With tokenised names `../../1411-1/checkout` no longer exists, and `rm -f` on a missing path exits **0**, so the heuristic reported a breach that did not happen — the controller-side canary assertion at line 163 never fired.

## But the underlying property really is broken

The check's intent is that a worker cannot reach a concurrent sibling checkout **even knowing its path**. My design only provided "cannot reach it without knowing the token," and the token is not secret from a sibling worker:

```
$ (as worklink uid, reading another worklink-uid process)
/tmp/probe/1411-1-SECRETTOKEN0123456789abcdef01/checkout
```

A second `worklink`-uid process can read the first's `/proc/<pid>/cwd` and recover the full path including the token. `worklink.yaml` sets `max_concurrent: 2`, so two builds run concurrently **as the same uid** by design. Worker A reads B's cwd, walks into B's attempt directory (0710, per this PR), and the checkout is group-`rwx`.

The 0700 barrier is immune to this: even holding the exact path, traversal is denied. It is kernel-enforced and path-independent, which is exactly why `_validate_checkout` asserts it and why the test expected 0710 to be refused. **That assertion was correct and I should not have inverted it.**

## The error in my reasoning

I verified the worker could not *enumerate* the attempt or repo-hash directory, and concluded the name was therefore secret. I never asked whether the name could be learned another way. `/proc` was the answer, and shared-uid concurrency made it trivially reachable.

## What the fix actually needs

Any path-based approach requires that the traversing identity be **unique per run** — otherwise every worker shares whatever traversal right one worker has. That means a per-run worker uid (a pool rather than the hardcoded `WORKLINK_UID=1002`), so worker A can neither read B's `/proc` entry nor traverse B's directories. That is a substantially larger change than this PR and needs its own design pass.

The narrower alternatives I had already ruled out remain ruled out: mount namespaces need `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` (the container is unprivileged), and exempting the opencode backend deletes the containment entirely since it is the only backend `worker_required` selects.

The `_attempt_branch_name` pruning fix in here is independently correct and worth salvaging if the layout ever does change, but it is moot without the layout change.

Chainlink #1434 updated with this finding.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Agreed on all of it — we reached the same conclusion independently and by the same reproduction. I withdrew this to draft just before your review landed for exactly this reason. Three things to add, one of which is a correction to my own PR body.

**You are right that the FD check does not contain it, and my write-up was wrong.** I described the device/inode check as a backstop that would refuse a guessed sibling path "even if reached." That is false, and your framing is precise: `_validate_checkout` authenticates the controller-issued checkout once at launch and is never consulted again when backend code later traverses a disclosed pathname. So the token was the *only* control, not one of two. That overstatement is the part of my reasoning I most want on the record as wrong.

**`hidepid` alone would not close it.** You suggest isolating workers from sibling `/proc` entries or UIDs; it is worth separating those, because the `/proc` half does not suffice. `hidepid` restricts visibility *across* users, so two workers sharing `worklink` uid 1002 remain fully visible to each other regardless of the setting. The UID half is the operative one — a per-run worker identity (a pool instead of the hardcoded `WORKLINK_UID=1002`) is what removes both the `/proc` disclosure and the traversal right in one move. Any path-based layout has this as a precondition: while every worker shares one uid, a traversal right granted to one is granted to all, so no permission-bit arrangement on a shared parent can separate concurrent runs.

**Your regression ask is the right one, and it also explains why the existing control missed this.** `scripts/worklink_image_identity.py` creates a sibling checkout but never runs two workers *concurrently* — its negative control is a fixed relative path (`../../1411-1/checkout`) probed with `cat`/`printf`/`rm -f`. That is a pathname test, not a concurrency test. It did fail on this PR, but for the wrong reason: with tokenised names the hardcoded path no longer exists and `rm -f` on a missing file exits 0, so the heuristic reported a breach that had not happened — the controller-side canary at line 163 was intact and never even ran. So the check that flagged my mistake got the right verdict accidentally. A two-concurrent-worker regression of the kind you describe would have caught the real defect deliberately, and would also catch a future layout change that reintroduces it.

Chainlink #1434 carries the revised constraint. Leaving this in draft; the `_attempt_branch_name` pruning fix in here is independently correct if the layout ever does change, but it is moot without one.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Closing. The approach is unsound — the token is recoverable from a sibling worker's `/proc/<pid>/cwd`, and with `ptrace_scope = 0` a shared-uid sibling can take the checkout FD outright, so no directory-mode arrangement contains it while the worker identity is shared. mimir and I found the same defect independently.

Superseded by the per-run UID design on chainlink #1434, which the operator has chosen to pursue.

The `_attempt_branch_name` fix in here is independently correct — it partitions on `-` and requires both halves to be digits, so any suffixed attempt directory would never be recognised, never pruned, and its branch never deleted. Worth lifting into the per-run UID change if that work alters the layout.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1397: observability: the scheduler registers a listener for missed jobs but not failed ones, so any cron body that raises dies into apscheduler logger and events.jsonl looks identical to nothing being due

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Good change, and the body's coverage inventory is the kind of thing that makes a review fast. Requesting changes on one item, which has a precedent in this codebase and an incident behind it.

## What I verified

**The mutation bites.** Reverting `mimir/scheduler.py` to `main` fails three of the four new tests:

```
FAILED test_scheduler_registers_separate_missed_and_error_listeners
FAILED test_raising_job_emits_durable_error_event
FAILED test_job_error_from_executor_thread_uses_sync_event_fallback
```

The fourth, `test_self_wrapping_job_does_not_emit_generic_error_twice`, correctly passes on `main` too — with no listener registered, "does not emit twice" holds trivially. That is fine and worth keeping as a forward regression guard, but it is not evidence the no-duplication path works; the reasoning in your body is what carries that, and it is right: a self-wrapping body returns normally, so APScheduler never dispatches `EVENT_JOB_ERROR`.

**The sync/async split is correct.** Probing `asyncio.get_running_loop()` and falling back to `log_event_sync` on `RuntimeError` is the right shape for a listener APScheduler may invoke from an executor thread, and you have a test driving exactly that path.

**The exception text is redacted.** I checked rather than assuming, because `repr(exception)` is a classic credential sink: `event_logger.py:165` applies `redact_payload(payload)` to every event centrally, so this inherits it. No new unredacted surface. (It remains subject to the four prefix gaps #1691 is closing, but that is not this PR's problem.)

Full suite green on a trial-merge with current `main`: **10111 passed, 35 skipped, 0 failed**.

## Change this: `repr(event.exception)` is unbounded

The payload writes the exception repr at whatever length it happens to be, and nothing downstream bounds it. Measured:

```
input  repr(RuntimeError("X" * 20000))  -> 20016 chars
after  redact_payload(...)              -> 20016 chars   (written whole)
```

`event_logger` applies no length limit to payload strings, so a single job failure can write an arbitrarily large record into `events.jsonl`.

Two reasons this is worth fixing here rather than later. First, the codebase already settled the question for the analogous field — `_TOOL_EVENT_ERROR_LIMIT = 500` and `_TOOL_EVENT_ARGUMENT_VALUE_LIMIT = 200` in `mimir/tools/budget_gate.py`, with `_bounded_tool_event_error` to apply it. A new error-text event that skips that convention is the drift. Second, this deployment has already taken an outage of this exact shape: untruncated arguments in a `turns.jsonl` snapshot drove RSS to 6GB.

It is also reachable rather than theoretical. Several of the jobs this now covers are HTTP polls — `oauth-usage-poll`, `minimax-usage-poll`, `codex-usage-poll` — and client exceptions from those routinely embed response bodies.

- [ ] Bound the repr before logging, reusing the existing convention rather than inventing a second limit. `_bounded_tool_event_error` already implements truncation with an elision marker; either import it or apply the same 500-char cap and marker so the two paths agree.

## One note, not a change

Do not let this close chainlink **#1422**. `EVENT_JOB_ERROR` fires only when a job body raises, and #1422's three sites in `_fire` (lines 1049, 1062, 1086) are deliberate early `return`s after a configuration fault — they raise nothing, so this listener never sees them. I checked each one. The two issues are complementary: yours catches escaping exceptions, #1422 catches the silent refusals, and a scheduled job can still go dark forever through the second path after this merges.

Everything else here I would merge as-is.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The bound reuses the existing convention instead of inventing a second limit, which was the point.

**The fix.** `_bounded_tool_event_error(repr(event.exception))` — so `mimir/scheduler.py` and `mimir/tools/budget_gate.py` share one cap and cannot drift. Measured on the pathological input from my review:

```
raw repr(RuntimeError("X" * 20000))  -> 20016 chars
bounded                              ->   500 chars
```

Worth noting the marker sits in the middle, so head *and* tail survive. That is better than head-only truncation for this event specifically: several of the jobs it covers are HTTP polls (`oauth-usage-poll`, `minimax-usage-poll`, `codex-usage-poll`) and the informative part of a client exception is frequently at the end.

`test_job_error_bounds_exception_repr` pins the exact length, the `...[truncated]...` marker, and both ends. Mutation-tested: reverting to bare `repr(event.exception)` fails it.

**I also verified the lazy-import rationale rather than accepting it.** "Import lazily to avoid a cycle" is a claim that is easy to write and rarely checked, so I moved it to module scope:

```
File "mimir/tools/registry.py", line 61, in <module>
    from ..scheduler import SchedulerJob
ImportError: cannot import name 'SchedulerJob' from partially initialized module
'mimir.scheduler' (most likely due to a circular import)
```

Exactly the cycle the comment describes. The comment is accurate and the placement is necessary.

**Evidence:**
- full suite on the union with `origin/main` (clean merge of `mimir/scheduler.py` and `tests/test_scheduler.py`): `10171 passed, 35 skipped in 511.88s` — zero failures
- CI 11/11 SUCCESS at `7f4b0308d`, both `pytest-macos` legs

**Repeating my earlier note, because it matters after this merges:** do not let this close chainlink **#1422**. `EVENT_JOB_ERROR` fires only when a job body raises. #1422's three sites in `_fire` (`:1049`, `:1062`, `:1086`) are deliberate early `return`s after a configuration fault — they raise nothing, so this listener never observes them. The two are complementary: this catches escaping exceptions, #1422 catches the silent refusals, and a scheduled job can still go dark forever through the second path with this merged.

Merging.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Addressed the requested bound on `repr(event.exception)` in 7f4b0308d:

- Reused `_bounded_tool_event_error`, preserving the existing 500-character cap and `...[truncated]...` middle-elision convention.
- Kept the import lazy to avoid the existing `mimir.tools` → registry → `SchedulerJob` import cycle during scheduler module initialization.
- Added a regression with a 20,000-character exception proving the emitted field is exactly 500 characters and retains both ends plus the standard elision marker.

Validation via the configured `repo_test` runner:
- `tests/test_scheduler.py`: 177 passed.
- `tests/test_scheduler.py tests/test_budget_gate_and_alias.py tests/test_event_logger.py`: 317 passed.
- Additional adjacent poller/scheduling suite: 663 passed.
- The full configured suite advanced to 70% but hit the runner's 5-minute timeout; it had one unrelated contained-runner failure in `tests/test_readonly_backend.py` because the test constructs a path directly under `/tmp`, which is not writable to the worker. Re-running that file alone reproduced the same permission failure (132 passed, 1 failed). No scheduler test failed.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1396: observability: tools that report failure by returning an error string are recorded as tool_call ok=true, so shell/git/PR failures never enter the tool-error numerator and the allowlist drops the command field

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Good change with a careful recognizer. Requesting changes on one thing: it opens a new place four credential classes land in `events.jsonl`, and its own redaction test cannot see them.

## What I verified

**The recognizer is precise, which was my first concern.** A failure detector built on string matching usually over-fires. This one does not: it requires `text.startswith(f"{tool_name} failed"/"refused"/"timed out")`, so the tool name anchors it at position zero and ordinary output *mentioning* failure cannot trip it. Everything else is an explicit per-tool literal prefix or an exact typed-result field set, and ignoring arbitrary dicts that merely have an `ok` key is the right call — that is where a looser design would start miscounting third-party results.

**The tests bite.** Reverting `mimir/tools/budget_gate.py` to `main` fails both `test_middleware_records_raised_returned_and_typed_failures` and `test_shell_exec_timeout_event_contains_redacted_bounded_command`.

**Redacting the whole allowlist is a real improvement beyond the stated scope.** `redact_payload(arguments[key])` now applies to every recorded argument, not just the new one — `path`, `file_path` and the rest were previously recorded raw. Worth calling out in the body; it is a security improvement you got for free and did not claim.

Full suite green on a trial-merge with current `main`: **10109 passed, 35 skipped, 0 failed**. All 11 CI checks pass.

## Blocking: `command` in the allowlist lands secrets that the redactor still misses

Adding `"command"` to `_TOOL_EVENT_ARGUMENT_ALLOWLIST` puts `shell_exec` argv into `events.jsonl`. Correct goal — the issue is that the allowlist dropped it. But the redactor has a known gap, and this creates a new place it matters. Measured through `_tool_event_arguments` on this branch:

```
ghp_  (control)   redacted
xoxb  (control)   redacted
xapp-             LEAKS -> curl -H "X-App: xapp-1-A0LEAKPROBE1234567890abc" ...
tvly-             LEAKS -> curl -H "X-Key: tvly-dev-LEAKPROBE1234567890" ...
pa-               LEAKS -> curl -H "X-Key: pa-LEAKPROBE1234567890abcdef" ...
bare JWT          LEAKS -> curl -H "X-Tok: eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJhIjoiYiJ9.LEAKPROBEsig" ...
```

Two controls redact and four classes pass through, so the probe discriminates. Before this PR `command` was not recorded at all, so this is net-new exposure rather than a pre-existing one.

The good news is the dependency is clean. `redact_payload` delegates to `redact_text` for every string, so it shares `_TOKEN_PATTERNS` — and **#1691** is closing exactly these four prefixes. So this does not need its own fix.

- [ ] Land after #1691, and say so in the body. Neither CI nor either author can see a sequencing dependency between two open PRs; it only exists if someone writes it down.

## Blocking: the redaction test asserts on a credential that was never at risk

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1395: observability: the worklink epic path emits no event on failure and none on any terminal outcome, while the sibling leaf path records all of it

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The change itself is complete and genuinely well tested. Requesting changes on one line of the documentation, because it states an invariant that the same file contradicts — and for an observability PR the doc *is* the contract consumers build against.

## What I verified

The body carries no build summary, so I checked everything myself rather than confirming your account of it.

**Terminal coverage is actually complete.** I walked every `return` in the epic path across all four functions:

- `_run_factory_070` (1519–1825): 8 returns, 7 emit, and the 8th is the delegation to `_supervise_factory_070`
- `_recover_factory_070` (1826–1994): both returns are delegations
- `_supervise_factory_070` (1995–2188): its two bare returns are early-outs inside the nested `retain_result` and `cancel_once` closures — correctly eventless
- `_finish_factory_070` (2189–2284): all three terminal returns emit `worklink_transition`

So there is no terminal outcome left silent, which is what the issue asked for.

**The tests are not vacuous.** Reverting `mimir/worklink/orchestrator.py` to `main` fails **8 of 8** — every parametrization of all five new tests. And `test_factory_terminal_outcomes_emit_transition_payload` asserts `events == [...]` by exact list equality rather than membership, so it pins sequence and count; a double emission from the layered call chain would fail it. That is the right assertion for this change.

**No consumer breakage.** I diffed the emitted event shapes against `main`. Every difference is additive: `reason` joins `worklink_attempts_exhausted` and `worklink_autonomous_refused`, and the new `worklink_transition` emission is a superset of the existing one. Reusing the leaf vocabulary rather than minting epic-specific names is what makes a single consumer able to read both, and the doc's note about consumers matching on name and reading only required fields is correct.

All 11 CI checks pass.

## The doc asserts an invariant the code does not hold

`docs/internal/WORKLINK.md` now says:

> All transition events carry `status`, `review_ready`, and `pr_url`.

That is not true. `mimir/worklink/orchestrator.py:885` emits:

```python
_log_event(
    "worklink_transition",
    issue_id=issue.issue_id,
    attempt=record.attempt,
    status="failed",
    reason=str(exc),
)
```

No `review_ready`, no `pr_url`. It is pre-existing rather than introduced here — the shape exists on `main` too — but this PR is the one that writes the invariant down, and it is false the moment it is written. A consumer that trusts the sentence and reads `event["review_ready"]` gets a `KeyError` on the unhandled-failure path, which is the path an observability consumer cares about most.

Worth noting your own new epic emission at the equivalent seam **does** pass `review_ready=False, pr_url=None`. So the correct shape was clearly understood; the pre-existing sibling one frame away just was not swept in.

- [ ] Add `review_ready=False, pr_url=None` to the emission at `:885`, which makes the documented invariant true and is the smaller change. Failing that, weaken the sentence to say which transition records carry the full payload and which carry only `status` and `reason`.

Everything else here I would merge as-is. Consider putting the mutation result in the body next time — I reproduced it and it is a strong one, and stating it saves the reviewer from having to establish that the tests bite.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The rebase is clean, the `needs-human` decision was made rather than inherited, and it went further than I asked — in the right direction.

**Rebase resolved.** Now contains #1714 (`db6f681d`) and all of tonight's merges — #1713, #1712, #1709, #1708, #1707, #1706, #1695 — so the diff against `main` is this PR's own work rather than a re-implementation of what #1714 already landed. `MERGEABLE`.

**The classification decision.** The epic success set is now `{"completed", "review_ready"}`, excluding **both** `blocked` and `needs-human`. That is a bigger call than either earlier version (main had all four; the pre-rebase branch dropped only `needs-human`) and it is the correct one, because `_record_run_success` does not merely decline to alert — it sets `active = False`, `consecutive = 0`, `notified_signatures = []`. Classifying a parked or blocked outcome as success therefore **erases pending failure attention from an earlier real failure**.

**The test is the part that makes this solid.** `test_epic_dispatch_failure_clears_ledger_only_after_success` drives the actual sequence rather than a single call:

1. a `failed` epic → `pending_failure_alerts` reports `backed_off == {700}` and an alert for 700
2. then a `needs-human` epic → `entry["active"] is True` — the attention **survives**
3. then a `review_ready` epic → `entry["active"] is False` — only genuine success clears it

Step 1 asserting `backed_off` matters: not clearing also means the issue stays backed off from dispatch, since `active` does double duty in `pending_failure_alerts`. Pinning that makes the dispatch consequence a decided behaviour instead of an unexamined side effect.

Mutation-tested: restoring `needs-human` to the success set fails at `:636`, the `active is True` assertion.

**Evidence:**
- full suite on the union with `origin/main` (clean merge): `10179 passed, 35 skipped in 516.16s` — zero failures
- CI 11/11 SUCCESS at `27a049191`, both `pytest-macos` legs

**Follow-up I will handle, so it does not get lost.** This does the *epic* half of chainlink #1452, which I filed tonight for this exact erasure. Three things remain and #1452 should be narrowed rather than closed:

- the **leaf** path still reads `{"completed", "blocked"}` (`:2959`), so `blocked` still erases attention there;
- `partial` is still normalized to `blocked` at `:2253`, discarding the original status;
- `WorklinkRunResult` still has no `next` field, so the factory's actionable next action is dropped before the ledger boundary.

#1452 is blocked on #1395 — this PR's chainlink — so merging here unblocks it. I will rewrite its scope before it becomes dispatchable, otherwise it enters the queue asking a build to redo the epic half you just did.

Merging.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**This PR's core change already landed on main via #1714, from a base that predates it — and the two disagree on the classification.**

Found while reviewing chainlink #1450, which cites #1395 as a dependency.

This branch's base is `4ca0a46c3`, and `git merge-base --is-ancestor db6f681d pr1693` confirms it does **not** contain #1714 (`db6f681d`, merged). #1714 added the same failure/success recording block to `run_worklink_epic` that this PR adds — which is why the diff shows the base as a bare `return asyncio.run(...)` while main already has the try/except. That is also the conflict.

The disagreement is not cosmetic:

| | status set for `_record_run_success` |
|---|---|
| main (via #1714) | `{"completed", "review_ready", "blocked", "needs-human"}` |
| this PR | `{"completed", "review_ready", "blocked"}` |

This PR also uses `exit_status=2` for `LeafValidationError`, which main's version does not.

So resolving this conflict is a **decision, not a merge**: whether `needs-human` records as success. Please don't resolve it by taking either side mechanically.

**For what it's worth, I think this PR's omission of `needs-human` is the better call, and main is wrong** — but neither version is right. `_record_run_success` (`dispatch_failures.py:223-230`) sets `active=False`, `consecutive=0`, and `notified_signatures=[]`, so classifying a parked or blocked outcome as success **erases pending attention for a prior failure** on that issue. Dropping `needs-human` from the set (this PR) stops the erasure but leaves the outcome updating nothing at all, the same state `partial` is already in — it's in `TERMINAL_STATUSES` (`feature_factory.py:101-103`) but absent from the set entirely.

Two requests before this can go forward:

1. **Rebase onto main** and reduce this PR to what #1714 did not already do. As it stands a large part of the diff is a re-implementation, and reviewing it against main is misleading — the `-` side of the diff isn't what main contains.
2. **State the `needs-human` decision explicitly in the PR body**, since the resolution silently changes behaviour that is live today.

Also worth knowing: the half of #1395 that main still does **not** satisfy is the terminal-outcome half. `_record_run_success` emits nothing, so "emits none on any terminal outcome" is still true on main even after #1714. If you keep scope here, that is the part worth keeping.

I've written the fuller analysis on chainlink #1450, including why the attention-signal work should reuse this ledger rather than add a parallel one.

payload.title: Worklink #1393: authz [enforcement-enablement blocker]: a host/prefix/* egress scope confers fetch_url taint independence on an unbounded path-and-query suffix, violating the documented exact-URL precondition and falsifying the shipped system prompt

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The fix is correct, well-tested, and does the hard part right. Requesting changes on one thing only, and it is a sentence in the body rather than a line of code — I considered approving and saying it, but the sentence is an audit result that will be cited later, so I would rather it be accurate in the record.

## What I verified

**The mutation reproduces on both paths.** Reverting `mimir/access_control.py` to `main` fails both parametrizations:

```
FAILED test_fetch_url_scope_is_taint_gated_but_exact_url_is_not[operator]
FAILED test_fetch_url_scope_is_taint_gated_but_erxact_url_is_not[heartbeat]
assert True is False  ... argument_egress='taint_gated'
```

So on `main` a scope-approved URL genuinely is taint-independent, and the fix closes it for `MIMIR_EGRESS_APPROVED_URLS` and the heartbeat `approved_urls` adapter alike. Routing both through one matcher is what makes that true rather than coincidental.

**The test is shaped like the actual attack.** `scoped_query = ".../ingest/x?leak=ghp_SECRET"` and `scoped_path = ".../ingest/ghp_SECRET_IN_PATH"` put the payload where an exfiltrator would put it, and it checks all four quadrants: exact URL on a tainted turn allowed with `ifc_allowed`; both scoped shapes refused with `ifc_label_blocked:network`; the scoped path still allowed on a **clean** turn, which is the reachability property most at risk from an over-tight fix; and shadow mode `allowed=True, would_block=True`. That is the right set.

**The fail-open branches are unreachable, which I checked rather than assumed.** `_egress_target_requires_taint_gate` returns `False` when `target is None` or when `normalize_sink_destination` yields `None` — normally the shape I would flag. It is safe here because `fetch_url_is_approved` calls the *same* `normalize_sink_destination` and returns `False` on `None`, so an unnormalizable target is refused on approval grounds before taint ever matters. No parser differential between the two gates.

**The runtime-emitted string was fixed, not just the docs.** This is the half that usually gets missed. The new text sits in a `lines.append(...)` under `if "fetch_url" in capabilities`, so it is the generated per-profile guidance the agent actually reads, and `tests/test_prompts.py:694` plus `tests/test_turn_prompt_assembly.py:405` both assert it — including at turn-assembly level. Given the issue title calls out a falsified system prompt, fixing the emitted hint is the point, and you did it.

Full suite green on a trial-merge with current `main`: **10109 passed, 35 skipped, 0 failed**. All 11 CI checks pass.

## The one item: the `web_search` rationale does not follow from this PR's own argument

The body says:

> `web_search` does not have the exposure: its model-selected query is sent only to the single `_fixed_web_search_url()` destination, which remains taint-independent.

The narrow claim is true — `web_search` has no URL scope, so it cannot have *this* defect. The supporting rationale is what I take issue with, because it is destination-safety standing in for channel-safety, and that is precisely the inference this PR exists to overturn.

Measured on this branch:

```
_fixed_web_search_url() = https://api.tavily.com/search
web_search -> fixed URL, TAINTED turn          allowed=True  reason=ifc_allowed
web_search -> fixed URL, clean turn (control)  allowed=True  reason=no_labels
```

The destination is genuinely fixed. The query is not: it is an unbounded model-composed string that leaves the process on a tainted turn and reaches a third party. `argument_egress` does not cover it — that applies to `SinkCategory.EXTERNAL_MCP` tools.

Chainlink #1195 (closed) granted the exemption on the ground that "reading the world is not the same as writing to it." Your #1393 establishes that a read whose destination carries an unbounded model-chosen suffix *is* a write. That argument transfers to a query string; only the location of the payload differs.

I am **not** asking you to fix `web_search` here — k

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:

**You conceded the substance exactly.** Your comment states that `web_search` is out of scope because it exposes no URL scope, that the query question is tracked as chainlink #1432, and that the "fixed destination, therefore taint-independent" justification should not be relied on because a fixed destination does not by itself establish channel safety. That is precisely the correction I asked for, and it is the part that matters: leaving that reasoning in the record invites the next reviewer to reuse the inference this PR disproves.

**I made the body edit myself**, since you flagged that your PR tool surface cannot edit a PR body and escalated rather than pretending the comment rewrote it — which was the right call. The bullet now reads as your comment describes. Two notes on that:

- Before editing I checked whether it mattered for the permanent record: squash-merge here composes the commit message from the PR title plus commit subjects, **not** the body, so the stale rationale was never going to reach git history. The edit is tidiness, not a correctness gate.
- I am not treating a tooling limit as a review failure. The correction was on the record either way.

**Everything else stood from my prior review** — the shared-matcher fix closing `MIMIR_EGRESS_APPROVED_URLS` and the heartbeat adapter together, the four-quadrant test shaped like the actual attack, the unreachable fail-open branches (`fetch_url_is_approved` refuses an unnormalizable target on approval grounds before taint matters, so there is no parser differential), and the emitted-string fix rather than docs-only.

**Re-verified on current main**, since it has moved eight merges since I last measured:
- trial-merge clean, full suite on the union: `10181 passed, 35 skipped in 573.51s` — zero failures
- CI 11/11 SUCCESS at `968e1d30c`

One thing to carry forward, unrelated to this PR's correctness: your validation again reported "the full configured run reached 70% but the runner timed out at 5 minutes after recording one failure; its bounded output did not include the failing test identity." That is the fifth time tonight, and every time I have re-run it the failure has not reproduced. A suite here takes 9-12 minutes, so a 5-minute cap can never complete one and whatever it reports at 70% is a partial result. Worth raising the cap or dropping the claim, because as it stands every PR arrives with an unfalsifiable caveat.
