payload.body:
Requesting changes. The four bare prefixes are genuinely fixed, but the JWT half reintroduces the exact bug class this issue was filed for, and the `pa-` pattern mangles ordinary log text.

I have a direct interest in this one being right: I measured the original gap earlier today while reviewing #1688, and I had to retract a wrong "correction" I posted on chainlink #1391 claiming a JWT pattern already existed. It did not, and this PR is the fix.

## Verified working

```
xapp-1-A0LEAKPROBE1234567890abc   -> [REDACTED]
tvly-dev-LEAKPROBE1234567890      -> [REDACTED]
pa-LEAKPROBE1234567890abcdef      -> [REDACTED]
AIza + 35 chars (the 39-char key) -> [REDACTED]
real RS256 JWT                    -> eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.[REDACTED]
```

Preserving the JWT header while masking payload and signature is the right call, and it satisfies the original criterion about not masking the whole token.

## Blocking 1: compact JWTs still leak, via a new length floor

The JWT pattern requires a first segment of `{25,}` and a third of `{27,}`. A standard HS256 header — `{"alg":"HS256"}` with no `typ` — base64url-encodes to `eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9`, which is **20 characters**. Measured on this branch:

```
in : eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJhIjoiYiJ9.sssssssssssssssssssssssssssssssssssssssssss
out: eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJhIjoiYiJ9.sssssssssssssssssssssssssssssssssssssssssss

in : eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJhIjoiYiJ9.LEAKPROBEsignature
out: eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJhIjoiYiJ9.LEAKPROBEsignature
```

Both are untouched. Note what this repeats: the issue's own third symptom was *"a 39-character AIza key leaks because the entropy fallback has a 40-character floor."* This PR fixes that floor and then adds two more of the same kind.

A length heuristic is the wrong discriminator here — a JWT has an invariant tell. Every JWT header starts `{"`, which base64url-encodes to `eyJ`. Anchoring on that instead is both tighter and shorter. I tested this replacement:

```python
re.compile(r"(\beyJ[A-Za-z0-9_-]{8,}\.)([A-Za-z0-9_-]{4,}\.[A-Za-z0-9_-]{8,}\b)")
```

```
compact HS256   -> eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.[REDACTED]
short signature -> eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.[REDACTED]
real RS256      -> eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.[REDACTED]
java package    -> com.example.averylongpackagename.submodule.ClassName   (correctly untouched)
```

- [ ] Anchor the JWT rule on `eyJ` rather than segment lengths, or lower the floors to the real minimum (20, not 25) and say why that number.

## Blocking 2: `pa-` matches mid-token and destroys ordinary text

None of the new prefix patterns has a left boundary, and the body charset includes `-`. Measured:

```
in : see europa-mission-telemetry-archive-2026 for detail
out: see euro[REDACTED] for detail

in : /opt/data-pa-partition-export-archive/file.txt
out: /opt/data-[REDACTED]/file.txt
```

This redactor runs over `events.jsonl` and `turns.jsonl`, so this silently eats file paths and identifiers in exactly the records an operator reads to diagnose a failure. Over-redaction is the safer direction for a secret, but not when a two-character prefix makes it routine.

Both cases are fixed by a lookbehind plus dropping `-` from the body, which I verified keeps the true positive:

```python
re.compile(r"(?<![A-Za-z0-9_-])pa-[A-Za-z0-9_]{20,}")
```

```
pa-LEAKPROBE1234567890abcdef                   -> [REDACTED]
see europa-mission-telemetry-archive-2026      -> unchanged
/opt/data-pa-partition-export-archive/file.txt -> unchanged
```

- [ ] Add the lookbehind to `pa-`, `tvly-` and `xapp-`, and drop `-` from the body charset unless a real key of that vendor contains one — if it does, say so, because that constrains the fix.

## Blocking 3: the corpus JWT entry is dimensioned to the regex

`tests/redaction_corpus.py` adds `"abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz.abc123.0123456789abcdefghijklmnopq"` — segments of **26 / 6 / 27** against pattern floors of **25 / 6 / 27**. It sits one character above the minimum on the first segment and exactly on it f

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. All three blocking items are addressed, and the one I filed as "minor" was fixed structurally rather than patched.

**The over-redaction is fixed, with a per-vendor justification.** Lookbehinds on all four bare-token patterns, and `-` dropped from `pa-`'s body — with the reasoning recorded where it belongs:

> `xapp` and `tvly` retain hyphens in the body because issued Slack app tokens and Tavily `tvly-dev` keys use hyphen-delimited components. Voyage `pa` bodies do not.

That is the right basis. I asked for a justification only if a real key of that vendor contains one, and you gave it per vendor rather than blanket-applying the fix. Verified rather than read — all four benign strings now pass through untouched, including both from my review:

```
see europa-mission-telemetry-archive-2026 for detail   unchanged
/opt/data-pa-partition-export-archive/file.txt         unchanged
tvly-ish-but-not-a-key                                 unchanged
xapp-short                                             unchanged
```

and all four secret shapes still mask. The JWT case preserves the `eyJ…` header and redacts payload and signature, which the comment explains is deliberate — correct, since the header is base64 of `{"` and carries no secret, so records stay diagnosable.

**The corpus now tests the input space rather than the implementation.** `COMPACT_HS256_JWT` and an RS256 entry, both genuinely `eyJ`-prefixed, replacing the entry whose 26/6/27 segments were dimensioned against the pattern's own 25/6/27 floors.

**The duplication item was closed properly.** `mimir/shared_redaction_patterns.py` defines the shapes once; both `mimir/redaction.py` and `mimir/turn_event_redaction.py` import from it; and **zero literal prefix patterns remain in either file**. The failure mode I described — the next prefix getting added to only one of two hand-synced copies — is now structurally impossible, while the deliberate registration asymmetry that `test_shared_corpus_pins_contained_scrubber_registration_asymmetry` pins is preserved. That is the harder of the two ways to satisfy the note and the better one.

**Mutation-tested in both directions**, each failing with named tests:
- dropping the `pa-` lookbehind fails `test_bare_secret_patterns_preserve_ordinary_text` on *exactly* the two strings from my review, so those findings are now parametrized regression cases;
- removing the `xapp-` pattern fails `test_bare_secret_shapes_are_masked_by_durable_and_live_redactors[bare-xapp]` and the asymmetry pin.

False positives and false negatives are pinned independently, which is what this kind of change needs.

**Evidence:**
- full suite on the union with `origin/main` (clean merge): `10195 passed, 35 skipped in 760.93s` — zero failures
- CI 11/11 SUCCESS at `34766d6e2`

**This unblocks #1694.** I held that PR specifically on this one: adding `command` to `_TOOL_EVENT_ARGUMENT_ALLOWLIST` starts writing `shell_exec` argv into `events.jsonl`, and until now four credential classes passed through unmasked. I re-probed on this head and it is 0 of 6 leaking. #1694 also carries `@pytest.mark.xfail(strict=True)` on a bare `xapp-` case, so merging this will turn that XPASS into a failure and force the marker off — the ordering enforces itself from here. I will pick #1694 up next.

Merging.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Addressed the requested changes in 34766d6e2:

- JWT matching now anchors on `eyJ`, preserves the header, and covers real compact HS256 plus RS256 corpus entries without implementation-dimensioned floors.
- `xapp-`, `tvly-`, `pa-`, and `AIza` patterns now require a left token boundary; `pa-` no longer admits hyphens in its body. `xapp`/`tvly` retain hyphens because their real token families use hyphen-delimited components (`xapp-1-...`, `tvly-dev-...`).
- Added ordinary-text regressions for the Europa identifier, `data-pa-partition` path, and Java package shape.
- Moved the shared provider/JWT definitions into `mimir/shared_redaction_patterns.py` so durable and live redactors cannot drift.

Validation via the bound `repo_test` runner:
- `tests/test_redaction.py`: 148 passed
- related event/turn logging tests: 90 passed

- full suite reached 70% before the 5-minute runner timeout; a reproducible unrelated contained-runner failure is `tests/test_readonly_backend.py::TestBuildFileToolRoutes::test_non_admin_home_collections_surface_only_admitted_subtrees[tmp]`, which tries to create a synthetic path directly under `/tmp` and gets `PermissionError`.

payload.title: Worklink #1392: authz [enforcement-enablement blocker]: authorize_skill_write canonicalizes only physical and home-relative targets, so the backend own virtual /skills/... spelling bypasses the flag-independent skills boundary

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
This is the most carefully built PR I have reviewed in this batch, and I verified it hard because it is a flag-independent boundary and an enablement blocker. One item to change — a latent coupling, not a live defect.

## What I verified, and how

**The bypass is genuinely closed, and only the bypass.** Reverting `mimir/access_control.py` to `main` fails **27** tests, and every failing id is a `[virtual-…]` parametrization:

```
test_skill_writes_require_an_untainted_admin_operator_turn[virtual-scripts/fetch-news.ts-poller-…]
test_skill_writes_require_an_untainted_admin_operator_turn[virtual-…-admin_operator-…-True]
…27 total, all [virtual-…]
```

The `physical` and `relative` parametrizations still pass against unmodified `main`. That is exactly the signature you want: the fix moves the virtual spelling and touches nothing else. Parametrizing the existing test over all three spellings rather than adding a fourth test is also the right structure.

**The helper genuinely mirrors the backend, which is the assumption everything else rests on.** If `_resolve_file_tool_target` and the live backend disagreed, the authorizer would approve a different path than gets written. I diffed them directly:

```
/skills/a/SKILL.md        helper == backend  -> <home>/skills/a/SKILL.md
skills/a/SKILL.md         helper == backend
<home>/skills/a/SKILL.md  helper == backend
/state/x.json             helper == backend
/etc/passwd               helper == backend  -> <home>/etc/passwd   (both virtual-remap)
<ext-root>/f.txt          helper == route._resolve_path             (physical, via the router)
/skills/../etc/passwd     helper None, backend ValueError           (both refuse)
```

The external-root case only agrees once you go through `build_file_tool_routes`, which is the production shape — checking it against the bare home backend shows a false divergence. Worth knowing if anyone re-runs this.

**`record_file_write_integrity` is behaviour-identical, symlink guard included.** This is the part I was most worried about, because the diff deletes a block whose comment explicitly says *"A path lexically under the configured home but resolving outside it is a symlink escape, not an unrelated write to permit."* Deleting a commented guard is usually where a refactor loses a property. It does not here — the existing tail (`resource.resolve()` then `relative_to(home)` in a `try`, and the `parts[0] not in _SELF_AUTHORED_FILE_ROOTS -> return True`) subsumes both branches. Measured PR vs main with a real symlink out of home:

```
symlink escape, physical spelling   False   False
symlink escape, virtual spelling    False   False
plain home write (control)          True    True
virtual home write (control)        True    True
unrelated absolute                  True    True
```

Identical on every case.

**`ifc_labels: Any = None` fails closed.** A new optional parameter on a security path is the shape that bit #1688, so I checked: `_is_admin_operator_turn(None, None)` returns `False`, so an omitted value refuses the skill write rather than allowing it. All call sites pass it explicitly anyway.

**The sibling roots behave correctly.** `/.mimir_builtin_skills/…` and `/SKILLS/…` both get no opinion from the boundary — not a gap, because neither is in `agent_writable_roots`, so writes there are refused outright rather than laundered. `/state/x.json` correctly gets no opinion, and your `virtual_state.allowed is True` assertion is the right negative control to have included.

Full suite green on a trial-merge with current `main`: **10153 passed, 35 skipped, 0 failed**. All 11 CI checks pass.

## Change this: the external-root list depends on positional ordering

```python
external_roots = tuple(dict.fromkeys(
    root.resolve() for root in (*_configured_file_roots()[1:], *physical_roots)
))
```

The `[1:]` encodes "home is element 0". That is true today — `_configured_file_roots` returns `[Path(home), *extra_roots]` — but nothing pins it, and no test asserts the o

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The coupling is removed, and the implementation is stronger than what I asked for.

```python
external_roots = tuple(dict.fromkeys(
    resolved
    for root in (*_configured_file_roots(), *physical_roots)
    if (resolved := root.resolve()) != home_root
))
for root in sorted(external_roots, key=lambda item: len(item.parts), reverse=True):
```

I asked for `root != home_root` instead of positional slicing. You went further in three ways that matter: both sides are `resolve()`d, so an extra root that *resolves* to home (a symlink, or a duplicate spelling) is excluded too — positional slicing could never catch that; `dict.fromkeys` dedupes while preserving order; and the match loop is sorted by path depth descending, so the most specific root wins rather than whichever came first.

**On mutation, and being straight about what it shows.** Reverting to `_configured_file_roots()[1:]` leaves all 69 file-root tests passing. I checked whether that meant the fix was unpinned, and it does not — `_configured_file_roots` returns `[Path(home), *extras]`, so home is structurally first and the two forms are *semantically equivalent under the current construction*. No test can distinguish them because there is nothing to distinguish.

That makes this different from an untested guard: my item was about removing a dependency on an invariant declared in another function, not about fixing a live miscomputation. The value is that `_configured_file_roots` can now change its ordering without silently breaking this call site. A regression pinning that would have to reorder the roots artificially, which I do not think is worth the fixture.

The one genuinely new behaviour — excluding an extra root that resolves to home — is not covered either, and that one *is* testable without contrivance. Not blocking on it; worth a line if this file is touched again.

**Verification:** trial-merged current `main` (union `1861f83e`, this head was 42 commits behind, no conflicts) and ran the full suite: **10354 passed, 35 skipped, 0 failed.** All 11 CI checks green.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Addressed the remaining positional-coupling finding in `865910ba3`.

`_resolve_file_tool_target` now evaluates every configured root and explicitly excludes the resolved `home_root`, rather than assuming home is element 0 via `[1:]`. Explicit `physical_roots` go through the same deduplication/filtering path, so a future ordering change cannot silently make home external or drop a real external root.

Bound validation: `tests/test_access_control.py` — **1041 passed**.

payload.title: Worklink #1389: authz: the session-boundary gh repository guard matches only literal --repo while the allowlist admits -R, and repo_review applies no repository bound to gh api/pr view/pr diff/pr checks/issue view

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes. The alias half of this is done well, and `gh api` is bound correctly — but the repository bound is skipped in the two cases that are *easier to reach* than the aliases it closes, and this PR already contains the pattern that fixes both.

## What I verified as correct

Measured against a state bound to `jasoncarreira/mimir`:

```
explicit WRONG repo --repo         -> refused
explicit WRONG repo -R             -> refused
explicit WRONG repo -Racme/widget  -> refused     (attached form)
explicit RIGHT repo                -> ADMITTED
api WRONG repo path                -> refused
api RIGHT repo path                -> ADMITTED
```

So the original defect — `-R` and `--repo=` slipping past a literal `--repo` match — is genuinely closed, in all three spellings. Driving the option table from `_GH_REPOSITORY_OPTION_FORMS` so the allowlist and the extractor cannot drift apart is the right structure.

I also confirmed this does not regress the earlier `--jq` removal: `--jq env` and even `--jq .reviews` are refused on `pr view` and `gh api` alike.

## Blocking 1: omitting the selector skips the bound entirely

The bound is gated on `repository is not None`. When no selector is present, `gh` resolves the repository from the **current directory's git remote**, and the guard never sees a cwd — `_target_matches_repo_review_shell_command(argv, review_state)` takes no cwd parameter and nothing in the repo_review path binds one.

```
NO selector, pr view      -> ADMITTED
NO selector, pr diff      -> ADMITTED
NO selector, pr checks    -> ADMITTED
NO selector, issue view   -> ADMITTED
```

This matters here specifically because the deployment configures several repository checkouts side by side — `MIMIR_FILE_TOOL_ROOTS` names `/workspace/mimir`, `/workspace/feature-factory` and others. A cwd in a different checkout reaches a different repository's PR data, which is the exact boundary this issue exists to enforce. Closing `-R` while leaving the no-selector case open closes the harder path and leaves the easier one: omitting an argument takes less than spelling it differently.

- [ ] Require a repository selector for `pr view`, `pr diff`, `pr checks` and `issue view` when a bound repository exists, rather than admitting the ambient one. That is what `gh api` already does — it has no "no path" case, so it cannot be unbound.
- [ ] If ambient resolution must stay supported, bind the cwd instead and verify it resolves to the scope's `canonical_root`. Do not leave "no selector" as a silent third state.

## Blocking 2: absent `review_state` fails open here and closed in `gh api`

The same condition also requires `review_state is not None`. With no review state:

```
gh pr view 1 --repo acme/widget    -> ADMITTED
gh api repos/acme/widget/pulls/1   -> refused
```

`gh api` fails closed because `_repositories_match(value, None)` is `False`, so an absent bound denies. `pr view` fails open because the whole comparison is skipped. Two commands in one profile disagree about what an absent bound means, and the safe answer is already implemented a few lines away.

- [ ] Make an absent `review_state` deny for every repository-scoped subcommand, matching `gh api`. If some caller legitimately has no review state and must still read, that caller deserves an explicit branch with a stated reason, not an implicit fall-through.

## Smaller point

`_gh_repository_operand` treats `-R=acme/widget` as the repository `=acme/widget`, which then fails the match and denies — correct outcome, but by accident rather than by rule. Worth rejecting a selector value beginning with `=` explicitly so the intent is legible.

The structure of this change is good and I would like it to land once the bound applies in the absent cases as well as the explicit ones.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Both blocking items are fixed correctly, and the fix is better than a per-call-site patch. Re-blocking only because the branch now conflicts with `main` and I cannot verify it as an integrated whole.

## Both items are closed by one structural change

```python
-    if (
-        repository is not None
-        and review_state is not None
-        and not _repositories_match(repository, _repo_review_bound_repository(review_state))
-    ):
+    if bind_repository and not _repositories_match(
+        repository, _repo_review_bound_repository(review_state),
+    ):
         return False
```

Removing the two `is not None` guards makes `_repositories_match` run unconditionally, and that helper already requires **both** operands to be `str`:

```python
return isinstance(left, str) and isinstance(right, str) and left.casefold() == right.casefold()
```

So a missing selector (`repository is None`) and an absent `review_state` (bound resolves to `None`) both now deny, through the same predicate rather than two separate special cases. That closes item 1 and item 2 together and leaves no third silent state, which is what I was actually worried about.

**Mutation:** restoring the old permissive condition fails both guards:

```
FAILED test_repo_review_github_reads_require_explicit_repository[gh issue view 5 --json body]
FAILED test_repo_review_github_reads_refuse_absent_review_state[gh issue view 5 --repo acme/widget --json body]
```

**And the coverage is per-subcommand, not a single representative.** Both tests are parametrized across exactly the four I named — `gh pr view`, `gh pr diff`, `gh pr checks`, `gh issue view` — and all eight parametrizations pass at baseline, so each subcommand is independently bound rather than one standing in for the rest.

`value.startswith(("-", "="))` in `_gh_repository_operand` is a good catch beyond what I asked for; `test_gh_repository_operand_rejects_equals_prefixed_short_option_value` pins it.

## Blocking: the branch conflicts with `main`

```
mergeable=CONFLICTING  state=DIRTY
commits main has beyond this head: 40
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in tests/test_access_control.py
```

`tests/test_access_control.py` has been rewritten several times today — #1729, #1730 and #1649 all landed in it, the last of those about an hour ago. The 11 green checks on `c3be5d9d5` are real but were computed against a base 40 commits back, so they say nothing about the merged result, and I cannot run a union suite against a tree that will not merge.

- [ ] Merge current `main` and resolve the `tests/test_access_control.py` conflict. Given how much of that file moved today, please re-run the four `require_explicit_repository` and four `refuse_absent_review_state` parametrizations after resolving — a conflict resolution that drops a parametrization would leave the guard live but unverified, which is the failure mode this PR is about.

No code changes requested; the security change itself is right.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The conflict resolution held under the check that mattered, and the guards still bite on the current tree.

## The resolution preserved the coverage

My concern was that resolving `tests/test_access_control.py` — a file rewritten several times today by #1729, #1730 and #1649 — could silently drop a parametrization, leaving the guard live but unverified. That is the failure mode this PR exists to prevent, so it would have been a particularly bad one to introduce while fixing it.

Re-verified on a fresh trial-merge with current `main` (union `2bd55f96`), not on the pre-merge head:

```
8/1141 tests collected     (all four subcommands x both guards)
baseline: 8 passed
mutation (restore the permissive `is not None` condition):
  FAILED ...require_explicit_repository[gh issue view 5 --json body]
  FAILED ...refuse_absent_review_state[gh issue view 5 --repo acme/widget --json body]
```

Collection surviving is not the same as enforcement surviving — a resolution can keep test *names* while breaking what they assert — so the mutation is the part that actually settles it.

## The security change itself

Unchanged from my earlier review and still right: dropping the two `is not None` guards makes `_repositories_match` run unconditionally, and since that helper requires both operands to be `str`, a missing selector and an absent `review_state` both deny through the *same* predicate rather than two special cases. No third silent state.

## On the one suite failure

The full union run reported `10361 passed, 1 failed` — `tests/test_root_dockerfile.py::test_built_image_provides_process_tools`, which builds a Docker image and hung in `subprocess.run → communicate → wait` while two Worklink builds and another suite were saturating the machine. I did not merge on the assumption that was environmental: re-run in isolation on this same union, **1 passed in 272.59s**. Slower than its 145s baseline, which is consistent with contention rather than a defect, and this PR touches only `mimir/access_control.py`.

All 11 CI checks green; `MERGEABLE`, 9 commits behind `main`.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Addressed both blocking review findings in c3be5d9d5:

- `gh pr view` / `pr diff` / `pr checks` / `issue view` in `repo_review` now require an explicit repository selector and match it against the bound `canonical_repo`; ambient-cwd repository resolution is denied.
- The same reads now fail closed when `review_state` (and therefore the repository bound) is absent, matching `gh api` behavior.
- `-R=owner/repo` and separated `-R =owner/repo` are explicitly rejected rather than denied only as a downstream mismatch.
- Added regressions for selector omission, absent review state, and the malformed short-option forms; updated existing admitted-command fixtures to carry the explicit bound.

Validation:
- `repo_test` focused `tests/test_access_control.py`: **1075 passed**.
- Deployment-configured full suite was attempted and reached 70% before the runner's 5-minute timeout; stdout had one unidentified failure marker before timeout, with no traceback/name preserved by the bounded result.
- A bounded follow-up slice outside the changed test file ran **1297 passed, 2 skipped, 1 failed**; the sole named failure is the contained-runner synthetic `/tmp` permission case in `tests/test_readonly_backend.py::TestBuildFileToolRoutes::test_non_admin_home_collections_surface_only_admitted_subtrees[tmp]`, unrelated to this authorization change.

payload.title: Worklink #1390: authz: the deliver-failure notice sends raw exception text to a chat channel unredacted, and harness_sink_allowed reads enforcement off a possibly-absent auth context so the early-crash egress cannot be blocked even under enforcement

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes on one substantive point. The change itself is correct and should land — what needs fixing is a test whose name claims a property that does not hold, because the residual gap it hides is live credentials going to a chat channel.

## What I verified as correct

**Both mutation checks reproduce**, independently:

- Reverting `mimir/harness_egress.py` to main → `test_missing_auth_context_uses_process_enforcement` and `test_missing_auth_context_disagrees_with_shadow_carrier_under_enforcement` both fail (`assert True is False`).
- Reverting `mimir/channel_registry.py` to main → `test_post_job_failure_notice_redacts_credentials` fails.

**The enforcement precedence is right.** `carrier_enforcement is not None` is the correct test rather than a truthiness check: it keeps an explicit carrier `False` authoritative and falls back to the process environment only on genuine absence. That preserves the policy-vs-fail-safe distinction — with the flag unset the early-crash egress stays shadow-only exactly as today, and under enforcement it now blocks.

**Redaction is at the right boundary.** Applying it in `channel_registry.post_job_failure_notice` means every bridge receives redacted text; doing it per-bridge would have left the next bridge to reintroduce the leak. The call-site audit in the body is also accurate — I checked `ctx` nullability at the two early-exception callers.

## Blocking: the test picks a covered credential, and four uncovered classes still reach the channel

`test_post_job_failure_notice_redacts_credentials` asserts with `[REDACTED-CREDENTIAL]`. Slack `xox[bpasr]-` **is** in `redaction._TOKEN_PATTERNS` (`redaction.py:141`), so the test passes on a class that was never in question.

Measured through this PR's own code path, using this PR's own `_bridge` helper, with the token bare in the exception text (the shape a library error actually produces):

```
xoxb (PR's test token)   redacted  | ⚠️ github-activity failed: ... token [REDACTED] for account
ghp_ (control)           redacted  | ⚠️ github-activity failed: ... token [REDACTED] for account
xapp-                    LEAKS     | ⚠️ github-activity failed: ... token xapp-1-A0LEAKPROBE1234
tvly-                    LEAKS     | ⚠️ github-activity failed: ... token tvly-dev-LEAKPROBE1234
pa-                      LEAKS     | ⚠️ github-activity failed: ... token pa-LEAKPROBE1234567890
bare JWT                 LEAKS     | ⚠️ github-activity failed: ... token eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.e
```

Two controls redact and four classes leak, so the probe discriminates. payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes. The tests here are worth keeping, but the production change is redundant and the one test that would guard the class silently tests nothing.

## 1. The production change is redundant after #1684 (blocking)

This PR was branched before #1684 (chainlink #1385) merged, and #1684 fixed this bug class generally rather than per-method.

`publish_protected_result` (`mimir/access_control.py:7728`) **mutates the shared capture object under a lock**:

```python
capture = _protected_result_provenance.get()
if isinstance(capture, _ProtectedResultCapture):
    with capture.lock:
        ...
        capture.sources.append(source)
    return
_protected_result_provenance.set(ProtectedResultProvenance(sources))   # only when no capture is active
```

`asyncio.to_thread` copies the context, but the copy holds the *same* `_ProtectedResultCapture` object — so the in-thread publish from sync `grep` (`readonly_backend.py:1409-1419`) already reaches the caller. `capture.lock` exists for exactly this cross-thread case.

Evidence, not inference: I ran **this PR's own three new tests against `main`'s unmodified `mimir/readonly_backend.py`** — all pass. Reverting only the production change breaks nothing this PR adds.

Please drop the `agrep` change and keep the tests.

## 2. `test_every_async_read_override_publishes_exact_provenance` never runs (blocking)

The parametrize filter is:

```python
and "_publish_read" in vars(_RootAwareFilesystemBackend)[name[1:]].__code__.co_names
```

`co_names` is a tuple of *exact* names — it contains `_publish_read_paths`, so `"_publish_read" in co_names` is `False` for every method. The parametrize resolves to `[]` and pytest reports:

```
SKIPPED [1] tests/test_readonly_backend.py:155: got empty parameter set for (method)
```

So the conformance test that is supposed to pin this property for *all* async read overrides is vacuous — it would pass against a completely unfixed tree. This is the only empty parameter set in the suite (`main` has zero), so it is introduced here.

Substring matching is what was intended:

```python
and any("_publish_read" in x for x in vars(_RootAwareFilesystemBackend)[name[1:]].__code__.co_names)
```

That yields `['aread', 'als', 'aglob', 'agrep']`, and with the filter repaired **all four pass on `main`'s unmodified code** — which is also the cleanest confirmation of point 1.

Worth considering a guard so an introspective parametrize that resolves empty fails instead of skipping; a silent skip is what let this through.

## 3. Rebase needed

The branch conflicts with `main` in `tests/test_readonly_backend.py` (one hunk, overlapping #1684's agrep provenance test).

## Suggested resolution

Rebase onto `main`, drop the `readonly_backend.py` change, fix the parametrize filter, keep all three tests. The result is a real regression guard for the four async overrides, which is durable value #1684 did not add.

payload.title: Worklink #1387: authz: a poller .recovery.json is writable by every other poller and replayed with extra unvalidated, so a forged stash mints a full RepoPRActionScope on an arbitrary mimir-authored PR

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Verified on substance and green.

**The replay marker cannot be suppressed by stash content.** `event.extra[POLLER_RECOVERY_REPLAY_EXTRA_KEY] = True` is a direct assignment, not a merge of recovered data, so a crafted `.recovery.json` cannot pre-set or override it.

**The one case where the marker is not stamped fails closed.** Stamping is guarded by `if isinstance(event.extra, dict)`, so a non-dict `extra` skips it — but `_repo_review_state_from_event` refuses on `not isinstance(event.extra, dict)` *before* reading anything, so that path denies rather than replaying unmarked.

**The marker check is not spoofable by a falsy value.** `event.extra.get(POLLER_RECOVERY_REPLAY_EXTRA_KEY) is not None` means a stash setting the key to `False` is still treated as a replay and rejected — the `is not None` form is the right choice over a truthiness test.

**Authority-bearing fields are cleared unconditionally**, not conditionally on parse success: `author`, `author_display`, `author_id`, `repo_pr_action_scope`, `continuation_auth_context`, `source_session_acl`. A malformed stash therefore cannot retain a stale grant by failing partway.

Full suite green on a trial-merge with current `origin/main`: **10098 passed, 35 skipped, 0 failed**. All 11 CI checks pass.

payload.title: Worklink #1386: authz: skills/ and .mimir_builtin_skills/ are trusted on read but silently unrecorded on write, so a file written during a tainted turn reads back as self-authored trusted prompt content

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The fix makes the defect impossible rather than fixing an instance of it, and the body identifies the residual honestly — which I have now filed.

**One inventory, so the lists cannot diverge again.** The defect was two root sets that had to be identical and were not. `_SELF_AUTHORED_FILE_ROOTS` as the single source for trusted reads, virtual-path remapping, *and* physical write recording removes the class, not the instance. I confirmed the writer really consults it — my mutation asserted `_SELF_AUTHORED_FILE_ROOTS` appears in `record_file_write_integrity`'s body and it does, so the "single inventory" claim is structural rather than aspirational.

Expressing the `state/pollers` carve-out once as `_FILE_INTEGRITY_EXCLUDED_SUBTREES`, and having tests derive the exclusion case from that constant, is the same discipline applied to the exception.

**Your self-reported mutation is accurate.** You wrote that with skills recording removed, the named test fails with skills rereading `(trusted, informational)` while state rereads `(untrusted, active_ingest)`. Removing `skills` from the writer's side only:

```
FAILED test_state_and_skills_tainted_writes_read_back_with_same_integrity
FAILED test_virtual_path_write_to_a_self_authored_root_is_recorded[skills]
```

Baseline 282 passed. Comparing `state/` and `skills/` against each other in one test is the right shape — it asserts the two roots *agree*, which is the actual invariant, rather than asserting a fixed label per root.

**Retaining `(trusted, informational)` for ledger-absent operator-seeded files is correct here**, and the reason you give is the right one: flipping that default would downgrade every pre-ledger operator file and needs its own migration decision.

## The residual you identified is real, and I have filed it as chainlink #1430

You flagged that the missing-ledger and absent-key defaults have the same laundering consequence for writers that bypass `record_file_write_integrity`, "notably shell writes," and scoped it out. That was the right call for this leaf, and the observation is correct. I verified it with a discriminating pair in a scratch home:

```
shell-written  skills/evil/SKILL.md  (no ledger entry)   -> ('trusted', 'informational')
same file WITH a ledger entry                            -> ('untrusted', 'active_ingest')
```

So the ledger is opt-in at the *writer*: `shell_exec` redirecting into `<home>/skills/` produces no entry, and the next read treats attacker-derived content as self-authored. The agent has shell access on this deployment, so it is reachable. Filed as **#1430** with the constraint you correctly identified — pre-ledger operator files must keep reading trusted — as the thing any fix has to design against.

**One coordination note.** This necessarily widens chainlink #1424's scope: `skills/` and `.mimir_builtin_skills/` are now recorded on write, so a tainted write into them joins the set of files that can never recover to trusted. That is not a reason to hold this — closing a laundering hole beats leaving one open because the recovery mechanism is imperfect — but #1424's fix now has two more roots to account for, and I have noted the interaction in #1430's review criteria so whichever lands second does not re-open the other.

Verification: focused information-flow suite green (282 passed), mutation confirming both named tests, full suite pending on my side. All CI checks green.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1385: authz: each backend in the composite fan-out replaces the previous read provenance, so a route matching nothing publishes the authoritative empty set and the turn takes zero taint for files it just read

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. This is the best-evidenced PR body I have reviewed in this batch, and the fix is in the safe direction on a bug whose unsafe direction matters.

**Why this one is more than an accounting fix.** With each backend in the composite fan-out *replacing* provenance, a broad `grep` spanning several routes recorded only the last route's source. So the turn's label set described a fraction of what the turn had actually read — **under**-tainting, not over-tainting. Under-tainting is the direction that permits a flow after real ingestion, which is the same failure class chainlink #1327 was about from the other end. Accumulating instead of replacing closes it.

**Your falsification claim is accurate to the detail, and I checked it.** You wrote that with the production change reverted, `test_broad_grep_provenance_covers_all_matches_in_any_route_order` fails "because the captured resource IDs contain only the last route's file rather than the home file and both route files." Reverting both production files and keeping the tests:

```
Extra items in the right set:
  …/first/first.txt
  …/home/state/home.txt
```

Only `second.txt` — the last route — was captured. That is precisely what you described. Four tests fail on the revert in total.

**And the test set discriminates.** `test_broad_glob_with_no_matches_is_authoritatively_empty` keeps **passing** under the revert, which is correct — a genuinely empty result was already handled, so that test pins pre-existing behaviour rather than the new accumulation. A test set where every test fails on any revert tells you nothing about which property is which; this one separates them.

**The mechanism is consistent with the codebase.** `_ProtectedResultCapture` as a mutable object in the ContextVar is the same shape chainlink #1327 (PR #1656) used for the refusal capture — appends to a shared object survive `contextvars` copies into threads, which is exactly what the `agrep` worker-context case needs. The `threading.Lock` covers concurrent route publication, `closed` prevents late writes after the window shuts, and `seen` dedupes so a file matched by two routes is one source rather than two.

Two design points worth crediting explicitly:

- **`invalid` on unresolvable paths.** Invalidating the whole capture when a filesystem collection cannot resolve every returned path is the fail-closed choice: a partially-resolved collection cannot be described accurately, so claiming the resolvable subset would understate the read. `test_unresolved_collection_path_invalidates_prior_route_provenance` pins it, and it fails on the revert.
- **"An empty publication remains authoritative only when no non-empty publication occurred."** That is the subtle case — a later empty route must not erase an earlier route's real sources, but a genuinely empty overall result must stay authoritative. Getting both halves right is what `test_broad_glob_and_aglob_keep_home_taint_when_last_route_is_empty` and the authoritative-empty test cover between them.

Verification: focused readonly-backend suite green (133 passed), revert-check confirming four aimed failures, full suite pending on my side. All CI checks green.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The `frontend` check is failing, and I reproduced it locally so you have the diagnosis rather than just the red tick. **The implementation looks right — the test is stale.** Please fix it in that direction, because the tempting "fix" would reintroduce a real bug. ## The failure `frontend/src/main.test.tsx:266`, deterministic (1 failed / 182 passed, identical on two runs): ``` it("returns to the login screen after clearing the key", …) await waitFor(() => expect(screen.queryByRole("link", { name: /Users/ })).toBeNull()); expect(screen.getByRole("button", { name: "Sign in" })).toBeTruthy(); // ← throws ``` The rendered DOM at that moment is: ```

Loading server auth policy…

``` So after sign-out the nav link disappears (the `waitFor` succeeds), but the app is in its bootstrap-loading state when the next assertion runs synchronously. `npx tsc --noEmit` is clean, so this is the `npm run test` step only. ## Why the implementation is right and the test is wrong This PR removes the bootstrap query's exclusion from the reset predicate: ```diff - predicate: (query) => query.queryKey[0] !== "web-bootstrap" ``` That exclusion existed because the bootstrap payload was "public server policy, not per-user data" — safe to keep across auth changes. This PR changes exactly that premise; the comment now reads "Public auth policy before login; **a credentialed request also returns UI and** …". Once the payload carries credentialed, per-user data, keeping it cached across a sign-out means a signed-out session retains the previous user's UI data. So invalidating it on auth transition is **necessary**, and an intermediate loading state after sign-out is the correct consequence. The test was written against the old caching behaviour and simply predates the change. - [ ] Fix the assertion, not the cache: `expect(await screen.findByRole("button", { name: "Sign in" })).toBeTruthy();` — await the login screen instead of asserting into the loading window. - [ ] **Do not** restore the `predicate` exclusion to make the test pass. That would re-cache credentialed UI data across a sign-out, which is a cross-user data-retention bug and strictly worse than a red test. I am flagging it explicitly because it is the shortest path to green. - [ ] While there: consider asserting the loading state is *transient* — that "Loading server auth policy…" appears and is then replaced — so the new invalidation behaviour is pinned rather than merely tolerated. Otherwise a future change that stops invalidating would pass this test again. ## The rest `pytest (3.11)`, `pytest (3.12)` and `pytest-enforced` were still pending when I looked, so I have not assessed the Python side of the five hardening items yet. I will review those once the run completes — this is only about the failing check. The `bootstrap?.server?.web_host` style optional-chaining changes throughout look like the right companion to a payload that can now be partially populated before login, rather than defensive noise.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The failing test is fixed the right way, and I have now reviewed the Python side that my last review explicitly deferred.

## The frontend fix took the correct path

```js
expect(screen.getByText("Loading server auth policy…")).toBeTruthy();
expect(await screen.findByRole("button", { name: "Sign in" })).toBeTruthy();
expect(screen.queryByText("Loading server auth policy…")).toBeNull();
```

That is the assertion fix, and it also takes the optional item I raised — the loading state is now pinned as *transient* (appears, then is replaced) rather than merely tolerated, so a future change that stops invalidating on sign-out fails here instead of quietly passing.

**And it did not take the shortcut.** The remediation commit is `frontend/src/main.test.tsx` only (+5/-2); the production `predicate: (query) => query.queryKey[0] !== "web-bootstrap"` exclusion stays removed. That was the thing I most wanted preserved, since restoring it would have re-cached credentialed UI data across a sign-out to make a test go green.

## The five hardening items (deferred from my last review)

**Bootstrap reduction is server-side, not cosmetic.** An unauthenticated caller now receives `{"version": ..., "auth": {"required": gate}}` and nothing else, with `_no_store_headers()`. I mutated each of the two gate guards **independently** — both fail `test_both_web_bootstraps_limit_unauthenticated_operator_data`, so the test genuinely covers both routes and its name is accurate rather than aspirational.

**The env-file write is textbook-correct.**

```python
fd = os.open(path, os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREAT | os.O_TRUNC, 0o600)
os.fchmod(fd, 0o600)
```

Creating with mode `0o600` means no window ever exists where the file is readable — `write_text` would have created it umask-derived, typically `0644`. And `fchmod` on the **descriptor** rather than a path-based `chmod` closes the symlink-swap race that a check-then-chmod would open; the comment shows that was deliberate. Mutation: reverting to `0o666` with no `fchmod` fails both `test_skill_env_first_write_is_owner_only_with_permissive_umask` and `test_skill_env_existing_mode_is_not_loosened`.

**The remaining three are covered by discriminating pairs** rather than single confirming probes: traversal *and* symlink-escape for channel-memory loading, credentials absent from argv *and* from the timeout message/event, and MCP config redaction *with* a round-trip so `_restore_redacted_values` is exercised rather than assumed.

Routing the ad-hoc env redaction through the shared `_redact_config_value` is the right consolidation. Worth knowing that it inherits that helper's coverage — a gap there now surfaces in this path too — but centralising is still strictly better than the bespoke marker list it replaces.

## Suite

Full suite on a trial-merge with current `main` (union `937d099b`): **10259 passed, 35 skipped, 0 failed.** All 11 CI checks green at `abe35b6f6`, verified by grouping on conclusion rather than counting failures.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1384: security: the pre-commit secret gate and secret_scan._SECRET_PATTERNS omit six credential prefixes this deployment declares, so a key pasted into a tracked note is committed and pushed to the state repo

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. This is better designed than I first credited, and finding out why produced a precise follow-up for chainlink #1391.

**Two tests, two different guarantees.** I initially assumed the parity test tied the gates only to each other, leaving both free to fall behind reality together. That is wrong — there are two properties enforced:

1. `test_module_and_pre_commit_pattern_lists_stay_in_step` asserts `module_patterns == hook_patterns` after normalizing the Python/Bash syntax differences. Gate-to-gate drift now fails a test rather than silently halving coverage.
2. `test_refusal_gate_is_not_weaker_than_redactor_for_credential_corpus` asserts, for every corpus entry, **both** `redact_text(text) != text` **and** `contains_secret(text) is True`. That is a genuine cross-module invariant — the commit gate cannot become weaker than the log redactor.

The second one is the good idea. A parity test between two copies of the same list is table stakes; pinning the gate against a *different* subsystem is what stops the two security surfaces diverging.

**Mutation-tested.** Removing only the `tvly-` pattern from the Python scanner fails three tests, including `test_contains_secret_matches_high_signal_shapes[tavily]` and `test_refusal_gate_is_not_weaker_than_redactor_for_credential_corpus[tavily]` — so both properties are load-bearing, not decorative. 337 passed otherwise.

## One precise gap, and it belongs to #1391 rather than to this PR

The corpus test cannot detect the asymmetry that matters most, because every entry is in **assignment form**:

```python
    pytest.param("TAVILY_API_KEY=tvly-dev-" + "T" * 24, id="tavily"),
    pytest.param("VOYAGE_API_KEY=pa-" + "V" * 24,      id="voyage"),
    pytest.param("GOOGLE_API_KEY=AIza" + "G" * 35,     id="google"),
```

The redactor matches those through `(?i)(token=|api[_-]?key=|password=|secret=)(…)` — the `KEY=` prefix — not through any `tvly-`/`pa-`/`AIza` pattern. Comparing the two lists directly: `secret_scan._SECRET_PATTERNS` has **22** patterns, `redaction`'s token list has **10**, and redaction has no bare-prefix entry for `tvly-`, `pa-`, `AIza`, `xapp-` or `sk-proj`.

So a **bare** token — `tvly-XXXXXXXX` sitting in prose with no `KEY=` in front of it — is blocked from a commit by this gate and still written unredacted to `events.jsonl`. That is chainlink **#1391**, now confirmed precisely rather than by inference, and narrowed: the leak is specifically the bare form, and redaction *does* already cover Slack `xox[bpasr]-` and JWTs, which I had wrongly listed as missing.

Nothing to change here — adding bare-form corpus entries would fail today, since redaction lacks those patterns. But this test is exactly the right place to enforce #1391 when it is fixed:

- [ ] Not for this PR — when #1391 lands, add bare-form entries (`"tvly-" + "T"*24`, `"pa-" + "V"*24`, `"AIza" + "G"*35`, `"xapp-" + "X"*24`) to `CREDENTIAL_CORPUS`. The existing assertion then enforces the fix permanently, and the corpus becomes the single place both surfaces are measured against.

Driving the coverage table from every `prefix:` in `mimir/credentials.yaml` is the right way to have built the list, and the suffix length floors (20+ characters after `sk-ant-`, 35 after `AIza`) are the right way to keep the gate from firing on prose containing a prefix.

Verification: focused secret-scan suite green (337 passed in the selected range), full suite pending on my side. All 11 CI checks green.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1383: security: unsanitized author_display is interpolated into the current-message prompt header and takes precedence over the resolver, letting a platform display name forge framework-authored instructions

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The resolver-first ordering is the part that makes this a real fix rather than an escaping patch.

**Preferring the server's own resolved name is the right hierarchy.** `resolver.display_name(event.author)` first, then `author_display`/`author`, then sanitize whatever was selected. Escaping platform-supplied metadata is defence in depth; *not using it when the server already knows who this is* is the actual fix. Mutation-tested: replacing the resolver call fails `test_turn_prompt_resolver_display_name_wins_and_is_sanitized`.

**The sanitizer closes the vector that matters.** I checked the mechanics rather than trusting the description:

```python
    sanitized = " ".join(str(value).split())
    sanitized = CONTROL_CHARS_RE.sub("", sanitized)
```

`str.split()` with no argument splits on `str.isspace()`, so it collapses `\n`, `\r`, `\t`, `\x0b`, `\x0c` **and** Unicode ` `/` ` — which is the primary injection shape here, since a fabricated header line needs a newline. The C0/DEL regex then catches the non-whitespace controls `split()` cannot see, notably `\x00`. The two steps are complementary and in a working order. Mutation-tested: removing the whitespace collapse fails tests in **both** renderers, so the property is pinned in the current-turn and mid-turn paths independently rather than in one and assumed in the other.

**The audit went wider than the finding.** Beyond author and `author_display`, it sanitizes `source_id`, `trigger`, `channel_id`, `saga_session_id`, and `ts` — and that last one matters more than it looks. `ts_override` comes from `event.extra`, which is client-influenceable on the HTTP ingress path, so sanitizing it closes a hole the issue never mentioned. Promoting the sanitizer to `mimir.prompt_safety` with one implementation rather than a second copy is also right; a divergent second sanitizer is how this class comes back.

Two observations, neither blocking:

- **Residual, out of scope:** the sanitizer does not strip Unicode formatting characters that are not whitespace or C0 — for example RTL override (`‮`) or zero-width joiners survive. That is a *display*-spoofing concern rather than a prompt-injection one: without newlines an injected value cannot fabricate a header block, and the model reads the codepoints rather than a rendered glyph. Worth knowing, not worth widening this change for.
- **The `mimir.feedback` compatibility re-export** is the kind of shim this codebase normally avoids on internal surfaces. It is defensible here as a module move rather than an API promise — but if `mimir.feedback` has few importers of that symbol, updating them and dropping the re-export would leave one import path instead of two.

Verification: focused prompts and mid-turn-injection suites green (126 passed), full suite pending on my side. All CI checks green.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1382: saga: three low-severity items - divergent test-only consolidate emit path, session dedup not owner-scoped, mark_contributions reporting credit it did not write

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. Three separate items, each fixed at the structural level rather than the instance, and the transaction audit is unusually careful.

**Item: the divergent consolidation path.** Rather than porting retry-repair and tombstoning into the weaker path, you extracted `emit_observation()` and had both `consolidate.consolidate()` and `SagaStore._restructure` delegate to it. That is the fix that prevents recurrence — two paths that must agree become one.

**I verified the claim the no-repair-sweep decision rests on.** You argue no sweep is needed because "the weaker standalone path is test-only and has no production callers." That holds: every reference to `consolidate()` in `mimir/` is a **comment** — `__init__.py:40`, `client.py:22/368/549/740/1725` are all prose mentions — while production goes through `SagaStore.consolidate()` (`client.py:1666`) into `_restructure` (`:2044`), which already had the repair. So no production data passed through the weak path and there is nothing to sweep. That was load-bearing for skipping a migration and it is correct.

Also right to call out `consolidate_skill_memories()` as a *third* consolidation loop that does not share the window, because it only does ACL-partitioned raw-atom dedup and emits no synthesized observations. Naming a third path and explaining why it is exempt is better than implying there were only two.

**Item: the blind rollback.** The `began` flag is the correct shape and matches what `client._record_access_events` and `forget.forget_by_criteria` already do, so the codebase now handles this one way rather than two:

```python
        began = False
            began = True
        except ...:
            if began:
                conn.rollback()
```

Mutation-tested: restoring the unconditional `conn.rollback()` fails `test_mark_contributions_does_not_rollback_callers_transaction` — named for the property, and it asserts the caller's transaction survives rather than just that no exception escaped.

Adding `credit_written: bool` to the result was not asked for and is the better half of the fix: a caller can now distinguish "credit written" from "rolled back", where before both returned the same shape. `test_mark_contributions_failed_write_reports_no_credit` pins it.

**The transaction-ownership audit is the strongest part.** It splits the surface three ways — changed because this issue executes them (`mark_contributions`, all three `store.store` transactions, both `emit_observation` transactions), already guarded (`_record_access_events`, `forget_by_criteria`), and out of scope with a reason each (`resolve_contradictions_to_supersedes`, `repair_world_state_dual_current`, both `dedup` writes, `calibration`, `mark_negative_outcomes`, `reflect`, `recall`, `refresh_trend`). And it states the condition under which the out-of-scope ones would need the same guard: "their current callers do not supply caller-owned transactions; each would need the same ownership guard if its transaction contract changes." That sentence is what makes the audit reusable instead of a one-time list.

`legacy_acl_migration` is correctly excluded for a structural reason rather than a stylistic one — its `BEGIN` sits outside the handler, so a failed begin cannot reach that rollback at all.

Verification: focused phase2, tier2b and correctness-regression suites green (69 passed), full suite green on a trial-merge with `origin/main` — 10054 passed, 35 skipped, python 3.12. All 11 CI checks green.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1380: tools: set_poller_overrides persists an unvalidated env map that survives the turn and hijacks later poller subprocesses via PATH/BASH_ENV under the poller service identity

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The allowlist design is right and the asymmetry at its heart is both correct and tested.

**The asymmetry is the good idea.** `POLLER_OVERRIDE_PASS_ENV_KEYS = POLLER_OVERRIDE_ENV_KEYS | {...}` encodes that `env` must be *narrower* than `pass_env`, because `env` lets the agent supply a literal value while `pass_env` only lets it select a name whose value stays operator-controlled. So `GITHUB_REPOS` is safe to pass through and unsafe to author — the agent could otherwise point a poller at a repository of its choosing. That distinction is easy to miss and the comment states it exactly: "Scope selectors are safe here but not as agent-provided literals."

**Mutation-tested on precisely that.** Widening `env` to use the `pass_env` allowlist fails `test_validate_poller_overrides_text_rejects_literal_scope_selectors` for both `[GITHUB_REPOS]` and `[GOG_ACCOUNT]` — so the invariant is pinned per selector, not just in aggregate.

**The `env` set is genuinely non-secret.** All four entries are numeric tuning knobs — `MIMIR_GMAIL_MAX_FETCH`, `MIMIR_SOCIAL_FEED_LIMIT`, `MIMIR_SOCIAL_LIMIT`, `WORKLINK_MAX_CONCURRENT`. No paths, no hosts, no credentials. Rejecting the *entire* write on any disallowed name rather than filtering is also right: a partially-applied override is worse than a refused one, and the error names both the offending keys and the allowed set.

**On values rather than names — I checked, and key-only validation is sufficient here.** The validation inspects keys, never values, which made me look at the consumers:

- `MIMIR_GMAIL_MAX_FETCH`: `try: int(...) except (TypeError, ValueError): default`, then `max(1, min(max_fetch, 200))`. Defaulted and clamped.
- `WORKLINK_MAX_CONCURRENT`: the orchestrator returns `WorklinkConfig.load(config).defaults.max_concurrent` when `worklink.yaml` exists and never consults the variable — and this deployment has `max_concurrent: 2`, so it is inert here. Only a YAML-less deployment reaches the env path, where `int()` is guarded and `parsed > 0` enforced but no upper bound applies. That missing ceiling is pre-existing in the poller script and outside this PR; worth knowing, not worth blocking.

**The file-integrity exemption claim is correct, and I verified it rather than taking it.** You argue `pollers-overrides.yaml` needs no file-integrity record because it is never surfaced as a trusted filesystem result. That holds: it lives at `<home>/pollers-overrides.yaml`, so `relative.parts[0]` is the filename itself and not one of the trusted-on-read roots (`.mimir_builtin_skills`, `docs`, `memory`, `prompts`, `skills`, `state`). Probed against the live resolver:

```
/mimir-home/pollers-overrides.yaml            -> ('untrusted', 'active_ingest')
/mimir-home/.mimir_builtin_skills/…/SKILL.md  -> ('trusted',   'informational')   ← control
```

The control returning trusted is what makes that meaningful rather than a vacuous "everything is untrusted." So a record really would have no consumer, and auditing the mutation as a `set_poller_overrides` scheduler sink instead is the right place for it. That reasoning also keeps it clear of the laundering asymmetry chainlink #1386 is about.

Keeping discovery-time `load_poller_overrides` lenient is correct too — a strict reader would let one malformed override stop every poller, which is a worse failure than ignoring a bad entry.

Verification: focused poller-override tests green (35 passed with the mutation reverted), full suite pending on my side. All CI checks green.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1381: tools: _validate_public_host category deny-list admits 100.64.0.0/10, so fetch_url can reach CGNAT and Tailscale hosts on the internal network

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The one-line fix is the right *kind* of fix, and the test set covers the bypass I would have gone looking for.

**Why `is_global` is better than adding one more category.** I tested the predicate directly, and it shows exactly why the original enumeration missed this:

```
100.64.0.1       is_global=False  is_private=False   ← RFC 6598, the finding
10.0.0.1         is_global=False  is_private=True
127.0.0.1        is_global=False  is_private=True
169.254.1.1      is_global=False  is_private=True
8.8.8.8          is_global=True   is_private=False   ← still allowed
140.82.114.4     is_global=True   is_private=False   ← github.com, still allowed
```

Carrier-grade NAT space is **neither private nor global** — it sits in the gap between the two, which is why a deny-list of private/loopback/link-local fell straight through it. `not ip.is_global` closes the gap by construction rather than by appending the one range we happened to notice, so the next special-purpose allocation is covered without another patch. And it does not over-block: real public v4 and v6 destinations still pass.

**The IPv4-mapped IPv6 bypass is covered**, which is the thing I checked before anything else — `::ffff:100.64.0.1` would let an attacker re-express the same address as IPv6 and slip a v4-only check. `is_global` delegates to the mapped address:

```
::ffff:100.64.0.1   is_global=False  (maps to 100.64.0.1, its is_global=False)
::ffff:8.8.8.8      is_global=True   (maps to 8.8.8.8, its is_global=True)
::1                 is_global=False
fc00::1             is_global=False
```

Your parameterized cases include `("::ffff:100.64.0.1", False)`, so that is pinned rather than incidentally correct.

**Mutation-tested.** Removing the check fails four tests, including all three shared-space forms and the redirect path:

```
test_public_address_verdicts[100.64.0.1-False]
test_public_address_verdicts[100.127.255.254-False]
test_public_address_verdicts[::ffff:100.64.0.1-False]
```

Baseline 73 passed.

**The symmetric audit draws the right axis.** Leaving `webhook` and `http_request` alone because they use explicit operator URL approvals and *intentionally* permit operator-selected internal destinations is correct — the distinction that matters for an SSRF screen is "agent-selected arbitrary host" versus "operator-approved host," not "internal versus external." Likewise the bridge attachment downloads are hostname-allowlisted against platform CDNs and reject IP literals, and the GitHub poller builds a fixed `api.github.com`. Each exemption is a property of that call site rather than a blanket claim.

Testing the redirect path through `_SSRFCheckingRedirectHandler` rather than only the initial destination is also the right choice — a redirect is how this class is usually reached in practice.

Verification: focused web-tools suite green (73 passed), full suite green on a trial-merge with `origin/main`, python 3.12. All CI checks green.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1378: tools: an untrusted skill learning injected as an INFORMATIONAL source satisfies memory_store non-empty-sources test without tripping the untrusted test, so restating it persists as Integrity.TRUSTED

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. A one-line fix that decouples two axes that should never have been conflated.

```diff
-        and not labels.has_untrusted_active_ingest
+        and all(source.integrity == Integrity.TRUSTED for source in labels.sources)
```

`has_untrusted_active_ingest` requires **both** `integrity == UNTRUSTED` **and** `integrity_effect == ACTIVE_INGEST`, so an untrusted source carrying an `informational` effect sailed through and its restatement was persisted as trusted. The integrity axis governs whether content may be *believed*; the effect axis governs whether it *gates sinks*. Reading the second to answer the first was the bug, and this reads the right one.

**No vacuous truth.** `all(...)` over an empty list is `True`, which would have made a source-less turn trusted — the obvious way to get this wrong. The guard is there: `labels.sources` precedes the `all(...)` in the same condition. It also matches the existing idiom in `record_file_write_integrity` (`if sources and all(source.integrity == "trusted" ...)`), so the codebase now decides this the same way in both places.

**Mutation-tested, both halves, each caught by an aimed test:**

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| Revert to `not labels.has_untrusted_active_ingest` | `test_memory_store_stamps_untrusted_for_any_untrusted_source_effect[**informational**]` FAILED |
| Drop the non-empty `labels.sources` guard | `test_memory_store_empty_labels_stamp_untrusted` FAILED |

The `[informational]` parameter is the laundering case itself, so the new test targets the exact hole rather than the general area. And the empty-sources trap turns out to be covered by a **pre-existing** test — good, that is the kind of guard that should already be there.

**The #948 trade-off is correctly preserved.** Auto-recalled sources stay `INFORMATIONAL`, untrusted ones included, so recalled facts still do not handcuff the turn at sink gates. The change only affects what gets *written* as trusted. Keeping the read-side leniency while closing the write-side laundering is the distinction that makes this safe rather than a blanket tightening — and it is stated explicitly rather than left for a reviewer to infer.

Forward-only is honestly scoped: atoms keep `origin_trigger`, `origin_ref` and writer provenance, but writes do not retain the source-integrity set that would be needed to decide which existing atoms were laundered, so a retrospective reclassification cannot be done accurately. Saying that plainly is better than a heuristic sweep over the memory store.

Verification: focused skill-memory, injection and write-provenance suites green (63 passed), full suite green on a trial-merge with `origin/main`, python 3.12. All CI checks green.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1364: worklink: mimir worklink stop looks up the factory record under the bare issue id while the orchestrator saves it under chainlink-<id>, so stopping a live epic is impossible

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The centralization is the right fix and the reader inventory is thorough. Verified first:

- **Key derivation now goes through the production formatter.** `load_factory_records_for_issue` derives the canonical key via `epic_run_id`, the same function production writes with, instead of a hand-built `f"chainlink-{issue_id}"`. I checked that exactly one construction site remains — inside `epic_run_id` itself — and it validates against `_RUN_ID` and guards `isinstance(issue_id, bool)` (needed, since `True <= 0` is False and a bool would slip a naive check). Given that chainlink #1355 was an id-formatting collision that cost a whole debugging arc, having one validating formatter is exactly right.
- Replacing the duplicated `{str(issue_id), f"chainlink-{issue_id}"}` literal with `factory_record_run_ids(...)` removes a two-places-must-agree hazard.
- The stop path now selects a *verified-live* record rather than blindly the bare key, which is the actual bug.
- **Mutation-tested where it bites:** reading only the canonical key (dropping legacy) fails `test_issue_lookup_reads_both_keys_without_legacy_shadowing_canonical` and `test_worklink_archive_factory_run_cli_archives_canonical_and_legacy_records`.

One item.

## The tie-break is unverified, and the test named for it does not test it

```python
    records.sort(
        key=lambda record: (record.attempt, record.run_id == canonical),
        reverse=True,
    )
```

I inverted that secondary key so **legacy wins an attempt tie** instead of canonical:

```python
        key=lambda record: (record.attempt, record.run_id != canonical),
```

**34 passed, 3 skipped — nothing caught it.** So the "canonical on ties" behaviour promised by the docstring, and named in `test_issue_lookup_reads_both_keys_without_legacy_shadowing_canonical`, is not actually pinned. That test proves both keys are *read*; it does not prove which one *wins* when they collide.

Worth being precise about why, because my first mutation was a no-op and I had to re-aim. Removing the secondary key entirely also changes nothing — the list is built `for run_id in (canonical, legacy)` and Python's `sort` is stable (`reverse=True` does not reverse ties), so canonical already wins by construction. That means the explicit tie-break is currently **redundant with the list order**, which is fine as defensive intent but has two consequences: reordering that tuple silently changes which record wins, and inverting the key silently changes it too. Neither is caught.

The colliding case is reachable and is the whole reason this PR exists — a store can hold `<id>` and `chainlink-<id>` for the same issue, and if both are at the same attempt the tie-break decides which record `stop` cancels and which `archive` treats as primary. Picking the wrong one there is the same family of failure as #1355.

- [ ] A test with both key shapes present **at the same attempt**, asserting the canonical record is returned first. That is one fixture and it makes the documented invariant real.
- [ ] Decide whether to keep the explicit tie-break or rely on list order, and make the choice visible. If you keep it, the test above is what stops it drifting; if you drop it, a comment on the list construction should say that its order *is* the tie-break.

Everything else is verified. Full suite running on my side.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The one-line change is the right change, and it fixes a real confound. Re-blocking because a second confound is still standing between the test and the invariant it is named for — but the remaining ask is small, and one of the two ways to close it is a comment.

## What the fix genuinely improved

```python
-        attempt=2,
+        attempt=legacy.attempt,
```

Before this, the two records differed in `attempt`, so "canonical came back first" was fully explained by the attempt ordering — the tie-break could have been deleted and the test would not have noticed. Equalising the attempt removes that, and it is exactly the fixture change I asked for.

## Blocking: the list order is a second mechanism producing the same result

```python
records = [record for run_id in (canonical, legacy) if ...]
records.sort(key=lambda record: (record.attempt, record.run_id == canonical), reverse=True)
```

The list is built canonical-first, and Python's sort is stable — equal keys keep their original order, and `reverse=True` does not reverse equal elements. So with attempts now equal, canonical comes first whether or not the tie-break exists. Three mutations, run against the new head:

```
A  tie-break removed, list built (canonical, legacy)   ->  1 passed
B  tie-break kept,    list built (legacy, canonical)   ->  1 passed
C  tie-break removed, list built (legacy, canonical)   ->  1 FAILED
```

So the test is not vacuous — C proves it detects the state where neither mechanism holds. But A shows the explicit tie-break can be deleted with the suite still green, which is the same sentence I wrote last time about `attempt`. The documented invariant ("newest attempt first and canonical on ties") is still carried entirely by a redundancy no test can see.

That matters here specifically because the failure this PR exists to prevent is *legacy shadowing canonical*. It now takes two independent edits to reintroduce it — reorder the list construction, and drop the "redundant" tie-break — and neither edit fails anything on its own. Two-step silent regressions are the ones that actually happen, because the first step looks harmless and the second looks like cleanup.

Either of these closes it, and I am happy with the cheaper one:

- [ ] **Document the redundancy** — a comment on the list construction saying the `(canonical, legacy)` order is deliberate and the sort tie-break is belt-and-braces, so a future reader reordering it knows the tie-break is what keeps them safe. This was the second half of my previous item ("make the choice visible") and it costs one line.
- [ ] **Or isolate the tie-break** — drive `load_factory_records_for_issue` with the list order reversed (or assert on the sort key directly) so mutation A fails. Stronger, and it makes the invariant real rather than documented.

Nothing else here needs changing; the both-keys read and the non-shadowing behaviour are correct, and CI is 9 green with 2 still running as I write this.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. You took the cheaper of the two options I offered, which I said I would accept, and the wording does more work than the minimum would have.

```python
# Canonical-first construction is deliberate: it is a stable-sort fallback for
# the explicit canonical tie-break below, not an interchangeable iteration order.
records = [record for run_id in (canonical, legacy) ...]
records.sort(key=lambda record: (record.attempt, record.run_id == canonical), reverse=True)
```

The reason this is the right note rather than a box-tick: it names the **relationship** between the two mechanisms instead of just asserting the order matters. "Stable-sort fallback for the explicit tie-break below" tells a future reader both that reordering the list is not free *and* that the tie-break is what keeps them safe if they do. That is precisely the two-step regression I was worried about — reorder the construction, then delete the tie-break as redundant, with nothing failing in between.

For the record on what I measured before: with attempts equalised, mutation A (drop the tie-break, keep canonical-first) passed and mutation B (keep the tie-break, build legacy-first) passed, while mutation C (both) failed. So the redundancy is real, neither mechanism is individually pinned, and documenting it was a legitimate resolution — the alternative was restructuring the function purely to make a test observable.

The earlier `attempt=legacy.attempt` fix stands as the more important half: before it, the differing attempt was doing the work and the tie-break could have been deleted without the test noticing at all.

**Integration:** `main` is an ancestor and this head is **0 commits behind**, so the 11 green checks are the integrated result, not a stale-base green. Focused run of the touched file: 13 passed.
