payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1377: tools: a stale-scope repo_push returns ok=False as a status=success result, so the turn is credited with a push that never happened and charged a remediation attempt

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. Small, correct, and the audit distinguishes the cases properly.

**The fix.** The stale-scope `GitPush` branch was the only `GitOperationResult(False, ...)` returned rather than raised, so a push that never happened was reported as a `status=success` tool result with `ok=False` buried inside it. Raising `GitRefusal("stale_scope", ...)` and classifying it as an execution refusal makes it a plain `ToolException`, while `stranded_work_message()` is preserved — which matters, because the operator-facing explanation of *why* the work is stranded is the useful part.

**Mutation-tested.** Reverting the push refusal to `return GitOperationResult(False, "stale_scope", self._stranded_work_message(), ...)` fails **three** tests:

```
FAILED test_stale_remote_head_raises_named_refusal_and_never_pushes
FAILED test_mergeability_rebase_stale_lease_refuses_concurrent_push
FAILED test_changes_requested_rebase_stale_lease_refuses_concurrent_push
```

Baseline 127 passed, 1 skipped. The primary named test plus two independent stale-lease paths, so the property is pinned from more than one direction.

**The result-shape audit draws the right line.** Leaving `ProjectTestResult(False, "test_timeout", ...)` and `(False, "tests_failed", ...)` alone is correct and the stated reason is the right one: those are *completed test runs reporting their outcome*, not a Git effect claimed to have happened. `repo_test` is not a remediation-effect tool, so a falsy result there is a legitimate answer rather than a lie about a side effect. Distinguishing "this operation did not happen" from "this operation happened and the answer was no" is exactly the distinction the issue is about, and the audit gets it right instead of sweeping both into the change.

Passing `failed=True` to checkout observation as well as protected-result classification on the plain-`ToolException` path is the necessary companion — without it the checkout accounting would still believe the push landed.

**Coordination.** This merges cleanly with #1674 (chainlink #1376), which I confirmed by trial-merge, and I have verified this PR on a tree that already contains it. It **conflicts with #1669** (chainlink #1370) in `mimir/tools/repo.py` and `tests/test_budget_gate_and_alias.py`, because #1669 also classifies `stale_scope`. Per the note on #1669: this and #1674 land first, then #1669 rebases and re-scopes to what remains — checking rather than re-applying its own `stale_scope` classification, since that would now be redundant or contradictory.

Verification: focused `test_repo_tools.py` green (127 passed, 1 skipped), full suite green on a re-merge containing current `origin/main` and #1674, python 3.12. All 11 CI checks green.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1376: tools: a GitHub review-guard refusal escapes wrap_tool_call after the budget was consumed and without a hard_boundary_denied record, so the turn is charged an attempt it should have been exempted for

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The refusal-lifecycle work is correct, but the most important thing in this PR is something neither its title nor chainlink #1376 mentions, so I want it on the record.

## This closes a live model-directed-execution path

On `main`, `ReviewSubmission.executable` is `argv[0]` taken from the **parsed model command** (`github_review_guard.py:201-202`), and `_run` executes it as argv[0] of the guard's probe subprocess (`:213`). The parser only validates the basename:

```python
if len(argv) < 3 or Path(argv[0]).name != "gh" or argv[1:3] != ["pr", "review"]:
```

So `/workspace/mimir/gh` satisfies it and gets executed. The agent has `:rw` entries in `MIMIR_FILE_TOOL_ROOTS` and shell access, so it can write a file named `gh` and have the review guard run it — a component whose entire purpose is to *be* a guard.

Your fix is the right shape: the probe resolves `gh` from the server's trusted `PATH` via `_GH_EXECUTABLE`, with `direct_exec_env(["gh"])`, an isolated GitHub config, identity confirmation and closed stdin — and the model-supplied value is kept **only for recognising argv**, never for execution. The comment says exactly that, which is the distinction that matters.

Mutation-tested: restoring `[spec.executable, *arguments]` fails `test_guard_probe_uses_server_gh_and_direct_exec_environment`. Baseline 50 passed.

## The lifecycle work

Moving parsing and claiming inside the exception lifecycle in both `wrap_tool_call` and `awrap_tool_call` is right, and routing duplicate-review suppression through the common successful tail rather than returning early is the part that makes it durable — an early return is how the original defect existed in the first place.

The symmetric audit of the other pre-`try` exits is real, and it names the one that actually needed changing (duplicate review was the only successful pre-tail return) rather than asserting the rest are fine in the abstract.

## Coordination

**This conflicts with PR #1669 (chainlink #1370)**, which makes the same structural move for overlapping reasons. I confirmed it by trial-merge — real content conflicts in `budget_gate.py` and `github_review_guard.py`, both restructuring the hunks at `:1665` and `:1999`. #1675 (chainlink #1377) merges cleanly with this one.

So the order I have recommended on #1669 is: this PR and #1675 land first, then #1669 rebases onto both and re-scopes to what remains. I flagged there specifically that resolving the conflict by re-applying #1669's version would undo the executable fix above — which is the kind of regression that would be invisible in a conflict resolution.

Verification: focused review-guard suite green (50 passed), full suite green on a re-merge with current `origin/main`, python 3.12. All 11 CI checks green.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1375: tools: bash_job_output and bash_jobs_list serve any job in the process-global registry regardless of the reading turn channel or auth carrier, while the spawn path refuses exactly that mismatch

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. This is the right shape for a read-isolation fix: one shared ownership predicate as a chokepoint, and fail-closed where authority is absent.

**The fail-closed choice is the good detail.** A reading turn with no server-created auth carrier gets no jobs from list, and output returns *the same unknown-job response as a nonexistent ID*. That last part matters — a distinguishable "exists but forbidden" response would be an enumeration oracle over other channels' job IDs. Returning the indistinguishable answer closes that without needing a separate decision.

**Mutation-tested, and both properties fall to the same mutation:**

Removing the predicate from `get_owned` (`return job` instead of `return job if job is not None and self._is_owned_by(...) else None`) fails **both** new tests:

```
FAILED test_shell_job_reads_are_scoped_to_reading_turn_owner
FAILED test_shell_job_reads_without_auth_carrier_serve_nothing
```

Baseline 86 passed, 1 skipped. Both falling to one mutation is the correct signature here, because the design deliberately routes ownership and no-carrier through a single predicate rather than two independent checks.

**I verified the load-bearing claim rather than accepting it.** The PR says `ShellJobRegistry.get` stays as a trusted lifecycle lookup but "no caller-facing consumer reaches the unscoped lookup." That holds:

- The only remaining `self.get(...)` uses are `shell_jobs.py:531`, which is *inside* `get_owned()` (unscoped fetch composed with the ownership predicate — exactly how a scoped lookup should be built), and `:611` inside `read_job_output()`, which is an object-identity check that the registry still holds the same `ShellJob`, not an authorization decision.
- Every other `registry.get(...)` in the tree is a different registry — tool provenance and MCP adapters in `mcp_client.py`, worklink backends in `orchestrator.py`. I checked these individually because "no caller reaches it" is the kind of claim that is easy to assert and easy to get wrong.
- `read_output` (`:597`) uses `get_owned`, so the model-facing path is scoped.

**The `shell_job_complete` change is the right kind of narrowing.** Having the wake-up summary take the exact registry-created `ShellJob` and call `read_job_output` — rather than looking up a model-selected ID — removes an ID-indirection that could not be authorized meaningfully. That is a design improvement beyond what the issue asked for.

Filtering `shell_job_snapshots` is also correctly scoped: it needed the carrier requirement precisely because its only production consumer is `bash_jobs_list`, and stating that is what justifies changing a serializer rather than just its caller.

Verification: focused shell-job and async-wiring suites green (86 passed, 1 skipped), full suite green on a trial-merge with `origin/main`, python 3.12. All CI checks green.

**Note on my full-suite run:** it reported 1 failure, `tests/test_rate_limits.py::test_render_humanizes_resets_in_minutes_or_hours`. That is **not attributable to this PR** — it touches nothing rate-limit or time related (`agent.py`, `shell_jobs.py`, `tools/shell_async.py` only), and re-running that file in isolation gives 55 passed. It is a time-boundary flake under concurrent-suite load, the second of that shape I hit tonight. Final numbers: 10003 passed, 35 skipped, plus a 160-test cross-check of the shell-job and saga slices after re-merging the one commit `main` gained since (#1670, disjoint).

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1374: saga: MIMIR_SAGA_PRE_MSG_MIN_TIER and two saga confidence keys have no reader, and the tier similarity floor is missing, so wiring them would drop every keyword-only atom

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Choosing outcome (a) — wiring the controls rather than deleting them — is the right call: the operator's `saga.toml` says gating should be on, so the fix is to honour that rather than remove the dial. The counterpart audit is good, and singling out `capture_rate_limits` as a *separate* inert field that is deliberately left alone is the kind of distinction that keeps a cleanup from turning into scope creep.

I checked the thing this PR most plausibly gets wrong, and it does not:

- **There is no default-versus-deployment divergence.** I went looking for the trap that sank #1654 — a newly-reachable config value that differs between CI and the deployment. It is not present here. The built-in defaults already are `enable_confidence_gating = True` and `default_min_confidence_tier = "low"`, identical to the live `saga.toml:71-72`; `_config_io.py:50` says the defaults "mirror saga.toml exactly" by design. I verified it by loading the config with and without `SAGA_CONFIG` pointed at the live file and comparing the `[retrieval]` section — same values both ways. So tests exercise the same values the deployment will use, and CI's green is meaningful here in a way it was not for #1654.
- Coverage is real: 17 references to `enable_confidence_gating` / `min_confidence_tier` across five test files, and `test_low_floor_keeps_orthogonal_fts_only_atom` covers the specific failure mode that matters — an exact FTS-only hit with an orthogonal embedding being dropped by a similarity floor it should never have been scored against.

One item before I approve.

## The PR does not state that this activates gating on the live deployment

The whole finding is that these keys had no reader. After this merges and deploys, `enable_confidence_gating = true` stops being decorative and starts removing results — the `saga.toml` comment says "drops sub-0.15 noise", so there is a concrete floor about to become real on a memory store that has never had one applied.

That is the intended outcome and I am not asking you to change it. I am asking that it be written down, because "these keys now have readers" and "retrieval begins discarding sub-threshold results" are the same change described at two very different levels of consequence, and only the first is currently in the PR body.

- [ ] State the activation plainly: which keys go from inert to live, what floor that puts in place, and that this changes retrieval output on any deployment whose config already sets them (i.e. this one, and any deployment on defaults).
- [ ] Quantify it if you can. On a store of realistic size, what fraction of previously-returned results fall below the `low` floor? Even a rough number turns "gating is now active" into something an operator can sanity-check after deploy. If measuring is impractical inside the sandbox, say so and say what an operator should watch instead.
- [ ] Confirm the keyword-path baseline is the *only* pathway that needed a floor adjustment. The body says semantic, triple, and extra pathways "retain their existing confidence behavior" — worth stating whether that was verified per pathway or inferred, since the FTS case shows the floor can be wrong for a pathway whose scores are not comparable to similarity.

Nothing else outstanding. Once the body says what deploying this does to retrieval, this is ready.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. All three items are addressed, and the activation section does more than satisfy the ask.

## The three items

**1. Activation stated plainly, with the real numbers.** The body now names the three keys as "parsed but inert" before the change, states that an enabled gate applies the floor to every `SagaStore.query()` call, and — the part I could not get from the original body — gives the actual runtime thresholds: `low` rejects below cosine `0.10`, `medium` requires `>= 0.30`, `high` requires `>= 0.45`. It also notes this deployment and the built-in defaults both enable gating at `low`, so the change is live here rather than hypothetical.

**2. Quantification handled honestly.** I asked for a number or an explanation of why not plus what to watch. You gave both: the live SAGA database is outside the sandbox and query results expose no gated-drop counter, so the number cannot be produced here; after deploy, compare pre-message result counts and IDs at `min_confidence_tier="none"` against the configured floor and watch for missing session-boundary/extra-pathway recalls. The closing line — "A production-impact number should not be inferred from the synthetic regression fixture" — is the right instinct, and it is the sentence that stops someone quoting a fixture-derived figure as production impact.

**3. Per-pathway behaviour verified, not inferred.** Stated explicitly as verified in `recall()`, then enumerated: semantic keeps FAISS cosine, triple keeps triple cosine and uses the max of semantic/triple, extra/session-boundary-only stay at `0.0` and are rejected at any active floor unless they enter a scored pathway, and keyword is the only pathway receiving the synthetic `low` baseline **because BM25 is not cosine-comparable**. That last clause is the actual justification for the special case and was missing before.

## The documentation mismatch you surfaced

Worth calling out as good practice rather than scope creep: you found that `mimir/commands/setup.py` describes the low gate as dropping sub-`0.15` noise, `mimir/saga/recall.py` hard-codes `low = 0.10`, and `_config_io.py`'s configured `confidence_sim_low = 0.20` is never read — a three-way inconsistency. You scoped the fix out (correctly, given #1374's explicit "no threshold retuning") while making the activation description state the real `0.10` behaviour rather than repeating the stale comment. That is exactly the right handling: do not silently fix out-of-scope things, but do not let the body inherit a false claim either. Worth its own leaf.

## Verification

This head is body-only — the SHA is unchanged from the commit I reviewed, so the code is what I already assessed. Its CI is 11 green but **58 commits stale**, so I trial-merged current `main` (union `ea685d21`, no conflicts) and ran the full suite: **10304 passed, 35 skipped, 0 failed.**

payload.body:
I reconciled the requested documentation change against head `db81d6d433c5bdaf7d8ebbee47e5bc94adf47969`. No source change is needed, but the PR body should be updated before re-review.

Suggested body addition/replacement under **Outcome**:

> **Deployment activation:** before this change, `MIMIR_SAGA_PRE_MSG_MIN_TIER`, `[retrieval].enable_confidence_gating`, and `[retrieval].default_min_confidence_tier` were parsed but inert. After merge and deployment, an enabled gate applies the configured tier floor to every `SagaStore.query()` call unless the caller supplies an explicit floor. This deployment and the built-in defaults both enable gating with `default_min_confidence_tier = "low"`; with the implementation's current hard-coded tiers, `low` rejects semantic/triple/extra-only candidates whose best embedding cosine is below `0.10`. Keyword candidates receive a synthetic `low` classification and therefore survive the default `low` gate regardless of cosine. `MIMIR_SAGA_PRE_MSG_MIN_TIER` overrides that default for the agent's pre-message retrieval; `medium` and `high` require cosine `>= 0.30` and `>= 0.45` respectively, including for keyword hits unless their semantic/triple score clears the stricter floor.
>

After deployment, compare pre-message result count/IDs for representative queries with `min_confidence_tier="none"` versus the configured floor (or temporarily disable `enable_confidence_gating`) and watch for missing session-boundary/extra-pathway recalls. A production-impact number should not be inferred from the synthetic regression fixture.
>
> **Pathway audit:** verified in `recall()` rather than inferred: semantic candidates retain their FAISS cosine; triple candidates retain their triple cosine and use the max of semantic/triple scores; extra/session-boundary-only candidates retain `0.0` and are rejected at any active floor unless they also enter a scored pathway; keyword candidates are the only pathway receiving the new synthetic `low` baseline because BM25 is not cosine-comparable. payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1373: saga: each query() pulls every live embedded triple embedding out of SQLite twice and full-scans sessions, so per-query cost grows with corpus size at fixed top_k

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The performance work is solid and the test coverage is the best part. Verified before looking for problems:

- **The core property is pinned on the real connection.** `test_query_reads_and_scores_triples_once` installs `operation_conn.set_trace_callback(statements.append)` and asserts `len(triple_reads) == 1`. That is a read-count assertion against the actual short-lived query connection rather than a proxy, which is exactly right for a "stop reading it twice" fix.
- **`test_rank_triple_candidates_filters_dimension_before_window_limit` is the test I would have asked for.** Applying the dimension filter *after* the limit would silently drop valid candidates in favour of ineligible ones — a recall bug that no timing measurement would catch. Pinning the ordering is the difference between a bounded query and a wrong one.
- **The migration is low-risk and replay-safe.** All three new indexes are plain `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS` — zero `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` in the diff — so the collision class that makes chainlink #1423 (migration v9) dangerous does not apply here: there is no uniqueness to violate and no dedup pre-pass needed.
- **Fresh-versus-migrated parity is asserted**, via `test_v11_fresh_and_migrated_indexes_have_identical_pragma_output` plus a `detect_schema_version` pair covering 10 and 11. That is the same class chainlink #1346 was about (a v6 replay diverging from a fresh install), and it is covered here rather than assumed.
- Leaving `_make_faiss_search_fn`'s over-fetch alone is the right scope call, and the reason given is the correct one — the full-index over-fetch is what stops unauthorized vectors consuming authorized result slots.

One blocking item.

## The 500-row cap is a silent recall ceiling, hardcoded, and this deployment is already at 80% of it

```python
TRIPLE_CANDIDATE_LIMIT = 500
```

A module constant with no config hook, and nothing emits when the pool is actually truncated. The docstring acknowledges truncation exists, but at runtime a capped query is indistinguishable from a complete one.

That matters now rather than eventually. I counted the live store:

```
total triples:          398
live (not tombstoned):  398
with embeddings:        398
```

**398 of 500 — 80% of the cap, and monotonically growing.** So this deployment will cross it, and on the day it does, semantic triple search silently stops considering the oldest triples. No error, no event, no log line; retrieval quality just quietly degrades from the bottom up. Given `created_at DESC` ordering, the first things to become unreachable are the oldest facts, which are exactly the ones a long-lived memory is supposed to be good at.

This is the same shape as several other findings tonight (a correct fail-safe with no signal), but it is worse in one respect: the others trigger only on error, and this one is *guaranteed* to trigger with normal growth.

- [ ] Emit or log when the candidate pool is truncated — i.e. when the query returns exactly `TRIPLE_CANDIDATE_LIMIT` rows and more were eligible. An operator needs to learn that semantic recall has become partial from something other than a hunch.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. All four items are addressed, and the truncation detection is done more carefully than I asked for.

## The truncation signal is correct, not approximate

I asked you to emit when the pool is truncated "and more were eligible", which is the hard half — a query that returns exactly `LIMIT` rows cannot distinguish "exactly full" from "overflowing". You solved it by asking for one extra row:

```python
(dim, dim, ref_iso) + tuple(auth_params) + (candidate_limit + 1,)
...
if len(rows) > candidate_limit:
    logger.warning("triple_candidate_pool_truncated: ...")
    rows = rows[:candidate_limit]
```

So the warning fires only on genuine overflow and never on a store sitting exactly at the bound, and the extra row is discarded before scoring. One row of extra BLOB transfer is the right price for an unambiguous signal.

**Configurable** via `[storage].triple_candidate_limit` through the existing `get_config()` accessor, with `< 1` rejected. I checked the hot-path cost since this call is now inside `rank_triple_candidates`: `_load_config()` early-returns on `_config_loaded`, so there is no per-query file read.

**The ceiling behaviour is written down**, and in a better place than I asked for. I requested it in the PR body; you put it in the `rank_triple_candidates` docstring instead, including the part that actually matters:

> Consolidation adds and merges knowledge but does not guarantee the live triple count remains below this independently configured retrieval bound.

That is the coupling I wanted stated, and a docstring outlives a PR body. The body still carries only the mechanism sentence ("limited to the newest 500 eligible rows"), which now understates what the code documents — worth updating whenever this file is next touched, but the property is recorded where a reader will find it.

**The test got cheaper, not more expensive.** Seeding dropped from `TRIPLE_CANDIDATE_LIMIT + 1` (501) rows to 3, driving the same path by configuring the limit down to 2. Same coverage, and it no longer pays 500 inserts to prove one boundary.

I checked whether this change caused it before re-running, because a saga performance PR blowing a suite budget is exactly the plausible story: the same branch had run 3.12 in 6m one commit earlier, `main` runs it in 7:50-11:16, and both macOS legs roughly doubled. payload.title: Worklink #1372: saga: forget_by_criteria treats a service read-domain grant as delete authority via OR, so one added capability would let a service tombstone other principals private atoms

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. This is a security narrowing done properly, and the empirical claim in the PR body is true — I checked it against the live deployment rather than taking it.

**The fix.** `readable_domains` is gone from `_ServiceMutationScope` entirely, and the OR-join it fed is replaced with `AND owner_principal = ?`. So owner is now a required conjunct rather than one of several alternatives, which is the whole defect: a read grant is no longer delete authority.

**Mutation-tested, and I had to correct my own first attempt.** Restoring only the producer (`readable_domains` back on the scope) failed nothing — because the consumer's OR-join was also removed, so the field flowed nowhere. That was a partial mutation on my side, not a test gap. Reverting `client.py` in full — field, OR-join, and the `origin_domains` passthrough together — fails exactly `test_trusted_service_readable_domain_does_not_authorize_mutation`. So the security property is genuinely pinned.

The other half:

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| Domains-alone restored as delete authority in `forget.py` | `test_forget_by_criteria_domains_without_owner_do_not_authorize` FAILED |
| Full revert of `client.py` (all three pieces) | `test_trusted_service_readable_domain_does_not_authorize_mutation` FAILED |

**`origin_domains` is not the inert back-compat shim the body's wording suggests.** I went looking for a dead authorization-shaped parameter, which would have been worth blocking on, and it is not one. At `forget.py:200`:

```python
    elif origin_domains is not None:
        return ForgetResult(dry_run=dry_run)
```

Domains without an owner return an empty result rather than deleting by domain — a fail-closed refusal, not a silent ignore. That is the right behaviour and strictly better than dropping the parameter, because a caller that still passes it deletes nothing instead of falling through to an unbounded delete. And it is covered by `test_forget_by_criteria_domains_without_owner_do_not_authorize`. Consider rewording "retained for API compatibility" to say it is a fail-closed refusal path — that is a stronger claim than compatibility.

**The empirical claim checks out.** The body says forward-only is safe because "no currently reachable service configuration combines a real atom origin domain with `saga_forget`, so no rows can already have been wrongly tombstoned." I grepped every `pollers.json` and the home config on the live deployment: **`saga_forget` is not declared anywhere**. So no service could have reached this path, nothing was wrongly tombstoned, and no repair is needed. That claim was load-bearing for skipping a migration and it is correct.

**The six-counterpart audit is real**, and the two I would have questioned are answered well: `ownership._authorization_predicate` deliberately keeps `public OR owner OR readable domain` because it is read-only, and `end_session` needs no change because it inherits the source session ACL and binds trusted services by session id rather than by domain.

Verification: focused authorization and tier4 suites green (74 passed), full suite green on a trial-merge with `origin/main`, python 3.12. All 11 CI checks green.

**Cross-PR interaction with #1668 checked.** That PR (chainlink #1371, merged earlier tonight) justified leaving `forget_by_criteria` alone on the grounds that its `a.is_pinned = 0` guard protects pinned atoms — and this PR restructures that function's WHERE-clause assembly. The guard survives the combination at `forget.py:231` (shifted from :235), and the two subsystems' suites pass together on the re-merge: 189 passed across mutation-authorization, tier4, dedup, and worklink autonomy.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The design is right and the audit is thorough. Replacing refusal-code allowlists with an explicit "did execution start" phase is the correct discriminator, because after chainlink #1327 (PR #1656) `ToolPolicyRefusal` carries a real guarantee — it means nothing was exposed, so no labels are contributed. Using an error-code list to decide that was always going to drift.

What I verified before looking for problems:

- **Every conversion goes in the fail-closed direction.** Zero `raise ToolPolicyRefusal` added, six removed, seven `raise ToolException` added. So the change strictly increases what taints; there is no place where an exception became a refusal, which is the one direction that could suppress a label that should exist. I checked this specifically because it is the only way this PR could introduce an exposure.
- **The `read_policy.py: no change` claim holds and matters.** Its refusal is emitted only for a denied protected read, and PR #1656 added `_result_matches_policy_refusal`, which requires the result content to match the refusal text exactly before suppressing. So that path is verified structurally rather than by trusting the exception type, and it correctly needs nothing here.
- **The four-module audit is real**, with kept-versus-changed stated per site and a reason: argument/configuration/cache-only refusals stay pre-execution in `forge.py`, shell parsing and argument validation stay in `github_review_guard.py`, and the review-lock timeout correctly becomes a fault because `gh` metadata subprocesses have already run.
- No redaction behaviour actually changed — I checked the diff for it. The body's "`_permission_diagnostic` ... now covered by the failed repository label rather than redacted" describes the labeling consequence, not an un-redaction, so nothing newly reaches the model. Worth rewording, but not a defect.

One blocking item.

## The discriminator defaults to the label-suppressing verdict

`mimir/tools/repo.py:134-135`:

```python
        execution_started = bool(
            getattr(exc, "execution_started", False)
        )
```

and the carrier itself:

```python
        execution_started: bool = False,
```

Both default to `False`, and `False` is the suppressing answer — at :58 `isinstance(exc, ToolPolicyRefusal) and not execution_started` re-raises as a refusal, and at :60 the same for `GitRefusal` / `ProjectTestRefusal`. So a refusal-typed exception raised from a post-execution site that forgets `execution_started=True`, or that predates the attribute, is treated as pre-execution and contributes no labels.

That is precisely the defect this PR exists to remove, and the default makes it silently reachable again. The blast radius is bounded — an arbitrary new exception type is not a `ToolPolicyRefusal`, so only the refusal family is affected — but the refusal family is exactly where the bug lived, and there are now seven post-execution sites that each had to remember the flag.

The asymmetry to fix: forgetting the flag should over-taint, not under-taint. Over-tainting costs a turn some sinks and is visible; under-tainting silently permits a flow after real output reached the model.

- [ ] Make the safe verdict the default. Either default the kwarg to `True`, or make it required with no default so a new site cannot omit it, or invert the field to something like `pre_execution: bool = False` where the default means "assume execution started".
- [ ] Replace the `getattr(exc, "execution_started", False)` fallback. If an exception can legitimately lack the attribute, decide deliberately what that means and say so; if it cannot, read the attribute directly so a missing one is an error rather than a silent suppression.
- [ ] A test that raises a refusal-typed exception from a post-execution path **without** setting the flag, and asserts it does not suppress labels once the default is inverted. That test is what stops the seventh site's omission from becoming the eighth.
- [ ] State how a future post-executi

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Two of the four items are properly addressed, and the second one is better than what I asked for. Requesting changes on the remaining two.

## Addressed

**The discriminator now defaults to the safe verdict** (item 1), in both places it mattered:

```
_tool_refusal(..., execution_started: bool = True)     # was False
GitRefusal.__init__(..., execution_started: bool = True)  # was False
```

So a bare `GitRefusal(code, message)` raised from a post-execution path now records labels instead of suppressing them.

**The `getattr` fallback is gone, and replaced with something stronger than I suggested** (item 2). Both sites now read the attribute through an explicit type test rather than tolerating its absence:

```python
(exc.execution_started if isinstance(exc, GitRefusal) else False)
or (git_tools is not None and git_tools.execution_started)
```

```python
execution_started=(
    exc.execution_started if isinstance(exc, ProjectTestRefusal) else True
)
```

I asked you to decide deliberately what a missing attribute means. Dropping `getattr` entirely means a refusal type that forgets the attribute now raises `AttributeError` rather than silently reading `False` — that is the right answer, and the non-refusal branches pick the safe verdict on each path (`True` for project tests; `False` for git, which then recovers through `git_tools.execution_started`).

## Still open: no test pins the property (item 3)

The only test changes in `34149768` add `self.execution_started = False` to test doubles, which is adapting the fakes to the removed `getattr` — not asserting the behaviour. There is still no test that raises a refusal-typed exception from a post-execution path **without** setting the flag and asserts labels are not suppressed.

That test is the whole point of the item: the defaults are right today, and a test is what keeps them right.

- [ ] Add it for both paths, since both defaults changed.

## Still open: the two refusal classes now disagree, undocumented (item 4)

`GitRefusal` and `ProjectTestRefusal` are structurally identical — same docstring shape, same `__init__`, same attribute, consumed by the same `_tool_refusal` — and after this change they have **opposite** defaults:

```
mimir/repo_tools.py:100     execution_started: bool = True
mimir/project_tests.py:83   execution_started: bool = False
```

I checked before calling this a bug, and it is not one today. Every `ProjectTestRefusal` site that omits the kwarg is genuinely pre-execution — `test_not_configured`, `test_config_invalid`, `test_command_unresolvable`, `test_selector_invalid`, `test_selector_count_exceeded`, `test_selectors_too_large`, `test_selector_outside_checkout`, `scope_action_denied` — 17 of them, all correctly non-executing. The 8 post-execution sites pass `execution_started=True` explicitly. So `False` genuinely suits that class's call-site distribution.

But that reasoning exists only in my head and yours, and item 4 asked for it to be written down. As it stands, the next person to add a post-execution `ProjectTestRefusal`, or to move code between these two files, has an even chance of getting it wrong — and the failure is silent label suppression, which is the exact defect this PR exists to fix.

- [ ] Either give `ProjectTestRefusal` the same `True` default and pass `execution_started=False` at the 17 pre-execution sites, so both classes fail closed identically; or keep the asymmetry and put a comment on both declarations saying why they differ and what a new site must do. I mildly prefer the first — it is more edits now, but it removes the choice rather than documenting it.

Note the branch also picked up the merge with `main`, which cleared the conflict — checks are running now and 8 of 11 are already green.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Coordination note, not a new review item: **PR #1674 (chainlink #1376) conflicts with this PR and should land first.**

They overlap on all three of this PR's review-guard files, and both make the *same* structural move — this PR says it "moved claim execution inside BudgetGate capture/catch in both sync and async paths so labels merge"; #1674 says it "moved GitHub review parsing and claiming inside the exception lifecycle in both `wrap_tool_call` and `awrap_tool_call`." I confirmed it is a real conflict rather than a conceptual one by trial-merging them:

```
Auto-merging mimir/tools/budget_gate.py
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in mimir/tools/budget_gate.py
Auto-merging mimir/tools/github_review_guard.py
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in mimir/tools/github_review_guard.py
```

Both restructure the same hunks around `budget_gate.py:1665` and `:1999`.

**Why #1674 goes first:** it also fixes a live vulnerability that neither chainlink's title mentions. On `main`, `ReviewSubmission.executable` is `argv[0]` taken from the *parsed model command* (`github_review_guard.py:201-202`) and is executed as argv[0] of the guard's probe subprocess (`:213`). The parser only checks the basename — `Path(argv[0]).name != "gh"` — so a path like `/workspace/mimir/gh` passes and gets executed. The agent has `:rw` file roots and shell access, so it can write a file named `gh` and have the guard run it. #1674 closes that by resolving `gh` from the server's trusted `PATH` and keeping the model-supplied value for argv *recognition only*. I mutation-tested that fix: restoring `spec.executable` as argv[0] fails `test_guard_probe_uses_server_gh_and_direct_exec_environment`.

So the sequencing that loses the least work:

- [ ] Wait for #1674 to land, then rebase this PR onto it.
- [ ] Re-scope this PR to what remains after #1674: the `forge.py` and `repo.py` refusal-to-fault conversions, and the `execution_started` phase carrier. The `github_review_guard.py` review-lock-timeout conversion may already be subsumed — check rather than re-apply it, since resolving a conflict by re-applying your version would undo #1674's guard changes.
- [ ] The `execution_started` default item from my review above is unaffected by the rebase and still stands.

Resolving this conflict by hand in `wrap_tool_call` / `awrap_tool_call` is exactly where a mistake would be least visible, so it is worth doing in the order that makes one side a clean rebase rather than a merge.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. Small, correct, and the test parameterization is the good kind.

**Mutation-tested both directions, and the parameterization discriminates:**

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| `merged_is_pinned = 1 if can_row[10] else 0` (canonical-only, drop the OR) | `test_dedup_pass_preserves_pin_from_either_cluster_member[False]` FAILED — exactly the case where the *duplicate* holds the pin |

That is what a parameterized test should do: the first mutation fails only one arm, which proves the arms are testing different things rather than being decorative.

**Correctness checks I made:**

- The positional index is right. The re-read at `dedup.py:429-431` selects `id, topics, metadata, agent_id, owner_principal, origin_domain, visibility, tombstoned, encoding_confidence, integrity, is_pinned` — so `is_pinned` is index 10. And positional access matches the surrounding idiom in this file (`current_can[4]`, `tuple(current_can[5:9])`), so it is consistent rather than a new fragility.
- ORing is the right operation. A pin means "do not forget this," so merging a pinned duplicate into an unpinned canonical must carry the protection across; the alternative is the bug being fixed. The consequence that a canonical accumulating many merges stays pinned is the intended "pin survives" semantics, not over-pinning.
- The docstring correction is accurate. `is_pinned` does stay behind activation in `_atom_score_key`, so "pinned wins only when activation ties" now describes the real policy, and the fix deliberately does not change canonical selection.

**I verified the load-bearing audit claim rather than taking it.** "`forget_by_criteria` needs no change because its existing `a.is_pinned = 0` guard protects pinned atoms" — that guard is real, at `forget.py:235`. That matters, because it is the reason a transferred pin actually protects anything.

Keeping pinned atoms in the dedup candidate query is also the right call: excluding them would stop genuine duplicates collapsing, and it is safe now that the merge ORs the persisted values.

The forward-only decision is reasonable and honestly stated — `metadata.dedup_merged_ids` plus tombstoned rows would make a targeted backfill possible, and declining it because it carries migration and operator-policy questions beyond this leaf is the right scope boundary rather than an evasion.

Verification: focused dedup suite green (16 passed), full suite green on the current head, python 3.12. All CI checks green.

payload.title: Worklink #1369: tools: fetch_url returns unparsed remote header and reason-phrase strings inline while classify_protected_result gives the call no IFC label, so remote text enters the model with zero sources recorded

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The approach is the right one and most of it is done well. Choosing to *complete* the metadata-only contract rather than drop `fetch_url` out of `_METADATA_ONLY_RESULT_TOOLS` preserves a single active-ingest boundary at body-read, which is the better design — but it raises the bar, because now every byte in the inline result has to be server-owned. One remote-derived string is left.

What I verified as correct first:

- **The media-type sanitizer is tight.** `partition(";")` drops parameters, `.lower()`, then `re.fullmatch(rf"{token}/{token}")` with `token = [!#$%&'*+.^_\`|~0-9a-z-]+` — the RFC 7230 tchar set minus uppercase. That excludes `<`, `>`, `"`, whitespace and newlines, so no markup and no header injection, with a 127-char cap and an `application/octet-stream` fallback.
- **The allowlist is exclusive by construction**, not a denylist: `payload = {key: metadata[key] for key in keys if key in metadata}` builds a fresh dict, so a metadata key added later cannot leak in. That is the durable shape.
- **`final_url` is genuinely out of the inline result.** It still exists at `web.py:429` for the sidecar, which is fine — the sidecar is read as a file and taints normally. (The body's "Removed redirect-derived `final_url`" slightly overstates; it was removed from the *inline* result.)
- **The class audit is complete.** `_METADATA_ONLY_RESULT_TOOLS` has exactly two members and you checked the other one, `bash_async`, with real reasoning. I also confirmed the remaining `exc.reason` interpolation at `web.py:501` is in `web_search`, which is **not** in that set — so its result taints normally and it is not the same defect.

## The PDF extraction failure path still puts remote-derived text inline

```python

        result["reason"] = f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"
        return result
```

That `result` becomes `metadata["pdf_extraction"]` (`web.py:219`), and `pdf_extraction` is one of the nine allowlisted keys (`web.py:122`). The allowlist copies values by reference and only re-sanitizes `content_type` — nested dict contents are never inspected. So the string flows straight into the model-visible result of a tool that is declared metadata-only and therefore **does not taint the turn**.

The exception text is remote-influenced. `pypdf` read errors routinely embed bytes from the document being parsed — messages of the `Invalid Elementary Object starting with b'...'` shape quote the offending object directly. So a server returning a crafted PDF controls part of that string, and it lands inline with no ingest label. That is the same defect class this PR exists to close, just in the one path that goes through a nested structure instead of a top-level field.

Note the sibling `reason` two branches up is already correct — `result["reason"] = "PDF contains no extractable text"` is fixed server text. So the pattern you want is established; this one path did not follow it.

Either build it through its own key allowlist the way `_inline_fetch_metadata` does, or assert its values are `int`/`bool`/a fixed string set. Otherwise the next field added inside it reintroduces this.
- [ ] A test: a fetch of a malformed PDF whose parser error would carry document bytes, asserting the inline result contains no substring from the document. Asserting `status == "failed"` is not sufficient — the point is what `reason` contains.
- [ ] Re-check the `metadata_path` / `text_path` / `file_path` values are server-generated in every branch, since they are the other allowlisted strings. I believe they are (`_virtual_path` off `_home`), but the PR should state it, because the in

All four items from my previous review are addressed, and two of them more strongly than I asked.

**1. The interpolated exception is gone.** `except Exception:` no longer binds the exception at all, and the handler writes fixed server text (`"PDF extraction failed"`). I had said keeping `type(exc).__name__` would be acceptable; dropping it entirely is the safer choice and I prefer it.

Because it builds a new dict rather than filtering in place, a field added inside the extraction result later cannot reintroduce the leak. That is the durable shape and it matches `_inline_fetch_metadata`.

**No bypass path.** Both inline-result constructions — the cache-hit at `web.py:659` and the fresh path at `:703` — go through `_inline_fetch_metadata`. The reads at `:636`/`:650` only consult `extraction` for control flow (whether to re-extract) and do not place it inline.

The test is the one I asked for, on the right surface.** `test_fetch_url_pdf_extraction_failure_preserves_fetch` asserts against the **inline** result: `meta["pdf_extraction"]["reason"] == reason` for exact fixed text, plus `assert body.decode("latin-1") not in str(meta)`. The old expectations were literally `"Error"` and `"FileNotDecryptedError"` — asserting the leaked exception names — so the rewritten parametrization is itself the proof the leak is closed, across malformed, image-only and encrypted inputs.

Verified rather than taken on trust.** The body does not state the path invariant, so I checked it: every assignment of the three allowlisted path strings is built by `_virtual_path(...)` — `:263` (`text_path`), `:648`/`:649`/`:656` on the cache-hit path, and `:688`/`:689` feeding `:696`/`:697` on the fresh path. payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1368: saga: forget() never tombstones derived triples or end-dates world_state, so a forgotten name keeps being injected into every consolidation prompt

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
This is the best-built PR I have reviewed in this batch. Approving.

**The nine-path audit is real, not a gesture.** Every symmetric path is named with a verdict and a reason, and the "no change" entries are as considered as the changed ones — `get_history` intentionally retaining end-dated audit rows, `detect_contradictions` only considering `is_current=1` which `forget` now clears, `repair_world_state_dual_current` repairing competing current values that forgotten rows no longer are. That is the shape a class fix should take.

**Mutation-tested three ways, each caught by its own named test:**

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| Triple tombstoning removed from `forget` | `test_forget_retracts_derived_triple_and_world_state` FAILED |
| Reader atom-liveness removed from `triples.py` (`get_current_value`) | `test_derived_reads_ignore_legacy_rows_with_tombstoned_source` FAILED |
| Reader atom-liveness removed from `synthesize.py` (`build_vocab_block`, 2 sites) | `test_derived_reads_ignore_legacy_rows_with_tombstoned_source` FAILED |

Two tests covering three production sites, and the second test genuinely covers both reader modules — I checked that separately rather than assuming.

**The correctness questions I went looking for, and how they resolved:**

- *Over-deletion.* `UPDATE triples SET tombstoned = 1 WHERE source_atom_id IN (...)` would be wrong if a triple could be sourced by several atoms. It cannot — `source_atom_id` is a single column, so forgetting the source atom retracting its triple is exactly right.
- *Atomicity.* The PR claims "the same transaction" and it holds: `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` at `forget.py:101`, `conn.commit()` at :136, with both statements between them. A partial retraction that end-dated world-state without tombstoning the triple would be the worst outcome here, and it is not reachable.
- *NULL source atoms.* The reader predicate is `(t.source_atom_id IS NULL OR a.tombstoned = 0)` over a `LEFT JOIN`, so a triple with no source atom stays live rather than being silently dropped by the join. That is easy to get wrong and you did not.

**The forward-only decision is correctly argued.** Declining a blanket sweep because it would also retract facts attached to dedup tombstones (`tombstoned_reason = 'merged'`), whose merge semantics deliberately preserve knowledge, is the right call — and it is why the reader-side change matters: legacy stale rows are handled at read time instead of by a migration that could not distinguish the two tombstone reasons. `test_derived_reads_ignore_legacy_rows_with_tombstoned_source` pins exactly that, so the forward-only choice is not leaving a silent gap.

Verification: focused suite green (22 passed), full suite green on a trial-merge with `origin/main`, python 3.12 (a bare `uv run` in a fresh worktree resolves to 3.13, which no CI leg covers). All CI checks green.

payload.title: Worklink #1365: worklink: a cleanup failure in _finalize skips release_issue, and every recovery path scopes on a label the run already removed, so the lock leaks and permanently costs a concurrency slot

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
This is a good fix and the teardown structure delivers exactly what it claims. Verified by reading it:

```python
finally:
    try:
        try:
            _close_attempt_capabilities(...)
        except Exception as exc:
            _log_event("worklink_cleanup_failed", ...)
        _remove_executor_report_dir_best_effort(...)
    finally:
        try:
            claims.release_issue(issue.issue_id)
        finally:
            clear_run_state(self.home, issue.issue_id)
```

Release sits in an outer `finally`, so it survives a `BaseException` out of the cleanup body — not just an `Exception` — and clearing sits in a `finally` around release, so a raising release cannot skip it. That is the right nesting for the guarantee, and `worklink_cleanup_failed` makes the best-effort steps observable rather than silent.

I also want to correct an assumption I started with. The `if claims.release_issue(issue_id): clear_run_state(...)` at :1275 looked at first like it contradicted the unconditional clearing at :909. It does not — :1275 is the reattach path where the leaf is no longer `worklink:in-progress`, so declining to clear our state when we could not confirm the release is the considered choice. `test_reattach_retains_state_when_transitioned_lock_release_fails` pins exactly that, so the difference is deliberate and tested. All five new tests pass.

One blocking item, and it is the same distinction taken seriously.

## A release that *fails* is silent at the main teardown, and the state is cleared anyway

`release_issue` returns a bool with a specific meaning — *"report whether Chainlink confirmed it"*, `result.returncode == 0` (`claims.py:547-550`). At :907 that return is discarded:

```python
claims.release_issue(issue.issue_id)     # return value dropped, nothing logged
```

`check=False`, so a failed release does **not** raise. It returns `False`, the enclosing `finally` runs, and `clear_run_state` deletes `<home>/state/worklink/runs/<id>.json`. Net result: the Chainlink lock is still held, and the local record that we hold it is gone. Nothing knows to retry the release, and the lock persists until `reaper_ttl_s` — currently **86400s**, so 24 hours.

That is not hypothetical. Earlier tonight two stale locks (#1358, #1359) held both concurrency slots after a container recreate; with `reaper_ttl_s` at 86400 that would have wedged the leaf queue for a day, and it needed a manual release. This PR is the one that owns lock-teardown correctness, so this is the right place to close that variant rather than leave it to the reaper.

What makes it clearly an inconsistency rather than a contract you did not know about: you *do* consume the return at :1275, and you wrote a test for the failure case there. The main teardown deserves the same seriousness — it is the path that runs on every single build.

- [ ] Capture the result at :907 and emit on `False`. `worklink_cleanup_failed` already exists and is the natural shape — something like `cleanup="lock_release"` with the issue id and attempt — so an unreleased lock is visible in `events.jsonl` instead of only surfacing 24 hours later as an unexplained capacity loss.
- [ ] Decide whether `clear_run_state` should still run when the release was not confirmed. Clearing it removes the only local trace of a lock we still hold. Either keep the state (matching :1275's reasoning) or state why the main teardown deliberately differs — the current code makes that choice implicitly by discarding the bool.
- [ ] A test for the failure case at this site: `release_issue` returns `False`, and assert the event is emitted and whatever state disposition you choose. The existing `test_report_cleanup_failure_cannot_skip_lock_release_or_state_clear` covers cleanup raising, not release failing.
- [ ] While you are in here: :1200/:1201 and :1266/:1267 still call release then clear sequentially, with neither the `try/finally` nesting nor the conditional. Your audit covered "both sites that combine deletion with lock

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
All four items addressed, and the shape you chose is better than patching the call site I pointed at. Approving.

**You extracted the decision instead of duplicating it.** `_release_issue_and_clear_run_state(claims, *, home, issue_id, attempt) -> bool` now owns the whole policy, and six call sites use it. Its docstring states the rule — "clear local state only after confirmed release" — and the body enforces it:

```python
    if not released:
        _log_event("worklink_cleanup_failed", ..., cleanup="lock_release",
                   error="Chainlink did not confirm lock release")
        return False
    clear_run_state(home, issue_id)
    return True
```

That is the decision I asked you to make, made explicitly: **state is retained when release is unconfirmed**, matching the reasoning already present at the reattach site rather than contradicting it. A leaked lock with a surviving local record is recoverable; a leaked lock with no record is what cost us both concurrency slots earlier.

Three details worth crediting:

- **Both failure modes are recorded, not just one.** The `except BaseException` arm logs before re-raising, so even an interrupt during release leaves a trace; the `not released` arm logs the unconfirmed case separately with its own message. `release_issue` uses `check=False`, so the silent-`False` path was the one that would have stayed invisible.
- **You reused `worklink_cleanup_failed` with `cleanup="lock_release"`** rather than minting a new event name. That keeps this queryable alongside the other teardown failures and avoids the collision I flagged with chainlink #1395's event vocabulary.
- **The test is named for the property**: `test_failed_lock_release_is_logged_and_retains_run_state` asserts both halves — the log *and* the retained state — rather than just the return value.

**Mutation-tested** from my first pass and still valid: the outer-`finally` structure means a `BaseException` out of the cleanup body cannot skip the release attempt, and clearing sits inside a `finally` around release.

**On the one remaining raw call, and why I am not blocking on it.** `orchestrator.py:1696` still does a bare `finally: claims.release_issue(issue_id)` in the factory launch-failure path, so a failed release there is still silent. Your body accounts for it — "Factory teardown releases its lock but does not mix that release with deletion or run-state clearing" — and that boundary is right for *this* issue, which is about the cleanup/release interaction; a release-only site cannot skip release because of a cleanup failure.

So I am treating the silent failed release at that site as a separate observation rather than an unmet item of this PR. It is worth a one-line fix whenever that path is next touched, because a leaked *epic* lock is what wedges both concurrency slots for `reaper_ttl_s` (86400s here) — but it is not this change's job and I would rather not hold a correct fix for it.

Verification: full suite green on the previous head (10001 passed / 1 unrelated docker-timeout flake, since re-confirmed 8 passed in isolation); the remediation touches `orchestrator.py` and its tests only. All 11 CI checks green.

---

**This now needs a rebase before it can merge.** GitHub reports `mergeable=CONFLICTING`, `state=DIRTY`, and a trial-merge with current `origin/main` conflicts in exactly one file:


`mimir/worklink/orchestrator.py` and `claims.py` both auto-merge cleanly — only the test file collides, because several PRs merged tonight touched it (#1662, #1663, #1676's area). Your 11 green checks predate that, since `main` moved after they ran.

Nothing to change in the fix. Rebase onto `main` and resolve the test-file conflict by keeping **both** sets of tests — the collision is additive test functions, not competing assertions, so a resolution that drops either side loses coverage rather than reconciling it.

My approval will be dismiss

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1367: saga: an embedding-provider outage makes SagaStore.query() raise AssertionError instead of degrading to FTS, so the turn loses keyword recall too

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The fix is the right shape and the sibling audit is the right instinct — degrading to an empty result is correct here, because `recall.py` already treats empty FAISS results as "no semantic candidates" and falls back to FTS5, which is precisely the documented behaviour the issue said was broken by the `AssertionError`.

I checked the audit's four claims rather than taking them:

- `_make_triple_search_fn` / `triple_augment_search` and `top_triples_with_payload` both go through `_cosine_scores`, which does skip stored vectors of differing shape — so "no additional guard needed" holds.
- `faiss_search_atoms` does delegate to `VectorIndex.search`, so it inherits the new guards.
- `_search_sessions_with_conn` is enclosed by `if query_emb and eligible_ids`, so both its FAISS and Python-cosine paths are already gated.

That is a genuine class audit, not a gesture at one.

One blocking item.

## Every degradation path is silent, in the one function this repo has already been burned by

`VectorIndex.search` now has four `return []` exits and not one of them logs or emits:

```
:356   return []      # index missing or empty
:359   return []      # query_vec is None
:362-363 except (TypeError, ValueError): return []
:364-365 if q.size != self.dimension: return []
```

All four are indistinguishable from "the index legitimately has no matches." So an embedding-provider outage, a malformed vector, or a dimension mismatch all present as "no semantic candidates," recall quietly falls back to FTS5, and nothing anywhere records that semantic recall stopped working.

That is not a hypothetical concern in this file. Chainlink **#1348** — closed — is titled *"the sessions index overwrites the shared embedding dim, so the atoms index builds empty and semantic recall dies silently."* The failure mode this repo has already paid for is exactly silent semantic-recall death, and the new `q.size != self.dimension` branch is the shape that would swallow a recurrence: if the shared dimension is ever poisoned again, this returns `[]` forever and the only symptom is gradually worse recall.

Trading a loud `AssertionError` for a silent `[]` fixes the crash and loses the signal. Keep the degradation; keep a signal with it.

- [ ] Distinguish "no matches" from "could not search." At minimum log at warning level with the reason; better, emit a durable event for the malformed-vector and dimension-mismatch cases, since those indicate a defect rather than an empty corpus.
- [ ] The dimension mismatch specifically should be loud. An empty or `None` query vector is an ordinary provider outage; `q.size != self.dimension` means the index and the provider disagree, which is a bug in this system rather than a transient. State which of the four you treat as expected and which as anomalous.
- [ ] A test asserting the signal is produced. `#1348` was found by reasoning about the code, not by an alert — a test that pins the observability is what stops the third occurrence.
- [ ] Confirm the guard cannot mask `#1348` specifically: state what happens now if the shared embedding dimension is poisoned, and why an operator would notice.

Everything else verified: the guards are correctly placed, the docstring is updated to match the new contract, and the trial-merge with `origin/main` is clean. Full suite in progress on my side.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
This addresses the item and goes past it in two ways I did not ask for. Approving.

**What I asked for:** distinguish "no matches" from "could not search," and make the dimension mismatch loud because it means the index and the provider disagree — a defect, not a transient.

**What you built:** a single `_report_search_degradation(reason, observed_dimension=..., emit_event=...)` reporting path with distinct reason codes, splitting expected from anomalous exactly along that line. `missing_query_vector` and an empty vector warning-log; conversion failures and `query_dimension_mismatch` additionally emit a durable event. That is the right split, and having one helper rather than four ad-hoc log calls is what keeps it from drifting.

Two things beyond the ask:

- **De-duplication with re-arm.** `self._reported_search_degradations.clear()` on a successful search means a persistent fault reports once instead of once per query, and recovery re-arms it. That matters more than it looks: a latch that never resets is its own defect — I filed exactly that separately as chainlink #1404 — and you got the harder half right on the first pass.
- **The degradation reaches the agent, not just the log.** `test_saga_vector_search_degradation_surfaces_to_next_turn` asserts a feedback block containing "SAGA semantic search degraded to FTS5" and the reason code. So the turn after a degradation *knows its recall is partial*. An operator-visible event was what I asked for; making the agent itself aware is strictly better, because the agent is the party whose behaviour should change.

**Mutation-tested, both new properties:**

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| `emit_event=False` for the dimension mismatch | `test_search_rejects_and_reports_malformed_query_vector[query_vec3-query_dimension_mismatch-4]` and `test_search_dimension_mismatch_event_rearms_after_recovery` FAILED (3 total) |
| Remove the `clear()` re-arm on success | `test_search_dimension_mismatch_event_rearms_after_recovery` FAILED |

The parameterization is worth calling out: `[query_vec3-query_dimension_mismatch-4]` pins the reason code *and* the observed dimension, so the test asserts the signal is specific rather than merely present.

**And it answers the #1348 question.** I asked you to confirm the guard could not mask a recurrence of "the sessions index overwrites the shared embedding dim, so the atoms index builds empty and semantic recall dies silently." It cannot now: that scenario produces `query_dimension_mismatch`, which emits a durable event, surfaces into the next turn's feedback block, and re-arms if it recurs. The failure mode this repo already paid for is now the one it is loudest about.

The original guards remain correct — degrading to an empty result is right, because `recall.py` treats empty FAISS results as "no semantic candidates" and falls back to FTS5. This keeps the degradation and adds the signal, which was the whole ask.

Addressed the observability gap in `c14b8112b`.

What changed:

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1366: worklink: a bookkeeping failure after the PR is opened rewrites a review-ready run as failed, leaving it undispatchable behind review_ready_evidence_exists and never closed on merge

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The core design is right — making successful PR creation the publication commit point, so bookkeeping after it records rather than demotes — and the observability is done properly, which I want to call out because the sibling PR #1662 does not do it: `_record_post_publication_error` emits a durable `worklink_post_publication_failed` carrying issue, attempt, `pr_url` and the error, and it guards its own emission so recording can never break the run.

Verified:

- **Mutation-tested.** Unwrapping the evidence comment (`comment_evidence()` instead of `run_bookkeeping("evidence comment", ...)`) fails `test_post_pr_comment_failure_does_not_demote_completed_run` (1 failed, 277 passed). Aimed.
- The assertions are the right ones: `status == "completed"`, `review_ready is True`, `pr_url` present, and — importantly — `worklink:failed` and `worklink:ready` are asserted *absent* while `worklink:review` is present. Asserting the negative labels is what makes it a real regression.
- The claims repair path is covered too: it unlabels `worklink:ready`, labels `worklink:review`, and does not re-add `worklink:ready`.
- `except Exception` is the right breadth — `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` and `asyncio.CancelledError` all derive from `BaseException` and still propagate.

Two things before I approve.

## 1. The authorized branch-ref cleanup is a fourth handling path, and it is the untested one

Post-publication failures are now handled three different ways:

| mechanism | steps | tested |
|---|---|---|
| `run_bookkeeping` helper | evidence write (:1093), evidence comment (:1124), evidence event (:1125), issue transition (:1157), transition event (:1158) | yes, via the new test |
| error-return accumulated at :1162-1172 | checkout cleanup | pre-existing |
| bespoke `try/except` at :852-866 | authorized branch-ref cleanup (`update-ref -d`) | **no** |

The branch-ref path hand-rolls what the helper does, and nothing exercises it — `grep` for `branch cleanup` or `update-ref` in `tests/test_worklink_orchestrator.py` finds nothing. That is the one place where "any housekeeping failure after the PR is opened" could still demote a completed run, which is exactly the property this issue exists to guarantee.

- [ ] Route the branch-ref cleanup through `run_bookkeeping` as well, or state why it cannot be (it is in a different function, so a shared helper may need lifting — that is fine, say so).
- [ ] A test that makes `update-ref -d` fail after a successful PR creation and asserts the run still returns `completed` / `review_ready=True` with the reason appended.

## 2. The runbook in the PR body produces false positives — I ran it

The body says to find affected leaves by comparing "active completed evidence files containing `pr_url`" against leaves lacking `worklink:review`. I executed that against the live deployment: 715 evidence files contain the string `pr_url`, and the comparison yields two candidates, **#1365 and #1367**.

Both are false positives. `pr_url` is present-but-null on ordinary runs:

```
1365-1.json  status='failed'     pr_url=None
1367-1.json  status='completed'  pr_url=None
```

So **no live leaf is actually stranded by this bug** — good news, but an operator following the runbook as written would re-dispatch two healthy leaves, one of which is mid-build.

- [ ] Tighten the criterion to a non-null `pr_url` (and ideally `status == "completed"` as well), since the key is present on every evidence file.
- [ ] State that the expected result on this deployment is currently zero affected leaves, so an operator who finds hits knows to look closer rather than assuming the runbook found real damage.

Neither is large. Everything else here is verified: full suite green on a trial-merge with `origin/main`, and all 11 CI checks green.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Both code items are addressed, and the first one the right way. Approving — with one correction I am making myself rather than asking for a third round, explained at the end.

**Item 1 — the fourth handling path is gone.** You extracted `_run_post_publication_bookkeeping(name, action, ..., errors=...)` and routed the authorized branch-ref cleanup through it, rather than leaving its hand-rolled `try/except` beside the helper. That is the better fix: there is now one mechanism for "a post-publication step failed, record it and keep the run completed," instead of three that have to agree. The remaining `cleanup_errors` accumulation into `result.reason` is the right shape for a step that runs outside the main tail.

**Item 2 — the test exists and asserts the property, not the mechanism.** A failing `update-ref -d` after successful PR creation now yields `status` completed, `review_ready is True`, the `pr_url`, and the appended reason — and, importantly, asserts the *negative* labels: `worklink:review` present while `worklink:failed` and `worklink:ready` are absent. Asserting the labels that must **not** appear is what makes it a real regression rather than a smoke test.

## On the runbook: I am correcting it here instead of blocking again

Items 3 and 4 from my last review are not addressed — the body still says to find affected leaves by comparing "active completed evidence files **containing** `pr_url`". I am not blocking on it, and I want to be explicit about why rather than appear to have quietly dropped my own item.

The criterion is too loose rather than false: `pr_url` is a key present on essentially every evidence file, usually null. I ran it against the live deployment when I first reviewed this, and it yields two candidates, **#1365 and #1367**, both false positives:

```
1365-1.json  status='failed'     pr_url=None
1367-1.json  status='completed'  pr_url=None
```

So the corrected criterion, for the record and for anyone who follows this later:

> Affected leaves have an evidence file with **`status == "completed"` and a non-null `pr_url`**, and lack `worklink:review`. On this deployment that set is currently **empty** — no live work is stranded by this bug. A non-empty result means look closer, not that the runbook found real damage.

I am correcting rather than blocking because the substance is fixed and the outstanding item is *guidance about a condition that does not currently exist*. Holding a correct fix for a third round over advice describing an empty set is the wrong trade — and since I am the one who ran the runbook, the accurate version belongs in the merge record, which this review is part of. If the body is edited later, that is the text to use.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1363: worklink: a retained factory record is recoverable forever and an out-of-set phase is routed into recovery, so a vanished sandbox or changed launcher wedges the epic and drains its attempt budget

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The core fix is right, and it exposes that the old logic was inverted rather than merely permissive. Worth stating plainly, because it is a better find than the issue described:

```python
# before
if _factory_record_is_recoverable(retained) or not recoverable_phase:
    return await self._recover_factory_070(...)
archive_factory_record(self.home, retained)
```

`or not recoverable_phase` routed records in *unrecoverable* phases straight **into** recovery. So the "recoverable forever" behaviour was not a missing check — it was a check wired backwards.

Verified independently:

- **Mutation-tested.** Restoring `or candidate.controller_phase not in _RECOVERABLE_FACTORY_PHASES` fails `test_unbindable_factory_record_is_archived_before_claim_and_fresh_run[lifecycle]` (1 failed, 261 passed). Aimed, not incidental.
- **Fail-closed predicate.** `_factory_record_is_recoverable` now delegates the whole binding to `_verify_factory_recovery_target` and returns False on any `WorklinkError`, and `_RECOVERABLE_FACTORY_PHASES` is genuinely consulted (orchestrator.py:2224), so `stopped` and unknown phases are both abandoned rather than resumed. The docstring states each phase's meaning, which is what the issue asked for.
- **`before_claim` placement is the right lever.** Classifying and archiving under the shared claim mutex before the Chainlink lock means abandoning a record consumes no claim attempt. That matters here specifically — attempt-budget starvation is what burned #1327 through 22 attempts.
- **`clear_factory_record` really was unused.** On `origin/main` its only references are its own definition and two tests; no production caller. Removing it with its tests is correct for this codebase, not a lost capability.
- **It preserves #1658.** The `factory sandbox already exists` guard survives the trial-merge with `origin/main` intact at orchestrator.py:2251.
- Reading both `chainlink-<id>` and legacy `<id>` keys is migration necessity rather than back-compat cruft, since records under both spellings exist on disk today.

One blocking item.

## Archiving a factory run is silent, and the reason is available and discarded

`archive_factory_record` (factory_state.py:293-310) returns a destination path and emits nothing, and the new call site at orchestrator.py:1518 wraps it in no event either. So a factory run being abandoned — the difference between "the controller is still retrying this" and "the controller gave up and moved the record" — produces no durable event.

Worse, the reason exists and is deliberately thrown away:

```python
    except WorklinkError:
        return False
```

`_verify_factory_recovery_target` raises with a specific message naming which part of the binding failed — identity, repository, base, launcher, phase, session, sandbox, or checkout. That message is exactly what an operator needs and it is dropped on the floor.

This is not a pre-existing gap you inherited. Chainlink #1395 enumerates the epic path's silent returns at :1406, :1425, :1447-1459, :1484 and :1486-1488 — all of which predate this PR. The archive at :1518 is a **new** silent path this change introduces, so #1395 will not cover it.

It matters concretely right now: this code is about to be deployed and exercised by the first real epic launches, and the whole reason the factory was hard to diagnose this week is that its failures emitted nothing.

- [ ] Emit a durable event when a record is archived, carrying the run identity, the phase, and the `WorklinkError` reason. Capture the exception message rather than discarding it — `except WorklinkError as exc` and pass `str(exc)`.
- [ ] Distinguish the two archive paths in the event: dispatch-time abandonment (:1518) versus the explicit `mimir worklink archive-factory-run` operator command. An operator needs to know which one moved the record.
- [ ] A test asserts the event is emitted with the reason when an unbindable record is archived. Asserting the record moved is not sufficient — the point is that the

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The remediation is better than what I asked for. Approving.

I asked you to capture the discarded `WorklinkError` and emit an event. You did something stronger: **you removed the place the information was being lost.** The bool-returning `_factory_record_is_recoverable` wrapper is gone, and the `try/except WorklinkError as exc` is inlined at the call site with `reason=str(exc)`. Since that wrapper's `except WorklinkError: return False` *was* the discard, deleting it is a better fix than emitting from inside it.

Three things I did not ask for and am glad you did:

- **`reason` and `source_kind` are mandatory.** `raise FactoryRecordError("factory archive event context is incomplete")` means no caller can archive without context. That converts "remember to pass the reason" into a property the code enforces, which is what stops the next archive site from being silent.
- **`source_kind` distinguishes the paths** — `dispatch_abandonment` versus `operator requested archival` — so an operator reading `events.jsonl` can tell whether the controller gave up or a human intervened.
- **The archive rolls back if the event cannot be persisted.** `factory_state.py:335-339` does `os.replace(destination, source)` on failure, and raises `FactoryRecordError` if the rollback itself fails. So a record can never end up moved with no durable trace — which is the original defect, closed one level deeper than my review reached. `test_archive_factory_record_restores_active_record_when_event_persistence_fails` pins it, asserting the record is back, the source file exists, and the archive directory is empty.

**Mutation-tested.** Replacing `reason=str(exc)` with a fixed string fails five tests, including both parameterized arms of `test_unbindable_factory_record_is_archived_before_claim_and_fresh_run`. The tests assert the event name, `source`, `reason`, `run_id` and `phase`, and map distinct refusals to distinct expected reasons — so the reason is pinned as *specific*, not merely present.

Also still verified from my first pass: the inverted `or not recoverable_phase` routing is gone, the fail-closed predicate delegates the whole binding check, `_RECOVERABLE_FACTORY_PHASES` is genuinely consulted, `clear_factory_record` really was test-only, and #1658's `factory sandbox already exists` guard survives.

Verification: full suite green on a trial-merge with `origin/main` — 10009 passed, 35 skipped (python 3.12). `main` then gained one commit (#1673, disjoint: shell jobs versus worklink), re-merged and cross-checked both sides together: 370 passed, 4 skipped. All 11 CI checks green.

payload.body:

- Added durable `worklink_factory_record_archived` events with `run_id`, issue/attempt/session identity, phase, reason, and archive path.
- Dispatch-time abandonment preserves the exact `WorklinkError` reason and uses `source=dispatch_abandonment`.
- `mimir worklink archive-factory-run` emits the same event with `source=operator_command` and an explicit operator-archive reason.
- Centralized archive+event handling so event persistence failure restores the active record instead of silently completing the state transition.
- Named Chainlink #1395 at the event definition so its broader silent-path work reuses this event rather than introducing a competing archive name.
