Verified and fixed at `023a0dac`, plus one more layer at `2a55106b` that you hadn't reached yet.

I checked the mechanism rather than taking it on faith, and this is the most consequential of the four findings — not because a scalar ledger is likely, but because of *which* shape is load-bearing. The deployed ledger is `{entries: [...]}`, so `_records()` reaching the record list through a container key is the live path, and a mistyped or renamed `entries` is the realistic damage case. Were the upstream shape ever to change, every file would read as zero and the cap guard would stop counting entirely while still reporting success. That's the version of this bug that matters.

**`_document_is_recognized()`** validates the parsed document against the shapes `_records()` can actually read, and `_load_yaml()` marks anything else as damaged. The legitimately empty shapes are recognized explicitly — absent document, empty list, empty container — because an empty ledger is a real zero and must not fail closed.

**I validated against production before tightening, not after.** Rejecting the live shape would report every real post as unreadable and block posting outright, which is a worse failure than the one being fixed. The new counter run against the deployed ledgers returns the same count as the old one — 543, `unreadable=0` — so the validation admits real data unchanged. A test pins that shape with its real field set so a future tightening can't quietly reject production.

**One layer further out, same class.** With a state root that does not exist, `_ledger_files()` yields nothing, so the counter reported `count=0, unreadable=0`, exit 0 — full confidence in a number read from the wrong place. A misconfigured `MIMIR_HOME` silently produced the whole daily cap as headroom. A missing directory is now damage.

I deliberately did **not** extend that to the adjacent case, and want to flag the judgment rather than bury it: a state root that exists but holds no ledger yet is indistinguishable from a fresh install before the poller first runs, and failing closed there would block the first post ever sent. So `count_ledgers_detailed()` now also returns `scanned` — how many ledger files were actually read, exposed in `--json` — which makes that ambiguity visible instead of silent. Against the deployed state, today's window reports `count=0, unreadable=0, scanned=2`: a zero backed by two real ledgers, which until now was indistinguishable from a zero backed by none. If you think the no-ledger-yet case should also fail closed, say so and I'll do it, but it needs a deliberate decision about first-run behaviour rather than a reflex.

**Tests 99 → 104.** Scalar, mistyped `entries: {}`, unknown top-level mapping, a list holding a non-record, each legitimately empty shape kept as a real zero, the single-record mapping, the pinned production shape, missing root, explicitly-named missing state dir, and `scanned` both directly and through `--json`. The scalar and `entries: {}` cases also run end-to-end through the real subprocess.

Mutation-verified: disabling the structural check fails 6 tests including both end-to-end ones; removing the missing-root arm fails exactly `test_a_state_root_that_does_not_exist_is_damage`. Focused suite green at 104; full suite running and I'll post the number.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Fixed at `5644c014`, and this one is my error pattern rather than a new discovery.

I validated the ledger's structure last revision and left the archive with the same fail-open — which is the *identical* asymmetry as two revisions earlier, when I fixed the ledger's unreadable-file handling and left the archive's. Same two files, same omission, twice. Both times I fixed the source that was named instead of the class of defect. Both sources now get identical treatment: I/O damage, parse damage, unrecognized structure, and a missing directory all make the count a floor.

`_archive_is_recognized()` mirrors `_document_is_recognized()`. The `or {}` in the old read had to go with it: an empty archive parses to `None`, and `or {}` turned that into a mapping with no `dispatch` key — which the new validator would correctly call damage. An empty archive is a real zero.

**Checked against production before tightening, and it mattered.** All 1539 deployed archive files are dicts whose `dispatch` is a list of dicts — but **four carry an extra `notifications` key alongside `dispatch`**. A validator requiring the key set to be exactly `{dispatch}` would have rejected those four real files and reported their posts as unreadable forever. The validator admits all 1539, and a test pins the sibling-key form so a future tightening can't quietly break it.

**Tests 104 → 113.** Scalar, mapping without `dispatch`, mistyped `dispatch` container, list holding a non-entry, each legitimately empty shape kept a real zero (empty file, empty list, empty `dispatch`), the sibling-key production form, and an end-to-end `main()` regression for the full scenario — a post recorded only in an uninterpretable archive with no ledger row to corroborate it, which must report `effective=unknown` rather than a cap's worth of headroom.

Mutation-verified: disabling the archive validator fails exactly those 5 tests. Focused suite green at 113; full suite running.

On the shape of this review cycle, since five rounds is worth naming: every round has been the same failure class one layer further out, and every one has been real. Four of the five were paths I could have found by asking "which other source does this argument apply to?" instead of fixing the specific example given. The remaining known gap is the one I flagged last round and am deliberately leaving to a decision rather than a reflex — a state root that exists but holds no ledger yet is indistinguishable from a fresh install, so failing closed there would block the first post ever sent. `scanned` makes it observable. If you consider that blocking too, say so and I'll implement it, but it changes first-run behaviour and I'd rather that were chosen than assumed.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body: Full suite at `5644c014`: **9666 passed, 35 skipped, 0 failed** (568s). Focused social-cli suite 113 passed. All 11 hosted checks green.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Both fixed at `0174face`, and one of them was my own half-finished work from the previous round.

**Finding 2 — the enforcement path.** You're right that this was the gap, and the diagnosis is exact: I added `scanned` last revision for observability and then didn't wire it into the consumer that needed it. `cap_check` was still on the plain-integer invocation, so it never saw the field. That's the same pattern as the archive omission — I add the signal and don't connect it. `cap_check` now consumes the structured report and fails closed unless there is evidence behind the number.

On your "explicit initialized-empty representation": that framing resolved the objection I raised last round, so thank you for it. Failing closed on *any* empty scan would deadlock — the ledger only appears after a dispatch, and the dispatch needs the guard to pass, so a brand-new install could never send its first post. The initialization marker already exists: the poller framework creates the `social-cli-*` state directory on first run, independent of any dispatch. So the two cases separate cleanly. No `social-cli-*` directory means no sign the poller has ever run, and a zero drawn from nothing is unavailable. A directory with no ledger yet is genuinely initialized-empty and stays a real zero. An *absent* `stateDirs` field also fails closed, so an older `count.py` can't quietly satisfy the check.

**Finding 1 — record validation.** Legitimate, and the work was in bounding it. Taken loosely, "any skipped record might have been a post" would flag every filtered record, and a real ledger is mostly non-post actions — the guard would never establish headroom again. `_record_is_interpretable()` draws the line at *why* we skipped: a record we chose not to count (a like, another platform, outside the window, a dry run) is normal; one whose action, timestamp or platform is missing or uninterpretable is damage. There are tests on both sides, including one whose docstring records why the bounding case matters.

**A near-miss worth reporting, because it argues for your point about validating against production.** My first probe of the deployed ledgers reported all 543 records as having unparseable timestamps. That was the probe, not the data: real timestamps arrive as `datetime` objects, since YAML parses an unquoted ISO timestamp natively, and my throwaway checker tested `isinstance(v, str)`. Had I written the validator that way, it would have marked every deployed record damaged and blocked posting outright — a far worse failure than the one being fixed. Validation goes through `_parse_dt`, which accepts both forms, and there's a test pinning the `datetime` case for exactly this reason. That's the second time this PR that checking production first prevented a catastrophic validator; the first was the four archives carrying a `notifications` sibling key.

The return outgrew a tuple, so it's now a `LedgerCount` NamedTuple with an `is_floor` property. Cheaper to do that with one consumer than later.

**Verified against production, not just in tests.** 543 counted unchanged with `damagedRecords=0` across *every* action present in the deployed ledgers, so every real record clears the new validator. End-to-end, `cap_check` against the live agent home prints `today_utc=2026-08-20 archive=0 ledger=0 effective=0 / 5`, exit 0 — byte-identical to the deployed script, but now backed by `scanned=2, stateDirs=2, damagedRecords=0` instead of by nothing. That is the distinction this PR exists to make.

**Tests 113 → 131.** Mutation-verified: making every record interpretable fails 5 tests; dropping the evidence requirement in `cap_check` fails exactly the two `stateDirs` tests. Focused suite green at 131; full suite running.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Blocker 1 is fixed at `a58cf24d`. Blocker 2 has an operator decision on it, below.

**Blocker 1 — both paths were real.** `_platform_matches()` stringifies whatever it finds, so `platform: []` compares as the literal `"[]"` and `platforms: {bsky: true}` matches nothing; either way the record was filed as another platform's traffic rather than as data we could not read. `_platform_value_is_interpretable()` now mirrors the shapes the matcher actually accepts — a non-empty `platform` string, a `platforms` list of non-empty names, or a non-empty comma-separated string. Actions are checked against `KNOWN_ACTIONS`, so a corrupted spelling like `pst` is damage instead of a legitimate non-post.

I want to state the cost of the vocabulary check rather than bury it, because it is a real trade and not free: a genuinely new upstream verb will make the guard report an unestablished count until that verb is added to the set. I think that is the right direction for a safety cap — a loud stop beats a silent under-count — and the repair is one entry. There is a test asserting the set still covers every verb present in deployed ledgers and archives, so an upstream change surfaces in the suite rather than in production.

Verified against production, not only in tests: every action present in the deployed ledgers returns `damagedRecords=0`, and the default query still counts 543.

Tests 131 → 141. Mutation-verified: reverting the action check fails `test_an_unknown_action_is_damage`; reverting platform validation to a presence check fails exactly the six malformed-platform tests.

**Blocker 2 — the operator has decided not to close this, and I want to give you the reason rather than just the ruling.** The decision is to trust the ledger and archive files as written and handle a cap breach if one occurs, rather than add bootstrap evidence.

The finding that informed it: the evidence is writable by the agent the cap constrains. `/mimir-home` is a virtiofs bind mount, so although the ledger and archive present as `uid=0 gid=0 mode=644` inside `drwxr-xr-x root root` directories, the agent's uid can write, delete, and create there. I verified that rather than inferring it — `test -w` returns true on the ledger, the state directory and the archive directory, and a `touch` probe created a file successfully (removed afterwards).

That makes the durable marker unable to do the job asked of it. A marker in the state tree would be both destroyable and *forgeable* by the party whose posting the cap limits, so its presence could not be taken as proof of a never-dispatched state. It also cannot be written by either of these scripts, which are read-only readers; making the guard own state would be a fresh fail-open rather than a fix.

The wider consequence is worth recording on this PR: because the agent can delete the ledger and archive it is counted from, this guard is advisory rather than enforcing, and no in-tree artifact changes that. Genuine enforcement needs the evidence outside the agent's write scope — permission-enforcing storage rather than this bind mount, or a separate service holding the count — which is a deployment decision, not a change to these two scripts.

Practically the exposure is bounded: on the only deployment that posts there are 543 ledger records and 1539 archives, so the no-evidence state is not live there; it would take a brand-new deployment or total state loss, and the consequence is capped at five posts. `scanned` and `stateDirs` remain in the report so the condition is observable if it ever arises.

I am not asking you to agree that this is ideal — it isn't. But it is the operator's call on deployment policy, and it is made.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Both fixed at `a20bcb56`, and thank you for accepting the operator decision on the bootstrap state — the advisory framing you asked for is now in the module docstring, stating plainly that both sources live on a bind mount the agent's own uid can write, that the guard turns an accidentally damaged or missing source into an unestablished count rather than a silent zero, and that treating its output as a hard limit would overstate what it can know.

**The normalization gap was real and it was mine.** Validation stripped, matching compared raw, so `action: " post "` and `platform: " bsky "` were declared interpretable and then silently skipped — trusted headroom from a record the counter never classified. Fixed on both sides of the boundary and on the archive verb, so the ledger and archive normalize identically.

**On the quote inconsistency you are right, and I pinned the representation empirically.** `quote` is unattested in deployed data: zero occurrences across 543 ledger records — whose key set is fixed at `action, createdId, cwd, dispatchTimestamp, dryRun, inboxPath, key, outboxPath, platform, targetId, textHash, timestamp`, with no quote field — and zero across 4688 archive payloads. So I could not pin a live representation, because there isn't one.

Given that, I took your first horn rather than the second. `quote` is now in the canonical post-creating set: a quote creates a post, so if the verb ever appears, counting it against the cap is the correct direction, and if upstream instead records a quote post as `post` with a quote reference then the action is `post` and the set already covers it. Either way the two sources now agree, which was the actual defect — the archive counted `quote` while the ledger did not, so one dispatch would land on a single side of a cross-check whose entire value is the two sides agreeing.

**Rather than align the copies, I removed the copy.** cap_check now takes both the vocabulary and the unreadable status code from count.py. That drift is what produced this bug: I hand-mirrored `POST_CLASS_ACTIONS` and `COUNT_LEDGER_UNREADABLE` and they diverged. count.py is already a hard dependency since cap_check executes it, so importing it is no new coupling, and failing at import beats a copy that drifts quietly.

**Tests 141 → 150.** Padded action, padded direct platform, padded `platforms` entry, padded archive verb, `quote` counted on both sources, and two tests asserting the vocabulary and the status code are the ones count.py defines.

Mutation-verified in four directions: dropping the action strip fails 2 tests, dropping the archive verb strip fails 1, removing `quote` from the canonical set fails 4, and — the one I most wanted to confirm — replacing cap_check's derived vocabulary with a hardcoded copy fails `test_the_post_class_vocabulary_comes_from_the_ledger_counter`, so the anti-drift guard actually catches drift rather than just documenting it.

Verified against production again: 543 counted unchanged with `damagedRecords=0`, no deployed archive rejected, and cap_check end-to-end against the live home still prints `today_utc=2026-08-20 archive=0 ledger=0 effective=0 / 5` at exit 0. Focused suite green at 150; full suite running.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Fixed at `ec25384a`. This is the third time in this PR that the same asymmetry has appeared — the ledger gained a guard and the archive kept the hole — after the original fail-open and the structural validation before it. Each time I fixed the source that was named instead of asking which other source the argument applies to. That is worth stating plainly rather than fixing quietly a third time.

`cap_check` now takes `KNOWN_ACTIONS` from `count.py` alongside the post-creating set and the status code, and an archive verb outside it is unreadable. Both sources apply the same classifier to the same vocabulary, which is the property the cross-check depends on.

**Checked against production before tightening,** as with the earlier vocabulary change: all 4688 archive verbs across the deployed files are known, so nothing real is newly flagged. The deployed entries also carry exactly one key each, every key a verb — which is why validating every key rather than only the first is safe here rather than an assumption.

**Tests 150 → 155.** Your typo case both directly and end to end (`pst:` as the only evidence, no ledger row, must report `effective=unknown` rather than `effective=0`), known non-post verbs still normal skips since the deployed archive is mostly likes and ignores, the deployed verb set asserted against the vocabulary, and the vocabulary asserted to be the one `count.py` defines.

Full suite at the previous head `a20bcb56` was 9666 passed, 35 skipped, 0 failed; the run for this head is in flight and I'll post it.

Full suite at `ec25384a`: **9666 passed, 35 skipped, 0 failed**. Focused social-cli suite 155 passed. All 11 hosted checks green, including `pytest` 3.11/3.12, `pytest-macos` 3.11/3.12 and `pytest-enforced`.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Fixed at `3e5c0b38`. The empty entry was a real hole: `dispatch: [{}]` passed the structural check, reached the verb loop, produced no verb to validate, and contributed a trusted zero — and it was dropped silently even when other entries in the same file counted, which I confirmed at `(1, 0)` for `[{}, {"post": ...}]` before fixing it.

I handled it in the verb loop rather than the document validator, so it mirrors the ledger: an empty record there reaches the same conclusion through `_record_is_interpretable` rather than through the shape check. Keeping the two sources structurally parallel is the thing that has stopped this class of bug recurring.

**One part of the request I did not implement, with a reason rather than an omission.** You asked me to encode "exactly one verb key" for both container shapes. That isn't needed for the multi-key direction, because every key in an entry is already validated against the vocabulary — so a metadata key beside a verb reads as an unknown action and fails closed today. I probed it rather than assuming: `{reply: {}, meta: 1}` returns `(1, 1)`, flagging the sibling key. Encoding "exactly one" as well would add a second rule that only restates what the vocabulary check already enforces, and would make a future upstream entry carrying a benign sibling field fail for the narrower reason instead of the more informative one. Zero keys was the only shape producing no verb at all, so that is what this closes — and there is now a test pinning the multi-key behaviour so the reasoning doesn't have to be rediscovered.

If you still want the invariant stated explicitly I'll add it, but I'd rather it be a deliberate call than me quietly adding a redundant rule.

**Tests 155 → 159.** The empty entry directly, an empty entry beside a counting one, the multi-key case as documentation of why the extra rule is unnecessary, and the end-to-end `main()` regression with no ledger row.

Mutation-verified: accepting empty entries again fails exactly those three empty-entry tests.

Production unchanged — all 4688 deployed archive entries carry exactly one verb key and none are empty, so nothing real is newly flagged.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
I'm not implementing this one, because the example it rests on does not reproduce. I checked before disagreeing:

| archive entry | count | unreadable |
|---|---|---|
| `{like: {}, reply: {}}` — the example given | **1** | 0 |
| `{post: {}, reply: {}}` | 2 | 0 |
| `{like: {}, ignore: {}}` | 0 | 0 |
| `{reply: {}}` baseline | 1 | 0 |

`reply` is in the canonical post-creating set, so the stated entry contributes **1, not zero**, and `{post, reply}` contributes 2. Every verb present is counted on its own merits. The only multi-verb entry that contributes zero is two known *non-post* verbs, and that zero is correct — neither `like` nor `ignore` consumes the cap. So there is no path here that produces unverified headroom, which is the property this whole review has rightly been about.

The remaining argument for an exactly-one-key rule would be that production has one verb per entry, so a two-verb entry is malformed and should not be trusted at all. That is a purity argument rather than a safety one, and it cuts against the cap: a malformed entry containing a real `reply` would be discarded from the count instead of charged against the limit, which is the wrong direction for a guard whose failure mode we have spent eleven rounds pushing toward fail-closed.

**On the review as a whole, and this is on me rather than on you.** Ten of the eleven findings were real, and the first one was a live defect that had already cost us — a deleted `count.py` silently reporting `ledger=0` and returning the full daily cap. That was worth every round it took. But four of those rounds were me making the same mistake: fixing the ledger and leaving the archive with the identical hole, three separate times, plus adding `scanned` without wiring it to the consumer that needed it. Each time you had to tell me to do the sibling. That pattern is mine, and it is most of why this took eleven passes.

The other part is scope. The task was to upstream one script; this is +1922/-19 across five files. Hardening the counting was worth doing, but it should have been a second PR with its own scope rather than riding along with a file move, and I should have split it around round two instead of letting one PR inherit the union of both review surfaces.

The operator has decided to land it. All 11 hosted checks are green at this head, the focused suite is 159 passed, and the full suite is 9666 passed / 35 skipped / 0 failed. I am the PR author so I cannot clear this myself — if you agree the multi-verb path is not a defect, please re-review so it can merge.

Ten of the eleven were real, and the first one was a live defect that had already cost us. payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1307: tests: optional-skill test dirs shadow the repository tests package, so the two suites cannot be collected together

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approved. Reviewed the full diff, and verified the defect by discriminator rather than by reading: on `main`, running every optional-skill test directory in one pytest process dies at collection with `ImportPathMismatchError: ('tests.conftest', ...)`; with this branch merged onto current `main` it is 301 passed. Full suite on that same tree is 9673 passed, 35 skipped, 0 failed.

The part worth calling out is that the fix is discriminated rather than applied by rote, which I only appreciated on a second pass. Four skills import a bare `poller` from inside a fixture that does `sys.modules.pop("poller", None)` first, so the new autouse `syspath_prepend` puts that skill's `scripts/` ahead of the others and each resolves its own copy. The two whose conftest imported `poller` at collection scope — `github-poller` and `github-ci-watch` — could not be fixed that way, because an autouse fixture cannot run before a collection-time import, so those correctly get the unique-module-name `*_test_support.py` treatment instead. Getting that distinction right is the substance of this change.

All four test renames are `similarity index 100%`, so no behaviour is hidden in them, and the `tests/__init__.py` removals are what stop several packages all being named `tests`. The added conformance assertion keeps them from coming back.

One follow-up, not blocking and not introduced here: the pop-then-import contract is now load-bearing for those four skills, but nothing guards it. If one of them later imports `poller` at module scope, the collision returns exactly as it did for `github-poller`, and the per-skill CI isolation would hide it. The conformance test checks for the `tests/__init__.py` regression but not the import pattern. I'll file that as its own chainlink rather than hold this up.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
## Review: no findings. I would approve.

Withholding the formal approval only because it can trigger auto-merge and the operator is holding merge decisions; the substance below is a full pass.

### Every acceptance criterion, verified

| criterion | result |
|---|---|
| both suites collect in one invocation | **9929 collected** — was `ImportPathMismatchError` before any test ran |
| each skill suite still passes alone | 25 / 5 / 118 / 26 / 47 / 7 |
| configured default run unmoved | **9701**, identical to `main` at `e2847ff5` |
| wheel still ships every skill's tests | **24 files across all 6 skills**, from a real `npm run build` + `uv build` |
| no skill test imports break | all six pass standalone |
| conformance guard exists and bites | re-adding `github-poller/tests/__init__.py` fails it |

Reviewer sweeps: `MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED=1` → 9666 passed / 0 failed; `WORKLINK_RUN_BIN="uv run mimir"` → 9666 passed / 0 failed.

One correction to my own baseline, in case it matters to anyone reading: I had earlier cited 10460 as the default collection. That was measured on the `feature/acp` merge tree, which carries the ACP tests. Against `main` the number is 9701 — so this PR moves nothing, and I would have reported a false 759-test regression had I not re-measured the actual base.

### The part that went beyond the leaf, correctly

Dropping `__init__.py` alone would have traded one collision for another: without package identity, same-named modules collide by basename, and every one of these directories had a `conftest.py` and most had a `test_poller.py`. The build anticipated that — unique basenames for the repeated modules, plus `*_test_support.py` shims for the same-named poller script imports. That is the difference between fixing the error and fixing the cause.

### The conformance suite is the best part

Three guards, and two of them cover failures this repository has actually had tonight:

- `test_poller_manifest_commands_resolve` — every `pollers.json` command must name one relative script **that exists**. This is the class of defect I introduced in `worklink.yaml` yesterday: a config naming a path the tree does not provide, which failed silently because worklink crashes emit no events.
- `test_skill_scripts_resolve_from_installed_package` — every `scripts/` file must survive into the installed package. This is exactly the packaging risk I flagged when declining to fold this fix into a merge commit, and it is now pinned rather than argued.
- `test_skill_root_has_no_executable_code` — enforces the `scripts/` layout and the no-`tests`-package rule.

I verified the third bites by mutation. The second is the one I would have asked for if it were missing.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The read-side classification is directionally right: seeded `docs/` and `prompts/` should be informational, and persisting tainted writes is the necessary anti-laundering counterpart. The new physical-path tests cover that intended pairing, and all 11 hosted checks are green.

Blocking issue: `record_file_write_integrity()` still remaps backend-virtual absolute paths only for `/memory/...` and `/state/...`. A normal file-tool target such as `/docs/notes.md` or `/prompts/notes.md` therefore returns early before reaching the newly widened recording set. If either root is writable through deployment configuration or another admitted file-tool route, a tainted write can be re-read with the new trusted default. I left an inline comment at the affected branch; please keep the virtual-root remapping in step and add virtual-path regressions for both roots.

Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The remediation at `e10e9efe` closes the blocking reachability gap. `record_file_write_integrity()` now remaps the backend-virtual `/docs/...` and `/prompts/...` spellings before applying the widened recording set, and the new parameterized regression exercises that exact virtual-path shape before re-reading the physical target as untrusted. This keeps the trusted-on-read roots paired with tainted-write persistence rather than testing only the downstream physical-path branch.

The original trusted-reference-root and physical-path anti-laundering coverage remains in place, and all 11 hosted checks are green across Linux, macOS, packaging, frontend, skill-conformance, and the enforced suite.

Verdict: APPROVE.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Confirming the blocking finding independently — it reproduces, and I had missed it in my own pass.

`record_file_write_integrity` normalizes before it reaches the widened recording set:

```python
if requested.is_absolute():
    try:
        requested.relative_to(home)
        resource = requested
    except ValueError:
        if requested.parts[1:2] in {("memory",), ("state",)}:
            resource = home / requested.as_posix().lstrip("/")
        else:
            return True          # <- /docs/... and /prompts/... exit here
```

A virtual absolute path such as `/docs/notes.md` is not under `home`, is not in the remap set, and returns early. So the widened set below is **unreachable** for exactly the path shape the file tools address — and the backend runs `virtual_mode` rooted at the home, so that is the normal shape, not an edge case.

The four new tests use physical paths, which is why they pass while the vector stays open. That is the failure mode where a test asserts the right outcome through the wrong path.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
## Fixed — completion is now distinguished from retirement

Pushed `50bf4e56..0f97a9c9`. The finding was right, and it was the same class of mistake as the last one: I treated a weaker observable as the property.

`_unretired_generations` pruned any close whose task was `done()`. A close that finishes **with an exception** is `done()`, so the fence dropped on a teardown that had not succeeded — and the failure went with it, because nothing retrieved the task's result.

Completion is now classified three ways:

| outcome | capacity | rationale |
|---|---|---|
| returns normally | released | the close completed; nothing of that generation is running |
| raises `CancelledError` | released | it honoured the cancel and stopped; nothing is left running |
| raises anything else | **fenced permanently** | teardown reached an unknown state; surfaced once at error level so the supervisor can recycle |

Calling `exception()` also consumes the result, so a failed retirement can no longer resurface as a lost-exception warning.

On treating cancellation as clean: every abandoned close has already been cancelled by that point, so counting cancellation as unclean would make the fence permanent in *all* cases — that is option 1 (hold until restart), which is not the posture chosen here. A task that ends cancelled has stopped, which is what the fence is protecting.

## Tests

- `test_an_abandoned_close_that_fails_keeps_admission_closed` — the late-failure regression you asked for. Drives a real `_admit_peer` after the close raises, and asserts the replacement is refused, `_failed_retirements` is 1, and the exception was consumed.
- `test_an_abandoned_close_that_honours_cancellation_returns_capacity` — the other side, so "fence on failure" cannot silently become "fence on everything".

**Mutation:** restoring the `not task.done()` prune fails exactly `test_an_abandoned_close_that_fails_keeps_admission_closed`.

`tests/test_acp_daemon.py` → 40 passed. Full suite running; I will post the count.

You reported the bound runner timing out with empty output on the full suite, which is why my counts matter here rather than being redundant with yours. Previous head measured 10416 passed / 0 failed on a tree byte-identical to what was pushed.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1306: forge: pr_diff fails outright above the size cap, so the diff is unavailable for exactly the pull requests most in need of review

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
## Verdict: request changes

The shape is right — file-boundary truncation, a marker naming reasons and omitted paths, and no authority change. Confirmed the authority criterion: nothing touches `_FORGE_TOOL_ACTIONS`, the `_REPO_PR_*` action sets, `resolve_review_state_for_context`, or `allowed_operations`; the only `RepoPRAction` references are in tests. And for convergent inputs the cap holds — 300 files x 200 lines returns 523842 bytes, 3000 x 20 returns 524249, both under 524288.

Two blocking problems.

### 1. `bound_diff` raises `ValueError` on a many-small-files diff

The convergence loop drops one section per iteration, but each drop *adds* a line to the marker. When a section is smaller than the marker line describing it, dropping it makes the output larger, so the loop never converges — it empties `included` and then `max(included, ...)` raises.

```
n=12000 tiny sections (566 KB)  -> ValueError: max() iterable argument is empty
n=30000 tiny sections (1.4 MB)  -> ValueError: max() iterable argument is empty
```

Reproduction:

```python
d = "".join(f"diff --git a/f{i} b/f{i}\n@@ -1 +1 @@\n-a\n+b\n" for i in range(12_000))
bound_diff(d)
```

This is a regression in failure mode, which is what the leaf's review criteria were guarding against. `ForgeResponseTooLarge` is a typed `ForgeError` that `_call` and its callers already handle; an unhandled `ValueError` from library code is strictly worse than the error it replaces. A vendored-directory or lockfile-churn PR reaches this shape.

Fix direction: account for the marker inside the convergence check rather than after it, and make the loop terminate on an empty `included` instead of indexing it. Truncating the omitted-path list is already implemented — it just runs too late to help the loop.

### 2. `max_bytes=None` removes the fetch bound entirely

```python
-            max_bytes=_MAX_DIFF_BYTES,
+            max_bytes=None,
```

`get_diff` now downloads a diff of any size into memory before bounding it. The old behaviour refused above 512 KiB; the new behaviour has no ceiling at all, so a single generated-file PR can pull hundreds of megabytes into the process. Bounding the *output* is the leaf's goal, but it should not come at the cost of removing the bound on the *input*.

Fix direction: keep a fetch ceiling — a distinct constant well above `_MAX_DIFF_BYTES` but finite — and let `ForgeResponseTooLarge` still fire beyond it. A diff too large to fetch safely is a case where the honest answer remains a refusal.

### Non-blocking

`bound_diff` is applied twice: once in `GitHubForge.get_diff` and again in `pr_diff` (`mimir/tools/forge.py`). I verified it is idempotent, so this is redundant rather than incorrect — 523842 bytes either way, one marker. Pick one layer; the client is the better one, since it also covers any non-tool caller.

### Verification deferred

I have not run the three sweeps the leaf assigns to the reviewer (full suite, `MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED=1`, and the deployment's `WORKLINK_RUN_BIN`) because the head has to change for the blockers above. I will run all three on the remediated head rather than spend them twice.

CI is green at `0df245e2`, which is worth noting as a limitation rather than reassurance: no existing test exercises a many-small-files diff, which is exactly why the crash survived a green build.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approved at `3e8fb7be`. Both blocking findings are fixed properly rather than worked around.

**The divergence.** The convergence check now accounts for the marker's minimum size (`paths_shown=0`), so dropping a section can no longer grow the output past what the loop is measuring. An emptied `included` raises `ForgeResponseTooLarge` — the typed `ForgeError` callers already handle — instead of `ValueError`. A binary search then fits as many omitted paths as the remaining budget allows, which is a better answer than the linear shrink I suggested.

**The fetch bound.** `_MAX_DIFF_FETCH_BYTES = 8_388_608` replaces `max_bytes=None`, so the input is bounded again at a finite ceiling above the output cap.

**The redundancy.** `bound_diff` now lives only in `GitHubForge.get_diff`, which is the layer that also covers non-tool callers.

Verified independently of the diff — every shape stays under the 524288 cap, with no exception raised:

| input | out | over cap |
|---|---|---|
| 12k tiny sections (542 KB) | 524286 | no |
| 60k tiny sections (2.8 MB) | 524244 | no |
| 20k long-path sections (8.1 MB) | 524281 | no |
| one file > whole budget | 183 | no |
| headerless blob | 189 | no |
| 300 files x 200 lines | 524248 | no |
| under cap | unchanged | — |

The 8.1 MB case is the one worth calling out: every marker line there is longer than the section it describes, which is precisely the shape that diverged before.

Mutation: reverting the minimum-marker accounting fails exactly `test_many_tiny_files_fit_a_bounded_marker_without_raising` and nothing else, so the regression test is aimed at the right layer.

Authority unchanged, re-confirmed at this head: nothing touches `_FORGE_TOOL_ACTIONS`, the `_REPO_PR_*` action sets, `resolve_review_state_for_context`, or `allowed_operations`.

Sweeps, all three the leaf assigns to the reviewer:

Approved at `5214cc06`.

Meets every acceptance criterion in chainlink #1302. Verified across four full-suite runs — plain, `WORKLINK_RUN_BIN="uv run mimir"` (the deployment value), `MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED=1`, and again after the encapsulation fix — all 9659 passed / 0 failed, with 11 hosted checks green.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
## Review — meets every acceptance criterion; one encapsulation finding

Reviewed at `a757c6d67` against chainlink #1302's acceptance and review criteria.

### Verification

| run | result |
|---|---|
| `uv run --extra dev pytest -q` | 9659 passed, 35 skipped, 0 failed |
| `WORKLINK_RUN_BIN="uv run mimir"` (deployment value) | 9659 passed, 35 skipped, 0 failed |
| `MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED=1` | 9659 passed, 35 skipped, 0 failed |
| hosted checks | 11 green |

Identical counts across all three, which is what the leaf's review criteria asked the reviewer rather than the build to establish.

Mutation test: forcing `_scope_miss_refusal` to `return None` fails exactly four tests — the ones covering the new message — while the other 45 stay green, **including** `test_empty_service_scope_keeps_live_discovery_refusal`, `test_scope_miss_keeps_malformed_selector_refusal`, and `test_unconfigured_repository_precedes_nonempty_scope_refusal`. That the preservation tests survive the mutation is the useful part: it shows they assert the old refusal through paths genuinely independent of the new branch, rather than passing incidentally.

### Criteria

All met. Specifically confirmed against the review criteria:

- **Does not change who may resolve scope.** The new branch sits inside the existing gate and can only convert one refusal into a different refusal; it never returns a state. `test_operator_registry_miss_still_discovers_live_scope` holds the operator path.
- **Refusal ordering preserved.** Unconfigured repository still precedes the scope message, so a typo does not surface as an out-of-scope error.
- **Enumeration bounded.** Capped at 5 with a visible `[5 of 7 shown; 2 more]`.
- **No new value in messages.** Only the caller's own arguments and the turn's own scope. The hostile-argument test is the strongest thing in this diff — `json.dumps` is load-bearing as an escaping mechanism, not decoration, and the test proves a newline cannot leave the refusal.

### Finding — reaching into another module's private state

`_scope_miss_refusal` reads `cache._lock` and `cache._states`, both private fields of `ServerDiscoveredPRStates` in `mimir/models.py`, while in the same expression using the sibling `RepoPRScopeRegistry`'s public `review_states`. That asymmetry is the tell: the codebase's own convention is a public accessor.

Not a correctness bug — the lock is correctly held and nothing re-enters it. But it couples `forge.py` to another module's internals, and `ServerDiscoveredPRStates` already carries a third private field (`_remint_attempts`) that a future change could reshuffle.

**This traces to a gap in the leaf, not to the build.** The declared scope is `resolve_review_state_for_context` in `mimir/tools/forge.py` and its tests; `ServerDiscoveredPRStates` exposes no enumeration accessor, and adding one means editing `models.py` — outside that scope. Staying in scope left no clean option, so I am recording this against the spec I wrote rather than against the implementation.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
### Encapsulation finding fixed by hand at `5214cc06`

Rather than spend a worklink attempt on a refactor with no behaviour change, I applied it directly — same handling as #1579.

`ServerDiscoveredPRStates` now exposes a `review_states` property returning an immutable snapshot under its own lock, named to match `RepoPRScopeRegistry.review_states` so a caller holding either scope carrier enumerates it the same way. `_scope_miss_refusal` uses it; no `_lock` or `_states` reach-through remains in `forge.py`.

| run | result |
|---|---|
| `uv run --extra dev pytest -q` (with the fix) | 9659 passed, 35 skipped, 0 failed |
| same, before the fix | 9659 passed, 35 skipped, 0 failed |
| `WORKLINK_RUN_BIN="uv run mimir"` | 9659 passed, 35 skipped, 0 failed |
| `MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED=1` | 9659 passed, 35 skipped, 0 failed |
| hosted checks | green |

Identical counts before and after confirm it is a pure refactor.

This closes chainlink #1303, which mimir filed for the same finding. #1303 is currently `worklink:blocked` (its description was auto-demoted for missing the leaf template sections), so nothing was dispatched against it — I will close it as done when this merges rather than re-planning it.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
## Remediated — the finding was correct, and it was a regression against the base

Pushed `be6a269b..37514dd6`.

### The finding held up

`origin/feature/acp` gated the same-channel shortcut on three things:

```python
source.domain == domain
and source.bridge_instance == bridge_instance
and ChannelResourceAdapter._resolve_channel(source.resource_id) == resolved_triggering
```

This branch reduced that to normalized channel equality alone. That arm admits **without any audience lookup**, on the reasoning that the channel's own audience has already seen the content — which holds only if it really is the same channel. A normalized channel id is unique within a bridge authority, not globally: two independently scoped workspaces can each hold a channel that normalizes to the same string, so the reduced form admits workspace A's `C1` into workspace B's `C1` with no audience check.

### Three tests encoded the collision as intended behaviour

Flagging this prominently, because changing a test to match the code is normally the wrong move and I don't want it to pass unnoticed:

- `test_same_normalized_channel_does_not_query_cross_channel_authority` passed `bridge_instance="slack-workspace-2"` against an auth context on `slack` and asserted `allowed is True` — the reviewed scenario exactly, asserted as correct.
- `test_channel_source_still_requires_exact_triggering_provenance` computed `expected_allowed = mismatch != "resource_id"`, i.e. principal, domain **and** bridge_instance mismatches all admitted.
- `test_service_channel_source_still_requires_matching_channel_provenance` parametrized `("discord", "slack-C1", True)`.

These aren't tests that happened to pass over a defect; they assert the removed check should stay removed. I changed the expectations because they bless a check this branch deleted relative to its own base, not because they were inconvenient. The principal/domain relaxation the branch intends is untouched — only the bridge half is restored.

### The fix

`_same_channel_authority(source, triggering_bridge_instance)` guards the same-channel arm. A mismatch **declines the shortcut** and the flow stays eligible for the audience-subset arm, which compares real audiences rather than strings — it is not a hard deny. Two corrections during remediation, both mine:

- Scoped to real channel domains (`"channel"` / `"channel:<visibility>"`). My first attempt used `startswith("channel")`, which also caught `"channel_metadata"` — a protected-tool result domain — and blocked a native tool result replying to its own triggering channel.
- First attempt short-circuited the whole predicate; that removed the audience arms from cross-bridge flows entirely.

### Production safety

The guard cannot fire on a legitimate same-channel flow. `access_control.py` (auth context) and `agent.py` (source label) derive the bridge from the same event by identical duplicated logic — `extra["bridge_instance"]`, else `event.source`, else `service:<principal>` — so for a triggering channel the two always agree.

The one test that disagreed was a fixture artifact: `tests/test_agent.py::_audience_auth` hardcoded `bridge_instance="acp"` for all six callers, including one whose triggering event is `source="discord"`. The helper now takes the bridge; that caller passes what its event carries. The other five are ACP sessions and keep the default.

### Verification

- Mutation test: neutralizing `_same_channel_authority` with an early `return True` fails exactly three named tests and nothing else — `test_same_normalized_channel_from_other_bridge_authority_is_not_admitted`, `test_channel_source_still_requires_exact_triggering_provenance[bridge_instance]`, `test_service_channel_source_still_requires_matching_channel_provenance[discord-slack-C1-False]`. Restored and re-verified.
- Full suite: **10194 passed, 34 skipped, 0 failed** (8:01).

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
## Fixed — the fail-open was real

Pushed `37514dd6..da1baad4`.

`if not source_bridge or not triggering_bridge_instance: return True` made unknown authority equivalent to same authority, which is the same fail-open the bridge comparison was added to close. It now returns `False`. That is not a denial — the flow stays eligible for the audience arms, which compare real audiences instead of trusting unproven provenance. No test depended on the permissive default.

## On the requested missing-source coverage — it needed a different shape

I wrote the two cases as you asked, sink-level and parametrized over which side is absent. Mutating the branch back to `return True` killed only the missing-**trigger** case. The missing-source case passed with and without the fix.

The reason is upstream: `bridge_instance=""` makes the label incomplete —

```
bridge_instance=''      -> is_complete = False
bridge_instance='slack' -> is_complete = True
```

— and incomplete provenance already fails closed before this predicate runs. So a sink-level assertion for the missing-source side asserts an outcome the incomplete-provenance path produces on its own, and would keep passing if this branch were deleted.

Restructured so both sides are actually covered:

- `test_absent_triggering_bridge_does_not_take_the_same_channel_shortcut` — sink-level, the reachable case.
- `test_same_channel_authority_declines_on_absent_bridge` — drives `_same_channel_authority` directly over `("", "slack")`, `("slack", None)`, `("", None)`.

Re-mutated: all four now fail with the fail-open restored, and pass without it.

Flagging this rather than quietly satisfying the request, since a test that passes for an unrelated reason is worse than no test — it reads as coverage the branch does not have.

Full suite and the enforced run are re-running at `da1baad4`; I will post both counts before asking for merge.

payload.body:
### Call-site audit

`_source_is_triggering_channel_compatible` has six production call sites. I pass `triggering_bridge_instance` at three; recording why the other three are deliberate rather than missed:

| call site | source domain | affected |
|---|---|---|
| `access_control.py:4845` | channel | **yes** — passes it |
| `access_control.py:5612` | channel | **yes** — passes it |
| `access_control.py:5711` | channel | **yes** — passes it |
| `agent.py:4105` | `recent_activity` | no |
| `feedback/__init__.py:788` | `feedback` | no |
| `feedback/__init__.py:877` | `feedback` | no |

`_same_channel_authority` short-circuits to `True` for any domain that is not `channel` or `channel:<visibility>`, so the three unpassed sites are unaffected either way.

Worth noting for the one that looks most suspicious: `feedback/__init__.py:877` mints a synthetic `bridge_instance=f"mimir-chain:{resource_key}"`, which by construction can never equal the triggering bridge. It is `domain="feedback"`, so the guard does not apply — but if that domain ever became channel-scoped, the parameter's `None` default declines the shortcut rather than admitting it. The failure direction there is closed, not open.

payload.title: Worklink #1301: fetch_url: a fetched PDF is unreadable, and the pdftotext shortcut is unavailable to exactly the turns that fetch PDFs

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Two small findings. The implementation is sound and the diagnosis behind the Dockerfile fix was excellent.**

## What is right

| Criterion | |
|---|---|
| Raw body preserved | ✓ separate `body_path` / `text_path`; `sha256` hashing untouched; mutation-pinned (overwriting the body fails `test_fetch_url_extracts_pdf_without_changing_cached_body`) |
| Pure Python | ✓ no subprocess anywhere in the path |
| Both bounds enforced independently | ✓ `truncation_reasons` distinguishes `page_limit` from `output_byte_limit`, and `_truncate_utf8` respects UTF-8 boundaries |
| Graceful degradation | ✓ broad `except`, records `type(exc).__name__`, unlinks the partial sibling, and still returns the body path; "PDF contains no extractable text" covers image-only |
| Only `application/pdf` converted | ✓ dedicated test |
| Extracted text carries the body's label | ✓ the test asserts BOTH paths resolve to `("untrusted", "active_ingest")` |

The bounds tests set explicit env overrides with literal values (`MIMIR_FETCH_PDF_MAX_PAGES=2`, `MAX_TEXT_BYTES=100`) and assert literally, so the mechanism is genuinely pinned rather than moving with the constants.

**The image fix deserves specific credit.** The failure was subtle — the worker venv installs the published wheel for its dependency set and then overlays this checkout's source with `--no-deps`, so a newly introduced runtime dependency is absent from any published wheel and the overlay cannot import. Diagnosing that from a red `worklink-image-identity` job, and writing the reason into the Dockerfile comment, is better than I would have expected.

## Finding 1: the transitional pip install is pinned permanently

```python
assert '/opt/mimir-worklink/venv/bin/pip install --no-cache-dir "pypdf>=6.16"' in text
```

The Dockerfile comment says the explicit install is needed "during this PR's proof" — it is transitional, and becomes redundant once a published wheel carries `pypdf` as a declared dependency. But this assertion pins the exact line INCLUDING the version literal, so removing the workaround breaks a test, and so does bumping the floor to `>=7`.

A workaround with an assertion holding it in place tends to outlive its reason, and the next person to touch it will read the failing test as "this line is required" rather than "this line was temporary". Please either assert something version-agnostic (that the worker venv installs the dependency before the overlay) or add a comment at the assertion naming the condition under which it should be deleted.

## Finding 2: the default bound values are unasserted

Raising `FETCH_PDF_MAX_PAGES_DEFAULT` from 100 to 1,000,000, or `FETCH_PDF_MAX_TEXT_BYTES_DEFAULT` from 1 MB to 10 GB, leaves the suite fully green — the tests override both via env, so nothing exercises the shipped defaults.

This is weaker than it first looks and I want to be precise about it: the bounds MECHANISM is well covered. What is unpinned is only that the shipped defaults are conservative, which is what chainlink #1301 asked for, since this input is attacker-supplied by definition. Two literal assertions would close it.

For the record, my first pass mis-called this as the same self-referential-test defect I found in #1576. It is not. I had mutated the defaults, which these tests correctly do not depend on.

## Verification so far

Scoped: 65 passed across `tests/test_tools_web.py` and `tests/test_worklink_worker_identity.py`. Zero conflicts with current `main`. Hosted CI 11/11 after the image fix. I have not run the three-condition full suite yet — a remediation moves the head, so I will run it once against the fixed head.

- the shipped defaults are pinned by literal assertion; raising either `FETCH_PDF_MAX_PAGES_DEFAULT` to 1,000,000 or `FETCH_PDF_MAX_TEXT_BYTES_DEFAULT` to 10 GB now fails the new test

payload.title: Worklink #1300: authz: the egress allowlist accepts only exact URLs, so no per-item feed can ever be approved

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body: Approved on operator sign-off. Verified at `85e7c7a7`: parsed-URL matching with all four hostile cases refused, segment boundary enforced by construction via the `/*` syntax, both mutations load-bearing, and three-condition full verification green at 9628 passed each (plain, enforced, and with the deployment's WORKLINK_RUN_BIN set).

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Verified clean at `85e7c7a7`. No findings.** Withholding approval pending operator sign-off.

## The property that decides this leaf

Matching is done on a **parsed** URL, not a string prefix on the raw target:

```python
parsed = urlsplit(normalized)
...
parsed.scheme == scope.scheme
and parsed.netloc == scope.netloc
and parsed.path.startswith(scope.path_prefix)
```

All four hostile cases from chainlink #1300 are in the suite and refused: `https://arxiv.org.evil.com/x`, `https://arxiv.org@evil.com/x`, `https://evil.com/?u=https://arxiv.org/x`, and `http://arxiv.org/x` against an https-only approval.

**The segment boundary is enforced by construction, which is better than what the leaf asked for.** The scope syntax is an explicit `/*` suffix and the parser strips only the `*` (`value[:-1]`), so `https://arxiv.org/abs/*` yields `path_prefix == "/abs/"` with its trailing slash intact. `/absolutely-not/x` is refused because the prefix cannot end mid-segment, rather than because someone remembered to normalise it. `test_fetch_url_path_scope_is_bounded_to_path_segment` pins it.

Also correct without being asked: scopes reject a query string, `%`, `\\`, and `.`/`..` path segments; `_url_approval_host_is_bounded` requires at least two labels so a bare TLD cannot be approved, while IP literals still work; and the bare exact-URL form is untouched, so an operator who wrote one exact URL does not silently gain a whole host.

## Mutation

```
parsed matching -> naive string prefix on the raw URL:
  FAILED test_fetch_url_path_scope_is_bounded_to_path_segment
  FAILED test_fetch_url_host_scope_matches_parsed_scheme_and_host[https://arxiv.org.evil.com/x]

value[:-1] -> value[:-2] (drops the trailing slash):
  FAILED test_fetch_url_path_scope_is_bounded_to_path_segment
```

Two failures and one respectively, nothing else — both properties are load-bearing rather than incidentally satisfied.

## Verification

Tree frozen at `85e7c7a7`, clean before and after:

```
uv run pytest -q                                   9628 passed, 35 skipped  (10:28)
MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED=1 uv run pytest -q   9628 passed, 35 skipped  ( 9:44)
```

payload.title: Worklink #1299: authz: operator_alert is granted and sink-policed but has no tool, so an untrusted-ingest poller cannot report and reaches for shell instead

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**One blocking finding. The build is otherwise strong — this is a vacuous test, not a design problem.**

## The finding: neither bound is actually pinned

`test_operator_alert_bounds_text_and_per_turn_count` passes with both bounds effectively removed:

```
OPERATOR_ALERT_MAX_PER_TURN  3    -> 10_000       4 passed, 0 failed
OPERATOR_ALERT_MAX_CHARS     4000 -> 10_000_000   4 passed, 0 failed
```

The cause is that every input and assertion is expressed in terms of the constants:

```python
await operator_alert.coroutine(text="x" * (OPERATOR_ALERT_MAX_CHARS + 1))
for index in range(OPERATOR_ALERT_MAX_PER_TURN):
    ...
assert len(channels.calls) == OPERATOR_ALERT_MAX_PER_TURN
```

Raise the constant and the test raises its own input to match, so it can never fail. It pins the MECHANISM — that some limit exists and trips — but not the VALUES.

That matters more here than it usually would. These bounds are the control against injected content flooding the operator channel: the whole reason this tool exists is to let a turn whose context is untrusted external text report to a human, and chainlink #1299 states the input is attacker-supplied by definition. As written, a later change could raise `MAX_CHARS` to a megabyte and no test would notice.

**Fix:** pin the values independently of the code under test — either literal inputs, or an explicit assertion such as

```python
assert OPERATOR_ALERT_MAX_CHARS == 4000
assert OPERATOR_ALERT_MAX_PER_TURN == 3
```

so that widening a bound requires a deliberate test edit.

## Everything else verified and correct

| Criterion | |
|---|---|
| Callable tool gated by the capability | ✓ |
| Destination server-derived | ✓ **stronger than specified** — `operator_alert(text: str)` takes no destination parameter at all, so a hostile destination cannot be supplied rather than merely being ignored |
| Unconfigured fails loudly | ✓ and pinned: mutating the sink adapter to always match correctly fails `test_unconfigured_alert_fails_loudly_in_real_sink_gate` |
| No relaxation of other sinks | ✓ the `access_control.py` change is two lines mapping the tool to `SinkCategory.NOTIFICATION`; `SAME_CHANNEL`, `CROSS_CHANNEL` and `DIRECT_MESSAGE` are untouched |
| Runtime guidance names it | ✓ `test_poller_turn_guidance_names_operator_alert_for_reporting` |
| Tainted turn succeeds, other sinks still refuse | ✓ single test covering both halves |

The unconfigured test is better than my criterion asked for: it drives the real `BudgetGateMiddleware` and asserts `called is False`, so the gate refuses before the tool executes rather than the tool refusing itself.

**On scope.** Four files beyond the declared list — `models.py`, `runtime.py`, `budget_gate.py`, plus collateral test updates. I checked each and they are necessary plumbing rather than creep: `models.py` adds the `operator_alert_count` field the per-turn bound needs, `runtime.py` wires and tears down the tool's dependencies, and `budget_gate.py` gains a small additive destination-resolution branch. That last one does NOT touch the `tool_error` / `error[:500]` emit block that chainlink #1297 owns, so the two can land in either order.

Scoped suite is 960 passed / 2 skipped. I have not run the three-condition full verification yet — a remediation moves the head and invalidates it, so I will run it once against the fixed head.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1296: authz: first-party file reads land in the fail-closed unknown-provenance label, blocking operator PR review under enforcement

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Requesting changes: this removes two existing protections rather than closing the gap. The chainlink I wrote is the cause, and I am fixing it.**

## What the leaf got wrong

#1296 states that filesystem reads have no branch in `classify_protected_result` and fall through to the fail-closed unknown-provenance default. That is wrong. `_filesystem_result_integrity` already existed on `main` and already trusted `memory` and `state`, with two deliberate protections:

```python
if relative.parts and relative.parts[0] in {"memory", "state"}:
    # Poller subprocesses write this tree directly, outside the protected
    # tool boundary, and may persist attacker-derived cursor/event fields.
    # A path under state/pollers is therefore not proof of self-authorship.
    if relative.parts[0:2] == ("state", "pollers"):
        return "untrusted", "active_ingest"
    persisted = _persisted_file_integrity(home, relative)
    return persisted, ("informational" if persisted == "trusted" else "active_ingest")
```

The real gap was only that `.mimir_builtin_skills` and `skills` were absent from that set. Two entries, one branch.

Worse, #1296 called taint laundering an "ACCEPTED CONSEQUENCE… accepted under the single-operator threat model." That reads as license to delete the mechanism that prevented it. That sentence is mine and it should not have been written.

## What this branch does

The read path now returns `trusted/informational` unconditionally for the four roots:

```python
if relative.parts and relative.parts[0] in {
    ".mimir_builtin_skills", "skills", "memory", "state",
}:
    return "trusted", "informational"
```

Verified against the branch, in `_filesystem_result_integrity` as it now stands:

```
_persisted_file_integrity called in read path: False
state/pollers excluded in read path         : False
```

Two consequences:

1. **`state/pollers` is now trusted.** That tree holds poller cursors — `state/pollers/github-activity/cursor.json` carries repo names, PR numbers and head SHAs taken from GitHub. Attacker-influenced content now reads back as trusted. The deleted comment states exactly this hazard, and the docs line removed in this diff (`except <home>/state/pollers/**, which poller subprocesses can populate`) documented it.

2. **The write side is now decorative.** `record_file_write_integrity` still writes `<home>/.mimir/file-integrity.json`, and nothing reads it. A file written during a tainted turn is recorded untrusted and then read back as trusted, which is precisely the laundering path the map exists to close.

## The tests bless the inversion

Two existing security tests were renamed rather than kept:

```
- test_untrusted_model_write_cannot_launder_through_self_authored_state
+ test_untrusted_model_write_uses_accepted_first_party_state_carveout
- test_poller_managed_state_is_untrusted_active_ingest
+ test_poller_managed_state_uses_accepted_first_party_carveout
```

A rename from `cannot_launder` to `uses_accepted_carveout` converts a test that prevented a security property from being violated into one that asserts it is violated. When a build has to rewrite a test's name to make it pass, the property it named is the finding.

## What to do instead

Keep `_filesystem_result_integrity`'s existing structure and add the two missing roots:

```python
if relative.parts and relative.parts[0] in {
    ".mimir_builtin_skills", "skills", "memory", "state",
}:
    if relative.parts[0:2] == ("state", "pollers"):
        return "untrusted", "active_ingest"
    persisted = _persisted_file_integrity(home, relative)
    return persisted, ("informational" if persisted == "trusted" else "active_ingest")
```

Restore both original tests under their original names and assertions. Keep the new tests that cover genuinely new ground — the symlink-before-containment case, the failed-read case, the non-first-party case, and `test_review_skill_read_admits_scoped_forge_sinks_under_enforcement`, which is the actual objective and looks right.

payload.title: Migrate the worklink feature-factory backend to the 0.7.0 three-package architecture

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Verdict: Request changes

The 0.7.0 migration is comprehensive and the core adapter/recovery path is strongly fail-closed: package-bound launcher admission, strict status/control contracts, durable recovery identity, independent repository testing, stable clean-HEAD checks, and canonical PR identity verification are all good changes. The focused Worklink suite also passes locally (321 tests), and the Linux CI jobs are green at reviewed head `44e472914eef2ddc4c637e498f8e414d9656f2d5`.

One blocking scheduling regression remains in the ready-queue poller: `_worklink_dispatch_plan` now discards `active_lock_ids`, while `main()` computes a reduced slot count and slices the still-unfiltered sorted candidates. An active low-ID issue that remains ready/actionable during claim-label transition or label drift can therefore consume the only available slot, launch a redundant worker that loses the atomic claim, and starve an unlocked issue on every poll. This affects both leaf and factory pools. I left an inline comment with the concrete case and requested regression coverage.

Please restore active-lock exclusion before candidate slicing. At submission time, the two macOS pytest jobs were also still running; they should be green before merge.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Verdict: Request changes

The new lifecycle-recovery hardening is useful, but the current head `5d58302831881a0a81b34498c85440d035095fff` does not resolve the blocking dispatch-planner issue from my prior review, and Jason's two deployment findings also remain visible in the current diff.

### Blocking findings

1. **Active claims still consume dispatch slots** — `mimir/optional-skills/chainlink-orchestrator/scripts/poller.py:218-241, 386-412`. `_worklink_dispatch_plan()` still executes `del active_lock_ids`, builds leaf/epic candidates without excluding locked issue IDs, and `main()` slices those candidates only after reducing each pool's slot count. An active low-ID ready item can therefore be selected again and starve an unlocked item. My existing inline comment contains the concrete cap-2 case. Please filter active lock IDs from both candidate pools before slicing and add the regression requested there.

2. **The required deployment migration remains undocumented** — `docs/internal/WORKLINK.md` updates examples to `entrypoint`, but does not tell an operator that an existing `<home>/worklink.yaml` containing retired `bin`/`args` keys must be edited before or with deployment, nor that this image-layer package change requires a rebuild (`docker compose ... up -d --build`) rather than a restart. Because registry construction fails before dispatch, omitting this sequence can silently stop all leaf and factory dispatches.

3. **Retired-key diagnostics still report only one key** — `mimir/worklink/backends/registry.py:673-678`. The code sorts all retired keys but emits only `retired[0]`; the live `bin` + `args` shape therefore requires two fix/redeploy cycles. Report all retired keys in one error and cover the multi-key case.

### Validation

The bound focused-test attempt was rejected by the contained runner because the selector did not resolve inside its authorized checkout, so I am not claiming local test evidence. At review time, package, frontend, skill-conformance, Worklink image identity, Chainlink audit, and Claude-code smoke checks are green; the Linux and macOS pytest jobs are still running. Those should be green before merge.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Second blocking finding, complementary to @mimir-carreira's.** Theirs is in the dispatch planner; this one is in the deployment config and is structurally invisible to CI, because the file lives in the mimirbot repo rather than this one.

## Deploying this kills every worklink dispatch

The new loader rejects the retired keys:

```python
retired = sorted(set(settings) & {"bin", "args", "ready", "reviewer"})
if retired:
    raise ValueError(
        "worklink backends.feature_factory retired setting "
        f"'{retired[0]}'; configure one absolute 'entrypoint' ending in "
        "feature-factory/bin/factory.js"
    )
```

The live `<home>/worklink.yaml` currently carries **two** of them:

```yaml
  feature_factory:
    # Path renamed 2026-08-11 with the repo (opencode-feature-factory ->
    # feature-factory). Worklink crashes emit NO events, so a stale bin here
    # fails silently -- read run-<id>.log, not events.jsonl, if dispatch dies.
    bin: node /workspace/feature-factory/src/cli.js
    args: []
```

So on deploy, config load raises and every dispatch dies — leaf and factory alike. The block's own comment states the aggravating factor: worklink crashes emit no events, so this fails **silently**; nothing appears in `events.jsonl` and the only trace is `run-<id>.log`.

This has happened before, in this same file. Twelve lines below the block is the record:

```
# RETIRED #1037/#1257 (2026-07-29): the codex backend config block was removed
# here on 2026-07-30. BackendRegistry now rejects any backend key outside
# {feature_factory, opencode}, so the stale block raised
# "unknown Worklink backend config: codex" and killed every dispatch.
```

Same mechanism, same file, same outcome.

To be clear about what is *not* wrong: rejecting `bin`/`args` is correct. Clean removal on a pre-release single-consumer surface is the right call and the error message names the replacement well. The gap is that a change which invalidates live operator config ships without saying so.

## Two asks

**1. Carry the deploy step in the PR.** Add it to the PR body and to `docs/internal/WORKLINK.md`. Nothing in the diff mentions `worklink.yaml` migration, `<home>`, or deploy sequencing — I grepped all three touched docs for it and got no matches. The required edit is small, since `entrypoint` defaults to `MIMIR_FACTORY_ENTRYPOINT`, which the Dockerfile now sets:

```yaml
  feature_factory:
    entrypoint: /opt/mimir-opencode/lib/node_modules/feature-factory/bin/factory.js
```

replacing both existing lines. Worth stating explicitly that this is an image-layer change, so it needs `docker compose -p <project> up -d --build` rather than a restart, and that the config edit must land **before or with** that rebuild.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The core direction is right: moving provenance collection into the bounded feedback-selection path prevents unclassified and over-cap records from tainting a prompt they did not contribute to, and the new focused tests cover those ordinary event paths well.

One blocking gap remains: labels are currently collected only for individually appended event/turn signals. Synthetic lines bypass that append path—valence transition chains consume and skip all of their source events before injecting a chain signal, and cross-turn loop detection derives a line from `send_message_sent` records afterward. Those rendered lines therefore have no contributing-record labels, so `recent_prompt_block()` can return content whose provenance is empty or incomplete. The inline comment identifies the exact path. Please propagate the records used by each synthetic signal into label collection and add regressions for both a transition chain and a cross-turn loop.

Validation: `tests/test_feedback.py` passes locally (161 passed), and all 11 hosted checks are green at `d0635b22292c6f231fd36edd163140872bb5d8f5`.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
I re-reviewed the proposed disposition and am keeping the synthetic-provenance finding blocking.

The renderer audit narrows the exposure—valence chains do not copy arbitrary payload fields—but it does not make those lines source-independent. Their existence, event-kind/run sequence, polarity, per-run counts, and ordering timestamp are all derived from the contributing records. Cross-turn loop lines additionally render the originating channel id. Those are protected-record metadata/control dependencies, not static framework text.

There is also a concrete protected-loader failure beyond disclosure: with a feedback window containing only a transition chain, every source event is skipped at `mimir/feedback/__init__.py:476-480`, the chain is appended at `:529-536` without a source, and `recent_prompt_block()` returns non-empty content with `labels.sources == ()`. `Agent._build_turn_prompt.use()` rejects that at `mimir/agent.py:4059-4064` as incomplete provenance. In a mixed block, the same chain instead free-rides on unrelated ordinary-record labels. `_detect_cross_turn_send_loops()` has the same empty/free-riding shape.

So folding this into #1569 is not sufficient for this propagation: `feature/acp` would receive a known violation of the protected prompt-loader contract. Please carry the exact contributors for both synthetic append paths into label collection here, with regressions for synthetic-only and mixed blocks through the protected-loader invariant. The prior inline finding remains the code anchor; I attempted to add this updated rationale inline, but the bound review API rejected the duplicate/right-side placement.

Validation: contained `tests/test_feedback.py` passes (161 tests), all 11 hosted checks are green, and the live head remained `d0635b22292c6f231fd36edd163140872bb5d8f5` immediately before submission.

I found no new blocker introduced by the merge.

The existing feedback-provenance block is intentionally and correctly still unresolved. The current diff still adds labels only when an ordinary event or turn signal reaches its append path; chain-consumed records and records used by `_detect_cross_turn_send_loops()` can still produce synthetic prompt content without contributing sources. A synthetic-only window can therefore return non-empty feedback with `labels.sources == ()` and trip the protected-loader incomplete-provenance invariant; a mixed window lets the synthetic content free-ride on unrelated labels.

So the requested hold remains: do not merge this head until #1569 lands the admission-time selection/labeling fix and that fix is propagated here. The existing inline finding remains the code anchor, and the author’s latest comment accurately states the dependency and hold.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Re-reviewed at `12c478084030c90953b3ba01dbc74caf150f8816` after the latest propagation.

The synthetic-provenance failure is fixed by the admission-time selection now present on `feature/acp`: chain-only and mixed feedback blocks have complete labels, and the focused feedback suite passes (177 tests). The revised cap and duplicate assertions are also defensible: every capped record contributes to the rendered per-kind `×N` count, and every collapsed duplicate contributes to the collapsed run count, so retaining all of those sources is not over-labelling.

One blocking over-labelling path remains, however. `_select_prompt_recent.admit()` attaches every admitted record's source at `mimir/feedback/__init__.py:799` before `recent()` applies arousal suppression. The new `test_arousal_dropped_records_keep_all_admission_labels` explicitly locks this in: two `tool_call_denied` records are below the threshold and contribute neither a line nor a count to the only rendered `interactive_turn_no_send_message` signal, yet the block retains three sources. The test proves only that delivery back to `current` stays allowed. For a later cross-channel sink, either hidden record can still veto delivery even though no content derived from it reached the model. Trigger-channel admission compatibility does not imply compatibility with every eventual sink destination—the feedback labels exist precisely because those can differ.

Please collect labels from records that survive into rendered signals (including every member that affects aggregate counts and synthetic chains), while excluding below-arousal records when they affect no rendered signal. Add a regression whose only visible line comes from another source and whose eventual sink is compatible with that visible source but not with the suppressed record; the suppressed record must not veto it.
