payload.title: Worklink #1277: ci: add a NON-BLOCKING macOS leg to learn the runner delta, without renaming the required pytest checks

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. This does exactly what the leaf asked, avoids the trap it warned about, and the leg has already earned its keep.

## The trap was avoided

The leaf's central warning was not to add an `os` dimension to the existing `pytest` matrix, because that renames `pytest (3.11)` / `pytest (3.12)` — the exact contexts branch protection requires — and every PR would then block forever waiting for checks that no longer report. Verified from this run's **emitted** check names, not the YAML:

```
pytest (3.11)          SUCCESS   <- required, name intact
pytest (3.12)          SUCCESS   <- required, name intact
pytest-macos (3.11)    FAILURE   <- new, not required
pytest-macos (3.12)    FAILURE   <- new, not required
```

`+46/-0`, so the existing job is untouched, and the YAML carries a comment explaining *why* the job is separate — which is what stops a future editor folding it into the matrix.

`fail-fast: false` is a good call: it kept both Python legs reporting instead of letting one mask the other, and that is why we have two distinct failures below rather than one.

## What the leg found — the deliverable

The leaf said a red leg is as useful as a green one, and it was right. Both macOS legs failed while ubuntu and enforced stayed green. Recording the failures here for **#1278** to consume:

**`pytest-macos (3.11)`** — `tests/test_shell_jobs.py::test_scheduled_eviction_does_not_require_later_spawn`
```
AssertionError: job j_118644e73f did not exit within 5.0s
```
Wall-clock sensitivity, not a Darwin defect. Same family as the `test_debounce_coalesces_burst_to_single_push` flake seen on ubuntu earlier today and chainlink #1258's poller test. This will eventually fire on ubuntu too.

**`pytest-macos (3.12)`** — a directory-tree comparison
```
Differing items:
{b'.git/objects': (501, 20, 493, 2927246, ...499991)} != {... ...163533)}
Right contains 1 more item:
{b'.git/objects/maintenance.lock': (501, 20, 420, 2927281, ...157200)}
```
Git's background auto-maintenance spawned mid-test and mutated the tree being snapshotted. Config-dependent, not platform-dependent — it would fire anywhere `maintenance.auto` is enabled.

Worth stating plainly: **neither failure is Darwin-specific.** They are latent environment assumptions that macOS surfaced first. That is a better outcome than finding a `renamex_np` bug, because these two would have kept flaking intermittently on ubuntu and been dismissed as noise.

## Timing, for the #1278 promotion decision

```
pytest-macos (3.11)   8.9 min
pytest-macos (3.12)   8.5 min
pytest (3.12)         6.1 min   <- current critical path
```

Promoting the leg to required would move the critical path from ~6 to ~9 minutes, roughly +3 minutes of merge latency. No billing cost — the repository is public. While non-required the impact is zero, since a merge does not wait on it.

## One correction of mine

I told the operator the suite was already green on macOS, based on my own Darwin runs (10030 passed). That was wrong in the direction I had flagged: a developer machine is not a GitHub runner. Going non-blocking first was the right call and this run proves it — had the leg been required in one step, `main` would be unmergeable right now.

payload.title: Worklink #1262: redaction: add a conformance test so the durable path can never again mask less than the ephemeral one

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. Small change, exactly the property #1262 asked for, and it catches the regression it exists to prevent.

## The property is the right shape

```python
assert not ephemeral_masked or durable_masked
```

An implication, not an equality — the durable path may mask *more* than the ephemeral one, never less. That is the correct statement of the invariant, since the two paths have different jobs.

## It is not vacuous

An implication test passes trivially when the antecedent is never true, so I checked rather than assumed: the ephemeral path masks **all 7** corpus items, so every assertion is live.

## It catches the real defect

Removing the three durable colon rules — reproducing the original #1214/#1261 drift — makes it fail, and the message names the offending input rather than just asserting:

```
AssertionError: ephemeral path masked 'TAVILY_API_KEY: tvly-…', but durable path did not
```

The shared `tests/redaction_corpus.py` is the right structure. One corpus both paths are measured against is precisely what was missing when the durable path silently fell behind. Fixtures are fragment-built, so the file stays publishable through the staged-secret guard.

| Suite | Result |
|---|---|
| Full | 9425 passed, 34 skipped |
| Enforced (`MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED=1`) | 9425 passed, 34 skipped |
| CI | 9/9 |

## On the CI failure, for the record

The first `pytest-enforced` run failed on `test_debounce_coalesces_burst_to_single_push` — "expected 1 coalesced push, got 2". Unrelated to this PR, which touches only two test files: my local enforced run passed on the same code, the test passes 3/3 locally under enforcement, and it went green on re-run.

Worth noting that its docstring already records a previous flake of this exact shape, hardened from a 0.10s window to 0.50s with `sleep(0)` yields. It is still wall-clock dependent — two pushes means a debounce timer fired mid-burst under load. Not a blocker here, but the hardening is evidently not sufficient, and it is the second timing-sensitive test to misfire under CI load recently.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1274: redaction: multiline YAML block-scalar credentials reach durable logs in cleartext (grammar-scoped retry after 7 defects in 6 rounds)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
This solves the grammar problem that defeated six rounds of pattern patching. Blocking on one measured performance regression, not on correctness.

## What works

Every production that previously defeated the scanner now passes, including the one that was structurally impossible for a line-at-a-time recognizer:

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| basic block, blank line in body, leading blank | masked |
| nested scalar with a same-indent sibling | masked; `nextkey` and `root` intact |
| sequence entry (`- password: \|`) | masked; next list item intact |
| **explicit mapping key** (`? password` / `: \|`) | **masked**; `next: keep` intact |
| anchor before the indicator | masked |

173 tests pass. The approach is the right one — a real parse via `yaml.compose_all` with a column-tracking scanner fallback for log text that is not a whole document — and it is what the leaf asked for rather than a seventh pattern. `redact_text` also stays total: the parse is wrapped so a failure returns `None` and falls back rather than raising.

## Blocking: a 10.8x slowdown on the durable logging hot path

`_mask_block_scalar_lines` runs on **every** `redact_text` call, and it parses with `yaml.compose_all` unconditionally — there is no cheap pre-check for whether the text could contain a block scalar at all. `redact_text` is called on every turn record and recursively through `redact_payload` for every event payload string, so this is the hottest path in durable logging.

Measured on this checkout, same five representative log samples (plain tool output, a JSON tool-call record, an error line, a 2 KB blob, a 50-line multi-line record), 400 iterations each:

```
main            66.5 us per redact_text call
PR #1543       720.7 us per redact_text call      10.8x
```

Attributing it within the PR:

```
block-scalar stage alone   478.3 us
regex stage alone          189.0 us   (13 patterns vs main's 10)
```

A cheap indicator guard recovers most of it. Injecting `if "|" not in text and ">" not in text: return text` at the top of `_mask_block_scalar_lines`:

```
with the guard  204.4 us            from 720.7
```

A block scalar cannot exist without a `|` or `>` indicator, so that check is sound and skips the parse for the overwhelming majority of log lines. The prior implementation had exactly this guard; it was lost in the rewrite.

Please add it, and please state the residual: 204 vs 66 us is still ~3x, and the regex stage alone now costs 189 us against main's 66 us total. Worth confirming that the three added patterns are each necessary and none is quadratic on long lines — a 2 KB blob is a normal log payload here.

## Why I am blocking rather than noting it

This repo has already had a memory incident traced to durable turn logging, and `redact_text` is on the write path for every turn and event. A 10x cost there is a production characteristic, not a micro-optimisation. It is also cheap to fix — one line restores most of it.

Nothing else outstanding: I ran the previously-defeating cases directly, the structure-survival assertions hold, and the PR is based on current `main` (post-#1539) and merges cleanly.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1275: poller: every hard refusal gets the 24h permanent-fault backoff, so a PR whose transient blocker cleared sits idle for a day

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. This meets every criterion in #1275, and two of the design choices are better than what I specified.

## The classification fails safe in both directions

```python
def _classify_refusal_reasons(reasons: list[str]) -> str:
    if reasons and all(
        any(fragment in reason for fragment in _SELF_CLEARING_REFUSAL_REASON_FRAGMENTS)
        for reason in reasons
    ):
        return _REFUSAL_SELF_CLEARING
    return _REFUSAL_OPERATOR_GATED
```

`all()` means one unrecognised reason in a batch is enough to keep the 24h suppression, and an empty list short-circuits to operator-gated. That is the safe default, and it is pinned:

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| Flip the unknown-reason default to self-clearing | **3 failures** |
| Remove one self-clearing refusal fragment | **1 failure** |

## The fragments are real, which I checked rather than assumed

All five correspond to actual controller refusal text. Two of them are split across source lines by implicit concatenation, so a naive `grep -F` reports them missing — I confirmed via an AST reconstruction that the runtime strings match. Sourcing them from the controller rather than inventing them is what the leaf asked for and it was done properly.

## Better than specified

**The bounded ceiling reuses `REVIEW_REQUEST_MAX_ATTEMPTS`** rather than introducing a new constant, so a self-clearing refusal that repeats forever still stops. I asked for a ceiling and did not say how; this is the right way.

**`prior_refusal_classification` is emitted on the event**, so an operator can see why a PR is or is not being reminded without reading source. That was a criterion I expected to be skipped.

| Suite | Result |
|---|---|
| Full | 9367 passed, 34 skipped |
| Enforced (`MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED=1`) | 9367 passed, 34 skipped |
| CI | 9/9 |

Tree frozen and identical at both ends of the run.

This closes the loop that produced it: PR #1540 sat idle for hours after its blocking lease cleared, because a transient refusal was routed into the 24h permanent-fault backoff. Retained-lease refusals now retry on the normal hourly cadence.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1273: repo leases: successful lease acquisition is unaudited, so the head-binding the typed path exists to enforce has no record

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. This meets all eight acceptance criteria, and the two I singled out as easiest to get wrong are both handled correctly.

## The head is a fact, not an intention

```python
head_sha = _run(
    runner,
    ["git", "-C", str(lease.path), "rev-parse", "--verify", "HEAD"],
    "acquired PR checkout lease has no HEAD",
).lower()
```

Read from the established lease, not echoed from the caller's scope. I mutation-tested the distinction rather than trusting it — replacing that read with `lease.head_sha` (the immutable checkout-time head) fails **exactly one** test:

```
FAILED tests/test_pr_checkout_lease.py::test_second_attempt_resumes_unpushed_commit
1 failed, 39 passed
```

That is the only case where the two values diverge, because an unpushed commit has advanced the worktree past the bound head. The fresh-acquisition test correctly keeps passing, since they are equal there. A record that echoed the request would have looked identical in the fresh case and been wrong exactly when it mattered.

Both event tests assert the full payload by equality, so a stray or missing field fails rather than passing quietly.

## Best-effort emission is real

Following `_report_retained_candidates` — lazy import, `except Exception: pass`, emitted after the lease is established — means a logging failure cannot change lease safety. Pinned:

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| Drop the fresh-acquisition emit | `test_fresh_acquisition_records_actual_checkout_head` FAILED |
| Echo the bound head instead of reading the worktree | `test_second_attempt_resumes_unpushed_commit` FAILED (only) |
| Let a logger failure propagate | `test_acquisition_succeeds_when_event_logger_raises` FAILED |

## No credential surface

The payload is `repository`, `pull_request`, `scope_id`, `head_sha`, `path`, `owner`, `acquisition`. `canonical_origin` — the one lease field that can carry a remote URL with userinfo — is **not** logged. The criterion holds by construction rather than by luck.

| Suite | Result |
|---|---|
| Full | 9321 passed, 34 skipped |
| Enforced (`MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED=1`) | 9321 passed, 34 skipped |
| CI | 9/9 |

Verified tree matched the PR head exactly (`9cdc0316`), clean at both ends of the run.

This closes the gap that surfaced while verifying the #1050 canary: the typed path was audited only when it failed. The bind itself — the security property the whole immutable-scope design exists to enforce — now has a record.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1272: repo leases: a REBASED head defeats publication-ancestry proof, so #1531's fix leaves the common case blocking

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
This is very close, and the core is right. One dead guard to resolve.

## Verified

The real-world case this was filed for now releases. I reproduced the exact shape from the lease that blocked #1537 — a rebased head whose only delta from the published head is content already on `main` — and the content-equivalence branch clears it while a genuinely unpublished path is still preserved.

`_tree_blob` compares per-path blob object ids with absence represented explicitly, uses a `:(literal)` pathspec so a filename can't be glob-interpreted, and rejects ambiguous `ls-tree` output. Requiring a *unique* merge base is the right strictness.

The dangling-commit test is better than what the leaf asked for. It creates a genuinely orphaned commit in the source, then pins the shared object store directly:

```python
assert source_object.stat().st_ino == lease_object.stat().st_ino
```

That is the trap that would otherwise make an automated recovery bundle most of the repository, and it is now a hard assertion rather than a comment. Using a **binary** payload (`b"\x00unpublished\xff"`) for the unexplained-path test is also well chosen — it exercises blob-id comparison on content that rendered diffs handle badly, which is exactly why the leaf asked for blob ids.

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Mutation — `head_blob not in {published_blob, base_blob}` → `!= published_blob` | `test_acquire_releases_rebased_published_work_by_blob_identity` **FAILED** |
| Full suite | **9324 passed**, 34 skipped |
| Enforced (`MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED=1`) | **9324 passed**, 34 skipped |
| CI | 9/9 |

## Blocking: the unrelated-base containment check cannot fire

```python
bases = _run(runner, ["git", "-C", ..., "merge-base", "--all", head, tracked_base], ...)
...
base = bases[0].lower()
contained = runner([... "merge-base", "--is-ancestor", base, tracked_base])
if contained.returncode == 1:
    raise RuntimeError("PR checkout lease HEAD base is unrelated to tracked base branch")
```

`base` is produced *by* `merge-base --all head tracked_base`, so it is an ancestor of `tracked_base` by construction. `--is-ancestor base tracked_base` is therefore always true and the `== 1` branch is unreachable.

Deleting the entire refusal — both the `== 1` and `!= 0` branches — leaves the suite green at **43 passed**. I checked this was not a mis-aimed mutation: `test_acquire_refuses_rebased_lease_when_tracked_base_is_unrelated` builds an `--orphan` base and asserts `match="no verifiable tracked base"`, which is the earlier `merge-base --all` guard. That test is correct and pins a real refusal; it simply never reaches this one.

So the leaf's criterion — the base is *verified* to be contained in the tracked base branch — is currently satisfied by construction rather than by that check, and the check reads as though it were doing the verifying. Either:

- **delete it** as tautological, leaving `merge-base --all` failure as the real guard (and say so in a comment), or
- **make it meaningful** by testing containment of something not derived from `tracked_base` — e.g. the lease HEAD's own first parent — and pin that with a test that fails when it is removed.

I have no preference between those; I do want the code to stop implying a check it isn't performing. Keep the `!= 0` arm either way so a git failure still fails closed.

Everything else here is ready to merge.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The blocking guard is resolved correctly, and the combined tree is verified.

## The tautological guard

Deleted, with a comment naming what actually does the verifying:

```python
    if len(bases) != 1:
        raise RuntimeError("PR checkout lease HEAD has no unique tracked base")
+   # A merge base computed against tracked_base is its ancestor by construction;
+   # _run above and the uniqueness check are the fail-closed verification gates.
```

That is the right resolution. The concern was never that the check was harmful — it was that the code implied a verification it was not performing, which is how a later reader trusts the wrong thing.

## Verified against the combined tree

This is the first run where #1540's content-equivalence work and #1541's acquisition audit execute together in `pr_checkout_lease.py`, so I ran the suites on the PR head merged with current `main` rather than trusting the clean auto-merge:

```
FROZEN TREE: 171348d5  clean=[]
  full      9326 passed, 34 skipped
  enforced  9326 passed, 34 skipped
TREE AT END: 171348d5  clean=[]
```

The PR's real diff against its merge-base is +305/−7 across two files and deletes nothing. CI 9/9.

## The unrequested change, which I am accepting with a caveat

`git bundle verify` now runs with `-C str(lease.path)` at both call sites. That was not part of my review and arrived unannounced, so I checked it rather than waving it through. It is a genuine fix:

```
from a non-repo cwd:   error: need a repository to verify a bundle
with -C into the repo: The bundle uses this hash algorithm: sha1
```

Without it `_preserve_checkout_head` fails outright whenever the process cwd is not a git repository — which is the normal condition for a daemon.

It is also **unpinned**: reverting `-C` at both sites leaves the suite fully green at 45 passed. The existing reclaim tests exercise the bundle path but cannot catch this, because pytest runs from the mimir repo, so `git bundle verify` finds *a* repository regardless of which one. Same shape as the `/proc` and `pwd.getpwnam` defects earlier today: the test passes for a reason unrelated to the code being correct.

I am not blocking on that. It is strictly better than a call that fails in production, and holding a correct fix for a test on a drive-by would be disproportionate. But it should not pass silently, and a real test would need to invoke the helper from a non-repo cwd — worth folding into whatever next touches this file.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The reported embedded-quote defects are fixed for the new regression cases: JSON/Python-style backslash escapes and YAML doubled-single-quote escapes now run past the embedded delimiter, current-head CI is fully green, and the durable turn-logger fixture exercises the double-quoted path.

Two blocking boundary cases remain in the narrowed quoted-value scope. First, a valid YAML double-quoted scalar can escape a physical line break; `\\.` does not consume that pair without DOTALL, and the matcher can again partially redact the first fragment while persisting the rest. Second, combining Python-style `\'` with YAML single-quoted syntax is ambiguous: YAML treats backslash literally, so a value ending in a backslash can cause the matcher to consume the real closing quote and then erase unrelated following durable context. Both root causes are amplified by matching without requiring an actual closing delimiter. Concrete reproductions and requested direct/durable regressions are inline.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
@mimir-carreira you were right on both counts, and the block-scalar one is the more serious of the two. Fixed in `0c92b593`.

I reproduced both against the real function before changing anything:

```
{"password": "correct horse battery staple"}  ->  {"password": "[REDACTED] horse battery staple"}
password: |                                   ->  password: [REDACTED]
  s3cr3t-value-here                                 s3cr3t-value-here     <- untouched
```

The second is worse than a plain miss: the indicator was consumed *as* the value, so the durable log presents an unredacted credential as though it had been scrubbed. Anyone auditing that line would conclude it was safe.

Worth noting how my own verification missed this. My false-positive corpus tested that benign text *survives* redaction, and my mutation test only proved the new pattern was load-bearing for the cases I had already written. Neither asks whether the pattern is **complete**. You tested the adversarial direction — a supported key with an awkward value — and that is where it broke.

## The fix

Split into three rules:

- **Quoted values run to the closing quote**, one pattern per quote style. A backreference for the quote character would push the capture count past two, and `redact_text` uses `pat.groups == 2` to decide whether to preserve the prefix.
- **Block scalars mask the indented body**, leaving the indicator so structure stays readable. Handling them beats declining to match, since the value is genuinely a credential.
- **The bare rule gains a negative lookahead** so an indicator can never be reported as a redacted value, even if the block rule misses.

## Verification

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| Remove the double-quoted rule | quoted-with-whitespace cases + durable turn-logger test **FAILED** |
| Remove the single-quoted rule | `test_quoted_credential_is_masked_through_the_closing_quote['my secret pass phrase']` **FAILED** |
| Remove the block-scalar rule | 6 block cases + durable turn-logger test **FAILED** |
| Remove only the block-indicator lookahead | block cases **FAILED** |

Coverage added per your request, including the durable-logger case with the supported `password` key and a whitespace-bearing value — it asserts no *fragment* of the passphrase survives, not merely that the string is absent:

```python
for fragment in passphrase.split():
    assert fragment not in line
```

Block scalars are parametrized over `|`, `>`, `|-`, `>-`, `|+`, `|2`.

The false-positive corpus is unchanged and still passes — prose, log timestamps, JSON config, a headers dict and URL userinfo all untouched. Full and enforced suites re-running now; I will post the numbers before merging.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
@mimir-carreira right again, and the blank-line case is the same failure mode as your first report rather than a smaller one. Fixed in `0da5eb2c`.

Reproduced both before changing anything:

```
password: |            ->  password: |
  first-half                [REDACTED]
                            
  second-half               second-half        <- persisted

password: | # supplied externally   ->  unchanged; body untouched
  the-secret-body
```

The first is what makes it blocking: the log reads as scrubbed while holding half the credential — exactly the property you flagged originally, just displaced one case over. The second went unmatched by the block rule while the bare-value lookahead correctly declined the indicator, so nothing masked the body.

## Fix

The body atom required `\S` on every line, which ended the match at the first blank line. Blank lines are part of a block scalar, so the body now accepts them — but **only when another indented line follows**, so a blank line separating the block from the next key is not swallowed and the following key survives:

```
password: |
  the-secret

nextkey: plain      ->  password: |\n[REDACTED]\nnextkey: plain\n
```

The scalar header now also accepts an optional trailing comment.

| Mutation | Failures |
|---|---|
| Require a contiguous body (revert blank-line support) | **10**, including the durable turn-logger test |
| Header cannot carry a comment | **4** |

Regressions parametrize three header styles (`\|`, `>-`, `\| # comment`) against three blank-run shapes (`\n`, `\n\n`, `\n   \n`) and assert **no fragment** survives — not merely that the joined string is absent. The durable turn-logger case now carries a header comment plus an internal blank line and asserts both halves are gone.

Scoped: 103 passed. Full and enforced suites queued behind two other PRs; I'll post the numbers before merging and won't merge without your re-review.

Worth saying plainly: you have now caught two real leaks in this file that my own verification missed. My corpus tests that benign text survives and my mutations test that a pattern is load-bearing — neither asks whether a pattern is *complete* against awkward-but-legal inputs. That is the gap, and it is mine, not a fluke.

@mimir-carreira correct a third time. Fixed in `9aab4eaa`.

Reproduced first: `password: |\n\n  secret-tail\n` was left wholly unredacted — the block rule did not fire because the body had to begin with an indented non-blank line, and the bare-value guard correctly declined the indicator, so nothing masked it.

The repetition now accepts a leading blank run on the same terms as an internal one — absorbed only when an indented non-blank line follows — and the body ends with a mandatory non-blank line, so a match can never consist of a blank run alone.

Three rounds, three separate holes in one pattern, each a legal YAML shape the previous fix had not considered. That is a pattern in *my* method, not bad luck: I was fixing the reported input instead of the input grammar.

So before claiming this one, I swept the grammar — header style (plain, folded, strip/keep chomping, indentation indicator, trailing comment, uppercase key, quoted key) crossed with leading blank runs, internal gaps, and trailing whitespace:

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Disclosure before you review this round: I probed grammar dimensions nobody has reported yet, and **found two more leaks**. I am deliberately not pushing fixes for them, because a new head would reset your review of `777e0deb` — but you should have them while forming that review.

```
LEAK   "a:password": |      →  "a:password": |\n  zz-probe-secret\n     (unchanged)
LEAK   password: &anchor |  →  password: &anchor |\n  zz-probe-secret\n   (unchanged)
```

- The key alphabet `[A-Za-z0-9_.-]*` cannot contain `:`, so a quoted key holding a colon is not recognised as a credential key.
- A YAML anchor between the `:` and the block indicator (`&anchor |`) is not allowed for by the header pattern. A tag (`!!str |`) will fail the same way.

Both leave the body wholly unredacted, the same shape as the sequence-entry miss you just caught.

Probes that came back clean, for the record: CRLF line endings, flow mappings, flow sequences of mappings, tab-indented bodies, and multi-document streams.

## Where I think this leaves the PR

Five rounds, five real findings from you, and now two more I found myself — all in a block-scalar rule that **I** introduced in round 1. The salvaged build never had one; your first review noted `password: |` was mishandled, I added a regex for it, and every finding since has been a hole in my code rather than the build's.

The underlying problem is that I kept extending a regex for an indentation-sensitive construct. `redact_text` dispatches on `pat.groups == 2`, so a backreference for the header indent was unavailable, which meant the pattern structurally could not express "indented beyond the key". Round 4 forced the move to `_mask_yaml_block_scalars`; round 5 then cost one parameter. That should have happened at round 2.

So I have recommended to Jason that we **split this PR**: land the quoted-value fix, which is small and complete on its own, and move block-scalar handling to its own chainlink whose acceptance criteria name the grammar explicitly — indentation and chomping indicators, anchors and tags, quoted keys, flow style, sequence entries — rather than accreting one case per review round.

He wants your review of this round before deciding, so please review `777e0deb` as it stands. If you think the current shape converges, say so and I will keep going; if you agree it should be split, that is useful signal for him.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Pushed `9af9363b` fixing the two leaks I disclosed above. Jason asked for these to land and then be reviewed as a round, so this is what to review now rather than `777e0deb`.

Both were complete misses — the header did not match at all, so the block rule never fired and the bare-value guard correctly declined the indicator:

```
"a:password": |        key alphabet excluded ':'      -> body survived
password: &anchor |    anchor not allowed for         -> body survived
password: !!str |      tag failed the same way        -> body survived
```

Quoted and bare keys are now separate alternatives, because a single alphabet either rejects the quoted form or lets a bare key swallow the separator. An anchor / alias / tag run before the indicator is skipped, in either order. Alternation is free here — the header pattern is used by `_mask_yaml_block_scalars`, not `_TOKEN_PATTERNS`, so it is not bound by the `pat.groups == 2` dispatch.

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Mutation — revert to the single key alphabet | **11 failures** |
| Mutation — drop the node-property skip | **17 failures** |
| Sweep: 5 key forms x 5 node properties x 5 indicators x 3 sequence nestings x 3 leading-blank runs | **1125 combinations, 0 leaked, 0 structure eaten** |
| Scoped | 611 passed |

Durable turn-logger coverage now carries a quoted-colon key with an anchor.

One known cosmetic effect I chose not to chase: `password: !!str |` renders as `password: [REDACTED] |`, because the bare-value rule masks the tag. That is over-masking rather than a leak, the body is correctly masked, and adding another lookahead to that rule is exactly the accretion that got this PR to six rounds.

payload.body:
@mimir-carreira split done, per your recommendation and Jason's decision. This PR is now the quoted-value fix only — `bc653852`.

**Removed:** `_mask_yaml_block_scalars`, `_BLOCK_SCALAR_HEADER`, `_indent_width`, and all nine block-scalar tests. Net change is +39 lines in `redaction.py`.

**Kept, deliberately:** the block-indicator negative lookahead in the bare-value rule. Removing the scanner without it would have reintroduced the very first defect you reported — `password: [REDACTED]` printed above an untouched body. The lookahead makes the miss honest instead of a false claim of redaction, and a new test pins it:

```python
def test_block_scalar_indicator_is_not_reported_as_redacted(indicator):
    assert out == text, "the indicator must not be masked as if it were a value"
    assert "[REDACTED]" not in out
```

| Mutation | Failures |
|---|---|
| Remove the double-quoted value rule | 4, including the passphrase case |
| Remove the indicator lookahead | 6, all of the above test |

The reasoning is in a code comment too, so the lookahead does not read as vestigial to whoever next edits that tuple.

**The other half is chainlink #1274**, filed with the failure history rather than a clean slate: all seven defects in the order you found them, the two I found by probing, and the three structural conclusions —

1. a regex in `_TOKEN_PATTERNS` cannot express indentation-relative body membership, because it needs a backreference and `redact_text` dispatches on `pat.groups == 2`;
2. explicit mapping keys break a line-at-a-time recognizer too, so the scanner must associate a key line with a later indicator line;
3. sweeps asserting only "the secret is gone" hide over-consumption entirely — every masking assertion must be paired with a survival assertion.

Its acceptance criteria enumerate the productions up front and require both directions in the same test.

Please review the narrowed scope. What I would most value your eye on: whether removing the scanner while keeping the lookahead leaves the module in a coherent state, and whether the comment explaining the deliberate miss is clear enough to survive a future refactor.

Suites re-running on a frozen tree; numbers to follow.

payload.body:
@mimir-carreira right, and this one is squarely in scope. Fixed in `193838df`.

Reproduced all three before changing anything:

```
{"password":"correct \"horse\" battery staple"}
  ->  {"password":"[REDACTED]"horse\" battery staple"}

password: 'can\'t share this'   ->  password: '[REDACTED]'t share this'
password: 'can''t share this'   ->  password: '[REDACTED]''t share this'
```

Same shape as the block-scalar failures — the output reads as redacted while the remainder of the credential persists.

Escapes are now consumed as units, so the value runs to the real closing quote. Single quotes carry two conventions and both are handled: Python-repr `\'` and YAML's doubled `''`. The alternations are non-capturing, so the capture count stays at two and the `pat.groups == 2` dispatch is unaffected.

| Mutation | Failures |
|---|---|
| Revert the double-quoted value class to `[^"]*` | 2 |
| Revert the single-quoted value class to `[^']*` | 2 |

Regressions cover JSON escapes, Python-repr escapes, YAML doubled quotes, and a value ending in an escaped backslash, plus a durable turn-logger case carrying embedded escaped quotes.

Worth recording: my first durable fixture for this was **wrong**, and the code caught me. I wrote `a \\"phrase\\" z`, which is an escaped *backslash* followed by a closing quote — so `phrase` genuinely sits outside the credential and correctly survived. The test failed, I assumed the fix, and the fixture was at fault. Corrected to a single escaped quote.

The false-positive corpus is unchanged. Suites re-running on a frozen tree.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
@mimir-carreira both confirmed and fixed in `e0ca66b9`. The second one was mine — my previous commit introduced it.

```
password: "first-part\        ->  masked "first-part" only, rest persisted
  second-part"

password: 'ends in \'         ->  password: '[REDACTED]
next: must-survive                 ENTIRE remainder erased
```

## Which construct holds which property

I mutation-tested each guard separately, and the first pass told me something I had to correct: neither the lookahead **nor** the newline exclusion failed a single test when removed alone. Chasing that gave the accurate picture, which differs from what I first wrote in the commit message:

| Property | Actually held by | Mutation result |
|---|---|---|
| Single-quote erasure | Dropping the `\.` escape — with YAML semantics nothing can skip past a quote, so a match always ends at one | restoring `\.` → **2 failures** |
| Double-quote runaway | Newline exclusion **and** lookahead, deliberately redundant — either alone bounds it | removing **both** → **1 failure** |

I amended the commit message and the code comments, because the first draft credited the lookahead for the single-quote fix and that is simply wrong. Attributing a property to the wrong construct is how a later refactor deletes the one that mattered.

## The trade-off I am taking deliberately

Single-quoted values now follow YAML — backslash literal, `''` the only escape. That costs the Python-repr `\'` form, which masks only up to the backslash. I checked how often that shape can actually occur: `repr` switches to **double** quotes for a value containing an apostrophe, and emits `\'` only when the value holds *both* quote styles.

```
repr("can't share")            ->  "can't share"        (double-quoted, masked fully)
repr('has \' and " both')      ->  'has \' and " both'  (the rare gap)
```

`test_single_quoted_values_follow_yaml_escaping_not_python_repr` documents this rather than leaving it latent. I would rather carry a bounded, named gap than an erasure — but flag it if you disagree, since it is a leak and I have been arguing all night that leaks matter.

Also added: unterminated quotes (`password: "abc` with no closing quote) now match nothing at all instead of consuming to end of input, with survival regressions for all three shapes.

Scoped: 101 passed. Full and enforced suites re-running on a frozen tree.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
@mimir-carreira you were right to push back, and the criticism of the test was the sharpest part of it — `startswith` codified partial masking as acceptable instead of proving removal. Fixed in `2ea6866a`.

I had concluded the two grammars were mutually exclusive. They are not. Neither can be dropped:

```
YAML-only     'has \' and " both'      ->  masked to the backslash, tail left
Python-only   'ends in \'              ->  ate the true closing quote and
              next: must-survive           every following line
```

So the value form is an **ordered alternation**, and the engine takes whichever reading actually reaches a closing quote — Python-repr escapes first, YAML as the fallback. Neither alternative may cross a newline, which is still what bounds an unterminated quote.

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| `password: 'has \' and " both'` | fully masked |
| `{'password': 'has \' and " both'}` (dict repr) | fully masked |
| `password: 'ends in \'` + `next: must-survive` | value masked, next line intact |
| `password: 'can''t share this'` | fully masked |
| `password: 'abc` (unterminated) | no match — honest miss, following lines intact |
| `password: 'a' and note: 'b'` | masks only `a` — preferring the longer reading does not become "consume the line" |

| Mutation | Failures |
|---|---|
| Drop the Python-repr branch | 2 — both `has \' and " both` cases |
| Drop the YAML branch | 2 — the literal-backslash case and the erasure test |

The regressions now assert no fragment survives under either grammar, plus a separate test proving the following line lives. Scoped: 105 passed.

I asked you to challenge that trade-off and you did, with a concrete alternative rather than an objection. That is the tenth defect you have found in this file, and the second time you have declined a compromise I had already talked myself into. Both were right.

Full and enforced suites re-running on a frozen tree.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
@mimir-carreira confirmed and fixed in `89865df2`. This one had the widest real-world reach of the eleven.

```
{'password': "correct horse battery staple"}   ->  survived unchanged
"password": 'correct horse battery staple'     ->  survived unchanged
```

The first is what `repr` produces for a mapping, so it is among the most common shapes in a durable log — not a corner case at all. Both matchers were constraining the *key* to the same quote style as the *value*, which is not how either grammar works.

Each value matcher now accepts either key quote style. The key-quote class is non-capturing, so the two-capture dispatch is untouched.

| Combination | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `{'password': "…"}` (dict repr) | **leaked** | masked |
| `"password": '…'` | **leaked** | masked |
| `{"password": "…"}` | masked | masked |
| `{'password': '…'}` | masked | masked |
| `password: "…"` | masked | masked |
| `password: '…'` | masked | masked |

| Mutation | Failures |
|---|---|
| Re-couple the key to the double-quoted value rule | 2 |
| Re-couple the key to the single-quoted value rule | 1 |

Regressions cover all six combinations asserting no passphrase fragment survives, plus durable turn-logger coverage for the dict-repr shape. Corpus unchanged; scoped run 111 passed.

Suites re-running on a frozen tree.

Eleven findings now, every one real, and this is the second where my mental model of the grammar was simply wrong rather than incomplete — I had been treating the key and value quoting as one decision. Worth saying because it is the argument for #1274 being written against an enumerated grammar rather than a case list: I clearly cannot enumerate this one from memory.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
@mimir-carreira confirmed against PyYAML and fixed in `0a6cbcb0`. The PyYAML citation was what made this unarguable — I could check your reading rather than weigh it against mine.

```
in:      {'password': 'ends in \', 'next': 'must-survive'}
PyYAML:  {'password': 'ends in \\', 'next': 'must-survive'}     two entries
before:  {'password': '[REDACTED]'next': 'must-survive'}         comma, space, quote erased
after:   {'password': '[REDACTED]', 'next': 'must-survive'}
```

The Python branch may now not escape a quote followed by **structural context** — comma, closing brace or bracket, colon, comment start, or end of line. There the quote is the real YAML delimiter. Where no such context follows, the Python reading still wins, so `'has \' and " both'` is masked whole. Your same-line-comment variant is covered too, with and without quotes inside the comment.

| Mutation | Failures |
|---|---|
| Drop the structural-context guard | 2 — the flow mapping and the quoted comment |

I had the survival guarantee scoped to *following lines* and you were right that it needed to extend to same-line delimiters. That is the third time in this PR the fix for a leak introduced an erasure, and the pattern is consistent enough to name: every time I widen what the matcher consumes, I need to ask what it now consumes that it shouldn't, in the same change rather than the next round.

One correction of my own while writing the durable regression: my first fixture asserted the fragment `flow` was absent while the survivor was named `keep-flow`, so the test contradicted itself and failed. My fixture, not the code — renamed so the words do not overlap.

Scoped: 115 passed. Suites re-running on a frozen tree.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
@mimir-carreira both cases confirmed on this checkout, and the operator decision is to stop arbitrating. `7bb99f47`.

```
repr({"password": "alpha', omega \"tail\"", ...})
  -> {'password': '[REDACTED]', omega "tail"', 'next': 'must-survive'}   tail disclosed

password: 'alpha\''omega-secret-tail'
  -> password: '[REDACTED]'omega-secret-tail'                            tail leaked
```

Your root-cause line is the one that settled it: the matcher "never proves that the quote selected by an alternative is followed by a format-appropriate closing boundary." Proving a boundary is parsing, and five rounds of trying to approximate it in a pattern produced five defects that alternated between leaking a tail and erasing surrounding context.

So this rule now **declines** the ambiguity rather than guessing at it. A backslash is exactly where the two grammars disagree:

| Input | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `password: 'my secret pass phrase'` | masked |
| `password: 'can''t share this'` | masked |
| `{'password': 'correct horse battery'}` | masked |
| anything containing a backslash | **declined, byte-for-byte untouched** |

An honest miss can neither disclose half a credential nor corrupt the record — the two failure modes the previous attempts alternated between. `test_ambiguous_single_quoted_values_are_declined_untouched` pins it, including both of your reproductions.

Mutation: re-admitting backslashes into the value class fails 5 tests.

Full arbitration moves to chainlink **#1274** alongside block scalars, with your PyYAML-verified cases written into its acceptance criteria. Both halves need the same thing — a parser, or a scanner that proves closing boundaries — so they should be built together rather than as more pattern patches.

For the record, thirteen reviews and thirteen real findings, several of which I would not have found and two of which were defects my own fixes introduced. The narrowing is a consequence of your evidence, not a shortcut around it.

Suites re-running; I will post the numbers.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Merging. Final verification on the frozen tree:

```
FROZEN TREE: 7bb99f47  clean=[]
  full      9367 passed, 34 skipped
  enforced  9367 passed, 34 skipped
TREE AT END: 7bb99f47  clean=[]
```

CI 9/9, approved at head `7bb99f476`.

## What lands

`redact_text` is the durable redactor behind `turns.jsonl` and `events.jsonl`. Before this, credentials in colon forms reached disk in cleartext, and quoted values were masked only to the first space:

| Shape | Before |
|---|---|
| `> X-API-Key: <32 hex>` | leaked in full |
| `MIMIR_API_KEY: <32 hex>` | leaked in full |
| `{"VOYAGE_API_KEY": "pa-…"}` | leaked in full |
| `{"password": "correct horse battery staple"}` | only the first word masked |
| `{'password': "…"}` (Python dict repr) | leaked in full |

All masked now, across every combination of key and value quote style, with escaped quotes and YAML line continuations running to the true closing delimiter.

## What deliberately does not land

Multiline block scalars, and single-quoted values containing a backslash. Both are **declined untouched** rather than half-masked, and the bare-value rule refuses to mask a block indicator so a log can never read as scrubbed while holding an untouched credential. Both are tracked in chainlink #1274 with the grammar enumerated and your PyYAML-verified cases as acceptance criteria.

## Thanks

Thirteen reviews, twelve real defects, several of which I would not have found: the block-scalar indicator masquerading as a value, over-consumption of nested siblings, sequence entries, the mixed key/value quote styles that left the commonest repr shape in the clear, and two defects introduced by my own fixes. You also declined a compromise I had already talked myself into, twice, and were right both times.

The most useful thing you did was cite PyYAML for the flow-mapping case. It turned a disagreement about grammar into something I could check, and it is what made the final scope decision obvious rather than arguable.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1271: worklink: the staged-secret guard scans whole blobs, so the factory can never edit the 8 files that already hold credential fixtures

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. This meets every acceptance criterion in the leaf, including the one that was easiest to get wrong, and I verified the outcome end-to-end rather than only through the tests.

## The property that matters

I ran the real `_assert_staged_diff_has_no_secret` against an innocuous edit to each of the eight files the old guard had locked the factory out of:

```
ADMITTED  tests/test_activity_panel.py       ADMITTED  tests/test_git_bootstrap_redact.py
ADMITTED  tests/test_codex_auth.py           ADMITTED  tests/test_git_tracking.py
ADMITTED  tests/test_event_logger.py         ADMITTED  tests/test_oauth_usage_poller.py
ADMITTED  tests/test_git_bootstrap.py        ADMITTED  tests/test_redaction.py
REFUSED   new credential in a base-dirty file (correct)
```

All eight unblocked, and a *different* credential-shaped value added to one of those same base-dirty files is still refused. That is exactly the widening the leaf asked for and no more.

## Fail-closed handling is the part I'd have expected to slip

The naive implementation treats any unreadable base blob as an empty base set, which quietly converts a read failure into "everything is new is fine." This one instead verifies via `ls-tree` that the path is genuinely absent from HEAD's tree, and raises otherwise — with a separate branch for an unborn HEAD. Both mutations confirm it is real:

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| `staged_matches - base_matches` → `staged_matches` | 3 tests **FAILED** |
| Unreadable base → silently empty base set | `test_staged_secret_guard_fails_closed_for_base_blob[unreadable]` **FAILED** |

The second is the one I care about, and it's pinned by a parametrized case rather than an incidental assertion.

Also right: comparison is on matched substrings per path (`secret_matches`), not a count, a whole-file hash, or the path; whole-blob byte reads with `surrogateescape` are preserved, so the binary / `-diff`-marked case still scans; and `test_staged_secret_guard_refuses_new_match_without_echoing_it` asserts the error does not leak the offending value.

## Buildability

Every fixture is fragment-built — `"ghp_" + "a" * 36`, `"AKIA" + "A" * 16` — so all four touched files stay scanner-clean and this PR does not poison its own paths for future edits. That constraint is easy to miss and it was followed exactly.

| Suite | Result |
|---|---|
| Scoped (`test_secret_scan.py`, `test_worklink_orchestrator.py`) | 160 passed |
| Full | 9306 passed, 34 skipped |
| Enforced (`MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED=1`) | 9306 passed, 34 skipped |
| CI | 9/9 |

This unblocks chainlink #1214 / #1261 / #1262, which had no path to build at all while the guard scanned whole blobs.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1270: Trigger remediation when CI fails on Mimir-owned pull requests

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Strong build. The durability engineering here is better than the leaf asked for — atomic cursor writes with `fsync` on both file and directory, `O_EXCL` delivery claims for overlapping polls, and receipts written *only* after enqueue succeeds. One authority narrowing needs justification or reversal before this lands, and two behaviours I want confirmed as intended.

## Checked against #1270's criteria

| Criterion | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Detect newly completed failures on owned open PRs, durable dedupe | Met. `_delivery_key` binds repo + number + head_sha + a sha256 of the sorted `(name, conclusion)` set, so a rerun with the same failures at the same head cannot re-dispatch. |
| Remediation turn carries repo/number/head/check names/log links | Met. `failed_checks` carries `id`, `name`, `conclusion`, `url`, `details_url`, `external_id`. |
| Re-check live state and head before mutation | Met, and in the right place. `remediation_checkout_preflight` re-reads the live PR, refuses on `head_sha` mismatch ("pull request head was superseded"), and re-lists checks to refuse when they have gone green. A stale payload cannot mutate. |
| No auto-edit of external PRs | Met. `author == me` gets `_emit`; everything else gets `_emit_signal("pr_ci_failure_external")`, which is notification-only. |
| No duplicate wakeups vs `github-ci-watch` | Met. `github-ci-watch` is hard-scoped to `BRANCH = "main"` (`scripts/poller.py:38`); this watches open PRs. Disjoint. |
| Authority from configured identity, not hard-coded | Met. `me` comes from `MIMIR_GITHUB_SELF_LOGIN`, and `if me and author == me` means an unset login routes *everything* to the signal path — fails toward no mutation, which is the right direction. |
| Focused tests for routing/dedupe/stale-head/red-to-green/overlap | Met, and they are real tests: owned-vs-external routing, overlapping-poll dedupe, receipt dedupe, closed-and-green race clearing the cursor, API failure preserving the cursor *and* not advancing the new-failure window, and baselining. |

## Blocking: CI remediation is the only remediation path that cannot speak on the PR

```python
_REPO_PR_CI_REMEDIATION_ACTIONS = _REPO_PR_REMEDIATION_ACTIONS - frozenset({
    RepoPRAction.PR_COMMENT.value,
    RepoPRAction.PR_EDIT.value,
    RepoPRAction.PR_REREQUEST.value,
})
```

That leaves `{INSPECT, CHECKOUT, TEST, WRITE, COMMIT, PUSH}`. Every sibling path keeps all nine — `_REPO_PR_CONFLICT_RESOLUTION_ACTIONS` is `_REPO_PR_REMEDIATION_ACTIONS` unchanged, and `pr_changes_requested_stale` gets the full set.

I understand the least-privilege reasoning: a red check means fix the code, not discuss it. But the consequence is that **a CI remediation that cannot succeed leaves no trace on the PR.** When the agent hits something it genuinely cannot fix — a blocked checkout, an exhausted lease, a defect in the leaf rather than the code — its only way to surface that today is a PR comment. Removing `pr_comment` converts those into silence, and the operator sees a PR that stayed red with no explanation.

That is not hypothetical: every blocked remediation I have worked through in the last day was diagnosable *only* because the agent commented on the PR explaining what stopped it.

`pr_edit` and `pr_rerequest` I have no objection to dropping — retitling and re-pinging a reviewer are not part of fixing a build. Please restore `PR_COMMENT.value`, or state in the diff why silence is preferable and how a failed CI remediation is meant to reach an operator instead.

## Confirm these are intended

**1. A PR that is already red when this ships is baselined and never fires at that head.** The first poll writes `baseline: True` and `test_old_red_head_is_baselined_without_later_retry` pins that it stays quiet on the next pass. Since `same_failure` is keyed on head + failure-digest, it only re-arms when someone pushes or the failure set changes. Skipping the backlog on rollout is sensible; I want it stated that "red today, untouched until the next push" i

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. All three blocking items are addressed, and the scope test is stronger than what I asked for.

## Verified at head `7b95b43d`, trial-merged with current `main`

**`pr_comment` restored, narrowing preserved.** `_REPO_PR_CI_REMEDIATION_ACTIONS` now excludes only `PR_EDIT` and `PR_REREQUEST`, so a CI remediation that cannot succeed can still leave an operator-visible trace on the PR — which was the whole concern — while retitling and reviewer-pinging stay out of a build-fixing turn.

**The scope test goes further than a bare equality update.** Adding

```python
assert "pr.edit" not in scope.allowed_operations
assert "pr.rerequest" not in scope.allowed_operations
```

means a future widening to the full remediation set fails loudly instead of silently passing an updated equality. That is the right shape for an authority assertion.

Mutation-tested: re-excluding `PR_COMMENT` fails `test_ci_remediation_scope_requires_checkout_before_every_mutation`.

**The documentation states the bounds honestly.** Both `docs/code-building-pipeline.md` and the poller SKILL describe the rollout baselining as deliberate, and the PR window as *"a bounded approximation, not complete enumeration of repositories with more than 100 open pull requests."* Naming a cap as a cap is exactly right — a silent truncation reads as full coverage.

| Suite | Result |
|---|---|
| Full | 9319 passed, 34 skipped |
| Enforced (`MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED=1`) | 9319 passed, 34 skipped |
| CI | 9/9 |

The durability work from the first round stands unchanged and is the strongest part of this PR: atomic cursor writes fsync'd on both file and directory, `O_EXCL` delivery claims for overlapping polls, and receipts written only after enqueue succeeds so a rejected handoff retries rather than being silently consumed.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Automatic stale-base remediation was withheld after rebasing the scoped checkout onto immutable base `5241f9024d40727d2f0ae868584cb083b9f2f58f`.

The mandatory repository test command did not produce validation evidence:

```text
/usr/local/bin/uv run --extra dev --extra bench pytest -q
repo_test: test_timeout
stdout: empty
stderr: empty
```

I did **not** push the rewritten head because the required full-suite gate did not pass. The unpublished scoped checkout is preserved for runner/controller recovery; starting-head lease was `3b67ceb75c5bfbe6f5c2786c712d5e2842d4b4f7`.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Agreed on the blocking point: CI remediation must retain `pr_comment` so a failed/blocked repair can leave an operator-visible trace. `pr_edit` and `pr_rerequest` should remain excluded.

The two observed behaviors are intentional:

1. Rollout baselines already-red heads. They stay quiet until a new head or changed failure set; this avoids a deployment-time backlog burst.
2. The open-PR query's `per_page=100`, updated-desc window is a deliberate bounded approximation for newly completed failures, not a claim of complete enumeration. That contract should be stated in the diff.

I attempted to apply those changes, update the scope test, and document both contracts. The scoped checkout controller refused mutation because the earlier unpublished rebase checkout is retained under another immutable scope after its mandatory full suite timed out with empty output. I escalated controller recovery as `apply_jason_s_requested_changes_to:03946c745496750f`; I won't bypass that retained-work guard.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body: Current remote head `3b67ceb75` is mergeable and all 9 GitHub checks are green, including Python 3.11, 3.12, and enforced mode. The requested stale-base update is still blocked before checkout by a retained unpublished candidate from another immutable PR scope (`b32cd31568b442d0a85cac10f6bdd1d83f01cd34` at `/workspace/pr-leases/ec3b9619ddd6449a-db3fd691bc4c4dbdac805f707a2b50ab`). I am escalating controller recovery rather than bypassing the scoped lease or discarding unpublished work.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Lease cleared — this is unblocked. Jason authorized the removal.

Before removing it I measured what it actually held, rather than trusting the refusal reason. The lease commit `b32cd315` differed from the published head `3b67ceb75` by exactly one file:

```
tests/test_turn_event_bus.py | 5 ++++-
```

That difference was not the build's work. The lease's parent was `5241f902` (`worklink: issue #1268 (#1535)`) while the PR head's parent was the older `22a9bb4b` — so the delta arrived through the rebase, and it is the payload change merged to `main` earlier today. Confirmed:

```
$ git diff origin/main refs/lease/1537 -- tests/test_turn_event_bus.py
(empty)
```

Byte-identical to `main`. **The lease held no unique work** — the second false refusal today, which is the case #1531 item 1 is about.

One thing worth recording for that issue: `git fsck` reported **965 dangling commits** in the lease, which looks alarming and is not. The lease is a local clone of `/workspace/mimir`, so its object store is *hardlinked* to the source — same inode `237360576`, 4 links — and the source itself carries 733 dangling commits. Removing the lease directory drops one hardlink; the source keeps its own objects. An automated recovery that tried to preserve every dangling commit it found would bundle the entire source history on every release. The authoritative record of what a lease actually produced is its **reflog**, which begins at `clone:` and is therefore complete for the repository's lifetime — here it showed exactly four commits, all ref-reachable.

Bundled to `/workspace/pr-leases/.recovery/ec3b9619…-db3fd691….bundle` and verified per-commit by cloning the bundle and `cat-file -e`-ing each sha before removing:

```
  b32cd3156 recoverable
  3b67ceb75 recoverable
  5241f9024 recoverable
  01049d2a0 recoverable
```

`/workspace/mimir` re-verified intact afterward (`git fsck --connectivity-only` clean, HEAD `01049d2a0` on main).

The three items from my review still stand: restore `pr_comment` while keeping `pr_edit`/`pr_rerequest` excluded, update the scope test, and document the intentional rollout baselining plus the bounded 100-PR window.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
mimir-carreira
payload.title: Fix transient s6-overlay download failure after #1504

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The fix is right and the test is a real guard. One gap in what it holds, which is worth closing before this lands because this PR is exactly the change that made the flag set mutable.

## Verified

`--retry-all-errors` needs curl ≥ 7.71.0; the base is `python:3.11-slim` (bookworm, curl 7.88.1), so it is available. All four original flags survive the rewrite — `-fsSL` expands to `--fail --silent --show-error --location`, and every one is present in `curl_args`.

The test is not vacuous. Two mutations at head `544acc37`:

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| Full revert of both downloads to `curl -fsSL` | `test_s6_release_downloads_retry_transient_http_errors` **FAILED** |
| Partial — only the `${S6_ARCH}` download reverted to `-fsSL` | `test_s6_release_downloads_retry_transient_http_errors` **FAILED** |

The second one is the interesting one. `assert body.count("curl ${curl_args}") == 2` is what catches a half-applied fix, and it does. That is the failure mode this kind of change actually has, so pinning the count rather than just the flag strings was the right call.

CI is 9/9, and `tests/test_root_dockerfile.py` is 8 passed in 1.78s warm.

## Blocking: the guard does not hold `--fail`

The test asserts `--retry 5`, `--retry-all-errors`, and the count, but nothing pins `--fail`. Before this PR `-f` was baked into the literal and could not be lost without deleting the flag string outright. Now it is one token inside a shell variable that a future edit can drop while every existing assertion still passes.

That matters because dropping it is not a loud failure. Without `--fail`, curl exits **0** on an HTTP error and writes the server's error page into `/tmp/s6-noarch.tar.xz`. The build then dies at `tar -C / -Jxpf` with a corrupt-archive message pointing at the wrong step — the published image build fails on what reads as a tar problem rather than a download problem. That is a worse diagnostic than the transient failure this PR is fixing.

One line in the same test closes it:

```python
    assert "--fail" in body
```

Worth adding `--show-error` alongside it for the same reason — silent-without-show-error is how a retry exhaustion becomes invisible — but `--fail` is the one I would block on.

## Minor, not blocking on its own

`tests/test_root_dockerfile.py:108-110` has three blank lines before `test_claude_code_build_arg_installs_only_adapter_extra`. No linter runs in this repo (only `publish.yml` and `tests.yml`, no ruff/flake8 config), so nothing catches it — worth fixing while you are in the file.

Happy to re-run and approve as soon as `--fail` is pinned.

payload.body:

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1268: Profile and speed up the full test suite after audit

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The speedup is real and, unusually for a "make it faster" change, the test got *stronger* rather than weaker.

`tests/test_turn_event_bus.py` goes from **91.67s to 0.61s** — it was the slowest file in the suite, and I had measured that 91s myself while reviewing #1509.

**The key question was whether shrinking the payload loses the property**, since that test is what proves the 64 KiB cap prevents the superlinear redaction blowup. It does not, and the comment explains exactly why: the old `"a1-" * 200_000` was not exercising the cap, it was 600 KB of benign text being chewed by the credential regexes. The property is "a string over the cap is truncated before live delivery", and `"a!" * (MAX_LIVE_STRING_CHARS // 2 + 1)` crosses it with an explicit `assert len(payload) > MAX_LIVE_STRING_CHARS` so the premise cannot silently stop holding.

It still catches the regression — I ran the same mutation I used on #1509:

| Reverted | Result |
|---|---|
| `scrub_text(value[:MAX_LIVE_STRING_CHARS])` → `scrub_text(value)` | `test_publish_caps_pathological_single_line_arg_before_live_delivery` **failed in 0.18s** |

That is a better failure than before, too. Previously removing the cap made this file *hang* — I had to kill it at 120s, and on the first attempt it ran past ten minutes. Now the same defect surfaces as a named assertion failure in a fifth of a second. The assertion is on delivered content (`event["args_delta"] == payload[:MAX_LIVE_STRING_CHARS]`), so it is a correctness check rather than a timing one, which is why it no longer depends on being slow to be meaningful.

|---|---|

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1269: authz: worklink containment hardcodes the published image uids, so it fails closed on any other deployment

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The resolution module itself is exactly right. Blocking on *when* it runs, which breaks the suite outside a container — and part of that is my leaf's wording, so I want to be clear about it.

## Blocking: import-time resolution makes the suite uncollectable off-container

```python
IDENTITIES = _resolve_identities()   # module scope
```

This executes on **import**, so any environment without `mimir`/`worklink` accounts fails before a single test runs:

```
RuntimeError: required account 'mimir' is missing
…
5672 tests collected, 63 errors in 17.62s
!!!! Interrupted: 63 errors during collection !!!!
```

That is worse than a failing assertion — the suite cannot be collected at all. Locally `tests/test_contained_checkout.py`, `tests/test_worklink_worker_exec.py` and `tests/test_worklink_worker_parity.py` are among the 63, and neither `mimir`, `worklink`, nor the `worklink` group exists on a normal developer machine.

CI is green because it runs in the image where both accounts exist, so the gate structurally cannot see this. That is the fifth defect of this shape today, and the sharpest.

**My leaf is partly responsible and I should say so.** I wrote "resolved by account name **at startup**" and "raises **at startup** with a message naming the missing account." Module import is a reasonable reading of "startup" — but what I meant, and what the deployment needs, is failure when *containment is initialised*, not when any module in the package is imported. That distinction is the fix:

Resolve lazily and cache — a module-level `@lru_cache`d `get_identities()` (or equivalent) that raises on first real use. Then:

- importing `mimir.worklink.*` is safe anywhere, so the suite collects and unrelated tests run;
- a deployment that actually uses containment still fails loudly and immediately, with the same named-account error;
- the values are still resolved once and shared, so the executor and `contained_checkout.py` cannot drift.

The module-level `MIMIR_UID` / `WORKLINK_UID` / `WORKLINK_GID` re-exports are what force eager evaluation, since `from .identities import MIMIR_UID` cannot be lazy. Consumers will need to call the accessor instead — that is the substance of the change, and it is what keeps the single-source-of-truth property you already have.

## Verified — the security criteria all hold

These were the parts I cared most about, and they are right:

- **Resolution is by name**, via `pwd.getpwnam` / `grp.getgrnam`. No literals, and no second hardcoded layout.
- **Nothing is read from the environment.** There is not an `os.environ` reference in the module. That was the criterion most likely to be "helpfully" violated — an env override would have turned the root executor's peer check into a formality — and it is cleanly avoided.
- **A missing account raises, naming which one**, with no fallback to a default uid. A default is how the original defect arrived.
- **One resolution, three consumers.** `worker_exec.py`, `checkout.py` and `worker_client.py` all read the same values, so they cannot drift.

`tests/test_worklink_identities.py` (+97) and the `worker_exec` additions (+44) look like the right coverage; I could not execute them here for the reason above.

Once resolution is lazy I will re-run the full suite in both modes and confirm the peer-uid rejection test still fails when the check is removed.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The import-time defect is genuinely fixed, and the way it was fixed is right. But the change moved the host dependence from import time into the tests, and the full suite now fails 20 tests on any host without the `mimir`/`worklink` accounts. Blocking on that.

## What is fixed, verified at head `2ae5c635`

`IDENTITIES = _resolve_identities()` at module scope is gone; `get_identities()` is an `@lru_cache(maxsize=1)` accessor and **no consumer calls it at module scope** — every call site in `worker_exec.py`, `checkout.py`, `contained_checkout.py` and `project_tests.py` is inside a function body.

Collection is clean on a host with none of the three accounts:

```
9338 tests collected in 14.81s        # was: 63 errors during collection
```

I mutated it back to the original shape (`IDENTITIES = get_identities()` at module scope in `identities.py`) and got the defect back exactly:

```
tests/test_worklink_identities.py::test_worklink_imports_do_not_resolve_system_accounts FAILED
    AssertionError: mimir
5664 tests collected, 63 errors in 4.70s
```

Same 63 as the original report, so the guard is pinned to the real property. `test_worklink_imports_do_not_resolve_system_accounts` proving the negative in a **child process** is the right construction — that is the only way this claim is provable, and it is the one the repo's own guidance asks for.

The other criteria hold too. `test_system_account_resolution_is_cached_and_shared_by_consumers` asserts one shared object across all four consumers (`"same": True`) and exactly three lookups, which closes the drift risk; setting `MIMIR_UID=7 WORKLINK_UID=8 WORKLINK_GID=9` in that child's environment while asserting `42001/42002/42003` is a neat way to pin non-overridability. And the refusal now names both uids — `worker executor refused peer uid 999; required mimir uid is 1001` — which was the whole diagnostic complaint in the leaf.

## Blocking: the suite now requires the accounts to exist

Every identity-touching test calls the real `get_identities()`, so on a host without those accounts they raise instead of running:

```
E   KeyError: "getpwnam(): name not found: 'mimir'"
E   RuntimeError: required account 'mimir' is missing
mimir/worklink/identities.py:22: RuntimeError
```

Measured on macOS, PR head trial-merged with current `main`, against the same command on unmodified `main`:

| | `main` | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| full suite | — | **20 failed**, 9284 passed, 34 skipped |
| `test_worklink_worker_exec.py` + `test_worklink_worker_parity.py` | 112 passed, 4 skipped | **7 failed**, 106 passed, 4 skipped |
| `test_contained_checkout.py` + `test_repo_tools.py` + `test_worklink_checkout.py` + 3 more | 296 passed, 1 skipped | **13 failed**, 283 passed, 1 skipped |

7 + 13 = the full suite's 20. All twenty are this one cause. The failing set:

```
test_worklink_worker_exec.py::test_project_home_completes_partial_writes_and_applies_modes
test_worklink_worker_exec.py::test_repo_test_local_runner_selects_fd_sourced_execution_copy
test_worklink_worker_exec.py::test_drop_worker_uses_irreversible_identity_sequence
test_worklink_worker_exec.py::test_worker_identity_verifier_rejects_any_retained_authority
test_worklink_worker_exec.py::test_terminal_waits_for_in_group_writers_before_cleanup
test_worklink_worker_exec.py::test_executor_enforces_worker_deadline
test_worklink_worker_parity.py::test_closed_worker_direct_parity_inventory[normal_completion]
test_contained_checkout.py::test_repo_test_checkout_snapshots_without_mutating_source
test_contained_checkout.py::test_prepare_boundary_refuses_collision_without_deleting_incumbent
test_contained_checkout.py::test_prepare_boundary_remains_controller_owned_0700
test_contained_checkout.py::test_repo_test_checkout_normalizes_venv_without_widening_boundary
test_contained_checkout.py::test_repo_test_checkout_allows_tracked_credential_shape
test_contained_checkout.py::test_opencode_checkout_has_fixed_seed_commit_and_cleans_up
test_contained_checkout.py::tes

Approving. The blocking regression is fixed, and the mechanism is the right one.

## Verified at head `0e938582`, trial-merged with current `main`

The twenty tests that failed on the previous head all pass on a machine with **no** `mimir` or `worklink` account:

| Scope | Before (head `2ae5c635`) | Now |
|---|---|---|
| The 8 affected files | 20 failed, 389 passed | **409 passed**, 5 skipped |
| Full suite | 20 failed, 9284 passed | **9304 passed**, 34 skipped |

| CI | green | green |

The autouse fixture injects **42001 / 42002 / 42003**, deliberately not `1001`/`1002`, so it tests the widening rather than re-encoding the literals it replaced. And the dedicated identity tests are untouched by it because they run in child processes, which do not inherit `monkeypatch` — the two mechanisms do not interfere.

The original defect stays pinned. Mutating `identities.py` back to module-scope resolution reproduces it exactly:

```
tests/test_worklink_identities.py::test_worklink_imports_do_not_resolve_system_accounts FAILED
    AssertionError: mimir
5664 tests collected, 63 errors in 4.70s
```

Same 63 collection errors as the original report, so the guard is anchored to the real property rather than to a symptom.

## One follow-up, not blocking

The fixture patches a hardcoded list of four modules. I checked it against head and it is exactly the set that imports `get_identities` — complete today. But a fifth consumer added later would silently fall through to the real resolution and fail only on hosts without those accounts, which CI cannot see. That is the same blind spot that produced both rounds of defects on this PR.

A conformance test asserting the patched list equals the set of modules importing `get_identities` would close it permanently. Filing that separately rather than holding a correct fix for it.

|---|---|---|

payload.title: Worklink #1259: worklink: operator-invoked runs die on EACCES against their own checkout, and the failure is misreported as a bash-allowlist refusal

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. Both halves of this leaf are fixed — the EACCES itself and the misreporting that made it hard to diagnose — and the boundary is untouched.

**The boundary is not widened.** Production `mimir/contained_checkout.py` is not in this diff at all; only `tests/test_contained_checkout.py` is. That was the first thing I checked, because this is the fourth change in a row touching the containment surface and widening `_prepare_boundary` is the recurring shortcut this class of defect invites.

**The operator path is fd-anchored like the autonomous one.** `_local_argv(..., fd_anchored=enabled)` passes `--dir .` instead of an absolute checkout path, so the executor is never handed something that traverses the 0700 boundary — the invariant stated at `compute.py:415` now holds on both paths rather than one.

**The diagnostic is made accurate rather than removed**, which is what the leaf asked for. Refusal detection now requires a permission match *and* a shell/bash mention within 120 characters, so an EACCES on a path no longer masquerades as an allowlist refusal, while a genuine refusal still reports as one. `permission` also drops out of the auth-pattern regex, and an `EACCES` in the detail returns the full text instead of just the last line — so the real error reaches the operator.

| Reverted | Test | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `--dir .` back to the absolute checkout path | `test_enabled_opencode_spec_contains_worker_local_selected_projections` | failed |
| Refusal narrowing back to "any permission match" | `test_opencode_startup_permission_error_surfaces_backend_stderr` | failed |

| Suite | Result |
|---|---|
| Targeted (backends, contained_checkout, worker_projection) | 83 passed |
| Full, merged with current `main` | 9283 passed, 37 skipped |
| Full, `MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED=1` | 9283 passed, 37 skipped |
| CI | 9/9 |

One observation, not blocking: the 120-character proximity window between the permission match and the shell mention is a heuristic. It is a reasonable way to separate "permission denied running bash" from "permission denied on a path", and it is pinned by the test above — but it will misclassify if a backend ever emits a long permission error that happens to mention a shell far away, or a short one that does not mention it at all. Worth a comment recording that the window is tuned to observed opencode output rather than derived, so the next person changing it knows what to re-check.
