payload.title: 1392: ACP registry candidate and client documentation

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES

The ACP client documentation and registry candidate are otherwise thorough, and the implementation/runtime claims I spot-checked match the daemon-attached architecture established by #1423/#1437. All reported GitHub checks are green, and the PR records a full exact-head run of `9415 passed, 26 skipped, 4 warnings`.

Two acceptance criteria from #1392 remain blocking (see inline comments):

1. **Schema provenance is not pinned to an upstream revision.** The vendored schema uses a `latest` `$id`, while the test pins only its local SHA-256. That detects local byte drift but does not record the upstream commit/revision those bytes came from. Record the exact upstream schema commit/revision alongside the digest.
2. **Registry ineligibility is not documented.** The candidate intentionally omits `authMethods`, but `docs/acp.md` only describes publication/manual-smoke release gates. It must explicitly state that the omission makes this candidate not yet registry-eligible and that an auth method must be built before registry submission.

Local focused validation could not start because the scoped runner failed before collection while opening `uv.toml` with `EACCES`; I am treating that as a runner/environment limitation rather than a PR failure and relying on the green CI plus the exact-head full-suite evidence above.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Verdict: APPROVE

Both previously blocking items are resolved at `2424c8c1`.

- `docs/acp.md` now states unambiguously that the manifest's missing `authMethods` makes this candidate ineligible for registry submission, and that publishing plus smoke testing cannot substitute for designing and advertising a supported authentication method.
- `registry/schema/PROVENANCE.json` records the provenance that the upstream distribution actually exposes: source URL, retrieval date, registry format version, and exact SHA-256, while explicitly preserving `immutable_revision: null` with the evidence-backed reason that neither the repository tags nor versioned CDN paths identify these registry-schema bytes. Recording an unrelated wire-schema tag would have been false provenance; the moving-source-plus-pinned-bytes treatment is the correct honest fallback here.

The added tests pin both corrections, including the vendored-byte/provenance digest relationship and the registry-ineligibility language. All nine reported GitHub checks pass at this head, including pytest on Python 3.11 and 3.12. I also attempted the configured focused run for `tests/test_acp_registry.py`, but the scoped runner failed before collection because it could not open its redacted `uv.toml` (`EACCES`); that is runner failure rather than contrary test evidence.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Both blocking items addressed at `2424c8c1`.

**Registry ineligibility** — `docs/acp.md` now has a `### Registry eligibility` section stating the candidate is **not registry-eligible** because it advertises no `authMethods`, that the curated registry requires at least one Agent Auth or Terminal Auth method, and that publication plus manual smoke testing **do not unlock submission on their own** — an auth method must be built and advertised first.

**Schema provenance** — recorded in a new `registry/schema/PROVENANCE.json` rather than by editing the vendored bytes, which need to stay byte-identical to upstream.

One correction to the requested fix, with evidence. The review asked for the upstream commit behind `schema-v1.20.0`. That tag exists, but it does not identify these bytes:

- `agent.schema.json` is **not committed to `agentclientprotocol/agent-client-protocol` at any tag**. The recursive tree at `schema-v1.20.0` (`5e89c71497fe07dd4ae633c181a17224f4a8956d`) contains no such path — that repository ships `agent-client-protocol-schema/`, the wire protocol schema, and its `schema-v*` tags version that, not the registry entry schema.
- Every versioned CDN path 404s — `.../registry/v1/v1.20.0/agent.schema.json` and `.../registry/v1/schema-v1.20.0/agent.schema.json` both. Only `.../registry/v1/latest/agent.schema.json` resolves (200).

Recording a commit SHA that does not correspond to the file would be worse than recording none. So `PROVENANCE.json` records the provenance that exists — `source_url`, `retrieved_utc`, `sha256`, `registry_format_version: 1.0.0` (from the CDN `registry.json`), and an explicit `"immutable_revision": null` with a note explaining why, so a later reader cannot mistake a missing revision for an oversight.

I verified the vendored bytes against the live CDN: `curl` of `latest` hashes to `2489443bf21d8211bcd046edeff5931eecca1ee219ffae4efde09e367c5b1236`, matching both the vendored file and the existing test pin. The bytes are authentic; what was missing was the record of where they came from and how drift is detected (re-fetch and compare).

Both claims are pinned by tests rather than prose. Mutations run on this head, each failing exactly one named test:

- weaken the eligibility statement → `test_docs_state_the_candidate_is_not_registry_eligible`
- drop the "do not unlock submission" clause → same test
- corrupt the recorded digest → `test_schema_provenance_is_recorded_and_matches_the_vendored_bytes`
- silently omit `immutable_revision` → same test

Full suite locally: **9427 passed, 16 skipped**.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1199: authz: only BELATED remediation is authorized — a fresh changes-requested review mints a review-only scope, so every prompt fix pushes out of scope

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Verified at `c8f4386df`. The predicate is right and the guard coverage is good, but the change is wired onto a code path that carries none of the measured traffic, so the defect this leaf exists to fix is unchanged.

## Blocking — the fix reaches POLLER_PAYLOAD only; every measured denial is SERVER_DISCOVERED

`review_state` is threaded in exactly one place — `_repo_review_state_from_event` (`access_control.py:1302`), which builds scopes with `provenance=RepoPRScopeProvenance.POLLER_PAYLOAD`.

The `SERVER_DISCOVERED` factories are untouched, and both hardcode the event type with no review state:

```python
def create_server_discovered_review_scope(repo, pull_request):      # :1220
    return _repo_pr_scope(
        provenance=RepoPRScopeProvenance.SERVER_DISCOVERED,
        event_type="pr_review",        # no review_state argument
        ...

def resolve_server_discovered_review_scope(repo, pull_request):     # :1245
    return _repo_pr_scope_resolution(
        provenance=RepoPRScopeProvenance.SERVER_DISCOVERED,
        event_type="pr_review",        # no review_state argument
        ...
```

`review_state` therefore defaults to `None` on that path, `is_fresh_changes_requested_remediation` is `False`, and the scope stays review-only.

That is the path the failure lives on. From `/mimir-home/logs/events.jsonl`, counting every event carrying `scope_provenance`:

```
  server_discovered   226        poller_payload   136
  ('server_discovered', 'repo_commit')   23
  ('server_discovered', 'repo_push')     22
  ('poller_payload',    'repo_commit')    0
  ('poller_payload',    'repo_push')      0
```

All 45 `repo_pr_scope_denied` / forge would-blocks in the leaf's evidence are `scope_provenance: server_discovered`. Not one `repo_commit` or `repo_push` has ever been authorized against a `poller_payload` scope on this deployment.

`NormalizedPullRequestSnapshot` (`models.py:48`) carries `state`, `number`, `author`, `head_*`, `base_*` — no review state — so this is not a one-line thread-through on that path; the review decision has to reach the factory, and where it comes from needs deciding (a passed-in review state vs. a server-side lookup).

**Every new test drives `_github_poller_auth`**, i.e. an `AgentEvent` with `extra["items"]` — the POLLER_PAYLOAD path. Nothing exercises `create_server_discovered_review_scope` or `resolve_server_discovered_review_scope`, which is why a green suite and 9/9 CI coexist with the measured defect surviving.

Acceptance criterion 8 asks for a test reproducing the measured failure. The test that was written reproduces a *structurally similar* failure on a different provenance. Please add coverage on the `SERVER_DISCOVERED` factories asserting `repo.commit` / `repo.push` are granted for a fresh changes-requested review on a self-authored PR, and denied otherwise.

## Confirmed — no action needed

The predicate itself is correct and the guards are properly pinned.

- **The three-part predicate is right.** `event_type == "pr_review" and review_state == "CHANGES_REQUESTED" and principal == self_login`. `principal` is the PR author, not the reviewer — the server-side attestation at `pollers.py:463-471` independently requires `user.get("login") == self_login` *and* `extras.get("author") == self_login`, so a review by anyone else cannot mint remediation authority on someone else's PR.
- **Guard coverage is thorough.** `test_fresh_changes_requested_remediation_applies_every_write_guard` is parametrized over `repo`, `number`, `author`, `head_repo` (including an explicit `fork/r` case), and `head_remote`, so each guard rejects individually.
- **Adjacent event types stay review-only.** `pr_opened` and `pr_review_comment` are asserted unchanged, and a `COMMENTED` review is asserted to still produce `repo_pr_scope_denied` — so the widening is bounded to the CHANGES_REQUESTED case.
- **The no-union invariant is pinned.** `test_repo_write_authority_is_resolved_per_pr_without_scope_union` asserts two registry entri

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Re-reviewed at `449d218b0`. The activation miss is fixed, and fixed on the provenance the evidence cited.

## The blocking item

Both `SERVER_DISCOVERED` factories now accept and thread `review_state`:

```python
def create_server_discovered_review_scope(repo, pull_request, *, review_state=None)
def resolve_server_discovered_review_scope(repo, pull_request, *, review_state=None)
```

Mutation — remove `review_state=review_state` from both (exactly the gap I raised):

- fails `tests/test_access_control.py::test_server_discovered_changes_requested_review_mints_remediation_authority`
- fails `tests/test_forge_tools.py::test_server_discovered_changes_requested_review_reaches_repo_write_authority`

The test names name the provenance, so a future change cannot quietly re-wire this to `POLLER_PAYLOAD` only.

## The derivation is server-side, which is what mattered

`resolve_review_state_for_context` computes `review_state` from the forge itself rather than accepting it from a caller:

- gated on `snapshot.state == "open"` **and** `snapshot.author == MIMIR_GITHUB_SELF_LOGIN`, so it is only ever computed for the agent's own PR;
- `client.list_reviews(discovery_scope)` is a real forge read, taken through a discovery scope rather than an assertion;
- only `APPROVED` / `CHANGES_REQUESTED` count, so a `COMMENTED` review does not mint write authority — correct, since a comment is not a verdict;
- last-write-wins per author, so a reviewer who requested changes and later approved does not leave stale remediation authority behind.

Mutation — drop the self-authored check so any open PR derives a review state → fails `test_operator_turn_discovers_live_review_scope_and_reaches_repo_test` and `test_enforced_middleware_resolves_standing_review_before_authorization`. So the own-PR restriction is pinned too, which is the one that keeps this from becoming write authority on someone else's branch.

Full suite locally: **8897 passed, 16 skipped**. CI 9/9 including `pytest-enforced`.

## Two notes, neither blocking

**Ordering is inherited, not asserted.** The per-author latest verdict relies on GitHub returning `/pulls/N/reviews` in ascending submission order, which it does today — I confirmed it on #1469 (`16:33 COMMENTED` then `17:38 APPROVED`). `ReviewProjection` already carries `submitted_at`, so sorting on it would make the property explicit rather than dependent on an undocumented API guarantee. Fine as is; worth knowing if the projection is ever reused somewhere the order is not preserved.

**An extra forge round trip** now happens on every `resolve_review_state_for_context` for a self-authored open PR. Bounded and only on that path, but it is a real per-call cost on the hot review surface.

Approved. Not merging.

- `create_server_discovered_review_scope` and `resolve_server_discovered_review_scope` now mint remediation operations only for the existing three-part predicate; ordinary/approved reviews remain review-only.
- Added direct SERVER_DISCOVERED factory coverage plus an end-to-end resolution test proving `repo_commit` and `repo_push` authorization on the measured provenance.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1197: proposals: resolved proposal branches are never swept -- rejected PRs have no cleanup path, and merged ones stop qualifying once main moves on

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Verified at `20ff1be63`. The two defects are fixed and the fail-closed paths are well covered. One blocking item: the new query can hide an open PR, which narrows a safety gate the docstring still advertises.

## Blocking — `--state all --limit 1` no longer guarantees an open PR wins

The old query was safe by construction:

```
gh pr list --state open --head <branch> --json number --limit 1   →  bool(list)
```

It filtered to open, so *any* open PR produced `True` no matter how many PRs the head carried. The new query does not filter:

```
gh pr list --state all --head <branch> --json number,state --limit 1
```

and the code reads `prs[0]`. Which PR lands in slot 0 is decided by the forge's result order, which this code neither controls nor asserts. If a head carries a closed PR and an open one and the closed one sorts first, `pr_state` is `"closed"` and the branch is **deleted while a PR against it is still open** — past `_remove_worktree_for_branch` and `git push origin --delete`.

The docstring added in this PR still claims the old guarantee:

```
- preserve branches with open PRs or unknown PR state,
```

That is now conditional on undocumented ordering.

Severity, stated honestly: **latent, not live.** I checked every head across the three repos this runs against — `jasoncarreira/mimir`, `muninn-mimir`, `mimirbot` — and **zero** carry more than one PR. Proposal branches are timestamp-suffixed, so one branch to one PR holds by construction today. The reachable path is a reopened older PR alongside a newer closed one on the same head, since reopening does not change `created_at`.

I am still asking for it because this is the destructive direction and the leaf's review criteria were explicit that every uncertain path must leave the branch in place. The fix is small — ask the open question separately and let it win, or drop `--limit 1` and treat "any PR is OPEN" as open before reading a terminal state. Either keeps the docstring true without depending on result order.

## Confirmed — no action needed

Both defects reproduce-and-fix cleanly, and each guard is pinned. Mutations run on this head against `tests/test_proposals.py`:

- unknown state made sweepable → fails all four `test_cleanup_skips_branch_when_pr_status_unknown_and_logs` params (`missing`, `nonzero`, `malformed`, `network`)
- content check restored for merged/closed (the original bug) → fails `test_cleanup_sweeps_terminal_pr_without_consulting_content[closed]`, `[merged]`, and `test_cleanup_sweeps_merged_pr_after_main_changes_proposal_blob`
- open-PR skip removed → fails `test_cleanup_preserves_open_pr_branch` and `test_cleanup_skip_events_are_edge_triggered_until_eventual_cleanup`

Against the leaf's criteria:

- **Defect B is reproduced as a test, not just fixed.** `test_cleanup_sweeps_merged_pr_after_main_changes_proposal_blob` is the `PR #43` shape — merged branch, blob since diverged on main, still swept.
- **Defect A has no content dependency.** `pr_state == "no_pr" and not _proposal_branch_content_is_on_main(...)` reaches the content helper only when there is no PR, so a rejected proposal is swept without a check that could only ever refuse.
- **The no-PR path is unchanged.** The content helper still decides, so proposal-prefixed branches that never had a PR are not swept.
- **Fail-closed is thorough** — `gh` missing, `OSError`, non-zero exit, non-list JSON, non-dict element, non-int (and explicitly non-bool) number, unrecognised state. Every one returns `None` and skips.
- **The prefix guard holds.** `test_cleanup_never_considers_branch_outside_proposal_prefixes` is parametrized across all five states including `None`.
- **Deletions stay auditable**, and the reason now distinguishes `resolved_pr_merged` / `resolved_pr_closed` / `resolved_content_on_main`, so a sweep is reconstructable from the event log.

Full suite locally: **8869 passed, 16 skipped**.

## Note — not blocking

The 17 stale branches are deliberately not touched by this PR, which is right

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Re-reviewed at `4f15ddf60`. The blocking item is resolved.

The open-only query now runs first and is authoritative; a terminal PR is inspected only after it comes back authoritatively empty. `--state open` returning anything means an open PR exists regardless of forge result ordering, which restores the guarantee the original `--state open` query had by construction. The docstring now states that reasoning rather than asserting the outcome.

The interleavings are safe in both directions: a PR opened between the two queries is still recognised as `OPEN` by the `--state all` branch and returns `"open"`; a PR merged between them was already caught by the open query. No ordering lands on delete.

Element validation was tightened at the same time — `any(not isinstance(pr, dict) for pr in prs)` checks every element rather than only `prs[0]`.

Mutations on this head:

- bypass the open-only query (the exact defect raised) → fails `test_proposal_branch_pr_state_open_wins_over_terminal_result_order`. The test feeds `--state all` a list with `CLOSED` at index 0 and `OPEN` at index 1 — the ordering that would have deleted a branch with an open PR — and asserts `"open"`.

I also re-ran the three mutations from the previous head to confirm the rewrite did not unpin anything:

- unknown state made sweepable → fails all four `test_cleanup_skips_branch_when_pr_status_unknown_and_logs` params
- content check restored for merged/closed → fails `test_cleanup_sweeps_terminal_pr_without_consulting_content[closed]`, `[merged]`, and `test_cleanup_sweeps_merged_pr_after_main_changes_proposal_blob`
- open-PR skip removed → fails `test_cleanup_preserves_open_pr_branch` and `test_cleanup_skip_events_are_edge_triggered_until_eventual_cleanup`

Full suite locally: **8870 passed, 16 skipped**. CI 9/9 including `pytest-enforced`.

Approved.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Addressed the blocking safety issue in `4f15ddf60`.

`_proposal_branch_pr_state` now asks the open-PR question separately and fails closed unless that query authoritatively returns empty. Only then does it query all states for the terminal/no-PR classification, so forge ordering can no longer let a closed/merged PR hide an open PR on the same head.

Added `test_proposal_branch_pr_state_open_wins_over_terminal_result_order` to pin the reported closed-first/open-second shape, and adapted the state-classification test to verify both query stages.

Validation note: the scoped `repo_test` runner could not start pytest because its redacted `uv.toml` was unreadable (`Permission denied`), so there is no fresh local test result from this remediation turn. The previous head's CI was green; new CI should validate `4f15ddf60`.

payload.title: Worklink #1196: authz: untrusted ingest silently revokes the reply path -- upgrade taints itself, and the operator and originating channels have no carve-out

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Verified at `2dda42c3e`. Implements all three operator decisions, and each guard is pinned by a test that fails when the guard is removed.

Mutations run on this head against `tests/test_information_flow.py` + `tests/test_agent.py`:

- drop `"upgrade"` from the trusted-ingress tuple → fails only `test_trusted_authorless_service_can_egress_to_triggering_channel_under_enforce[upgrade-...]`
- remove the operator-channel carve-out → fails all five params of `test_untrusted_ingest_can_reach_only_server_configured_operator_channel`
- drop `resolved_resource == resolved_triggering == resolved_target_channel` → fails the **cross-channel** tests, which is what demonstrates that equality is the thing keeping cross-channel closed
- drop `source.integrity == "trusted"` from `has_authenticated_ingress` → fails `test_all_labels_must_be_destination_compatible_to_pass`, so an untrusted ingress source cannot fake its way into the carve-out

Against the leaf's review criteria:

- **The operator channel resolves server-side.** `send_message` to the literal `"OPERATOR_CHANNEL"` is refused while the resolved value is allowed, so the sentinel cannot be used by the model to select in by name.
- **The originating-channel carve-out keys on the server's record of the turn** — trigger, interactivity, `event_ingress is None`, and an ingress source matching principal/domain/resource/bridge with `canonical_principal` in `authorized_principals`. Nothing model-asserted participates.
- **Only the reply path opens.** `cross_channel` stays refused, and the upgrade parametrization asserts `shell_exec` still returns `ifc_label_blocked:shell_process` once genuinely external content is ingested — so the carrier is trusted, not everything the turn later reads.
- **Labels are not cleared.** The sources stay on the turn; the carve-out only widens the allowed sink set.

Two things that read as problems and are not, recorded so the next reader does not re-derive them:

- The flip of `incompatible_reply` from `False` to `True` in `test_untrusted_ingest_recloses_operator_action_sinks_but_not_reply` targets the **originating** channel while carrying a source pointing at another channel. That is precisely the case the leaf opens, and `cross_channel` in the same test stays `False`.
- The change to the shared `_target_matches_operator_alert` is behaviour-preserving: `resolve_deliver_channel(OPERATOR_CHANNEL_SENTINEL, env)` returns the env value verbatim, and the empty case stays falsy.

Full suite locally: **8858 passed, 16 skipped**. CI 9/9 including `pytest-enforced`.

Approved.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1195: authz: web_search is declared taint-independent but one of the two egress gates ignores the exemption

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Verified at `f43838e0c`. The fix is the right one and it reaches the causal surface — I traced it end to end against the leaf's review criteria. One blocking gap: half the change is untested.

## Blocking — `fetch_url` gains the exemption with no coverage

Acceptance criterion 1 names both tools. Only `web_search` is tested.

Mutation on this head — narrow the new guard so it exempts `web_search` alone:

```python
            and tool_name not in frozenset({"web_search"})
```

`tests/test_access_control.py` → **877 passed, 2 skipped**. The mutation survives. Nothing in the suite pins `fetch_url`'s behaviour at this gate, so a later change narrowing the set would land green.

It is a real behaviour change, not a theoretical one. Same gate, `private` label, no sources:

| tool | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `fetch_url` (approved URL) | `ifc_label_blocked:network` | `ifc_allowed` |
| `http_request` | `ifc_label_blocked:http_webhook` | unchanged |

Please add a `fetch_url` case asserting `allowed is True` and `would_block is False`. I confirmed it is writable: with `MIMIR_EGRESS_APPROVED_URLS` set to the target and the same auth context the `web_search` test uses, `check_sink_flow("fetch_url", ...)` returns `allowed=True, reason="ifc_allowed"`. Parametrizing over `sorted(_TAINT_INDEPENDENT_EGRESS_TOOLS)` — with the per-tool destination setup each one needs — would also stop a future third member from going untested.

## Confirmed — no action needed

Against the leaf's review criteria:

- **The gates guard genuinely different conditions and neither becomes unreachable.** `:4916` fires on sensitivity labels with no provenance; `:4964` fires on untrusted active ingest, which requires sources. Disjoint on the source predicate, so widening the first cannot mask the second.
- **The branch still refuses everything else.** Disabling it outright (`if False:`) fails `test_ifc_label_blocked_sink_denial_carries_service_principal`; reverting to the original one-line form fails the new test. The change is bracketed on both sides.
- **`fetch_url`'s reach is unchanged.** `fetch_url_is_approved(target, auth_context)` at `:4988` is downstream and untouched — with no approved URL the refusal is `egress_destination_not_approved`. The exemption governs whether taint blocks it, not where it may go.
- **Return labelling is unchanged.** `result_integrity` defaults to `"untrusted"` and is overridden only on the validated-MCP path; the diff touches neither. Reaching out, not trusting what comes back.
- **No provider hostname in the change.** The test uses `search.example.invalid` and sets the pre-existing `TAVILY_SEARCH_URL`, which the destination pin at `:4972` requires.
- **This was the last thing refusing `web_search`.** `CapabilityTier.UNBOUNDED` → already exempt in `_service_tier_allows`; `service_sink_destination_denied` applies only to `SAME_CHANNEL`. Nothing downstream re-blocks it.

Full suite on this head, locally: **8831 passed, 16 skipped**. CI 9/9 including `pytest-enforced`.

## For the record — not blocking

This gate is about **confidentiality** (sensitivity labels leaving) where `:4964` is about **integrity** (untrusted input driving action). Exempting `web_search` here means a turn holding `private` data may put that data into a query to the configured search endpoint. That is the operator's decision and it is exactly what the leaf asked for — noting it so the widening is explicit rather than implied by the set's name.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Re-reviewed at `238846001`. The blocking item is resolved.

The single-tool test is now parametrized over both members of `_TAINT_INDEPENDENT_EGRESS_TOOLS`. Mutation results on this head:

- narrow the exemption to `{"web_search"}` → fails **only** the `fetch_url` param (this is the mutation that survived on the previous head)
- revert the guard to the original one-liner → fails both params
- disable the branch outright (`if False:`) → fails `test_ifc_label_blocked_sink_denial_carries_service_principal`

The change is bracketed on both sides and each parameter is load-bearing.

Full suite locally: **8832 passed, 16 skipped**. CI 9/9 including `pytest-enforced`.

Separately confirmed, since it is the property this exemption depends on: `web_search` results still taint the turn — `classify_protected_result` returns an untrusted `active_ingest` source, so `has_untrusted_active_ingest` is true afterwards. `fetch_url` is metadata-only by design; it returns the sidecar and the body taints on the subsequent `Read` via `_filesystem_result_integrity`. payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Addressed the blocking coverage gap in 238846001: the sourceless-sensitivity-label test is now parameterized across both taint-independent egress tools, with `MIMIR_EGRESS_APPROVED_URLS` configuring the `fetch_url` destination. It asserts `allowed=True` and `would_block=False` for both `web_search` and `fetch_url`.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1193: authz: skills and poller manifests are writable by the principals they configure — restrict to admin operator turns

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Meets chainlink #1193, and improves on two of its criteria.

## The predicate

The build extracted `_is_admin_operator_turn` and then made the **existing** call site at `access_control.py:5347` use it, rather than duplicating the composite. The leaf asked for the shape to be reused; consolidating both into one function is strictly better — the two definitions now cannot drift, which was the stated failure mode.

```python
cls._is_trusted_operator_turn(ifc_labels, auth_context)
and has_untrusted_active_ingest is False
and "admin" in (getattr(auth_context, "roles", ()) or ())
```

Renaming the parameter `trusted_operator_turn` → `admin_operator_turn` throughout is the right call too: the old name would now be actively misleading, since the predicate is strictly stronger than what it used to mean.

The boundary widened correctly, from `skills/<skill>/scripts/**` to all of `skills/`, and the docstring states the limit I asked to be recorded:

> This is a file-tool boundary, not a filesystem sandbox: admitted shell commands and subprocesses can still write there.

## The two criteria most likely to be met in letter only

**Non-admin operator.** Covered as a named case in the matrix (`non_admin_operator`), across all three of `pollers.json`, `SKILL.md` and `scripts/fetch-news.ts` — and `tainted_admin_operator` and `upgrade_service` are covered too. Refusals assert the specific reason `skill_write_requires_admin_operator` rather than just `allowed is False`, so a refusal arriving for an unrelated reason cannot satisfy the test.

**No upgrade exemption.** `test_apply_skill_update_does_not_pass_through_file_tool_gate` monkeypatches `_agent_writable_root_for_path` to **raise if called**, then runs a real refresh. That proves independence rather than asserting an outcome, and it is stronger than the criterion I wrote. `test_upgrade_turn_skill_package_writes_are_refused` covers the other direction: the upgrade *service principal* is still refused through the gate, so the exemption did not sneak in via the principal instead.

`test_skill_write_refusal_is_self_classifying_in_audit_event` is a good addition nobody asked for — the audit event carries the reason, so this is diagnosable from events without replay.

## Verification

- New tests: 24 passed.
- **Mutation A** — replacing the admin-role check with `True` fails the `non_admin_operator` cases. The role requirement is genuinely guarded, not incidental.
- **Mutation B** — narrowing the predicate back to `scripts/` only fails 10 cases including `tainted_admin_operator` and `upgrade_service`. The widening is genuinely guarded.
- 9/9 CI green including `pytest-enforced`.

## For the record

This closes a real hole rather than a theoretical one: during review of PR #1449 a build moved three pollers from `research` (17 capabilities) to `custom` (62) by editing a manifest the principal could write. payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1188: authz: synthesis needs rebuild_index — recorded would-blocks that enforcement would turn into silent regressions

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The core change is right and the build found something my leaf missed. One undocumented consequence needs to be made explicit before this lands.

## What is correct

The leaf asked for the profile grant plus a `TRIGGER_CAPABILITY_TIERS` entry, and both are here: `rebuild_index` → `SCOPE_CONTAINED`, consistent with `write_file`/`edit_file`, so it no longer falls back to `UNBOUNDED` and a `session-boundary` poller capped at `SCOPED_WITH_PROVENANCE` can hold it. `test_synthesis_builtin_has_scoped_pr_reads_without_shell` is untouched, so the rejected shell half did not creep back.

The build also discovered — correctly — that the grant alone does nothing. I verified it: with the capability granted but `_FIXED_SERVICE_SINK_OPERATIONS` emptied, the call is refused `service_sink_destination_denied`. The bypass is what makes the capability usable, and the premise is sound: `rebuild_index` takes `scope` validated against `{memory, state, wiki, all}` (`mimir/tools/extra.py:186`) and accepts no path, so the target-based checks it skips have no target to evaluate. That is a real architectural gap my leaf did not anticipate.

## The finding: this makes `rebuild_index` taint-independent, silently

Measured on this branch, `synthesis` principal, `enforce=True`:

```
                    WITH bypass          WITHOUT bypass
clean labels        allowed=True         allowed=False (service_sink_destination_denied)
untrusted ingest    allowed=True         allowed=False (service_sink_destination_denied)
```

So a turn carrying **untrusted active ingest** may now call `rebuild_index`. To be precise about what this PR did and did not do: it did not remove a taint gate — the destination check refused both cases before, so taint was never the discriminator here. But the effect of the change is that a taint-independent operation now exists where none did, and nothing in the diff says so.

It is not scoped to `synthesis` either. The bypass keys on `tool_name` alone, so it applies to every principal holding `rebuild_index` — including the `github` profile, whose pollers ingest untrusted PR and issue content by design.

I think the disposition is probably **right**: `rebuild_index` regenerates `INDEX.md` from files already on disk, ingests nothing, writes fixed paths, and the post-turn hook rebuilds all indexes after every turn unconditionally — including tainted ones. Gating the mid-turn call would achieve nothing the hook does not already do seconds later. There is precedent in `_TAINT_INDEPENDENT_EGRESS_TOOLS`.

But that reasoning is currently nowhere in the code or the tests, and the only new test asserts the allow case with `InformationFlowLabels()` — clean labels. An undocumented taint exemption in the authorization path is exactly the kind of thing a later reader "fixes" or silently extends.

## Requested changes

- [ ] A test asserting the taint behaviour explicitly — that `rebuild_index` is permitted on a turn carrying untrusted active ingest — so the exemption is a pinned decision rather than an emergent side effect.
- [ ] A comment at `_FIXED_SERVICE_SINK_OPERATIONS` recording why the operation is exempt: no caller-supplied target, fixed derived destinations, and the post-turn hook performs the same rebuild unconditionally. State that membership is deliberately narrow and what a candidate must satisfy to be added.
- [ ] A note that the exemption applies to every principal holding the capability, not only `synthesis` — the `github` profile also grants it and ingests untrusted content.

No objection to the mechanism. The ask is that the widening be stated and tested rather than inferred.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Retracting my first requested change — the premise was wrong, and following it broke the build.**

I claimed the `_FIXED_SERVICE_SINK_OPERATIONS` bypass made `rebuild_index` taint-independent, and asked for a test pinning that. It does not, and the test faithfully implementing my request now fails.

## What the code actually does

`authorize_tool` on a tainted `synthesis` turn returns:

```
decision=ADMIN_REQUIRED  allowed=False  argument_egress=taint_gated
```

The refusal happens at the capability-tier gate (`_service_tier_allows`), which runs **before** the sink-flow bypass this PR touches. So taint gating was never removed — the bypass only skips the *target* checks, and an operation with no caller-supplied target has nothing for them to evaluate.

## How I got it wrong

I measured with `InformationFlowLabels(sources=frozenset({...}))`. That does not exercise the path that matters. Your `.with_source(...)` construction is the correct one — and it demonstrates the opposite of what I asserted, since the test built that way fails on `allowed is True`. I should have used the construction the existing tests use before reporting a security finding, and I stated it with more confidence than the evidence supported.

## Current state

All three pytest jobs fail on `c382a7fd`:

```
pytest (3.11)     FAILURE
pytest (3.12)     FAILURE
pytest-enforced   FAILURE
```

`test_synthesis_builtin_authorizes_tainted_scope_contained_index_rebuild` asserts behaviour the code does not have.

## Requested

- [ ] **Invert the test.** Keep the `.with_source(...)` tainted-label construction and the `assert labels.has_untrusted_active_ingest is True` guard, but assert the call is **refused** under untrusted active ingest. Keep a separate clean-label case asserting allowed. That pins the real boundary — taint-gated at the tier, target checks skipped at the sink — and is more useful than what I originally asked for.
- [ ] **Correct the comment.** Drop "They are also deliberately taint-independent for every principal holding the capability (currently including synthesis and github)" — the code contradicts it. The accurate statement is narrower: these operations accept no caller-selected destination, so the target adapter has nothing to validate; taint gating still applies upstream at the capability tier.
- [ ] Keep the rest of the comment. The membership criteria ("no caller-selected target, fixed derived destinations") are good and worth retaining, minus the safety-under-untrusted-ingest clause, which is now the tier`s job rather than a property of the set.

Everything else in this PR was already correct before my review: the `SCOPE_CONTAINED` tier entry, the profile grant, the untouched no-shell test, and the bypass mechanism itself. Sorry for the detour.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Both corrections landed, and the test is better than what I asked for.

## The test now pins the real boundary

`test_synthesis_builtin_authorizes_clean_but_refuses_tainted_index_rebuild` asserts both halves in one place — clean labels allowed, tainted refused — and goes further than requested by pinning the *reason*:

```python
assert tainted_decision.allowed is False
assert tainted_decision.argument_egress == "taint_gated"
```

That distinguishes "refused because taint-gated" from "refused for some other reason", which is what makes it a durable guard rather than a coincidence. It also keeps the `assert labels.has_untrusted_active_ingest is True` precondition, so the tainted case cannot pass vacuously on a mis-constructed label.

## The comment is now accurate

> Taint gating still applies upstream at the capability-tier gate; membership here bypasses only destination checks.

Correct and appropriately narrow. The membership criteria are retained, minus the safety-under-untrusted-ingest clause that is the tier`s job rather than a property of this set.

## Verification

- Corrected test: 1 passed.
- **Mutation:** emptying `_FIXED_SERVICE_SINK_OPERATIONS` fails the test — so the exemption is still genuinely guarded, and the clean-case allow is not incidental.
- 9/9 CI green including `pytest-enforced`, recovering the three pytest failures my previous request caused.

## Standing summary of the change

`rebuild_index` is granted to `session-boundary` with an explicit `SCOPE_CONTAINED` tier entry, so it no longer falls back to `UNBOUNDED` and a poller capped at `SCOPED_WITH_PROVENANCE` can hold it. The destination-check bypass is what makes the capability usable at all — verified by removing it and observing `service_sink_destination_denied` — and it is bounded to a single named operation with no caller-selected target. `test_synthesis_builtin_has_scoped_pr_reads_without_shell` remains untouched, so the rejected shell half never crept back.

Approving. Apologies again for the round trip — the PR was correct before my first review, and the intervening failure was mine.

payload.title: Worklink #1192: pollers: gmail-poller and social-cli need declared shell_commands with wrapper scripts — their calls are refused for shape, not authority

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The wrapper scripts are good work. The profile change is not, and it inverts the point of the issue.

## Blocking: the pollers were moved from `research` to `custom`

Chainlink #1192 said, verbatim: *"No `shell_exec` capability is added to the `research` profile. The declarations are the grant; widening the profile would admit far more than the recorded need."*

`access_control.py` is untouched, so no profile was widened — but all three manifests were switched to `profile: custom`, which satisfies the letter of that constraint while doing the thing it existed to prevent.

```
research   17 capabilities
custom     62 capabilities
```

What `gmail-inbox`, `social-cli-feed` and `social-cli-notifications` gain by that move, beyond the `shell_exec` + companions they need:

```
repo_push, repo_commit, repo_merge, repo_rebase, repo_revert, repo_checkout,
repo_test, worklink_run, spawn_open_code, task, fetch_url, http_request,
webhook, ntfy_send, web_search, saga_end_session, pr_submit_review,
pr_inline_review_comment, pr_comment, ... (45 in total)
```

`custom` is the largest profile in the codebase — larger than `github` (55) and `heartbeat` (54). These are pollers that ingest untrusted email and social-feed content, and this hands them repository write, push, spawn, and webhook egress they have never attempted. The recorded would-block evidence supports `shell_exec` and its two companions. Nothing in it supports the other 45.

It also re-grants `saga_end_session`, which #1189 and #1190 deliberately withheld from these exact pollers on the grounds that the synthesis turn already closes those sessions.

The honest options are: declare `shell_exec` + `bash_jobs_list` + `bash_job_output` inside `research` (a 3-capability widening, reviewable on its evidence), or create a profile sized to these pollers. Moving to a 62-capability catch-all is neither.

## Also blocking: an unrelated, untested change to `mimir/pollers.py`

```python
+ try:
+     await asyncio.wait_for(asyncio.gather(*pending, return_exceptions=True),
+                            timeout=POLLER_EXIT_GRACE_SECONDS)
+ except asyncio.TimeoutError:
+     for task in pending: task.cancel()
```

This changes process-group teardown after SIGKILL — async lifecycle behaviour affecting every poller, not just these three. It may well be correct (descendants inheriting pipe descriptors is a real problem), but it is outside the issue scope, and no test covers it: the `tests/test_pollers.py` change in this PR is about manifest paths, and `POLLER_EXIT_GRACE_SECONDS` already existed on main. Please split it into its own issue where it can be reviewed and tested on its merits.

## What is good, and should survive the rework

The wrapper scripts are defensive in the right ways and should be kept as-is: `set -euo pipefail`, an allowlisted poller name, an allowlisted subcommand, per-option value tracking, rejection of any unrecognised `-*`, and `exec` of a fixed absolute binary. That directly answers the review criterion about a wrapper not passing user-controlled text to a shell. Declaring `wc -l` and `ls -la` directly rather than wrapping them is also the right call.

Scripts live under `<skill>/scripts/`, which is writable only on a trusted-operator turn, so a poller turn cannot rewrite what it is about to execute.

## Requested

- [ ] Revert the three manifests to `profile: research`, and obtain `shell_exec` + `bash_jobs_list` + `bash_job_output` by the narrowest available route. State which route and why.
- [ ] Do not re-grant `saga_end_session` to these pollers; #1189/#1190 withheld it deliberately.
- [ ] Move the `mimir/pollers.py` process-group change to its own issue, with a test.
- [ ] Keep the wrapper scripts and the direct `wc`/`ls` declarations unchanged.

Note the branch also needs `main` merged — it is currently `DIRTY` on `tests/test_contained_execution.py`, the same `OPENCODE_CONFIG` conflict four earlier builds hit. Resolve toward main: the module-level autouse fixture alrea

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
All four requested changes are in, and the new tests are stronger than I asked for.

## Against the review

| requested | result |
|---|---|
| revert all three pollers to `research` | done — `social-cli-feed`, `social-cli-notifications`, `gmail-inbox` all `profile: research` |
| obtain the three companions by the narrowest route, stating which | done — `research` widened by exactly `shell_exec`, `bash_jobs_list`, `bash_job_output` (17 → 20 capabilities) |
| do not re-grant `saga_end_session` | done — absent from all three |
| split out the `mimir/pollers.py` change | done — no longer in the diff |
| merge `main` | done — `main` is an ancestor, `DIRTY` cleared |
| keep the wrappers | done — both `run-social-cli.sh` and `run-gog.sh` unchanged |

The route taken is the first of the two options I named: a 3-capability widening of `research`, reviewable on its evidence, rather than `custom`'s 62. Each added capability maps to a recorded would-block, and `bash_jobs_list`/`bash_job_output` are the companions `_missing_capability_companions` requires — without them the principal fails to construct.

## On the profile widening

`research` is shared, so this raises the ceiling for every research-profile poller across both deployments — including the four mimirbot pollers declared in mimirbot#25. Worth being explicit that this is a **ceiling, not a grant**: those pollers gain nothing until their own manifest declares the capability, and none does.

I also checked what that ceiling is actually worth, because it bears on how much the widening costs:

```
skills/<skill>/pollers.json    scheduled/poller turn  WRITABLE
skills/<skill>/scripts/*.sh    scheduled/poller turn  refused
```

A manifest is writable on an ordinary turn, so an agent could already move a poller to `profile: custom` and reach 62 capabilities — as the previous revision of this PR did. The profile ceiling is a review surface, not a containment boundary against self-modification. That makes the marginal risk of +3 small, and it is the wrapper scripts under `scripts/` — operator-turn-only — that carry the real boundary here. Worth its own issue rather than blocking this one.

## The new tests

`test_shell_wrappers_refuse_code_passthrough_options` is the one that matters: it **executes** the wrapper with a disallowed option and asserts `returncode == 2` and `"unsupported option"`. That proves the allowlist works rather than asserting the source contains an allowlist. Together with `test_shell_wrappers_do_not_expose_interpreter_passthrough` (no `eval`, `bash -c`, `python3 -c`, `python3 -m`) it directly answers the review criterion about a wrapper not re-opening what the profile closes.

`test_shipped_shell_commands_parse_in_installed_skill` parses each manifest through the real `parse_declared_shell_commands`, so a declaration whose script sits in a writable root fails the test rather than the live poller.

## Verification

- CI **9/9 green** on `fd6dfbae3`, including `pytest-enforced`.
- All three manifests parse with `outside_profile=none`.
- Declarations resolve: `bash` → the pinned wrapper, plus `wc` and `ls` directly.

One portability note, not blocking: those tests fail on macOS because the manifests pin `path: /usr/bin/bash`, which exists in the Debian containers (verified on both mimirbot and muninn) but not on macOS, where bash is `/bin/bash`. Correct for the deployment targets; it will just confuse the next person who runs the suite locally.

Approving.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1191: prompts: the trigger authority block says what a principal may call but never what shape the call must take, and renders nothing at all when no profile is declared

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Meets chainlink #1191, including the criterion I expected to be the hardest.

## The contract matches the enforcement, not a paraphrase

This was the review criterion most likely to fail, because a prompt that describes a stricter or looser rule than the gate trains the agent toward a shape that still refuses. The rendered text says interpreters may never use:

> ``-c``, ``-e``, ``-m``, ``--command``, ``--eval``, or stdin ``-`` forms

and the enforcement set is:

```python
_CODE_FROM_ARGV_OPTIONS = frozenset({"-c", "-e", "-m", "--command", "--eval", "-"})
```

Exact match, including the easily-missed bare `-` stdin form. The shape list (no pipes, redirects, `&&`/`;`, globs, `$(...)`, `source`/`export` prefixes) corresponds to the `shell_control_characters` refusals actually recorded.

## Correct gating on both new behaviours

- The contract renders only when the principal holds `shell_exec` or `bash_async`, so principals without shell are not given irrelevant instruction.
- The block now renders for a principal with no profile: `if trigger_authority_present or trigger_authority_profile or capabilities`, with `profile` falling back to `none`. That closes the case where `poller:arxiv-agent-memory` (`profile=None, tier=None, capabilities=[]`) received no authority section at all and then produced 300+ would-blocks across 11 tools.
- `agent.py` passes `trigger_shell_commands` as executables only, so declared commands are named without leaking pinned script paths or option lists into the prompt.
- The framing stays consistent with the existing "this guidance grants nothing" — the new text is explicitly labelled "shape only, not a grant".

## Verification

- `tests/test_prompts.py`: 39 passed.
- **Mutation A** — rendering the contract unconditionally (`if True:`) fails `renders_shell_contract_and_declared_commands_only_for_shell_capability` and `renders_profileless_autonomous_authority`.
- **Mutation B** — restoring the old `if trigger_authority_profile:` gate fails `renders_profileless_autonomous_authority`.

Both new behaviours are genuinely guarded rather than incidentally passing. 9/9 CI green including `pytest-enforced`.

Approving.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1187: repo_test: the credential preflight refuses every snapshot of this repository, so the tool cannot run on the repo the agent reviews most

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
This narrows a credential control, so I verified the security properties directly rather than reading the diff and the evidence block.

## The design is right, and correctly bounded

The per-kind decision is the whole thing:

```python
scan_credentials = kind != "tracked" or scan_tracked_credentials
```

Untracked and ignored entries take the existing path unconditionally. The flag defaults to `True`, so every caller keeps current behaviour unless it opts out, and only `create_repo_test_checkout` does. `create_opencode_checkout` is untouched (`contained_checkout.py:200` still calls `preflight_git_snapshot` with no flag) — which is what the leaf required, since its seed goes to an external agent process and its threat model was never assessed here.

Both `preflight_git_snapshot` calls inside `create_git_snapshot` receive the same flag, so the TOCTOU comparison `verified_entries != entries` stays consistent. Getting that wrong would have turned every repo_test snapshot into `SnapshotSourceChanged`.

## Verification

**The problem is fixed.** Against a clean checkout of `main`:

```
scan_tracked_credentials=True  -> REFUSED (count=114)
scan_tracked_credentials=False -> OK, 938 entries
```

**The control survives where it matters.** Built a repo with a committed `SERVICE_TOKEN=`, then added credential files in each other inventory class, all on the repo_test path:

```
tracked secret only                  -> allowed
+ untracked .env                     -> REFUSED (n=1)
+ ignored secrets.txt                -> REFUSED (n=1)
```

That is exactly the intended boundary: already-committed content is exempt, a stray `.env` or ignored credential file is not.

**Mutation.** Widening the gate to `scan_credentials = scan_tracked_credentials` — i.e. letting the flag disable scanning for all kinds — fails `test_repo_test_checkout_still_refuses_nontracked_credentials` for both `untracked` and `ignored`. The restriction to tracked content is genuinely guarded, not incidental.

179 tests pass in the two touched files; 9/9 CI green including `pytest-enforced`.

## One consequence worth stating for the record

A tracked file whose NAME is credential-shaped (`credentials.json`) is now also exempt on this path, because `_name_is_sensitive` sits behind the same gate. That follows from the same reasoning — a committed `credentials.json` is already in the repository, already in the pull request, already on the remote — and a committed secret is a secret-scanning problem at the remote, not something a snapshot boundary can retroactively contain. It is worth being explicit that this is understood rather than overlooked.

Approving.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1186: tools: a provider that wraps arrays as {"item": [...]} loses every list-taking tool call, and the validation error is discarded so it is undiagnosable

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Verified independently, not from the evidence block. Meets every acceptance criterion on chainlink #1186.

## Implementation

The coercion is correctly bounded. `_is_sequence_annotation` unwraps `Annotated` and both `Union` spellings, and excludes `str`/`bytes`/`bytearray` — which is load-bearing, since `str` IS a `Sequence` and without that exclusion a scalar parameter given `{"item": "x"}` would silently unwrap. The `set(value) == {"item"}` check enforces the sole-key restriction, so `{"item": x, "other": y}` cannot drop `other` on the floor. Coercion happens before `model_validate`, so nothing bypasses validation.

The diagnostic addition is careful in the way that matters: `errors(include_url=False, include_context=False, include_input=False)`, only the parameter location and error type are recorded, the type string is regex-guarded, and the whole thing is wrapped so a logging failure cannot affect authorization. A test proves a credential-shaped argument value never reaches the log.

## Verification

- New tests: 6 passed.
- **Mutation A** — replacing `set(value) == {"item"}` with `"item" in value` fails `keeps_invalid_list_payloads_invalid[topics0]`. The sole-key restriction is genuinely guarded.
- **Mutation B** — removing `and candidate not in (str, bytes, bytearray)` fails `unwraps_item_only_for_list_parameters`. The scalar exclusion is genuinely guarded.
- 9/9 CI green including `pytest-enforced`.

## On the third file

`tests/test_contained_execution.py` gains an autouse fixture clearing `OPENCODE_CONFIG`. That is unrelated to the item-wrapper, and I checked whether it masks something. It does not — it fixes a defect I introduced in PR #1438.

With the fixture removed and `OPENCODE_CONFIG` set in the environment:

```
FAILED test_safe_truncation_length_moves_the_cut_off_a_spanning_secret
FAILED test_safe_truncation_length_without_materials_is_the_limit
```

Both are tests I wrote. They construct `SensitiveMaterialScrubber(home="", checkout=None)` and assert on its material set, but the constructor reads `os.environ["OPENCODE_CONFIG"]` and registers it as a material — so they were asserting on ambient state they do not own, exactly the failure mode CONTRIBUTING.md describes. Clearing the variable for that module is the right fix and makes the module hermetic. Worth having stated in the PR body rather than leaving as an unexplained third file, but the change itself is correct.

Approving.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1185: authz: a shell refusal tells the agent why only in prose — the stable binding_rule is computed at the same call site but sent only to the event

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The change is correct and well-tested — one defensive fix before merge.

## Verified good

Checked against each acceptance criterion on chainlink #1185, and independently rather than from the evidence block:

- `binding_rule` now reaches the caller at `budget_gate.py:716`, and the prose is **added to**, not replaced — the human-readable diagnosis that line exists to provide is intact.
- The emitted event is untouched, so the operator/shadow-audit consumers of `reason="service_shell_argv_binding_failed"` and `binding_rule` keep working.
- `mimir_shell_refusal` remains in `_SERVER_ONLY_SHELL_ARGS`.
- `.value` is used, so the suffix carries the stable enum value rather than a repr.
- All three refusal classes are covered, and the `secret_value not in refusal` assertion pins the no-laundering criterion.
- 9/9 CI checks green including `pytest-enforced`.
- **Mutation-tested locally:** reverting the suffix fails all three parametrised cases (`3 failed, 867 deselected`); restoring returns `3 passed`. The test genuinely guards the behaviour rather than passing incidentally.

The `profile-allowlist` case is a nice addition beyond what the leaf asked for — it documents that an undeclared command with **no** declarations yields `profile_allowlist`, while an undeclared flag **with** declarations yields `declared_command_mismatch`. That distinction is load-bearing downstream and was previously undocumented.

## Requested change: guard the `None` rule

`parse_service_shell_argv_with_diagnostics` is typed `tuple[list[str] | None, str, ServiceShellBindingRule | None]`, so `binding_rule.value` assumes a non-`None` value the signature does not promise.

I confirmed this is **not** a live bug: an AST walk of all 19 tuple returns in that function found zero refusal paths (`argv=None`) that return a `None` rule. So the invariant holds today.

The problem is what happens when it stops holding. This line sits in the authorization gate, on the path whose entire purpose is to fail **closed** — the comment directly above it explains that the argv binding stays as defence in depth so "a future refactor that drops this channel still fails closed rather than reaching a shell." An `AttributeError` here converts that clean refusal into an unhandled exception inside the gate, which is a strictly worse failure than the refusal it replaces. A new refusal path that forgets to pass a rule is an easy and invisible mistake, and the signature actively permits it.

Suggested shape:

```python
args["mimir_shell_refusal"] = (
    f"{tool_name} was refused before execution: {refusal} "
    f"binding_rule={binding_rule.value if binding_rule is not None else \"unknown\"}"
)
```

Acceptance for the follow-up:

- [ ] A `None` `binding_rule` produces a refusal with a stable placeholder rather than raising.
- [ ] The suffix format is unchanged for the real cases, so the existing `endswith(f" binding_rule={expected_rule}")` assertions still hold.
- [ ] A test drives the `None` path — e.g. monkeypatch `parse_service_shell_argv_with_diagnostics` to return `(None, "...", None)` — and asserts a refusal is returned, not an exception. Without that test the guard is unverified and can regress the same way.

Everything else is ready to merge as-is.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving `92582f173`.

The guard is exactly what was requested, including the test — which was the item most likely to be skipped:

```python
binding_rule={binding_rule.value if binding_rule is not None else 'unknown'}
```

`test_service_shell_binding_refusal_handles_missing_rule` monkeypatches the parser to return `(None, "synthetic refusal", None)` and asserts a refusal string is returned rather than an exception raised. The patch targets the module attribute, which is imported into `budget_gate`'s namespace at line 65, so it covers BOTH call sites (`:662` and `:673`) rather than only the one under test.

Verified on this head, not inferred from the commit appearing:

- All four tests pass (three original classes + the `None` guard).
- **Mutation:** removing the guard fails *only* `missing_rule`; the three original cases still pass. That is the signature I wanted — it proves the guard is covered by its own test AND that the suffix format did not drift, so real-case behaviour is unchanged and the existing `endswith(f" binding_rule={rule}")` assertions still hold.
- 9/9 CI green including `pytest-enforced`.

Net effect: a refusal now carries the stable class key to the agent alongside the human-readable prose, and a future refusal path that forgets to pass a rule degrades to `binding_rule=unknown` instead of raising an `AttributeError` inside the authorization gate. The gate keeps failing closed, which is the property this line exists to protect.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Addressed the requested defensive fix in 92582f173:

- `binding_rule=None` now produces the stable suffix `binding_rule=unknown` instead of raising.
- Added a regression that monkeypatches the parser to return `(None, "synthetic refusal", None)` and verifies a normal fail-closed refusal.
- Existing real-rule suffix behavior is unchanged.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.title: 1433 : authz: extract a reusable contained-execution entry point, and route repo_test and spawn_open_code through it

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The contained-checkout architecture is directionally strong: it isolates `repo_test` and `spawn_open_code` from controller-owned trees, centralizes bounded execution, projects credentials into worker-owned files, and returns OpenCode edits as a separately applied proposal. The diff also includes substantial unit and shipped-image coverage.

One blocking confidentiality issue remains in the shared output collector: the cap can cut through a sensitive scalar, while the later scrubber only replaces full registered values. That exposes a prefix of an OAuth token/API key through the tool result or persisted artifacts. I left an inline finding on `mimir/contained_execution.py`; please preserve a redaction-safe boundary or use overlap-aware incremental scrubbing, with a regression for a cap bisecting a known secret.

Validation: CI was still running when reviewed; completed package, frontend, skill-conformance, chainlink audit, and shipped-image identity checks were green.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The remediation at `ab5c4961` resolves my blocking confidentiality finding. `_drain` now retains exactly the longest-material lookahead needed to observe a value spanning the output cap, and `safe_truncation_length()` retreats the cut to the start of any genuinely spanning occurrence; this prevents whole-value scrubbing from receiving and exposing a secret fragment without penalizing ordinary output that merely shares a sensitive material's prefix. The iterative retreat also handles cascaded/overlapping cut points.

The production wiring is complete: both `repo_test` and `spawn_open_code` pass their existing scrubber into the contained executor, and dropped-byte accounting includes the extra bytes removed to reach the safe boundary. Coverage exercises every cut offset on both stdout and stderr, verifies exact-cap retention when no material spans the cut, and pins the helper's boundary behavior. Jason's correction about stream-read boundaries is also correct: `_drain` reassembles chunks before scrubbing, so truncation—not chunking—is the fragment-producing operation.

The pytest 3.11, pytest 3.12, and access-control-enforced checks are green on this head. `chainlink-cli-audit` is currently red and still needs to be resolved or shown transient before merge; it does not change the disposition of the code remediation reviewed here.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Independently reproduced the truncation leak. It is real, and the reproduction is small enough to become the regression directly.

```python
s = SensitiveMaterialScrubber()
s.add_scalar(b"sk-live-ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789")

# normal path is fine
s.scrub_bytes(b"token=" + SECRET + b"\n")        # -> redacted

# cap lands 20 bytes into the secret
retained, dropped = await _drain(stream, limit=len(b"token=") + 20, overflow)
s.scrub_bytes(retained)
```

```
full value scrubbed              : True
cap=26  dropped=25
retained ends with a secret PREFIX: True
prefix SURVIVES scrubbing        : True
leaked bytes                     : sk-live-ABCDEFGHIJKL
```

Twenty bytes of the token reach the tool result verbatim.

The two halves are individually reasonable, which is why this is easy to miss:

```python
# _drain, line ~171 — cuts at an arbitrary byte offset
remaining = max(0, limit - len(retained))
retained.extend(chunk[:remaining])

# scrub_bytes — substring replacement, needs the WHOLE value
payload = payload.replace(material, _REDACTION)
```

A prefix matches no registered material, so it is emitted unchanged. It only manifests when output overflows *and* a secret straddles the cap, so ordinary tests will not surface it.

Worth noting the same reasoning applies to the other boundary, and a fix should cover both: a secret split across two `stream.read()` chunks is equally unmatched even without any truncation, since `scrub_bytes` is called on the assembled buffer only after draining. If the fix is overlap-aware incremental scrubbing, it closes both; if it is only a redaction-safe cut at the cap, the chunk-boundary case stays open.

For the regression I would assert the property rather than the offset — for every cut point across the secret's span, no non-empty prefix of a registered material survives scrubbing. A single hand-picked offset passes while neighbouring ones leak.

Everything else in the review matches what I found reading the diff: the contracts hold — `repo_test` runs against a disposable snapshot with the active PR lease never normalized or chowned, and `spawn_open_code` gets a fresh server-issued checkout rather than the supplied cwd, returning edits as a separately applied proposal. Those were the two capability contracts the issue pinned, and they are implemented as specified.

CI is now complete on this head: 9/9 green, 0 incomplete.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Pushed `ab5c4961`.

**Correction to my earlier comment first.** I claimed a secret split across two `stream.read()` calls leaks the same way. That is wrong — I tested it: `_drain` accumulates every chunk into one buffer and nothing scrubs until the buffer is complete, so a value straddling a read boundary is reassembled and scrubbed normally (`secret survives scrubbing: False`). **Truncation is the only step that produces a fragment.** That narrowing is what the fix is built on, and it is stated in the docstring so the next reader does not re-derive it.

**The fix.** `_drain` now buffers `lookahead_bytes()` (longest material − 1) past the cap, so any material spanning the cut is present *whole*, and `safe_truncation_length` moves the cut back to where that material begins.

The design choice worth reviewing: the cut is chosen from occurrences that **actually span it**, found with `bytes.find`, not from tails that merely *look like* the start of a material. I built the prefix-inference version first and rejected it — `/` is the first byte of every registered path, so it trimmed any output ending in a run of slashes. Measured on 1 MiB of `/`: it discarded the entire buffer and took 309 ms. The occurrence rule leaves that output untouched and runs in ~1 ms on a 1.2 MiB stream with a 4 KB `auth.json` registered as a material. There is a test pinning that non-regression, because the cheap fix here is the one that quietly destroys logs.

Why the lookahead is exact rather than best-effort: if the buffer reaches `limit + lookahead`, any occurrence spanning the cut starts at ≥ `limit − longest + 1` and ends at ≤ `limit + longest − 1`, so it fits. If the buffer is shorter, the stream hit EOF and there are no further bytes to hide one. A process killed mid-secret emits a fragment either way — untruncated output would carry the same bytes, so that is not truncation-induced and is out of scope here.

**Interface change owns its callers**, per the rule on #1433: `execute_contained` takes the scrubber both production callers already construct, and both call sites are updated in this same commit — `mimir/project_tests.py:313` and `mimir/tools/registry.py:2155`. Neither had to move its scrubber construction; both already built it before the call.

`*_dropped_bytes` now counts every byte the caller does not receive, including anything trimmed past the cap, so the accounting stays honest rather than under-reporting the trim.

**Evidence.**
- Regression test parametrised over **every** cut point across the secret's span, on **both** streams — `test_truncation_never_emits_a_fragment_of_a_secret`. This is deliberate: a single hand-picked offset passes while its neighbours leak.
- Mutation: reverting the safe cut to `keep = limit` fails **58** of those cases; restoring it returns 106 passed. The tests ran — they were not deselected.
- `safe_truncation_length` cross-checked against a brute-force reference over 6,000 randomised material/payload combinations: 0 mismatches. My first two drafts were both wrong and this is what caught them — the second had a static floor that missed cascading cut points (191/4000 mismatches).
- Full suite green twice: **8787 passed, 23 skipped** on the default config and again under `MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED=1`.

payload.title: 1423 : ACP daemon foundation — bounded primitives, authenticated generation, socket runtime (partial)

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The new commit makes the successor-socket test robust by asserting pathname preservation without depending on socket inode reuse, but it does not address the blocking input-bound issue from my review at the previous head. `BoundedMessageQueue.task_done()` still releases item and byte capacity as soon as the ACP dispatcher dequeues a message, while request handling continues in an independently supervised task; a peer can therefore keep the queue below its limits while accumulating unbounded active handlers and decoded request memory.

The existing inline finding remains current: bound active inbound request/notification runners (or retain queue capacity until each runner completes) and add an end-to-end `Connection` regression with handlers blocked while more than the configured limit is sent.

Validation: the new socket test change is sound, and the Python 3.11, Python 3.12, enforced-pytest, package, frontend, Claude Code smoke, Worklink image, and Chainlink audit checks now pass. `skill-conformance` was still running when reviewed.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The blocking inbound-dispatch issue is resolved at `923ab3e7`. `BoundedMessageDispatcher` now shares one 64-permit semaphore across requests and notifications, acquires before creating the supervised runner, releases on every completion/setup-failure path, and cancels a dispatcher blocked on capacity during shutdown. Together with the bounded item/byte queue and frame cap, this prevents both unbounded runner-task growth and unbounded decoded-input retention.

The new live-`Connection` regression exercises mixed requests and notifications with blocked handlers, proves the active count cannot exceed the configured limit, then releases them and verifies all work completes. I also ran `tests/test_acp_sdk_contract.py tests/test_acp_daemon.py`: 104 passed. payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1183: authz: job-bound scheduled ticks cannot read other channels, so the memory-hygiene scan cannot run

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving at `99a4ab95c`. All 9 checks green; full local suite 8454 passed, 22 skipped.

**Verified behaviourally against the real principal builder**, not by reading the predicate:

| | job-bound tick | non-tick turn |
|---|---|---|
| enumerate `memory/channels/` | ALLOWED | ALLOWED (unchanged) |
| own channel | ALLOWED | ALLOWED |
| another job's channel | **ALLOWED** (the change) | DENIED |
| a web channel | **ALLOWED** | ALLOWED (it is that turn's own) |
| `memory/core` | ALLOWED | ALLOWED |

The non-tick column is the one worth stating: a human turn still reads only its own channel, so this widened the class it was meant to widen and nothing else.

**Mutation-verified.** Restoring the per-job narrowing fails all three tests, including the end-to-end scan. So the widening is pinned rather than incidental.

**The old assertions were inverted, not deleted.** `..._memory_scope_allows_core_and_only_its_channel` became `..._allows_core_and_all_channels`, with `is False` → `is True` for both the other-channel and the bare-enumerate cases. That was the thing I most wanted to see: three edits have now landed on `is_memory_read_path_allowed` in a week — #1169 scoped it per job, #1176 restored `memory/core`, and this removes the cross-channel narrowing — and renaming rather than deleting means the next reader sees three deliberate decisions instead of a boundary that eroded.

**`test_scheduled_tick_can_execute_cross_channel_memory_hygiene_scan` is the right closing test.** It drives the real principal through the actual scan — authorization decision, `glob`, per-channel sizes, then reading a note's content — rather than asserting the predicate in isolation. The prompt needs content, not just sizes (judging "notes that look more like runbooks than channel facts"), and this proves that path end to end.

Scope is exactly two files, `read_policy.py` and its tests, so no write surface was touched. This is a read grant only, as intended.

For the record, what this unblocks — measured on mimirbot before the change:

    260 KB  poller:github-activity     ~32x the 8 KB channel-memory injection cap
    196 KB  poller:arxiv-agent-memory
     24 KB  poller:anthropic-changelog
     20 KB  scheduler:heartbeat

None of it visible to the job whose contract is to find exactly that.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1161: image: the shipped Dockerfile has no ps, so a routine liveness check reports a healthy build as dead

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving at `f88c59037`. All 9 checks green.

**The test asserts the artifact, not the source.** It builds the image and runs `command -v ps && command -v pgrep` inside it. That was the criterion that mattered here — grepping the Dockerfile for `procps` would pass while the binary was still absent, which is the exact shape of the defect being fixed.

**Mutation-verified:** removing `procps` from the install list fails `test_built_image_provides_process_tools`. It completes in ~18s locally on a warm layer cache, so the build-in-a-unit-test cost I expected does not materialise.

**It runs rather than skips in CI.** The `skipif(shutil.which("docker") is None)` guard is the right shape for local machines without Docker, and ubuntu-latest ships it — confirmed from the pytest (3.12) log: skip count stayed at 19 while passes rose to 8465, so the new test is not among the skipped. Worth stating because "never ran" and "passed" are indistinguishable from a green check.

The fix itself is one package on the existing `apt-get install --no-install-recommends` line — no new layer, nothing else touched, and `scripts/worklink_image_identity.py` correctly left alone. Its `/proc` scan stays host-independent and works where `docker top` does not; adding `procps` does not make it obsolete.

Non-blocking observation: this duplicates a build the `worklink-image-identity` job already performs, so the same assertion could have lived there for free. Placement was not specified in the leaf and the cache makes it cheap, so it is not worth a change request — noting it only in case a future image assertion is added, where that job is the natural home.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1182: github-poller: a PR already reviewed at its current head can be re-emitted by another pass, producing a duplicate review turn

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
This is the right shape. `_emit_pr_review_needed` is a genuine choke point rather than the same guard pasted into three call sites, so a pass added later inherits the suppression instead of having to remember it — which was the acceptance criterion I was least sure would be met.

Two details in it are better than what the leaf asked for:

- **Comment passes resolve the live PR head.** `head_sha or new_head`, falling back to a live `pulls/{number}` lookup, so an old comment cannot make an already-reviewed head actionable. The leaf only asked that comment passes consult the guard; resolving the current head is what makes that correct rather than approximately correct.
- **API failures fail open.** That preserves the #299 recovery deliberately, and it is the difference between fixing this defect and trading it for a worse one.

## Verified

**Both mutations fire, in opposite directions** — this is the pair that matters here:

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| never suppress (reintroduce the defect) | **3 failed** — including `test_current_head_review_suppresses_a_later_poll_from_another_pass` |
| always suppress (over-correct) | **32 failed** across the recovery and trust suites |

The second is the one I care about. Suppressing unconditionally collapses a third of the suite, which demonstrates the #299 recovery is genuinely pinned rather than merely unbroken-by-accident. A fix that stopped duplicate reviews by reintroducing silently-dropped ones would have passed the first mutation and failed nothing.

The test set covers each criterion directly: a **cross-poll** assertion (the within-poll suppression already existed and would have masked the defect), `test_review_on_previous_head_does_not_suppress_updated_pr` for head re-opening, per-pass coverage for the new-PR and review-comment paths, `test_pr_parent_lookup_failure_fails_open`, and `test_synchronize_coalesces_review_request_and_preserves_retry_state` for the retry cursor.

**Routing is complete.** The three remaining raw `_emit` sites are all inbound signals about *our own* PRs — `pr_changes_requested_stale`, the mergeability events, and `pr_review` (someone else's review, carrying `state` and `author`). None can start a review turn on another PR, so none belongs behind the choke point.

95 tests pass in the skill's isolated suite, and CI is 9/9 green.

## One thing I checked and was wrong about

I initially flagged that `testpaths = ["tests"]` means the default `pytest` run collects **zero** of these tests — which would have made them decorative. That is wrong: `tests.yml:184` runs each optional skill's tests in its own isolated pytest process, deliberately, because each ships its own conftest. The workflow even errors when no skill test dirs match, guarding against exactly the silent-skip I was worried about. Recording it because "the tests never ran" and "the tests passed" look identical from a green check, and the next reader may have the same doubt.

No findings.
