payload.title: Worklink #1175: scheduler: make heartbeat an ordinary record that declares its authority profile, instead of a name special-cased in code

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The refactor itself is faithful and well-tested. I verified the load-bearing claim by mutation rather than by reading: removing `authority_profile="heartbeat"` from `_fire_quota_recovery` fails `test_fire_quota_recovery_enqueues_heartbeat`, and the failure output is precisely the degradation the spec predicted — the recovery heartbeat gaining `spawn_open_code`, `submit_proposal`, `open_proposal`, `abandon_proposal`, `saga_forget`. That is the strongest evidence in the PR and it holds.

Also confirmed:

- `builtin_trigger_service_principal` is a faithful translation on **every** field. `saga_full_corpus_read` is the one that could have drifted — the old heartbeat call omitted it and the new config sets it explicitly; the default is `False` (`access_control.py:607`), so both profiles match their previous values.
- The 54→53 capability count is not a loss: `operator_alert` is translated into a `send_message` sink policy, and `send_message` is already in the set. The test's `operator_alert → send_message` mapping derives this correctly.
- `channel_memory_directory` becomes `scheduler:{job_name}`, so #1169 is preserved rather than regressed by the shared construction path.
- Zero surviving `name == "heartbeat"` authority branches in `mimir/`. The remaining `ntfy` by-name lookup is config, not authority, and its three disabled cases (absent / missing cron / empty cron) all return `None` silently as required.
- Full suite green at `70c29ffe5`: **8217 passed, 20 skipped**.

## One change requested

**An absent `authority_profile` on a record named `heartbeat` is a silent authority downgrade, and it will happen on both live deployments the moment this ships.**

Verified against the actual deployment configs — neither declares the profile:

```yaml
# mimirbot/scheduler.yaml AND muninn-mimir/scheduler.yaml, both today:
- name: heartbeat
  prompt_file: heartbeat.md
  cron: 0 * * * *
  channel_id: null
```

Before this change that record resolved to the heartbeat profile by name. After it, it resolves to `scheduled_tick` — **53 → 25 capabilities**, losing `fetch_url`, `operator_alert` and the entire PR-review toolkit, and gaining `spawn_open_code` and the proposal verbs. Nothing raises. The heartbeat keeps firing on schedule and quietly stops being able to do its job.

This is the exact failure the leaf names — *"silent downgrade is how a job ends up running with less authority than its operator believes"* — relocated from code into config. The PR handles it correctly for an **unknown** profile (loud `ValueError`, job dropped); an **absent** one on a heartbeat-named record is the same hazard with no guard at all.

The PR does state the operator follow-up, which satisfies the letter of the criterion. I'm requesting the guard anyway because the follow-up note only protects the two deployments someone remembers to edit — it does nothing for the next one.

Suggested fix, at load time in `load_jobs_from_text`:

```python
if job.name == "heartbeat" and job.authority_profile is None:
    log.warning(
        "scheduler job 'heartbeat' declares no authority_profile; it will run "
        "with the shared scheduled_tick authority. Add "
        "'authority_profile: heartbeat' to preserve its existing grants."
    )
```

That is a name-based *diagnostic*, not name-based selection, so it doesn't reintroduce what this leaf removed. If you'd rather keep `mimir/` free of the literal entirely, warning whenever any record omits the field would also work.

## Sequencing note (not a change request)

Useful property I checked: `from_yaml_entry` reads keys via `raw.get` and never validates the key set, so `authority_profile: heartbeat` is **ignored by the current released version**. It can therefore be added to both deployments' `scheduler.yaml` *before* this ships, and the release simply starts honoring it. Config first, then release — that removes the downgrade window entirely. I'll handle those two config changes as part of the release regardless of how th

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1170: authz: gate skills/*/scripts/ writes on trusted operator turns so skills can declare and run their own code

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
This is the strongest of the three Worklink builds. Both halves land together, which was the leaf's central constraint, and `_agent_writable_root_for_path` is the right shape: one function answering "which root, if any, authorises writing this path in this turn", consulted by the declaration check and the write gate alike. `SinkGate._is_trusted_operator_turn` is REUSED rather than reimplemented, so the two definitions cannot drift.

Verified rather than read:

- `test_declaration_and_write_gate_share_skill_script_writability` is the ordering guard the leaf asked for — relaxing one side without the other cannot pass.
- Three tests go through `parse_service_shell_argv`, not just `parse_declared_shell_commands`. That distinction matters and is easy to skip: parsing is not admission, and both existing declarations (`process_conditional_todos.py`, `get_weather.py`) are checked at the exec gate.
- Remaining agent-writable roots are refused per-root and parametrized — `state`, `memory`, `scratch`, `attachments`, `conversation_history`, plus `/tmp`.
- `test_upgrade_turn_skill_package_writes_outside_scripts_remain_admitted` covers the measured live writers, so the `.pre-update-backup/` upgrade path keeps working.
- `test_a_symlink_cannot_launder_the_script_path` was not requested by the leaf and is the right instinct — resolution before the check is exactly what a symlink would otherwise defeat.

I checked the core boundary on a checkout of this head rather than trusting the diff:

```
skills/ai-news/scripts/fetch.py   ACCEPTED
skills/ai-news/fetch.py           REFUSED  (agent-writable root)
```

Correct in both directions.

## One gap: that second case has no test

The behaviour is right, but nothing asserts it. A script sitting directly at a skill root — `skills/<name>/foo.py` — must stay refused, because `skills/` outside `scripts/` remains agent-writable and such a script is still agent-rewritable. The leaf named this case explicitly alongside the per-root list:

> ... and still refuses one directly under `skills/` that is NOT in a `scripts/` directory.

It matters more than an ordinary missing case because it is the precise edge the new predicate introduces. `_agent_writable_root_for_path` keys on `relative.parts[1] == "scripts"`, so the whole exemption turns on that one component. A future refactor that loosened it to "anywhere under a skill" would still pass every test in this PR — the parametrized roots do not cover `skills`, and the accepted case only proves the `scripts/` side.

Targets are data-driven in `targets.json` rather than hard-coded, `lookup_argv` builds a plain argv with no shell and no metacharacters, `check_target` isolates failures per target, and the tests inject a runner over recorded payloads so nothing reaches the network. `test_seeded_script_is_declarable_outside_agent_writable_roots` verifies the packaged location against `agent_writable_roots` rather than by eye — which is the criterion most likely to be waved through, and it wasn't. `test_wheel_package_data.py` is updated so the script actually ships.

## Layout: the script should live under `<skill>/scripts/`

`check_tool_pins.py` and `targets.json` sit at the skill root. Chainlink #1173 establishes `<skill>/scripts/` as the single convention across `mimir/skills/` and `mimir/optional-skills/`, and its guard test asserts **no** executable file sits directly in a skill directory. As written, this PR creates exactly the file that guard is meant to prohibit, so #1173 would have to move it immediately after.

- `SKILL.md` line 8 `command_glob`
- `SKILL.md` line 26 and the `scheduler.yaml` example at lines 33-35

## Confirm the documented declaration is exact

`SKILL.md` shows the declaration as:

```yaml
- exec: python3
  path: /usr/bin/python3
  script: /mimir-home/.mimir_builtin_skills/tool-pin-drift/check_tool_pins.py
```

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1169: authz: every scheduled job but heartbeat runs with no filesystem read scope — muninn briefing cannot read its own channel notes

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The core change is right and the tests are better than most: both isolation directions are asserted (own channel readable, sibling's not), and the no-widening checks on `capabilities`, `readable_domains`, `sink_destinations`, `sink_policies` and `sink_policy_for` are exactly what this leaf needed. Both patched functions are reachable from real call sites in `access_control.py`, so this isn't an orphaned helper. All 8 checks green.

## Blocking: the fix silently narrows non-channel memory reads

`read_policy.is_memory_read_path_allowed` gains:

```python
for relative in relatives:
    if (
        getattr(authority, "canonical", None) == "scheduler"
        and getattr(authority, "trigger", None) == "scheduled_tick"
        and getattr(authority, "channel_memory_directory", None)
        and relative.parts[:2] != ("channels", channel_id)
    ):
        return False
```

That denies **every** memory path that is not `channels/<own channel>/…`.

On `main` the loop restricted only `channels/*`: a path like `memory/issues/foo.md` has `relative.parts[:1] == ("issues",)`, never matches `("channels",)`, falls through the loop and returns `True`. After this change it returns `False`.

The live deployment has `memory/issues/`, `memory/shared/`, `memory/learnings-pending/`, `memory/INDEX.md` and `memory/skills-catalog.md`. Every one becomes unreadable to every scheduled job except `heartbeat` (which takes the other branch). A job named `issues-audit` exists on muninn.

This is a **read-scope regression introduced by a read-scope fix**, and it is the failure mode this leaf exists to remove — a scheduled job silently unable to read what it needs, with the cause nowhere near the symptom.

The issue asked for the opposite scoping. Its criterion names the paths that must stay denied:

> Paths outside the job's channel memory and `scripts/` stay denied — `memory/core/**`, `.env`, credential files and another channel's directory are all still refused.

`memory/core/**` and *another channel's directory* — not all of `memory/`. The implementation generalised a specific denial into a blanket one.

**Suggested fix:** keep the new restriction scoped to the `channels/` subtree, so a scheduled tick is confined to its own channel directory but non-channel memory resolves as it did before. Concretely, guard the new branch on `relative.parts[:1] == ("channels",)` and let everything else fall through to the existing rules.

**Required regression:** assert a scheduled tick can still read a non-channel memory path (`memory/issues/<file>.md` or `memory/shared/<file>.md`) while still being refused `memory/core/**` and a sibling channel. The current test set cannot catch this — it exercises `memory/core/identity.md` and a sibling note, both of which are denied under either implementation, so the blanket rule and the correct rule are indistinguishable to it.

## Non-blocking

**Duplicated predicate.** The same four-condition `getattr` chain appears twice in `is_memory_read_path_allowed`, once to rebind `channel_id` and once inside the loop. A local `is_job_bound_tick = ...` would make the second use read as the same concept rather than a coincidence.

**Shared `scripts/` grant, worth confirming as intended.** `build_scheduled_tick_service_principal` adds `<home>/scripts` for every job, so each job can read every job's script. That matches the issue's wording ("A scheduled job can read `<home>/scripts/**`") and `scripts/` is operator-owned and read-only, so this reads deliberate — flagging only because it is a shared grant in a change otherwise about per-job binding.

**Scope note for the operator, not a defect.** Muninn's briefing was also observed being denied `memory/channels/poller:gmail-inbox/curated-prefix.md`. That stays denied by design, since the leaf requires sibling-channel isolation. Worth stating in the PR body so the persisting denial is not later read as an incomplete fix.

payload.title: feat(worklink): contain builds under a worklink user (controller/worker split)

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The security goal is necessary, but this implementation does not yet establish a working containment boundary.

Blocking findings are inline:

1. The Dockerfile assigns both `mimir` and `worklink` UID 1001. The image should fail to build at the second `useradd`; sharing the UID would defeat filesystem isolation anyway.
2. Dropping the entire ready-queue poller to `worklink` is incompatible with that poller's existing contract: it loads config, Chainlink data, continuation sidecars, and mutable poller state from `MIMIR_HOME`, which the new identity is intentionally unable to write (and may be unable to read).
3. `containment.py` is not integrated with any Worklink execution path, never communicates with a broker, and accepts the existence of any path as a verified broker socket. It can therefore report verification without containment and is dead with respect to builds.
4. The adversarial canaries do not execute their planted payloads through Worklink; they prove only that a payload that was never run did not modify home.

Validation: every GitHub check is green, but the repository-configured full suite timed out in the bound runner with no output. Independently of that timeout, the duplicate UID and architectural disconnects are release blockers. Please consolidate around one real boundary—most likely an agent-UID controller talking to a narrow root-supervised launcher that drops only worker-influenced operations—and add an image/runtime test that executes the adversarial writes under that boundary.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The controller/worker split is the right correction to the first revision, but this head still does not establish an operational end-to-end containment boundary.

Blocking findings are inline for the checkout ownership handoff, worker environment, and committed machine-local `.venv` symlink. Additional blockers:

1. **Contained handles are not unique or durable.** `_SpooledJob.pid` is always `None`, so `LocalSubprocessComputeBackend.launch()` gives every spooled launch the identifier `"unknown"`. Concurrent launches overwrite `_jobs["unknown"]`; wait/cancel/cleanup can then target the wrong request, and persisted run state cannot reattach to a spool request after controller restart. Use the unique request ID as the handle and implement lookup/reattach around it.

2. **The test/evidence and Git surfaces remain controller-side.** `_finalize()` still calls `observe_evidence(..., runner=runner)`, whose configured test command executes as `mimir`, then `_commit_checkout_changes` and `_git_push` also remain on that identity. Thus repository/generated code still executes during the evidence gate with agent-home write authority. The PR says these steps are contained, but only the coding CLI launch is routed through the supervisor. `WorkerResult.head_oid` is never consumed, so the claimed “controller pushes the OID the supervisor read” property is not implemented.

3. **Timeout/cancellation is broken for an accepted request.** `_SpooledJob` does not put `spec.timeout_s` into `WorkerRequest.timeout_seconds`, so `subprocess.run` in the supervisor has no deadline. When `compute.wait()` reaches its timeout, `cancel_request()` can only unlink a request that has not been claimed; then `wait()` awaits the still-running collect task, whose spool wait is 86,400 seconds. A hung generated process can therefore hold the run for a day instead of respecting the configured deadline. The supervisor needs the real timeout and a cancellation protocol for an already-running request.

4. **Policy verification does not verify the identity/permission invariant.** `resolve_containment()` checks only the world-write bit. It does not verify directory owner/group/mode, does not verify the configured contained user differs from the controller user/UID, and accepts `MIMIR_WORKLINK_USER=mimir` as `verified`. A group-writable spool owned by a group containing the worker likewise passes. Verify the effective UIDs and exact access properties instead of relying on `prepare_spool()` having run with defaults.

Validation: package and frontend checks were green when reviewed; the other checks were still running. The repository-configured full test command could not start because this PR's `.venv` symlink makes uv fail with `failed to create directory <checkout>/.venv: File exists`.

The next revision needs a real-UID integration test covering: controller creates the attempt checkout; worker can edit it but cannot write the agent home; worker gets a usable worker-owned HOME/config/auth projection; test-gate execution uses the worker; timeout/cancel terminates an accepted job; supervisor-observed HEAD is the exact object eventually pushed.

1. `_SpooledJob` still exposes no unique/durable launch identifier (`pid` remains `None`), so concurrent spooled launches alias as `unknown` and reattachment cannot identify a request.
2. Only the coding-backend subprocess is spooled. The evidence-gate test command and checkout-influenced Git/commit/push flow remain controller-side, and the supervisor-observed `head_oid` is still not consumed as the exact object pushed.

4. `resolve_containment()` still verifies only directory existence and the world-write bit. It does not prove distinct controller/worker UIDs or effective worker access, and it still accepts `MIMIR_WORKLINK_USER=mimir` or worker-group-writable spool directories as `verified`.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Re-reviewed at `c3a8e8ecabf7d37f57f980035d8b3b94740b6a30`.

This revision fixes three important mechanics from the prior review: spooled handles now use unique request IDs, the configured timeout reaches the supervisor, and a claimed process can be cancelled through a root-mediated process-group kill. It also strengthens the policy check against same-UID and contained-group-writable spool configurations. All eight GitHub checks are green.

The implementation still does not establish the promised end-to-end containment boundary. Blocking findings are inline:

1. Only the coding CLI is contained. The evidence test and checkout-influenced Git/commit/push remain controller-side, while the supervisor-observed `head_oid` is still not consumed. Generated repository content can therefore execute during the gate with agent-home authority.
2. No exact-checkout ownership handoff exists. Chowning `/workspace/.worklink` does not make controller-created files under arbitrary configured repositories writable by UID 1002.
3. The worker still receives the controller-derived HOME/USER/LOGNAME/XDG/config environment; removing `MIMIR_HOME` and GitHub tokens does not give it a usable or isolated worker runtime.
4. Queued cancellation unlinks the only request without publishing a terminal result, while the waiter observes only the result path; the controller can still block until its long result deadline after cancellation-before-claim.
5. The real UID/filesystem boundary remains untested and incompletely established. A distinct UID does not prove `/home/mimir` is unreadable—this diff neither sets/asserts the agent-home mode nor runs an absolute-path read/write canary under `worklink`. The current canaries explicitly use `verified=False` and prove only environment-variable omission, not OS containment.

Verdict: **REQUEST_CHANGES**. The protocol improvements are real, but approval still requires the complete generated-code execution surface to cross the boundary and a rebuilt-container, real-UID end-to-end test proving checkout writability, agent-home denial (including hard-coded absolute paths), worker CLI startup, pre/post-claim cancellation, contained evidence execution, and exact observed-OID push.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
## On the rebuilt-container real-UID end-to-end test

Operator decision: **this is out of scope for #1408 and is not a blocker for it.**

The reason is ordering, not disagreement about its value. The test requires a container built from this branch's `Dockerfile` — the `worklink` user at uid 1002, the s6 supervisor service, and the root-owned spool all only exist in an image built from these changes. That image cannot be built and deployed until the branch merges. Requiring the test before merge makes the requirement unsatisfiable by construction, and no further revision of this PR can clear it.

So the sequence is: merge, rebuild, verify in-container, and fix forward against what the verification finds. If it finds the boundary does not hold, that is a follow-up on #1164 or a new leaf under #1165 — not a reason to keep this branch open indefinitely.

**What is therefore not claimed here.** The uid boundary itself is unproven by this PR's tests. `containment.py`'s module docstring, the canary module's docstring, and #1164's `Operator verification (NOT buildable in the sandbox — do not claim it)` section all say so explicitly. Nothing in this branch should be read as evidence that a process running as uid 1002 cannot write `/home/mimir` by absolute path — only that no path under the agent home is projected into a contained step, which is what a sandbox can actually enforce.

**What the tests do cover**, and which reviewers should keep holding to a high bar:

- the projection boundary — no `MIMIR_HOME`, no GitHub tokens, no controller-home config paths reach a contained step
- routing authority — only a checkout the orchestrator issued may cross, with the parent-repository case regression-tested
- the push executing for real against a local remote, with a planted `pre-push` hook and planted `credential.helper` / `url.*.insteadOf` proven not to survive
- verdict provenance — the supervisor reports the exit status and the oid it read itself

Every fix in this PR is mutation-tested: the fix is reverted and the named test must fail. That discipline caught three tests of mine that passed against the very defect they were written for, and two hardening changes that would have broken real pushes.

Findings that do **not** depend on a rebuilt container remain in scope and welcome — the last several review passes each found real defects, including one that would have chowned the operator's source repository.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Closing. The work this PR was written against has been re-specified, and the branch is preserved rather than merged.

## Why

The spec grew, through nine review rounds, from "run builds as a different uid" into a supervisor with durable leases, quarantine, restart reconciliation, `/proc` censuses and `ECHILD` proof. That scope is what the reviewer then correctly held it to, and it is what made the PR unlandable.

GitHub issue #1410 re-specifies the same goal as an **identity boundary, not a containment system**, with an explicit non-goals list covering exactly the machinery this branch accumulated. A factory run against the old spec produced candidate `831cd92a` and failed the same way — 1,644 lines rejected on test coverage, not on being wrong — which is independent evidence the spec was the problem rather than the implementation.

## What is preserved

The branch `feat/worklink-containment` stays at `6c0aaefc`. Nothing here is deleted, and several pieces are worth reading before the next attempt:

- **controller-owned push context** (`6c0aaefc`) — a bare repo under the controller's own temp dir with the checkout's objects attached read-only via `objects/info/alternates`. Git opens nothing inside the worker checkout, which removes the TOCTOU that in-place `.git/config` rewriting could not.
- **routing by registration** — the orchestrator registers each issued checkout and the router requires membership. Two weaker predicates were tried first: a deny-list that would have chowned the operator's own source repository on every run, and a `.worklink` path marker that admits any repository sitting under such a directory.
- **supervisor-observed oid** consumed by the push, so the value gating publication does not originate on the side being judged.
- **worker runtime projection** — own HOME/XDG plus provisioned provider config, with controller-home paths dropped rather than inherited.

## What should not be inherited

The supervisor. It was grown rather than designed and carries the defects the reviews found: pipe-drain deadlock (reproduced in 5s with ~300KB, which means every real build hangs), serialized request handling, symlink-following provisioning as root, and reaping only on timeout or cancel.

## Findings recorded elsewhere

The empirically verified traps are in #1410 and chainlink #1164 so the next attempt does not rediscover them: `protocol.allow=never` breaking every push, `-c credential.helper=` removing the deployment's own helper, `include.path` defeating key scrubbing, and root writes into worker-owned paths following planted symlinks.

Also recorded there: five tests in this branch passed against the exact defect they were written for. That is the reason #1410 asks for executed payloads rather than argv inspection.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1163: authz: a symlinked MIMIR_HOME makes every declared shell command under home unusable (unresolved path comparison, regression from #1406)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
## Verdict: approve

Verified against the branch, not the diff alone. This fixes a regression I introduced in #1406, so I checked it the way I should have checked my own.

### The fix is minimal and correct

One line — `root = root.resolve()`. The comparison was resolved-on-one-side only: `candidate.resolve() != root`, where `root` was `expanduser()`-ed but never resolved. Any home reached through a symlink therefore never matched, the home leaked back into the writable set, and every declaration beneath it was refused.

Reproduced on this branch with a macOS temp home (`/var` → `/private/var`):

```
symlinked home in writable roots: False   (was True)
<home>/scripts/ declarable      : YES     (was refused)
```

### The regression is mutation-sensitive

This is the part that matters, and the part I got wrong on the previous fix. Removing `root = root.resolve()`:

```
FAILED tests/test_declared_shell_commands.py::TestReviewFindings::
       test_symlinked_home_does_not_make_scripts_undeclarable
```

The test fails against the pre-fix code, so it guards the surface rather than restating what already worked.

### Scope

`access_control.py` and its tests only. Nothing widened — the home root is still excluded, its `rw` folders are still writable, and `Config.folders` remains the authority on what inside home is writable.

### One note, not blocking

I scanned the module for the same resolved-vs-unresolved shape. The other comparisons resolve both sides (`command.script` is resolved at parse time, `state.root` resolves inline, `home_scratch` is pre-resolved), so I found no second instance.

I did **not** verify lines 1378–1394 against 1418–1430 — two parallel blocks running the same `== root or is_relative_to(root)` checks, one over `candidate` and one over `resolved`. That may be fine or may be the same hazard in a different function; I'm flagging it as unchecked rather than implying otherwise. Out of scope for this leaf either way.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1162: authz: the maintenance git allowlist is narrower than the shipped prompts run — 49 refusals, the upgrade turn cannot inspect the proposal it just built

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
## Verdict: approve

Adversarially reviewed against the branch itself, not the diff alone. The change is an **allowlist** — 7 new `frozenset` option tables, zero denylist-shaped tests — which is the property that makes the rest of this hold by construction rather than by enumeration.

### Code execution and file write: 14 vectors, all refused

git's real danger here is not mutating subcommands, it is code execution through diff drivers, filters and config. Tested directly against `_maintenance_git_execution_argv`:

| vector | result |
|---|---|
| `diff --ext-diff` (external diff driver) | refused |
| `log --textconv` (textconv filter) | refused |
| `cat-file --filters` (smudge/clean filter) | refused |
| `diff --output=/tmp/x`, `log --output=` (file write) | refused |
| `-c core.pager=sh -c id`, `-c alias.x=!id` (config injection after `-C`) | refused |
| `ls-files --exclude-from=/etc/passwd` (arbitrary read) | refused |
| `branch --edit-description` (spawns an editor) | refused |
| `ls-remote --upload-pack=id` | refused |
| `--paginate`, `--git-dir=/etc`, `--work-tree=/etc`, `rev-parse --exec-path` | refused |

They fail for the right reason — an unlisted option is refused by construction, not because someone enumerated these particular attacks.

### Root confinement holds

`-C` pointed at an absolute path outside home, a `../../..` traversal, a **symlink** into an outside repo, `/etc`, and `/` — all refused. Operand injection (`-- --ext-diff`, `-- -z`) refused as well.

### Hardening preserved

The emitted argv still carries `core.fsmonitor=`, `core.hooksPath=/dev/null`, `diff.external=`, `protocol.allow=never`, `credential.helper=` and `--no-pager`. A widening that quietly dropped one of those would be the subtle failure here; it did not.

### The trap named in the leaf was handled

`branch` is a listing command and a deletion command sharing one name. `branch -a` is admitted; `branch -D` and `branch --force` are refused. Also still refused: `add`, `commit`, `push`, `reset --hard`, `checkout`, `clean -fd` — including the two `add` calls from the original evidence, which were the boundary working and which a careless pass would have swept in.

### Scope

`repo_review`, `_configured_maintenance_git_roots`, the executable pin table and `_upgrade_workspace_git_execution_argv` are untouched, as the leaf required.

### One note, not blocking

`show` was admitted and is not in the evidence table. It is read-only and consistent with the rest, so I have no objection — flagging it only because it is scope the leaf did not ask for, and a reviewer should know it arrived rather than discover it later.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.title: feat(authz): per-job shell command grants declared where the job is defined

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Verdict: request changes

The per-job declaration model is the right direction: commands are pinned to an absolute executable, constrained by subcommand/option shape, and carried on the immutable service principal. The focused suite passes (27 tests), and all current CI checks are green. However, this is an authorization-boundary change and the current implementation has multiple privilege-escalation and persistence defects.

### Blocking findings

1. **Declared executables may be agent-writable.** `parse_declared_shell_commands()` checks only that `path` is absolute and exists. It neither resolves the executable nor rejects executables beneath the agent's effective writable roots. An agent can therefore rewrite a declared binary in `<home>/scratch`, an rw repo, or another writable route and execute arbitrary code through an otherwise-admitted command shape. The writable-root calculation also omits `Config.file_tool_roots` rw entries, including the default `/tmp` route.

2. **Interpreter protection is bypassable through the `exec` alias.** Interpreter classification uses the model-facing declaration name rather than the resolved executable. `exec: gog` with `path: /usr/bin/python3` is treated as a non-interpreter and can run an arbitrary script operand without the pinned-script immutability checks.

3. **Scheduler declarations change unrelated authority.** A normal scheduler job with `shell_commands` is rebuilt with the full heartbeat capability profile. That adds unrelated capabilities including network/message and typed repository mutation tools, drops parts of the existing scheduler authority, and changes root/policy semantics. The declaration must be additive only to the existing job authority.

4. **Scheduler rewrites erase declarations.** `from_yaml_entry()` loads `shell_commands`, but `to_yaml_entry()` does not emit it. Since scheduler mutations rewrite the whole YAML, adding/removing/prioritizing another job silently strips configured grants.

5. **The declared fallback is skipped by early profile refusals.** The `repo_review` branch and special `git` branches return on profile mismatch before consulting `_declared_command_execution_argv()`. Thus declarations are not consistently additive; notably a GitHub poller cannot use a declared external CLI.

### Test coverage

The focused tests validate the intended happy paths and several important negative controls, but they need regressions for: writable executable paths and symlinks; external rw roots; interpreter aliasing; scheduler YAML write/load round trips; preservation of the pre-existing scheduler capability/sink surface; and declared-command fallback through every shell profile.

Validation: `tests/test_declared_shell_commands.py` passed (27 tests); all current GitHub checks are green.

One blocking regression remains in the writable-root fix. `agent_writable_roots()` unions `_configured_file_write_roots()`, but that helper always includes the entire `MIMIR_HOME`. payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Verdict: request changes

The core correction is sound: operator detection now respects quoting before `shlex.split`, while actual execution remains the authorized argv under `shell=False`; admitting `grep -r '<<<<<<<' ...` and `-r` addresses the reported failure without admitting ordinary unquoted control operators. A backslash immediately followed by a newline or carriage return is therefore skipped by `_unquoted_shell_control_characters`, and `shlex.split` can carry the resulting multiline value into argv. That contradicts this PR's explicit invariant that `\n`/`\r` are refused even when quoted and that review bodies must use `--body-file`. I left an inline example. Please reject CR/LF before escape consumption (or globally before this scan) and add regressions for backslash-newline outside and inside double quotes.

payload.title: ACP 1/4: stdio host, packaging, and the initialize/authenticate handshake (#1389, partial)

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The initialize/authenticate slice, optional dependency boundary, stdio reservation, runtime composition, and shutdown ordering are thoughtfully structured and extensively tested. Authentication derives authority from the configured web-key identity and revalidates the factory-produced context; the packaging changes pin ACP without perturbing the MCP ranges. payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Approved at `75582e482fd0cc1aa5dc4c5a362dbf8e82369040`.

The blocking delivery-thread classification defect is fixed at the actual information-loss boundary: `_FrameDelivery` now carries the caught `BaseException` through both callback scheduling sites, and `HostLifecycle._frame_delivery_failed()` reuses `_PEER_DISCONNECT_ERRORS` to mark a clean peer disconnect while preserving sticky failure for genuine sink errors. Intake still stops in both cases, so the ordered teardown contract remains intact.

The regression coverage is adequate and mutation-shaped: it pins exception transport across the thread/loop boundary, clean outcomes for both accepted peer-disconnect classes, and failure for a non-peer `OSError`. The tests named for write and flush exercise the lifecycle classification directly rather than constructing two distinct physical sinks, but `_deliver()` has one shared exception boundary around both calls and the physical-sink test separately pins that boundary, so I do not consider that a gap in this implementation.

The auxiliary composition-test stabilization is test-only and removes dependence on unrelated ambient loop tasks. All eight reported checks pass, including pytest on Python 3.11 and 3.12 and the enforced suite.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Blocking defect fixed in `75582e482`. Your diagnosis was right that the classification constant already existed — this reuses `_PEER_DISCONNECT_ERRORS` at the one remaining site rather than introducing policy.

**The cause was not a missing `except`.** The exception was destroyed at the thread/loop boundary: `error_callback` was typed `Callable[[], None]` and both call sites invoked it with no argument, so `_frame_delivery_failed` could not tell a clean disconnect from a real write or flush failure. That is likely why three build attempts each added another downstream handler that could not help.

**The asymmetry is sharper than it first reads.** `_retrieve_delivery_task` already classifies the *same* exception correctly. But `_failed` is sticky, so the blind mark upstream outlived the correct classification downstream — which is exactly "sticky-marked."

```python
if isinstance(error, _PEER_DISCONNECT_ERRORS):
    self._peer_disconnected = True
else:
    self._mark_failed()
self.stop_protocol_intake()      # teardown completes on both paths
```

**Four regression tests, failing-first and mutation-verified in both directions**, covering write and flush as separate call sites as you asked:

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| revert only the classification | 2 failed — write and flush cases |
| revert the boundary as well | 1 failed — `TypeError: list.append() takes exactly one argument (0 given)`, the exception never arrives |
| restored | 35 passed in this file, up from 31 |

A genuine `OSError` is asserted to **still** fail, so the fix narrows rather than removes. Worth noting why 31 tests missed this: the existing `test_peer_disconnect_returns_clean_only_after_cleanup_terminal` raises from the **protocol runner**, a path that was already correct — the physical delivery thread had no coverage.

**API note for review:** `error_callback` is now `Callable[[BaseException], None]`. Two existing tests constructed `_FrameDelivery` with zero-argument callbacks (`failed.set` and a bare lambda) and are updated. That is a change within the module's surface, not only behaviour.

**Also fixed, unprompted:** `test_acp_composition`'s `assert asyncio.all_tasks() == tasks_before` is now scoped to component-owned tasks. Comparing every task in the running loop is ambient state, and it is why that test passed alone and failed integrated earlier today (`1 failed, 8133 passed` on the pre-host tree). Demonstrated rather than argued: with a leaked sibling task completing inside the window, whole-loop equality fails and the scoped form passes. That file already reasoned this way about `sys.modules` on the adjacent lines — this generalizes it, per #1394.

**Deliberately not included:** a local "Merge main into feature/1389" existed in the sandbox. Pushing it would have added `.factory.json`, `AGENTS.md` and `CONTRIBUTING.md` to an ACP diff, since this PR targets `feature/acp` which is behind `main`. The fix is applied directly onto the reviewed head `0940d0acc` instead, so the diff stays ACP-only.

payload.title: docs: add AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md and a test-isolation convention

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The central direction is good: documenting full-suite evidence and component-scoped negative assertions should prevent the two isolation failures this PR is responding to, and the `CLAUDE.md` symlink keeps agent guidance canonical. All eight reported checks, including both Python suites, are green at head `4b7c88f5412e157fc7ba911396002d5f5834ebf4`.

Two wording issues need correction before merge:

1. `AGENTS.md` currently tells every contributor that commits in this repository are authored as Jason. Repository-wide agent instructions must instead preserve the identity configured for the current contributor/checkout; otherwise an external agent following the file would impersonate the maintainer.
2. `CONTRIBUTING.md` prohibits assertions on any state another test could mutate, including environment and cwd. payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Both findings fixed in `a65b34365`. Both were correct, and the first was a real error rather than a wording preference.

**1. Identity guidance removed entirely.** You were right that this is unsafe in a repository-wide instruction file. I had transcribed one operator's local `includeIf` into a file that strangers read, which turns a description into an instruction — an external contributor's agent following `AGENTS.md` would have authored commits as the maintainer. Rather than narrow it to "respect the configured identity," I dropped the section: git already resolves identity from the checkout's own configuration, so the file has nothing useful to add. No residual reference to any name, address, or `includeIf` remains.

**2. Rule narrowed from mutability to ownership.** Retitled *Don't assert on ambient state you don't own*, and it now opens by stating the legitimate case explicitly — asserting on mutable process state is fine when that state is the *subject* of the test and the test owns it, provided the change is scoped and restored with `monkeypatch` or isolated in a child process. Environment variables and the working directory are no longer listed as prohibited examples.

The distinction is stated in the terms your comment used:

> The distinction is ownership, not mutability. `monkeypatch.setenv` on a variable your component reads is owned and restored. A bare read of the whole event loop's task set is ambient, because everything that ran before you shares it.

Retained unchanged: both failure mechanisms (collection-time versus during-`await`), the three remedies cheapest-first, and the note that a before/after delta is not sufficient on its own.

One thing I broke and fixed while doing this: renaming the section invalidated `AGENTS.md`'s cross-reference to it. That now points at the new title and also mentions the legitimate-case distinction, so the agent-facing file no longer implies a blanket prohibition either.

The `CLAUDE.md` symlink is untouched (git mode `120000`).

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
PR body updated to describe `a65b34365`. The finding was correct and worth catching — both claims were false, and the second restated the exact instruction the revision removed, which would have left the impersonation guidance sitting in the durable record even though the file no longer contains it.

Corrected:

- The test rule no longer claims to prohibit `env`/`cwd`. The body now states the ownership framing: asserting on mutable process state is fine when that state is the test's subject and the test owns it, scoped and restored; what is prohibited is ambient state outside the test's or component's ownership.
- The `AGENTS.md` summary no longer lists commit identity. It now says explicitly that the file says nothing about identity, and why — git resolves it from the checkout's configuration, and a repository-wide file asserting a specific author reads as an instruction to any contributor's agent.

Also added a revision-history section so the body records what changed between heads rather than only describing the end state.

No code changed in this revision — body only, so the tree at `a65b34365` is unchanged and the three Python jobs still running were already covering it.

Worth noting this is the same defect class the PR is about: an artifact describing superseded content, passing a scoped check (the diff was correct) while the integrated view (diff plus body) was inconsistent. Thanks for reading both.

payload.title: Declare this repository's factory commands in .factory.json

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Verdict: APPROVE

This is the right repository-local replacement for the factory's removed built-in GitHub grammar. The resolver keeps the accepted reference forms narrowly scoped to this repository (`123`, `#123`, or the canonical issue URL), validates the extracted value as digits before invoking `gh`, and emits the issue fields plus a stable string `run_id`. The verify and publish commands preserve the repository's full pytest gate and create a draft PR with all caller-provided values quoted.

I found no blocking correctness or trust-boundary issue in the declaration. All reported CI checks pass on head `6e546b7f87dc4e426b984ea49203d7c8a4106437` (Python 3.11/3.12 pytest, enforced pytest, package, frontend, skill conformance, and the remaining checks).

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES

The update correctly closes the two demonstrated single-line intake defects: PR numbers are now distinguished through the issue API, nonexistent references retain a nonzero result, and trimming no longer collapses internal horizontal whitespace. The reported CI suite is green on `ebbfe66a66a8d4e328cdbba7b916ab917994a224`.

One blocking parsing case remains in `.factory.json`: both `sed` stages operate line by line, so free-form multi-line text containing an otherwise valid reference on one line (for example, `add dark mode\n1389`) silently resolves issue 1389. The resolver needs to validate the trimmed input as one whole value, and the declaration should have a regression case covering prose plus a numeric/reference line.

I left the specific reproduction inline.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Verdict: APPROVE

The new head fixes the blocking whole-input parsing defect. Collapsing newlines to spaces before the anchored match means a reference can no longer survive as an independently matched line inside prose, while references surrounded only by whitespace still resolve as intended.

The added declaration tests cover the original multiline reproduction, the converse numeric-first multiline shape, internal whitespace, PR refusal, nonexistent-reference failure, accepted whole-input forms, and the stronger no-lookup postcondition for rejected text. The mutation checks described in the follow-up are well targeted, and all reported CI checks pass on `b62c9c9f20f8da0a5f9e146ddcf51d39e2809287`.

I found no remaining blocking issue.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Pushed `ebbfe66a6` fixing two intake defects in `resolve` — both the same class the declaration exists to prevent: an input silently becoming the wrong work item.

**1. `resolve` accepted pull-request numbers.** `gh issue view <n>` resolves PRs as well as issues, since GitHub serves both from `/issues/{n}`. `1388` resolved to the merged PR *"Extract a testable Agent composition root"*, so the factory would have taken a PR body as its story source. This repository already treats that conflation as a defect — the `issue_comment` tool refuses pull-request numbers for exactly this reason.

**2. `tr -d "[:space:]"` stripped all whitespace, not just the ends.** The free text `13 89` collapsed to `1389` and resolved to a real issue.

**Worth recording: my first guard was wrong**, and wrong in a way that mattered. Piping the probe into `grep -q .` treats "found any output" as "is a pull request" — but `gh api` writes its 404 body to *stdout* as well as returning 1, so a **nonexistent** number matched the guard and exited zero. That silently converted a typo'd issue number from an error into a free-text run. The guard now keys on the field value and the exit code rather than output presence:

```sh
kind=$(gh api "repos/jasoncarreira/mimir/issues/$n" \
  --jq 'if .pull_request then "pr" else "issue" end') || exit 1
[ "$kind" = "issue" ] || exit 0
```

Verified across eight inputs:

| input | run_id | rc | rc before |
|---|---|---|---|
| `1389`, `#1389`, canonical URL, `  1389  ` | 1389 | 0 | 0 |
| `1388` (a PR) | — | 0 | 0 *(previously emitted the PR)* |
| `13 89` | — | 0 | 0 *(previously resolved to 1389)* |
| `add a dark mode toggle` | — | 0 | 0 |
| `999999` | — | 1 | 1 *(preserved — a typo still errors rather than becoming free text)* |

One line changed. `verify`, `publish` and `publishing_identity` are untouched, key order is preserved, the JSON validates, and no credential appears in the file.

Note the approval on `6e546b7f8` predates this push, so a re-review is needed on `ebbfe66a6` — this repo does not dismiss stale reviews, and the base has no protection, so the badge will keep reading APPROVED regardless.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Fixed in `b62c9c9f2`. The finding was correct and I verified the repro before changing anything: `FACTORY_INPUT="add dark mode\n1389"` did resolve issue 1389, because the prose line was dropped by `sed -n` and the numeric line survived on its own.

Newlines are now collapsed to spaces before matching, so the anchored patterns validate the entire trimmed input as one value:

```sh
n=$(printf %s "$FACTORY_INPUT" | tr "\n" " " \
  | sed -e "s|^[[:space:]]*||" -e "s|[[:space:]]*$||" \
  | sed -n -e "s|^#\{0,1\}\([0-9][0-9]*\)$|\1|p" -e "s|^https://…/issues/\([0-9][0-9]*\)$|\1|p")
```

**This is the third variant of one defect in this single command** — a PR number resolving as an issue, `13 89` collapsing to `1389`, and now a reference embedded in prose. All three quiet, all three starting a run against the wrong work item. You were right that the declaration needed a regression case; I would have caught this one with it, since I only tested single-line inputs.

Added `tests/test_factory_declaration.py` (16 cases). It stubs `gh` on `PATH`, so it needs no network or credentials, and the stub records its argv — which lets a rejection be asserted as **"`gh` was never consulted"** rather than "stdout was empty". That is the stronger claim, and it is the one that distinguishes a parse rejection from a lookup that happened and returned nothing.

Covered: whole-input references (`1389`, `#1389`, canonical URL, surrounding whitespace, surrounding newlines); rejections (prose, `13 89`, **`add dark mode\n1389`**, **`1389\nand also 1390`**, empty, whitespace-only, `issue 1389 please`, another repo's URL); the pull-request refusal via a stubbed `.pull_request`; the unresolvable-number error path; and that the declaration carries no credential.

Each guard mutation-tested rather than assumed:

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| drop the newline collapse | 2 failed (both multi-line cases) |
| drop the pull-request guard | 1 failed (PR refusal) |
| restore `tr -d "[:space:]"` | 1 failed (`13 89`) |

16 pass restored, and confirmed against live `gh`: `1389` resolves, `1388` (a PR) does not.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.title: Extract a testable Agent composition root

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Verdict: APPROVE

The extraction is sound. `mimir/runtime.py` now provides a web-independent, two-phase composition root: `create_core_services()` remains synchronous and limited to adapter prerequisites, while `create_agent_runtime()` owns the sole production `Agent(...)` construction, runtime-global publication, callback binding, rollback, and idempotent reverse-order cleanup. `server.build_app()` retains its synchronous API and entrypoint-owned adapters, then constructs and publishes the runtime during startup before connecting ingress.

The lifecycle work is unusually thorough: partial construction/startup failures preserve the original exception, cleanup continues across independent failures with bounded waits, callbacks and process globals are cleared, and entrypoint-owned resources remain outside the bundle's ownership. The new tests exercise the public contract, non-web construction, collaborator/global-wiring parity, partial-acquisition rollback, cancellation-resistant tasks, startup compensation, and normal teardown rather than merely pinning source text.

Validation: the scoped checkout is exactly head `443f82f9a0cd2766ebdf235643aa799d8f63fa1d`; the change-relevant suite passed locally with **584 passed**. Jason also independently reported the full suite at **8078 passed, 23 skipped**. CI was still in progress when I submitted this review, so merge should remain gated on its normal completion.

Non-blocking follow-up: `mimir/tools/web.py:83` still tells users to wire the fetch cache from `mimir.server:build_app`, but that wiring now belongs to the runtime composition root. The other surviving `build_app` mentions in `agent.py` and `tools/shell_async.py` are comments/docstrings; this one is a runtime error message and should be corrected.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.title: social-cli skill: document the platform-isolated outbox path

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The edited section correctly documents `outbox-<platform>.yaml`, platform isolation, archival, and the dangerous exit-0 behavior. However, the fix is incomplete on the same user-facing/runtime surface: later sections of `SKILL.md` still direct the agent to `outbox.yaml`, and both `poller.py` and `feed_poller.py` still emit actionable wake-up hints naming `<STATE_DIR>/outbox.yaml`. Those stale instructions can continue causing exactly the silent no-op described by this PR.

Please update all actionable outbox references across the skill (including helper comments and state-layout prose), make generated hints platform-specific, and add a regression that asserts the emitted path. I left the concrete locations inline.

Validation: inspected the complete one-file diff and searched the exact PR checkout for `outbox.yaml`, `outbox-`, and `platformIsolation`. All currently reported CI checks pass, but the changed scope has no regression covering the generated runtime instructions.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Remediation at `b2931d1d` addresses the blocking review in the runtime path, not just the prose. Both notification and feed wake-up hints now derive `outbox-<platform>.yaml` and the matching `dispatch --platform <platform>` command from the event platform; stale actionable references across `SKILL.md` and the wrapper comments are corrected; and the state-dir ignore pattern now covers isolated outboxes.

The new regressions pin the generated Bsky path/command, verify the suffix tracks an X event rather than being hardcoded, reject the old actionable `<STATE_DIR>/outbox.yaml` path, and cover the ignore glob. The dispatch-resolution table also preserves the important nuance that no-platform dispatch can fall back to a shared file while platform-specific dispatch cannot.

All reported checks pass, including pytest on Python 3.11 and 3.12, skill conformance, packaging, and the enforced test gate. I found no remaining blocking issue in the updated diff.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Remediated in `b2931d1db`. The review was right and it found the more important half — my first pass fixed prose while the runtime prompt kept telling the agent the wrong filename, which is the thing that actually causes the silent miss.

### What I verified before changing anything

I read the resolution out of the installed `social-cli` (`/opt/social-cli/dist/commands/dispatch.js`) instead of trusting the docs or the agent's issue notes, and it is subtler than either:

| invocation | file read |
|---|---|
| `dispatch --platform bsky` | `outbox-bsky.yaml`, **no fallback** — a bare `outbox.yaml` is skipped with `No outbox file found` and exit 0 |
| `dispatch` (no platform) | every `outbox-*.yaml` present; falls back to shared `outbox.yaml` **only if none exist** (`dispatch.js:820-826`) |
| `dispatch --file <path>` | exactly that path |

Two consequences: the old hint's unsuffixed path is invisible to the `--platform` form the pollers tell the agent to use, and because the no-platform form *prefers* suffixed files, a stale `outbox-bsky.yaml` silently beats a fresh `outbox.yaml`.

This also corrects a claim **this PR itself introduced** — step 2 said dispatch "never looks at a shared `outbox.yaml`". The fallback branch disproves that, so it is now a table of the three real rules.

Confirmed live rather than assumed: `state/pollers/social-cli-feed/config.yaml` has `platformIsolation: true`, so the hints named a file dispatch never reads on the deployment that files the bugs.

### Fixed

- **`poller.py` / `feed_poller.py` hints** — now `outbox-<platform>.yaml` + a matching `dispatch --platform <platform>`, plus one line on why the suffix is required. Measured **+150 chars/event**; I updated the overhead comments to the new figures rather than leave them stale.
- **All actionable `SKILL.md` references** — reply path (289), quick commands (315), batching (404-408), both state-layout blocks (436, feed), success criteria (522).
- **`dispatch-outbox.sh`** — header and usage comments, including what passing vs omitting the platform arg does.

### Two things the review did not name

- **The seeded `.gitignore` listed `outbox.yaml`, not the glob.** Its siblings already use `inbox-*.yaml` / `feed-*.yaml`, so under isolation the suffixed outboxes the agent writes were the one transient *not* ignored — a turn ending before dispatch leaks one into tracked home state. Now `outbox*.yaml`.
- **Misleading inbox references in the same files.** The module docstring said `sync` writes `inbox.yaml`, contradicted by `_load_inbox` twelve lines below, which documents that per-platform files are *mandatory* and that the pre-refactor code "looked at `inbox.yaml` and emitted nothing." The `SKILL.md` troubleshooting steps told the reader to inspect an `inbox.yaml` that never exists. Left alone: the two refs that deliberately discuss the shared name.

Worth noting this is the same defect already fixed once on the read side — the outbox hint was the unfixed write-side half. muninn filed it five times (`memory/issues/social-cli-outbox-*.md`).

### Regressions

- `test_action_hint_names_the_platform_suffixed_outbox` in both pollers' suites — pins `outbox-<platform>.yaml` and `dispatch --platform`, and asserts the unsuffixed path is **not** offered.
- `test_action_hint_suffix_tracks_the_platform` — the suffix follows the event's platform rather than being hardcoded to `bsky`.
- The `.gitignore` tests now assert the emitted pattern actually matches both `outbox-bsky.yaml` and `outbox.yaml` via `fnmatch`, so replacing the glob with either literal fails.

**Each guard mutation-tested**, since a passing test proves nothing until seen failing: reverting the notifications hint fails 2 named tests (2 selected / 23 deselected), the feed hint 1 (1 / 14), the gitignore glob 2 (2 / 45). Restored → 47 pass.

One measurement note: `tests/test_skill_conformance.py::...[list]` fails in my local venv, and does so identically on the unmodified PR head. It is a stale-venv artifac

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Correction to my remediation comment above: I wrote that muninn "filed it five times." That overcounts — I globbed `memory/issues/social-cli-outbox-*.md` instead of reading each one.

Accurate breakdown of the five files:

- `social-cli-outbox-filename-mismatch` — the filename bug
- `social-cli-feed-outbox-filename` — the filename bug (feed poller)
- `social-cli-outbox-write-on-existing` — downstream effect (write refused on the stale outbox)
- `social-cli-outbox-stale-queue-fire` — downstream effect (stale queued actions firing)
- `social-cli-outbox-path` — a **different** bug: STATE_DIR not respected for outbox lookup

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1159: upgrade reconciliation has never delivered a proposal, and submit_proposal records the failure as a successful tool call

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving — but read the chainlink first: **#1159's premise was wrong and I retracted it.** The upgrade flow was never broken. Proposals go to the home repo `jasoncarreira/mimirbot`, I searched `jasoncarreira/mimir`, found none, and concluded from that plus `submit_proposal` returning `ok=True` that the tool reported success while delivering nothing. It had in fact pushed the branch and opened the PR both times — #17 at 15:12 and #18 at 14:08, matching the tool calls to the minute. My "returns failure as a string, so ok=True is compatible with failure" reasoning explained away the very signal that should have corrected me.

So this PR fixes a bug that was not occurring. I am approving it anyway because two of its changes are correct independent of that:

**The `pushed` asymmetry is a real latent defect.** Previously, when PR-open failed, the code left the proposal marked open "rather than strand a valid worktree" — but `finalize_proposal` had already removed the worktree after pushing, so there was nothing for a reconciliation turn to recover, and the failure was reported as a non-error. Distinguishing pushed from not-pushed, and returning `ok=False, action="error"` when the worktree is already gone, is right. Mutation-verified: forcing that branch false fails its test.

**Typed failures beat string returns.** `ProposalSubmissionError(ToolException)` carrying `reason` and `lane`, and `ProposalPrError` for the three PR-open failure modes, means a failure is distinguishable from a success by shape rather than by parsing message text for the word "failed". Mutation-verified: reverting one raise to a string return fails its test. That this pattern let me construct a plausible-but-false story about silent failure is itself an argument for the change.

CI 8/8; local full suite 8012 passed, 20 skipped.

**What I would want changed if this were load-bearing, but am not blocking on:** `test_version_bump_opens_upgrade_pull_request_end_to_end` is the criterion I wrote as "a version bump produces a proposal PR." It now passes against a fake opener, which is the right unit-level shape — but the real end-to-end evidence was always available and I did not look for it: the actual PRs in the home repo. If that test ever fails, check the home repo before believing the flow is broken.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1158: the agent cannot read its own skills directory, so skills silently never load on non-admin or service turns

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The fix is right and it anticipated a regression its own change would have caused.

**All three read-policy sites are updated** — `is_protected_read_path`, `configured_non_admin_read_roots` and `resolve_non_admin_read_target` — which the leaf called out specifically because updating only the first leaves the virtual-path resolver disagreeing with the boundary check.

**The narrowing is the best part of this PR, and I initially misread it.** I flagged the shared-root `SKILL.md` restriction as unrequested new policy. It is not: mutating it away fails the *pre-existing* `test_poller_read_scope_is_limited_to_its_server_bound_skill`. Adding the shared skill roots to service read scope would otherwise have handed every poller read access to every other skill's files — including the `runtime-notes.txt` holding a `ghp_` token in that test's own fixture. Full access stays scoped to `owned_skill_directory`, which is exactly the mechanism the leaf's review criterion asked you to consider. That is a regression avoided rather than a rule invented.

**The observable-symptom test is the one that matters here.** `test_skills_middleware_loads_home_sources_without_errors` instantiates the real `SkillsMiddleware`, runs `before_agent`, and asserts no "Skills load errors" record. This defect existed for an unknown length of time precisely because nobody was asserting the symptom — only the policy predicate — so pinning the loader's own output is what stops it recurring silently.

**Verified.** Three mutations, each killed: removing `skills` from the read carve-out, removing it from service read roots, and removing the shared-root narrowing. Read/write separation is asserted directly — both roots in read roots, neither in write roots. Local full suite 8007 passed, 20 skipped; CI 8/8.

I also checked the thing that would have made this a half-fix: whether ordinary turns can read a skill's *supporting* files, not just its `SKILL.md`. They can — `helper.py` and `reference.md` under a skill both read fine on a non-admin turn, and `ls` returns all three entries. A fix that cleared the warning while leaving referenced files unreadable would have been the same defect wearing a different face.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1156: forge: the review poller cannot comment on an issue, and the first fix modelled the authorization wrongly

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. This is a better implementation than the one I wrote and closed, in three specific ways.

**Better than the spec:**

- **Server-returned identity is validated.** `get_open_issue_target` checks `observed_number == issue` and derives `observed_repo` from the response's own `repository_url`, refusing on mismatch — then returns `IssueTarget(observed_repo, observed_number)`. My version trusted the request. This closes redirect and alias cases the leaf did not name.
- **A repository-derived source is required**, not merely matched. The leaf asked which check constrains an unbound turn; you added `issue_repository_source_required` and made it explicit. The test asserting `client.calls == []` for that case is the right detail: the gate runs before resolution, so an unbound turn cannot even cause a forge fetch.
- **`issue_comment` is removed from the `custom` profile's implicit grant** (`frozenset(TRIGGER_CAPABILITY_TIERS) - {"issue_comment"}`). Custom profiles would otherwise have inherited a brand-new sink capability silently. I did not think of that.

**The recorded IFC rule is implemented exactly.** For an issue scope, `_forge_repository_scope_mismatch` compares repository and then `continue`s past the pull-request and head comparisons — repository must match, resource within it need not. Pull-request destinations keep exact `(repo, pr_number, head)` matching, and the existing tests still prove it.

**The trap I recorded in the leaf was avoided.** The static `_OPERATION_SINK_DESTINATION` entry is preserved for `service_can_invoke_operation`'s capability check while `repo#issue/220` is the resolved flow target, and a test asserts the static value. Collapsing those two would have silently denied the poller the capability it was just granted.

**Verified, not taken on trust.** Four mutations, each with the selected count confirmed non-zero:

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| drop the repository match in the issue branch | authorization test fails |
| drop the repository-source requirement | authorization test fails |
| drop the pull-request refusal in the client | client test fails |
| drop the server-identity mismatch check | client test fails |

The authorization test exercises the real `ToolRegistry.authorize_tool()` with `enforce=True` and asserts `resolved_sink_target == "repo-a/project#issue/220"`, cross-repo `ifc_label_blocked:forge`, and no-source `issue_repository_source_required`. That is the boundary my own attempt bypassed by testing `.func` directly, and it is why that attempt shipped a tool that would have been unusable for the one principal it was for.

Local full suite 7998 passed, 20 skipped. I also merged current `main` into this head and ran both PRs' affected tests together — 1072 passed — because this PR's CI predates #1381 landing, so its green did not reflect the current base. Clean, no semantic conflict.

**Non-blocking, two notes.** `resolve_issue_comment_target` runs at authorization and again inside the tool body, so a successful comment costs two GETs; the second is the stricter one and fails safe if the issue closed in between, so this is efficiency rather than correctness. And the PR body is the plain evidence block — the build-authored `Build summary` channel from #1153 is deployed on mimirbot now, so future builds can use it.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. Implements the decision and goes beyond it in one worthwhile way.

**Verified.** Mutation-tested all three guards, each with the selected count confirmed non-zero:

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| drop `pr_changes_requested_stale` from `_HISTORY_REWRITE_EVENT_TYPES` | `test_changes_requested_rebase_push_uses_exact_head_lease` fails |
| drop the `_PROTECTED_BRANCH_REFS` condition | 2 tests fail |
| drop the `ls-remote` freshness comparison | `test_changes_requested_rebase_stale_lease_refuses_concurrent_push` fails |

I am noting the selection count because my first attempt at this review was itself vacuous: a failed `git checkout` left me on the wrong branch and every `-k` run reported "114 deselected" with zero selected, which reads exactly like a pass. The numbers above are from a run where the head was verified as `04638b324` first.

**Better than the spec.** `_PROTECTED_BRANCH_REFS` makes `main`/`master` unforceable *in this code path* rather than relying on the prohibited-action guard elsewhere. The leaf asked for a test proving it; you added a structural guard as well, which is the stronger answer for a change whose whole subject is who may rewrite published history.

**A behaviour change to the existing triggers, which I checked rather than assumed.** Renaming `rewritten_rebase` → `rewritten_history` also changes its meaning from "this event type may rewrite" to "history actually diverged". So `--force-with-lease` is now attached only when the push is genuinely non-fast-forward, where previously a `pr_mergeability_rebase` scope carried it even on a fast-forward. That is a real change to those paths, and it is an improvement — not forcing when forcing is unnecessary — but it is worth saying out loud rather than letting a rename hide it.

payload.author: mimir-carreira

```
  no repository sources   : allowed, and ANY configured repo selectable
```

- destination is a **server-fetched** `repo#issue/<n>`, never the model's selector

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1155: glob and ls hide read-policy denials as empty results, so the agent cannot tell empty from withheld

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The design is implemented faithfully and the hard part — the `ls` channel — is solved well. Requesting changes on one concrete defect and one deviation that needs to be a deliberate choice rather than an unremarked one.

## Verified working

Named-denied-target now returns an error from both surfaces, matching `read`:

```
glob(path='/logs') -> error='Read denied: mimir_home_read_boundary. Use an allowed state path instead.'
ls('/logs')        -> error='Read denied: mimir_home_read_boundary. Use an allowed state path instead.'
```

That was the core inconsistency and it is fixed. The `ls` withheld-count channel — the open design point, since `LsResult` has no `truncated` field and vendoring the upstream type was ruled out — is answered with a mimir-side `ContextVar` plus `_create_ls_tool`/`_create_glob_tool` wrappers that append to `ToolMessage.content`. No upstream type touched, and it works for both the sync and async tool paths. Good answer to a question I left open. 121 tests pass.

## Blocking — `truncated=True` on a policy withhold makes the model read a falsehood

`truncated=truncated is not None or withheld_notice is not None` sets the upstream truncation flag for policy withholds. Upstream renders that flag as a fixed string:

```
GLOB_TRUNCATION_NOTE = "Note: the search stopped early because it hit its time limit. The paths above
are valid but incomplete. Narrow the search (a more specific pattern or a narrower path) to see the rest."
```

So on a withhold with no actual truncation, this is what the model receives:

```
['/state/a.md']

Note: the search stopped early because it hit its time limit. The paths above are valid but
incomplete. Narrow the search (a more specific pattern or a narrower path) to see the rest.

Note: read policy withheld 2 entries (mimir_home_read_boundary), one or more entries
(protected_name_match). The permitted results above are valid but incomplete.
```

Two problems. The first note is **false** — no time limit was hit, the walk completed. And its advice **cannot work**: narrowing the pattern will never reveal a policy-withheld entry, so an agent that follows it retries forever and learns nothing. That is the same self-correction failure this leaf exists to fix, reintroduced through the truncation flag. The two notes also contradict each other in one message.

Verified fix: change it to `truncated=truncated is not None`. The withheld notice still reaches the model, because the `ContextVar` channel is independent of the flag:

```
contains 'hit its time limit'  : False
contains 'Narrow the search'   : False
contains 'read policy withheld': True
```

`truncated` should keep meaning what its docstring says — the walk stopped early — because #1123's time bound depends on that meaning. One of your tests asserts `glob_result.truncated is True` for a withhold, so it needs updating with the fix; please assert the notice instead, which is the signal that actually reaches the caller.

## Blocking — the coarse class still advertises presence, contrary to the leaf

`_withheld_notice` withholds the count for `protected_name_match` but still names the reason:

```
Note: read policy withheld one or more entries (protected_name_match).
```

The leaf's criterion was "not given a distinguishable per-reason count, **so the presence of a credential or key file is not advertised**." This satisfies the letter and not the stated purpose: it confirms a secret-shaped file exists in that listing.

I want to be straight that your choice may be the better one. Total silence for that class reintroduces exactly the confusion this leaf fixes, and telling the agent "something was withheld by naming rules" lets it stop rather than loop. What I am not willing to do is credit a criterion as met when it was changed silently. Either restore the leaf's behaviour (omit `protected_name_match` from the notice), or keep yours and say so explicitly with the threat-model reasoning — that in a single-operator deployment reading its

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Both of my blocking items are fixed correctly and I verified them. A new blocker has appeared that is not your fault: base drift against #1376, which merged after you branched.

## Both previous findings resolved

**`truncated` no longer conflated.** The model now receives only the accurate notice:

```
Note: read policy withheld 2 entries (mimir_home_read_boundary). The permitted results above are valid but incomplete.
```

with `hit its time limit` and `Narrow the search` both absent. `truncated` is back to meaning what its docstring says, which #1123's time bound depends on. Mutation-verified: re-conflating the returned flag fails `test_allowed_root_returns_partial_results_with_scope_denial_notices`.

I should note that this took me three attempts to mutate correctly — my first two hit the `truncated=` kwarg passed to `_record_glob_search` (telemetry) rather than the one in the `GlobResult` return, two lines apart, and both times the test "survived." The test is not vacuous; my mutation was. Flagging it because a reviewer skimming for that pattern could reach the wrong conclusion.

**Naming-rule denials no longer advertise presence.** `protected_name_match` alone now yields no notice at all, and in a mixed case only the boundary count appears — verified directly. You restored the leaf's criterion and recorded the reasoning in both the comment and a code comment, which is what I asked for. For the record, the residual is deliberate: when a listing withholds *only* naming-rule entries the caller still cannot distinguish empty from withheld, and that trade is the criterion's intent rather than an oversight.

## Blocking — silent semantic conflict with #1376

`test_denied_named_target_errors_for_ls_and_glob_without_disclosing_path` builds `<home>/docs/` and asserts `ls("/docs")` and `glob(path="/docs")` are denied with `mimir_home_read_boundary`. Chainlink #1154 (PR #1376, merged `d8c80e27`) made `<home>/docs` a **read-only root**, so that path is now legitimately readable and the error is `None` — which is exactly the CI failure:

```
AssertionError: assert None == 'Read denied: mimir_home_read_boundary. Use an allowed state path instead.'
```

Confirmed it is base drift, not your code. Merging current `main` into this branch locally is **textually clean** — no conflict markers — and then that one test fails and only that one:

```
merge: CLEAN (no textual conflict)
docs carve-out present after merge? 2
1 failed, 121 passed
```

Check-run history matches: all three pytest jobs were green at `c647fcb0c` and red at `4064c9c1b`, because CI tests the head merged with current `main` and #1376 landed in between.

This is the dangerous shape — git had nothing to flag, and only that assertion caught it. Please rebase on `main` and pick a target that is still withheld (`/logs`, `/skills`, or any home subdirectory outside the `state`/`memory`/`docs`/artifact/turn-scratch carve-out). Keep the "without disclosing path" assertions; only the fixture directory needs to change.

I also owe you a correction: in my previous review I called the stale base non-blocking and said it "will resolve on rebase." That was wrong — it breaks a test rather than resolving itself, and I should have caught that then.

## Non-blocking, unchanged

`_read_denied_message` still duplicates guidance strings that `read_policy` produces for the `read` path; worth collapsing to one source later so they cannot drift.

payload.body:
