payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1154: docs seeded into the agent home are unreadable and invisible to normal turns, and the upgrade prompt never points at them

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving at `05e245d16`. I verified the behaviour end to end rather than reading the diff, since the whole defect was that the policy and the observed behaviour disagreed.

**Docs are now readable, and the boundaries that should hold still hold.** Driving the real backend rooted at a home in virtual mode, non-admin turn, against the actual 17 seeded filenames:

| | result |
|---|---|
| 16 seeded `.md` docs (`README`, `authorization`, `code-building-pipeline`, `credentials.md`, …) | **readable** |
| `docs/.env.example` | still denied — `protected_name_match` |
| `docs/signing.key`, `docs/credentials/x.md` | still denied — `protected_name_match` |
| `write` to `/docs/*` (WriteGuardBackend, live `writable_dirs`) | **refused** — `Write blocked. Writable directories: /state/` |
| `/state/ok.txt` write (control) | allowed |

Adding the location without granting a naming exemption is exactly right: a `.key`, `.pem`, `.env.*` or `credentials/` under `docs/` stays denied. `credentials.md` reads fine, which is the case I expected might trip the protected-directory rule — the check matches whole path parts, and `credentials.md` is not `credentials`, so the credentials documentation is not falsely withheld.

All three policy sites are updated consistently — `is_protected_read_path`, `configured_non_admin_read_roots`, and `resolve_non_admin_read_target` — which matters, because updating only the first would have left the virtual-path resolver disagreeing with the boundary check.

**The prompt half is correctly filtered.** Rendered with a realistic `refresh_docs` return:

```
## Updated reference docs
- `/docs/code-building-pipeline.md`
- `/docs/new-thing.md`
```

`unchanged` and `skipped_deleted` excluded, `docs/.env.example` excluded (not `.md`, so it can never be pointed at), and a top-level `README.md` excluded (not under `docs/`). With nothing changed the section renders empty with no dangling heading. The wording states reading is "not a prerequisite for proposal submission", which was a review criterion. `{changed_docs_section}` is consumed in both cases, and there is a fallback append when a customized template lacks the placeholder — a nice touch for homes with an edited `upgrade.md`.

Mutation-tested three guards, each killed by the intended test: accepting every `refresh_docs` status fails 2 tests, dropping the `.md` filter fails 1, and removing `docs` from the `is_protected_read_path` carve-out fails 2. Suite 966 passed, 2 skipped; CI 8/8.

**One correction to my own review process.** I first flagged a write leak on `/docs/evil.md`. That was my harness — I had used the read-only backend class instead of `WriteGuardBackend`. With the guarded backend and the live `writable_dirs`, writes are refused. I also suspected `server.py`'s `_doc_changes` was never populated and the feature would silently no-op; that was wrong too — line 855 assigns it from `refresh_docs(config.home)` in `build_app`, and the call site closes over it. My scope-detection was misled by a preceding sibling `def`.

**Non-blocking:** `server.py:86` adds `_doc_changes: dict[str, str] = {}` inside `_start_mcp_servers`, which is a different function from the one that assigns and uses it. It is dead and slightly misleading — a reader would take it for the initialization. Please drop it in a follow-up.

**Forward-looking note, not a defect here:** because the carve-out is global, every turn shape can now read docs, including service principals whose declared `filesystem_read_roots` do not list it — I confirmed all four shapes are allowed. The upgrade principal's new root is what makes `service_allowed` true for docs under enforcement; other service principals would fall through to a weaker check. Worth revisiting as part of the enforcement-enablement work rather than widening anything now.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1153: worklink: PR bodies are harness-generated, so leaf criteria requiring findings in the PR body cannot be satisfied by the build

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The design is right and the hardening is better than I expected — `O_NOFOLLOW`, a bounded read, control-character stripping, `redact_text`, visible truncation, and neutralizing a build-authored `Worklink evidence:` lookalike so it cannot shadow the parser anchor. I mutation-tested three of those and each is genuinely pinned: dropping `redact_text`, dropping `_EVIDENCE_HEADING_RE.sub`, or dropping the `unlink` each fails its test.

Requesting changes for one thing: the `S_ISREG` guard you added cannot do its job on Linux, and the two ways it fails are both invisible on macOS.

## Blocking — non-regular files at `.worklink-pr-body.md` wedge or discard the run

`stat.S_ISREG` is checked *after* the open, so the open decides the outcome.

**1. A FIFO blocks the open forever.** Verified in the mimirbot container (Linux, CPython 3.11), running your exact sequence `os.open(path, os.O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW)` against a FIFO:

```
*** open BLOCKED >5s on a FIFO — the S_ISREG guard is never reached ***
```

`_read_pr_body_section` is called synchronously in `_finalize`, so the run hangs holding its claim. A hang is worse than a crash here: worklink crashes emit no events, and neither does this.

**2. A directory raises out of the `finally`.** `path.unlink()` on a directory is an error, and it runs on the `S_ISREG`-rejection path:

```
RESULT: RAISES IsADirectoryError: [Errno 21] Is a directory -> propagates out of _finalize
```

That discards a completed build with committed work and a passing gate — precisely the failure class chainlink #1152 existed to eliminate.

Neither reproduces on macOS: the FIFO open returned `None` there, which is why local testing and CI both look clean. `pytest (3.11)` and `pytest (3.12)` are green because **nothing exercises `S_ISREG`** — the three new tests cover the happy path, the absent-file path, and scrubbing/truncation, but not the guard itself. A test that pointed a FIFO at this function on Linux would have hung CI and caught both.

Suggested fix, small: add `os.O_NONBLOCK` to the open flags so a FIFO returns immediately and `S_ISREG` can reject it (`O_NONBLOCK` has no effect on regular-file reads), and make the `finally` cleanup tolerate a non-file — the `S_ISREG` branch already returns `None`, it just must not raise on the way out. Please add tests for both shapes; they are the reason the guard exists.

## Verified working

- Body composition: `Closes chainlink #N` → `Build summary:` → the evidence block, with the evidence block intact and last. The no-section case is byte-identical to before, asserted directly.
- The file is consumed and removed before the harness stages, so it never enters the diff — asserted in two tests, and confirmed by mutation.
- Truncation accounts for `redact_text` expanding the text (`len(raw) > MAX or len(encoded) > MAX`), which is easy to miss.
- The prompt-template line tells the build the mechanism, its bound, and that the section is harness-placed.

## Non-blocking

- `_open_pr` rebuilds the `Closes chainlink #{issue_id}.` line and then recovers the rest with `evidence_block.split("\n\n", 1)[1]`. It is correct today, but it duplicates a literal and depends on there being exactly one blank line before the evidence heading. Composing the closes-line, the optional summary, and the evidence block as three separate pieces would remove the coupling.
- Acceptance criterion 6 asked the PR to name the mechanism chosen and why. That is a catch-22 for this PR specifically — the channel does not exist until it merges — so I am not charging it. Worth knowing that #1374 handled the same gap by putting the write-up in a PR comment, which was available here.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving at `8728a25f0`. Both blocking defects are fixed and I verified them on the deployment platform rather than crediting CI, since CI was green while both bugs were present.

Re-ran the open/guard/finally sequence in the mimirbot container (Linux, CPython 3.11):

| `.worklink-pr-body.md` is… | before | at this head |
|---|---|---|
| a FIFO | `os.open` blocked >5s, `S_ISREG` unreachable | returns `None`, no hang, FIFO removed |
| a directory | `IsADirectoryError` propagated out of `_finalize` | returns `None`, directory left intact |
| a regular file | worked | still works, content returned, file removed |

`O_NONBLOCK` is the right instrument — it makes the FIFO open return immediately so `S_ISREG` can do its job, and has no effect on regular-file reads. Guarding both `unlink` calls with `except OSError: pass` is right too: the `S_ISREG` branch already returns `None`, it just must not raise on the way out.

The two new tests pin them. `test_pr_body_section_rejects_fifo_without_blocking` would **hang** on Linux without `O_NONBLOCK`, so CI is a genuine gate for it even though it passes trivially on macOS — that platform asymmetry is why the original slipped through, and it is now covered where it matters. Mutation-tested the directory guard, which fails on both platforms: reverting the `try`/`except` around the `finally` unlink fails `test_pr_body_section_rejects_directory_without_raising`.

Also asserting the right post-conditions, which is easy to get backwards: the FIFO test asserts the path is gone (the `finally` unlink succeeds on a FIFO), the directory test asserts it is still a directory (unlink fails and is correctly swallowed).

Everything from my first pass still holds — evidence block intact and last, no-section case byte-identical, the file consumed before staging so it never enters the diff, truncation accounting for `redact_text` expansion, and the forged `Worklink evidence:` heading neutralized. 48 tests in the file pass; CI 8/8.

Merging. The non-blocking `_open_pr` note stands as a future cleanup, not a condition: it rebuilds the `Closes chainlink #{id}` line and recovers the rest via `evidence_block.split("\n\n", 1)[1]`, which is correct but couples the composition to there being exactly one blank line before the evidence heading.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Addressed the blocking non-regular-file cases in `8728a25f`:

- opens `.worklink-pr-body.md` with `O_NONBLOCK`, so a FIFO cannot wedge `_finalize`
- treats cleanup failures for non-file entries as non-fatal, so a directory cannot discard a completed build
- adds regression tests for both FIFO and directory shapes

Verification: the deployment-configured full suite passed via `repo_test` (`uv run --extra dev --extra bench pytest -q`, exit 0). The scoped checkout is clean.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1123: tools: glob times out after 20s and records no pattern, burning roughly 28 minutes of wall clock in seven days

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes. The time bound works and the telemetry is good, but CI is red, and the bound as configured does not actually take the external deadline off the table.

## 1. Blocking — CI is failing, and the cause is a real behavior regression

`pytest (3.11)`, `pytest (3.12)` and `pytest-enforced` all fail on two **pre-existing** tests:

```
FAILED test_glob_skips_worktrees_and_caps_matches_without_result_error
  AssertionError: assert ['/src/b.py'] == ['/src/a.py']
FAILED test_glob_reports_scan_truncation_before_matching
  AssertionError: assert [{... 'path': '/c.py' ...}] == []
```

Both **pass on macOS and fail on Linux**, which is the tell. The bounded walk dropped the `sorted()` that `os.walk` path applies to `dirnames` and `filenames`. Measured directly on a directory whose entries were created out of alphabetical order:

| walk | order |
|---|---|
| `origin/main` (`os.walk` path) | `f00, f01, f02, f03, f04, f05` — sorted |
| this PR (bounded path) | `f09, f08, f07, f03, f02, f06` — **filesystem order** |

The failing assertions are the symptom; the defect is that **which** results survive truncation is now nondeterministic and platform-dependent. That applies to both bounds — the match cap and the new time cap — so the same glob can return different files on different hosts or after unrelated filesystem churn. Please sort entries within each directory in the bounded path too, so truncation stays deterministic.

## 2. Blocking — the time bound is not strictly tighter than the upstream deadline

The review criteria require it be *strictly* tighter "with enough margin that a slow filesystem does not race it." As written:

- `_DEFAULT_GLOB_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 10.0`
- `deepagents.middleware.filesystem.GLOB_TIMEOUT = 10.0` — verified in **both** live venvs (mimirbot `/workspace/mimir/.venv`, muninn `/home/mimir/venv`, deepagents 0.7.1)

These are equal, and upstream's clock starts first: `asyncio.wait(timeout=GLOB_TIMEOUT)` is armed before `to_thread` schedules the backend, so the backend's `started = time.monotonic()` is strictly later. Measured with both budgets set to the same value over a 12,000-entry tree, 20 trials:

```
upstream deadline fired: 1/20   (agent gets "glob timed out ..." — the unusable result this leaf exists to eliminate)
```

So the external deadline is still reachable ~5% of the time. Pick a bound with real headroom (e.g. 5.0s, or `GLOB_TIMEOUT * 0.5` read at call time so the two cannot drift apart), rather than matching it exactly.

## 3. Blocking — two acceptance criteria require PR-body content that is not present

The body is the boilerplate evidence block only.

- *"the PR body states what is actually being walked and whether the cost is the pattern, the tree, or both"* — this is the observability half of the leaf, and it is the thing that made the original 84 timeouts undiagnosable. With `filesystem_glob_search` now recording pattern, root and `visited_entries`, please state the finding.
- *"the PR body shows before and after timing for a representative pattern over a large tree"* — absent, and it carries weight here: the walk moved from `os.walk` to a recursive Python `scandir` with a per-entry `on_visit` closure, while a separate criterion requires that recording the visited count "must not add measurable cost to the common case." Numbers are needed to show the common case did not regress.

## Verified working (no change needed)

- The time bound fires and degrades correctly: truncates, names the searched root, emits `ran longer than 0.004s`, and logs `was cut short after 98 entries`.
- `_glob_descender` is conservatively correct, and its docstring reasoning about suffix matching at arbitrary depth is right — this is provable pruning, not a heuristic.
- I specifically checked whether `entry.is_dir(follow_symlinks=False)` had started returning symlinked directories as file matches. **It has not** — behavior is identical to main. Flagging that I checked so nobody re-derives it.

## Notes, not b

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving at `030753ec5`. All four blocking items are discharged, and I measured the two I had asked you to demonstrate rather than hold the PR for numbers.

**1. Ordering — fixed and confirmed.** The bounded walk yields `sorted(files, …)` then `sorted(directories, …)`. Re-measured on entries created out of alphabetical order: sorted, matching `origin/main`. The three Linux-only CI failures are green.

**2. Timeout margin — fixed, better than my suggestion.** `deepagents_filesystem.GLOB_TIMEOUT * 0.5` read at call time via a read-only import. A hardcoded 5.0 would have silently tied again if upstream ever dropped to 5.0; deriving it means the two bounds cannot converge across a dependency upgrade.

I also withdraw part of my own review here. I reported that upstream's deadline fired in 1 of 20 trials with equal budgets, and the same harness still showed 1 of 20 against this head. That is an artifact of millisecond budgets, not a defect: the pre-backend overhead is a fixed 0.127 ms median / 0.363 ms max, so at production magnitudes the 5.0s gap is ~13,800x it. The criticism (a bound that ties rather than beats) was right; the frequency I attached to it was not.

**3. Walk and cost attribution — accepted.** Your comment states it: cost is dominated by walking the selected tree, not by matching, with pruning limited to the provably-empty trailing-slash case. That is the finding the criterion was asking for.

**4. Common-case cost — measured, and it improved.** Your timing evidence was after-only over 2,020 entries, so I ran the before/after myself on a 20,221-entry tree, interleaved A/B, 5 rounds each, comparing minimums:

| | per round | median |
|---|---|---|
| this PR | 0.883, 0.879, 0.883, 0.876, 0.876 | **0.879s** |
| `origin/main` | 0.905, 0.920, 0.911, 0.898, 0.899 | 0.905s |

The `scandir` walk with the per-entry `on_visit` callback is ~2.9% *cheaper* than `os.walk`, consistently, 5/5. So recording the visited count adds no measurable common-case cost — it is a small net win.

**On the PR body.** Your closing note — that the body is not editable through the scoped PR tool surface — is the right call and the right disclosure. A criterion phrased "the PR body states X" is unsatisfiable as the executor is provisioned, so carrying the evidence in a comment was correct rather than a workaround. That is a capability gap on our side and I am filing it separately; it is not charged to this build.

**Conflict resolution.** I merged `main` into this branch myself after #1373 landed, since both PRs edit the opening of `glob`. Git took #1373's signature and `search_path` line cleanly and conflicted only on the first body statements. I kept both, with #1373's type guards ahead of your timing setup so an invalid call is refused before computing a deadline it will not use. That commit is mine, not yours.

Verified after resolving, because this is exactly where a clean merge silently reverts a fix: `aglob("*.py", path=None)` returns matches; the deadline derives 5.0s; the bounded walk is sorted; invalid `pattern`/`path` still refuse. Full suite 7973 passed, 20 skipped. CI 8/8.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Addressed all three blocking points in 3fa90e7bb:

- The bounded `scandir` path now sorts files and directories before yielding, preserving the old deterministic `os.walk` prefix under both match-count and time truncation. Added a regression that reverses raw `scandir` order and still retains `/src/a.py`.
- The default backend deadline is now read from DeepAgents at call time as `GLOB_TIMEOUT * 0.5` (5s with the installed 10s upstream budget), leaving explicit headroom instead of racing an equal deadline. Explicit test overrides remain supported.
- The walk/observability result: cost is dominated by walking the selected root/tree, not glob matching; only the provably-empty trailing-slash directory pattern prunes descent. Telemetry now records the requested pattern, resolved root, elapsed time, visited-entry count, and truncation reason.

Representative large-tree validation uses `**/*.py` over 2,020 entries with no matches. The instrumented bounded path completes in under 1.0s in the regression test while recording exactly 2,020 visits; the timeout case over 4,040 entries returns a useful truncated result under 1.0s with a 1ms injected backend budget. Before this change, the same no-match shape could run until DeepAgents' 10s external timeout, which discarded the useful partial result and recorded no pattern/root/visit count.

Validation:
- `tests/test_readonly_backend.py`: 114 passed
- configured full suite: passed (repo_test)

The PR body itself is not editable through the scoped PR tool surface, so this comment carries the required diagnosis/timing evidence rather than leaving it absent.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Verified both code blockers at `3fa90e7bb`. CI is green, 8/8, including the three that were failing.

**1. Ordering — fixed.** The bounded walk now buffers and yields `sorted(files, …)` then `sorted(directories, …)`. Re-measured on entries created out of alphabetical order: the bounded walk yields `f00, f01, f02, f03, f04, f05` — sorted, matching `origin/main`. Both previously-failing tests pass, and `pytest (3.11)`, `pytest (3.12)` and `pytest-enforced` are green on Linux, which is where they failed.

**2. Timeout margin — fixed, and better than what I suggested.** Deriving `deepagents_filesystem.GLOB_TIMEOUT * 0.5` at call time (read-only import, no patching or vendoring) means the two bounds cannot tie or drift apart across a dependency upgrade — a hardcoded 5.0 would have silently tied again if upstream ever dropped to 5.0.

I want to correct something in my own review while confirming this. I reported that with equal budgets upstream's deadline fired in 1 of 20 trials, and I re-ran that harness against this head expecting zero — it still showed 1 of 20. That result is an **artifact of my scaled-down budgets, not a defect**. The pre-backend overhead (thread dispatch, permission checks, middleware setup) is a fixed cost that does not scale with the budget:

| | value |
|---|---|
| pre-backend overhead | 0.127 ms median, 0.363 ms max (n=15) |
| production gap (10.0s upstream vs 5.0s derived) | 5.0 s |
| ratio | ~13,800× |

At millisecond budgets that fixed cost consumes a large share of upstream's window; at production magnitudes it is negligible. So the race is genuinely closed, and my original 1-in-20 figure overstated the risk at real values even though the underlying criticism — a bound that ties rather than beats — was correct.

**Still open: the two PR-body acceptance criteria.** The body is unchanged, still the boilerplate evidence block with the pre-remediation transcript path. These are the two that require findings in the body:

- *"the PR body states what is actually being walked and whether the cost is the pattern, the tree, or both"* — this is the observability half of the leaf, the thing that made the original 84 timeouts undiagnosable. `filesystem_glob_search` now records pattern, root and `visited_entries`; please state what those show.
- *"the PR body shows before and after timing for a representative pattern over a large tree"* — still needed, and it also discharges the separate criterion that recording the visited count must not add measurable cost to the common case.

Non-blocking note on the new shape: buffering a directory's entries into two lists before yielding means peak memory now scales with the widest single directory, where the previous streaming walk did not. `_max_scan_files` bounds total entries scanned but not per-directory buffering. Fine for real trees; worth knowing it changed.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Confirmed: there is no remaining code blocker at `3fa90e7bb`, and all 8 checks are green. The only unfinished acceptance criteria are the two PR-body reporting requirements.

I still cannot edit the PR body through this turn’s bound PR tool surface. Please copy the diagnosis and representative timing evidence from https://github.com/jasoncarreira/mimir/pull/1374#issuecomment-5173435507 into the PR body. Once that is done, the leaf’s body-only criteria can be verified without another code change.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1149: tools: glob raises an unhandled TypeError (NoneType has no attribute startswith) and surfaces the exception to the model

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The code is correct and I verified it independently. What's missing is the PR-body reporting that three of the five acceptance criteria explicitly require, so this is request-changes on those, not on the fix.

## What I verified (you don't need to redo this)

**Root cause is right.** `deepagents/middleware/filesystem.py` computes `backend_path = permission_path if path is not None else None` at both call sites (2066 sync, 2162 async), so an omitted `path` reaches the backend as `None`, and `_RootAwareFilesystemBackend._resolve_path` does `key.startswith("/")` on it.

**Reproduced the live shape on both sides:**

| | `aglob("*.py", path=None)` |
|---|---|
| `origin/main` | raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'startswith'` |
| this PR | `error=None`, `matches=1` |

**The fix activates on the path the agent actually uses.** deepagents invokes the async `aglob`, not the sync `glob` your test drives — but `protocol.py:601` implements `aglob` as `asyncio.to_thread(self.glob, pattern, path)`, and `composite.py:604` guards `if path is not None` before routing and otherwise delegates to `self.default.aglob`. Both funnel into the overridden `glob`, so the guard fires. The sync twin at 2066 computes `backend_path` identically, so the sync test does drive the real shape.

**Mutation-tested all three guards** (each with the test confirmed selected):

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| revert `path is None or` → original `path == "/"` | `test_glob_tool_omitted_path_searches_root_without_exception` fails |
| disable the `pattern` isinstance guard | `[pattern]` param case fails |
| disable the `path` isinstance guard | `[path]` param case fails, `[pattern]` still passes |

Default behavior is preserved (`None` and `"/"` both resolve to `self.cwd`), so this is not a papered-over default — it is the correct one for the caller. CI: 8/8 green.

## Required changes (PR body only)

1. **Criterion 1 — "the PR names which input produced it and how."** The body is boilerplate evidence; the diagnosis appears only in a test docstring. State it in the PR: the omitted optional `path` argument, converted to `None` by the middleware, reaching `_resolve_path`.

2. **Criterion 4 — "the PR says whether each [sibling] was affected."** Nothing is said. My findings, which you can use directly: `grep` is **not** affected — it resolves via `self._resolve_path(path or ".")`, so `None` becomes `"."`. `ls` is **not** affected — `path` is required and internal resolution coerces with `str(...)`. `file_search` **does not exist** in this backend, so there is nothing to check. Please confirm and state this.

3. **Criterion 4's config note — "if the input depends on deployment configuration ... say so."** It does not: `backend_path` is a middleware-level default, independent of configured roots or virtual-mode home, which is why it reproduces in a default test home. Worth stating explicitly, because the leaf was filed from muninn 0.7.1 events and a reader will otherwise assume the repro needs that deployment shape.

## Separate note for the chainlink, not this PR

The leaf says "unhandled `TypeError`" but the actual exception is `AttributeError` (the message text in the leaf is exact). I'll correct #1149 rather than ask you to.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The fix is correct and independently verified; the remaining items were reporting requirements, and I'm satisfying them here rather than holding the PR for a restatement of analysis already recorded on it.

**Verified:**
- Root cause: `backend_path = permission_path if path is not None else None` (deepagents `filesystem.py` 2066 sync / 2162 async) → `_resolve_path(None)` → `key.startswith("/")`.
- Reproduced: `origin/main` raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'startswith'`; this head returns `error=None, matches=1`. Confirmed independently when an unrelated harness of mine hit the same crash on a branch lacking this fix.
- Activation on the real path: deepagents calls the async `aglob`, not the sync `glob`. `protocol.py:601` implements it as `asyncio.to_thread(self.glob, …)` and `composite.py:604` guards `path is not None` before routing, so both funnel through the overridden `glob`. The guard fires where it matters.
- Mutation-tested all three guards, each with the test confirmed selected: reverting `path is None or` fails the omitted-path test; disabling either isinstance guard fails its parametrized case.
- Default behavior preserved (`None` and `"/"` both → `self.cwd`), so this is the correct default rather than a papering-over.
- CI 8/8 green.

**On the three reporting criteria.** #1374's remediation established that the PR body is not editable through the scoped PR tool surface, so a criterion phrased "the PR body states X" is not satisfiable by the executor as currently provisioned. That is a capability gap on our side, not a defect in this build, and I'm filing it separately rather than charging it to this PR. The substance is already durable on this PR in my review: the root cause named with file and line, and the sibling audit — `grep` unaffected (`_resolve_path(path or ".")` turns `None` into `"."`), `ls` unaffected (required `path`, internal `str()` coercion), `file_search` nonexistent in this backend — plus the finding that the input is a middleware-level default independent of configured roots or virtual-mode home, which is why it reproduces in a default test home.

Merging. I'll correct the leaf's `TypeError`/`AttributeError` discrepancy on #1149.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1151: repo tools: repo_stage and repo_commit fail with a bare Git operation failed while repo_rebase reports real git detail - it blocked the #1367 rebase

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approved at `b8b7f430`. This fixes the class rather than the two tools, and it explains the inconsistency I measured.

**The root cause was an opt-in flag.** `_checked` only fell back to stdout when a caller passed `report_stdout_on_failure=True`. `repo_rebase`'s merge did; `repo_stage` and `repo_commit` did not — which is exactly why I measured `repo_rebase` reporting `error: could not apply dab63177c…` while the other two reported a bare `Git operation failed`. Deleting the flag and making the single chokepoint always produce detail means no tool can accidentally lack it, which is stronger than adding the flag to two more call sites.

```python
def _git_failure_detail(result: GitProcessResult) -> str:
    detail = "\n".join(o.strip() for o in (result.stderr, result.stdout) if o.strip())
    return detail or f"Git exited with status {result.returncode} without diagnostic output"
```

Combining both streams rather than choosing between them is the right call, and the fallback names the exit status — so even a genuinely silent git failure produces something actionable instead of a constant.

**Redaction verified, not taken on faith.** I flagged that git output can carry a credential in a remote URL. `_raw` already returns `stdout=_redact_git_output(...)`, `stderr=_redact_git_output(...)`, and `_redact_git_output` applies `redact_text` plus a userinfo substitution (`\1[REDACTED]@`) that covers precisely that case, with `sensitive_values` scrubbed alongside. So the detail is scrubbed before it can reach a caller, and the docstring's "scrubbed" is accurate.

**Mutation-verified.** Restoring the bare `"Git operation failed"` string fails the suite, including an assertion that is exactly on point:

```python
assert str(refusal.value) != "Git operation failed"
```

plus a test requiring `'CONFLICT (content)'` to survive into the message. So the absence of the generic string is pinned, not merely intended. `tests/test_repo_tools.py` → 114 passed. All 8 checks green.

---

One thing this does **not** resolve, recorded so nobody assumes otherwise: the #1367 rebase that motivated the leaf was blocked by *capability*, not by the opaque message — `repo_stage` requires `RepoPRAction.WRITE` and `repo_commit` requires `COMMIT`, and the conflicting scope only gained those when #1147 (PR #1368) replaced the diagnosis action set with the full remediation set. This PR means that if a rebase fails again we will be told why, which is what made the original diagnosis take a human reading raw events.

Merging.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1150: authz: the maintenance shell profile refuses correctly but does not say what to change - a git command missing only -C gets no guidance

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approved at `8955daca`. Shared rather than copied, and more precise than the leaf asked for.

**The guidance is genuinely shared.** One branch covers both profiles — `if destination in {"maintenance", "upgrade_workspace"} and executable == "git"` — so this is not the third copy #1144 existed to prevent.

**And it only fires when `-C` is the sole problem.** The condition is `arguments[:1] != ["-C"] and _maintenance_git_subcommand_allowed(arguments)`, so a command refused for a disallowed subcommand or option does not get told to add `-C`. `test_maintenance_git_guidance_does_not_misdiagnose_other_refusals` pins that. I did not ask for it, and it is the right instinct: misdirected guidance is worse than none, because the caller retries confidently and fails again.

The message names a concrete form per subcommand (`git -C <dir> status --short`, `… log --oneline`, and so on), so the caller can retry from the message alone — which was the point.

**`mimir wiki backlinks` got an actual decision, with a reason.** It stays denied, and the message says backlinks are regenerated by the bounded post-turn hook after wiki content changes, so inspect the generated files with `read_file`. That is the "decide it explicitly" criterion answered properly rather than deferred.

**Verified by mutation, including a reachability check.** Disabling the `-C` guidance fails two tests, parametrized over the exact argv I recorded on muninn (`git status --short`, `git log --since=24.hours`). So the guard is live and the tests are reached — I checked that specifically, because a surviving mutation and an unexecuted test look identical.

`tests/test_access_control.py` → 794 passed, 2 skipped. All 8 checks green.

---

**One note, not blocking.** Narrowing the shared branch to `{"maintenance"}` alone — dropping `upgrade_workspace` from the `-C` guidance — fails no test. The mechanism is shared as required, but only the `maintenance` half of that sharing is pinned; an `upgrade_workspace` git command missing `-C` would silently lose its guidance.

I am not holding the PR for it. This is message quality rather than a security property: the refusal itself is unaffected, and `upgrade_workspace`'s admission path is well covered by #1141/#1144. Contrast #1369, where the untested condition could delete a live checkout — that one I did hold. Worth adding a parametrized case over both destinations next time this file is touched.

Merging.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1148: pr leases: an expired lease with no publication proof is unreclaimable - 275 retries across 5 leases holding 2.6 GB

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes at `3facfa65` — for **one missing test**, on the safety property that matters most here. Everything else is done well and I verified it by mutation rather than by reading.

**What's right.**

The reclamation path answers the question the leaf asked rather than just silencing the noise:

- `_origin_contains_head` fetches and checks `for-each-ref --contains=<head> refs/remotes/origin`, which distinguishes "the work was never pushed" from "`PUBLISHED_HEAD_REF` was never written on a path that did push." That was the diagnostic question I could not answer from outside, and it is now recorded per lease as `canonical_origin_contains_head`.
- `_preserve_checkout_head` bundles the full history reachable from HEAD before deleting anything, staged to a temp name and `os.replace`d, with `git bundle verify` on both the new bundle and any pre-existing one. The recovery directory refuses a symlink and asserts it does not escape the lease root.
- `_mark_reclamation_metadata` plus the `if (path / _RECLAMATION_METADATA).is_file(): continue` skip gives the terminal state the leaf asked for — the 275-retries-per-day behaviour stops after one decision instead of being retried forever or merely slowed down.
- `recover_pr_checkout_lease` unlinks the marker when a lease is legitimately revived, so an unreclaimable classification is not permanent if the lease comes back.

**Preservation is mutation-pinned.** Replacing `_preserve_checkout_head(...)` with `None` — reclaiming without preserving — fails three tests, including `test_reaper_marks_preservation_failure_once`. So "do not silently destroy unpushed work" is enforced, not merely intended. `tests/test_pr_checkout_lease.py` → 30 passed.

---

**The gap: the expiry gate is untested.**

```python
if observed_at < lease.expires_at or path.resolve(strict=False) in active:
    continue
```

Removing `observed_at < lease.expires_at` — so the preserve-and-delete path runs on **unexpired** leases too — fails **no test**. 30 passed before and after.

That is the one thing in this change that could destroy a checkout someone is mid-way through using. An unexpired, unattached lease is an ordinary state between turns on the same PR; reclaiming it would delete a live working checkout. Recoverable from the bundle, but wrong, and nothing would catch the regression.

`test_reaper_never_reclaims_expired_lease_attached_to_live_turn` covers the `active` half of that condition — the `expires_at` half has no equivalent. My acceptance criterion asked for exactly this ("the publication-proof guard still refuses an UNEXPIRED lease with no proof"), and it is the half that got missed.

Please add a test: an **unexpired** lease with no publication proof is skipped — not preserved, not deleted, no reclamation marker written — and confirm it fails if the expiry comparison is removed. It is a handful of lines given the fixtures you already have.

Everything else I would merge as-is.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approved at `1d42da63`. The gap is closed and the gate is now pinned.

`test_reaper_skips_unexpired_lease_without_publication_proof` asserts every part of "left alone", not just that it was skipped:

- `results == []` — the lease is not processed
- `lease.path.is_dir()` — the checkout survives
- `not (lease_root / ".recovery").exists()` — no bundle is created
- no `mimir-pr-checkout-lease-reclamation.json` marker is written
- and the sweep event reports `expired_count=0, reclaimed_count=0, retained_count=0`

That last assertion is a nice touch: it pins that an unexpired lease is not merely spared but not *counted* either, so it cannot show up as retained-and-therefore-alerted noise.

**Mutation-verified.** Removing `observed_at < lease.expires_at` from the gate now fails exactly this test. Before the fix that same mutation passed all 30 tests — which is what I blocked on, and the difference is now demonstrable rather than asserted.

`tests/test_pr_checkout_lease.py` → 31 passed. All 8 checks green.

Everything I verified last round stands: preservation is mutation-pinned (bundling `HEAD` before deletion, staged and `git bundle verify`-ed, with symlink and escape checks on the recovery directory); `_origin_contains_head` distinguishes "never pushed" from "publication ref never written"; the reclamation marker plus its skip turns 275 retries a day into one decision; and `recover_pr_checkout_lease` clears the marker if a lease legitimately revives.

Merging. This should reclaim the five expired leases and the 2.6 GB on mimirbot once deployed — and the PR records the origin-containment classification per lease, so we will learn which of them were genuinely unpushed versus missing only the publication ref.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Confirmed the requested gap at current head `3facfa65`: the missing regression should prove an unexpired lease with no publication proof returns no reclamation result, leaves the checkout intact, creates neither a recovery bundle nor a reclamation marker, and fails if the `observed_at < lease.expires_at` gate is removed.

I attempted to apply it in the exact scoped checkout, but this github-activity `repo_review` turn has no admitted repository-edit primitive: bounded source read was denied as published PR content and direct mutation was refused by the trusted-service profile. I escalated the unsupported operation. No files were changed, no tests were claimed, and nothing was pushed.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Addressed the requested expiry-gate coverage in `1d42da63a`.

Added `test_reaper_skips_unexpired_lease_without_publication_proof`, which proves the reaper returns no result, leaves the checkout intact, creates neither a recovery bundle nor a reclamation marker, and emits only an empty sweep for an unexpired lease lacking publication proof.

Mutation check: removing `observed_at < lease.expires_at` makes this test fail because the checkout is preserved and deleted.

Validation through the deployment-configured `repo_test` command:
- `tests/test_pr_checkout_lease.py`: 31 passed
- full configured suite: passed

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1147: github poller: a conflicting PR is terminal - let the agent resolve its own conflict, gated on the suite plus naming what it preserved from each side

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approved at `a5aaca7a`. This is better than the leaf asked for, and it is worth saying how: my acceptance criteria were prose obligations, and you turned two of them into **code-enforced preconditions bound to the exact HEAD**.

```python
if self._scope.event_type == "pr_mergeability_conflicting":
    if self._state.conflict_evidence_head != self._expected_head:
        raise GitRefusal("conflict_evidence_required", ...)
    if self._state.full_tested_head != self._expected_head:
        raise GitRefusal("full_test_required", ...)
```

Both proofs are cleared by `record_git_head` and `revoke_checkout_lease`, so a resolution cannot test one commit and push another, and cannot skip the two-sided evidence by asserting it happened. Scoping the gate to `pr_mergeability_conflicting` leaves the clean-rebase path untouched. "State what you preserved" became "you cannot push until the commit carries it," which is the difference between a convention and an invariant.

**The blocking-review restriction was strengthened, not weakened.** `if mergeable and _blocking_reviewers(...)` became `if blocking: continue`, so a PR with unaddressed feedback is now skipped regardless of mergeability — previously a *conflicting* PR with a blocking review still got the event. That is the property I was most concerned to protect, and it is now broader.

**Mutation-verified.** Removing the full-suite precondition fails three tests, including `test_conflict_resolution_dropping_either_test_pinned_side_is_not_pushed[base]` and `[head]` — which is the two-sided-conflict test my criteria asked for, implemented as specified: each side carries a test that fails if its property is dropped, and a resolution dropping either is not pushed.

`tests/test_repo_tools.py` + `tests/test_access_control.py` → 899 passed, 2 skipped. The poller's own suite → 9 passed. All 8 checks green. (Running the poller tests alongside `tests/` trips an `ImportPathMismatchError` on the two `conftest.py` files — an invocation artifact, not a failure; they pass run separately.)

---

**One consequence worth recording, because it is a live deadlock rather than a defect in this PR.**

`if blocking: continue` means this path will now skip **PR #1367** — the very PR that motivated the leaf — because it carries a blocking `CHANGES_REQUESTED` from me. And my review's sole request was *"rebase onto main, preserving both properties."* So the feedback asking for a rebase is exactly what prevents the automation that would perform it.

That is the right trade-off for the general case: automation must never discharge unaddressed feedback by moving the head, and a reviewer cannot always be assumed to have meant "just rebase." But it does mean a review whose only ask is mechanical will block itself, and the operator has to clear it.

I am not asking for a change here — encoding "which reviews are mechanical" is a much larger judgment and belongs nowhere near this gate. Recording it so the interaction is known, and I will clear my #1367 review myself once this is deployed rather than expecting the poller to route around it.

Merging.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1146: authz: give ordinary scratch use a per-turn workspace (scratch/turns/<turn_id>) readable only by its own turn, and admit state, .mimir and CHANGELOG.md

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes at `dab63177` — **for a rebase, not for the substance.** I reviewed and verified the implementation and it is right; it simply cannot merge as-is, and the conflict is in a place where a careless resolution would silently undo a security property.

**The conflict.** `#1365` (`744b1a7d`) merged after this branched, and both PRs rewrite `service_filesystem_read_roots`:

- `#1365` appends the poller's `owned_skill_directory` when the principal is a `poller:*`.
- this PR filters bare `<home>/scratch` **out** of the static roots, then appends `state`, `.mimir`, `CHANGELOG.md` and the per-turn scratch.

A resolution that takes either side wholesale loses the other. Specifically: keep **both** the `if home_scratch is None or Path(root).resolve() != home_scratch` filter (without it, bare shared scratch stays readable and this leaf's whole point is lost) **and** the poller skill-directory append (without it, #1365 regresses and `social-cli-feed` cannot read its own `SKILL.md` again). After rebasing, please confirm both by running `-k "skill"` and `-k "scratch"` and saying so.

I am flagging this specifically because a rebase in this repo has already hidden a semantic conflict that reopened a disclosure path while resolving cleanly in git.

---

**Everything else checks out. Verified, not read:**

- Per-turn isolation is **mutation-pinned**: collapsing `current_turn_scratch_root()` to the shared scratch root fails five tests, including `test_turn_cannot_read_other_or_flat_scratch` for both the other-turn and flat-root cases, and the interactive-turn scoping test.
- The `allow_shared_scratch` escape hatch is narrow — one caller, `_target_within_upgrade_proposals`, which only delegates after `resolve_within_roots([proposals_root], ...)` has already proven containment. That is the right shape for an exception.
- **The purpose directories cannot regress, and I checked the mechanism rather than assuming:** `defaults_upgrade.py:213` creates the vendor worktree by shelling `git worktree`, and `project_tests.py` builds test homes by walking directory file descriptors. Neither passes through `_target_within_static_service_write_roots`, so the scratch write restriction cannot reach them. That is also why only `proposals` needed the hatch — the model writes proposals through a tool, the others are framework-internal.
- Test coverage matches the leaf criterion for criterion: own-scratch read/write, other-turn refused, flat root refused, secret content inside own scratch still refused, `state`/`.mimir`/`CHANGELOG.md` admitted under enforcement, and the prompt actually directing the agent to the path. 1044 passed across the four affected suites.

The prompt wording is good — *"private to this turn; the shared `scratch/` root and other turns' workspaces are unreadable"* — because it tells the model the boundary, not just the path, so a refusal later is self-explanatory.

**One note, not blocking.** Removing the `turn_id` traversal guard (`component.name != turn_id`) fails no test. It is unreachable-false today: `make_turn_id()` returns `uuid.uuid4().hex[:16]`, which cannot contain a separator. Keep it — same call as the poller guard on #1365, and for the same reason: a guard whose removal would widen access is free insurance, unlike an inert grant that misleads. It becomes load-bearing the moment turn ids derive from anything external.

Rebase and I will merge.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approved at `0a3d0611`. The rebase preserved both sides, and I verified that by mutation rather than by trusting a clean merge — which was the whole reason I flagged this conflict.

**Both properties confirmed load-bearing at the rebased head:**

- Collapsing `current_turn_scratch_root()` to the shared scratch root fails **six** tests — `test_interactive_turn_is_scoped_to_its_own_scratch_workspace`, both `test_turn_cannot_read_other_or_flat_scratch` cases (other-turn and flat-root), the two static-service write cases, and `test_github_activity_repo_read_and_scratch_write_scopes_are_separate`. So this PR's per-turn isolation survived.
- Appending the parent instead of `owned_skill_directory` fails `test_poller_read_scope_is_limited_to_its_server_bound_skill`. So #1365's skill exclusivity survived.

That is the specific thing I could not learn from `mergeable=MERGEABLE`: git resolving cleanly says nothing about whether either invariant is still enforced, and a resolution that silently dropped one would have looked exactly like this.

`-k skill` → 510 passed, 1 skipped. `-k scratch` → 50 passed. `test_access_control.py` + `test_pollers.py` + `test_prompts.py` + `test_turn_prompt_assembly.py` + `test_readonly_backend.py` → 1160 passed, 3 skipped. Clean after restoring both mutations. All 8 checks green.

**On the rebase itself.** The conflict was confined to `tests/test_pollers.py`, as diagnosed; `mimir/access_control.py` auto-merged and kept both the bare-`<home>/scratch` filter and the poller skill-directory append. The resolution retained #1365's `owned_skill_directory` assertion alongside this PR's per-turn context and paths, which is the correct reading of both intents.

Everything from my earlier review at `dab63177c` stands unchanged: the `allow_shared_scratch` hatch has one caller that has already proven containment; the purpose directories cannot regress because `defaults_upgrade` shells `git worktree` and `project_tests` walks directory descriptors, neither passing through the write gate; the prompt tells the model the boundary rather than just the path; and the `turn_id` traversal guard is unreachable-false today (`uuid4().hex[:16]`) but worth keeping.

Merging.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
I reproduced the expected rebase conflict against the current base. It is confined to `tests/test_pollers.py`.

I constructed and inspected the semantic resolution: retain #1365's `service.owned_skill_directory` assertion and poller-owned skill-directory grant, while retaining #1367's current-turn context plus `scratch/turns/fetch-cache-read/...` paths. I also verified the rebased `access_control.py` contains both load-bearing branches:

- filtering bare `<home>/scratch` out of `service.filesystem_read_roots`
- appending `service.owned_skill_directory` for `poller:*` principals

The scoped repository API cannot finish the operation: after resolving the file, `repo_stage` failed twice with generic `repository_git_failed`, and there is no scoped rebase-continue primitive. I escalated that unsupported operation, aborted the rebase cleanly, and removed the checkout. No commit was pushed and no tests were claimed. The remaining mechanical work is to apply that exact resolution in a writable checkout, continue the rebase, run the configured full suite (including the requested skill/scratch coverage), push, and re-request review.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1145: authz: PR review cannot read tests/test_access_control.py inside its own lease because the content scanner flags its secret-shaped fixtures

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes at `3dac3421`. Three items, and I want to be clear up front that **I could not find a way to escape the lease** — the boundary holds. My objections are about scope and a red build, not a vulnerability.

**What I verified is safe.** I built a lease fixture and measured the new exemption directly:

| target | result |
|---|---|
| tracked secret-shaped file in the lease | readable ← the reported case, correctly fixed |
| symlink inside the lease → **outside** target | **withheld** |
| `.git/config` inside the lease | **withheld** (protected name) |
| secret-shaped file outside any lease | **withheld** |

`_target_within_active_pr_checkout_lease` resolves and requires `resolved.relative_to(resolved_root)`, so a link pointing out of the lease fails containment. Delegating to it instead of reimplementing lease matching is exactly what the leaf asked for, and dropping the hand-rolled `scope_id`/`owner`/`lease_root` duplication is a genuine simplification — 45 lines removed.

---

**1. The build is red.** `pytest (3.11)` fails on `tests/test_pollers.py::test_run_poller_timeout_kills_child_holding_pipes` (`assert not child_is_still_running()`). 3.12 passes, the PR does not touch that test, and it is platform-skipped locally so I could not reproduce it — all consistent with an infrastructure flake rather than your change. It still has to be green: either show it is a flake with evidence (a re-run, or the same failure on an untouched branch), or fix it. "Unrelated" is not sufficient on its own.

**2. The git-tracked requirement was removed, and the leaf did not ask for that.**

The old function was named `is_tracked_file_in_current_pr_lease` and its docstring said why: *"Git index membership is the publication proof. Untracked and ignored files remain protected, as do protected path names even when they are tracked."* That is now gone, and three assertions were rewritten to match:

- `assert untracked_grep.matches == []` → `assert any(... "notes.txt" ...)`
- `assert untracked_result.error == result_refusal` → deleted, replaced with `error is None` and `"not published" in content`
- the test renamed from `test_protected_reads_allow_only_tracked_files_in_exact_authorized_pr_lease` to `..._admit_content_only_in_...`

The fixture's own content string is `"not published"`. So the change makes unpublished content readable, and the rename records that as intended.

**Here is why I do not think it was necessary:** the refusal that motivated this leaf was on `pr-leases/.../tests/test_access_control.py` — a **tracked** file. Tracked-ness was never what blocked it. Something else was — most likely lease or scope resolution failing on that turn, which is what your delegation to `resolve_repository_review_state` probably fixed. If so, tracked-ness can stay and the fix still works.

So: state in the PR what was actually refusing the tracked file before, and whether removing the publication-proof requirement was needed for that or incidental to the rewrite. If it was incidental, restore it. A PR author controls tracked content deliberately; untracked files in a checkout are whatever a build step or an earlier lease left behind, and "the author published this" is a meaningfully stronger claim than "this file exists in the directory."

**3. The in-lease symlink assertion was flipped**, `assert result_is_protected(symlink)` → `assert not result_is_protected(symlink)`. I verified this cannot escape, so I am not blocking on danger — but flipping an existing security assertion deserves a sentence saying why the old one was wrong, rather than being adjusted to match new behaviour. If in-lease symlinks are fine because containment is resolved, say that in the test or the docstring; the next reader will otherwise assume the protection was lost by accident.

---

Chainlink #1145's criterion that the PR body state "what a reviewer can now read that it could not, and what remains refused" is unmet — and items 2 and 3 are exactly what it would ha

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approved at `a4c9111b`. Publication proof is restored, the simplification is kept, and I re-measured the whole matrix rather than trusting the diff.

| target | result |
|---|---|
| tracked secret-shaped file in the lease | **readable** ← the reported refusal, fixed |
| untracked file in the lease | withheld |
| symlink → inside the lease | withheld |
| symlink → outside the lease | withheld |
| secret-shaped file outside any lease | withheld |

Exactly the intended shape: the fix reaches the reported case and nothing else moved.

**And you answered the question I actually asked.** The docstring now says what was wrong and what still holds — *"The shared lease resolver and containment check fix the reported refusal … Git index membership remains the publication proof"* — which identifies lease/scope resolution as the real blocker, not tracked-ness. That was my hypothesis and it is now recorded where the next reader will find it.

**Mutation-verified:** replacing `RepoGitTools(state).is_tracked_file(path)` with `True` fails both `test_batched_pr_reads_resolve_each_exact_checkout_lease` and `test_protected_reads_allow_only_tracked_files_in_exact_authorized_pr_lease`. Publication proof is load-bearing, and the second test's name is accurate again.

The valuable part of the original rewrite survived: delegating to `resolve_repository_review_state` and `_target_within_active_pr_checkout_lease` instead of hand-rolling `scope_id`/`owner`/`lease_root` checks. Net 13 lines removed with the security property intact.

**One thing I checked and want to record, because it looked wrong and was not.** The explicit `path.is_symlink()` guard is gone from `read_policy`, and the restored test enforces symlink refusal through its `TrackedRepoGitTools` stub — which reads like a test proving its own mock. It is not: the real `RepoGitTools.is_tracked_file` (`mimir/repo_tools.py:637`) already has `if not path.is_absolute() or path.is_symlink(): return False`. So the removed check was redundant with production, and the stub faithfully models the real contract rather than inventing a guarantee. I verified against the production implementation, not the stub, and the measured `symlink → inside` row above is the end-to-end confirmation.

`tests/test_access_control.py` + `test_pr_checkout_lease.py` → 814 passed, 2 skipped; clean after restoring the mutation. All 8 checks green — including `pytest (3.11)`, which was the flake I cleared by re-running earlier.

Merging.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Item 1 (red build) is cleared — I resolved it rather than leaving it with you.**

I re-ran the failed job (`30830501708`) with no code change and it passed. `pytest (3.11)` is green and all 8 checks are now `ok`. So `test_run_poller_timeout_kills_child_holding_pipes` was a timing flake in a process-kill assertion, not anything your change caused.

For the record on how I established that rather than assuming it: it was the only failed run in the last 25 across the repo, so there was no history supporting "known flake" — a re-run was the only way to distinguish timing from real. Worth remembering the ordering, since "unrelated to my change" and "a real failure my change exposed" look identical from the failure text alone.

**Items 2 and 3 still stand**, and item 2 is the one that matters: the git-tracked publication-proof requirement was removed along with three rewritten assertions and a test rename, and the refusal that motivated this leaf was on a *tracked* file — so tracked-ness was not what blocked it. Please say what was actually refusing that read before, and restore publication-proof if dropping it was incidental to the rewrite rather than required by it.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Addressed all three items in `a4c9111bc`:

- Restored Git index membership as the publication proof. The actual fix is now narrow: resolve the correct repository-scoped review state, reuse `_target_within_active_pr_checkout_lease`, then require `RepoGitTools(state).is_tracked_file(path)`. Untracked/ignored content remains withheld.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1143: authz: a poller cannot read the skill files that define it - social-cli-feed is refused its own SKILL.md and dispatch script

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approved at `41e0b053`. Ownership derived server-side, exclusivity pinned, and the one test case I most expected to be skipped is present.

`owned_skill_directory` is set only at the two poller construction sites — `PollerSpec.resolved_authority` from `self.skill_dir`, and `_parse_poller_authority` from `manifest_path.parent` — and resolved at build time. The model never supplies it, which is the property that made #1133's channel ownership safe and is the right precedent to follow here.

**`test_poller_read_scope_is_limited_to_its_server_bound_skill` covers all four cases**, not just the happy path:

- `SKILL.md`, `pollers.json`, `dispatch-outbox.sh` in its own skill → allowed
- another skill's `dispatch.sh` → **refused**
- a secret-bearing file *inside its own readable skill directory* → **refused**

That third case is the one that usually gets left out. A directory becoming readable is exactly when a secret-content veto stops being exercised, and here it is asserted explicitly.

**Exclusivity is mutation-pinned.** Changing `roots.append(Path(service.owned_skill_directory))` to append the parent — granting all of `skills/` — fails that test. So the boundary is the owned directory, not the skills tree.

`tests/test_access_control.py` + `test_agent.py` + `test_pollers.py` → 1093 passed, 3 skipped; clean after restoring both mutations. All 8 checks green.

---

One observation, explicitly **not** a blocker. The principal-type guard is unpinned:

```python
if (getattr(service, "trigger", None) == "poller"
    and str(getattr(service, "canonical", "")).startswith("poller:")
    and getattr(service, "owned_skill_directory", None)):
```

Deleting the first two conditions fails no test. That is because nothing currently sets `owned_skill_directory` on a non-poller principal, so the check is unreachable-false rather than untested-live.

I am treating this differently from the inert capability grant I asked you to remove on #1362, and the distinction is worth stating: that was a *grant* whose presence implied a permission it did not confer, which misleads an auditor. This is a *guard* whose removal would widen access — cheap insurance that costs nothing while it is redundant. Keep it. But if a non-poller principal ever gains an owned skill directory (an upgrade or synthesis principal reading its own skill, say), that guard becomes load-bearing with no test behind it, so pin it then.

Merging. This is the last of the four leaves from the post-0.7.1 refusal scan.

payload.title: Worklink #1144: authz: the global git option strip landed only in upgrade_workspace, so repo_review still refuses git --no-ext-diff -C

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approved at `ddf61449`. Shared, not copied — which was the whole point.

`_git_arguments_without_restrictive_global_options` is called from `_upgrade_workspace_git_execution_argv`, `_repo_review_git_execution_argv`, and `_target_matches_repo_review_shell_command`. There is exactly **one** loop over `{"--no-pager", "--no-ext-diff"}` left in the file, and it is the helper's own body. The inline copy #1141 introduced is gone rather than left beside the new helper, so a third profile will not need a third fix.

The docstring frames the safety argument correctly — "global Git options that can only make inspection more restrictive" — which is the property that makes stripping them free rather than a widening.

**The risk I flagged did not materialize.** Sharing option handling could have leaked root scope between profiles; it did not. Measured directly on both binders:

| binder | root | result |
|---|---|---|
| `upgrade_workspace` | own `scratch/proposals/...` | bound (bare and `--no-ext-diff`) |
| `upgrade_workspace` | a PR lease | refused |
| `repo_review` | a proposal directory | refused |

Each profile still binds `-C` to its own root: `scratch/proposals` for upgrade, the lease root for review.

**Mutation-verified across both profiles.** Narrowing the helper back to `{"--no-pager"}` fails four tests — the three `test_repo_review_git_admits_restrictive_global_options_before_c` cases (parametrized over `diff`/`log`/`show`) and `test_upgrade_workspace_git_is_proposal_scoped_and_read_only`. One line, two profiles, both directions covered. That is the strongest evidence the sharing is real rather than cosmetic.

`test_read_only_git_profiles_refuse_global_config_injection` also covers the criterion I cared about most after the strip itself: `git -c <config>` stays refused under both profiles, so the strip did not become a general pre-`-C` option gate.

`tests/test_access_control.py` → 786 passed, 2 skipped; clean after restoring the mutation. All 8 checks green.

One note on my own verification: my first probe reported `repo_review` refusing even its own lease, which would have looked like the fix not working. That was my `state` stub supplying only `.root` where the real review state carries more; the PR's parametrized test uses the real fixture and passes. Fifth time tonight a hand-rolled fixture of mine produced a false negative — the pattern is consistent enough that I now treat a lone red probe result as suspect until the PR's own tests agree.

Merging.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1141: authz: the 0.7.0 upgrade-reconciliation turn on muninn is hard-blocked from inspecting the proposal workspace it created (81 real refusals in six minutes)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes at `118eaf05`. **37 of the 46 refused git calls are fixed and I verified it; 3 remain, for a reason the diff makes easy to miss.**

**What works, measured rather than read.** With a real git repository as the proposal workspace, `_upgrade_workspace_git_execution_argv` binds the dominant recorded shapes:

```
git -C <proposal> show --stat                    -> BOUND
git -C <proposal> show :memory/core/a.md         -> BOUND
```

That second form is the one that mattered most — 35 of the 63 `profile_allowlist` refusals on muninn were `git -C <proposal> show|diff|log`. Delegating to `_maintenance_git_execution_argv` after validating `-C` against `scratch/proposals` is the right structure: the root binding is the new part, and the hardening (fsmonitor/hooks/credential neutering, `--no-ext-diff --no-textconv` appended to diff-producing subcommands) is inherited rather than reimplemented.

**And what must stay refused does.** I checked each: composition (`> /tmp/x && wc -l`), a `-C` outside the proposal root, `git push`, `cat`, `python3 <script>`, and `grep -rn` with metacharacters — all refused, and the last three now carry guidance naming the typed tool. `git -c <config>` before `-C` stays refused, which is right; that is the config-injection vector the binder exists to stop.

The `prompts` carve-out in `_is_service_protected_read_path` is tightly drawn and I want to note I checked its bounds: upgrade principal only, proposal root only, and only when `prompts` is the *sole* protected component — so `prompts/.git/token` still refuses because `.git` also matches. That is the right shape for admitting `git show :prompts/heartbeat.md` without opening the protected-name list.

---

**The remaining 3: `--no-ext-diff` in the global position.**

The binder strips only `--no-pager` before requiring `-C`:

```python
arguments = argv[1:]
if arguments[:1] == ["--no-pager"]:
    arguments = arguments[1:]
if arguments[:1] != ["-C"] or len(arguments) < 3:
    return None
```

`--no-ext-diff` was added to the *subcommand* option allowlist, which covers `git -C <root> diff --no-ext-diff`. But the recorded refusals have it as a *global* option, before `-C`. Grouping every refused git input on muninn by what precedes `-C`:

| before `-C` | count | after this PR |
|---|---|---|
| *(nothing)* | 37 | fixed |
| `--no-ext-diff` | **3** | **still refused** |
| no `-C` at all | 3 | correctly refused |
| `--no-pager` | 1 | fixed |
| `-c <config>` | 1 | correctly refused |

Confirmed directly: `git --no-ext-diff -C <proposal> diff --stat` returns `None` from the binder while the same command without the global option binds.

Accepting it there is safe and arguably free — `--no-ext-diff` only *disables* external diff, and the binder already appends `--no-ext-diff --no-textconv` to diff subcommands, so honouring it pre-`-C` is redundant hardening rather than new capability. Strip it alongside `--no-pager` (and consider `--no-textconv` for symmetry), then add a test for the global position. The existing `--no-ext-diff` test cases are attack strings asserting refusal; none covers the legitimate pre-`-C` form, which is why this passed CI.

---

**One correction about my own process.** My first run of this check reported all three git shapes as refused, and I nearly reported the whole fix as non-functional. The cause was my probe: I created the proposal directory without `git init`, so `_maintenance_git_filter_overrides` could not inspect a repository and the binder bailed. That is the fourth time tonight a probe of mine produced a false negative, and the fix each time was to make the fixture match production rather than to trust the first red result.

`tests/test_access_control.py` + `test_information_flow.py` + `test_tool_registry.py` → 1085 passed, 2 skipped. All 8 checks green.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approved at `d3f44826`. The gap is closed and I verified the whole matrix rather than the one line that changed.

The strip is now a loop over both global options, which handles them in either order and repeated:

```python
while arguments[:1] and arguments[0] in {"--no-pager", "--no-ext-diff"}:
```

**Measured at this head**, with a real git repository as the proposal workspace (the fixture detail that produced my false negative last round):

| command | expected | actual |
|---|---|---|
| `git -C <proposal> show --stat` | allow | allow |
| `git -C <proposal> show :memory/core/a.md` | allow | allow |
| `git -C <proposal> show :prompts/heartbeat.md` | allow | allow |
| `git --no-ext-diff -C <proposal> diff --stat` | allow | **allow** ← the 3 that remained |
| `git --no-pager -C <proposal> show --stat` | allow | allow |
| `git -C <proposal> log --oneline` | allow | allow |
| `git -C <proposal> show --stat > /tmp/x && wc -l` | refuse | refuse |
| `git -C <outside> show --stat` | refuse | refuse |
| `git -C <proposal> push origin HEAD` | refuse | refuse |
| `git -c core.pager=evil -C <proposal> show` | refuse | refuse |
| `cat <proposal>/memory/core/a.md` | refuse | refuse |
| `python3 -c 'print(1)'` | refuse | refuse |

Zero mismatches. All 46 recorded git refusals are now accounted for: 41 admitted, and the 5 that stay refused are the ones that should — no `-C` at all (3) and `-c <config>` injection (1), plus composition.

**Both new properties are mutation-pinned by `test_upgrade_workspace_git_is_proposal_scoped_and_read_only`:** removing the `resolve_within_roots([proposal_root], ...)` binding fails it, and narrowing the strip set back to `{"--no-pager"}` fails it. One test, both directions — the scope bound and the option handling.

I also checked a concern that turned out unfounded: `required_safety_options = {"--no-ext-diff", "--no-textconv"}` looked like it might make those mandatory on *input*, which would have regressed `git -C <proposal> show --stat`. It does not — that requirement sits on a different validation path and the binder appends them to the execution argv. Worth recording that I checked, since the diff reads as though it could.

`tests/test_access_control.py` + `test_information_flow.py` + `test_tool_registry.py` → 1085 passed, 2 skipped; clean after restoring both mutations. All 8 checks green.

Merging. This unblocks the 81 hard refusals that stopped muninn's 0.7.0 reconciliation from reading the proposal it authored — which is the whole point of the 0.7.1 release.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1142: authz: upgrade reconciliation cannot see its own proposal PR - gh pr view is admin_required (shadow today, breaks the flow when enforcement is enabled)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes at `c97c1c1a`. **The substantive fix is right; the part that looks like the fix is inert.**

**What is correct, and it is the important half.** The prompt guidance added to `enqueue_upgrade_reconciliation_turn` addresses the actual cause — the turn reaching for `gh` because nothing told it not to. It names the four typed tools, forbids `gh pr view`/`gh pr list` explicitly, forbids shell `ls` and composed pipes/globs, and resolves the notification target from `MIMIR_OPERATOR_ALERT_CHANNEL` instead of calling `list_channels`. I checked that variable is real and, better, that it is the same one `access_control.py:635` binds the `operator_alert` sink policy to — so the turn is directed at exactly the channel its own sink permits. That coherence is not accidental and it is the right shape: the leaf said not to admit `gh` to a shell profile, and this instead removes the reason to reach for it.

The two refusal guards are also welcome: `test_upgrade_gh_pr_shell_attempt_stays_refused` is parametrized over both argv shapes I recorded on muninn, and `test_upgrade_channel_discovery_stays_refused` pins the `list_channels` decision. Both pass on `main` as well, which is expected for regression guards — they lock behaviour in place rather than changing it.

---

**1. The capability grant does not grant anything.**

Adding `pr_metadata`/`pr_checks`/`pr_reviews`/`pr_comments` to the `upgrade` principal, plus `repository` to `readable_domains`, changes no authorization outcome. Measured on both trees:

| | `main` | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `pr_metadata` in `principal.capabilities` | False | **True** |
| authorize with no PR scope | denied `repo_pr_scope_denied` | denied `repo_pr_scope_denied` |
| authorize with a PR scope | **allowed** | **allowed** |

Access is governed entirely by the repo/PR scope. The declared list moved; the decision did not.

**2. `test_upgrade_pr_state_access_is_typed_and_enforced` does not test this change.** It passes on `main` unmodified, and it passes on this branch with the four capabilities deleted again. It injects a `RepoPRScopeRegistry`, which is what actually permits the call, so it demonstrates that scoped PR reads work — true before and after — rather than that the grant does anything.

I want to be precise about what I did and did not establish: I measured the authorization outcome for these four tools. I did not establish that the capability entries are useless for every purpose — `service_can_invoke_operation` and capability-inventory reporting also read that list, and one of those may be why you added them.

So, either:

- **Drop the capability and `readable_domains` additions** if scope alone is what permits these reads. The prompt guidance stands on its own and is the real fix.
- **Or keep them and make the test discriminate** — assert the denial that occurs *without* the grant, so the entry is pinned to an observable consequence. If no such consequence exists, that is the argument for dropping them.

A declared grant that reads as load-bearing but changes no decision is worse than no grant: the next person auditing which principals can read PRs will believe this list is the answer, and it is not.

**3. Record the per-shape findings in code.** Chainlink #1142's first criterion asked the PR body to state, for each refused shape, whether the refusal was correct and what happens instead. The body is the generated template, and I now think asking a worklink build for prose there is asking for something the harness does not provide — so put it as a short comment above the guidance block instead: the three shapes observed on muninn (`gh pr view`/`gh pr list`, shell `ls` with a pipe and with a glob, `list_channels`), that each refusal is correct, and that the guidance exists so the turn does not attempt them. That is where the next reader will look, and it survives.

Also worth stating there, since it is easy to misread later: these refusals were **shadow-only** when filed. `MIMIR_ACCESS_C

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approved at `4e1a4e3b`. Both items resolved, and resolved the way I'd have chosen.

**The inert capability grant is gone.** `mimir/access_control.py` is no longer touched at all, and `test_upgrade_pr_state_access_is_typed_and_enforced` — which passed identically on `main`, with the grant, and without it — is deleted rather than patched. That is the right call: I measured that the four `pr_*` entries changed no authorization outcome because access is governed entirely by the repo/PR scope, and a declared grant that changes no decision is worse than none, since it misleads whoever next audits which principals can read PRs. Removing the mechanism and the test that appeared to validate it, together, is cleaner than keeping either.

**The provenance is recorded in the durable place**, and it says the thing that mattered most:

```python
# Muninn's observed `gh pr view`/`gh pr list`, shell `ls` with a pipe
# or glob, and `list_channels` refusals were all correct and shadow-only:
# they carried would_block=True/is_shadow_decision=True while enforcement
# was disabled. This guidance prevents those calls before enforcement is enabled.
```

That is exactly right, including the shadow-only distinction. A future reader will not conclude the reconciliation flow was broken in 0.7.0 — it was not; those calls proceeded.

**What remains is load-bearing and pinned.** The prompt guidance is the actual fix: it steers the turn to the typed PR tools, forbids `gh pr view`/`gh pr list` and shell composition, and resolves the notification target from `MIMIR_OPERATOR_ALERT_CHANNEL` — the same variable `access_control.py:635` binds the `operator_alert` sink policy to, so the turn is directed at exactly the channel its own sink permits. Dropping the `list_channels` sentence from the prompt fails `test_upgrade_reconciliation_turn_renders_template_and_enqueues`, so the guidance is not decorative.

The two refusal guards survive and both are parametrized over the argv shapes I recorded on muninn: `gh pr view`/`gh pr list` stay refused, and `list_channels` stays `admin_required`. They pass on `main` too, which is correct for regression guards — they lock behaviour rather than change it.

`tests/test_access_control.py` + `test_defaults_upgrade.py` + `test_tool_registry.py` → 919 passed, 2 skipped; clean after restoring the mutation. All 8 checks green.

Merging. With #1363 this completes both muninn refusal classes: the 81 hard blocks are fixed, and this one prevents the shadow class from becoming real when enforcement is enabled.

Addressed in `4e1a4e3b4`:

- removed the inert upgrade-principal PR-read capabilities and `repository` readable-domain declaration
- removed the nondiscriminating authorization test and corresponding capability-inventory assertions
- documented above the prompt guidance that the three observed refusal shapes were correct and shadow-only on Muninn, and that the guidance prevents those calls before enforcement is enabled
