payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1140: docs: document the code-building pipeline end to end for 0.7.0 - repositories.yaml, worklink config, the strict leaf format and its silent auto-demotion, the ready-queue poller, and the github poller

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approved at `0397cbb9`. I spot-checked the factual claims against code rather than reading for plausibility, and they hold — including one that is more precise than I would have written myself.

**The marker pin is the right mechanism and it is load-bearing.** `test_documented_leaf_markers_match_validator` imports `_REQUIRED_SECTIONS` and asserts **tuple equality** against the documented block, not substring presence. Dropping a single trailing colon from `- Suggested test command:` in the doc fails it. That is exactly the failure mode that cost real filing round-trips — a marker that looks right and silently fails validation — now caught mechanically.

**Claims I verified against source at this commit:**

| doc claim | code |
|---|---|
| `max_concurrent` default 2 | matches; `WORKLINK_MAX_CONCURRENT` is legacy-only when the YAML key is absent |
| leaf claim budget is three charged attempts | `ChainlinkClaims.__init__(max_attempts: int = 3)` |
| `defaults.max_claim_attempts` is compatibility-only and does not change the budget | **correct** — parsed at `backends/registry.py:216`, and no call site passes it to `ChainlinkClaims`, so it is genuinely inert |
| at most two reset markers honored | `MAX_CLAIM_RESETS = 2` |
| invalid leaf loses `worklink:ready`, gains `worklink:blocked`, gets a `WORKLINK_BLOCKED` comment, no attempt consumed | matches observed behaviour |

The `max_claim_attempts` line deserves specific credit: it documents a latent wiring gap — a config key that is parsed and then ignored — instead of describing what the key looks like it should do. That is the harder and more useful thing to write, and it is the kind of claim I would normally have to go check because prose usually gets it wrong in the optimistic direction.

**§4 distinguishes `worklink:ready` from `chainlink issue ready`** with the consequence spelled out: an unblocked issue can appear in `chainlink issue ready` and never be claimed. I hit that confusion twice tonight — on #1123 and again on #1138 — so having it written down is worth more than its two lines suggest.

**It ships.** The new file is top-level `docs/*.md`, and `doc_seed` enumerates with `sorted(docs_dir.glob("*.md"))` excluding `docs/internal/`, so it lands in the wheel force-include and gets seeded to `<home>/docs/` with no packaging change required. `test_worklink_pipeline_docs.py` + `test_doc_seed.py` + `test_wheel_package_data.py` + `test_docs_enforcement_claims.py` + `test_config_docs_complete.py` → 26 passed. All 8 checks green.

**And it correctly stayed out of the environment-variable area**, which was the instruction I got wrong when filing this leaf: I claimed 52 undocumented vars and no detecting test, having measured `.env.example` when `docs/configuration.md` is the reference. It documents all 96 and `test_config_docs_complete.py` already enforces it bidirectionally with a meta-test against scanner vacuity. Nothing here duplicates or contradicts that.

Merging. This is the last leaf before the 0.7.0 release, and it is the one whose output ships to every install.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1139: authz: memory read access is a growing exact-path allowlist - state one rule instead: any turn may read all of memory except another channel's directory

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approved at `01edb607`. This is the right shape — one invariant replacing the allowlist, with `mimir/read_policy.py` net **−80 lines**. The carve-outs were removed rather than layered, which was the criterion I cared about most.

**The rule reads as the invariant:**

```python
for relative in relatives:
    if relative.parts[:1] == ("channels",) and len(relative.parts) > 1:
        if relative.parts[1] != channel_id:
            return False
return True
```

Checking both the resolved and the lexical relative is a good call I did not ask for — it closes the gap where a symlink inside `memory/` resolves outside the channel it appears to be in.

**Measured posture at this head**, enforcement unset as live, session bound to `channel-a`:

| target | read boundary |
|---|---|
| `memory/core/00-identity.md` | allowed |
| `memory/channels/channel-a/**` (own) | allowed |
| **`memory/channels/channel-b/**` (other)** | **withheld — `service_scoped_read_boundary`** |
| `memory/issues/note.md` | allowed ← the gap that started this |
| `memory/learnings-pending.md`, `memory/INDEX.md` | allowed |
| `state/liveness.json`, repo file | allowed (unchanged) |
| `memory/issues/.git/token` | withheld — `protected_name_match` |

**Exclusivity is strongly pinned.** Dropping the other-channel comparison fails six tests across three files, including the new `test_memory_read_rule_compares_session_channel_ownership`. `tests/test_agent.py` + `test_access_control.py` + `test_readonly_backend.py` + `test_pollers.py` → 1194 passed, 3 skipped; clean after restoring. All 8 checks green.

**The `authorize_tool` reordering is better than what I asked for.** I expected the memory rule to be additive at the read-boundary only. Instead:

```python
allowed = scoped_read_allowed or (service_allowed and not targets_memory)
elif service_allowed: allowed = True
```

Capability alone still admits non-memory reads — repo roots, artifacts, `state/` — while anything under `memory/` must pass the rule. That gets the property I blocked #1357 over (no silent revocation of the capability fast-path) *and* moves exclusivity into the authorization layer instead of relying on the backend, which is where I said on #1353 the coverage was thin. Verified on Linux that `resolved_read_target_from_arguments` handles both the virtual (`/memory/...`) and absolute (`<home>/memory/...`) forms, so `targets_memory` is not form-dependent on the deployment platform.

Removing `test_missing_owned_channel_file_does_not_report_missing_root` and `test_missing_declared_service_channel_memory_root_is_observable` is correct: both existed to observe a per-principal derived root that can no longer be missing, because the rule no longer derives one. Deleting obsolete guards along with the mechanism they guarded is the right instinct.

One note for whoever reads this later, not a defect: `non_admin_read_filter_enabled` now treats any service principal as having read scope (`filesystem_read_roots or is_service`) rather than requiring non-empty roots. That is necessary for the rule to apply to principals with no declared roots, and it widens which turns are subject to the read filter — a tightening, in the safe direction. Worth knowing it changed.

Merging. This closes the third leaf in a row on memory read policy; the difference is that this one states a rule, so a fourth directory does not need a fourth leaf.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1138: authz: every turn should be able to read core memories, but service principals are refused - the heartbeat cannot read its own core files

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Closing unmerged. The premise of chainlink #1138 was false and the fault is mine, not this build's.

I filed #1138 from 27 `protected_read_target` denials on `memory/core` for the `heartbeat` principal without checking their timestamps. All 27 fall between 2026-08-01T12:00 and 21:00; mimirbot restarted 2026-08-02T15:03; there have been zero since. The reason string `protected_read_target` no longer exists in the source — it is the old catch-all that #1336 replaced — so those events came from code that had not run in over a day.

Measured against the deployed code (`dc310c79`) with `MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED` unset exactly as live, and with the read filter genuinely active (`filesystem_read_roots`=2, `non_admin_read_filter_enabled()`=True):

    protected_read_denial_reason(memory/core/00-identity.md) -> None
    WriteGuardBackend.read('/memory/core/00-identity.md')    -> content returned, error None

Confirmed again on current main after #1357 merged (`f2993e4e`): core reads return `None` for a service principal. There was nothing to fix.

Beyond the false premise, this change is not behaviour-neutral. Adding `<home>/memory/core` to `roots` in `is_current_service_protected_read_path` newly applies the trigger-service protected-NAME list inside core memory — your own test pins that with `core/config`. Core memory is readable today because it is simply not protected; this makes it explicitly scoped and simultaneously withholds a subset of it. The operator's stated posture is that **every turn should be able to read core memories**, so a change whose net effect is to withhold more of core moves the wrong way, however small the affected set.

The work itself is competent and the test is well constructed — it separates readable, protected-name, and secret-content cases cleanly. If we later want the carve-out made explicit as hardening rather than relying on core happening not to match the protected predicate, that is worth doing on a truthful premise and with the name-filtering decision made deliberately rather than as a side effect. It would need its own leaf.

Sorry for the wasted build. The specific error was reading a tail of the events log as current state, which I had explicitly checked for earlier the same night on a different set of events and then failed to check here.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1137: authz: synthesis can write a channel's memory for its own session but cannot read it back, because the read path has no session binding

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes at `4735214a`.

**The part I was most worried about is done correctly.** `_synthesis_target_matches_session` is split so the channel-matching arm is shared while the write predicate keeps its own `except ValueError: return True`, and the new read arm returns `False` there instead. That was the trap I named on the chainlink — reusing the permissive branch for reads would have admitted `memory/core` — and it is avoided. `synthesis_session_channel_memory_root` guards `channel_id` against traversal the same way #1133 did, `_is_synthesis_shared_memory_path` admits `learnings-pending.md` by exact resolved equality rather than a prefix rule, and both the authorization layer and the read-boundary layer were updated together rather than one drifting from the other. That is careful work.

Two things block it, and the first is the significant one.

---

**1. This replaces synthesis's read scope rather than extending it, and pins the replacement.**

On `main`, synthesis reads are admitted at the authorization layer by capability alone:

```python
elif service_allowed:        # service_can_invoke_operation(principal, tool_name)
    allowed = True           # no target check at all
```

`synthesis` holds `read_file`/`aread`/`ls`/`glob`/`grep` in `TRIGGER_AUTHORITY_PROFILES["session-boundary"]`, so every read target is admitted here today, with only the read-boundary layer withholding protected paths.

The new branch is inserted **before** that `elif`, and inside it:

```python

relative = resolved.relative_to(home_root)   # ValueError for anything outside MIMIR_HOME
except (OSError, RuntimeError, ValueError): return False
```

So every path outside `MIMIR_HOME` now returns `False` — including every repository checkout. `/workspace/mimir` is in synthesis's own `filesystem_read_roots` (they are built from `repo_roots` plus `artifact_root`), so this revokes read access the principal currently has and that its declared roots still advertise. `test_synthesis_reads_only_its_session_channel_and_explicit_shared_memory` locks that in as intended behaviour.

I want to be fair about this: capability-allowed-with-no-target-check is a weak posture, and narrowing it is defensible on the merits. But three things make it wrong to land here. The leaf asked to fix an asymmetry by **adding** the read half of an existing write rule; silently revoking a broad existing capability is not that. Nothing tests what synthesis **retains** — every new assertion is about what is now denied, so a legitimate session-end read that breaks tomorrow has no failing test today. And session-end reflection plausibly reads repo files, which is exactly the workload with no coverage either way.

Two acceptable resolutions. Make the grant **additive** — admit the session channel and `learnings-pending.md` in addition to what the principal is already allowed, leaving the `service_allowed` path intact. Or keep the tightening, say so explicitly in the body with its blast radius, and add a test for what synthesis must still reach. My preference is additive here and a separate leaf for narrowing `service_allowed`, because the narrowing deserves its own operator decision rather than arriving as a side effect.

**2. The body omits the statement the pre-claim note required.**

The executor note added to #1137 before claim said: if `channel_id` is absent from read denials, implement against the code-level asymmetry and **state plainly in the PR body that measured attribution was unavailable because the telemetry was not yet deployed**. The telemetry (#1136, `47b62258`) is merged but not deployed — I verified 0 of 300 sampled `hard_boundary_denied` events carry the field — so this build necessarily took the no-data branch, and the body is the bare template.

That statement is not bookkeeping. It is the difference between "the scope was confirmed against measured attribution" and "the scope was inferred from the write-side rule, a

**The permissive-branch guard is not pinned, and the test is shaped to look as though it is.**

**Correcting my previous review — the core-memory finding was framed backwards, and there is a real regression I mis-described.**

The operator's intent, stated directly: a session-boundary turn **should** be able to READ core memories; it should not write them. My chainlink criterion said "a test proves `memory/core` stays refused for synthesis." That criterion was wrong, and my last review built on it.

I measured both versions at the read-boundary layer, with a synthesis turn bound to `channel-a`:

| target | `main` | this PR (`89c9d989`) |
|---|---|---|
| `memory/core/00-persona.md` | allowed (`None`) | **withheld — `service_scoped_read_boundary`** |
| `memory/channels/channel-a/summary.md` | withheld | **allowed** ← the intended fix |
| `state/liveness.json` | allowed (`None`) | **withheld — `service_scoped_read_boundary`** |

`authorize_tool` allows all three in both versions; the change is entirely at the read-boundary layer, so the authorization decision looks clean while the backend withholds the content.

**So the defect is `synthesis_scope_denied` in `protected_read_denial_reason`**, not a missing test:

```python
synthesis_scope_denied = (
    ... canonical_principal == "synthesis" ... and not service_scoped
)
general_protected = (not service_scoped and is_protected_read_path(path)) or synthesis_scope_denied
```

For synthesis, `service_scoped` is satisfied only by `filesystem_read_roots` (repo roots plus the artifact root) or the two new grants. `memory/core` and `state/` are in neither, so both flip from readable to withheld. That is a revocation of exactly the access a session-boundary turn needs — reading its own identity and reflection policy is the point of the trigger.

**What to change:** remove `synthesis_scope_denied` entirely. The channel-memory and `learnings-pending.md` grants are additive on their own — they add `service_scoped` cases without taking any away, which is what the leaf asked for. With that clause gone, `memory/core` and `state/` return to `None`, the session channel becomes readable, and nothing else moves.

**And withdraw my previous item.** I reported that mutating the read arm to `except ValueError: return True` "opens a hole admitting core memory." Admitting core memory on READ is desired, so that mutation surviving is not a defect. What the read arm must still do is keep the *write* predicate's non-channel permissiveness out of the *channel-ownership* decision, so another channel's directory is never matched — and `test_poller_turn_cannot_read_another_pollers_channel_memory` plus the cross-channel fixtures are the right place to pin that. The unasserted `other_note` fixture in the retention test is still worth an assertion for that reason. `core_note`, `protected_note` and `operator_secret` should be asserted as **allowed or refused according to the intended posture**, which for core is now allowed — not refused as I previously wrote.

I have not verified the write side. Whether `memory/core` **writes** are still refused for synthesis is unchanged by this PR as far as I can tell, but I did not measure it, and I am not asserting it. Worth confirming before merge given the read posture just changed.

Apologies for the churn — two of my three items on this PR were wrong, and both errors came from a chainlink criterion I authored on an assumption I never checked.

payload.title: Worklink #1130: project tests: exceeding the 64 KiB output cap SIGKILLs the test run, so a passing suite is reported as a failure

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes at `4c299bfa` — for one line, with everything else verified. The head move from `55a2c7f78` was a pure rebase (parent `d9af005b` → `47b62258`, patch byte-identical), so my verification below applies to this head.

**The fix is right and it is pinned.** The kill is now conditioned on `timed_out` alone; the cap became a ring buffer that keeps the tail. Re-adding the cap to the kill condition — `if timed_out or any(dropped_bytes.values())` — fails **both** new parametrized cases, so the central behaviour is load-bearing rather than incidentally passing.

The tests replaced a mocked `ProjectTestProcessResult` with a real subprocess emitting 8000 lines and a final marker, parametrized across exit 0 and exit 1. That is the difference between asserting the code says "passed" and asserting a passing suite is actually reported as passing, and it is the right call.

Verified as well:

- **Memory stays bounded.** `os.read(..., 8192)` per chunk with an immediate trim puts the peak at `output_limit + 8192`, so hundreds of megabytes cannot grow the parent.
- **The no-newline edge case is correct, not a bug** — I measured it rather than reasoning about it. A subprocess emitting 200,000 bytes with no newline at all, exiting 0, yields `returncode=0`, `output_limited=True`, `stdout_dropped_bytes=200000`, `len(stdout)=0`. Everything is discarded, which is the consistent application of the partial-line rule: with no newline the whole buffer is one bisected line and prefix-based redaction cannot be trusted on it. Crucially the status is still correct and the drop is still declared, so a reader cannot mistake it for a clean short log. I want it on the record that I checked this and consider it right, so nobody later "fixes" it into leaking a bisected token.
- The partial-first-line discard and its comment are a real improvement I did not ask for, and they are what preserves the old code's security property while dropping its false failure.
- `tests/test_repo_tools.py` → 109 passed.

---

**The one item: the removal is half finished.** This PR deletes the only producer of the `test_output_limit` code, but `mimir/tools/repo.py:58` still lists it in `_PROJECT_TEST_EXECUTION_REFUSAL_CODES`:

```python
_PROJECT_TEST_EXECUTION_REFUSAL_CODES = frozenset({
    "test_execution_failed",
    "test_output_limit",      # <- no longer reachable
    "test_timeout",
    "tests_failed",
})
```

That set is what `_tool_refusal` uses to separate execution faults from policy refusals, so the entry is inert — nothing can misclassify, because nothing emits the code any more. I am still asking for it, for two reasons. It is a stated convention here that a removal on a pre-release surface is done cleanly rather than leaving a compatibility residue. And an unreachable entry in a refusal-classification set reads, to the next person auditing that classification, as a case that can still occur — which is a small lie in exactly the place where precision matters.

Delete the entry. If `repo.py` also documents the code anywhere in a docstring or tool description, that goes too. Nothing else is outstanding; add that and I will approve on the next push.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approved at `bb8f8707`. The residue is gone — `test_output_limit` deleted from `_PROJECT_TEST_EXECUTION_REFUSAL_CODES`, and zero real references remain repo-wide. The only remaining grep hit is the substring inside the test function name `test_project_test_output_limit_preserves_real_status_and_final_lines`, which I checked rather than assumed.

`mimir/project_tests.py` and `tests/test_repo_tools.py` are byte-identical to `4c299bfa`, so everything I verified there carries over unchanged:

- Re-adding the output cap to the kill condition fails **both** new parametrized cases, so the central fix is load-bearing.
- Peak memory is `output_limit + 8192` given the per-chunk read and immediate trim.
- The no-newline case discards everything while still reporting `returncode=0`, `output_limited=True` and the full dropped-byte count — measured, correct, and deliberately so.

All 8 checks green. Merging.

The practical effect is worth stating plainly: before this, any suite whose output exceeded 64 KiB was SIGKILLed and reported as a failure regardless of whether it passed. Every worklink build runs its suite through this path, so a chatty-but-green suite could fail a build for reasons that had nothing to do with the change under test — and the evidence would show a kill, not a cause.

Approved at `f67f3bc5`. One line of implementation, in the right place, with tests that pin the property I actually cared about.

`"channel_id": getattr(auth_context, "channel_id", None)` sits inside the existing `payload` dict, which is built *after* the function's two-step fallback resolution of `auth_context` — so it uses the resolved context rather than the raw parameter, which was the first acceptance criterion. `getattr(..., None)` always writes the key, so an unbound channel records an explicit null instead of a missing field. No second emitter, no admit/deny change.

**The tests are better designed than the criterion required.** Both deliberately deny a target under `/memory/channels/denied-target/secret.md` while the bound channel is `session-channel` — so the path and the answer disagree by construction. I mutated the implementation to derive the channel from the denied path:

```python
"channel_id": str(target).split("/memory/channels/")[1].split("/")[0] ...
```

Both new tests fail. That is exactly the circularity the review criteria forbade, and it is now caught rather than merely prohibited in prose. The three existing exact-dict assertions in `test_access_control.py`, `test_prohibited_action_guard.py` and the alias suite were updated, which doubles as the consumers-still-parse check.

`test_budget_gate_and_alias.py`, `test_access_control.py`, `test_prohibited_action_guard.py` → 889 passed, 2 skipped, tree clean after restoring the mutation. All 8 checks green.

---

**A limitation to record, and it is my spec's fault rather than this PR's.** I wrote `shadow_tool_decision` events as out of scope on chainlink #1136, so this change covers `hard_boundary_denied` only. The `read_scope` denial class takes a different path — `authorize_tool` sets `reason = "read_scope"` and it surfaces through `_emit_shadow_decision` → `AuthorizationDecision.as_log_fields()`, whose payload has no `channel_id` and still does not. So read denials are now attributable for the `protected_read_target` and `service_scoped_read_boundary` reasons but not for `read_scope`.

That does not block the leaf this was filed to unblock. Every synthesis denial I measured on 2026-08-02 was `protected_read_target` or `service_scoped_read_boundary` — both `hard_boundary_denied` — so #1137 gets the datum it needs. The `read_scope` rows in that corpus were `poller:pypi-deps-watch` and `poller:github-activity`, which #1133 has since addressed by a different route.

Adding `channel_id` to `as_log_fields()` would finish the job and is a one-field change of the same shape. payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1134: worklink: factory cleanup fails every ten minutes and records its reason as None

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes at `eeeca657`.

**The root cause is correctly identified and removed.** `reason=f"Cleanup failed: {alert.reason}"` propagated the *input* alert's reason — which is `None` for a cleanup-eligible alert — so every failure rendered as `Cleanup failed: None`. Deleting that block and having each branch name its own reason is the right fix, and `command_failure` synthesizing `"failed without a reason"` for empty output is exactly #1349's approach rather than a parallel one, which was the first review criterion. Setting `status="failed"` also corrects a real absurdity: the 30 recorded events all carry `status: "completed"`, because the old code copied the run's status onto a cleanup-failure alert.

Three things block it.

---

**1. The escalation key is the full reason text, and that text embeds raw CLI output.**

`record_failure` decides repetition with `repeated = entry.cleanup_failure_reason == reason`, and `command_failure` interpolates `msg`, which `_run_factory_cleanup` returns as `proc.stderr or proc.stdout` (line 695) or `str(exc)`. If that output varies between polls by even one character — a path, a run count, a timestamp, a differing git message — then `repeated` is `False` every cycle, `failure_count` resets to 1, `already_escalated` resets to `False`, and the poller emits a fresh `worklink_factory_cleanup_failed` on **every** poll. It never escalates and never suppresses.

That is the 28-repetitions-in-a-row symptom this issue was filed for, reproduced exactly, with better text on each line.

The escalation test cannot catch it because it stubs cleanup as `(False, "", None)` — an empty message, so the synthesized reason is constant by construction. Key the counter on a stable classifier instead: the failing stage plus which branch produced it (`preview`, `execution`, `digest-not-eligible`, `worktree-unidentified`), and carry the variable text as payload on the alert rather than as part of the identity. Then add a case where the stub returns a *different* message each call and assert it still escalates on the second failure.

**2. Silence after escalation is terminal, and that is pinned as intended.**

`assert poller._run_lifecycle_reconciliation(tmp_path, state_dir) == []` on the third cycle makes it explicit: once `cleanup_failure_escalated` is set, that failure never emits again. Nothing clears the flag except a fingerprint change.

I do not think that is the right trade, and the argument is this issue's own history: the 28 events repeated from roughly 14:00 to 17:20 and nobody acted on them — they surfaced only because I went looking through `events.jsonl`. Under this change that becomes one escalation, and if it is missed, a permanently broken cleanup is invisible while disk keeps growing. That is the failure mode that produced the 11 GB of stranded worktrees in the first place. The criterion asked for escalation instead of per-poll repetition; it did not ask for terminal silence. A bounded re-alert — every Nth failure, or once a day — satisfies both, and keeps the signal alive for whatever eventually looks at it.

**3. Criterion 4 is unmet, and the answer changes how this should be read.**

> The PR body states whether the 740/813 failures still reproduce after the 2026-08-02 sweep, so a fix is not written against a trigger that no longer exists.

The body is the bare worklink template. From `/mimir-home/logs/events.jsonl`: 30 `worklink_factory_cleanup_failed` events total, the **last at 17:20:02**, none since — zero in the 23:00 hour. The `chainlink-740` and `chainlink-813` run directories were removed by the sweep, so the trigger is gone and this fix is not validated against the condition that produced it.

payload.body:
Approved at `078cd165`. All three blocking items are fixed, and I mutation-verified the two that could regress silently.

**1. Dedup now keys on a stable classifier.** `repeated = entry.cleanup_failure_kind == kind`, with `kind` drawn from four branch identities — `worktree-unidentified`, `preview`, `digest-not-eligible`, `execution` — and the variable text carried as payload. Removing the modulo clause fails the same test at the re-alert assertion. The sequence is right: alert at 1, escalate at 2, silent through 143, re-alert at 144, silent again — and a *change* of kind resets to a fresh alert, so a new failure mode is never swallowed by an old one's suppression.

**On chainlink criterion 4, which asked the body to state whether 740/813 still reproduce — I am answering it here rather than holding the PR.** They do not. payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1133: authz: a service principal cannot read the channel memory it wrote itself, so pollers are denied their own notes

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes at `a2e32b9f`.

**The mechanism is the right one.** Ownership is derived server-side from `authority.canonical` and cross-checked against `auth_context.canonical_principal`, so the principal cannot influence it; `Path(canonical).name != canonical` blocks traversal; the root symlink is rejected; protected names are still enforced *inside* the owned root because `is_current_service_protected_read_path` folds the owned root into its scan. The generalization that deletes the hardcoded `memory/channels/<canonical>` from `build_trigger_service_principal` is exactly the "ownership, not an allowlist" shape criterion 3 asked for, and the `test_agent.py` probe going through `BudgetGateMiddleware` rather than the bare predicate is the right response to criterion 4. None of that is in question.

The problem is what it actually fixes. I pulled the denial corpus from `/mimir-home/logs/events.jsonl`:

| principal | path | count | fixed by this PR? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `synthesis` | `channels/poller:github-activity/pr-reviews.md` | 25 | no |
| `synthesis` | `channels/poller:github-activity/open-issues.md` | 12 | no |
| `synthesis` | `channels/poller:github-activity/pr-ownership-routing.md` | 6 | no |
| `synthesis` | `memory/learnings-pending.md` | 8 | no |
| `poller:pypi-deps-watch` | `channels/poller:pypi-deps-watch/notes.md` | 6 | **yes** |
| `heartbeat` | `channels/scheduler:heartbeat/notes.md` | 2 | no |

**1. The canonical name is not the channel directory name.** `builtin_trigger_service_principal` builds the heartbeat with `canonical="heartbeat"`, but the directory on disk is `scheduler:heartbeat` — `ls /mimir-home/memory/channels/` has no `heartbeat` entry. `service_owned_channel_memory_root` therefore returns a path that does not exist, `is_service_owned_channel_memory_path` fails its `resolve(strict=True)`, and the heartbeat stays denied its own notes. Same for `synthesis`: canonical `synthesis`, no `channels/synthesis` directory. Of the three principals in the corpus, exactly one — `poller:pypi-deps-watch` — is actually fixed, because its canonical happens to match its directory.

This needs an explicit mapping from principal to channel directory, verified against the real directory names, not an assumption that the two strings coincide.

**2. The failure is silent, which is why it would have shipped.** A canonical that names a nonexistent directory is indistinguishable from having no owned memory: both return `None`/`False`, no event, no log. That is the same dead-guard shape as the reasonless failures in #1349 — a check that produces a correct-looking negative while verifying nothing. Please make a canonical whose channel directory is missing observable, so the next naming drift surfaces instead of quietly denying.

**3. Criterion 5 is unmet, and the answer is in the data.** The criterion asked the body to state whether `learnings-pending.md` is per-principal or shared and scope access accordingly. The body is the bare worklink template. The evidence says shared — only `synthesis` touches it, 8 denials — so it is not channel memory and the ownership rule cannot reach it by construction. That is a defensible outcome, but it has to be *stated*, because right now the PR closes an issue whose cited symptom it leaves in place.

---

**A correction that is mine, not yours.** I filed #1133 as "a service principal cannot read the channel memory it wrote itself" and cited `channels/poller:github-activity/pr-reviews.md` as the leading example. The corpus shows those reads are `synthesis` reading **github-activity's** files — a different principal's channel memory, not its own. So the dominant pattern behind the issue is cross-principal aggregation, and under criterion 2 this PR correctly refuses it. The spec pointed at the wrong case; you built the right rule for the case as written.

That leaves a real open question the leaf cannot answer: **is `synthesis` supposed to read across channels?** If session-boundary synthes

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Re-review at `4bc4c1f9`. **The mapping defect is properly fixed.**

`channel_memory_directory` is now declared rather than inferred from `canonical`, with `builtin_trigger_service_principal` pinning the heartbeat to `"scheduler:heartbeat"` and both poller call sites — `resolved_authority` and `_parse_poller_authority` — deriving it as `f"poller:{name}"`. I specifically checked the thing that "declared" could have broken: the value is **not** read from the manifest JSON, so a `pollers.json` cannot point one principal at another principal's channel directory. It comes from the same server-side name that produces `canonical`, at the same call sites. That keeps the ownership property the chainlink's first review criterion demanded. `test_heartbeat_turn_reads_explicitly_mapped_channel_memory` covers the case that was silently broken.

Two items remain, one of them new and one of them mine to have missed earlier.

---

**1. The new telemetry reports the wrong cause in the ordinary case.**

```python
try:
    resolved_root = root.resolve(strict=True)
    resolved = path.resolve(strict=True)
except (OSError, RuntimeError):
    ...
    emit_hard_read_denial(..., "service_owned_channel_memory_root_missing")
```

Both resolutions are inside one `try`. If the root exists but the *file* does not — an agent reading a note it has not written yet, which is routine — `path.resolve(strict=True)` raises `FileNotFoundError`, `targets_owned_root` is lexically true, and the event claims the **root** is missing. The root is fine; the file is absent.

This matters more than a wrong label usually would, because the entire purpose of this item was to make a missing owned root observable. An event that fires for the common missing-file case and names the rare missing-root cause is worse than no event: it will be the loud, ignorable majority, and the real mismatch will hide inside it. Resolve the root and the path in separate `try` blocks and emit only when the root itself fails.

**2. Chainlink criterion 5 is still unanswered.**

> The PR body states whether `learnings-pending.md` is per-principal or shared, and scopes access accordingly rather than admitting it by path.

`learnings-pending` appears nowhere in `read_policy.py`, `access_control.py`, or the tests, and the body is still the bare worklink template. The evidence answers it — 8 denials, all `synthesis`, so it is shared and not channel memory — and the correct outcome is that the ownership rule deliberately does not reach it. As on #1352, please put that where it lasts: a short comment on `service_owned_channel_memory_root` saying shared memory files such as `learnings-pending.md` are intentionally out of scope because they have no owning principal. Then the next reader knows it was decided, not overlooked.

---

**3. Criterion 2 has no test, and I should have said so in my first review.**

> A service principal still cannot read another principal's channel memory; **a test proves one poller cannot read another's channel file.**

There is no such test. The `channels/` references in `test_access_control.py` are pre-existing write-binding cases, and the three new `test_agent.py` tests all cover the positive path or the missing-root path. Exclusivity is structurally true — `is_service_owned_channel_memory_path` compares against the caller's own root — but "structurally obvious" is exactly the property a regression test exists to hold, and this PR widens reads, so the exclusivity direction is the one that must not silently drift. A turn as `poller:a` attempting `memory/channels/poller:b/notes.md` and getting denied is a handful of lines given the harness you already built.

I raised the other three items and missed this one; introducing it in round three is my error, not a moving target. It is still the right thing to add before this merges.

Non-blocking: `is_service_owned_channel_memory_path` reads as a predicate but now emits telemetry as a side effect, and it is reachable more than once per re

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approved at `fc5a1a13`. All three items are addressed, and I mutation-verified the one that was a real bug.

**1. The telemetry no longer misattributes a missing file.** Root resolution and path resolution are now in separate `try` blocks, so only a failure to resolve the *root* emits `service_owned_channel_memory_root_missing`. Refolding `path.resolve(strict=True)` back into the root `try` — recreating the original shape — fails `test_missing_owned_channel_file_does_not_report_missing_root`. The test reads `scheduler:heartbeat/not-written-yet.md` inside an existing root, which is the routine case that would otherwise have generated the loud, ignorable majority of these events.

A note on my own process here: my first two mutation runs did *not* fail, and I nearly reported this test as vacuous. The cause was my own `-k channel_memory` selector, which does not match `test_missing_owned_channel_file_does_not_report_missing_root` — the test was never being executed. I only caught it by probing whether the function was reached at all. Worth recording because "the mutation passed" and "the mutation was never run" look identical in a summary line.

**2. Criterion 5 is answered where it lasts** — the `service_owned_channel_memory_root` docstring now states that shared memory such as `learnings-pending.md` has no owning principal and is intentionally outside the grant. That is the decision recorded as a decision.

**3. `test_poller_turn_cannot_read_another_pollers_channel_memory` covers criterion 2** — `poller:memory-probe` attempting `/memory/channels/poller:other/notes.md` under `access_control_enforced = True`, asserting the call is refused before execution. Correct and end-to-end.

`tests/test_agent.py`, `tests/test_pollers.py`, `tests/test_access_control.py` → 1062 passed, 3 skipped, tree clean after restoring every mutation. All 8 checks green.

---

**One observation, deliberately not blocking.** Making the ownership comparison unconditional — `return True` in place of `resolved == resolved_root or resolved.is_relative_to(resolved_root)` — does **not** fail the cross-principal test. The denial in that scenario comes from `_trigger_service_read_target_is_allowed`, whose roots never include another principal's directory; the `read_policy` predicate is the second layer, and its widening alone cannot admit a read.

So the security property is real and tested, but it is pinned at one layer of two. If someone later widens `is_service_owned_channel_memory_path`, nothing fails — and that function gates `is_current_service_scoped_read_path`, which suppresses the `service_scoped_read_boundary` reason. The composite still denies, so this is redundancy rather than exposure, which is why I am merging rather than holding: unlike the three items I did block on, a failure here cannot make the fix silently not fire.

It is still worth a direct unit test of the predicate at some point — the layer that stops being tested is the layer that quietly stops working.

Merging.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Head moved `a2e32b9f` → `fd12c41e`, but this is a **rebase, not a remediation**. I diffed the PR's own change set at both heads against their respective bases and the patch is byte-identical (same 11,361 bytes across `read_policy.py`, `access_control.py`, `test_agent.py`, `test_pollers.py`). The new base is `c872792f`, which is main after #1351 merged — that is the entire delta, and it explains the extra `scheduler.py` / `worklink/claims.py` files that appear in a naive head-to-head compare.

2. The mismatch fails silently: a nonexistent owned root and no owned memory are indistinguishable, both returning `None`/`False` with no signal.
3. Criterion 5 is unanswered — `learnings-pending.md` is shared, not per-principal (only `synthesis` touches it, 8 denials), and the body should say so.

The corrected denial corpus is on chainlink #1133 as a comment, including the part that was my error: the `pr-reviews.md` denials I cited in the leaf are `synthesis` reading github-activity's files, not a poller reading its own. Item 1 is the real defect here; please do not try to solve the synthesis cross-channel question inside this PR.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Addressed the blocking review at `4bc4c1f9a`:

- Added an explicit server-owned `ServicePrincipal.channel_memory_directory` mapping rather than deriving the directory from `canonical` at read time.
- Wired heartbeat to `scheduler:heartbeat` and poller authority constructors to their `poller:<name>` channel directories. Synthesis declares no owned channel-memory directory; the cross-channel synthesis question remains out of scope.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1135: authz: the repo_review shell profile refuses npm, and the refusals were invisible until argv logging landed

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes at `9aacfe59`.

**The core judgment call is right.** The chainlink's first review criterion was "do not widen the profile to make the events stop," and this PR does not widen it — `npm run` and inline `python -c` stay refused, and the refusal gains a pointer to the typed tool. That was the outcome I most wanted and the hardest one to choose, so I want to be clear the direction is correct before the specifics.

Three things block it.

---

**1. `repo_test` is named unconditionally, and the codebase already documents why that is wrong.**

`_service_shell_typed_tool_guidance` returns "Repository scripts must run through the typed repo_test tool" with no capability check. One file over, `mimir/optional-skills/github-poller/poller.py::_verification_guidance` guards the identical sentence:

> `repo_test` is only registered when `MIMIR_CODING_ENABLED` is true, and that setting defaults to false (`mimir/config.py` `coding_enabled`), so naming the tool unconditionally would point a default deployment at something it does not have.

That reasoning applies here verbatim. On mimirbot `MIMIR_CODING_ENABLED=true`, so the guidance resolves correctly today and no test catches it — but in a default deployment the refusal now instructs the agent to call a tool that is not registered, which is a worse failure than the generic message it replaced: the agent burns a turn discovering the suggestion is dead. Gate on the same flag and fall back to runner-neutral wording, as `_verification_guidance` does.

The test reaches for env handling but picks the wrong variable — `monkeypatch.delenv("MIMIR_PROJECT_TEST_COMMAND")` — so the flag that actually governs registration is never exercised in either state.

**2. The most recent real refusal is not covered.**

I pulled the recorded argv corpus from `/mimir-home/logs/events.jsonl`. Since argv logging landed there are exactly three shapes, all `poller:github-activity`:

| when | argv | rule | covered? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 17:32 | `['npm', 'run']` | `profile_allowlist` | yes |
| 18:01 | `['python', '-c', …]` | `shell_control_characters` | yes |
| **22:46** | `['python', '-', '<<PY', …]` | `shell_control_characters` | **no** |

The third is a heredoc — `argv[1]` is `'-'`, not `'-c'`, so the branch falls through and returns `""`. It is the same class the PR exists to address (arbitrary code execution through the shell profile), it is the *most recent* occurrence, and it happened tonight, hours before this build. After this change that turn still gets a bare metacharacter complaint.

**3. For the workload that actually produced these, the suggested alternative cannot do the job.**

The `python -c` guidance says to use "the typed read_file or grep tool for repository inspection." The 22:46 command was not repository inspection — it was parsing a fetched HTML attachment out of `/mimir-home/attachments/fetch-cache/` with BeautifulSoup to pull an issue body. `read_file`, `grep`, and `repo_test` cannot do that. Pointing there is not just unhelpful, it misdescribes what the agent was doing, and an agent that follows the advice will fail and retry.

Either name a tool that covers HTML/attachment extraction, or say plainly that this workload has no typed equivalent yet and the refusal stands — an honest dead end is better than a wrong redirect. If it has no equivalent, that is worth its own chainlink rather than papering over it here.

---

**Acceptance criterion 1 is unmet, and it is what would have caught 2 and 3.**

> The PR body reports what repo-review turns actually attempt with `npm` and inline `python -c`, grouped from recorded argv, and states for each whether the refusal is correct.

The body is the bare worklink template. That criterion was not decoration — the whole premise of the chainlink was that the refusals might be *correct* and the decision had to be grounded in what the turns actually do. Grouping the three recorded shapes takes one grep, and doing it surfaces the uncovered hered

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Re-review at `5b6b0e19`. **All three blocking items are addressed, and I mutation-verified the two subtle ones rather than trusting the green run.**

| item | resolution |
|---|---|
| `repo_test` named unconditionally | `_service_shell_coding_enabled()` gates it; runner-neutral fallback when disabled |
| `python - <<PY` uncovered | `argv[1] in {"-c", "-"}`, with the message distinguishing `python -c` from stdin/heredoc |
| wrong redirect for attachment parsing | now says plainly there is no typed equivalent and to report the workload as not performable |
| npm normalization (non-blocking) | `Path(argv[0]).name` for npm too; `npm ci` / `npm install` handled explicitly |

Mutation results, at this head:

- Forcing `_service_shell_coding_enabled()` to `return True` fails `test_repo_review_guidance_does_not_name_unavailable_repo_test` on **all five** env states — `None`, `""`, `false`, `0`, `invalid`. The `invalid` case is the one I care about most: it confirms an unparseable value falls back to disabled rather than to enabled.
- Reverting the predicate to `argv[1] == "-c"` fails exactly the heredoc case and nothing else, so the new coverage is load-bearing and isn't shadowed by another assertion.
- Restored, tree clean, full `tests/test_access_control.py` → 771 passed, 2 skipped.

The flag parsing also agrees with `config._env_bool` on the truthy set (`{1, true, yes, on, y}`, lower-cased and stripped) and on defaulting to `False`, so the guidance cannot claim `repo_test` is available when config would have registered it off. Worth a short comment noting it is a deliberate copy of that contract — `access_control` importing `config` would risk a cycle, so the duplication is justified, but the next person changing the truthy set needs to know there are two copies.

---

**One item remains, and it is the only thing between this and approval.** Chainlink acceptance criterion 1 asks the PR to report what repo-review turns actually attempt, grouped from recorded argv, with a correct/incorrect call for each. That is still unmet — the body is the bare worklink template.

I want to be precise about why I am still holding on it, because the reason has narrowed. Last round the criterion mattered *instrumentally*: doing the grouping would have surfaced the uncovered heredoc and the wrong redirect. That purpose is now fully discharged — both are fixed and pinned. What is left is provenance: five command shapes are now special-cased, and nothing in the tree says where they came from or why each refusal is correct.

So rather than the PR body, please put it **in the code**, next to `_service_shell_typed_tool_guidance` — a short comment listing the three observed shapes with their source (`poller:github-activity`, from `/mimir-home/logs/events.jsonl` after argv logging landed) and the two added by inference (`npm ci` / `npm install`), each with the one-line reason its refusal stands. A PR body is read once; a comment there is read by whoever next wonders why `npm ci` is enumerated but `npm ls` is not. That satisfies the criterion in the place where it keeps paying.

Everything else is verified. Add that comment and I will approve.

payload.body:

The only item I was holding on is done, and done in the durable place. `_service_shell_typed_tool_guidance` now carries the provenance inline: the three shapes actually recorded for `poller:github-activity` after argv logging landed (`npm run`, `python -c`, `python - <<PY`), why each refusal stands, and an explicit note that `npm ci` / `npm install` are *inferred* rather than observed. That distinction is the part that will matter to the next reader. The `config._env_bool` alignment comment with the import-cycle rationale is a good addition I did not ask for.

I re-verified rather than assuming the comment was harmless: the delta from `5b6b0e19` is 9 lines in `access_control.py`, all comments, and `tests/test_access_control.py` is byte-identical. So the mutation testing I did at the previous head carries over unchanged — forcing `_service_shell_coding_enabled()` to `True` fails the guard on all five env states including `invalid`, and reverting the predicate to `argv[1] == "-c"` fails exactly the heredoc case. All 8 checks green at this head.

Merging. Net effect: the `repo_review` profile is not one command wider than it was, and three refusal classes that were opaque this morning now tell the agent what to do instead — or tell it honestly that there is nothing to do instead, which was the harder call to get right.

payload.title: Worklink #1132: worklink: a claim whose heartbeat stops is never reaped, so the issue stays worklink:in-progress forever and cannot be re-dispatched

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Fresh pass on current head `3853492ed` — implementation approved from my review, but GitHub will not accept a formal approval on my own PR.

The root-cause fix is correct: Chainlink lock ownership and Worklink claim ownership are different identity namespaces, so comparing the lock's tracker owner with the claim's process `agent_id` suppressed legitimate stale-claim recovery. The replacement guard correctly asks only whether the issue still consumes a Chainlink lock; freshness and claim identity come from the latest structured claim comment.

payload.title: Worklink #1131: pr leases: expires_at is written and never read, and cleanup has one caller, so any turn that ends without calling it leaks a 0.5 GB checkout forever

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. Every acceptance criterion is met, and the two failure directions I was most worried
about are both pinned.

**Reuses the existing predicate.** Deletion goes through `cleanup_pr_checkout_lease`, so the
publication-proof rule from #1326 remains the single definition of "safe to remove" — a lease
lacking the proof is retained, not deleted. No second mechanism to disagree with the first.

**Retention is observable.** It emits `pr_checkout_lease_reclaimed` **or**
`pr_checkout_lease_retained`, with `expired_by_s`, `size_bytes`, `publication_proof_present`, and
`error`. A reaper that reclaims nothing is now distinguishable from one that is not running, which
was the specific review criterion.

**Expiry comes from the lease**, not a hardcoded scheduler constant, and
`active_pr_checkout_lease_paths()` excludes any checkout attached to a live turn — so a long build
that outlives its window is not reaped mid-use.

Three tests, matching the three cases:

| Test | Covers |
|---|---|
| `test_reaper_reclaims_expired_published_lease` | the normal path |
| `test_reaper_retains_and_reports_expired_unpublished_work` | the failure that matters |
| `test_reaper_never_reclaims_expired_lease_attached_to_live_turn` | live-turn safety |

Mutation-tested: dropping the live-turn guard fails the third test specifically.

Full suite: **7878 passed, 20 skipped, 0 failed**.

Context for the record: `expires_at` had been written into every lease and read by nothing —
grepping `mimir/` for it returned only capability expiry and OAuth tokens. Cleanup had exactly one
caller, the `repo_cleanup` tool, so any turn that ended without invoking it leaked a checkout
permanently. 43 leases totalling 5.4 GB were removed by hand on 2026-08-02, and six more had
accrued twelve hours later with four already past expiry and five belonging to merged PRs. This
turns that manual sweep into a control.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1129: config: consolidate scattered per-repository settings into one declared record, and make an unbindable repo a startup error

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The design is right and most of it should land verbatim. Requesting one structural change to where
the inventory lives, because it is far cheaper now than after a deployment declares one.

## What I verified, and what is good

The record shape, the validation, and the migration are all correct, and I checked them rather than
reading them:

- **The startup preflight actually fires.** `_configure_declared_repositories(home)` is wired on the
  boot path at `config.py:1170`, before application construction. A checkout whose remote disagrees
  with the declared origin raises:
  `repository owner/declared did not bind: expected origin '...declared.git', found '...ACTUAL.git' at /...`
  That names the repository, the expected origin, and the observed one — exactly the criterion, and
  exactly what was missing when a bad root surfaced only as per-call refusals for 8.5 hours.
- **The conflation is designed out.** `RepositoryConfig` and `AllowedRootConfig` are distinct types,
  `repository roots cannot also be allowed_roots` is enforced at parse, and allowed roots never
  participate in binding. A parent directory can no longer stand in for a checkout.
- **Fail-closed on a malformed inventory.** `authorize_tool` returns `allowed=False reason=write_scope`
  rather than raising. Correct direction.
- **No flag day.** Everything is gated on `repository_config_declared`, so deploying this changes
  nothing until the inventory is declared, and legacy variables are projections whose disagreement
  is a startup error reporting both values.

Keep all of that as written.

## Required change: the inventory does not belong in worklink.yaml

`access_control.py` now calls `WorklinkConfig.load(Path(home) / "worklink.yaml")` to determine
file-tool write scope, and imports `mimir.worklink.backends.registry` at four sites. The
authorization layer reads its security boundary out of the build subsystem's config file, through
that subsystem's loader.

That inverts the argument the change is built on. GitHub issue #1345 objected that a repository's
test command should not live in Worklink's deployment defaults because it belongs to the
repository. The fix moved the entire repository inventory further into Worklink's file, then made
access control depend on it. Concretely: a `worklink.yaml` typo now denies all repository writes,
and editing a build timeout means editing the file that defines the file-tool write boundary.

Please split it:

- Move `repositories:` and `allowed_roots:` to their own file, e.g. `<home>/repositories.yaml`.
- Move `RepositoryConfig`, `AllowedRootConfig`, and their parsing/validation out of
  `mimir/worklink/backends/registry.py` into a neutral module — `mimir/repository_config.py`, or
  into `mimir/config.py` alongside the preflight that already validates them.
- `access_control` reads the inventory directly. It must not import from `mimir.worklink`.
- Worklink reads the same inventory for `base_branch`, and keeps `backends:`,
  `compute_backends:`, and its own defaults in `worklink.yaml`.

**Keep `test_command` and `base_branch` on the repository record.** `test_command` has two
consumers, and only one is Worklink: `repo_test` / `project_tests.py` is the PR-review path, where
the reviewer independently executes the repository's suite. Putting that command in Worklink's
config is precisely what produced #1345, where reviewing a Node repository attempted `pytest` and
executed nothing. `base_branch` is the repository's default branch, not a build setting.

**Invert `worklink: true`.** Have `worklink.yaml` name its target instead:

    # worklink.yaml
    repository: owner/service

The flag is a back-reference from a neutral inventory to one specific consumer — the same inversion
in data form. Add a second consumer and you start adding `benchmark: true` beside it, so the flag
set grows with consumers. And "multiple `worklink: true` records are fatal" is really a statement
that Worklink has one target, enforced in the inventory's parser

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The restructure is exactly what was asked, and everything I verified as good in the
first pass survived it.

**All four required items, checked at head `6d84f831`:**

| Requirement | Result |
|---|---|
| `access_control` free of `mimir.worklink` | no imports remain — the security layer no longer depends on the build subsystem |
| Dataclasses in a neutral module | new `mimir/repository_config.py` (165 lines) |
| Inventory in its own file | `repositories.yaml`, loaded by `RepositoryInventory.load()` from both `config.py` and `project_tests.py` |
| `worklink: true` inverted | `repository:` key read in `worklink.yaml` (`registry.py:223`) |

`registry.py` drops from +144 to +8 — it now reads one key naming Worklink's target and nothing
else. That is the right size for what Worklink actually owns.

**Preserved, and re-verified rather than assumed:**

- `RepositoryConfig` still carries `base_branch` and `test_command`, and the `worklink` field is
  gone from the record. Both consumers of `test_command` — the reviewer's `repo_test` and the
  builder — now read it from the repository, which is what #1345 was about.
- The startup preflight still fires with the same precise message:
  `repository owner/declared did not bind: expected origin '...declared.git', found '...ACTUAL.git' at /...`
  Named repository, expected origin, observed origin. That is the check whose absence cost 8.5
  hours this morning, and it is on the boot path before application construction.
- Legacy projections still fail loudly and now name the right file:
  `MIMIR_FILE_TOOL_ROOTS disagrees with repositories.yaml` and
  `GITHUB_REPOS disagrees with repositories.yaml`, both reporting each value.
- The repository/allowed-roots separation, the origin-must-match-slug check, and the
  declared-gating that makes this a no-op until a deployment opts in are all intact.

Full suite: **7821 passed, 20 skipped, 0 failed**.

Worth stating what this buys beyond tidiness. Per-repository settings were spread across
`GITHUB_REPOS`, `MIMIR_FILE_TOOL_ROOTS`, `WORKLINK_REPO`, and two globals in `worklink.yaml`, and
one list expressed both "a repository checkout" and "an allowed file root" — which is why a parent
directory could be a valid root and bind to nothing at the same time. That state is now
unrepresentable, and a declared repository that does not bind stops the process instead of
producing per-call refusals nobody attributes for hours.

One thing to sequence carefully when you adopt it: declaring the inventory is the moment the new
path goes live, and the preflight runs before the socket binds. Get the origins exactly right in
`repositories.yaml` first, because a mistake there is a startup failure rather than a degraded
runtime — which is the correct trade, and also a harder failure to miss.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Head moved `68d661c4` → `350c067e`, but that is a **rebase onto current main**, not a remediation — the delta between the two heads is only the merged content of #1344 and #1347 (`repo_tools.py`, `tools/repo.py`, `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock`). The branch is still a single commit, `worklink: issue #1129`.

The blocking item is unchanged at head `350c067e`:

- `mimir/access_control.py` still imports `from .worklink.backends.registry import WorklinkConfig` at lines 732, 752, 864, and 888.
- `RepositoryConfig` and `AllowedRootConfig` are still defined in `mimir/worklink/backends/registry.py`.
- The inventory is still read from `worklink.yaml`; there is no separate inventory file.
- `worklink: true` is still a field on the repository record rather than `repository:` in `worklink.yaml`.

Rebasing was the right call given main moved four times today, and the rebase itself looks clean. Just noting it so a moved head is not read as a cleared review — the required change from the previous review still stands as written, and everything I verified as good there is still good and should be preserved verbatim.

- made an undeclared Worklink target a startup error and added regressions rejecting the old `worklink: true` back-reference

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1128: packaging: the suite requires the bench extra but no default install provides it, so every non-CI runner fails a test

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. Minimal change, and I verified every criterion against a clean dev-only install rather
than reasoning from the diff.

**The broken case now works.** A fresh `uv sync --extra dev` (no bench flag) takes **2s** from a
removed `.venv`, and `saga.benchmarks.longmemeval.harness` imports afterwards. That is the exact
invocation that was failing, and it is the one a new contributor or any non-CI runner uses.

**The guard is preserved, not defeated** — this was the criterion I cared most about, since making
the collection test pass by letting the module skip again would undo chainlink #1113 and re-hide
the memory pipeline:

| Condition | Result |
|---|---|
| dev-only install | `1 passed` |
| harness renamed away (genuinely unavailable) | `1 failed` |

So it passes because the dependency is really present, not because the assertion was loosened.

**Resolution stays local.** The lock records
`{ name = "saga", marker = "extra == 'dev'", editable = "benchmarks/saga" }` — the in-repo workspace
member, so a plain dev install does not reach an index. The `bench` extra is untouched
(`marker = "extra == 'bench'"` still present), so nothing referencing it breaks and the explicit
choice remains available.

Full suite on a dev-only install: **7806 passed, 20 skipped, 0 failed**.

This closes the regression I let through this morning. I approved #1340 after confirming CI's four
sync steps were updated, and never checked the other runners that execute the same suite — the
Worklink scoped runner used `uv run pytest -q`, so every build reported a failing gate until the
deployment config was patched. With this merged, installing the documented dev dependencies gets
you a green suite, and that deployment override becomes belt-and-braces rather than load-bearing.

Worth noting the two explicit `--extra bench` flags in CI are now redundant. Leaving them is fine
and arguably clearer about intent; I would not churn the workflow to remove them.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.title: deps: upgrade DeepAgents to 0.7.1

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Verdict: request changes

The DeepAgents 0.7.1 adaptation is thorough: it preserves Mimir-owned prompt composition, restores Todo middleware without duplicating it in the real graphs, keeps the token-schema cache shared across main/general/critic summarizers, exercises sync and async history/media offload, and explicitly constrains the model-visible filesystem surface so `delete` is not bound. The added integration tests are materially stronger than version-shape mocks.

One create-only write invariant is not yet safe: once `_exclusive_write` has created the destination, an encoding or I/O failure during `handle.write()` returns an error but leaves an empty/partial destination behind. The accompanying tests currently assert that leak. That consumes the path despite the reported failure, makes a corrected retry collide, and can persist partial model content. I left the blocking finding inline; please ensure failed creates leave no destination and add a retry regression.

Validation: the deployment-configured full suite passed in the scoped PR checkout. GitHub's Python 3.11 and 3.12 suites, packaging, frontend, Claude Code smoke, skill-conformance, and Chainlink audit are green. `pytest-enforced` is currently red, so this revision is not merge-ready independently of the code finding; the bounded checks projection did not expose its failure detail.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Verdict: approve

The blocking create-only write defect is fixed at `15590a00`. `_exclusive_write` now removes a destination after a post-create write failure through the same open parent `dir_fd`, preserving the symlink-resistant path resolution while keeping a transient encoding or I/O failure from consuming the create-only path. The updated assertions plus `test_failed_create_leaves_path_free_for_a_corrected_retry` test the externally important property: a failed create leaves the destination absent and a corrected retry succeeds.

The enforced-mode prompt test is also corrected to assert containment rather than equality, so it preserves the test's create-only-guidance intent without rejecting the required declassification suffix under `MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED`.

Validation: the focused scoped run passed (`118 passed` across `tests/test_readonly_backend.py` and `tests/test_agent_system_prompt_refresh.py`). All current GitHub checks are green, including Python 3.11/3.12, `pytest-enforced`, packaging, frontend, Claude Code smoke, skill conformance, and the Chainlink audit. No remaining blocking findings.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Review — blocking finding.** (Posted as a comment: GitHub refuses a changes-requested review on a
PR authored by the same account I review from.)

## One test this PR adds fails in a configuration CI gates on

`pytest-enforced` is the only red check; 3.11 and 3.12 pass. Reproduced locally with
`MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED=1`: **1 failed, 7849 passed, 20 skipped** — the same single test and
nothing else in the upgrade.

`tests/test_agent_system_prompt_refresh.py::test_fallback_system_prompt_includes_create_only_write_guidance`
is new here and asserts two things that cannot both hold under enforcement:

```python
monkeypatch.setattr("mimir.core_blocks.load_core", lambda _home: 1 / 0)   # force the fallback
prompt = agent._build_system_prompt()
assert prompt == _DEFAULT_SYSTEM_PROMPT                                    # exact equality
assert ("`write_file` creates a new file only. ...") in prompt
```

`_DEFAULT_SYSTEM_PROMPT` already contains the create-only guidance, so the second assertion passes
in either mode — the equality is what breaks. Under enforcement the agent appends the
declassification guidance block from `mimir/prompts.py:129`, so the actual value ends
`"...do not blindly retry the same call."` while the expected ends `"...Be concise."`.

That appended block is correct behavior — with access control enforced, the agent is told how to
handle declassification. The test encodes an enforcement-off assumption as an exact match.

Its own name is `..._includes_create_only_write_guidance`. Containment is the property; equality is
over-specification that holds in only one of the two configurations CI runs.
`assert _DEFAULT_SYSTEM_PROMPT in prompt` keeps the intent and passes in both.

The `ZeroDivisionError: division by zero` in the CI log is this test's own `lambda _home: 1 / 0`
fallback trigger, not a separate defect.

## The upgrade otherwise

`deepagents>=0.6.1,<0.7` → `>=0.7.1,<0.8`, lock moved to the 0.7.1 sdist and wheel. Compatibility
work lands where issue #1321 predicted: `_deepagents_patches.py`, `_deepagents_summarization.py`,
`readonly_backend.py` (+202), `subagents.py`, and the token-counter path.

I went to the failing gate first because it blocks. I have **not** reviewed the 21-file diff line by
line yet, and I will not approve until I have — particularly `readonly_backend.py`, since that is
where the filesystem-backend contract changed and it carries the write guard. Two things I will be
checking there specifically, given today's history: that core-memory writes remain refused with the
proposal flow as the only path, and that the create-only `write_file` semantics are unchanged.

Fix the assertion and I will do that pass.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Review complete at `15590a00`.** Both findings are fixed and I have now done the substantive pass
on the compatibility work. No remaining objections from me. (I cannot post a formal approval —
GitHub refuses reviews on a PR authored by the account I review from — so this is a comment, and
@mimir-carreira's `CHANGES_REQUESTED` is the blocking review that needs clearing.)

## Fixed in `15590a00`

**The create-only write leak** (mimir's finding — a real production defect, and the better of the
two). `_exclusive_write` opens with `O_CREAT | O_EXCL`, so a failure during `handle.write()` left an
empty or partial destination behind while returning an error. Because `write_file` is create-only,
the corrected retry then hit FileExistsError and was told to use `edit_file` on content that was
never written — a transient encoding or I/O error made permanent. The write is now wrapped so any
failure unlinks through the **same `dir_fd` used to create it**, so cleanup cannot be redirected by
a symlink swapped in after the open, then re-raises so the existing handler returns an identical
error.

Three tests asserted the leak and now assert absence, plus
`test_failed_create_leaves_path_free_for_a_corrected_retry` — the property that actually matters,
since asserting the file is gone is only a proxy for the retry succeeding. Reverting the guard
fails all three.

**The enforced-mode gate.** `assert prompt == _DEFAULT_SYSTEM_PROMPT` cannot hold under
`MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED`, where the declassification block from `mimir/prompts.py` is
appended — which is why `pytest-enforced` was the only red check. Relaxed to containment, which is
the property the test is named for and which held in both modes all along.

## Compatibility pass — verified, not assumed

**The model-visible filesystem surface is correctly constrained.** DeepAgents 0.7.1's stock
`FilesystemMiddleware` exposes `delete` **and `execute`**. `test_structured_subagents.py:735-736`
asserts both are absent from the actually-bound tool names while requiring the six expected
filesystem tools to be present. That is the right shape — a positive assertion of the expected set
plus negatives on the new surfaces — and it is checked against real graph construction rather than
version-shape mocks. `execute` is the one I most wanted to see excluded: an upgrade that silently
bound it would hand the model shell outside the authorization gate.

**The token-schema cache survived the rewrite.** The `-191` in `_deepagents_patches.py` is
restructuring, not removal. Bypassing `_cached_tools` fails four tests including
`test_real_main_general_and_critic_graphs_share_schema_cache`, so the cache really is shared across
the main, general, and critic summarizers and it is pinned against real graphs.

**Core memory stays proposal-only** — `_is_core_memory_write_blocked` retains all four call sites.

**Full suite: 7851 passed, 20 skipped, 0 failed — both plain and with
`MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED=1`.**

## One note for the record

Mimir found the better defect here. Mine was a test assertion; its was a production invariant
violation in the write guard — and it found it in `readonly_backend.py`, the exact file I had named
as where I would spend my time and had not yet reached. Its review also flagged that it could not
see the enforced failure detail, which is the half my review supplied. The two passes were
genuinely complementary rather than redundant.
