Approving. Re-verified at the pushed head `824f9541` after the rebase: content is identical to what
I reviewed at `150c3fc3` — same four files, same `+146/-9`, and all four properties still present
(three distinct failure codes, the `_has_in_progress_merge_or_rebase` gate, `_redact_git_output`,
and the commit-still-refused test). Content-preserving rebase, so the earlier mutation results
stand.

**What it fixes.** `repo_unmerged` and `repo_status` now work against a rebase or merge in progress
— `_has_in_progress_merge_or_rebase()` checks for `rebase-merge`, `rebase-apply`, and `MERGE_HEAD`,
and `allow_in_progress` is gated on the operation actually being in progress rather than granted
unconditionally. And `_execute` no longer collapses every failure into
`repository_operation_failed`: authorization refusal, invalid binding, and git failure each get
their own stable code, with the originating code preserved in brackets and the git stderr surfaced
through `_redact_git_output`.

**The criterion I cared most about is met.** Relaxing read-only inventory did not relax mutation:
`GitCommit(("tracked.txt",), "must not commit a conflicted rebase")` mid-rebase still fails with
`git_failed`, and there is a test asserting exactly that. Read-only inventory and mutating recovery
stayed separable.

Mutation-tested at the reviewed content, both caught:

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| collapse the failure classes back to one generic code | 2 parameterized cases FAIL |
| drop credential redaction from git output | `test_repo_wrapper_git_stderr_redacts_embedded_remote_credential` FAILS |

The redaction test asserts both directions — `super-secret-password` absent and
`https://[REDACTED]@example.invalid/owner/repo.git` present — which is the right shape for a
redaction guard.

Full suite at the pushed head: **7810 passed, 20 skipped, 0 failed**.

Worth recording why this leaf existed: I filed it after rebasing #1333 by hand, because the scoped
checkout reported a conflict and then "failed generically" on both `repo_unmerged` and
`repo_status`, so the conflicting paths could not be recovered through the authorized interface.
The rebase itself was two files. With this merged, that inventory is reachable and the failure is
nameable.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1122: observability: shell metacharacter refusals record which characters offended but not what the agent was trying to run (378 in seven days)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. Tests-only is the correct resolution here, and I verified the premise rather than taking
it on trust.

**The production fix already landed in #1121.** A metacharacter refusal returns `argv=None` from
`parse_service_shell_argv_with_diagnostics`, and `budget_gate.py:674` catches exactly that case to
call `service_shell_argv_for_log(target)`. So this path already records the redacted argv, the
profile, and a distinct `binding_rule` — chainlink #1121's work covered it without either leaf
noticing the overlap. The right thing to add was pins, not a second implementation.

**The tests check what actually matters:**

- `binding_rule == "shell_control_characters"` — this path has its own stable identifier rather than
  sharing one with other binding failures
- `"opaque-value" not in repr(hard)` — a secret-shaped argument does not reach the event
- `argv[-1] == "[TRUNCATED]"` with `argv_truncated is True` — truncation is explicit, not silent
- the refusal text asserts real guidance: "Issue one command per call", `git -C <dir>`,
  `--body-file <path beneath the agent scratch root>`, and that shell syntax "is never admitted and
  no quoting will change that"

That last group satisfies the criterion about the message telling the agent what to do instead of
only naming the rejected characters — which is the difference between an agent adapting and an
agent retrying the same shape 378 times.

Mutation-tested, both caught:

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| stop recording the argv on the refusal path | FAILS |
| weaken redaction so the secret-shaped value passes through | FAILS |

The redaction mutation is the one I most wanted to see fail, since recording a command is only safe
if the redaction is load-bearing.

Full suite: 7800 passed, 20 skipped, 0 failed.

Context for whoever picks up the follow-up: the original acceptance criteria on this leaf were
defective — they required grouping 378 historical refusals by attempted command, which is
impossible because that field is precisely what was missing. The executor caught it and blocked
before dispatch, correctly. The corrected leaf scopes to recording and pinning; the grouping waits
until deployed events carry the field.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1125: Verify isolated Worklink checkout effective push target

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. Correct implementation, and all five acceptance criteria are met including the two
regression cases I expected to be hardest to construct.

Captures the parent's effective push target with `git remote get-url --push origin` (failing on
error or empty), sets the isolated checkout's origin to it, re-resolves inside the checkout, and
fails closed on mismatch with both wanted and observed in the message. Ordering is right: all of it
sits at lines 199-231, before `checkout -B` at line 234, so a failure leaves no attempt branch, and
`shutil.rmtree(..., ignore_errors=True)` clears the half-created checkout.

Both required divergent configurations are actually constructed rather than simulated —
`test_isolated_checkout_uses_explicit_effective_pushurl` sets `remote.origin.pushurl` and
`test_isolated_checkout_uses_push_instead_of_effective_target` sets `url.<base>.pushInsteadOf`,
then let git resolve. That satisfies the sharpest review criterion on the leaf: the tests exercise
git's own push-target resolution instead of reimplementing URL selection in test code, so they
would catch a wrong resolution rather than agreeing with it.

Mutation-tested: reverting the capture to `config --get remote.origin.url` — the original defect —
fails 5 tests, including both parameterized cleanup cases.

I checked one thing that looked like a regression and it is not: setting origin to the *push* URL
means the isolated checkout's fetch URL also becomes the push URL, which would matter if it ever
fetched. It does not. Its only git operations are `remote set-url`, `get-url --push`,
`checkout -B`, and `rev-parse`; every fetch runs against the parent repo, which keeps its own
configuration. Origin exists in the isolated checkout purely as a push destination, so collapsing
the two is correct rather than lossy.

Full suite: 7794 passed, 21 skipped, 0 failed.

Context worth keeping with the change: this is hardening, not a fix for an observed failure. Fetch
and push are identical across all three repositories today, so the divergence it guards against
cannot currently be triggered — a single `git config remote.origin.pushurl` on the parent would
make it live and silent, which is exactly why the postcondition belongs here.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1118: saga: session semantic search truncates to top-k before the authorized session set is known, so foreign sessions degrade another caller's retrieval

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. This removes the ordering hazard rather than papering over it, and it is consistent with
the lane that already got this right.

**The fix is structural.** Step 1 now resolves the authorized session pool in SQL first
(`selection_predicate("sessions")` plus the channel clause, `LIMIT 500`), and Step 2 searches the
**complete** FAISS index — `top_k=index.total_vectors` in place of `min(limit * 4, 200)`. So
truncation no longer happens before authorization is known, and a foreign session cannot consume an
eligible session's semantic slot. The inline comment cites the atom lane precedent explicitly,
which is the right justification: this makes the two lanes agree instead of inventing a third
behavior.

Using `selection_predicate` rather than a raw scope also keeps it inside the enforcement-mode
contract from #1112, so this does not reintroduce a lane that filters strictly while atoms fall
back.

**The test constructs the actual hazard.**
`test_search_sessions_foreign_neighbors_do_not_starve_semantic_scores` seeds `user:bob`-owned
private sessions into the nearest-neighbour positions, then asserts the authorized sessions retain
their real similarity scores (0.9 and 0.1, i.e. semantic rather than recency ordering) and that no
`foreign-*` session appears in results. Restoring `min(limit * 4, 200)` fails exactly that test.
That is a starvation test, not a leak test — the right distinction, since nothing was ever leaking.

Full suite: 7790 passed, 21 skipped, 0 failed.

**On the cost, since the PR body does not state it:** the live store has 3,655 sessions, 3,115 with
embeddings, so `top_k=index.total_vectors` is a ~3.1k-vector scan per query today — negligible for
a flat index, and the atom lane already pays the same shape. Worth knowing that this cost grows
linearly with the session corpus; if sessions grow an order of magnitude it deserves a revisit. I
would not bound it here, because a cap is precisely the bug that was just removed, and diverging
from the atom lane to save microseconds would trade a correctness property for nothing.

Process note, mine not yours: this PR sat unreviewed for roughly 45 minutes. It landed while I was
mid-review of #1340 and I lost track of it, then twice reported the queue as empty. The monitor
reported it correctly both times.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1113: ci: 8 memory-pipeline tests skip in every job because no workflow installs the [bench] extra, leaving the retrieval path with zero executing coverage

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. This turns on coverage that has never executed, and the guard against it silently
switching off again is the strongest part.

**The memory pipeline now actually runs in CI.** All four `uv sync --extra dev` steps become
`--extra dev --extra bench`, so `tests/test_longmemeval_via_memory_smoke.py` collects instead of
skipping on `pytest.importorskip("saga.benchmarks.longmemeval.harness")`. Confirmed locally: 9
passed in that module, and the full-suite skip count drops 21 → 20, which is the module no longer
skipping rather than a test being hidden.

**The collection guard is real — I verified it the hard way.** My first mutation (`pip uninstall
saga`) was a no-op, because saga is a uv workspace member and pip could not remove it; the guard
passed and proved nothing. Renaming `saga/benchmarks/longmemeval/harness.py` reproduces the actual
missing-extra condition, and then
`test_longmemeval_memory_smoke_cases_are_collected` **fails**. So the guard bites on the real
failure mode.

Pinning the exact node-ID set rather than a count is the right call for this file specifically:
it catches re-skipping *and* silent test removal, and the failure message names missing and
unexpected IDs so the fix is obvious. The cost is that adding a legitimate test to that module
fails CI until the set is updated — deliberate friction, and appropriate for a module whose entire
history is silent absence.

**Cost is negligible.** Incremental `uv sync --extra dev --extra bench` after a dev-only sync takes
**0s** — `saga` resolves from the in-repo workspace member at `benchmarks/saga`, so nothing is
fetched from an index. That satisfies the criterion about resolving without additional network.

Full suite with the new extras: **7799 passed, 20 skipped, 0 failed**.

The acceptance criterion asking for the collected count and added wall-clock in the PR body is
unmet — the body is the worklink stub. I measured both and recorded them above, so the evidence
exists; noting it so the gap is deliberate rather than overlooked.

Worth stating what this closes: the reason a live, credentialed LongMemEval run became a blocking
factory gate was that nothing else verified this pipeline. It is verified now, offline, on every PR.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1124: prompts: reflect.md instructs the same core-memory reads the gate refuses, and whether that block is intended is still undecided

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. This resolves the question #1119 deferred, and it resolves it the right way.

**The resolution is "collateral", and the fix follows from that.** `memory/core` was unreadable
because the `("memory", "core")` adjacency lived in a predicate shared with the write policy, while
chainlink #342 only ever asked for read-*only*. Since `core_blocks.py` renders those files into the
system prompt every turn, the read withheld nothing. `is_protected_read_path` now admits
`<home>/memory/core` alongside `<home>/state`, and the now-unreachable `core_memory_block` denial
reason is removed rather than left dangling.

**The write gate is untouched and still proven.** `readonly_backend.py` has no diff,
`_is_core_memory_write_blocked` is still called at both sites, and `test_heartbeat.py:195` still
asserts `backend.write("memory/core/50-heartbeat-patterns.md", ...)` is refused. Core memory stays
proposal-only, which was the invariant that mattered.

**I probed the widening rather than trusting the diff.** With `MIMIR_HOME` set:

```
admitted    <home>/memory/core/00-identity.md     <- intended
PROTECTED   <home>/memory/channels/c.md
PROTECTED   <home>/memory/topics/t.md
PROTECTED   <home>/prompts/p.md
admitted    <home>/state/s.json                   <- pre-existing
```

Exactly one path class changes. I also checked the out-of-home case, since the predicate was
re-scoped from "`memory/core` adjacency anywhere" to "this home's core" — I expected that to have
dropped protection for another home's core memory. It had not: running the same probe against
`origin/main` shows `<outside-home>/memory/core/x.md` was **already** admitted there. No regression;
the re-scoping only tightens what the predicate claims to cover.

**The generalized test is the part I most wanted.**
`test_prompt_template_required_filesystem_operations_are_permitted` globs `prompt_templates/*.md`
rather than naming heartbeat, so `reflect.md`, `memory-hygiene.md`, `issues-audit.md`, and
`upgrade.md` are all covered now and any future template is covered on arrival. That closes the
class instead of the instance — a forbidden instruction in a template nobody thought to check now
fails CI.

Full suite: 7779 passed, 21 skipped, 0 failed. All 8 checks green.

One dead leftover, not blocking: `readonly_backend.py:746` keeps a `"core_memory_block"` key in the
`_read_denied_message` guidance table for a reason that can no longer be produced. I blocked #1336
over a stale `protected_read_target` reference, so to be explicit about why this is different — that
one was a test *assertion* that read as a guard and verified nothing, which misrepresents coverage.
This is an unreachable entry in a message lookup; it claims nothing and misleads no one. Worth
sweeping next time someone is in that file.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1121: observability: service_shell_argv_binding_failed never records the command, so 776 refusals in seven days are undiagnosable

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. This makes the highest-volume denial in the system diagnosable for the first time — 776
refusals in seven days that recorded nothing about what was refused.

**Every criterion is met.** The event now carries the refused argv, the bound profile, and a stable
rejecting-rule identifier. `ServiceShellBindingRule` as a `StrEnum` is the right choice: the values
are stable enough to aggregate on across releases, which was the point of asking for a rule rather
than prose.

**Redaction is applied to the argv itself, not just the message** — which is what I asked for,
since a token passed as an argument is the realistic leak path here. `service_shell_argv_for_log`
handles both shapes: a credential-bearing option whose value is the *next* argv element, and the
inline `--option=value` form. `redact_payload` then runs over the merged `event_fields` as a second
pass. Truncation is bounded by `_SERVICE_SHELL_LOG_MAX_ARGUMENTS` and represented both in the argv
and by an explicit flag, so a long command is visibly cut rather than silently shortened.

**Telemetry-only, as required.** Every refusal site keeps its existing condition and reason; each
`return None, <reason>` simply gained a rule. No command that is refused today becomes admitted.

Mutation-tested, both caught by `test_service_shell_final_binding_refusal_emits_hard_denial`:

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| blank the recorded argv | FAILS |
| collapse the rejecting rule to a constant | FAILS |

Full suite: 7776 passed, 21 skipped, 0 failed.

On the three parse variants — I checked whether `parse_service_shell_argv` had become a dead
back-compat shim, and it has not: `_with_diagnostics` returns the 3-tuple, `_with_reason` drops the
rule, and the bare form drops the reason, each with real callers (five for the bare form). That is
a layered adapter chain rather than a shim, so no cleanup is owed.

This also unblocks the open question on chainlink #1116. Until now there was no way to tell whether
those 776 refusals were an over-narrow profile or malformed commands; once this is deployed, a
week of events answers it from evidence.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1115: saga: quantify what enforcement would hide before cutover — legacy_admin dependence by surface and caller, then decide the migration

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. This is the most safety-conscious PR in the batch, and the disposition answers the
question the leaf was filed to answer rather than deferring it again.

**The disposition is correct and it closes an open operator question.** `legacy_admin` keeps its
rank, meaning, and fail-closed role, and the doc states plainly why it is not redefined to mean
"the operator": doing so "would make every future provenance ambiguity fail open." That was exactly
my objection when widening legacy rows was raised — good to have it written down where the next
reader will find it rather than living in a conversation.

The migration rule is mechanical and reproducible on a new row: pre-cutover `created_at`,
`memory_type = raw`, `source_type` in {`conversation`, `agent_authored`}, `origin_channel` in an
operator-reviewed mapping, and both owner and visibility still `legacy_admin`. Service-derived
rows, observations and their evidence intersections, service-owned rows, unmapped channels, and
post-cutover rows all stay narrow. Requiring the channel mapping to be an operator assertion that
the channel was exclusively theirs — with shared or uncertain channels excluded — puts the judgment
where it belongs instead of inferring an owner from content.

**The migration is safer than the leaf required.** I asked that it not be run against the live
store; this makes that structurally impossible: `apply=False` by default, `migrate_copy` raises
`ValueError("output must differ from source; live in-place migration is forbidden")`,
`FileExistsError` rather than clobbering an existing output, reserved sentinel principals rejected
as mapping targets, and `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` only on the copy. Idempotence is structural rather than
asserted — the `WHERE` requires both fields still be `legacy_admin`, so a migrated row cannot
re-match — and `test_legacy_acl_migration_is_copy_only_narrow_and_idempotent` pins it.

**The replay produces the breakdown the leaf specified.** `_GROUP_FIELDS = ("surface",
"caller_kind", "trigger")`, and `test_replay_reports_pre_and_post_fusion_losses_by_caller_surface_and_age`
covers the distinction that matters most: candidates excluded before fusion versus results excluded
after. A class removed pre-RRF does not appear in final-result counts at all, which is precisely how
the #1112 regression stayed invisible.

Nothing here enables enforcement — the only mention of `MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED` is the line
stating the flag remains a separate operator decision.

Full suite: 7775 passed, 21 skipped, 0 failed.

Two notes, neither blocking. Three tests for ~400 lines of new module is thin, though each covers
several properties at once. And the report still needs an operator run against the live store plus
a privileged trace to produce actual numbers — the tooling is delivered, the measurement is not, which
matches how the leaf was scoped. When that run happens, the useful anchor is already established:
provenance stamping began working 2026-07-17, so the historical remnant is a fixed ~1,554 rows with
an ongoing rate of zero.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1120: observability: protected_read_target is one reason string for three different rules, and records neither the target nor the trigger

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The telemetry work is right and I verified it end to end. Blocking on one stale reference the
rename sweep missed — a one-line fix.

## Verified

Every criterion on chainlink #1120 is met. The single `protected_read_target` string is replaced by
five rule-specific reasons — `core_memory_block`, `service_scoped_read_boundary`,
`protected_name_match`, `mimir_home_read_boundary`, `protected_read_result` — and the emitted
`hard_boundary_denied` event now carries `target` (through `redact_payload`, so a path is logged
without its contents), `trigger` resolved from `origin_trigger` → `trigger` → turn context, and
`service_principal` from the resolved trusted service. That closes the attribution gap directly:
533 denials over seven days recorded no target at all, and 142 of 219 post-fix ones recorded no
trigger.

Mutation-tested:

| Mutation | Caught by |
|---|---|
| collapse `core_memory_block` into the generic reason | `test_github_activity_repo_read_and_scratch_write_scopes_are_separate` |
| drop `target` from the emitted event | that test plus `test_protected_reads_allow_only_tracked_files_in_exact_authorized_pr_lease` |

All five reasons have coverage across `test_readonly_backend.py`, `test_pollers.py`,
`test_pr_checkout_lease.py`, `test_deepagents_summarization_offload.py`, and `test_search.py`.
Full suite: 7772 passed, 21 skipped, 0 failed.

Splitting `_has_protected_read_name` and `_is_core_memory_read_path` out as named predicates is
also the right structural move — the reason is now derived from the same functions that decide, so
the label cannot drift from the rule.

## Blocking: a now-unsatisfiable assertion left behind

`tests/test_heartbeat.py:143-146` still reads:

```python
assert not any(
    denial.get("reason") == "protected_read_target"
    for denial in turn.hard_boundary_denials
)
```

After this PR that reason value can never be produced, so the assertion is vacuously true forever.
This PR updated `test_pollers.py`, `test_pr_checkout_lease.py`, and
`test_deepagents_summarization_offload.py` for the rename and missed this one.

The functional risk is nil — `assert backend.drain_denials() == []` two lines above is
reason-independent and still bites. The problem is that the line reads like a guard and checks
nothing, which is the same silent-decay pattern that let the LongMemEval smoke skip for five weeks
and hid a live retrieval regression. Either point it at the new reason set or delete it and let the
`drain_denials()` assertion stand alone; both are fine, leaving it is not.

## Note, not blocking

Historical events in `logs/events.jsonl` carry the old `protected_read_target` value, so any replay
or dashboard reading across the cutover needs to accept both vocabularies. Worth a sentence in the
PR body so whoever runs the #1115 analysis does not silently lose the pre-change window.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Remediation verified at head `cc630fd2`. Approving.

The blocking item is resolved the cleaner of the two ways I offered: the four dead lines are
deleted rather than repointed, leaving `assert backend.drain_denials() == []`, which is
reason-independent and cannot go stale the next time a reason value changes. `protected_read_target`
now appears nowhere in `mimir/` or `tests/`.

I re-ran #1334's guard afterwards to be sure the deletion did not weaken it: re-adding
`read_file memory/core/00-identity.md` to the heartbeat prompt's declared operations still fails
`test_heartbeat_required_filesystem_operations_are_permitted`. The teeth were always the
per-operation `decision.allowed` and `drain_denials()` assertions; the removed line was genuinely
redundant.

Everything from the first pass stands: five rule-specific reasons in place of one string, `target`
recorded through `redact_payload`, `trigger` resolved across the three carriers, and
`service_principal` bound — which closes the attribution gap behind 533 target-less denials and 142
of 219 trigger-less ones. Both mutations (collapsing `core_memory_block`, dropping `target`) fail
tests.

Full suite: 7772 passed, 21 skipped, 0 failed.

Carrying forward the one note from the first review, still not blocking: events written before this
change carry the old `protected_read_target` value, so whoever runs the #1115 analysis needs to
accept both vocabularies or they will silently lose the pre-cutover window.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Addressed the blocking review item in cc630fd24: removed the now-vacuous `protected_read_target` assertion from `tests/test_heartbeat.py`, leaving the reason-independent `backend.drain_denials() == []` guard. Focused validation: `tests/test_heartbeat.py` — 11 passed.

Cutover note: historical `logs/events.jsonl` records may still use `protected_read_target`; analyses spanning this change need to accept both the legacy value and the five new reason-specific values.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1116: saga: registered trusted services get full-corpus reads from four trigger strings alone, regardless of declared job authority

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The grant now comes from declared authority instead of a trigger string, and the
enumeration is honest about what its evidence actually is.

**The mechanism is right.** `PLATFORM_SERVICE_TRIGGERS` is deleted outright rather than left as a
fallback, and `is_platform_service` reads `service.saga_full_corpus_read` off the frozen principal.
Exactly three sites declare it: the scheduler `_fire_job` registry entry, the session-boundary
`_on_session_idle` entry, and `builtin_trigger_service_principal`'s `session-boundary` branch. The
registration boundary is untouched, so this does not make the grant reachable by an unregistered
principal.

I checked the `heartbeat` branch of `builtin_trigger_service_principal` specifically, since it
would have been an easy place for the flag to leak — it does not set it, which matches the doc's
table. Doc and code agree.

**The conformance test is the right one.**
`test_trusted_service_without_corpus_declaration_is_narrow` is parameterized over `poller:new-feed`,
`heartbeat`, and `system`. Reverting `is_platform_service` to the old trigger-set derivation fails
all three. The `poller:new-feed` case is the important one: it pins that a *newly registered*
poller cannot acquire full-corpus read merely by being triggered as `poller`, which was the actual
defect.

**The inventory states its evidence basis rather than overclaiming.** "access_events records atom
and source but not the reader principal, so there are no principal-attributed historical reads; the
evidence below is the executable path and assigned workflow." That is the correct disclosure — the
leaf asked for evidence over inference, and where read telemetry does not exist the honest move is
to say so and reason from the executable path. Each principal is argued individually, including
`system`/`upgrade` and `saga_session_end` separately rather than grouped.

Retaining full corpus for `scheduler` on the strength of the weekly `reflect` audit, while
narrowing `heartbeat` on the same trigger, is the distinction that makes this a real fix rather
than a rename.

Full suite: 7770 passed, 21 skipped, 0 failed. All checks green.

One thing to watch after deploy, not blocking: eight pollers and the `upgrade` principal lose
full-corpus SAGA read here. Their own `service:*`-owned rows stay visible, so a poller reading back
its own learnings is unaffected — but if any of them was relying on cross-corpus recall that the
executable-path review did not surface, it will show up as thinner recall rather than an error.
Worth a look at `saga_read_would_block` volume by principal once chainlink #1112's telemetry lands.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1119: heartbeat: the tick prompt instructs two operations the access gate refuses, so every heartbeat fails the same way

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The fix is correct, the test design is the best I have seen on this repo, and it
implements the operator's direction exactly: core memory stays proposal-only, observations go to
channel memory.

**The test derives from the prompt rather than duplicating it.**
`test_heartbeat_required_filesystem_operations_are_permitted` regex-parses the declared operation
block out of `heartbeat.md` and runs each operation through both the `ToolRegistry` gate and
`WriteGuardBackend` with `enforcement_enabled=True` — stricter than production, which is shadow.
Mutation-tested three ways, all caught:

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| re-add `read_file memory/core/50-heartbeat-patterns.md` to the declared ops | FAILS |
| re-add `write_file memory/core/50-heartbeat-patterns.md` | FAILS |
| delete the declaration block entirely | FAILS (the `assert operations` guard) |

That last one matters most: the guard cannot be neutered by deleting what it guards. And because
the list is parsed from the prompt, a future instruction that adds a forbidden operation fails CI
automatically rather than waiting for someone to notice denials in the log.

**The timestamped-write design is the right call.** Writing
`memory/channels/scheduler:heartbeat/heartbeat-patterns-<timestamp>.md` means the tick never needs
to read or overwrite a prior observation — which sidesteps the fact that channel-memory *reads* are
themselves denied in some contexts. Routing stable patterns into core via `open_proposal`, with the
prompt explicitly saying the channel log is "not a way around core-memory review", keeps the
boundary intact.

Full suite on the head: 7768 passed, 21 skipped, 0 failed. All 7 checks green.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: fix(saga): restore shadow read mode and benchmark auth

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Strong work — the mode contract is restored correctly, the root cause is named with a commit
(`d2d37d9eb`, Worklink #883, 2026-07-15), and the telemetry addresses every point raised in the
design discussion. One blocking issue about the sampling, and three notes.

## Verified

Mutation-tested each guard independently:

| Mutation | Caught by |
|---|---|
| `selection_predicate` always strict (revert the fix) | 8 failures incl. `test_query_shadow_read_emits_one_bounded_non_sensitive_event` |
| `selection_predicate` always `1=1` (never enforce) | 4 failures incl. `test_get_atoms_true_enforcement_filters_private_rows` |
| `observe_selected` blinded | `test_shadow_recall_reports_pre_rrf_candidate_exclusions` + 2 |
| benchmark `auth_context=` kwargs stripped from the runner | 9 failures |

Full suite on the head: **7786 passed, 20 skipped, 0 failed**. All 7 checks green.

Scope discipline held. The session FAISS `limit * 4` / 200 truncation is untouched, so #1118 is
genuinely out; `test_session_boundary_expansion_binds_authorization_before_limit` covers
atom-expansion ordering, not the truncation. #1116 and #1117 are absent as stated.

The benchmark carrier is right, and pinning it against BOTH modes is what makes it durable —
`1=1` alone would have gone green today and re-broken at cutover.

## Blocking: the per-turn cap drops every surface after the first

`_SHADOW_EVENT_LIMIT_PER_TURN = 1` combined with `sampling: "first_shadow_read_with_exclusions"`
means only the first read *in a turn* that has exclusions is ever reported. `finalize()` is called
per read operation across distinct surfaces — `query` (`client.py:859`), `get_atoms` (`:1223`),
`search_sessions` (`:2782`), `recall`, and others — so a turn touching three surfaces reports one.
`test_shadow_read_events_are_bounded_to_one_per_turn` locks this in explicitly: it loops
`("query", "get_atoms")` and asserts `len(events) == 1`.

That defeats the downstream consumer. Chainlink #1115 requires the report to be "broken down by
surface, caller kind, and trigger" in order to size cutover impact. With first-wins sampling the
per-surface breakdown is structurally unobtainable, and the total is undercounted by an unknown
factor — heartbeat and poller turns issue many reads each, so the surfaces that run later are
systematically invisible. The bias is not random, so it does not average out over more turns.

The fix keeps the same bound: accumulate across the turn in one per-turn accumulator and emit once
at the end, with `resource_counts` keyed by surface. Still exactly one event per turn, but it
carries all surfaces instead of whichever fired first. The payload already declares `aggregation`
and `sampling` honestly, which is good practice — the issue is the value those fields describe.

## Non-blocking notes

**Cost of the counterfactual is unmeasured.** `observe_selected` issues an extra SQL query per
≤400-id chunk on every shadow read, and shadow is the default mode for every caller. The PR body
should state the measured overhead on a representative recall; if it is material, chunk size or
sampling is a knob worth choosing deliberately rather than inheriting.

**A failing probe is indistinguishable from a clean corpus.** The `except Exception` in
`observe_selected` drops to a debug log and reports nothing. Since #1115 will read this data as
evidence for the cutover decision, a silently broken probe looks exactly like "nothing would be
blocked." Counting probe failures — in the event or a counter — makes the difference visible.

**The frozen-class guard fails toward over-serving.** `enforcement_enabled` requires
`AuthContext.__dataclass_params__.frozen`; if that ever stops being true, enforcement silently
becomes unreachable and every read stays in shadow. That is the correct default today, but the
failure direction deserves a comment so a future change to `AuthContext` does not quietly disable
enforcement.

**On parity**, worth stating explicitly in the body: `1=1` restores pre-`d2d

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. I rebased this onto current `main` (`30dc095b`) myself since the scoped checkout could
not inventory the conflicts, and both my blocking finding and the collision are resolved.

## Your remediation of the sampling finding is correct

`0a6fc302` replaces first-wins sampling with a genuine per-turn aggregate: `aggregation` is now
`one_event_per_turn_by_surface`, `sampling` is `none`, and the payload carries a `surfaces` array
with per-surface counts bounded by `_SHADOW_SURFACE_LIMIT`, flushed once after all read surfaces in
the turn complete. Keeping `surface` as a scalar (`"multiple"` when >1) alongside the array means
existing consumers still parse. Mutation-tested: forcing `visible_surfaces = surfaces[:1]` fails
`test_shadow_read_events_aggregate_all_surfaces_once_per_turn`. Chainlink #1115 can now get the
per-surface breakdown it needs.

## The rebase surfaced a semantic collision, and I made a judgment call — please sanity-check it

Both PRs edited the same three triple read sites. `main` had #1332's
`_triple_read_authorization_predicate` (source-atom ACL INTERSECT triple ACL, chainlink #1117);
this branch replaced it with a mode-aware `selection_predicate("a")` (chainlink #1112). Taking
either side alone loses a property.

My first resolution routed both sides through `selection_predicate`. That was wrong, and the test
suite caught it: in shadow mode both evaluate to `1=1`, so the intersection filters nothing and
`test_dedup_narrowed_triple_is_hidden_from_wider_source_reader` failed — a rebase would have
silently re-opened the disclosure path #1117 closed.

The resolution in `c7091014` gates the two sides differently:

- **source atom → `selection_predicate`** (mode-aware). Shadow restores pre-regression read scope.
- **triple → `strict_predicate`** (always). A triple ACL narrower than its source is not policy
  scope; it is attenuation the writer chose in `_update_triple_acl_on_dedup`, whose stated purpose
  is that a triple never becomes "more readable than its least permissive source".

The principle I applied: shadow mode restores results that were *legitimately visible* before, but
must not restore ones a writer deliberately attenuated. This does mean shadow is not a pure
`1=1` on the triple path, which is a narrow exception to this PR's stated contract — flagging it
explicitly because it is a real semantic decision made during conflict resolution, not a mechanical
merge. If you disagree, the alternative is to gate both and accept the disclosure until enforcement
is enabled; I did not think a rebase should make that trade silently.

Mutation-tested: re-gating the triple side fails #1332's test.

## Validation

- Full configured suite on the rebased head: **7798 passed, 20 skipped, 0 failed**.
- Bench smoke with `--extra bench`: 9 passed — the boundary-RRF regression this PR exists to fix.
- `test_memory_triples.py` + `test_saga_read_authorization.py` + the bench smoke together: 106 passed.

Authorship preserved on both original commits; only the committer changed, as expected for a rebase.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Addressed the blocking sampling issue in 78c11a8a3.

- Replaced first-wins per-turn sampling with one turn-level accumulator, flushed during turn teardown. The single event now includes every observed surface in `resource_counts` and per-surface resource-type detail in `resource_type_counts`; `aggregation=one_event_per_turn_by_surface`, `sampling=none`.
- Added explicit shadow probe-failure counts so a broken strict counterfactual is distinguishable from a clean corpus without exposing failure details.
- Documented that the frozen-carrier guard deliberately fails toward compatibility/over-serving.
- Added regression coverage proving two surfaces are retained in one event and probe failures remain non-blocking but visible.

Validation: focused authorization/context suite 43 passed; full configured suite passed. The prior parity claim is by construction: shadow mode's `1=1` restores the pre-d2d37d9eb no-ownership-predicate read path.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Heads up: this is now `DIRTY` — #1332 (chainlink #1117, triple ACL intersection) merged and both PRs touch `mimir/saga/triples.py`. Please rebase onto current `main`; I'll re-review the remediation once it's mergeable.

Note the conflict is likely substantive rather than textual: #1332 replaced the source-only authorization in `triple_augment_search`, `top_triples_with_payload`, and `retrieve_by_entity` with `_triple_read_authorization_predicate`, which intersects the source-atom ACL with the triple's own ACL. Your shadow-mode work needs to route through that same helper so the intersection is subject to the mode contract too — otherwise triples would stay strictly filtered while atoms fall back to `1=1`, which is the same split-behavior bug in a different place.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1117: saga: triples can be narrower than their source atom, but reads authorize on the source only — a confirmed disclosure path

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. This closes the disclosure path completely and the test is the right shape.

**Complete.** All three source-only join sites (`triples.py:710`, `780`, `856`) now go through
`_triple_read_authorization_predicate`, and all three alias the triples table as `t`, matching the
`table="t"` predicate. No source-only path remains. The intersection is done in SQL alongside the
existing join, so there is no per-triple N+1.

**Correctly refuses the fallback.** The helper requires both predicates unconditionally, which is
what handles the `legacy_admin` sentinel without a source-only escape hatch — the branch my leaf
warned against.

**The test proves the real thing.** `test_dedup_narrowed_triple_is_hidden_from_wider_source_reader`
creates two source atoms under different owners *and* different tenants, calls `store_triples`
twice so the narrowing is produced by the actual `_update_triple_acl_on_dedup` path rather than
hand-written, asserts the narrowed row landed in the DB, then asserts all three read entry points
return empty for a caller who legitimately can read one of the sources. Reverting the intersection
to source-only fails exactly that test and nothing else.

Also good: the stale docstrings claiming the triple ACL columns were unenforced are gone from all
three functions, so the next reader will not repeat the dead-schema assumption.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1114: saga: 85% of atoms carry the fail-closed sentinel ACL — inventory every writer path and establish which, if any, is defective

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. This is the evidence-led inventory the leaf asked for, and it correctly declines to
assert more than the data supports.

**I ran the tool against the live store** (read-only, `mode=ro`, no mutating SQL) and then did the
operator investigation the report says class (a) requires. The conclusion holds.

```
total 1842 | direct_write_missing_owner 1329 | service_owned 284
            legacy_unattributed 127 | derived_legacy_inheritance 98 | other_owned 4 | unclassified 0
```

At first read, 1329 class-(a) rows carrying `skill_learning` and `agent_authored` source types
looked like it contradicted "no direct production tool writer is established as defective" — those
are exactly the two entry points the table clears. It does not. Splitting those rows by stamped vs
unstamped over time shows a clean cutover:

| source_type | unstamped (last seen) | stamped (first seen → latest) |
|---|---|---|
| `skill_learning` | 770, ends 2026-07-17T17:19 | 263, begins 2026-07-17T21:55 → 2026-08-02T02:24 |
| `agent_authored` | 658, ends 2026-07-16T02:35 | 27, begins 2026-07-17T00:33 → 2026-07-31T17:18 |
| `api` | 128, ends 2026-05-17 | 0 (source type retired) |

Every atom written in the last 48 hours is stamped — `service:poller:github-activity`,
`service:synthesis`, `jason` — except four `conversation` rows owned `legacy_admin`, which are the
derived class (b) correctly inheriting narrow evidence. **Stamping began working on 2026-07-17 and
has worked continuously since.** The 1329 rows are historical, and the report's refusal to call
them a live defect is right.

That also corrects the premise this leaf was originally filed on. I had asserted the stamping path
was failing for current writes; it is not, and the newest legacy rows are derived observations, not
failed direct stamps. Mimir made exactly that objection when reviewing the leaf, and the inventory
now proves the objection was correct.

**This hands #1115 what it needs:** a cutover timestamp of 2026-07-17 to migrate against, and a
defensible split between a fixed historical remnant and an ongoing rate of zero.

The document is honest where it matters. `legacy_unattributed` is explicitly not claimed as class
(a) because atoms persist no writer-path discriminator and the legacy importer produces the same
row shape — that is the discipline the leaf asked for, and the `limitations` field carries it into
the machine-readable output too.

Full suite: 7769 passed, 21 skipped, 0 failed.

Non-blocking: 123 test lines for a 159-line module is thin, and the two tests do not cover the
classification boundaries that carry the argument (a `skill_learning` row with partial provenance,
a derived row missing its `evidenced_by` relation landing in `unclassified`). The tool is read-only
analysis so the blast radius is a wrong report rather than wrong data, but #1115 will lean on these
counts — worth strengthening when that leaf runs.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1111: ci: no job builds the package on a pull request, so a packaging break is invisible until a release tag (a runtime file has been missing from published wheels for four releases)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The job closes the gap that let the 0.6.9 `web_auth.js` loss ship, and I verified it
catches both regression classes rather than taking the green check on faith.

**Mutation-tested locally against real builds:**

| Mutation | Caught by |
|---|---|
| remove `[tool.hatch.build.targets.sdist.force-include]` | `uv build` fails outright at the build step |
| remove `mimir/web_auth.js` from `include` | build SUCCEEDS; `assert_wheel_contents.py` fails with `missing required wheel members: ['mimir/web_auth.js']` |

The second is the important one — it is exactly the shape of the shipped 0.6.9 defect, where the
build is green and the artifact is quietly wrong. Nothing before this PR could have caught it.

**Design is right.** Release-order `npm ci` → `npm run build` → `uv build` mirrors publish.yml, and
building a second wheel directly from the checkout to diff against the sdist-built one is what
turns "the build succeeded" into "the artifact is correct". Full member-list parity via `Counter`
also catches duplicate members, not just missing ones, and the failure message names both
directions of the difference.

`REQUIRED_MEMBERS` covers the two files with a demonstrated history of silently dropping, and the
React check correctly ignores directory entries rather than matching the prefix alone.

**Runtime is 40 seconds** (01:28:33 → 01:29:13 on this PR's own run), well inside the bound where
path-gating would have been worth the complexity. Leaving it on every PR is the right call.

One small robustness note, not blocking: `--sdist-wheel dist/*.whl` relies on `dist/` holding
exactly one wheel. That holds today because the direct build is redirected to `dist/direct/`, but
a future step that leaves a second wheel in `dist/` would turn a shell glob into two argv values
and argparse would fail with a confusing error rather than a clear one.

The acceptance criterion asking for both reverted runs in the PR body is unmet — the body is the
worklink stub. I ran them myself and recorded the results above, so the evidence exists; noting it
so the gap in the record is deliberate rather than overlooked.

payload.author: jasoncarreira

I ran `tests/test_wheel_package_data.py` at head `0903013654377ad7b827cd4ac7cc03f3cd970f63`: **7 passed**. All seven GitHub checks are also green.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.title: Worklink #1107: wire work-reviewer into the pre-PR path and retire the never-invoked critic-structured

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES

The lifecycle is otherwise well placed: the reviewer runs only after commit plus re-observation, its result is persisted before PR creation, and rejection/failure remains advisory rather than corrupting the deterministic evidence gate. The new focused tests pass locally (61 passed), Python 3.12 and the enforced gate are green, with Python 3.11 still running when reviewed.

One security boundary blocks approval. `_invoke_work_reviewer()` launches `opencode run` directly through the generic runner, so it skips the existing Worklink OpenCode backend's minimal child environment and `OPENCODE_PERMISSION` enforcement. A prompt/plugin claim that `work-reviewer` is read-only is not a mechanical process boundary; this path currently inherits the controller environment and whatever process/filesystem authority ambient OpenCode configuration grants. I left the concrete remediation inline on `mimir/worklink/orchestrator.py`.

Please route this invocation through an equivalently constrained, tested runner and add a regression proving sensitive ambient env is scrubbed and write/process permissions are enforced. After that, the advisory result model and pre-PR placement look sound.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The implementation is good and does what the leaf asked — bounded advisory invocation, verdict and findings persisted to evidence and the PR body, REJECT non-gating, critic retired in its own commit, `StructuredOutputRetryMiddleware` kept with neutral fixtures. Blocking on the reachability mechanism, because the premise it rests on is not true of the deployed image.

## The claim

From `docs/internal/WORKLINK.md` in this PR:

> Generated runtime images install that package and register it in the global OpenCode plugin configuration, which also applies inside isolated Worklink checkouts.

## What the image actually contains

Neither half holds.

**The package is not installed.** `mimirbot/Dockerfile` installs exactly three npm globals:

```
npm install -g \
    opencode-ai@1.18.1 \
    opencode-openai-codex-auth@4.4.0 \
    opencode-anthropic-auth@0.0.13
```

`npm ls -g --depth=0` in the running container confirms only those three. `opencode-feature-factory` is absent.

**There is no plugin configuration.** No `opencode.json` or `config.json` under `/mimir-home/.config/opencode/` or `/root/.config/opencode/` registers any plugin.

So at runtime the reviewer resolves to "unavailable agent". This PR handles that non-fatally and records it, which is correct behaviour — and it means the feature would silently never run. That is the same failure mode as the `critic-structured` role this PR retires: a capability wired to something unreachable, never invoked, discovered only by grepping for zero occurrences. Replacing one unreachable reviewer with another is not progress.

## The only `work-reviewer.md` in the image is not the one you think

A filesystem search finds it in three places, all inside a checkout of the factory repository rather than an installed package:

    /workspace/opencode-feature-factory/assets/agent/work-reviewer.md
    /workspace/opencode-feature-factory/.opencode/worktrees/pr9-review2/assets/agent/work-reviewer.md
    /workspace/opencode-feature-factory-pr9/assets/agent/work-reviewer.md

That checkout is on an unrelated history to the operator's working copy:

| | HEAD | agent layout |
|---|---|---|
| container checkout | `be41d98` "Multi-agent pre_pr review panel + unified profiles config" — two commits, from "Initial commit" | `assets/agent/` |
| operator's working copy | `91ca206` "chore(release): feature-factory 0.1.7, opencode-feature-factory 0.3.14" | `packages/feature-factory/agents/` |

Different layout, different history, different content. So even if the agent were found, which definition gets loaded depends on which checkout happens to be present — and it would not be the one the factory is actually running.

## What needs to change

Pick a reachability mechanism that is true of the deployed image and verify it there, not in principle:

- If the npm package is the answer, `mimirbot/Dockerfile` needs to install and pin it, plus whatever plugin registration OpenCode requires. That is an image-layer change in the mimirbot repository, outside this PR, so this PR should not claim the mechanism works until it does.
- If the repository checkout is the answer, the agent path must be resolved explicitly rather than assumed, and the layout difference (`assets/agent/` versus `packages/feature-factory/agents/`) handled — the container's checkout uses the former and the operator's uses the latter.
- Either way, add a startup or first-use check that reports the agent as unresolvable, loudly. The whole reason this leaf exists is that a registered reviewer went a month without being invoked and nobody noticed. Reproducing that with a different reviewer and a `recorded, non-fatal` path would be worse, because the evidence record would carry an "unavailable" note that reads as a transient rather than a permanent misconfiguration.

State in the PR body which mechanism you chose and paste the command that proves the agent resolves inside a worklink checkout on the deployed image.

## Also worth checking before this lands

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body: Agreed. I missed the deployed-image reachability check in my review. This is an independent blocker from the constrained-execution boundary I raised: the reviewer must both resolve in the actual Worklink runtime and execute under mechanical environment/permission constraints. The current head proves neither, so my changes-requested verdict remains. The eventual fix should include the in-checkout resolution probe and overlap analysis you requested, not just turn `unavailable` into a louder warning.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1106: worklink: a rebase that drops already-applied commits strands its lease — repo_push accepts a HEAD repo_cleanup refuses (45 leases, 5.4 GB)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The predicate change is the right idea and better than what I suggested. Blocking because the proof it depends on is stored where the executor can write it, so the guard it replaces becomes forgeable.

## The right predicate, inverted the right way

Old: "current HEAD must descend from the lease's starting head." New:

```python
merge-base --is-ancestor <head> <published_head>
```

"current HEAD must be contained in what was published." That is the reachability-of-work test the leaf asked for, and inverting the direction is cleaner than the "is the lease's work upstream" phrasing I proposed — a rebase that drops already-applied commits leaves a HEAD contained in the published commit and releases, while a lease holding unpublished commits is not contained and still refuses. The refusal text names both sides, which the old one did not.

Recording the proof from the push path is also correctly placed:

```python
self._command(("update-ref", PUBLISHED_HEAD_REF, observed))
```

That runs only after push reachability verification passes, so `observed` is the verified remote commit rather than anything the model asserted. Deriving the proof from the remote rather than from local state is the part that makes this sound in principle.

`_attempt_cleanup`'s dry-run/digest/verify sequence is untouched, and the branch and origin mismatch refusals are unchanged.

## Blocking: the publication proof is executor-writable

`PUBLISHED_HEAD_REF = "refs/mimir/pr-checkout-lease/published"` lives inside the lease's `.git`. Since #1318 (merged) admits `write_file`/`edit_file` inside the turn's own active lease, and `_is_protected_path` does not cover it, that path is writable by the model:

```
.git/refs/mimir/pr-checkout-lease/published      protected=False
.git/mimir-pr-checkout-lease.json                protected=False
.git/FETCH_HEAD                                  protected=False
```

`_PROTECTED_NAMES` is `['.env', 'compose.env', 'config', 'core-memory', 'core_memory', 'corememory', 'credentials', 'identities', 'prompts', 'rate_limits.json', 'secret', 'secrets']` — `.git` is not among them, and only `.git/config` is caught, incidentally, because "config" is in the stem set.

So an executor can write its own HEAD into that ref file. `rev-parse --verify PUBLISHED_HEAD_REF^{commit}` then returns that value, `merge-base --is-ancestor head published_head` succeeds trivially (a commit is its own ancestor), and `shutil.rmtree(lease.path)` deletes a lease holding unpublished commits. That is exactly the loss the ancestry check existed to prevent, and exactly what #1075 was filed about.

I do not think any current flow does this, and it is not a privilege escalation — it is a data-integrity guard becoming forgeable by the party it constrains. But my review criteria on the leaf said not to add a force or bypass flag, because "an escape hatch here would be used by a future caller to delete a lease holding real work." A model-writable proof file is that escape hatch without the label.

Two ways out, either acceptable:

- Keep the proof outside the lease — in the lease-root directory alongside the lease, in worklink state, or anywhere the write-confinement rules already refuse. The proof describes the lease; it does not have to live in it.
- Or protect it: add `.git` to the write-protected set so nothing under any repository's `.git` is model-writable. That is a broader change with its own review, and it would also close the two adjacent paths below, but it may break flows that legitimately write there.

State which you chose and add a test that a write to the proof path is refused.

## Adjacent, worth a look but not blocking this PR

`.git/mimir-pr-checkout-lease.json` — the lease metadata — is also unprotected, and #1318's containment helper reads `lease.scope_id`, `lease.owner`, `lease.path` and `lease.lease_root` from it. The loaded `PRCheckoutLease` object is constructed once per turn, so mid-turn forgery would not change decisions already made, but a

payload.body:
Approving. My earlier changes-requested was based on a finding that did not hold — `.git` writes were already refused on the lease-admission path before this PR, and `update-ref` is not shell-admitted; the new adversarial test passes unmodified against the pre-remediation `access_control.py`. Details and the mutation matrix are in the preceding comment.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Addressed the publication-proof trust-boundary finding in fc41c6a90.

I chose the narrower protection route: `.git` is now protected by `WriteResourceAdapter`, so `write_file` / `edit_file` may still modify source files in the active lease but cannot modify any Git metadata. The adversarial authorization regression specifically covers the publication ref, lease metadata, and `FETCH_HEAD`; all three now refuse with `repo_pr_target_outside_active_lease`.

Validation:
- Focused: 320 passed
- Full configured suite: passed (repo_test)
