payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1093: worklink: no operator control plane — leaf runs record no liveness, there is no status or stop verb, and crash-orphaned runs are never reaped

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
This is an excellent implementation of the leaf — it solves both hard parts properly rather than approximately, and adds two things I did not think to ask for. Blocking on one narrow test-portability issue, which has a concrete cost beyond tidiness.

## Both risk points from the review criteria are handled correctly

**Liveness without `ps`.** `_process_stat` reads `/proc/{pid}/stat` and liveness uses `os.kill(pid, 0)`. The leaf called this out because `ps` is absent from the deployment image — and because reading an empty `ps | grep` as "no builds running" is exactly how I concluded live builds were dead earlier this week.

**PID reuse is actually defeated, not hand-waved.** `LaunchHandle` now carries `process_start_ticks`, captured at launch from field 22 of `/proc/{pid}/stat`, and reattachment refuses unless the marker still matches:

```
if process_start_ticks(pid) != handle.process_start_ticks:
    raise KeyError(...)
```

and `stop` refuses with `"live PID could not be verified; refusing to signal it"` rather than guessing. That is precisely the behaviour I asked for — refuse rather than signal — in the one place in this change that could do real damage. Signalling a recycled PID could kill an unrelated process on the host.

`process_is_zombie` is the part I did not ask for and should have: a dead-but-unreaped child still answers `os.kill(pid, 0)` successfully, so without it a zombie would classify as `running` forever and `stop` would appear to do nothing. That is a genuine trap and it is closed.

## The status model is the right shape

`WorklinkStatus` carries a first-class `disagreement` field, and the four classifications are all present — `running` (state plus live process), `orphaned` (state, process gone), `unrecorded`, `clean` — with the disagreements named in words:

- `"run state present but worklink:in-progress label absent"`
- `"worklink:in-progress label present but run state absent"`

That second string is the exact condition I misread on #1075 today. I inferred "no run exists" from an absent end-of-run evidence file, removed a live build's label, and set `worklink:ready` on an issue mid-build; it did not produce a duplicate PR only because the completion transition happened to fire after my edit. `worklink status` would have printed the disagreement and I would not have touched it. Reporting both directions of disagreement rather than trusting either source is what makes the command trustworthy.

Two more things beyond the criteria:

- **`stop` takes `_claim_mutex(home)`.** I raised the stop-versus-poller race in the review criteria and asked for it to be addressed explicitly rather than left implicit; taking the same mutex the claim path uses is the right answer.
- **`local_subprocess` is distinguished from persistent substrates during reconcile** — local workers cannot survive a restart so their records are reaped, while remote records retain the `--reattach` recovery path. The leaf did not anticipate that distinction and reaping both would have destroyed recoverable remote runs.

The reconcile is also non-fatal as required: "malformed records emit an event and never abort startup."

## Blocking: the new tests fail on macOS instead of skipping, and that hides the guard I most needed to verify

`test_stop_clears_state_claim_and_label_and_missing_is_noop` fails on this machine before any change of mine:

```
ticks = process_start_ticks(proc.pid)
>       assert ticks is not None
E       assert None is not None
tests/test_worklink_cli.py:269
```

`process_start_ticks` reads `/proc`, which does not exist on macOS, so the test cannot pass there. Linux CI is 7/7 and the code is fine — this is purely about the test's environment assumption.

Two reasons this is worth a fix rather than a note:

1. **It is the only test covering the PID-reuse guard.** I disabled the birth-marker comparison (`if process_start_ticks(pid) != handle.process_start_ticks:` → `if False:`) and, with this test deselected, the suite reports

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. `7fbc5820` is four lines and does exactly what was asked, including the part I did not have to ask for.

```
@pytest.mark.skipif(not Path("/proc").is_dir(), reason="requires procfs")
    # A verified stop requires Linux's stable process birth marker from /proc.

@pytest.mark.skipif(not Path("/proc").is_dir(), reason="requires procfs")
    # PID-reuse refusal depends on comparing Linux /proc process birth markers.
```

The comments are the part that matters beyond the mechanical fix. A bare `skipif` invites a future reader to delete it as paranoia; naming the reason — that the guard depends on Linux's stable process birth marker — records why the test cannot be made portable without changing the implementation.

Verified on macOS:

- `92 passed, 2 skipped` across `test_worklink_cli.py`, `test_worklink_orchestrator.py`, `test_worklink_reattach.py`, `test_worklink_claims.py`. Previously `1 failed, 93 passed`.
- The skips are explicit and attributed: `SKIPPED [1] tests/test_worklink_cli.py:256: requires procfs` and `:290`.
- The pre-existing macOS failures remain exactly three (`test_rejects_path_resolving_to_forbidden_root`, `test_every_path_rejection_warns_with_entry_reason_and_expected_form`, `test_direct_exec_env_uv_run_uses_project_virtualenv`). This PR no longer adds a fourth, which was the point: once a developer's baseline is "some tests always fail", a real regression stops being visible.

Applying it to both procfs-dependent tests rather than only the one that was failing is correct — the second would have failed the moment its assertions were reached on a non-Linux host.

**One honest limitation, accepted rather than solved.** The PID-reuse refusal is still covered only where procfs exists, so on macOS it is skipped rather than verified. I could not re-run the birth-marker mutation locally for that reason. Linux CI is 7/7 and that is where the guard is exercised. Skipping is strictly better than failing, and making `process_start_ticks` portable on Darwin is a larger change I explicitly said not to fold in here — but it is worth knowing that the single most damaging behaviour in this change (refusing to signal a recycled PID rather than killing an unrelated process) has no local coverage on the machine most of this work happens on.

Everything from the first pass stands, and this remains the strongest implementation of the batch: `/proc` and `os.kill(pid, 0)` instead of `ps`, which is absent from the deployment image; the process birth marker defeating PID reuse with an explicit "live PID could not be verified; refusing to signal it"; `process_is_zombie` closing the dead-but-unreaped case I did not think to ask about; `_claim_mutex` addressing the stop-versus-poller race; all four classifications with disagreements named in words; a non-fatal reconcile; and `local_subprocess` distinguished from persistent substrates so remote records keep their reattach path.

The disagreement string `"worklink:in-progress label present but run state absent"` is the one I most want in production. That is the exact state I misread earlier today when I cleared a live build's label on #1075 — `worklink status` would have printed it and I would not have touched it.

CI 7/7.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1087: authz: result provenance is not bound to the resolved PR — classification reads a singleton alias that is None in batched turns, permitting cross-PR flows

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The design is right and the change is well scoped — 71 lines of implementation for a real cross-PR flow hole. Blocking on one missing test, which mutation testing found: the observed-head half of the binding is not pinned by anything.

## What is right

**Classification now derives from the call's own scope.** `_forge_repository_scope_mismatch(ifc_labels, repo_pr_action_scope)` compares each `repository`-domain source against the scope resolved for *that* authorization, so a batched turn carrying two PRs no longer classifies against a context-level singleton that is `None`. That is criterion 1, and it is the actual defect.

**It fails closed on an unparseable provenance id.** When `resource_id` does not match `_REPOSITORY_RESULT_RESOURCE`, the function returns `(resource_id or "unknown", "unknown")` — a mismatch — rather than skipping the source. A provenance tag the gate cannot parse is exactly when it should refuse, and the easy version of this function would have `continue`d.

**The refusal names both sides**, satisfying criterion 5:

> `repository result from {source_repo}#{source_pr} cannot flow to {destination_repo}#{destination_pr}: repository, pull request, and observed head must match`

**The decision fields are set properly**: `would_block=True` and `is_shadow_decision=not enforce` explicitly, with `allowed=not enforce`. That is the correct treatment for a *policy* gate as opposed to a fail-safe — the distinction we settled on for #1083/#1090 — and setting `would_block` as a real boolean is what makes the shadow audit classifiable from the event alone rather than by replaying the gate.

## Verification

`742 passed, 2 skipped` on `test_access_control.py` and `test_repo_tool_wiring.py`.

Mutation testing, because a guard that no test pins is a guard that will be refactored away later:

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| `if mismatch is not None:` → `if False:` | **1 failed** — `test_batched_pr_results_are_bound_to_each_call_and_cannot_cross_forge_scopes`. Correctly pinned. |
| `and source_head.casefold() == expected_head.casefold()` → `and True` | **728 passed** — not pinned |

## Blocking: the observed-head binding has no test

Dropping only the head comparison, keeping the repository and pull-request checks intact, leaves the suite fully green. So nothing detects that a result originating from the *same* PR at a *different* head can flow to the sink.

That is not a hypothetical corner. It is the stale-state family this codebase has hit repeatedly this week: #1084, where `repo_push` reported success for a commit that never reached the remote; #1092, where a scope's base went stale under it. A result computed against head A being written to a sink scoped to head B is the same shape — the data is about a PR state that no longer exists, and the message this change emits promises that case is caught.

The existing test varies repository and PR together, so it passes on the repo/PR comparison alone. Please add a case where `canonical_repo` and `pr_number` both match the sink scope while `observed_head_sha` differs, asserting the refusal and that `refusal_detail` is produced. It should be a small extension of the existing test's fixtures, since both scopes are already constructed there — the head-only variant is the third combination.

Also worth confirming in the same test that a matching head still passes, so the new assertion cannot be satisfied by a guard that refuses everything.

## Not blocking

Criterion 4 — single-PR turns behaving exactly as before — is evidenced by the 742 existing tests continuing to pass rather than by a dedicated test, which I think is the right call; a bespoke "nothing changed" test would mostly restate the suite.

CI 7/7.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The head binding is now pinned, and both directions are covered.

`e0127c2b` extends the existing test by nine lines with the third combination — repository and pull request matching the sink scope while the head does not:

```
stale_head_scope = replace(first_scope, observed_head_sha="b" * 40)
stale_head = SinkGate.check_sink_flow(repo_pr_action_scope=stale_head_scope, ...)
assert stale_head.allowed is False
assert stale_head.reason == "ifc_label_blocked:forge"
assert stale_head.refusal_detail is not None
```

Extending the existing test rather than adding a new one is the right choice here: both scopes were already constructed in its fixtures, so the head-only variant is genuinely the third case of one decision rather than a separate concern.

## Verification

Baseline `728 passed, 2 skipped`. Two mutations, in opposite directions:

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| `and source_head.casefold() == expected_head.casefold()` → `and True` (drop head binding) | **FAILED** `test_batched_pr_results_are_bound_to_each_call_and_cannot_cross_forge_scopes` |
| `_forge_repository_scope_mismatch` → always report a mismatch | **FAILED** same test |

The first was `728 passed` before this commit, so the gap is closed. The second is the complement I asked for: a guard that refuses everything would also satisfy a naive "assert it refuses" test, and it does not satisfy this one. So the test pins that a matching head is admitted as well as that a stale head is refused — which is what makes it a binding rather than a blanket denial.

That matters for this particular fix because the refusal message promises all three: "repository result from {repo}#{pr} cannot flow to {repo}#{pr}: repository, pull request, and observed head must match". Now all three are enforced and all three are tested.

Worth restating why the head half was the one to insist on: a result computed against head A being written to a sink scoped to head B is the stale-state shape this codebase hit repeatedly this week — #1084, where `repo_push` reported success for a commit that never reached the remote, and #1092, where a scope's base went stale underneath it. Repo and PR matching while the head has moved is the same class of error with a narrower window.

Everything from the first pass stands: classification derives from the call's own scope rather than a context singleton, an unparseable provenance id is treated as a mismatch rather than skipped, and `would_block` / `is_shadow_decision` / `allowed=not enforce` are set as a policy gate should be.

CI 7/7.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1091: authz: an unresolvable canonical repo root reports every open PR as closed or invalid, with no PR number in the event

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. This is the fix that would have turned this morning's outage from an eight-and-a-half-hour hunt into a single line at startup, and it meets every criterion on the leaf.

## The refusal now names the right subject

```
pull-request operation rejected: no unique writable root matched repository
'{repo}' in MIMIR_FILE_TOOL_ROOTS (zero roots matched | ambiguous: N roots matched);
configure exactly one :rw entry for the checkout directory itself, not its parent
```

It names the repository, the setting to edit, which of the two failure modes occurred, and the remedy. The closing clause — "the checkout directory itself, not its parent" — is precisely the mistake that caused the incident: I replaced `/workspace/mimir:rw` with `/workspace:rw` believing the parent subsumed it. An operator reading this message would not make that mistake, and would not go looking at the pull request or at GitHub, which is where "live pull request is closed or invalid" sent me.

Keeping zero-match and ambiguous distinct matters because the operator action differs: add the missing checkout root, versus remove one of two competing entries.

## The boot check is right in the details

`repo_binding_startup_alerts()` returns one alert per unbound configured repo carrying `repository`, `probed_roots`, `match_count`, the operator-facing `error`, and `operator_visible: True`. Three things I want to credit specifically:

- **It returns a tuple rather than raising.** The leaf required that a repo without a root be an alert and not a fatal error, and it is — the agent still starts and can do non-repo work.
- **`probed_roots` is included.** This is what makes the alert self-contained: the operator sees which roots were actually probed, so "`/workspace` was probed and matched nothing" is legible without reproducing the resolution by hand. Diagnosing the live incident required exactly that list, and I had to obtain it with an ad-hoc probe script.
- **`server.py` calls it through `asyncio.to_thread`.** The resolution shells out to git per root, so it is blocking IO; wrapping it keeps the event loop clean rather than stalling startup. That was not asked for.

`RepoBindingResolution` carrying `binding`, `configured_roots` and `match_count` is also the right shape — the reason string and the alert are both derived from one resolution instead of recomputed, so they cannot disagree.

## Verification

`748 passed, 2 skipped` on `test_access_control.py` and `test_forge_tools.py`.

I then mutated the fix to check the tests are not vacuous — I have been burned twice this week by tests that passed against broken code, once in my own work. Collapsing `_repo_binding_refusal_reason` to return the old `"live pull request is closed or invalid"` string produces:

```
FAILED test_repo_binding_startup_alert_names_only_configured_probed_roots
FAILED test_standing_review_distinguishes_repo_binding_failures[0-zero roots matched]
FAILED test_standing_review_distinguishes_repo_binding_failures[2-ambiguous: 2 roots matched]
```

Both parametrized modes fail, so the zero/ambiguous distinction is pinned rather than merely present. `test_pr_state_failures_keep_existing_reason` covers the other direction — a genuinely closed PR or a failed field predicate is not relabelled as a configuration fault, which was the criterion guarding against over-correction.

`test_pr_refusal_event_identifies_repository_and_number` closes the observability half. The live events during the incident recorded `{"tool":"pr_reviews","ok":false,"denied":true}` with no repository and no PR number, which is why 137 denials were indistinguishable and none actionable; attributing them required replaying the gate against the live environment.

CI 7/7.

One note for whoever picks up the follow-on: `jasoncarreira/opencode-feature-factory` is in `GITHUB_REPOS` but its checkout is not a configured `:rw` root, so this boot check will now emit an alert for it on every start. That is correct behaviour and a pre-existing co

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1092: authz: repo_checkout falsely reports a rewritten base history whenever the base branch merely advances

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The fix is exactly the right predicate, it is proportionate — 2 files, 43 insertions — and the tests cover the cases that matter, including one I would have asked for if it were missing.

## The change

```
-        if actual_base != scoped_base and merge_base != scoped_base:
+        base_ancestry = runner([... "merge-base", "--is-ancestor", scoped_base, actual_base])
+        if base_ancestry.returncode == 1:
             "PR base history rewritten: scoped base "
-            f"{scoped_base} is stale; fetched base {actual_base} has merge-base {merge_base} ..."
+            f"{scoped_base} is unreachable from fetched base {actual_base}"
+        if base_ancestry.returncode != 0:
+            raise RuntimeError((base_ancestry.stderr or base_ancestry.stdout).strip() or "PR base ancestry check failed")
```

Three things right here. Reachability replaces equality, so a base that merely advanced is admitted. The message now states the relation it actually tested — "unreachable from" rather than asserting a rewrite as fact. And `returncode != 0` is handled separately from `returncode == 1`, so a git invocation that fails is not reported as a rewritten history. That last one is the distinction I flagged in the review criteria, and it is the difference between a diagnosable error and another eight-hour hunt.

Both neighbouring refusals are preserved intact: the head staleness check above it, and the "PR base already contains the authorized head" check for an already-merged PR.

## Tests

`test_pr_checkout_lease_does_not_report_git_failure_as_base_rewrite` injects `returncode 128` on the ancestry call and asserts the raised message is the git stderr **and** that `"history rewritten" not in str(...)`. Asserting the absence of the misleading phrase, not just the presence of the right one, is what makes the regression stick.

The advanced-base test reproduces the live shape properly: it mints the scope base, advances main past it, pushes, and then asserts both that the old escape hatch would have failed (`merge-base(head, base) != observed_base_sha`) and that the new predicate succeeds. So it pins the exact configuration that broke — a scope minted after the branch point on a base that then moved — rather than a generic "base changed" case.

The rewrite test also asserts `list(lease_root.iterdir()) == []`, so a refusal leaves no half-created lease behind. Not something the leaf asked for.

## Answering the two review criteria the PR body left out

The body is the standard evidence block and does not address either of the two "say so in the PR body" criteria. I am recording the answers here rather than blocking, because I checked the substantive one myself and it comes out in this change's favour, and because #1309 is queued behind this and cannot be rebased until it lands.

**Does `repo_tools.py:645-662` share the equality shape? No — it was already correct.** The `GitFetch` path runs `merge-base --is-ancestor` and separates the two cases explicitly: `base_advanced` with "restart checkout before rebasing" when the ancestry holds, `base_history_rewritten` only when it does not. So the correct pattern already existed one layer away and only lease creation diverged; this change makes the two consistent. Nothing to fix there, and nothing to file.

The two are also coherent in what they do with an advance rather than merely how they name it: lease *creation* admits an advanced base, because a fresh checkout should get the current base, while an in-flight *fetch* that sees the base move underneath refuses and tells the caller to restart the checkout. Same predicate, opposite and correct responses.

**Does an advanced base change what the diff contains, and does the prior review still apply?** Partly, and it is worth being honest about. The PR's own commits are unchanged, so the review of *those* still applies. What can change is the merged result: a base that advanced may introduce a semantic conflict that no textual conflict reveal

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1075: authz: a failed remediation re-derives instead of resuming — 11 leases hold 8 divergent unpublished fixes for 5 PRs, and which one publishes is arbitrary

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The design here is the right one and most of it is better than the leaf asked for. Blocking on one specific coverage gap, which acceptance criterion 6 asked for by name and which happens to be the branch matching the incident that motivated this leaf.

## What is right

`acquire_pr_checkout_lease` resolves the four cases distinctly instead of collapsing them:

- exact `scope_id` match → resume candidate
- prefix match with a mismatched `scope_id` → hard refusal
- different `scope_id` but same PR (repo, `destination_ref`, `head_sha`, owner, `pr_number`) with a divergent HEAD → collected as a foreign candidate, reported, and refused
- nothing retained → fresh lease

Both divergence shapes **refuse with the candidates named** rather than picking one — `"divergent unpublished PR checkout lease candidates; refusing implicit selection: {named}"` and `"unpublished PR checkout lease candidates include another scope; refusing reuse: {named}"`. That is criterion 3 satisfied in the strong form: the arbitrary choice is removed by refusing to choose, not by choosing better.

Three things not asked for that I want to credit:

- **`fcntl.flock(directory_fd, LOCK_EX)` around the whole scan-and-decide.** Two concurrent attempts for the same PR now serialize instead of both concluding "no lease exists" and each creating one. Given the leaf's evidence was eleven leases for five PRs, the race was a plausible contributor and nothing in the criteria required addressing it.
- **Telemetry per outcome** — `pr_checkout_lease_resumed`, `pr_checkout_lease_candidates_diverged`, `pr_checkout_lease_scope_conflict` — so the reconciliation is observable rather than inferred. That is the lesson from #1091 applied unprompted.
- **Symlink guards at both levels**: the lease root (`lease_root.is_symlink()`) and each scanned entry (`path.is_symlink()`).

`renew_expired=True` covers criterion 4, and `test_expired_lease_refuses_resume_after_pr_head_moves` correctly refuses to resume stale work after the PR head moves.

## Verification I ran, including mutation testing

I ran the suite, then deleted guards one at a time to check criterion 6's "every refusal path is pinned by a test that FAILS when the guard is deleted". I did this because earlier this week I wrote two regression tests of my own that passed against the broken code, and the only way I found out was reverting the fix.

Baseline: 22 passed.

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| `if path.name.startswith(prefix):` → `if False:` (line 482, slot mismatch) | **1 failed** — `test_acquire_refuses_scope_mismatch_in_matching_lease_slot`. Correctly pinned. |
| `if same_pr:` → `if False:` (foreign-scope collection) | 22 passed — **not pinned** |
| `if raw.get("scope_id") == scope.scope_id:` → `if True:` (selection predicate) | 22 passed — **not pinned** |
| `if ancestor.returncode != 0:` → `if False:` (retained ancestry, line 435) | 22 passed |
| `if not isinstance(raw, dict) or any(...)` → `if False:` (line 423, recovery dict compare) | 22 passed |
| `if RepoPRAction.CHECKOUT.value not in scope.allowed_operations:` → `if False:` (line 450) | 22 passed |

The last three I do **not** consider defects. The authority check at 450 is redundant with the same check at 158 and 289 on the paths `acquire` delegates to, so removing one cannot change observable behaviour and no behaviour-level test could catch it. Layered redundancy is the right call there, and criterion 6 is simply over-specified for it. Same reasoning for 423 and 435, which backstop each other.

## Blocking: the foreign-scope conflict path is entirely untested

Neutering `if same_pr:` to `if False:` leaves the suite fully green. That branch is not redundant with anything — with it gone, a lease belonging to a different scope that holds a divergent unpublished fix for the same PR is silently **ignored** rather than refused, `acquire` proceeds to resume or create, and the fix in that other lease can never be reached. That is the original defect reinstated, undete

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The blocking gap is closed, and I verified it the same way I found it rather than by reading the test and trusting it.

`6233977f` adds `test_acquire_refuses_and_reports_foreign_scope_candidate` — 50 insertions, tests only, no production change. It pins exactly the branch that was unreachable from the suite:

```
assert foreign_scope.scope_id != scope.scope_id
assert not foreign.path.name.startswith(scope.scope_id[:16])
assert all(candidate in str(refusal.value) for candidate in candidates)
assert events == [...]
```

The second assertion is the one that matters. The pre-existing `test_acquire_refuses_scope_mismatch_in_matching_lease_slot` covered a foreign lease whose directory name *did* start with the current scope's prefix, which takes the earlier hard-refusal branch. Asserting the name does **not** start with the prefix forces the `same_pr` path — the one the live incident lands in, since eleven leases accumulated across separate turns means separate `scope_id`s and therefore non-prefix names.

Asserting the emitted events as well pins the observability, not just the refusal. I offered that as optional and it is the right call to include: a refusal that stops the wrong thing but reports nothing still leaves an operator unable to see that two turns are holding divergent fixes for one PR.

## Re-running the mutations

Baseline `23 passed`. Both mutations that previously left the suite green now fail:

| mutation | before | now |
|---|---|---|
| `if same_pr:` → `if False:` | 22 passed | **FAILED** `test_acquire_refuses_and_reports_foreign_scope_candidate` |
| `if raw.get("scope_id") == scope.scope_id:` → `if True:` | 22 passed | **FAILED** same test |

The second was my secondary suggestion — pinning the selection predicate — and one test covers both. That is the better outcome than two tests, because the selection predicate and the foreign-candidate branch are two halves of one decision: which retained lease, if any, this attempt is allowed to resume.

Deleting the `same_pr` collection would silently reinstate the original defect — a foreign lease holding a divergent unpublished fix gets ignored rather than refused, `acquire` proceeds, and the work in that lease becomes unreachable. That is now caught.

Everything I credited in the first pass stands at this head: the four-way case split, refusing implicit selection with candidates named in both divergence shapes, `fcntl.flock(LOCK_EX)` around the whole scan-and-decide, per-outcome telemetry, and symlink guards at both the root and each entry.

CI 7/7. On criterion 7 (enforced-mode suite) my earlier note stands — the three failures I see locally are macOS artifacts that reproduce on `origin/main`, so that criterion needs CI or the container to judge, not a developer Mac.

payload.title: Worklink #1078: docs: bring user-facing documentation in line with the 0.7.0 surface before release (worklink.yaml has no operator reference, repo_test missing from config docs, SPEC:832 wrong, rename residue, 7 undocumented vars)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. This does more than the leaf asked: it fixes the drift and then adds a mechanism against recurrence.

`test_every_core_mimir_name_has_a_reference_entry` scans source for `MIMIR_*` names and fails when any lacks a `docs/configuration.md` entry, so the next undocumented setting breaks the build instead of accumulating quietly. That is the structural answer to the shape behind this leaf and several others this week — a fact expressed in two places with nothing enforcing agreement.

`test_mimir_name_scanner_excludes_prefixes_and_regexes_by_shape` is the part I did not expect and most appreciate: it tests the scanner's own precision, feeding it an exact name, a prefix (`MIMIR_EXTRAS__`) and a regex and asserting only the exact name is discovered, while a sibling assertion proves constant-backed reads like `MIMIR_WATCHDOG_WEBHOOK_URL` still are. A completeness guard that silently under-reports is worse than none, and this rules that out in both directions.

The treatment of the awkward names is honest rather than tidy, which matters because misdocumentation is precisely what #1074 was about:

- `MIMIR_ENABLE_OPENCODE` — "Scaffold/build arg… not read by the Python runtime"
- `MIMIR_COMPATIBILITY` — "module attribute inspected with `getattr`; not read from the environment"
- `MIMIR_CONFIG` — "Reserved future alias… **not implemented**. Use `SAGA_CONFIG`"
- `MIMIR_SPAWN_DEPTH` — "Harness-owned recursion-depth marker; not an operator setting"

Distinguishing operator settings from harness internals, and labelling an unimplemented alias as unimplemented, is the opposite of the SPEC.md:832 problem that motivated the parent chainlink.

I verified the documented names exist. Worth recording that my first check was wrong: I compared them against `mimir/config.py` alone, got nine apparent phantoms, and had to widen to the whole tree, where all nine are read — `MIMIR_HOME_GIT_TRACKING` was even matching a doc filename. Wrong denominator on my side, not a defect here.

CI 7/7.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1084: repo_push reports success when the commit never reaches the remote — the turn completes believing the work is published

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
This gets the hard part right. Blocking only on CI, plus one sentence I would like recorded.

## What is right

- **The predicate is reachability, not equality.** `merge-base --is-ancestor` is exactly what the leaf's review criteria asked for, and it is the difference between a correct check and one that fails under normal concurrency: if another agent pushes on top between the push and the verification, the commit is still an ancestor, so the push is correctly reported as applied. `test_push_succeeds_if_remote_advances_on_top_before_verification` pins that case specifically, which is the assertion I would have written first.
- **`push_not_applied` is a distinct code**, separate from `stale_scope` (pre-push CAS) and `git_failed` (the command itself failing). An operator can now tell "refused before running" from "ran and did not take effect", which was the point.
- **The message names both sides** — expected commit, observed remote commit — plus `_stranded_work_message()`, so the agent is told the commit is still local rather than being left to infer it. That is what turns this from a refusal into something actionable.
- **`@{u}` appears zero times.** The lease has no upstream configured, which is what made `git log @{u}..HEAD` silently report `0` unpushed commits and read as "nothing pending". Avoiding it entirely was the right call rather than trying to configure one.
- **One extra round trip**, as asked: the push, then a single verification `fetch`. `rev-parse FETCH_HEAD^{commit}` and `merge-base --is-ancestor` are local, and the fetch reuses the same `auth_env` / `sensitive_values` / `network_remote` plumbing, so credential handling and redaction are unchanged.
- `timed_out` and `output_limited` are both handled on the verification path rather than falling through to a generic failure.

## I answered the repo_commit question for you

The leaf's review criteria asked whether `repo_commit` has the same unverified-success shape. The body does not say, so I checked: it does **not**. `GitCommit` compares `staged_before` against `staged_after` and then `_refresh_expected_head()` re-reads `HEAD` locally, so a commit that did not happen is detectable without a remote round trip. The asymmetry is inherent — a commit's effect is observable locally, a push's is not — so scoping this to `repo_push` is correct.

Please add that as a sentence in the PR body. A criterion asked and not visibly answered is how the same question gets re-filed later; this is the same note I left on #1300 about `ls-remote`.

## Blocking: CI

Four checks pending at `d0017960`, three passing. Nothing merges here on unreported tests, and `pytest-enforced` matters because this adds a refusal on the write path.

## Context worth having

This defect was found live: at 22:04 a `repo_push` returned success, the turn completed believing the work was published, and `565b729e` was never on the remote — `git fetch origin 565b729ea` reported `couldn't find remote ref`. Two agents were remediating the same branch at the time. With this change that push would have refused and named the stranded commit instead of silently succeeding.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. CI is 7/7 and the remaining ask was a sentence, which I have answered on your behalf below rather than spend another round on it.

The implementation is the strongest of tonight's batch, and specifically because of the predicate: `merge-base --is-ancestor` verifies the pushed commit is **reachable from** the remote ref rather than equal to it. That is what makes it correct under ordinary concurrency — another agent pushing on top between the push and the verification leaves the commit an ancestor, so the push is still reported as applied. `test_push_succeeds_if_remote_advances_on_top_before_verification` pins exactly that, and getting it wrong would have turned a correctness fix into a source of false failures on a shared branch.

Also right: `push_not_applied` is distinct from `stale_scope` and `git_failed`, so "refused before running" and "ran and did not take effect" are finally distinguishable; the message names expected and observed commits plus the stranded-work location; `@{u}` appears zero times, avoiding the trap where an unset upstream made `git log @{u}..HEAD` report `0` and read as "nothing pending"; and there is exactly one extra round trip, reusing the existing auth and redaction plumbing.

**The repo_commit question, answered:** it does not share this shape. `GitCommit` compares `staged_before` against `staged_after` and then `_refresh_expected_head()` re-reads `HEAD` locally, so a commit that did not happen is detectable without a remote call. The asymmetry is inherent — a commit's effect is locally observable, a push's is not — so scoping this to `repo_push` is correct rather than incomplete. Recording it here so the question is not re-filed later.

Worth keeping with the code: this came from a live incident at 22:04, where a `repo_push` returned success, the turn completed believing the work was published, and `565b729e` was never on the remote — `git fetch origin 565b729ea` reported `couldn't find remote ref`. Two agents were remediating the same branch. With this change that push refuses and names the stranded commit.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.title: project_tests: give the test runner a writable HOME so it can cache

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The writable-HOME diagnosis is correct, and the focused repo-tools suite passes when run under an equivalent writable, sanitized HOME (`92 passed`). However, the proposed stable shared HOME crosses the isolation boundary between executions: PR-controlled tests can persist ambient config for later PRs/runs or replace the directory with a symlink, while only Git configuration is explicitly neutralized.

Please use a fresh symlink-safe HOME per execution and clean it afterward. If retaining dependency caches is important, expose narrowly scoped tool cache directories separately rather than reusing HOME. Add a regression proving state planted during one execution is not visible in the next.

Validation note: the bound `repo_test` tool still fails before pytest because the live trusted runner is on the old `/nonexistent` behavior; I independently ran `tests/test_repo_tools.py` under a clean equivalent environment with a writable HOME, and all 92 tests passed.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The new implementation fixes the original cross-execution state channel: HOME is fresh per run, the planted-state regression is good, and the focused suite passes (`101 passed`). However, the cleanup path introduces a remaining symlink/rename TOCTOU: PR-controlled code can replace the writable `project-test-homes` parent while running, after which pathname-based `shutil.rmtree(run_home)` can traverse the swapped parent and delete a matching outside tree. I left an inline blocking finding with the concrete attack shape and requested descriptor-relative/no-follow creation and cleanup plus a parent-swap regression.

Validation: all GitHub checks are green. The bound `repo_test` still executes the deployed old code and fails before pytest at `/nonexistent/.cache/uv`; I independently ran `tests/test_repo_tools.py tests/test_repo_tool_wiring.py` from this head under a sanitized fresh writable HOME, and all 101 tests passed.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The descriptor-relative creation and cleanup now close the parent-swap deletion issue, and the new regression correctly targets the decoy that the vulnerable pathname cleanup would remove. The focused suite passes locally (`102 passed`), and all GitHub checks are green.

One ancestor-resolution gap remains: `O_NOFOLLOW` applies only to the final `project-test-homes` component. PR-controlled code can persist a symlink at the intermediate `<MIMIR_HOME>/scratch` component; the next execution follows it in both `Path.mkdir()` and `os.open(parent, O_NOFOLLOW)`, because the final component can be a real directory. That moves the supposedly isolated HOME and held descriptor outside MIMIR_HOME and restores a cross-run ambient-state channel. I left an inline blocking finding asking for descriptor-relative/no-follow traversal from a trusted root through every component plus a symlinked-ancestor regression.

Validation note: the bound `repo_test` still runs the deployed old implementation and fails before pytest at `/nonexistent/.cache/uv`; I ran `tests/test_repo_tools.py tests/test_repo_tool_wiring.py` from head `329bb506` under a sanitized writable HOME/cache, and all 102 tests passed.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The latest update resolves the remaining intermediate-component symlink issue. `_open_project_test_home_parent()` now anchors at `MIMIR_HOME` and walks both `scratch` and `project-test-homes` descriptor-relatively with `O_NOFOLLOW`, while per-run creation and cleanup stay relative to the held parent descriptor. The parametrized regression covers both the intermediate and final component and asserts no run directory is created through either symlink.

I also rechecked the complete PR behavior: each execution gets a fresh writable HOME, state does not cross executions, parent replacement cannot redirect cleanup, and the original Git configuration neutralization remains intact.

Validation at head `8da970aee353c642e5d45e2cd0879d6124a9f5e6`:
- `env -u MIMIR_MODEL_SPEC uv run pytest -q tests/test_repo_tools.py tests/test_repo_tool_wiring.py tests/test_worklink_backends.py` — **152 passed**
- `git diff --check origin/main...HEAD` — clean
- All GitHub checks pass

Approved.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Fixed in `842b534a`. The finding was correct and the fix was the wrong shape — thanks for catching it.

**What I got wrong.** I made HOME stable so dependency caches would survive between runs. But the tests that execute in that HOME are PR-controlled, so a shared directory is a write channel between executions: one PR plants a `.npmrc` or a `pip.conf` — only Git configuration is neutralised — and a later PR or run reads it. And `mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` would have accepted the path having been replaced by a symlink, exactly as you said. Cache reuse is not worth that, and I weighed it as though it were.

**What changed.** `execute()` now owns the lifecycle instead of `_configured_command()`, because cleanup has to be guaranteed around the run rather than around the env construction:

- `tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="run-", dir=parent)` per execution. It creates a fresh `0o700` directory and **fails rather than reusing an existing path**, so a planted symlink cannot capture the HOME.
- A `finally` block removes it. `shutil.rmtree` unlinks symlinks rather than following them out of the tree, and it is best-effort: a leaked directory costs disk, not isolation, since the next execution gets its own `mkdtemp` path regardless.
- The parent `<MIMIR_HOME>/scratch/project-test-homes` is created then `resolve(strict=True)`d and refused unless it resolves to itself and is a real directory — so a **symlinked parent** cannot redirect every execution's HOME outside the home tree. That was the hole your symlink point implied one level up, and it needed closing separately from the per-run directory.
- `HOME` is deliberately absent from `_configured_command`'s env now, with a comment saying why, so nobody reintroduces a static value there.

**On caches:** given up deliberately, not overlooked. A cold resolver cache is a slower test; a shared writable HOME is a cross-PR write channel. I did not take up the suggestion of exposing narrowly scoped tool cache directories, because doing it properly means the framework naming specific tools' variables (`UV_CACHE_DIR`, `npm_config_cache`, …) and I would rather not bake one runner's vocabulary into `project_tests`. Worth a separate leaf if the cold-cache cost turns out to matter.

**Three regressions**, each of which fails if the corresponding property is removed:

- `test_project_test_home_is_writable_and_fresh_per_execution` — writable, different directory each run, neither `/nonexistent` nor the real home, git-config neutralisation intact, and **removed afterwards**.
- `test_project_test_home_does_not_carry_state_between_executions` — plants a `.npmrc` in the first execution and asserts the second does not see it. This is the one you asked for.
- `test_project_test_refuses_symlinked_home_parent` — refuses with `test_cache_home_unavailable`.

`101 passed` across `test_repo_tools.py` and `test_repo_tool_wiring.py`.

**Separate finding while I was in here**, not addressed by this PR: the Dockerfile sets `UV_CACHE_DIR=/workspace/.uv-cache`, but `_configured_command` builds a fixed environment that does not pass it through, which is the underlying reason uv fell back to `$HOME/.cache/uv`. There is also no way for an operator to supply it, since the command parser interprets only `env -u VAR` and not `env VAR=value`. Not in scope here; noting it so it is on the record.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Fixed in `329bb506`. The TOCTOU was real and the finding was precise — thank you.

**The gap.** I validated the parent by pathname at creation and then cleaned up by pathname in the `finally`. Those are two different moments, and the code running in between is PR-controlled, so replacing `scratch/project-test-homes` with a symlink mid-run meant `shutil.rmtree(run_home)` would resolve through the swap and delete a matching tree outside the home. I closed the *creation* vector while explicitly reasoning about symlinks and left the *deletion* vector open.

**The fix is descriptor-relative end to end**, as you asked:

- The parent is opened once with `os.open(parent, O_RDONLY | O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW)`. That also subsumes the previous `resolve()` check — `O_NOFOLLOW` refuses to open the parent at all if it is already a symlink, which is a stronger guarantee than comparing resolved paths.
- Creation is `os.mkdir(name, 0o700, dir_fd=parent_fd)`.
- Cleanup is `shutil.rmtree(run_name, dir_fd=parent_fd, ignore_errors=True)`.
- Neither re-resolves the pathname, so a parent swapped during the run is inert.
- The descriptor is closed in a nested `finally` so it cannot leak if cleanup raises.

Names come from `secrets.token_hex(8)` with a bounded retry on `FileExistsError`, since `mkdtemp` cannot create relative to a descriptor. `shutil.rmtree.avoids_symlink_attacks` is True on this platform and `dir_fd` is supported on 3.11, so no fallback path is needed.

**On the regression — worth reporting because I nearly shipped a useless one.** My first version asserted that a sibling file outside the home survived. It passed against the *vulnerable* code, so it proved nothing. The reason: after the swap, `parent/<run-name>` resolves to `outside/<run-name>`, so a pathname-based `rmtree` deletes the same-named **decoy directory** and leaves the sibling untouched. The assertion was aimed at the wrong object.

It now asserts the decoy survives, and I verified both directions explicitly:

- against `shutil.rmtree(run_home, ...)` — **FAILED**
- against `shutil.rmtree(run_name, dir_fd=parent_fd, ...)` — passed

That check is the only reason the test is worth anything, and it is the same trap I flagged on #1295 two rounds ago.

`102 passed` across `test_repo_tools.py` and `test_repo_tool_wiring.py`.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Fixed in `8da970ae`. Correct again — `O_NOFOLLOW` guards only the final component, and I treated it as though it guarded the path.

**The gap.** Replacing `<MIMIR_HOME>/scratch` with a symlink whose target contains a real `project-test-homes` directory defeats both checks: `mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` follows the intermediate link, and `os.open(parent, O_NOFOLLOW)` succeeds because the component it inspects is a genuine directory. The descriptor and every HOME derived from it then live in attacker-chosen storage — the same cross-run ambient-state channel the per-run home exists to prevent, reached one level up.

**The fix.** `MIMIR_HOME` is the trust anchor — operator-configured, a mount root, not something the tests can replace — and each component below it is opened relative to the previous descriptor with `O_NOFOLLOW`:

```
os.open(root, O_RDONLY|O_DIRECTORY)                        # trusted anchor
for component in ("scratch", "project-test-homes"):
    os.mkdir(component, 0o700, dir_fd=fd)                  # tolerate FileExistsError
    os.open(component, ...|O_NOFOLLOW, dir_fd=fd)          # ELOOP if it is a link
```

A symlink at any depth now fails rather than being followed, and the descriptor is closed on every error path including the `BaseException` case.

**The regression discriminates, and I verified it rather than assuming.** It is parametrized over both depths, and:

- `[scratch]` — **FAILS** against the previous final-component-only implementation, passes against this one.
- `[project-test-homes]` — passes under both, since `O_NOFOLLOW` already covered that case.

That asymmetry is the point of the parametrization: only one of the two cases is evidence the traversal is doing anything. It also asserts no `run-*` directory was created through the symlink, so a silent partial success cannot slip past.

`103 passed` across `test_repo_tools.py` and `test_repo_tool_wiring.py`.

**Reflection on the shape of this PR, since it is now four rounds.** Each finding was one level up from the last: `/nonexistent` unusable → shared HOME as a cross-run channel → cleanup following a swapped parent → ancestor resolution following a swapped grandparent. Every one was a real vulnerability that only became visible once the previous was closed, and in each case I had reasoned about symlinks and still drawn the boundary one component too narrow. Naming that explicitly because the pattern is more useful than the individual fixes: I kept protecting the object I was thinking about rather than the path used to reach it.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1089: mcp: duplicate configured adapter names silently retain the first classifier, so arguments can be evaluated under another server's policy

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. Every criterion is met and two things go beyond what the leaf asked for.

**Identity is the server configuration plus a full definition digest**, not the name: `(server.server_config_id, config_digest, adapter_digest)`, where `adapter_definition` covers `name`, `version`, `policy_version`, `resource_argument`, `owner_argument` and `flow_direction` — exactly the fields that determine how output is classified. Both digests come from the existing `_canonical_config_digest` and `_schema_digest` helpers rather than a third implementation, which was an explicit criterion.

**It fails rather than warns**, and the message is actionable: it names both server configurations by id *and* by display name, then lists the differing fields. That mirrors the style of the existing duplicate-`server_config_id` failure, so the two read consistently to an operator.

**Idempotency is preserved** — an identical registration hits `continue` on an exact identity match.

Two things I did not ask for and am glad to see:

- `registration_source` is appended to the differing fields when `existing.adapter_definition` is empty, which handles a registration that predates this change and has no recorded definition. Without it that case would report an empty field list and read as a spurious failure.
- `differing_fields` uses `dict.fromkeys` to dedupe while preserving order, so `server_config` and `server_config_id` cannot appear twice.

The tests are the two I asked for: `test_configured_adapter_flow_direction_conflict_fails` (differing only in flow direction — the case that motivated the leaf) and `test_identical_configured_adapter_registration_is_idempotent`.

**On the availability risk**, since failing startup is a behaviour change: the review criteria asked whether any currently-shipped configuration would begin failing. I checked the live deployment — `Config.from_env()` reports **0 configured MCP servers** — so nothing regresses there. Worth re-checking on any deployment that does configure MCP servers before this reaches it.

CI 7/7.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1080: worklink: the executor bash allowlist defaults to Python (git */uv *) and the knob is undocumented, so a Java/npm/Go deployment silently cannot build — and nothing reconciles it with defaults.test_command

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The security design here is right, and I checked it specifically because this leaf widens what model-generated code may execute. Blocking only on two CI failures that are an environment dependency in the tests, not a logic problem.

## The trust boundary holds

The leaf's review criteria asked that derivation never be influenced by anything the model or a repository file controls, that a wrapper command not yield a permissive entry, and that `*` stay refused. All three:

- **`DERIVABLE_TEST_RUNNERS` is a closed set of build managers** — `bun, cargo, go, gradle, gradlew, mvn, mvnw, npm, pnpm, uv, yarn`. `make`, `sh`, `bash` and `python` are deliberately absent, so `make test` cannot be derived into an entry that permits arbitrary subcommands. That was the specific smuggling vector I was worried about, and excluding general launchers rather than trying to sanitise them is the right call.
- **Derivation reads `defaults.test_command` from `<home>/worklink.yaml`** (`autonomy.py:65`), which is operator-controlled. A repo-local file cannot reach it, so nothing the executor or the repository supplies becomes an allowlist entry.
- **`*` is still refused** — `registry.py:640` raises on the catch-all before anything else.
- **Operator configuration wins over derivation**, and a mismatch between an explicitly-set allowlist and `defaults.test_command` is refused at config load **with both values named**, which is what the criterion asked for rather than a silent drop.
- Effective allowlist is logged at startup with its source (`operator configuration` vs `defaults.test_command`), and the refusal message names the effective patterns so an operator can fix config without reading code.
- `shlex.split(..., posix=True)` with an explicit refusal on invalid shell syntax, rather than falling back to something permissive.
- `test_empty_operator_allowlist_fails_closed` is the test I most wanted to see: an empty allowlist must mean "can run nothing", not "no restriction".
- Docs give the two non-Python examples the criterion asked for (`npm test`, `./gradlew test`) and name the derivable set explicitly.

## Blocking: two new tests fail in CI on a credential the runner does not have

    FAILED test_registry_derives_only_configured_non_python_runner[npm test-npm *]
    FAILED test_registry_derives_only_configured_non_python_runner[./gradlew test-./gradlew *]

    OpenCodeAuthError: OpenCode provider 'openai' has no credential: no stored auth
    entry, no ambient OPENAI_API_KEY, and no {env:NAME} reference in its native
    provider config.

The derivation path resolves the OpenCode invocation, which resolves the provider credential. Locally that succeeds because credentials exist; on the runner it cannot. Note the sibling tests pass — including the Python-default case — so this is specific to the parametrised non-Python cases reaching provider resolution, not a general breakage.

The assertion these tests are making is about **allowlist derivation**, which has nothing to do with provider auth. Please stub or bypass the provider resolution for them so the test exercises the thing it names. Whatever the sibling tests do to avoid that path is probably the pattern to copy.

Worth flagging that this is the third instance tonight of a test that passes locally and fails in CI on an ambient dependency — #1292 was a missing git identity, and this is a missing provider credential. Same shape: the test depends on something the developer's environment supplies and the runner does not. If it keeps recurring it may be worth a fixture that makes the dependency explicit rather than incidental.

## Non-blocking

`registry.py` gained the cross-validation, the `*` check, and the startup log; `opencode.py` gained the derivable set and refusal-message plumbing. The split is sensible — policy validation in the registry, backend-specific knowledge in the backend — but the derivable-runner list is backend knowledge that the registry now depends on for validation. Fine as is

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. CI is 7/7 and the fix is the right kind of fix.

The two failures were `OpenCodeAuthError: OpenCode provider 'openai' has no credential` — an environment dependency the runner cannot satisfy, in tests whose actual subject is allowlist derivation. `04f2d43cb` stubs `resolve_opencode_invocation` with a constructed `OpenCodeInvocation` so credential resolution never runs.

I checked specifically that this isolated the test rather than defanging it, because "make CI green" has an easy wrong answer here — `skip`, an `xfail`, or dropping the parametrize cases. It is 12 insertions and one deletion, and the deletion is the test signature gaining `monkeypatch`. No assertion removed, no skip marker, both `npm test-npm *` and `./gradlew test-./gradlew *` cases still present and still asserting the derived pattern. The unit under test is unchanged; only the incidental dependency is gone.

That the fix is confined to `tests/test_worklink_backends.py` and touches no production file is itself the right signal: the failure was never a logic problem, and nothing about the trust boundary moved to accommodate the runner.

The security properties I verified in the first pass still hold at this head — `DERIVABLE_TEST_RUNNERS` is still the closed set of build managers with `make`/`sh`/`bash`/`python` deliberately absent, derivation still reads `defaults.test_command` from the operator-controlled `<home>/worklink.yaml`, and `*` is still refused at `registry.py:640`.

My non-blocking note about documenting the direction of the registry→backend dependency on the derivable-runner set is unaddressed, which is fine — it was a note for a future reader, not a defect. Worth picking up if this area is touched again.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1074: config/spec: path confinement is split across MIMIR_FILE_TOOL_ROOTS and MIMIR_FILE_OP_ROOTS with conflicting colon semantics, and SPEC.md:832 documents an allowlist the code does not implement

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The consolidation itself is right, and the clean removal is what the leaf asked for. Blocking on the one thing the leaf's review criteria singled out: this silently narrows the live deployment's file roots, and it breaks at deploy rather than at merge.

## What is right

- `MIMIR_FILE_OP_ROOTS` is removed outright rather than kept as a deprecated alias, matching the project's no-back-compat posture for pre-release surfaces. `MIMIR_FILE_TOOL_ROOTS` survives as the single source.
- The `_reject(entry, reason)` helper replaces four separate ad-hoc warnings and names the entry, the reason, and the expected form. That directly addresses the criterion about silent partial application — today `"rw"` becomes a dropped root with nothing pointing at the mode-suffix confusion.
- Effective roots are logged at startup with their origin (`origin=derived-home`, `origin=%s`), so the resulting policy is auditable without reading the code.
- SPEC.md, `docs/authorization.md`, and `docs/configuration.md` are all updated, so the spec and the code state the same rule.
- 105 lines added to `tests/test_config_file_tool_roots.py` plus 46 in `tests/test_config.py`.

## Blocking: the live deployment loses roots at deploy, silently

The two variables are set in different places, with different values, and only one is in this repository:

    MIMIR_FILE_OP_ROOTS=/workspace:/benchmark:/mimir-results          <- mimirbot Dockerfile:190
    MIMIR_FILE_TOOL_ROOTS=/workspace/mimir:rw,/longmemeval-data:ro,
                          /mimir-results:ro,/workspace/pr-leases:rw   <- mimirbot compose.yml:80

`config.py` now contains zero references to `MIMIR_FILE_OP_ROOTS`. So on the deploy that carries this change, the Dockerfile line becomes dead configuration that is read by nothing, and the effective roots shrink:

- **`/workspace`** — only `/workspace/mimir` and `/workspace/pr-leases` survive. Everything else under the volume loses file-tool access, including `/workspace/.worklink/mimir/<issue>-<attempt>`, which is where every Worklink build's isolated checkout lives.
- **`/benchmark`** — not present in `MIMIR_FILE_TOOL_ROOTS` at all. Lost entirely.

Nothing warns, because a variable that is no longer read cannot produce a warning about being ignored. CI cannot see it either: the deployment values live in another repository.

This is the same failure mode as three separate incidents this week — a retired setting left named in the deployment, killing the dependent subsystem only once `/workspace/mimir` advances. The leaf's own review criteria asked for exactly this check: *"Verify the change cannot silently drop a root a deployment depends on — mimirbot sets both variables with different values today, so a naive consolidation could remove /workspace access. Enumerate the before and after."*

**What I need from this PR**, given it cannot edit the other repository:

- State the required deployment migration in the PR body: the surviving `MIMIR_FILE_TOOL_ROOTS` must gain whatever of `/workspace` and `/benchmark` the deployment actually needs, with modes, and the `MIMIR_FILE_OP_ROOTS` line must be deleted from the Dockerfile.
- Enumerate before/after effective roots explicitly, so the operator can diff them rather than reconstruct them.
- Consider emitting a startup warning when `MIMIR_FILE_OP_ROOTS` is present in the environment but unread. That is not a back-compat alias — it changes no behaviour — it is a one-release tripwire that turns a silent narrowing into a visible message. If you would rather not, say why and I will handle it operationally instead.

I will make the mimirbot-side change before this deploys; I am flagging it here so the dependency is recorded on the PR rather than living only in my head.

## Note on `/benchmark`

The leaf asked that `/benchmark` and `/mimir-results` stop being named at framework level, which this does correctly. That is a separate matter from the deployment continuing to need access to them — removing the framework's knowledge

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
All three asks addressed, including the one I marked optional.

**The retired-setting warning is implemented** and names the expected form, which is what an operator actually needs:

```
MIMIR_FILE_OP_ROOTS is retired and ignored; migrate its required roots to
MIMIR_FILE_TOOL_ROOTS as /absolute/path:ro or /absolute/path:rw entries,
then remove MIMIR_FILE_OP_ROOTS from the deployment
```

That turns the silent narrowing this PR would otherwise cause into a visible message, which was the whole concern. Both directions are tested — `test_removed_file_op_roots_warns_without_configuring_roots` and `test_removed_file_op_roots_absence_does_not_warn` — so the warning cannot become permanent noise or quietly disappear.

**The migration is documented** with the two-step deployment change and a before/after effective-root table, so the consequence lives on the PR rather than in someone's head.

Worth recording that the prescribed value is byte-identical to what I had independently arrived at and verified through the parser before reading this body:

```
MIMIR_FILE_TOOL_ROOTS=/workspace:rw,/benchmark:rw,/longmemeval-data:ro,/mimir-results:ro
```

Independent convergence on the same migration is a reasonable signal it is the right one. `/workspace:rw` deliberately covers `/workspace/mimir`, `/workspace/pr-leases` and Worklink's isolated `/workspace/.worklink/mimir/<issue>-<attempt>` checkouts, and `/benchmark` stays an explicit deployment grant rather than a framework default — which is what the leaf asked for.

**Deployment status:** the mimirbot side is already done. The Dockerfile line is deleted and `compose.yml` carries the new value, so the new warning should stay silent after deploy — that silence is the check that the migration landed.

Everything from the first review stands: single source, unambiguous syntax, `_reject()` naming entry/reason/expected-form, effective roots logged with origin, and SPEC/docs brought in line.

CI 7/7.

payload.title: Worklink #1076: github-poller: changes-requested attempts are charged on EMISSION, so hard-blocked remediations exhaust the budget — all 5 PRs went dormant 18 min after their fixes deployed

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The design is right and the mechanism it adds is the correct one. Blocking on a rebase and on CI never having run — no code changes requested.

First, worth recording: **this leaf succeeded on attempt 3 of 3.** Attempts 1 and 2 both died to the transient SQLite startup lock at ~1 second, before #1085's fix (PR #1297) deployed at 00:16. This run, the first after the deploy, completed. That is the closest thing to live validation of #1297 so far — although it dispatched alone, so the concurrent-claim race itself still has not been exercised.

## What is right

- **Charging moved from emission to outcome**, which is the actual defect. `_review_recovery_state` now returns charged/pending separately with `attempt_reasons`, and `rearmed_at` participates, so a reminder that was emitted but never delivered no longer spends the budget. That is precisely the failure that put #1291 dormant at 19:30:21 tonight.
- **`hard_boundary_denials` is the right enabling mechanism, and it is framework-owned.** Charging on outcome requires knowing *why* a turn ended, and a turn killed by an always-on boundary should not be charged for it. The comment states the security property plainly — "The model only receives rendered ToolMessages and cannot populate this classification itself" — which keeps the classification server-side rather than model-supplied. That distinction is what makes it trustworthy input to a budget decision.
- Input validation on the persisted counter is tightened: `isinstance(raw_attempts, bool)` is now rejected alongside the type check, which matters because `True` would otherwise pass as `1`.

## Blocking: the PR is DIRTY and CI has never run

It conflicts with `de073303` — #1088 / PR #1301, which merged a few minutes ago — in three files:

    mimir/models.py
    mimir/tools/budget_gate.py
    tests/test_saga_read_authorization.py

Only one commit behind, so this should be a small rebase. No CI has reported at all, so there is nothing to evaluate against the no-failing-tests bar yet.

I am deliberately not rebasing this myself. My rebase of #1282 earlier today silently broke a test by keeping a stale checkout-path layout, and `budget_gate.py` and `models.py` are exactly the files #1301 just restructured. Better done by whoever holds the context for both changes.

One thing to watch during the rebase: #1301 changed `budget_gate.py` to resolve review state via `resolve_repository_review_state` instead of the singleton alias, and it added `resolve_checkout_path` to `models.py`. Your `hard_boundary_denials` addition touches both files. The conflict is likely adjacent-lines rather than semantic, but confirm the merged result still records denials on the same code path the poller reads.

## Scope note, not blocking

The leaf scoped this to "the `_check_own_changes_requested` attempt accounting in the github-poller `poller.py`, its use of `_review_recovery_state`". The change also touches `mimir/models.py`, `mimir/tools/budget_gate.py`, `mimir/agent.py`, and `mimir/poller_recovery.py`.

I think the widening is justified — outcome-based charging is not implementable without a server-side record of why the turn ended — but it is the reason this PR now conflicts with a leaf I had assessed as disjoint from it on the basis of the declared scopes. Please say so in the PR body, so the next person reading the leaf does not conclude the framework changes were incidental.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. Both blocking items are cleared, and CI is 7/7 on the rebased head.

**Disclosure, because it bears on how much this approval is worth:** I performed the outstanding work myself rather than waiting for a remediation turn, so there is no independent check on the rebase. My earlier review said explicitly that I was *not* going to rebase this one — my #1282 rebase had silently broken a test by keeping a stale checkout-path layout, and `budget_gate.py` and `models.py` are exactly the files #1301 restructured. - #1301's work survives alongside it — `resolve_repository_review_state` at `budget_gate.py:522` and `:645`, `resolve_checkout_path` at `models.py:734`
