payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1088: authz: batched PR turns refuse valid file reads and repo shell commands — #1067 migrated authorization to the registry but not read_policy or budget_gate

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. Every criterion in the leaf is met, and the part I flagged as delicate was done correctly.

**The containment test is exact, not a prefix.** `resolve_checkout_path` ends in `resolved.relative_to(checkout)` — pathlib's component-based test, which raises rather than matching a sibling. That was the specific hazard I called out: a string prefix would let `/leases/abc-def-evil` satisfy lease root `/leases/abc-def`. It also rejects relative paths and any path containing `..`, resolves both the lease root and checkout with `strict=True`, and requires the checkout to sit directly under the lease root.

**A lease must actually belong to the scope.** `is_active`, `scope_id == state.action_scope.scope_id`, and `owner == state.action_scope.principal` are all verified before a lease is considered, so resolution cannot borrow another scope's lease.

**Both consumers migrated, and the singleton was not reintroduced for convenience.** `read_policy.py` resolves via `resolve_checkout_path(path)`; the shell path uses `resolve_repository_review_state(..., command=, cwd=)`. The singleton is read only in the `else` branch when no registry is present, so single-PR turns behave exactly as before.

**The no-match case refuses with a reason that says what happened** — "no matching checkout lease was found for the requested path" — rather than a generic denial.

**The read-policy fail-safes are untouched.** I diffed the counts against main: `symlink` 2/2, `file_contains_secret` 3/3, `resolve(strict` 17/17. This change alters only how the state and scope are obtained, not what is checked afterwards — which is the right seam.

Tests cover both halves of the defect: `test_batched_pr_reads_resolve_each_exact_checkout_lease` and `test_batched_pr_shell_commands_bind_each_exact_checkout_lease`.

CI 7/7.

Worth noting for the record: this and #1087 are the two halves of #1067's incomplete migration — it moved authorization onto `RepoPRScopeRegistry` and left the alias consumers behind. This one fixes the half that was *refusing valid work*; #1087 covers the half that *permits* something it should not.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1071: authz: repo_review admits far fewer read-only git shapes than #1040's retain-in-shell premise assumed (grep/blame/merge-base/rev-list all refused)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Careful work. This is an allowlist *widening*, so the hardening matters more than the coverage, and the hardening is right. One gap against the leaf's own evidence.

## What is right

- **The two arbitrary-command-execution vectors in read-only Git are closed.** `--no-ext-diff --no-textconv` on `diff`/`log`/`show` and `--no-textconv` on `blame`/`grep` shut off `diff.external` and textconv filters. Those are the paths that turn a "read-only" Git invocation into arbitrary execution, and they are easy to miss precisely because the subcommands look inert.
- **No `upload-pack` or `receive-pack` anywhere.** Zero occurrences, so no remote-helper execution path was opened.
- **`grep` excludes the dangerous options.** `-f` (read patterns from an arbitrary file) and `--open-files-in-pager` are both absent from the allowlist, and the operand check requires at least one non-flag operand.
- **`credential.helper` is emptied for `INSPECT`**, so a read-only shape cannot reach a credential store.
- I checked the `-c` occurrences specifically, since arbitrary `-c` would be config injection and would undo everything else. All of them are server-constructed overrides. The `-c` entries inside the `diff`/`grep` option sets are those subcommands' own flags — combined-diff and count — which cannot be top-level config because the allowlist validates arguments *after* the subcommand. Correct, but worth a comment saying so, because it reads alarmingly at first glance.
- `_arguments_match_allowlist` with explicit `exact_options` and narrow `option_prefixes` keeps this an allowlist rather than a denylist, which is the right structure for something that will be extended again.

## Blocking: `ls-remote` was cited evidence and is not covered

The leaf named three shapes observed being refused on the live agent. Two are now admitted — `status`, and `branch --show-current`. `ls-remote` has **zero** occurrences in this change, and `git ls-remote origin refs/pull/*/head` was one of the three.

I suspect the omission is deliberate and correct: `INSPECT` empties `credential.helper`, so an authenticated `ls-remote` against a private remote could not work anyway, and admitting a network shape under a read-only local profile is a different decision with its own credential story. If that is the reasoning, it is a good one.

But a symptom named as evidence in the leaf and then silently not addressed is how the same finding gets re-filed later. Please state the decision — in the PR body or a comment next to the local-only shapes — so the next reader knows `ls-remote` was considered and excluded on purpose rather than overlooked. If instead it should be admitted, it needs its own credential handling and probably its own leaf.

## Non-blocking

`option_prefixes=("-U", ...)` admits any `-U<suffix>`, so `-Ufoo` is admitted and Git rejects it downstream. Harmless, but `--unified=` is already handled by prefix and `-U` could take a digit-only check if you want the allowlist to be exact rather than merely safe.

## Verification note

122 lines of new tests, and the suite names the observed refusals, which is the right way to tie an allowlist change to the evidence that motivated it.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The blocking item is addressed, and addressed better than I asked.

I asked for the `ls-remote` decision to be stated so it would not be re-filed as an oversight. `ea05c63b5` does that in `access_control.py`:

> This allowlist is intentionally local-only. In particular, ls-remote is excluded even though it is read-only: it contacts a remote and would need a separate authenticated-network policy instead of INSPECT's disabled credential helper.

That is the reasoning I guessed at, now on the record. But the part I did not ask for is what makes it durable: `test_repo_review_git_deliberately_excludes_ls_remote` asserts both that the argv is refused **and** that the reason contains "contact a remote". A comment rots silently; a test that pins the refusal *and its stated reason* means anyone later admitting `ls-remote` breaks the build and has to revisit the decision deliberately. That is the right shape for encoding a deliberate exclusion.

The second added comment is a good unprompted catch: noting that subcommand options like grep's `-c` are parsed only after the subcommand is selected, and so cannot reach Git's top-level `-c` config-injection form. That is exactly the question a reviewer would raise about admitting short options into a git allowlist, answered before it was asked.

CI 7/7.

Two notes, neither blocking:

The `-U` prefix nit from my earlier review stands unaddressed and remains fine — `-Ufoo` is admitted and Git rejects it downstream, so it is safe rather than exact.

Separately, and outside this leaf: with this deployed, the poller was still refused `git branch` (bare), `git checkout <value>` and `git ... add` during last night's window. Those are write or ambiguous shapes that a read-only review profile should not admit, so I read them as the profile behaving correctly rather than as a gap here. If the agent genuinely needs them to remediate a PR it should be going through `repo_checkout`/`repo_commit`/`repo_push`, which carry the scope. Flagging it so the residual denials are not later mistaken for this leaf being incomplete.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1090: authz: finish the #1083 consolidation — repo_tools action checks still refuse unconditionally while typed PR actions are flag-aware

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
This finishes the consolidation correctly and the part I was most worried about is clean. One small finding, in a direction that matters.

## What is right

- `_require` now routes through `authorize_repo_pr_tool` and the real flag is genuinely threaded in — `enforce=bool(getattr(context, "enforcement_enabled", False))` — rather than the check being consolidated in name only. That was the first thing I checked, because a default of `enforce=True` with nothing passing the real value would have made this cosmetic.
- **Every fail-safe stayed unconditional.** I verified each one individually: `force_push_refused`, `stale_scope`, `cross_pr_checkout`, `invalid_path`, `unsafe_repo_config`, and `_assert_checkout_identity` — none routed through the gate. That was the single largest risk in this leaf, since flattening a CAS or confinement check into a flag-controlled policy decision would have been a real security regression dressed as a refactor.
- Multi-action semantics are right. `missing_actions` is a set difference and `in_scope` requires `not missing_actions`, so `_require("repo_commit", WRITE, COMMIT)` still needs both rather than either.
- `refusal_detail` names which action is missing, so the enforced-path message stays as informative as the old hand-built string.
- `allowed=in_scope or not enforce` matches the typed PR path exactly, which is the consistency the leaf was about.
- Good test set: shadow-then-enforce with the same reason, `test_scope_action_check_is_shadowed_when_enforcement_is_disabled`, and `test_repo_tools_does_not_decide_pr_scope_policy_locally` as the conformance guard against this drifting back.
- CI 7/7.

## Blocking: the enforcement state defaults permissive when it cannot be determined

```python
context = getattr(runtime, "context", None) if runtime is not None else None
...
enforce=bool(getattr(context, "enforcement_enabled", False)),
```

Both fallbacks resolve to `False`, which means **permissive**. If `runtime` is absent, or a context ever lacks `enforcement_enabled`, `repo_*` actions run unenforced — and nothing reports that the enforcement state was unknown rather than deliberately off.

It is moot in production today because enforcement is off anyway. It stops being moot the moment the flag is armed, which is the entire purpose of this line of work: an armed deployment with a missing context would silently behave as an unarmed one.

It also runs against the instinct the codebase applies elsewhere. `models.py` documents "Unknown labels fail closed (deny). Unknown sinks fail closed (deny)", and #1295's classifier treats `code is None` as taint precisely because unclassified should not mean safe. Here unknown means permissive.

Please either default to `True`, or refuse when the enforcement state cannot be resolved. If you default to `True`, check whether any test constructs `RepoGitTools` without a runtime and relies on the permissive default — those should pass `enforce=False` explicitly, which is better anyway because it states the intent rather than inheriting it.

Whichever you choose, an unresolvable enforcement state is worth an event. "We could not tell and assumed X" is exactly the class of thing that was invisible before #1083.

## Note

`repo_tools.py` importing from `access_control` is a new dependency edge. It looks fine — `access_control` does not import `repo_tools` — but worth a glance for cycles under a different import order, since `mimir/tools/repo.py` sits between them.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Resolved in `f3ad6feb`, and the telemetry detail goes past what I asked for.

`_enforcement_enabled` now fails closed: it returns the flag only when it is an actual `bool`, and anything else — missing runtime, missing context, absent attribute — falls through to enforcing rather than to permissive. That was the finding: both former fallbacks resolved to `False`, so an armed deployment with a missing context would have silently behaved as an unarmed one.

It also emits `repo_enforcement_state_unknown` with the repository, pull request, and `fallback_enforcement=True`, which is the part I asked for in passing — "we could not tell and assumed X" was exactly the class of thing that was invisible before #1083.

The detail I would not have thought to specify: the event emission is wrapped so that a telemetry failure cannot change the decision, with `# noqa: BLE001 — telemetry must not alter the decision` and a `log.warning` fallback that still records the fail-closed choice. A bare `log_event_sync` call there could have raised and turned an observability path into a control-flow path. Getting that ordering right is the difference between a guard and a liability.

Tests: `test_unknown_repo_enforcement_state_fails_closed_and_emits_event` and `test_repo_enforcement_state_preserves_explicit_flag` pin both directions, alongside the shadow/enforce pair and the conformance test from the earlier round.

Everything from my first review stands: `_require` routes through `authorize_repo_pr_tool`, multi-action calls still require all actions, `refusal_detail` names the missing action, and — the thing I checked most carefully — every fail-safe in `repo_tools.py` stayed unconditional: `force_push_refused`, `stale_scope`, `cross_pr_checkout`, `invalid_path`, `unsafe_repo_config`, `_assert_checkout_identity`.

CI 7/7. This completes the #1083 consolidation: the same authority question now gets one answer regardless of which tool asks it.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
mimir-carreira
mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1086: authz: GitHub effects are never verified against the declared bot identity — scopes trust MIMIR_GITHUB_SELF_LOGIN while effects use ambient credentials

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
This is a thorough implementation and the security-sensitive details are right. One blocking finding about how the identity check decides when to run.

## What is right

- **The cache is keyed to the credential, not just populated once.** `_credential_fingerprint` is a SHA-256 of the token, and `confirm_github_identity` refuses with a distinct reason when the active credential's fingerprint differs from the verified one. A rotated or swapped token therefore fails closed rather than reusing a stale binding — which was the actual attack shape in the finding.
- **No TTL, deliberately, with the reasoning recorded**: "Identity bindings intentionally expire only with the process. Effects never refresh this cache, so a changed or missing credential fails closed." That satisfies both criteria I cared about at once — no per-effect network round trip, and no window in which a changed credential silently re-verifies.
- **Fails closed in all three directions**: empty cache, fingerprint mismatch, login mismatch. Verification is under `_identity_lock`.
- **No token reaches an error message.** Every `ForgeError` names logins only, and the credential is hashed rather than stored. I checked specifically for an f-string interpolating the token and there is none.
- `GH_CONFIG_DIR` is a `tempfile.mkdtemp` at mode `0o500`, and `GH_TOKEN` / `GH_HOST` are scrubbed from the admitted-shell child. `_is_gh_argv` comparing `Path(argv[0]).name` rather than the literal string, with a comment explaining that authorization pins an absolute path, is the kind of detail that usually gets missed.
- The push path in `mimir/repo_tools.py` is covered — `confirm_github_identity(self._scope.principal, token)` — which answers the review criterion asking whether the executor's push shared the exposure. It did, and it is handled.

## Blocking: `_gh_has_account_effect` is a second list that must agree with the shell allowlist

The identity check runs only for `gh` invocations that `_gh_has_account_effect` classifies as effectful: `pr`/`issue` followed by one of `close, comment, create, edit, merge, ready, reopen, review`, or `api` with a non-GET `--method` / `-X`.

That is a parallel enumeration of "which admitted commands change account-visible state", maintained separately from the profile that decides which commands are admitted at all. Nothing keeps the two in sync. If a mutating `gh` shape is ever added to the profile — and #1071 and #1080 are both open leaves that widen the admitted set — the effect executes with **no identity verification**, silently, because this function returns `False` for anything it does not recognise.

That is the same shape as most of what we fixed this week: a fact expressed in two places with nothing enforcing agreement, failing open rather than closed.

The fix is cheap because the check is cheap. `confirm_github_identity` is an in-process comparison against a cached fingerprint — no network, no I/O. There is no performance argument for being selective. **Verify identity for every admitted `gh` invocation**, not only the ones currently believed to mutate. A read-only `gh api` call under a mismatched credential is also wrong — it reads as the wrong account — so running the check unconditionally is both simpler and more correct.

If you want to keep the distinction for some reason, it needs a conformance test asserting that every mutating shape the profile admits is also recognised here, so the two lists cannot drift. But I would rather delete the function than test it.

Minor, while you are in there: with `arguments = ["api", "path", "-X"]` — flag present, value absent — the `index + 2 < len(arguments)` guard falls through and returns `False`. Harmless today since the command would fail anyway, but it is another instance of an unrecognised shape defaulting to "no check needed".

## CI

Four checks pending, three passing.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The parallel-list finding is fully resolved — `_gh_has_account_effect` is gone (0 occurrences) and `confirm_github_identity` now runs for every `_is_gh_argv`. `env.pop("GH_CONFIG_DIR", None)` on the non-`gh` branch is a good addition I had not asked for: it stops an inherited config dir leaking into other children.

But making the check unconditional widened the blast radius of how it fails, and that is now blocking.

## Blocking: an identity mismatch terminates the turn

`confirm_github_identity` raises `ForgeError`, and `ForgeError` is `class ForgeError(RuntimeError)` (mimir/forge/client.py:12) — **not** a `ToolException`. It is raised from `direct_exec_env`, called at mimir/tools/extra.py:451. The enclosing `try:` catches exactly two things:

    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
    except FileNotFoundError as exc:

`ForgeError` matches neither, and `extra.py` mentions `ForgeError` nowhere. So it propagates out of `shell_exec`. And because it is not a `ToolException`, the handler #1295 just added to `wrap_tool_call` / `awrap_tool_call` — which exists precisely to return refusals to the model instead of killing the turn — does not catch it either.

The result is that a credential/identity mismatch produces an uncaught exception that terminates the turn. That is the exact failure mode of #1072, which took six review rounds to fix and merged about an hour ago, reintroduced through a new path.

It is worth being explicit that this got worse with the last commit, not better, and that the widening was my request. Before `24f9ef54`, only shapes `_gh_has_account_effect` recognised would reach the raise. Now every admitted `gh` invocation does, so any mismatch kills any turn that touches `gh` at all. Verifying unconditionally is still right — the delivery mechanism just has to match.

**Raise `ToolPolicyRefusal` instead** (`mimir/tools/refusals.py`, added by #1295). Two reasons it is the correct type rather than merely a convenient one:

1. It subclasses `ToolException`, so the middleware returns it to the model as a `ToolMessage(status="error")` and the agent can report the problem instead of the turn dying with a traceback.
2. #1295 classifies `ToolPolicyRefusal` as a *policy* refusal and deliberately skips the IFC taint merge for it. That is right here: an identity mismatch is detected during environment preparation, before anything executes, so nothing was read and there is nothing to label. Raising a bare `ForgeError` would, if it were ever caught as a generic fault, taint the turn for a call that never ran.

Keep `ForgeError` as the internal signal from the forge client if you prefer, and translate at the `_shell_env` boundary — that keeps the forge module free of tool-layer types.

payload.body:
**Superseding my previous ask.** I said to raise `ToolPolicyRefusal` so the mismatch reaches the model as a tool result. The operator has proposed something better and I agree: an identity mismatch should **disable the coding capability entirely, as though `MIMIR_CODING_ENABLED` were false, and fire warning events** — rather than refusing call by call.

Why that is the stronger design:

- It degrades into a **mode that already exists and is already exercised** — coding-disabled is the *default* configuration (`config.py`: `_env_bool("MIMIR_CODING_ENABLED", False)`), not a novel half-broken state. My version invented a new one: coding tools present but refusing.
- `coding_enabled` is consulted at **registration** time (`mimir/tools/registry.py:2398`), so on a startup mismatch the tools are simply never registered. There is nothing to refuse, which removes the turn-killing problem at the root instead of catching it.
- The prompt side is already handled. #1291's `_verification_guidance()` branches on the flag and, when coding is unavailable, tells the turn not to present changes as verified. That path is installed and live, so a degraded deployment already reads correctly to the agent.
- An identity mismatch is not a per-call authorization question. It means the deployment's configured identity and its actual credential disagree — a whole-process condition. Answering it once at the boundary is the right granularity.

## What I would like instead

**At startup** — verify, and on mismatch do not register the coding tools, exactly as if the flag were false. Emit a negative event plus an `operator_alert`. There is a precedent to follow rather than a new pattern to invent: `mimir/core_blocks.py` fires `core_prompt_degraded` as a negative algedonic event when its checks fail, and the feedback rules classify it. Mirror that — something like `github_identity_degraded` carrying both logins (never the token).

**Mid-flight** — the fingerprint check is the valuable part of what you already built, because it catches a credential changing *after* registration. At that point the tools are registered and cannot be cleanly withdrawn, so:
- refuse that call as `ToolPolicyRefusal` (subclasses `ToolException`, so #1295's handler returns it to the model rather than killing the turn, and #1295 classifies policy refusals as non-tainting — correct here, since nothing executed);
- **latch coding off for the remainder of the process** so subsequent turns behave like the startup-mismatch case;
- fire the same degraded event and operator alert.

**Do not auto-recover.** A security signal should not self-heal on the next successful check. Once latched, it stays off until an operator restarts with a corrected credential. Silent recovery would hide exactly the condition the check exists to surface.

## What must not regress

- Do not let the degradation be quiet. If coding switches off and nothing alerts, Worklink builds simply stop and the cause is invisible — a worse failure than the one being fixed. The `operator_alert` is load-bearing, not decoration.
- Keep everything already correct in this PR: the credential-fingerprint cache, fail-closed on empty cache or mismatch, no token in any message, `GH_CONFIG_DIR` at `0o500`, `GH_TOKEN`/`GH_HOST` scrubbing, the `repo_tools` push-path coverage, and verifying for **every** admitted `gh` invocation rather than a guessed-effectful subset.
- The `ForgeError` escaping as an uncaught `RuntimeError` still needs to stop happening; this design mostly removes the opportunity, but the mid-flight path must use a type the middleware delivers.

## Tests

- Startup mismatch: coding tools are absent from the registered set, the degraded event fires, and an operator alert is emitted.
- Startup match: tools registered, no event.
- Mid-flight credential change: the call is refused via a type the middleware returns to the model, the turn survives, coding is latched off, and a later call in a new turn finds coding disabled.

payload.body:
Approving. Every blocking item from the three earlier reviews is addressed, and the degradation design is implemented the way it needed to be rather than approximated.

## The latch is genuinely one-way

`_github_identity_degraded` is a module global guarded by `_github_identity_degraded_lock`, and the only assignments are `False` at import and `True` inside `_latch_github_identity_degraded`, which early-returns if already latched. There is no path that sets it back. That was the requirement I was most concerned about — a security signal that self-heals on the next successful check would hide precisely the condition the check exists to surface — and it is met structurally, not by convention.

`github_identity_is_degraded()` reads under the same lock, and `agent.py` derives `coding_enabled = not github_identity_is_degraded()`, so a rebuilt agent in a later turn simply has no coding tools rather than having tools that refuse individually. That is the design as specified.

## The mid-flight path returns a refusal the middleware can deliver

`confirm_github_tool_identity` raises `ToolPolicyRefusal` in both cases — when already latched, and when verification fails now (latching first, then raising). The `ForgeError` is caught and converted, so it no longer escapes as an uncaught `RuntimeError`. Combined with #1295, that means the refusal reaches the model as a `ToolMessage` and the turn survives instead of being destroyed, which was the whole point of routing it through a policy refusal rather than an exception.

## Two details I did not ask for and want to credit

**`set_github_identity_degraded_callback(..., notify_current=True)` replays an existing degradation to a newly installed callback.** If the latch fires before the server has wired its event/alert callback — entirely possible during startup — the event and operator alert still get emitted once the callback arrives. Without this, the earliest and most important degradation would be the one that goes unreported, which is the failure mode I called out as unacceptable ("do not let the degradation be quiet").

**An alert delivery failure does not un-latch.** The `except Exception as alert_exc:  # noqa: BLE001 — degradation remains latched` makes the separation explicit: notification is best-effort, the security state is not. Getting this backwards — treating a failed alert as a reason to continue as normal — is a natural mistake and it was avoided.

The one-shot guards (`degradation_recorded`, `degradation_alert_scheduled`) also keep a repeated mismatch from flooding the alert channel while still latching on the first occurrence.

## Verification

`103 passed` on `test_tool_registry.py`, `12 passed` on `test_forge_github.py`, `137 passed` across the forge/shell/agent suites.

Mutation testing on both halves of the latch, since a guard nothing pins is a guard that gets refactored away:

|---|---|
| `github_identity_is_degraded()` → `return False` | **FAILED** `test_identity_degradation_removes_coding_tools_and_does_not_auto_recover` |
| `_latch_github_identity_degraded()` → no-op | **FAILED** `test_midflight_forge_identity_change_returns_policy_refusal_and_latches` and `test_startup_identity_verification_degrades_coding_on_mismatch` |

So both the read path and the write path are pinned, in the two directions that matter: coding must actually disappear when latched, and the latch must actually be set on both the startup and mid-flight mismatch paths.

## Retained from the earlier passes

Still present and still correct at this head: the credential-fingerprint cache with fail-closed behaviour on an empty cache or mismatch, no token in any message, `GH_CONFIG_DIR` at `0o500`, `GH_TOKEN`/`GH_HOST` scrubbing (including for non-`gh` direct exec), the `repo_tools` HTTPS push path refusing when the acting identity is unverified, and `test_every_gh_command_requires_cached_declared_identity` verifying every admitted `gh` invocation rather than a guessed effectful s

payload.title: Worklink #1085: worklink/opencode: a transient SQLite lock at backend startup is fatal — no busy timeout or retry, so a run dies 1s in for a condition that clears itself

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The classification and backoff are right and closely mirror #1064's precedent, which is what I asked for. One blocking finding: the retry is named "startup" but is applied to the whole invocation, and the invocation is not idempotent.

## What is right

- `_SQLITE_CONTENTION_PATTERNS` classifies rather than blanket-retrying — `database is locked`, `database table is locked`, `database is busy`, `SQLITE_BUSY`. A non-transient failure is not retried, and `test_opencode_non_transient_startup_failure_is_not_retried` proves it with `attempts == 1` and `sleeps == []`.
- The bound is stated with its reasoning next to the constant: 5 attempts, 0.1 + 0.2 + 0.4 + 0.8 = 1.5s, justified against the observed sub-second window. That was an explicit criterion.
- `retrying` / `succeeded` outcomes plus a distinct `opencode_startup_sqlite_contention_exhausted` reason, so a delayed run is visible rather than merely slower, and exhaustion is distinguishable from the raw backend message.
- `sleeper` is injectable, so the tests do not actually sleep.
- The `orchestrator.py` change is a pure refactor — the launch / persist / wait block is moved verbatim into `invoke_backend()` so it can be passed to the retry. Nothing was removed, including the dormant `persistent_after_disconnect` branch. I checked line by line because an 81-line diff on that file is where I would expect something to be quietly dropped.

## Blocking: the retry covers the entire run, not startup

`_is_sqlite_contention` (mimir/worklink/backends/opencode.py:223-227) inspects the *finished* result:

```python
if result.exit_code == 0:
    return False
detail = f"{result.stderr}\n{result.stdout}"
return any(pattern.search(detail) for pattern in _SQLITE_CONTENTION_PATTERNS)
```

And `invoke_backend` — the thing being retried — is the whole invocation: `compute.launch(spec)`, `_persist_run_state`, and `_heartbeat_while(compute.wait(handle, spec.timeout_s), ...)`.

So a run that starts cleanly, works for twenty minutes, commits, and only then emits a matching string with a non-zero exit is classified as startup contention and **re-invoked from scratch, up to five times, in the same lease and checkout**.

Two problems with that:

1. **The re-run is not idempotent.** By the time a long run fails, the agent may already have staged, committed, and — per #1084, possibly without knowing — pushed. Re-invoking OpenCode against a checkout that already carries its own commits is not a retry; it is a second agent pass over mutated state. That is a materially different operation from re-opening a session store two seconds after launch.
2. **`stdout` is included in the match.** A run that merely *mentions* `database is locked` — echoing an error it recovered from, quoting a log line, printing a test failure that contains the phrase — triggers a full re-run on any non-zero exit. The signal is a substring of arbitrary agent output, not a launch failure.

The observed failure was unambiguous about the window: `worklink_backend_invocation` at 22:20:07, failure at 22:20:08, three git commands already run. One second in, no work produced. That is what needs retrying.

**Please bound the retry to the startup window.** Options, in the order I would prefer them:

- Retry only when the failure is a launch failure rather than a run result — the code already distinguishes these, since `ComputeLaunchError` is caught separately and sets `launch_error`.
- Or gate on no work having been produced: an elapsed time below a small threshold, or an unchanged checkout, so a run that got anywhere is never re-invoked.
- Or have the backend surface startup contention distinctly from run output instead of inferring it from combined stdout/stderr.

Whichever you choose, `stdout` should probably come out of the match, or be restricted to the pre-work portion.

**And please add the missing test.** All three new tests exercise immediate contention; none asserts that a *late* failure is left alone. A test where the fake invocation r

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Resolved, and the fix is stronger than what I asked for.

I proposed three options and leaned toward detecting a launch failure. You implemented a conjunction that is more robust than any of them:

```python
retryable = (
    _is_sqlite_contention(result)                  # stderr only now
    and elapsed_s <= startup_window_s              # temporal bound
    and checkout_snapshot() == initial_checkout    # no work produced
)
```

The third condition is the one that matters most — it directly answers the non-idempotency concern. If the agent mutated the checkout, there is no re-invocation, so a run that got anywhere is never repeated. And both `checkout_snapshot` and `clock` are injectable, so each condition can be driven independently rather than inferred.

`stdout` is out of the match, so a run that merely mentions the phrase no longer triggers a re-run.

The three boundary tests are the right ones, and one I did not ask for is the best of them:

- `test_opencode_late_sqlite_failure_is_not_retried`
- `test_opencode_sqlite_failure_after_checkout_mutation_is_not_retried`
- `test_opencode_stdout_only_sqlite_mention_is_not_retried`

The checkout-mutation test pins the non-idempotency guard specifically, which is the assertion that would catch a future refactor quietly widening the window.

Everything from the first review stands: classification rather than blanket retry, the bound stated with its reasoning next to the constant, `retrying`/`succeeded` outcomes plus a distinct exhausted reason, and the `orchestrator.py` change being a pure refactor with the dormant `persistent_after_disconnect` branch intact.

CI 7/7.

This is also the leaf that makes concurrent dispatch safe again — it fixes the failure that cost #1076 its first attempt when two builds started two seconds apart.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
This implements the leaf faithfully and the consolidation is the right shape. I am requesting changes on one consequence — and the defect is in **my** acceptance criteria, not in your reading of them.

## What is right

- `authorize_repo_pr_tool` is now the single policy decision for typed PR actions, and `_scope()` in `mimir/tools/forge.py` is reduced to resolving the server-issued scope with an explicit comment saying policy lives in the gate. That is exactly the consolidation #1083 asked for.
- `test_pr_scope_policy_shadows_then_enforces_with_the_same_reason` pins criteria 2, 4 and 5 together: `shadow.allowed is True`, `shadow.would_block is True`, `enforced.allowed is False`, `shadow.reason == enforced.reason == "repo_pr_scope_denied"`, and exactly one `shadow_tool_decision` event carrying that reason. The shadow stream now describes the gate that actually decides, which was the whole point of the leaf.
- `test_tool_modules_do_not_decide_pr_scope_policy_locally` with `assert offenders == set()` is criterion 6, and it is the assertion that stops a fourth decision point reappearing.
- Leaving `mimir/repo_tools.py` untouched was correct. Its `_require()` still raises `GitRefusal("scope_action_denied", ...)` unconditionally across 13 callsites covering CHECKOUT, WRITE, COMMIT and PUSH, so the git write path is unaffected by the flag.

## Blocking: outward-facing PR effects become unenforced in the live configuration

`allowed = in_scope or not enforce`. With `MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED` unset — which is production right now — `allowed` is unconditionally `True`. For reads that is the intended shadow behaviour. For these four it is not:

    pr_submit_review          (PR_REVIEW)
    pr_inline_review_comment  (PR_REVIEW)
    pr_comment                (PR_COMMENT)
    pr_rerequest_review       (PR_REREQUEST)

Those are effects that leave the system and appear on GitHub. Before this PR they were refused unconditionally by `_scope(runtime, RepoPRAction.X, ...)`. After it, in the live configuration, nothing refuses them.

That matters specifically because of what just landed in #1293. Review authority is now *standing* for any open PR in a configured repository, and the review action set deliberately excludes `PR_REREQUEST` and `PR_EDIT` — we removed a carve-out across three sites, with a test asserting `client.calls == []`, precisely so a reviewer could not manipulate the review state of a PR it does not own. This PR reinstates that capability by a different route: the action set still says no, and nothing consults it.

Note the resulting asymmetry is the mirror image of the defect #1083 was filed to fix. Git actions now enforce always; forge actions enforce never. The file that was left alone is the one behaving correctly.

**The bad criterion is mine.** I wrote "with enforcement unset, a PR-scope policy refusal records a shadow decision and ALLOWS the call", and separately "confirm the permissive path cannot allow something the gate would refuse when armed". Those two cannot both hold — shadow mode allowing what enforcement would refuse is its definition. You implemented the first, which was the explicit one. The contradiction is my error, not yours.

## What I am asking for

Split by effect direction rather than by module, so the audit benefit is kept without the outward-facing hole:

- `INSPECT` — shadow-allow under `not enforce`, exactly as implemented. These are reads; nothing leaves the system, and they were the majority of the observed refusals, so the enablement evidence still gets what it needs.
- `PR_REVIEW`, `PR_COMMENT`, `PR_REREQUEST`, `PR_EDIT` — refuse regardless of the flag, and still emit the decision so the audit records it.

`repo_tools._require` is the precedent to match: unconditional refusal for actions with effects, and it already coexists with the gate without being a second policy decision — it enforces an already-issued scope rather than deciding what the scope should be. Keep `authorize_repo_pr_tool`

payload.title: Worklink #1072: authz: a tool refusal terminates the turn instead of being returned to the model — so the agent cannot adapt, and the escape hatch for reporting it can refuse too

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The delivery fix is at the right seam and the escape-hatch redesign is exactly what #1072 asked for. One blocking finding, which I verified rather than inferred: the refusal path now permanently taints the turn.

## What is right

- **The seam is correct.** Catching `ToolException` in `wrap_tool_call` / `awrap_tool_call` and returning `ToolMessage(status="error")` intercepts it where it would otherwise reach langgraph's `_panic_or_proceed`. Fixing this in the middleware rather than `mimir/agent.py` is the better choice — `agent.py` would have had to distinguish refusals from genuine faults after the fact.
- **Observability survives.** The handler still emits the `tool_call` event with `denied=True` and a duration, so a refusal that no longer kills the turn is still visible in `events.jsonl`. A silent recovery would have traded one blind spot for another.
- **The escape hatch no longer refuses its caller.** Replacing `operation: str` (which had to match `[a-z][a-z0-9_.:-]{0,127}`) with a prose `description` plus `attempted_operations`, and deriving `operation` via `_operation_key`, is the fix for item 2 of the leaf. The old signature meant an agent that described its blocker in natural language got refused *by the tool that exists for reporting refusals*. This is not the fence violation it first looks like — the leaf explicitly scoped in "`unsupported_operation` and its validation."
- It also explains four turn deaths I observed live earlier today on `ToolException: operation must be a short stable operation name`. That was this exact regex rejecting escalations.
- `_bounded_escalation_text` bounds bytes, strips control characters via `unicodedata.category`, and routes through `redact_text` — the right treatment for prose that reaches an operator notification.

## Blocking: a policy refusal now monotonically taints the turn

Both new handlers do this before returning:

```python
result_labels = _result_labels_for_call(
    tool_name, request, auth_context, authorization, failed=True,
)
_merge_result_labels(auth_context, result_labels)
```

Following that through:

1. `_result_labels_for_call(failed=True)` → `classify_protected_result(..., failed=True)`.
2. `mimir/access_control.py:5802` — for the thirteen `pr_*` / `repo_*` read tools, `if scope is None or failed: return _incomplete_protected_result("repository", args)`.
3. `_incomplete_protected_result` (`:5763`) returns a `SourceLabel` with `integrity="untrusted"`, `integrity_effect="active_ingest"`.
4. `has_untrusted_active_ingest` (`mimir/models.py:281`) is **exactly** that pair, and it is the predicate that gates shell, file, spawn and message sinks with `ifc_label_blocked:*`.
5. `_merge_result_labels` is documented as *"Monotonically taint the exact turn and rebind harness egress"* — it rebinds `active_ctx.ifc_labels` and `active_ctx.auth_context`, and monotonic means it cannot be undone for the remainder of the turn.

So a refused `pr_metadata` now poisons every later shell, file, and message sink in the same turn. This is reachable and common — in today's live logs the refusals were `pr_metadata` ×8, `pr_checks` ×7, `pr_comments` ×7, `pr_reviews` ×6, `pr_files` ×5, `pr_diff` ×4, `repo_checkout` ×4, all inside the covered set.

The result is that this PR trades a loud failure for a quiet one. Before, a refusal ended the turn and the traceback named the cause. After, the turn continues and then loses shell/file/message access several steps later, attributed to `ifc_label_blocked` rather than to the refusal that actually caused it. For the specific goal of #1072 — "so the agent can adapt" — the agent now *cannot* adapt, because the tools it would adapt with are being denied for a reason with no visible connection to the refusal.

**The distinction to draw.** `except ToolException` wraps the handler, so it catches two different things:

- a **policy refusal** raised before anything executes — `_scope()` in `mimir/tools/forge.py` raises before any Forge call, so nothing was r

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The mechanism is right and the turn-survival test is exactly what I asked for. But the conversion is incomplete in a way that leaves out the two refusals that most needed it, so this still blocks.

## What is right

- **`ToolPolicyRefusal(ToolException)`** is the correct shape: a subclass, so every existing `except ToolException` keeps working, and the discriminator lives in the type rather than in a string match on the message.
- **`if not isinstance(exc, ToolPolicyRefusal)`** draws exactly the line I asked for — policy refusals do not taint, mid-execution faults still do.
- **forge.py's split is deliberate and correct.** 11 sites converted; the 4 left as plain `ToolException` are genuine faults — `ForgeError` from the live snapshot fetch (`:114`, where data may have flowed) and escalation-state read/write failures (`:386`, `:420`). Leaving those tainting is the right call, and it shows the split was reasoned rather than mechanical.
- **`test_tool_refusal_is_a_result_and_next_tool_call_can_run`** is precisely the assertion I requested: refuse `pr_metadata`, then run `shell_exec` in the same turn, and check `calls == ["refused", "adapted"]`, `adapted.content == "adapted"`, `ctx.ifc_labels == before`, and `has_untrusted_active_ingest is False`. Asserting the *second call actually executed* is what makes it meaningful.

## Blocking: `mimir/tools/repo.py` was not converted, so `repo_*` refusals still taint

Counts at this head:

| file | `ToolPolicyRefusal` | plain `ToolException` |
|---|---|---|
| `mimir/tools/forge.py` | 11 | 4 (correctly — genuine faults) |
| **`mimir/tools/repo.py`** | **0** | **6** |
| `mimir/tools/registry.py` | 0 | 4 |
| `mimir/mcp_client.py` | 0 | 3 (correctly — MCP faults) |

All six in `repo.py` are policy refusals, and they include the two I watched kill turns on the live agent earlier today:

- `:78` `repository checkout rejected: {exc}` — this is `scope does not grant PR checkout`, which terminated a turn at 19:10:08.
- `:139` `project test rejected ({code}): {exc}` — this is `scope does not grant repo.test`, which terminated a turn at 19:15:53.
- `:45` `repository operation rejected: {detail}` — the no-authorized-PR path.
- `:97` / `:101` — the checkout-lease cleanup refusals, including the identity mismatch.

And `repo_checkout`, `repo_fetch`, `repo_status`, `repo_test`, `repo_diff` and `repo_unmerged` are **all** inside `classify_protected_result`'s covered set (`mimir/access_control.py:5796-5799`), so `failed=True` → `_incomplete_protected_result` → `untrusted` / `active_ingest` still fires for every one of them.

So a review turn that gets refused on `repo_test` — the single most likely refusal now that #1293 has landed and reviewing involves checking out and testing — still poisons its own turn. The PR fixes the `pr_*` half of the exact problem it was filed for and leaves the `repo_*` half in place.

**A blanket conversion would be wrong here, which is probably why it was skipped.** `repo.py:60` and `:139` wrap `GitRefusal`, and those codes are genuinely mixed:

- *Policy — nothing executed:* `scope_action_denied`, `stale_scope`, `cross_pr_checkout`, `force_push_refused`, `inactive_checkout`, `invalid_checkout`, `invalid_scope`, `invalid_shape`, `invalid_path`, `invalid_paths`, `invalid_commit`, `invalid_message`, `invalid_revert_ancestry`, `dirty_out_of_scope`, `explicit_paths_required`, `unsafe_repo_config`, `unsupported_transport`, `test_selector_invalid`
- *Execution — git ran:* `git_failed`, `timeout`, `output_limit`, `invalid_git_output`

Please discriminate on the refusal code rather than converting the raise sites wholesale — otherwise genuine git faults (a real `git_failed` after git executed, a timeout mid-fetch) stop tainting, which would be the same bug in the opposite direction. The four execution codes are a short, closed list, so an explicit membership test reads clearly.

## Blocking: the test proves the mechanism but not the conversion

`test_tool_refusal_is_a_result_and_next_t

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Both previous items are properly resolved. One narrow gap left, in the direction that matters more.

## Resolved

**`repo.py` is converted, with the discrimination I asked for.** 7 `ToolPolicyRefusal`, 0 plain raises, and `_tool_refusal` gets the direction right:

```python
if isinstance(exc, ToolPolicyRefusal) or (code is not None and code not in execution_codes):
    return ToolPolicyRefusal(message)
return ToolException(message)
```

`_GIT_EXECUTION_REFUSAL_CODES` is exactly the four codes where git actually ran, and splitting out `_PROJECT_TEST_EXECUTION_REFUSAL_CODES` separately — with `test_selector_invalid` deliberately *not* in it — is more precise than I asked for. `code is None` falling through to `ToolException` is also the right default: unclassified means taint, which fails toward safety.

**The test goes through a real refusal now.** `test_real_repo_test_policy_refusal_does_not_taint_turn` asserts `"scope does not grant repo.test"` in the content, `calls == ["repo-refused", "adapted"]`, and no taint. That is the exact refusal that terminated a live turn at 19:15:53 today, so the test is anchored to a real failure rather than a hypothetical.

## Blocking: the discrimination is only tested in one direction

Every taint assertion in `tests/test_budget_gate_and_alias.py` is `has_untrusted_active_ingest is False` (lines 2433 and 2533), and no test raises a non-policy `ToolException` through the middleware at all. So `_GIT_EXECUTION_REFUSAL_CODES` has nothing pinning the half that matters most.

The asymmetry is worth being explicit about:

- A policy refusal that wrongly taints is an **availability** bug — the turn loses tools it should have. Annoying, and now covered.
- An execution fault that wrongly **stops** tainting is a **safety** bug — git or the test runner executed, output may have flowed into the result, and the IFC labels no longer record it. That weakens the boundary rather than the ergonomics.

Today the sets are correct, so nothing is wrong. But nothing prevents a later edit from moving `git_failed` to the policy side, or from dropping the `code=` argument at a call site, and the suite would stay green while the boundary quietly loosened.

Please add the mirror assertion: raise a `GitRefusal("git_failed", ...)` (or `timeout`) through a `repo_*` tool, and assert the turn **does** gain `has_untrusted_active_ingest is True`. One test next to the existing one closes the pair, and then the classification is enforced rather than merely correct.

## Blocking: CI has not reported

Four checks pending at `2649364a`; three pass. `pytest-enforced` is the one that exercises the taint predicate.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
CI is red and the three new tests fail deterministically — not from ordering or CI environment. They fail on a focused run in about six seconds. Blocking on that, with the diagnosis below so it does not need re-deriving.

```
$ uv run --frozen pytest tests/test_budget_gate_and_alias.py -q
FAILED test_tool_refusal_is_a_result_and_next_tool_call_can_run
FAILED test_real_repo_test_policy_refusal_does_not_taint_turn
FAILED test_real_repo_execution_fault_taints_turn
3 failed, 67 passed in 6.11s
```

## Root cause: `_ifc_auth()` is pre-tainted

`_ifc_auth()` (line 779) builds its context from `_ifc_labels()`, which carries a channel source with `integrity=UNTRUSTED, integrity_effect=ACTIVE_INGEST`. I evaluated it directly:

```
has_untrusted_active_ingest: True
```

That is correct for the fixture's original purpose — it exists to drive IFC tests — but it is the wrong starting state for these three, and it breaks each one differently:

1. **`test_tool_refusal_is_a_result_and_next_tool_call_can_run`** — the follow-up `shell_exec` never runs. It is refused with `shell_exec requires an admin identity (ifc_label_blocked:shell_process). The tool call was refused before execution.`, so `adapted.content == "adapted"` fails. Note `roles=("admin",)` is already the fixture default; the taint gate disables the trusted-operator exemptions, which is why holding admin does not help.
2. **`test_real_repo_test_policy_refusal_does_not_taint_turn`** — same refusal on the follow-up call.
3. **`test_real_repo_execution_fault_taints_turn`** — `repo_fetch` is refused with `ifc_label_blocked:forge` *before execution*, so the handler that would `raise GitRefusal("git_failed", ...)` is never entered. The assertion on `repository operation rejected (git_failed)` fails against the IFC message instead.

## Why this matters beyond a red build

With a pre-tainted context, none of the three can demonstrate the property it names:

- The two "does not taint" tests assert `has_untrusted_active_ingest is False` on a carrier that starts `True`. They cannot pass, and if they did it would mean something else was wrong.
- The "does taint" test asserts `is True` on a carrier that is **already** `True`. Even if `repo_fetch` reached the handler, that assertion would hold whether or not the taint were applied — it is tautological, and it is the security-relevant direction I asked to have pinned.

So the production change in `budget_gate.py` and `repo.py` is currently **unverified**. Having read it, I think the classification is correct — `_tool_refusal`'s direction is right, `_GIT_EXECUTION_REFUSAL_CODES` is the right four codes, and the `isinstance(exc, ToolPolicyRefusal)` guard is in the right place. But nothing demonstrates it, which is what the tests were added for.

## What is needed

Start these three from an **untainted** auth context, so the transition is observable:

- policy refusal: `has_untrusted_active_ingest` is `False` before and `False` after;
- execution fault: `False` before and `True` after.

Asserting the before-state explicitly (rather than only the after-state) is what makes the second test non-vacuous — worth doing even once the fixture is right, so a future change to the fixture cannot quietly re-hollow it.

Keep `_ifc_auth()` as it is for the tests that legitimately need a tainted carrier; this needs a sibling helper, not a change to the existing one.

Everything from my previous three reviews stays resolved — `repo.py` is converted, the code discrimination exists, and both directions are now *attempted*. This is the last step.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
`_untainted_ifc_auth()` is the right fix and the before/after assertions are what I asked for. Confirmed locally: `_untainted_ifc_auth() → False`, `_ifc_auth() → True` and unchanged for its existing callers.

Still red though — two remaining causes, both in the tests, both diagnosed below. **The production change is correct**; I verified that directly rather than by inference, see the first item.

## Tests 1 and 2: `assert ctx.ifc_labels == before` is the wrong assertion

`tests/test_budget_gate_and_alias.py:2450` and `:2551`. The labels do differ after the turn, but not because of the refusal. The added source is:

```
SourceLabel(principal='service:user-1',
            domain='shell', resource_id='repo_review',
            sensitivity='internal', source_kind='protected_tool',
            integrity='untrusted', integrity_effect='informational')
```

`domain='shell'` and `resource_id='repo_review'` identify this as the **successful follow-up `shell_exec`** recording its own result labels — which is exactly what should happen. And `integrity_effect` is `informational`, not `active_ingest`, so it does not satisfy `has_untrusted_active_ingest`.

**This confirms the fix works.** The refused `pr_metadata` contributed nothing; the only new source is the legitimate one from the call that succeeded. So object equality on the whole carrier can never hold in a test whose point is that a *second call still runs* — any successful call adds labels.

Drop the `ctx.ifc_labels == before` assertion and keep `has_untrusted_active_ingest is False`, which you already assert on the following line and which is the property that actually matters. If you want something stronger than the predicate, assert that no source has `integrity_effect == ACTIVE_INGEST`, or that no source has `domain == "repository"` — either stays true regardless of what the successful call legitimately contributes.

## Test 3: the injected fault is unreachable

`:2618` now fails with:

```
assert 'repository operation rejected (git_failed)' in
       'repository operation rejected (inactive_checkout): an active matching checkout lease is required'
```

`repo_fetch` refuses on `inactive_checkout` before the handler that raises `GitRefusal("git_failed", ...)` is ever entered. Worth noting the classifier is behaving correctly here — `inactive_checkout` is not in `_GIT_EXECUTION_REFUSAL_CODES`, so it is treated as a policy refusal and does not taint, which is why the `is True` assertion fails rather than the message assertion being the only problem.

You need a path that actually reaches execution. Either provide an active matching checkout lease so `repo_fetch` proceeds, or pick a tool/entry point where the injected `GitRefusal` is reachable without lease setup. The assertion should stay as it is — `False` before, `True` after — since that pair is the whole point.

## Note on this PR's shape

Five rounds now, and worth saying plainly because it is a useful signal rather than a complaint: the production code has been correct since round three. Rounds four and five have both been tests that did not exercise what they claimed — first a pre-tainted fixture that made the key assertion tautological, now an unreachable fault injection. Both would have shipped as green-looking coverage of an unverified behaviour.

That is the same failure mode as the finding this PR exists to fix: something that looks like it is working because the check cannot fail. Worth a moment's attention to the test's *reachability* before the next push — run it and confirm the injected fault actually fires, rather than confirming the assertion passes.

payload.title: Worklink #1082: repo_merge reports nothing on conflict: git writes conflict output to stdout but _checked only reads stderr

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The implementation is correct and the tests are the right tests. Requesting changes only on unreported CI and one design point; the engineering here needs no rework.

## What is right

- **It consults the unmerged index rather than parsing git's English.** `_unmerged_paths()` is the authoritative signal, and the leaf explicitly warned against inferring "conflict" from output text. This is the part I most expected to be done the easy way.
- **Non-conflict failures are genuinely unchanged.** The `except GitRefusal` re-raises when `exc.code != "git_failed"` and again when `not unmerged`, so an unknown SHA still surfaces git's own stderr. `test_merge_non_conflict_failure_preserves_git_stderr` pins that, including asserting the recovery text is *absent* — testing the negative was the right instinct.
- **The refusal is actionable**: distinct `merge_conflict` code, names the conflicting paths, and points at `repo_unmerged` / `repo_merge_abort`. The test then proves `GitMergeAbort` actually works from that state, which is more than the leaf asked for.
- **Redaction is verified on the new path.** `test_checked_failure_stdout_is_redacted_but_commands_must_opt_in` asserts `"diagnostic [REDACTED]"`, so `sensitive_values` scrubbing covers stdout reaching a refusal. `output_limit` still bounds it upstream.
- The new `merge_conflict` code surfaces cleanly — `mimir/tools/repo.py:64` reads `getattr(exc, "code", ...)` generically, so a new code needs no downstream registration.

## I verified the revert/stage question for you

The leaf's review criteria asked you to check whether `repo_revert` / `repo_stage` share this blindness and say so in the PR body. The body is the worklink boilerplate, so that is unanswered — but I tested it rather than send it back:

| operation | exit | stdout | stderr |
|---|---|---|---|
| `git merge` | 1 | 129B | **0B** |
| `git rebase` | 1 | 63B | 455B |
| `git revert` | 1 | 63B | 399B |
| `git cherry-pick` | 1 | 63B | 418B |

Only `merge` has the empty-stderr quirk. `rebase`, `revert` and `cherry-pick` all write `error: could not apply/revert …` to stderr, so `_checked` already reports something useful for them and scoping this fix to `GitMerge` is **correct**, not an oversight.

Please put that conclusion in the PR body or a comment — not to redo the work, but so the next reader knows merge-only was a determination and not an omission. `test_rebase_conflict_has_separately_modeled_working_abort` already exists nearby, which makes the asymmetry look accidental otherwise.

## Blocking: CI has not reported

At `b4805ac89`: `chainlink-cli-audit`, `pytest (3.11)`, `pytest (3.12)` and `pytest-enforced` are all still pending; the other three pass. Nothing merges here on unreported tests.

## Change request: `_checked` should be safe by default

The two layers have opposite defaults:

```python
def _checked(..., report_stdout_on_failure: bool = True)
def _command(..., report_stdout_on_failure: bool = False)
```

`_command` is safe-by-default, and it is currently the **only** caller of `_checked` — and it always passes the flag explicitly — so there is no live leak, and the test deliberately pins both directions. I am satisfied it is intentional.

Still, the lower and more general layer defaults to the more disclosing behaviour, and safety holds only because exactly one caller happens to override it. A future direct `_checked(...)` call — a new operation, a probe, a refactor — silently opts into echoing stdout into an exception message. Please flip `_checked`'s default to `False` and keep `_command` passing through explicitly; the merge branch already passes `report_stdout_on_failure=True` at its own call site, so nothing else changes and the existing test only needs its `_checked` call to pass the flag.

If you would rather keep it as-is, say why in a comment on `_checked` — the reasoning should not have to be reconstructed from the test name.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body: Both items resolved. `_checked` now defaults `report_stdout_on_failure=False` with merge as an explicit opt-in, so the safe behaviour no longer depends on one caller remembering to override it — and the regression test was genuinely updated to prove both directions (`_command` omits stdout; explicit `_checked` includes it, redacted). The merge-only scoping is now stated, and it matches what I measured independently: only `git merge` writes conflict output to stdout with empty stderr; rebase/revert/cherry-pick all report usable stderr. CI 7/7.

The regression test now proves the default `_command()` path omits stdout and direct `_checked()` only includes redacted stdout when explicitly enabled. Focused validation: `tests/test_repo_tools.py tests/test_repo_tool_wiring.py` (96 passed). Scope is intentionally merge-only: merge is the operation whose conflict diagnostics can be stdout-only; rebase, revert, and cherry-pick already emit useful stderr and remain unchanged.

payload.title: Worklink #1081: authz: PR review authority is gated on event type and requested-reviewer — most turns holding PR work cannot act on that PR

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Both halves of #1081 are implemented correctly, and the design is better than the leaf asked for. Requesting changes on one contradiction plus a pending-CI blocker.

## What is right

- The event-type gate and the `requested_reviewer == self_login` condition are both gone. `is_review` no longer exists.
- `_REPO_PR_REVIEW_ACTIONS` is exactly `{INSPECT, CHECKOUT, TEST, PR_REVIEW, PR_COMMENT}`, and `WRITE` / `COMMIT` / `PUSH` / `PR_EDIT` / `PR_REREQUEST` stay out. This was the half I most expected to be missed — a fix that removed only the gate would have looked successful while `scope does not grant repo.test` kept killing turns.
- `resolve_review_state_for_context` gets the security ordering right: `is_configured_github_repo()` is checked **before** any network call, the snapshot comes from `client.get_pull_request_snapshot()` rather than from the model (the model supplies only a selector, which is then validated), `scope.pr_number != pull_request` is cross-checked, and closed PRs are refused.
- `checkout_ref` = `refs/pull/{number}/head` is a good addition I had not specified. A provider-owned immutable ref is the right way to let a review scope obtain code it does not own, and folding it into `scope_id` keeps it part of the authority binding.
- The async path wraps the sync fetch in `asyncio.to_thread`, and the 20s client timeout bounds it. Putting network I/O in an authorization path is a real hazard and this handles it correctly.
- `"this turn carries no authorized pull requests"` is gone as a reachable string, replaced by specific refusals. That was the actual goal.

## Blocking: the parity projection now contradicts the gate it models

`mimir/repo_pr_parity.py:140-146` adds a carve-out with no explanatory comment:

```python
if (
    _OPERATION_ACTION[probe.operation] not in actions
    and not (
        probe.operation == "pr_rerequest_review"
        and RepoPRAction.PR_REVIEW.value in actions
    )
):
    return TypedProjection("refuse", "scope_action_denied")
```

So under a review workflow this module projects **allow** for `pr_rerequest_review`. Four things in this same PR disagree with that:

1. `mimir/access_control.py:803` maps `pr_rerequest_review` to `RepoPRAction.PR_REREQUEST`.
2. `_REPO_PR_REVIEW_ACTIONS` does not contain `PR_REREQUEST`, so the real gate refuses it with `scope_action_denied`.
3. This PR's own new test asserts it is denied: `for denied in (..., RepoPRAction.PR_REREQUEST): assert denied.value not in scope.allowed_operations`.
4. `pr_rerequest_review` is in this module's `_WRITE_OPERATIONS`, so the projection also returns `planned=("pr_rerequest_review",)` — it predicts a write effect the system will never perform.

This module's stated purpose is offline shadow parity between the legacy and typed paths. It cannot authorize anything (no Forge client, no Git runner), so this is **not** a privilege escalation. But making the parity model deliberately disagree with the typed path defeats what the model is for: it will now report allow-vs-refuse divergence as expected behaviour, which is exactly the mismatch class it exists to surface.

Please resolve it in one direction and say which:

- **(a)** Drop the carve-out so the projection matches `_REPO_PR_REVIEW_ACTIONS`. This is what #1081 specified — "a reviewer must not be able to modify, push to, or retitle someone else's pull request."
- **(b)** If re-requesting review genuinely belongs in review authority, add `PR_REREQUEST` to `_REPO_PR_REVIEW_ACTIONS`, update the test that currently asserts it is denied, and justify it in the PR body — re-requesting review is a write to another PR's review state, so it needs an argument, not a silent exception.

Either way the carve-out needs a comment explaining why, or a future reader hits the same contradiction.

## Blocking: CI has not reported

`pytest (3.11)`, `pytest (3.12)` and `pytest-enforced` are all still pending at `e2a9e6a95`. The other four checks pass. No PR merges here with unreported or failing t

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Resolved, and thoroughly. payload.title: Worklink #1079: authz: a PR checkout lease that committed work can never be cleaned up — the identity check requires HEAD to equal the checkout-time head, so 14 of 19 leases are permanently unreleasable

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Reviewed against every acceptance and review criterion on chainlink #1079. No defect found. Not approving — operator's call — and three checks were still pending when I looked.

**The HEAD check is replaced with the right pair.** My review criteria warned that a descendant check *alone* is not discriminating, because several leases of one scope share a base and any of them would contain `lease.head_sha`. This implements branch identity **and** descendant:

```python
expected_branch = lease.destination_ref.removeprefix("refs/heads/")
if branch != expected_branch: refuse          # "<detached>" handled explicitly
merge-base --is-ancestor lease.head_sha head  # HEAD must descend from the recorded head
```

`test_pr_checkout_lease_cleanup_refuses_unrelated_head_on_expected_branch` pins exactly the case that motivated the warning — right branch, unrelated commit — so the weaker single check cannot creep back in.

**What still prevents deleting the wrong directory** — the question that matters for a destructive operation — is intact and now stronger: path containment under the lease root (with an improved message naming both paths), `canonical_origin` equality, `scope_id`, and branch identity. `test_pr_checkout_lease_cleanup_refuses_directory_from_another_lease` covers the case I was most worried about given 19 leases across 6 scopes.

**Schema tolerance does not become a bypass.** The required identity fields are enumerated explicitly — `canonical_repo`, `canonical_origin`, `head_sha`, `destination_ref`, `owner`, `scope_id`, `path`, `lease_root`, `recovery_id` — so a field added later (`scope_base_sha`, from #1287) is tolerated while omitting a required one is refused. Both directions are pinned: `..._accepts_metadata_before_additive_field` and `..._refuses_missing_required_identity_field`. That was the subtle half of this leaf and it is handled precisely.

**Refusals now name both values** (`expected X; actual Y`), which is what turned this defect into an hour of lease-metadata archaeology rather than a readable error.

**Existing leases recover.** I checked a real stuck lease rather than assuming: `destination_ref=refs/heads/issue/1060-a2` matches the checked-out branch, and the recorded head is an ancestor of the current HEAD — so it passes both new checks. The 14 previously-unreleasable leases become cleanable without manual `rm`, satisfying that criterion empirically.

Worth stating what this fixes in operational terms: a remediation that *succeeded* was ending its turn on a failed cleanup, so success reported as failure to anything reading turn outcomes. Two remediations published today and both would have looked like failures.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes for one narrow fix. **The change itself is correct** — my earlier review stands, and nothing in the implementation needs rework. The new tests just cannot run in CI.

`pytest (3.11)`, `pytest (3.12)` and `pytest-enforced` all fail on the same two tests, with the same cause:

```
FAILED tests/test_pr_checkout_lease.py::test_pr_checkout_lease_cleanup_accepts_commit_on_lease_branch
  subprocess.CalledProcessError: Command '['git', '-C', '…/leases/…', 'commit', '-q', '-m', 'fix']'
  returned non-zero exit status 128

FAILED tests/test_pr_checkout_lease.py::test_pr_checkout_lease_cleanup_refuses_unrelated_head_on_expected_branch
  … 'commit', '-q', '-m', 'unrelated history' … exit status 128
```

Exit 128 from `git commit` in a fresh temporary repository is the missing-author-identity failure ("unable to auto-detect email address" / "Please tell me who you are"). The GitHub runner has no global `user.name` / `user.email`, and these are the only two new tests that create a commit — every other new test passes, which is what points at the environment rather than the assertions.

Note the production path already handles this: the merge and rebase invocations in `repo_tools.py` pass `identity=True` precisely because the executor cannot rely on ambient git config. The tests need the same treatment.

Fix is one of:

- pass identity per invocation in the `_git` helper: `-c user.name=… -c user.email=…`
- or set `GIT_AUTHOR_NAME` / `GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL` / `GIT_COMMITTER_NAME` / `GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL` in the test environment
- or `git init` the fixture with an identity already configured

Prefer whichever matches how other tests in the suite create commits, so the fixture stays consistent rather than gaining a local idiom.

One thing worth drawing out, because it is the interesting part rather than a criticism of this PR: these tests passing locally and failing in CI is a small instance of the gap this whole cycle has been about. A `repo_test` run inside a lease would likely have passed too, because the container *has* a git identity. So verification-before-push would not have caught this one — CI is the only place it shows. Worth knowing when we judge how much protection `repo_test` actually buys.

Everything else from my previous review is unchanged: branch identity plus descendant is the right check, the required-identity-field split is correct, the refusal messages name both values, and I confirmed on a real stuck lease that the 14 previously-unreleasable leases become cleanable.

payload.body: The CI blocker is resolved: `_git` now passes `-c user.name=test -c user.email=test@example.com` per invocation, matching how the production merge/rebase paths use `identity=True` rather than relying on ambient git config. Both previously-failing tests are still present and CI is 7/7 — I checked the head content, not just the check marks. The implementation itself I had already confirmed correct against a real stuck lease.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.title: github-poller: direct remediation turns to verify with repo_test

payload.author: jason-visotrust
payload.body:
## Findings

1. **[High] Make the `repo_test` instruction capability-aware.** `mimir/optional-skills/github-poller/poller.py:1552-1556` unconditionally tells every deployment to use `repo_test`, but coding tools are only registered when `MIMIR_CODING_ENABLED` is true (`mimir/tools/registry.py:2398-2427`), and that setting defaults to false. On a valid default deployment this prompt directs the agent to a nonexistent tool. Qualify the instruction with availability, or explicitly say not to publish unverified changes when `repo_test` is unavailable.

2. **[Medium] Tighten the selector guidance.** Selectors must resolve to existing non-symlink paths inside the checkout (`mimir/project_tests.py:205-232`), and `::node_id` is runner-specific rather than portable across the npm/Gradle/Cargo/Go runners cited by this PR. Describe existing non-symlink repo-relative paths and qualify `::node_id` as supported only when the configured runner accepts it; keeping “omit for the whole suite” is good.

3. **[Medium] Add regression coverage for the prompt contract.** The PR changes only the prompt, while the closest test merely checks for `stuck at CHANGES_REQUESTED`. Add assertions for `repo_test`, no shell flags, selector/whole-suite guidance, and the unavailable-capability behavior.

Focused github-poller changes-requested tests pass (`17 passed`) and all CI checks are green, but neither currently covers these semantics.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1077: authz: delete the scoped push proxy — it 403s legitimate pushes, its CAS duplicates the existing ls-remote check, and its credential hiding is unnecessary; push with an origin-scoped extraheader from the child env

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Reviewed against every acceptance and review criterion on chainlink #1077. No defect found. Not approving — operator's call — and four checks (`chainlink-cli-audit`, `pytest` 3.11/3.12, `pytest-enforced`) are still pending, so the green-suite gate is not yet cleared.

**Net -191 lines**, and the deletion is real: `mimir/repo_push_proxy.py` (-210) and `tests/test_repo_push_proxy.py` (-124) are both `deleted file mode`, with the `push_proxy_factory` seam gone rather than left as an unused parallel path.

**The credential moves to the child environment, not argv:**

```
GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=1
GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0=http.<canonical_origin>.extraheader
GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0=Authorization: Basic <b64 x-access-token:...>
```

That is the stronger option on the axis that motivated the proxy in the first place — argv is readable by anything that can read `/proc`, a child's environ is owner-only. Scoping the key to `http.<origin>.extraheader` rather than bare `http.extraheader` means the header is not offered to any other host, and `test_push_credential_is_available_only_for_exact_canonical_github_origin` pins it.

**The properties the proxy held are held elsewhere, which was the review's central question.** Walking each:

- *ref restriction and compare-and-swap* — the pre-existing `ls-remote --heads` equality check survives, re-pointed at the origin rather than the loopback remote (removed at :416, re-added at :435). Still refuses with `stale_scope` unless the remote ref is exactly `observed_head_sha`.
- *force-push refusal* — the `merge-base --is-ancestor` guard is untouched; zero removed lines, `force_push_refused` intact.
- *destination restriction* — server-built refspec, unchanged.
- *credential concealment* — now environment plus the origin-scoped key.

**Two hardening additions beyond the ask.** `http.followRedirects=false` is asserted in the argv, so a redirect cannot carry the header off-host — I asked for redirects to be refused or the header dropped, and refusing the redirect outright is the cleaner answer. And `test_repo_url_rewrite_config_is_refused_before_authenticated_push` closes the `insteadOf` laundering vector: a hostile lease git config cannot redirect an authenticated push.

**The diagnosability regression I reported is fixed.** The push failure now reads `f"push failed: {exc}; {self._stranded_work_message()}"` — the underlying git cause survives alongside the stranded-commit note. That mattered: the 403 that motivated this change reached no event at all, and I had to recover it from a Python traceback in `docker logs`.

Also good: the credential is scoped to the invocations that need it. A test asserts `ls-remote` and `push` both carry it while every other git call has no `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT` in its environment — so the token is not ambiently present for local operations.

Once the four pending checks are green this should be merged and deployed. It is the last known blocker on a completed remediation: five PRs currently hold committed fixes that cannot be published, and this is what publishes them.

Each property the proxy held is held elsewhere and I checked them individually: ref restriction and compare-and-swap by the surviving ls-remote equality check, force-push refusal by the untouched merge-base --is-ancestor guard, destination restriction by the server-built refspec. The diagnosability regression is also fixed — push failures now carry the underlying git cause alongside the stranded-work note, which is what made the original 403 invisible.
