payload.title: Worklink #1070: authz: the repo-review principal cannot run the project's tests, so it commits unverified remediations (9 refused invocations, fell back to compileall)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Reviewed against every acceptance and review criterion on chainlink #1070. No defect found, and two properties exceed what the leaf asked for. Not approving — operator's call.

This grants what is in substance arbitrary code execution (a test suite runs project code), so containment was the whole review, and it holds:

- **The command is the deployment's own**, resolved from `worklink.yaml` `defaults.test_command`. The model supplies no runner, no flags, no environment.
- **No shell.** `subprocess.Popen(argv, stdin=DEVNULL, ...)` with a fixed argv, so there is no metacharacter surface at all.
- **The runner is validated before use**: `resolve(strict=True)`, `is_file()`, and `os.access(X_OK)`.
- **Selectors are narrowed, not trusted.** Bounded by `_MAX_SELECTORS=32`, `_MAX_SELECTOR_LENGTH=256`, `_MAX_SELECTOR_BYTES=4096`; each must resolve to an existing path inside the checkout; and the symlink check runs on **every path component**, not just the leaf, which is what stops a mid-path symlink escape. `resolve(strict=True)` then `relative_to(root)` — resolution before containment, in that order. A flag cannot pass as a selector because a selector must be an existing path.
- **Failure is actionable rather than opaque**: `tests_failed` for a nonzero suite, distinct from `test_not_configured`, `test_config_invalid`, and `test_runner_unavailable`.

Two things beyond the ask:

**The lease path itself is redacted from output**, asserted by `assert str(state.checkout_lease.path.resolve()) not in result.stdout`. I asked for credential scrubbing; leaking the lease path would have been a smaller but real disclosure and it is closed.

**`test_project_test_output_limit_returns_no_partial_unredactable_output`** guards the subtle interaction between truncation and redaction — truncating mid-secret can defeat a scrubber that matches whole patterns. That is the kind of thing usually found after an incident rather than before.

The test names map one-to-one onto the criteria, including `test_project_test_resolves_selector_before_checkout_containment` (the ordering) and `test_repo_test_schema_exposes_no_execution_authority` (schema level). CI green on all seven checks.

This is the capability whose absence had the agent running `python -m compileall` as a substitute for testing, and committing fixes it could not verify. Worth landing.

payload.body: Approved on operator sign-off. Verified against every criterion on #1070: the test command comes from the deployment's own worklink.yaml defaults.test_command, runs with a fixed argv and no shell, the runner is validated (resolve strict / is_file / X_OK), and selectors are bounded and must resolve to existing paths with the symlink check applied to every path component — resolution before containment. Failure is actionable (tests_failed distinct from test_not_configured / test_config_invalid / test_runner_unavailable). Beyond the ask: the lease path is redacted from output, and test_project_test_output_limit_returns_no_partial_unredactable_output guards truncation defeating redaction. CI green on all seven checks.

payload.title: Worklink #1066: worklink: clone-path code is named 'worktree' though builds use git clone --local; delete the retired integrated-epic worktree helpers

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Reviewed against every acceptance and review criterion on chainlink #1066. No defect found. Not approving — mimir implementing a spec I wrote is the operator's call.

**Net -297 lines** (332 added, 629 removed), all seven checks green. The three retired integrated-epic helpers are gone with their tests: `create_integration_branch`, `create_slice_worktree`, `merge_slice_into_integration` — each removed once, added nowhere. That was the substance of the leaf.

**The naming now states the mechanism.** `worktree.py` becomes `checkout.py`, and the lease/evidence/orchestrator vocabulary follows. payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1069: authz: repo_push has NO credential channel (credential.helper emptied + GIT_ASKPASS=/bin/false) — the agent commits a fix then cannot publish it

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Reviewed against every acceptance and review criterion on chainlink #1069. This is the strongest change I have reviewed today, and it solves the problem in a better way than the leaf contemplated. I cannot substantiate a defect. Not approving — mimir implementing a spec I wrote is the operator's call, and four checks are still pending.

**The design avoids the credential-leak problem instead of managing it.** Rather than handing git a credential through any channel, it stands up a loopback receive-pack proxy: git's remote becomes `http://127.0.0.1:<ephemeral>/<repo>.git`, and the proxy attaches `Authorization` when forwarding upstream. The token never enters git's argv, environment, config, or credential cache, because git never has it. The leaf's own enumeration of leak channels — `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`, `/proc/<pid>/environ`, the lease git config, git's credential cache, the reflog, error text — is answered structurally rather than channel by channel. That is a better answer than `http.extraheader`, which I ruled out for exactly the argv-visibility reason.

**Crucially, the hardening was not relaxed.** `GIT_ASKPASS=/bin/false` and the emptied `credential.helper` stay in place; the proxy becomes git's only network authority. The instinct that produced the original defect was right, and this keeps it while routing around it.

**Containment is by construction, not by secrecy.** This was my main worry, since the agent has `shell_exec` and could reach a loopback port. It does not matter, because the proxy validates the receive-pack body itself and refuses anything but one exact state transition:

```
old.lower() != scope.observed_head_sha.lower()   # compare-and-swap against the scope's observed head
or new.lower() != expected_head
or ref != scope.destination_ref
or new == "0" * 40                                # no deletion
```

So a process that finds the port can only cause the push that was already authorized. Note what the first line buys: force-push is prevented *by construction* rather than by inspecting a flag, because a history rewrite cannot present a matching `old`. The leaf only asked that force-push "remain refused"; a compare-and-swap is a stronger guarantee than the flag check I would have accepted. `test_force_push_guard_refuses_before_any_network_call` adds a second layer ahead of the network.

Everything else on the surface is closed too: only `GET .../info/refs?service=git-receive-pack` and `POST .../git-receive-pack` are reachable and everything else is a 403; the origin is revalidated for scheme, host and path and rejects embedded userinfo, port, query and fragment; request and response are both bounded (411/413/502); `log_message` is suppressed so no request line is logged; and only `Content-Type`/`Content-Encoding` are echoed back, so no upstream header can be reflected. The listener is `127.0.0.1` on an ephemeral port and is shut down in `__exit__`.

**It also implements the amendment I added to this leaf an hour ago.** `_stranded_work_message()` and `test_push_failure_reports_and_preserves_stranded_local_commit` mean a failed push now says that a local commit remains unpushed in a preserved lease, rather than losing it silently. That was the mechanism by which five completed fixes ended up stranded on disk today, and it is addressed rather than merely noted. Non-HTTPS scopes are refused with the same stranded-work message rather than failing obscurely.

**One precision note, not a defect.** The module docstring says "One-use", but there is no used-flag; the listener serves until `__exit__`. In substance the guarantee is "one authorized transition" rather than "one HTTP request", because the compare-and-swap makes a repeat idempotent rather than an escalation. The behaviour is right; only the word overstates it slightly.

Once the four pending checks are green, merging this should publish five remediation commits that are currently sitting in leases — for PRs #1278, #1279, #1280, #1281 and #1282 — and in d

payload.body: Approved on operator sign-off. Verified against every acceptance and review criterion on #1069; the loopback receive-pack proxy keeps the token out of git's argv, environment, config and credential cache, and the compare-and-swap on `old == scope.observed_head_sha` makes force-push impossible by construction rather than by flag check. CI green on all seven checks.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1068: authz: a secret-shaped TEST FIXTURE makes tests/test_access_control.py unreadable (hard denial) — the agent cannot read the file a PR asks it to fix

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Reviewed against every acceptance and review criterion on chainlink #1068. This relaxes a confidentiality control, so the narrowness of the relaxation was the whole review — and it is narrow in every direction I probed. I cannot substantiate a defect. Not approving: mimir implementing a spec I wrote is the operator's call, and five checks are still pending.

**The carve-out is bound to the turn's own authorized lease, not to "a lease".** `is_tracked_file_in_current_pr_lease` requires an active `PRCheckoutLease` whose `scope_id` equals the turn's scope and whose `owner` matches the scope principal. So it is not enough for a file to sit in some lease; it must be *this* turn's authorized one. That is tighter than the criterion asked for.

**Laundering is closed on all three vectors I named.** The lease root and checkout are `resolve(strict=True)`d and containment-tested *after* resolution — the ordering I asked for, since testing before resolution is how symlink escapes slip through. `checkout.parent != lease_root or checkout == lease_root` rejects aiming at the lease root itself. `resolved.is_relative_to(checkout)` rejects anything escaping the checkout. And the tests cover all three: another PR's lease (`other_tracked = other_lease.path / "tests/test_access_control.py"`), a symlink, and untracked content.

**Protected names remain protected even when tracked.** The name checks still `return True` early; the carve-out applies only to the content-scan result at the end (`contains_protected_content and not is_tracked_file_in_current_pr_lease(path)`). A tracked `.env` inside the lease is still refused — and that is tested explicitly by adding `.env` to the index and asserting denial. Git index membership as "publication proof" is the right framing, and correctly does not extend to files whose *name* marks them sensitive regardless of publication.

**Tracked-ness is established server-side by asking git**, via `RepoGitTools(state).is_tracked_file(path)` — never inferred from path shape and never model-supplied.

**The refusal now answers the incoherence I raised.** It reads "Read denied: protected_read_target. For published PR content, use pr_files or pr_diff." The original complaint was that the same principal could fetch identical bytes through the API while the disk read was refused, with an opaque message. Now the boundary is coherent *and* it tells the agent where to go, so it can route around deliberately instead of falling back to shell and getting refused again.

**Verified against the real file.** `fixture_source = Path(__file__).with_name("test_access_control.py")` copies the actual 3000-line test file into the fixture repo rather than synthesizing a small stand-in. That was the criterion I most expected to be satisfied with a synthetic fixture, and it wasn't — so the test proves the specific file that triggered this is now readable.

One implementation detail worth praising because it is easy to get wrong: the expensive git query sits second in a short-circuit (`contains_protected_content and not ...`), so it only runs for files the scanner already flagged. Had the operands been ordered the other way, every read in a `grep` walk would have spawned a git process.

Confirm the five pending checks land green before merge.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1067: authz: a BATCHED poller turn derives no PR scope, so every typed pr_*/repo_* call is refused — remediation capability is zero (live failure on #1278)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Reviewed against every acceptance and review criterion on chainlink #1067. I probed the three things I considered most likely to be wrong and all three came back clean — I cannot substantiate a defect. Not approving: this is mimir implementing a spec I wrote and the operator signs off on those, and `chainlink-cli-audit` plus the three pytest checks are still pending, so the green-suite gate is not cleared. Recording the verification so it need not be repeated.

**The widening is correctly bounded.** This changes authority from one PR per turn to N, so that was the whole review. `RepoPRScopeRegistry` is a frozen dataclass whose `__post_init__` enforces tuple type, element type, and **rejects duplicate targets**. `resolve()` type-checks strictly and matches exactly against payload-derived entries, returning `None` otherwise — so a model-supplied selector can *choose from* the authorized set but can never *add to* it. Worth calling out that `resolve` explicitly excludes `bool`: without that, `pull_request=True` would match PR #1 through `isinstance(True, int)`. That is a real trap, caught.

My criterion said no model parameter may "add, widen, or select" a scope. On reflection the third verb was too strict — the agent must be able to name which PR it is acting on. The property that matters is that selection cannot reach outside the payload-derived set, and that holds.

**Cross-PR confusion — the failure I flagged as most dangerous — is closed.** `authorize_tool` and `_extract_sink_target` both resolve per named PR, and the sink target embeds `scope_id`, so a commit or push naming PR A cannot borrow PR B's proof even though both are authorized in the same turn. I checked the routing is exhaustive rather than trusting it: every one of the 26 typed `repo_*`/`pr_*` capabilities the poller is granted is present in `_TYPED_REPO_PR_TOOL_ACTIONS`, so no typed tool falls through to the legacy single-scope branch. An incomplete list here would have produced exactly the wrong-scope resolution the leaf warns about.

**Conflicting snapshots fail closed rather than picking one.** Two trusted items for the same target with different `scope_id` poison that target to `None`, and later items for it are skipped so it stays poisoned. "Never choose between conflicting trusted snapshots of one target" is the right instinct — arbitrating between two head SHAs would have been the subtle wrong answer. Pinned by `test_poller_scope_drops_conflicting_snapshots_for_same_pr`.

**Zero valid items still yields zero authority.** Invalid items are skipped, and an empty result returns `None` rather than an empty-but-permissive registry — the specific way removing the `len(items) != 1` test could have gone wrong.

**The refusals are distinguishable and do not leak.** "this turn carries no authorized pull requests" versus "requested pull request is not authorized" answers the diagnosability criterion. And `assert "owner/repo" not in str(denied.value)` / `assert "19" not in ...` pins the criterion that an improved message must not disclose repo or PR details to a caller that had no authority for them. That was a subtle ask and it is tested, not just satisfied.

**Heartbeat scopes are preserved.** I expected this to regress, since typed tools now consult only the registry while server-discovered heartbeat scopes arrive as a carried `repo_pr_action_scope`. Lines wrapping `carried_scope` into a single-entry registry when no poller registry exists keep that path working, and `repo_pr_action_scope` is still populated for the single-scope case. Epic criterion 1 (both poller payloads and heartbeat scopes) survives.

**Per-PR checkout proof** is isolated by `test_checkout_proof_is_isolated_to_named_pr`, and the schema-level tests (`..._requires_exact_repository_and_pr_selectors`, `..._only_name_exact_registry_selectors`) mean the selectors are enforced at the tool surface rather than only in the gate.

One operational note: this is the change that unblocks batched remediatio

payload.body: Approved on operator sign-off. Verified against every acceptance and review criterion on #1067. `RepoPRScopeRegistry.resolve` bounds selection to payload-derived scopes (and excludes `bool`, without which `pull_request=True` would match PR #1); all 26 granted typed capabilities are present in `_TYPED_REPO_PR_TOOL_ACTIONS` so none falls through to the legacy single-scope branch; conflicting trusted snapshots fail closed; heartbeat scopes are preserved via the single-entry registry wrap. payload.title: Worklink #1065: worklink: checkout shape is chosen from a hardcoded backend-name set — retired 'codex' still tested, and feature_factory falls through to the abandoned git-worktree shape

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Reviewed against every acceptance and review criterion on chainlink #1065 — I could not find a defect. Not approving, because this is mimir implementing a spec I wrote and the operator signs off on those; and `pytest (3.11)`, `pytest (3.12)` and `pytest-enforced` are still pending, so the green-suite gate is not yet cleared. Recording the verification so it does not have to be redone.

**Acceptance criteria**

- Selection is driven by a declared property, not a name set: `CheckoutShape` is documented as the "server-owned containment shape", and `checkout_shape_for_backend` replaces `backend_name in {"codex", "opencode"}`.
- The retired `codex` name is gone from the condition, and `create_worktree` is no longer imported by the orchestrator at all — so the abandoned shape is unreachable from selection rather than merely unselected.
- `feature_factory` and `opencode` each declare `checkout_shape = CheckoutShape.ISOLATED_CLONE` explicitly, so neither depends on falling through a test.

- *Fails toward the safe shape*: confirmed. A backend declaring nothing gets the isolated clone; the enum currently has a single member, so there is no way to select a worktree even deliberately.
- *Declaration is server-side and not operator-settable*: confirmed by inspection **and** by probe. `_build_opencode` extracts `bin`/`args`/`bash_allowlist` by name, and `_build_feature_factory` builds `kwargs` from an explicit allowlist (`bin`, `extra_args`, optional `ready_for_review`/`reviewer`). I constructed a registry with `backends.feature_factory.checkout_shape: "WORKTREE_EVIL"` in config; it was silently ignored, not honored. A containment property staying out of operator reach was the criterion I most expected to be missed.
- *opencode behavior unchanged*: it still reaches `create_isolated_checkout` with the same arguments, and the diff is a net reduction in the orchestrator (+22/-38).

**Beyond the ask, in the right direction**: the safety net that detected a non-isolated checkout was two backend-named events (`worklink_unsafe_codex_checkout` / `..._opencode_checkout`); it is now a single `worklink_unsafe_backend_checkout` covering any backend. Previously a third backend would have slipped past the net silently — the same selection-by-omission flaw this leaf exists to remove, fixed in the detection path too without being asked.

One note for whoever merges: #1066 (the naming rename plus deleting the retired worktree helpers) is deliberately sequenced after this, so `create_worktree` and `WorktreeLease` intentionally still exist here. That is expected, not an oversight.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1064: worklink: simultaneous dispatches race on the shared chainlink locks worktree; the loser dies at attempt None with no event (25% of dispatch instants, 36 runs)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes on two points. This is the strongest of the five worklink PRs — the design is right and the tests are the best I have reviewed today.

What lands well:

- The mutex is scoped to **only** the claim call. `_claim_lock_with_retry` holds `flock` across `self._run("locks", "claim", ...)` and releases in a `finally`, nothing more. That was the primary review criterion: a mutex held across the build would have reduced effective concurrency to one, which is the defect restated rather than fixed.
- Transient contention and real denial are genuinely separated. `_is_git_contention` matches on the three signatures that actually occur, and a non-contention failure returns immediately without retrying — `test_real_claim_denial_is_not_retried` pins exactly the case where getting this wrong would turn a retry into a steal.
- `test_simultaneous_claims_are_serialized_and_both_succeed` uses real `threading.Thread` rather than simulating the race. That is the criterion I expected to be fudged.
- Retries are bounded and the bound is explicit, with the comment stating it is a total-attempt bound including the first call — so the constant reads the way it behaves.
- The `retrying` / `succeeded` / `exhausted` outcomes plus the new `worklink_claim_failed` event mean a lost claim is no longer invisible. Previously it produced `attempt None`, no evidence file, and no event.
- Retry cannot double-claim, because the pre-existing "already hold" branch treats a same-agent re-claim as success. Worth noting the new retry path lands safely on machinery that already existed.

---

### 1. The mutex silently disappears when `home_path` is None

`_claim_lock_with_retry` branches:

```python
if home_path is None:
    result = self._run("locks", "claim", str(issue_id), check=False)   # no mutex
else:
    ... flock ... self._run("locks", "claim", ...) ...
```

Production is fine — `orchestrator.py` constructs `ClaimManager(..., home_path=self.home)`, so serialization applies on the real path. But a caller that omits `home_path` gets retry-only protection with **no signal that the mutex was skipped**, and the two paths are indistinguishable in the logs.

That is the same shape as several defects found today: a guard whose protection can lapse quietly. Please either require `home_path` for the claim path, or log/emit when serialization is unavailable so "we were protected" and "we were merely lucky" are distinguishable after the fact. Cheap either way.

### 2. The retry budget may be too small for the contention it is absorbing, and exhaustion still lands in the failure ledger

With `CLAIM_CONTENTION_MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3` and `CLAIM_CONTENTION_INITIAL_BACKOFF_S = 0.1`, total sleep is 0.1 + 0.2 = **0.3 s**. Then `claim_issue` returns `reason="claim_contention_exhausted"`, which is a failed run.

The comment correctly notes the retry exists for callers outside Mimir's mutex — but those are precisely the callers that may hold `index.lock` for a while. The contending operations observed in the run logs were `git reset --hard origin/chainlink/locks` and `git add locks.json`, and the same worktree is also used by `chainlink sync`, which fetches over the network. 0.3 s does not obviously outlast a lock held across a fetch.

I do not know the real hold-time distribution, so I am not asserting the bound is wrong — I am asking for it to be justified or widened. If 0.3 s is deliberate, say so in the comment next to the constant; if it is a placeholder, a second or two of total budget costs nothing on a path that only runs when already contended.

Related, and worth coordinating since both are in flight: PR #1279 adds a durable failure ledger with backoff keyed on error signature. An exhausted contention here still returns a failed status, so it will enter that ledger and earn 15 → 240 minutes of backoff for what began as a sub-second collision. This PR makes that far less likely by absorbing the common case, but it does not remove it — the classification request I

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body: Both items resolved. `worklink_claim_serialization_unavailable` now makes a skipped mutex observable rather than silent, and the retry budget is 5 attempts / 1.5s total with the reasoning stated next to the constant — that answers "justify or widen" in the direction I hoped. Verified in the code at this head, not inferred. CI 7/7.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1063: worklink/opencode: backend-injected model flag duplicates the configured one (opaque CLI crash), and the model actually used is unrecorded

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes for one item — a leak channel. The rest of this PR is the most complete implementation of the three worklink leaves so far.

What lands well:

- `_INJECTED_FLAGS` covers `-m`, `--model` **and** `--dir`, so the check is about every flag the backend injects rather than just the one that broke. `validate_extra_args` also catches the `=` form and the bundled `-mVALUE` short form, and `__post_init__` means it fails at registry construction — which, with #1280's startup and poller-side validation, surfaces before a leaf is consumed.
- The refusal names the offending argument, the injected flag, and the exact fix (`remove it from backends.opencode.args`). An operator can act on it without reading the code.
- The discarded side effect is gone. `model_spec_at_call_time(...)` is now consumed as `dotenv_model_spec`, and `resolution_env.setdefault("MIMIR_MODEL_SPEC", configured_model_spec)` makes resolution explicit instead of depending on a hidden dotenv mutation — that was the subtle half of the original defect and it is properly fixed, not papered over.
- Divergence is both logged and recorded (`worklink_model_divergence`, plus `model` / `configured_model` / `model_diverged` / `model_source` in the backend config), so a silent model substitution can no longer happen unobserved.
- `skip_test_reason="executor exited nonzero before the test gate"` is exactly right. A green test run against an unmodified tree was the most misleading artifact of the original failure, and it is now explicitly not treated as evidence.
- Test names map one-to-one onto the criteria, including `test_executor_crash_skips_gate_and_preserves_stderr_reason` and the parametrized `test_registry_rejects_opencode_injected_flags`. CI green on all seven checks.

---

### Blocking: raw executor stderr is stored and then published, unredacted and unbounded

`failure_reason=raw.error` flows straight from the OpenCode CLI's stderr into three places with no scrubbing and no length limit:

1. the attempt evidence file (`WorklinkEvidence.failure_reason`),
2. `validate_evidence`'s `reasons` — `reasons.append(evidence.failure_reason)`,
3. and from there to the tracker, via `orchestrator.py`:

```python
reasons = f"\nReasons: {', '.join(validation.reasons)}" if validation.reasons else ""
...
"issue", "comment", str(evidence.issue), summary + reasons + tail
```

So a failing executor's stderr is posted as an issue comment. That is the one surface where this matters most, because provider **authentication** failures are exactly the class of error most likely to quote a key, a bearer token, an `Authorization` header fragment, or a URL with an embedded credential — and `opencode.py` already has an `auth_error` status, so authentication failures are a known path into `raw.error`. Add environment fragments and absolute paths and this becomes a durable, published disclosure channel rather than a transient log line.

`#1063`'s review criteria asked specifically to "confirm no credential, token, or provider key reaches the evidence file or the events alongside the model." As written, one can.

The fix is small and already exists in the tree: `mimir/redaction.py` provides `redact_text`, and PR #1279 adds `dispatch_failures.terminal_error()`, which does precisely the right three things — take the last meaningful line, `redact_text` it, and bound it to 1000 characters. Please route `failure_reason` through that same helper rather than a second, differently-behaved treatment of "the executor's terminal error". Two PRs in flight now handle the same concept and only one of them scrubs; they should share one function.

While you are there, bound the length independently of redaction: an unbounded stderr blob in a published comment is a log-size problem even when it contains no secret.

---

### Minor, not blocking

payload.title: Worklink #1062: worklink: an unreferenced stale backend key in worklink.yaml aborts every dispatch; retiring a backend did not migrate the config

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes for one item. Everything else here is right, and two parts are better than the leaf asked for.

What lands well:

- The referenced-vs-unreferenced split is exactly the distinction that matters. `_reject_unknown_references` raises naming the offending setting (`defaults.backend`, `defaults.backend_by_category.<category>`, `routes[<i>].backend`) plus the valid choices, while `_drop_unreferenced_unknown_settings` warns and continues. A typo still fails closed; dead residue no longer kills dispatch.
- Reachability covers all three reference sites, not just `defaults.backend`, which was the gap I was most worried about.
- Compute backends were brought into the same discipline via `SHIPPING_COMPUTE_BACKENDS` instead of being left asymmetric.
- The startup check in `server.py` **warn-and-degrades** — Worklink is disabled, the server still boots, and `worklink_config_invalid` carries a `fix` field. That was an explicit review criterion (a config problem must not prevent the operator from booting in order to fix it) and it is honored precisely.
- The poller-side guard is beyond scope in the good sense: `worklink_poller_misconfigured` and an early return mean a bad config surfaces as a signal *before* a leaf is consumed. Had this existed this morning, the outage would have announced itself instead of appending tracebacks to a run log nobody reads.
- Error text names the file path and the concrete edit in both directions ("change X in <path> to one of: ...", "remove backends.<name> from <path>"). An operator holding a YAML file can act on that.

---

### Blocking: `SHIPPING_BACKENDS` can drift from the registry it describes, and nothing pins them together

`SHIPPING_BACKENDS` is a hardcoded frozenset, while the registry separately builds its dict from literals:

```python
SHIPPING_BACKENDS = frozenset({"feature_factory", "opencode"})
...
self._backends: dict[str, ToolBackend] = {
    "feature_factory": self._build_feature_factory(...),
    "opencode": self._build_opencode(...),
}
```

Consolidating the loader and `BackendRegistry.__init__` onto one constant is a genuine improvement over the two inline sets that existed before. But the constant and the dict are still two independent lists of the same names, and their agreement is not asserted anywhere — I grepped the diff for it.

Both drift directions are live failures:

- A backend added to `_backends` but not to `SHIPPING_BACKENDS`: config that legitimately references it is rejected as "unknown backend" even though the registry supports it.
- A name in `SHIPPING_BACKENDS` that `_backends` does not build: `get()` raises `KeyError` at dispatch instead of at load, which is the late-failure shape this leaf is removing.

That is precisely the defect class the leaf exists to prevent — a guard whose two halves can disagree. Please pin it: derive `SHIPPING_BACKENDS` from the constructed backends (or vice versa), or add a test asserting `set(registry._backends) == SHIPPING_BACKENDS` and the same for compute backends. Cheap, and it makes the invariant enforced rather than remembered.

---

For the record, the three new tests map cleanly onto the criteria (stale-unreferenced warns, every referenced-unknown rejects with path and fix, poller degrades before dispatch), and CI is green on all seven checks including `pytest-enforced`. Once the drift invariant is pinned this is ready.

payload.title: Worklink #1061: worklink: a run that crashes before claiming emits no event and notifies nobody (silent 10-minute crash-loop)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes. This is good work — the durable ledger with an `fcntl.flock` transaction is the right shape for concurrent detached runs, `redact_text` is applied to both the error and the log path, the terminal line is bounded to 1000 chars, `terminal_error` correctly takes `lines[-1]` (which is exactly the useful line for a Python traceback), the dedupe key is a content signature rather than the issue id, backoff is bounded at 240 minutes instead of circuit-breaking, and `attempt_consumed` makes the claim-budget question auditable. CI is green across all seven checks including `pytest-enforced`.

Two things block, and the first is the same class of defect this leaf exists to eliminate.

---

### 1. An alert is marked "notified" before it is emitted, so a lost alert is permanently silent

In `_reconcile_dispatch_failures` the signature is recorded as notified *inside* the transaction:

```python
notified.append(signature)
entry["notified_signatures"] = notified
```

and `failure_state_transaction` persists state in its `finally`. But emission happens **after** the transaction has already returned and saved:

```python
backed_off_ids, failure_alerts = _reconcile_dispatch_failures(state_dir)
for alert in failure_alerts:
    _emit(alert)
```

So if `_emit` raises, or the poller is killed between the state write and the emit, the ledger permanently believes the operator was told. Because dedupe is keyed on `notified_signatures`, that signature will **never** be alerted again — the failure becomes silent forever, which is precisely the outage shape #1061 was filed to fix. The window is small, but the consequence is unbounded and self-concealing.

Mark as notified only after emission succeeds — either emit inside the transaction, or reopen it to record delivery. If a crash must leave *some* inconsistency, prefer duplicating an alert over losing one: a repeated notification is noise, a dropped one is the original bug.

### 2. Transient claim contention now earns exponential backoff (interaction with the locks race)

`record_failure` is reached for any `result.status == "failed"`, including `attempt=None`. That is exactly the shape produced by the Chainlink locks-cache race — two runs dispatched in the same instant collide on git's `index.lock` and the loser dies before it is even assigned an attempt number.

Measured today: #1061 lost that race at 12:30:04 and recovered at the very next scan, 12:40, because the issue kept its `worklink:ready` label. Under this PR the same collision instead sets a 15-minute floor, and since the error text (and therefore the signature) is identical each time, `consecutive` increments and the delay walks 15 → 30 → 60 → 120 → 240 minutes. A sub-second contention that resolves by itself would cost up to four hours.

That race is filed separately (it lives in the third-party `chainlink` binary, reported upstream as dollspace-gay/chainlink#32, with the mimir-side mitigation as its own leaf), so you could not have seen the coupling from this leaf alone — but the two changes land in the same system and the combination is worse than either alone.

Please classify before backing off: git contention signatures (`Unable to create ... index.lock`, `cannot lock ref`, `Could not write new index file`) are transient and should not enter the backoff ledger at all, or should retry immediately rather than accrue `consecutive`. Persistent failures — the `ValueError: unknown Worklink backend config` shape that motivated this leaf — are what the exponential curve is for.

---

### Also worth addressing (not blocking on their own)

- **A manual run cannot clear the ledger.** `_record_run_success` is only called under `elif autonomous and result.status in {"completed", "blocked"}`. An operator who fixes the cause and verifies with a manual run leaves `active: True`, so the poller keeps skipping the issue for the remainder of the backoff. Manual verification is the most likely recovery path after a config-level failure,

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approved on operator sign-off. Both blocking findings from my earlier review are addressed at head 992a1200d, verified against the head content rather than inferred from the commit message:

1. **Notified-before-emitted is fixed.** `notified.append(signature)` inside the state transaction is gone. The flow is now `pending_failure_alerts(state_dir)` → `_emit(alert)` → `mark_failure_notified(...)`, so a crash or failed emit leaves the signature unnotified and it re-fires next poll. That accepts a possible duplicate alert to eliminate a silently-lost one, which is the trade I asked for.

2. **Transient contention no longer enters the backoff ledger.** `_TRANSIENT_CONTENTION_MARKERS` matches `("unable to create", "index.lock")` and `("cannot lock ref",)`, gated by `is_transient_contention` and — a good detail — `attempt is None`, which scopes the exemption to pre-claim failures where contention actually occurs. Transient collisions get `retry_after: None` instead of 15→240 minutes, while persistent failures keep the exponential curve.

CI green on all seven checks. The earlier `pytest (3.11)` failure was `test_run_poller_timeout_kills_child_holding_pipes`, a timing-sensitive subprocess-teardown test unrelated to this change; 3.12 and pytest-enforced passed on the same commit and a re-run went green, so it was flake.

payload.title: Worklink #1060: authz: ifc_label_blocked decisions record no causing source, so interactive taint denials cannot be attributed

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes. The shape is right and the tests are unusually good for this kind of work — all four `ifc_label_blocked:*` reasons are parametrized through the real `authorize_tool` path, redaction and the 1024-byte bound are both asserted (and `redact_payload` correctly runs *before* truncation, so a bisected secret can't slip past the redactor), `same_channel` is proven to skip the first source, and the failure-injection test proves the classifier cannot move a decision. Three things block, and all three are the same underlying issue: **the event asserts a degree of certainty the code hasn't established.**

---

### 1. `ifc_source_scope` always claims `"causing_source"`, including for an arbitrary pick

`_ifc_blocking_source` ends with:

```python
# For other label-gated sinks, any one source is sufficient to introduce
# the label that makes the otherwise-unlabelled flow subject to the gate.
return current.sources[0]
```

but the emission site hardcodes the scope regardless of which branch produced the source:

```python
fields["ifc_source_scope"] = "causing_source"
```

So a denial that reached the fallback reports `sources[0]` — whichever source happens to be first — as the *cause*. #1060's review criteria named this exact failure: "otherwise the audit will attribute denials to whichever source happens to sort first."

The `ifc_source_scope` field is the right idea; it just needs to tell the truth. Have `_ifc_blocking_source` return `(source, scope)` and emit a distinct value (`representative_source`, or similar) for the fallback. Keep `causing_source` for the two branches that genuinely establish causality — the SAME_CHANNEL incompatible-source match and the `UNTRUSTED`/`ACTIVE_INGEST` match. Then a reader knows when they must apply the gate's rule themselves.

### 2. A sourceless denial is indistinguishable from a crashed classifier

The application-egress branch blocks precisely when labels exist and sources do **not**:

```python
if is_application_egress and ifc_labels.labels and not ifc_labels.sources:
    ... reason=f"ifc_label_blocked:{sink_category.value}"
```

`_ifc_blocking_source` returns `None` on `not current.sources`, so `ifc_source` is omitted. But the `except` branch *also* omits it — this PR's own test asserts exactly that:

```python
assert "ifc_source" not in captured[0]
```

Two entirely different situations therefore produce byte-identical events: "the block was caused by labels carrying no sources" and "classification threw." That leaves `NETWORK` / `HTTP_WEBHOOK` / `EXTERNAL_MCP` egress denials unclassifiable from the event alone, which is criterion 1 unmet for a real production class, and it reintroduces the ambiguity #1056 existed to remove.

Emit an explicit scope for each case — e.g. `no_sources` when labels are present but `sources` is empty, and `classification_failed` in the `except` branch. Then *every* `ifc_label_blocked` event is classifiable without replaying the gate.

### 3. The SAME_CHANNEL rule is a second copy of `_get_allowed_sinks`

`_ifc_blocking_source`'s SAME_CHANNEL branch reimplements the per-source compatibility rule that `_get_allowed_sinks` (defined line 3770) owns in its loop at 3912+ — `is_complete`, `effective_principal not in source.authorized_principals`, the `channel` / `service` / `protected_prompt` kind handling, and the `_resolve_channel` comparison.

Two copies of a security-adjacent predicate will drift. When they do, the failure is not a missing field: the event still asserts `causing_source` and names the **wrong** source. A confidently mislabeled audit is worse than an absent one, because it will be believed.

`_get_allowed_sinks` returns `frozenset()` on its first failing source, so it can't name the offender as written — but that's an argument for extracting a per-source predicate both call sites share, not for maintaining a parallel copy. Please extract it and have both use it.

Related and folded in here: the emission site derives the branch from `get_s

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
All three items resolved, and the third one properly rather than superficially.

1. Scope is now truthful — `causing_source` / `representative_source` / `no_sources` — so the event no longer claims certainty the code has not established.
2. `classification_failed` in the `except` branch means a crashed classifier is finally distinguishable from a labels-without-sources denial. That was the ambiguity #1056 existed to remove.
3. The SAME_CHANNEL predicate is genuinely extracted: `_source_is_triggering_channel_compatible` is defined once and called from **both** `_ifc_blocking_source` and `_get_allowed_sinks`, so the two copies can no longer drift into confidently naming the wrong source.

The folded-in sub-item is handled too, and better than I asked: the emission site now takes the category the gate used and raises `ValueError("IFC sink category was not supplied by gate")` rather than falling back to re-deriving it. Failing closed there is the right instinct. CI 7/7.

payload.title: Worklink #1058: authz: read_scope denials record no target, so the class cannot be diagnosed from events

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The design is right on both points I cared about. Blocking on a failing test — and it is the case this leaf exists to fix.

**Blocking — CI is red and the failure reproduces on the branch alone**

```
pytest (3.11): FAILURE   pytest (3.12): FAILURE   pytest-enforced: FAILURE
```

`test_shadow_denial_records_bounded_redacted_requested_target[read_file-arguments0-...-read_scope]` fails. I checked whether this was a merge interaction and it is not: standalone on `96cf1c9c4` it is `1 failed, 1 passed`, and on the tree merged with `main` it is the same single failure in both enforcement modes (7426 passed, 1 failed).

The failing assertion is:

```python
assert "/outside?token=[REDACTED]&part=" in str(fields["target"])
```

and the parametrisation sets `target_channel=(requested_target if reason == "admin_required" else None)` — so for the `read_scope` case `target_channel` is `None` and the value has to come from `arguments`. Meanwhile the implementation populates

```python
"target": redacted_resolved_target,
"requested_target": redacted_requested_target,
```

So `target` carries the *resolved* path while the redacted *request* lands in `requested_target`. Either the assertion is checking the wrong field, or resolution legitimately cannot preserve a query string like `?token=…&part=…` and the test's expectation is wrong for the `read_scope` parameter. Worth deciding which, because the answer determines the contract: if `target` is always the resolved path, then an unresolvable request has no `target` and the auditor must read `requested_target` — which is fine, but the test should say so.

This is the `read_file` + `read_scope` combination, which is exactly the class the leaf was filed for (13 of the 15 audit denials were github-activity `ls`/`read_file`/`glob`/`file_search`), so it is the one case that most needs to work.

**What verifies clean**

- Both values are captured, not just one. `requested_read_target_from_arguments` and `resolved_read_target_from_arguments` are distinct, and the event carries both — which was my review criterion, since logging only the model-supplied string would have reproduced the current ambiguity in longer form.
- Redaction reuses `redact_payload` rather than inventing a second policy, and the length is bounded by `_MAX_REQUESTED_TARGET_LENGTH`. The parametrised test proves a secret embedded in a path is redacted rather than logged, which was the disclosure-channel concern I asked to be weighed deliberately.
- `test_read_scope_audit_resolution_failure_cannot_change_live_decision` covers the criterion that this is observability only — a resolution failure in the audit path must not alter an authorization outcome. That is the right shape: proven by test rather than asserted in a comment.
- Tool coverage is there: `read_file`/`aread`, `ls`/`als`/`glob`/`aglob`/`grep`/`agrep`, `file_search` (with its `path_prefix`/`scope` distinction), and `get_turn`.
- The comment on `requested_target` — "Caller input is evidence only. It is never resolved, compared with policy, or fed back into an authorization decision" — is the correct invariant and worth keeping.

**One criterion of mine that is not buildable, and I am withdrawing it.** I required "re-run the audit and state whether the virtual-path hypothesis holds." That needs the change running in the deployment to produce events, so a sandboxed build cannot do it — the same mistake I made on #1054's measurement and #1049's live canary. It moves to a post-deploy step; I will run it against real events once these merges are deployed, and it is the thing that finally answers whether `/state/...` versus `/mimir-home/state/...` is the cause.

Fix the failing parameter and this is ready.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Still blocking — CI is red on all three pytest jobs, and the fix changed the symptom rather than resolving the contract question.

The caller-spelling assertion moved to `requested_target`, which is correct and the accompanying comment states the contract well. But the replacement assertion on the resolved field now fails:

```
>   assert fields["target"] is not None
E   assert None is not None
```

reproduced locally on `ecac7f2d9`: `1 failed, 8 passed` for the `read_file` + `read_scope` parameter.

So for this case the resolved `target` is genuinely `None`. That is presumably *why* the original assertion could not find the redacted path in it — resolution produces nothing for a request that lies outside the read roots, which is exactly the class of request that gets denied with `read_scope`.

This is worth a design answer rather than another assertion swap, because it goes to the leaf's purpose. #1058 exists so that a `read_scope` denial is classifiable from the event alone. If `target` is `None` precisely for unresolvable requests, then the resolved field is empty in the case that matters most, and the diagnosis rests entirely on `requested_target`.

Two coherent resolutions:

1. **Make resolution produce something for an out-of-roots path** — the normalised absolute path it *would* have been, distinct from "resolves inside a permitted root". Then `target` is populated for every denial and the assertion holds as written. This gives an auditor both halves: what was asked for, and where the server placed it before refusing.
2. **Accept that `target` may be `None`** and say so. Change the assertion to `fields["target"] is None` for the `read_scope` parameter, document that an unresolvable request records only `requested_target`, and make sure the audit story still works — because the acceptance criterion is that the class is classifiable from the event, and "requested a path outside the roots" is a classification.

Either is fine. What is not fine is asserting `target` is populated when the code returns `None`, since that is the current state and it is red.

If you take (2), note the criterion I wrote asks the event to "distinguish what the model asked for from what the server resolved it to" — `None` *is* a meaningful distinction there, so (2) satisfies it, but only once the contract is written down and the test matches.

Everything else from my previous review still stands: both values captured, `redact_payload` reused with a bounded length, the redaction proven by test, `test_read_scope_audit_resolution_failure_cannot_change_live_decision` covering decision-invariance, and full tool coverage including `file_search`'s `path_prefix`/`scope` split.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The contract question is settled properly rather than by another assertion swap.

**The resolution.** `requested_target` always carries the caller spelling, redacted and bounded. `target` carries the server-resolved path and is `None` only when a request genuinely cannot resolve — which is why the original assertion could never find `/outside?token=…` in it. The comment states this, and the tests now pin both halves rather than conflating them.

The assertion that matters most for the leaf's purpose:

```python
assert event["requested_target"] == requested_suffix
assert event["target"] == str(home / resolved_suffix)
```

That is the virtual-path question made answerable: a request spelled one way, recorded alongside the home-mapped path the server actually resolved. Once deployed, that pair is what will finally show whether `/state/...` versus `/mimir-home/state/...` explains the 15 `read_scope` denials from the audit — which no amount of replaying the gate could tell us.

**Verification.** Rebased onto current `main` (an ancestor), merges cleanly with 0 conflicts, all six CI checks green, and **7508 passed / 18 skipped** locally both unenforced and with `MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED=1`.

Two mutations, both caught:

- Replacing `"target": redacted_resolved_target` with `None` fails 5 tests, including `test_read_scope_shadow_event_records_requested_and_resolved_target_via_middleware` parametrised over `grep` and `file_search`. So the resolved-target recording is pinned across tools, not just for `read_file`.
- Replacing `redact_payload(requested_target)` with the raw value fails 2 tests, including the secret-bearing path case. So the redaction is enforced, not incidental.

Carried over from earlier rounds and still true: both values captured rather than only the model-supplied string, bounded length, full tool coverage including `file_search`'s `path_prefix`/`scope` split, and `test_read_scope_audit_resolution_failure_cannot_change_live_decision` proving this is observability-only by test rather than by comment.

One criterion of mine I withdrew earlier and am not holding against this: "re-run the audit and state whether the virtual-path hypothesis holds" needs the change running, so it moved to a post-deploy step. I will run it against live events once this is deployed.

Merging.

payload.title: Worklink #1056: authz: tracker read surface is incomplete (issue tree refused); enumerate it against the CLI help

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The classification work is careful and correct. Two blocking items, and both are the same shape: a guard that looks present but cannot fire.

**Blocking 1 — the CLI-help audit test skips everywhere, including CI**

`_chainlink_help_commands` calls `shutil.which("chainlink")` and skips when it is absent. That helper is the mechanism behind criterion 3 -- "a test enumerates the admitted read set explicitly, so adding a subcommand to the CLI without considering it shows up as a failing assertion rather than a silent refusal."

It does not run:

```
local:  7460 passed, 18 skipped   ->  SKIPPED tests/test_access_control.py:4948: chainlink CLI is not installed
CI:     7468 passed, 18 skipped   ->  same count, and .github/workflows/tests.yml installs no chainlink
```

The skip counts match exactly and the workflow has no install step, so the audit never executes in either place. The leaf's central drift-detection mechanism is inert -- which is the same failure I flagged on #1266 (tests that never went through `.invoke()`) and #1271 (a rejection test that passed vacuously once nothing was declared).

Two ways to fix it and I would take the first: install `chainlink` in the test workflow, since detecting real upstream CLI drift is the entire point and a live `--help` parse is what does that. Failing that, check in a fixture of the help output and assert against it, plus an opt-in live test -- weaker, because a refreshed fixture is a human step, but at least it runs.

**Blocking 2 — misclassifying a mutation as a query is not caught**

Adding `relate` to `_CHAINLINK_QUERY_SUBCOMMANDS` leaves **656 passed, 2 skipped**. Nothing fails.

That is the dangerous direction. #1052 downgrades a tainted turn to queries only, so a mutation sitting in the query set becomes reachable on a turn carrying untrusted ingest -- exactly the self-dispatch-adjacent hole #1052 exists to close. The current tests pin that queries stay available and that `delete`/`close-all`/`init`/`locks` are refused, but not that every admitted mutation is *classified* as a mutation.

Please assert the partition directly: every name in `_CHAINLINK_MUTATION_SUBCOMMANDS` must classify as a mutation, and the two sets must be disjoint. Then moving a name across the boundary fails.

**What verifies clean**

I checked each newly admitted subcommand against the CLI's own help rather than its name, which was the review criterion:

```
related   List related issues
cascade   Show falsification cascade -- what breaks if this assumption is wrong
next      Suggest the next issue to work on
tree      Show issues as a tree hierarchy
```

All four are reads. I had specifically suspected `cascade` (could have applied a cascade) and `next` (could have claimed the next item); both are display-only, so the suspicion was unfounded.

The two-character trap is handled correctly, and this is the part I was most worried about:

```
chainlink issue related 1056        ADMIT  query
chainlink issue relate 1056 1040    ADMIT  mutation
chainlink issue unrelate 1056 1040  ADMIT  mutation
chainlink issue delete 1056         REFUSE
```

`related` is a query while `relate` remains a mutation, so #1051's boundary and #1052's downgrade both stay intact. Arities match the help too -- `show`/`related`/`cascade` share the one-ID shape, and `tree` correctly accepts both `tree` and `tree <id>`.

Suite: 7460 passed / 18 skipped locally, unenforced and with `MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED=1`; CI green. The refusal-hint text was updated to name the new queries, so a near-miss still self-corrects.

Once the audit test actually runs and the partition is asserted, this is ready.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The audit earned its keep on its first real run, which is the best possible outcome for this leaf. Two items before merge, plus one finding that belongs elsewhere.

**Both of my previous blocking items are fixed.** The dedicated `chainlink-cli-audit` job is a better structure than what I suggested — a cargo build in a separate job rather than slowing both pytest matrices. And the partition is now pinned: adding `relate` to `_CHAINLINK_QUERY_SUBCOMMANDS` fails `test_chainlink_query_and_mutation_subcommands_are_disjoint`, where before it left 656 tests passing. All six pytest/frontend/skill jobs are green.

**Blocking 1 — the audit found real drift, so finish the decision it is asking for**

`test_chainlink_top_level_help_has_an_explicit_scope_decision` fails because the CLI exposes two top-level commands with no explicit classification:

```
Extra items in the left set: 'cascade', 'falsify'
```

These are not phantoms of the CI pin — the running container has them too:

```
cascade   Show falsification cascade — what breaks if this assumption is wrong
falsify   Mark an assumption as falsified and propagate to downstream issues
```

`falsify` is a **mutation**, and a propagating one. It is currently refused only by accident: top-level commands are not among the admitted shapes, so it falls through. That is exactly the difference this test exists to expose — refused-by-omission versus refused-by-decision. Please classify both explicitly: top-level `cascade` is a read and can be admitted or excluded with a reason, and `falsify` should be excluded with its propagation named, alongside `delete`/`close-all`/`init`/`locks`.

Note there are now two `cascade` surfaces — `issue cascade <id>`, which this PR admits as a query, and top-level `cascade`. Worth confirming they are the same read and that admitting one does not imply the other.

**Blocking 2 — rebase.** `DIRTY` after #1275 landed. It is the trivial import-block collision in `tests/test_access_control.py` I flagged; keep both sides' imports.

**Separate finding, not for this PR: CI audits a different CLI than production runs.**

Three sources agree on the pin and the deployment does not:

```
tool_pins.py  pin="chainlink-1.6.0"
dockerfile.fragment  --tag chainlink-1.6.0
CI (this PR)  --tag chainlink-1.6.0
container     chainlink 0.2.0+9909d7e-dirty
```

The running binary was built from a dirty working tree at 0.2.0, not from the pinned tag. So the audit's guarantee — "upstream command drift cannot silently widen or break the service allowlist" — holds against 1.6.0 while the agent executes against 0.2.0. The two happen to agree about `cascade` and `falsify`, but nothing enforces that.

That is a deployment/tool-pin problem rather than a defect in this change, and it is precisely what the tool-pin drift poller exists to catch, so I am not blocking on it. I will file it separately unless you would rather fold it in. It also means the container should be brought to the pinned tag as part of the next rebuild, since `smoke="chainlink --version && chainlink issue ready"` would currently report a version the inventory does not expect.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving. The audit found real drift on its first run and the response was to make the decision explicit rather than to loosen the test — which is the right instinct.

**Both blocking items resolved.** Rebased (`origin/main` is an ancestor), and all seven checks green including `chainlink-cli-audit`.

**The classification is more complete than I asked for.** `_CHAINLINK_REFUSED_TOP_LEVEL_COMMANDS` now records a reason for every top-level root, not just the two the audit caught:

```
cascade  "use the bounded issue cascade form"
falsify  "dependency mutation"
tested   "test-reminder mutation"
export   "bulk serialization with a filesystem output option"
locks    "Worklink-owned coordination lifecycle"
sync     "coordination fetch and local lock-state update"
...
```

Two things I want to note. `tested` is one I had not spotted, so the audit surfaced more than my manual read of `--help` did. And `export` being called out for its "filesystem output option" is the kind of reasoning I would have missed entirely — a read-sounding command that can write files.

The comment states the principle precisely: these roots are recorded "so a CLI addition cannot disappear into a silent refusal." That is the refused-by-decision versus refused-by-omission distinction, which was the whole point.

**My question about the double surface is answered directly**: top-level `cascade` is refused *in favour of* `issue cascade <id>`, so admitting the bounded form does not imply the unbounded one.

**Verification.** 7502 passed / 18 skipped locally, unenforced and with `MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED=1`. The partition guard bites — adding `relate` to the query set fails `test_chainlink_query_and_mutation_subcommands_are_disjoint`.

One honest limit on my own checking: I tried to mutate the refusal set by deleting `falsify`, and locally that left 238 passed / **2 skipped** — the audit tests skip on my machine because chainlink is not installed there. So I could not verify that mutation myself; the guard lives in the `chainlink-cli-audit` job. The stronger evidence is empirical rather than mutational: that job *failed* on genuine drift and passes now that the drift is classified. A test that has already caught a real regression is better evidence than one I have only broken artificially.

**Separate finding I raised and am not blocking on**: the container runs `chainlink 0.2.0+9909d7e-dirty` while `tool_pins.py`, `dockerfile.fragment`, and this CI job all pin `chainlink-1.6.0`. So the audit's guarantee holds against a CLI the agent does not currently execute. They agree about `cascade`/`falsify`, but nothing enforces that. Worth resolving on the next rebuild.
