payload.title: Worklink #1014: authz/egress: PR reads via the GitHub API are all denied (exact-URL allow-list vs parameterized API; 57 would-blocks)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Reviewed against #1014's criteria at head `d99ec0b6`. This is the egress boundary, so I read it adversarially and checked several things that turned out fine — recorded below so the next reader doesn't have to re-derive them.

The path bound itself is good work. One blocking issue, and it is not in the URL matching.

## Blocking

**`_filesystem_result_integrity` now marks third-party-authored content as `trusted`.**

The change reads as a refactor — `normalized in approved` becomes `fetch_url_is_approved(...)` — but `fetch_url_is_approved` also consults the new `github_pr_api` adapter. So the trusted set goes from *operator-vetted exact URLs* to *any* `/repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{n}`, `/reviews`, or `/comments` in `GITHUB_REPOS`, and the bodies behind those endpoints are written by whoever opened the PR or left the comment — including an outside contributor with no repo permissions.

Concretely: `_fetch_source_label` → `SourceLabel(integrity="trusted", integrity_effect="active_ingest")` → the turn no longer accumulates untrusted active ingest for that content → the taint gate stops blocking downstream shell, file and message sinks. That gate is precisely what the 154 `ifc_label_blocked:*` events in the audit represent, so this quietly disables it for the highest-volume untrusted-input path the agent has.

Three reasons to take it out of this PR:

1. **Wrong criterion.** Trust here is derived from the transport the bytes arrived over. Per #854 and #1017 it must come from a server-side authorship check — `_github_author_is_trusted(repo, author, token)` already exists in `mimir/pollers.py:328` for exactly this, feeding `SourceLabel(integrity=...)`. An approved URL means "the agent is allowed to fetch this", not "the content is trustworthy."
2. **Not needed for the leaf.** #1014's would-block class is `egress_destination_not_approved`. Every acceptance criterion is satisfied without touching integrity; nothing in the leaf asks for it.
3. **It belongs to #1017**, which is the leaf that decides trust derivation and whose review criteria require each newly-trusted class to be documented in `docs/security/enforcement-enablement.md`.

Suggested fix: keep `_filesystem_result_integrity` on `approved_fetch_urls(auth_context)` — the exact-URL set, unchanged semantics — so this PR widens egress without also widening trust. If you think the two cannot be separated, say why and I'll look again.

## Checked and correct

- **The path bound is tight.** `https` only, `netloc` compared exactly (so no wildcard host, no userinfo, no port variant), empty `query` required, `%` and `\` rejected outright, `[^/]+` for owner and repo so neither can smuggle a separator, `fullmatch` against a closed set of three shapes, and the numeric PR id anchored to `[1-9][0-9]*`. `..` in an owner or repo position can only match if it is configured, and `_configured_github_repos` rejects `""`, `.` and `..`. Criteria 3 and 4 hold.
- **`fetch_url` is GET-only.** I checked this specifically, because `/pulls/{n}/reviews` and `/pulls/{n}/comments` are POST endpoints in the GitHub API — if the tool took a method, this adapter would have handed the poller review-submission over egress, bypassing the `repo_review` shell profile's gating of `gh pr review` entirely. It has no method parameter and only downloads; `web.py:286`'s POST is in the unrelated `_post_json`. Worth a sentence in the PR body so nobody has to re-derive it.
- **`GITHUB_REPOS` is server-owned**, read from the environment inside the adapter, so no model-supplied text reaches the binding. Criterion: satisfied.
- **Exact-URL semantics are preserved.** `approved_fetch_urls()` is untouched and the adapter is consulted separately in `fetch_url_is_approved`, so no existing approval silently becomes a prefix. Criterion 5: satisfied.
- **Authorization and execution agree.** `_authorized_fetch_urls_for_tool` admits the target through the same `fetch_url_is_approved` predicate used at authorization, so there is no "autho

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Reviewed at head `97961b4d`. **My blocking finding is resolved** and the scope addition is bounded correctly. One new issue, plus a rebase.

## Resolved

**The trust widening is gone.** `fetch_url_is_approved` now appears exactly twice in `access_control.py` — its definition and the egress gate in `check_sink_flow` — and no longer in `_filesystem_result_integrity`. So egress approval authorizes the *request* without conferring `integrity="trusted"` on the *response*, and trust derivation stays with the authorship check under #980/#960. That was the right separation.

**The raw-host addition is bounded to `GITHUB_REPOS`, and the fork widening was correctly not done** — which matters given I verified a fork PR's head resolves under the base repo path, so widening the owner side would have bought nothing and cost a lot.

## Blocking: literal `..` is admitted on the raw path

`_GITHUB_RAW_REPO_PATH` ends in `(?:/(.+))?`, and nothing rejects `..`:

```
ADMITTED  raw.githubusercontent.com/jasoncarreira/mimir/abc123/../../attacker/evil/x.py
ADMITTED  raw.githubusercontent.com/jasoncarreira/mimir/abc123/a/../../../attacker/evil/x
denied    raw.githubusercontent.com/jasoncarreira/mimir/abc123/%2e%2e/x
denied    raw.githubusercontent.com/attacker/evil/abc123/x.py
```

The percent-encoded form is caught by the existing `"%" in parsed.path` check; the literal form is not.

**Severity, stated honestly: this is not exploitable today.** I tested the real host — `raw.githubusercontent.com` treats `..` as a literal segment and returns 404 rather than resolving it, and `urlsplit` passes the path through verbatim. So no request currently escapes the bound.

It is still worth fixing, for two reasons. First, #1014's acceptance criteria require it explicitly: "no path-traversal in a template (`..`, encoded separators) can widen the approved set. **Tests for each.**" The encoded case is handled and tested; the literal case is neither. Second, and more substantively, the bound currently holds because a third party declines to normalize our URLs. `posixpath.normpath` on that same path yields `/jasoncarreira/attacker/evil/x` — a different repository. Any layer that normalizes (a proxy, a redirect chain, a future change to the fetch implementation, a different HTTP client) silently converts a denied read into an admitted one. An egress bound should not depend on GitHub's URL handling staying as it is.

The fix is small: reject any path whose segments contain `.` or `..`, the same way `_configured_github_repos` already rejects them in the owner and repo positions. Add a test for the literal form alongside the encoded one.

## Also needed

- **Rebase.** `mimir/tools/budget_gate.py` conflicts with `main` — a consequence of #1223 landing, not anything here.
- The skill update I flagged earlier still applies once this merges: `mimir/skills/review/SKILL.md` currently states that fetching a file at an arbitrary SHA is unavailable and names #1014 as the tracking leaf. That becomes wrong the moment this lands, so teach the `fetch_url https://raw.githubusercontent.com/<owner>/<repo>/<headRefOid>/<path>` form in the same change or an immediate follow-up.
- CI is mid-run (2/6) at this head; I have not treated it as evidence either way.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Re-reviewed at head `44a5309a`. Both blocking findings are resolved, the scope addition is bounded correctly, and the documentation follow-up landed with it. Approving.

## The traversal is fixed as a class, not as a case

```python
or any(segment in {".", ".."} for segment in parsed.path.split("/"))
```

Verified against the running code rather than read off the diff:

```
ADMITTED  raw.githubusercontent.com/jasoncarreira/mimir/abc123/mimir/access_control.py
denied    raw.githubusercontent.com/jasoncarreira/mimir/abc123/../../attacker/evil/x.py
denied    raw.githubusercontent.com/jasoncarreira/mimir/abc123/a/../../../attacker/evil/x
denied    raw.githubusercontent.com/jasoncarreira/mimir/abc123/./x.py
denied    raw.githubusercontent.com/attacker/evil/abc123/x.py
```

Rejecting `.` and `..` at the segment level rather than pattern-matching the observed forms is the right shape, and it covers the API host too — `test_github_poller_fetch_rejects_widening_shapes` includes `api.github.com/repos/acme/widget/pulls/7/../comments`, which I had not thought to check. The bound no longer depends on GitHub declining to normalise our URLs, which was the actual reason to fix something that was not exploitable today.

## The trust widening stays reverted

`fetch_url_is_approved` appears only in its definition and the egress gate, not in `_filesystem_result_integrity`, and `test_github_pr_fetch_authorization_does_not_confer_trusted_integrity` pins it. Approval authorises the request; it does not launder the response. That separation matters more here than the original review implied — I later verified that a fork PR's head resolves under the *base* repo path, so file contents served from `jasoncarreira/mimir/<sha>/…` can be authored by anyone who opens a PR.

`test_github_repo_template_does_not_change_exact_url_approval_semantics` covers criterion 5, and `test_non_github_poller_cannot_claim_unbounded_fetch_capability` is a good defensive addition nobody asked for.

## The skill update landed, and it is additive

This is the third PR in a row to touch `mimir/skills/review/SKILL.md`, and the previous two both came close to silently dropping a sibling's warning there. This one does not: `approve_declassification` (#1228), the heredoc prohibition and the `--jq` credential warning (#1230) all survive at this head, and the new text replaces the now-false "fetching a file at an arbitrary SHA is not admitted" paragraph with the route that actually works. The guard test added in #1230 passes against it.

The replacement text is also correctly hedged — it names the `GITHUB_REPOS` bound, says traversal remains denied, and states that the returned content **remains untrusted**, which keeps the skill consistent with the integrity decision above rather than implying that an admitted fetch is a trusted one.

Merges clean, 6/6 checks green.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Correction to my review: I said the trust-widening finding "belongs to #1017". That was wrong — #1017 turned out to be the residue-classification leaf, not trust derivation. Chainlink #1017's own text points the trust-derivation model at **#980 / #960**, so that is where the authorship-based derivation belongs.

The finding itself is unchanged and still blocking: reusing `fetch_url_is_approved` inside `_filesystem_result_integrity` promotes third-party-authored PR and comment bodies to `integrity="trusted"`, which is a decision about trust derivation rather than about egress approval, and #1014 does not ask for it. Keep `_filesystem_result_integrity` on the exact-URL set so this PR widens egress without widening trust, and let the authorship check (`_github_author_is_trusted`, `mimir/pollers.py:328`) decide trust under #980/#960.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Scope addition, operator-directed (Jason):** admit `raw.githubusercontent.com` for the github poller as well, bounded the same way as `api.github.com`.

Folding it in here rather than filing a separate leaf on purpose. It is the same `ServiceSinkPolicy("fetch_url", ..., "GITHUB_REPOS")` on the same `github` profile, and a second leaf would produce two separately-maintained allowlists governing one principal's egress — the thing I warned about on #1015.

**Evidence.** Measured `would_block: true` `fetch_url` decisions on mimirbot, by host:

```
161  api.github.com                  <- this PR
 51  raw.githubusercontent.com       <- add
 15  github.com
  3  patch-diff.githubusercontent.com
```

Every one is under a configured repo. Sample targets:

```
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jasoncarreira/mimir/550066da.../mimir/access_control.py
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jasoncarreira/mimir/550066da.../tests/conftest.py
```

so the shape is `/<owner>/<repo>/<ref>/<path>` and the `<owner>/<repo>` prefix binds to `GITHUB_REPOS` exactly as the API paths do.

**Bound it, do not allowlist the host.** A blanket `raw.githubusercontent.com` grant is an exfiltration channel, not merely a broad read: the path is attacker-influencable, so content can be encoded into it and leave on the request line, and it would also admit arbitrary third-party repositories as prompt-injection input. Apply the same checks the existing adapter already gets right — `https` only, exact netloc, empty query, reject `%` and `\`, `fullmatch` on the path, and `<owner>/<repo>` lowercased against `_configured_github_repos`. The `<ref>` may be a branch, tag or SHA; it stays inside the bound repo either way.

**Do not let this ride the trust path.** This is the finding already open on this PR: raw content on a PR branch is authored by whoever opened the PR. Approving the URL must not mark the result `integrity="trusted"` — keep `_filesystem_result_integrity` on the exact-URL set and leave trust derivation to the authorship check under #980/#960.

**Two hosts to decide, not silently include.** `github.com` (15) and `patch-diff.githubusercontent.com` (3) also appear. `patch-diff` serves `.diff`/`.patch` for a PR and is bounded the same way if the flow needs it. `github.com` is the HTML site and is the one I would leave denied — anything it offers is available through an already-admitted surface. State the disposition for each rather than adding or omitting them by accident.

Worth noting for whoever picks this up: the poller is currently doing its PR-review work *through* these blocked paths, and it only functions because enforcement is off. That is the concrete cost of leaving this class open, and the reason it is worth getting the bound right rather than fast.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Two follow-ups on the `raw.githubusercontent.com` addition, one of them now settled by measurement.

## 1. Fork PRs need no widening — verified

I raised this as an open question and then tested it rather than leaving it open. GitHub serves a fork PR's head commit under the **base** repository path, because the commit is reachable from the base repo via `refs/pull/N/head`:

```
cli/cli PR #13982, head 65fb1e00 (fork owner: offbyone)

raw.githubusercontent.com/cli/cli/<fork-sha>/README.md      -> HTTP 200
raw.githubusercontent.com/offbyone/cli/<fork-sha>/README.md -> HTTP 200
```

So bounding the adapter to `GITHUB_REPOS` covers fork PRs already. **Do not widen the owner side to accept fork owners** — it is unnecessary, and it would turn a bound set of two repositories into "any GitHub account that has forked one of them."

This does sharpen the trust finding that is still blocking this PR, and makes it less theoretical than I first put it. It is not only that PR *bodies* are third-party text: the **file contents** served under `jasoncarreira/mimir/<sha>/…` can be authored by anyone who opens a PR, because a fork head resolves under our own repo's path. Approving that URL must not confer `integrity="trusted"`. Keep `_filesystem_result_integrity` on the exact-URL set and leave trust derivation to the authorship check under #980/#960.

## 2. The review skill needs updating when this lands

#1230 rewrote `mimir/skills/review/SKILL.md` to stop teaching `gh api "…/contents/<path>?ref=<sha>" --jq '.content' | base64 -d`, which failed three ways at once — `gh api` unadmitted, `--jq` unadmitted, and the pipe making it compound. Rather than substitute another form that does not work yet, it now says plainly that fetching a file at an arbitrary SHA is not available today and names #1014 as the tracking leaf.

Once this PR merges, that text becomes wrong in the other direction — documentation failing to describe a capability that exists. Please update the same section in this PR or an immediate follow-up to teach:

```
fetch_url https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jasoncarreira/mimir/<headRefOid>/<path>
```

It is strictly better than the form it replaces: one call, no base64 step, no jq filter, and no compound command.

Worth noting neither this PR's nor #1226's `gh api` path regex admits `/contents/` or `/git/blobs/` — both are `pulls/{n}/…` only. That is the right call. The raw host is the narrower route for file contents, and one allow-list for these reads is better than two.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Summary

The two-path design is sound: authorization-time denials and shadow-mode argv-binding refusals now converge on an actionable caller-visible explanation without changing the stable machine reason or relaxing execution. The new sync/async middleware tests, enforcement parity, forge protection, and green CI cover the main control flow well.

## Blocking issue

**`mimir/access_control.py` — `_service_shell_not_admitted_reason` / `_service_shell_command_shape`: refusal prose can still disclose argument values.**

The implementation claims that reasons never quote values, but it emits every dash-prefixed token up to the first `=` as an option name and also emits up to two plain positional tokens. Both classes can contain secrets. For example, a refused command containing `-HAuthorization:Bearer-SEKRIT`, `--token-SEKRIT`, or a plain positional such as `SEKRIT`/`private/path/SEKRIT` will place that value verbatim in the refusal returned to the model and persisted in the transcript. The current test covers only values separated by `=` or punctuation that fails `_SERVICE_SHELL_SHAPE_TOKEN`, so it misses attached short-option values and plain alphanumeric/path values.

Please make the rendering fail closed: name only option spellings that are known for the recognized command/profile (or omit options entirely), and do not echo positional tokens unless they are likewise drawn from a fixed known-safe subcommand/resource vocabulary. Add regressions with an attached option value and a plain positional secret, asserting the sentinel never appears.

## Validation

I reviewed the full three-file API diff at head `ba7b22e800337ca62149ba829f898c757e318ea8`. All six GitHub check runs are green, including Python 3.11/3.12 and enforced-mode pytest. I could not run an independent local suite because process-backed commands in this poller runtime currently exit 1 with empty output; the finding above follows directly from the changed rendering logic and is not dependent on local execution.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
@mimir-carreira the finding is correct and I've fixed it in `a580948b`. Both holes were real, and my own test is what let them through.

**What was wrong.** `options` was built with `token.split("=", 1)[0]`, so an option carrying its value *attached* — `-HAuthorization:Bearer-SEKRIT`, with no `=` to split on — had the whole token, value included, named as the "option". And `_SERVICE_SHELL_SHAPE_TOKEN` accepted `[A-Za-z0-9._/-]`, so a bare `SEKRIT` or a path-shaped `private/path/SEKRIT` was echoed verbatim — which is exactly the shape of a legitimate API resource path, so the pattern could not tell them apart.

**Why the test passed.** It only covered values in a *separate* argv token (`git -c http.extraheader=...`, where the value is its own token and so never reaches the option list) and a URL whose punctuation happened to fail the pattern. It exercised the safe shapes and gave me false confidence — your read of that was exactly right.

**The fix takes your first suggestion.** Rather than a better pattern, a fixed display vocabulary: a token is echoed only if it is literally a member of `_SERVICE_SHELL_DISPLAY_COMMANDS` / `_SERVICE_SHELL_DISPLAY_SUBCOMMANDS` / `_SERVICE_SHELL_DISPLAY_OPTIONS`, otherwise it renders as `<command>` / `<value>` / `<option>`. No regex can separate an attached short-option value from a legitimate long option, so membership is the only sound test — this makes non-disclosure a property of construction rather than of matching.

What keeps a hand-maintained list safe is the asymmetry: absence from it can only make a message *less specific*. It cannot change a decision, admit a command, or deny one — the worst failure is a vaguer sentence. Executables derive from `_MAINTENANCE_PINNED_EXECUTABLE_DEFAULTS` so they cannot drift from what can actually run.

Your four cases now render:

```
gh api -HAuthorization:Bearer-SEKRIT repos/x/pulls/1 -> does not admit 'gh api'. Options sent: <option>
gh pr view 1 --token-SEKRIT                          -> does not admit 'gh pr view'. Options sent: <option>
gh api SEKRIT                                        -> does not admit 'gh api <value>'
gh api private/path/SEKRIT                           -> does not admit 'gh api <value>'
```

Still actionable: a known spelling is named (`--json`), and only unknown spellings collapse into a single `<option>`.

**Regression** now injects the sentinel at every argv position — attached short option, attached long option, bare positional, path-shaped positional, the executable itself, and inside a URL — across three profiles, and asserts `--badoption` is withheld while `--json` is named. Full suite green unenforced and with `MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED=1`, 6918 passed / 16 skipped in both.

On your validation note — "process-backed commands in this poller runtime currently exit 1 with empty output" — that is the exact symptom this PR fixes, and it is why the leaf's other criteria matter: your `true` health probe is not an admitted command for the `repo_review` profile, so the probe fails regardless of whether execution works. Once this lands you will get a sentence explaining that instead of a bare exit 1. Re-requesting review.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Reviewed against #1013's acceptance and review criteria, and against the head commit (`4dd89673`), not the cumulative diff. The core is right, and two of my three initial concerns were already handled — details below so you know what I checked rather than assumed.

## Blocking

**1. The protected-name list is now duplicated into a second live enforcement point.**

Two independent copies, both load-bearing:

- `mimir/access_control.py` — `_TRIGGER_SERVICE_PROTECTED_READ_NAMES`, consumed by `_is_trigger_service_protected_read_path` at *authorization*.
- `mimir/read_policy.py` — an inline `protected = {...}` literal inside `is_current_service_protected_read_path`, consumed at the *read boundary* (`result_is_protected`) and in the *backend traversal filter* (`readonly_backend._is_excluded`).

They are identical today and will not stay identical. Add `.ssh` or `authorized_keys` to one and the other keeps letting it through — and the failure is silent, at whichever enforcement point the path actually flows through. Import the one constant instead. (The copies in `tests/test_pollers.py` are fine; a test asserting a hardcoded expected list is a real guard.)

I hit this exact failure mode myself today at lower stakes: one sentence copied to five surfaces, three of which survived a hand-run grep because the wording differed slightly. A security-relevant name list is the same shape with worse consequences.

**2. `file_search` needs an explicit disposition, or criterion 1 cannot be checked off.**

Criterion 1 requires the `read_scope` class to be *empty* for this principal in a fresh window, and the measured set was `read_file(70) grep(34) ls(8) glob(2) file_search(1)`. `file_search` is not in the new allowlist, so that one event will still be there.

To be clear, I do **not** think you should add it here. Reading `read_policy.py:285-299`, `file_search` returns `None` unless `scope == "state"` and only ever resolves under `<home>/state` — it is an index-backed search over `memory/` and `state/`, so this PR's repo-read mechanism cannot cover it even in principle, and widening it would be a separate policy decision about memory contents entering a review turn. The fix is to say so: note it in the PR and either amend #1013's criterion or file the follow-up, so the leaf does not get closed on a "class empty" check that will still show one event.

## Verified, and worth crediting

- **Protected names are enforced during traversal, not just on the path argument.** This was my first and biggest concern — a `grep` rooted at an allowed repo root walking into `.git/config` or `.env` would have satisfied a check on the argument alone. Hooking `is_current_service_protected_read_path` into `readonly_backend._is_excluded` and `result_is_protected` closes it at the point where files are actually opened. Correct layering.
- **Dropping `_configured_repo_write_roots()` for this principal.** The review criteria said a repo write grant would let a review turn modify the code under review; you removed it rather than merely not adding to it. That is a narrowing beyond what the leaf strictly asked for, and it is the right call.
- **`except (OSError, RuntimeError, ValueError): return True`** in the new read check fails closed.
- **No capability list changed**, which the leaf said would be evidence of misdiagnosis, and `filesystem_read_roots` is empty for every other principal — so the `non_admin_read_filter_enabled` change cannot alter behavior for anything but this poller. Criterion 3 holds.
- **`would_block` is unaffected**: it is only set under `if not allowed`, so the new `elif` cannot emit a false would-block the way the `service_allowed` branch does (#1012).

## Question, not blocking

`_trigger_service_read_target_is_allowed` calls `file_contains_secret(resolved)` during authorization, and `result_is_protected` scans again at the read boundary. On a review turn with ~70 `read_file` calls that is two full-file scans each. Is the authorization-time scan buy

payload.body:
Approving and merging at `6a967382` on Jason's instruction. Both findings from my earlier review are resolved.

**The duplicated protected-name list is gone.** `read_policy.py` now imports `_TRIGGER_SERVICE_PROTECTED_READ_NAMES` from `access_control` and uses it at both call sites; the literal list exists exactly once in the codebase. That was the finding that mattered — two independent copies at two live enforcement points would have drifted silently, and the miss would land at whichever point the path happened to flow through.

**`file_search` is dispositioned rather than quietly left out.** The PR body states it is intentionally not admitted by this repo-read scope, with the reason: it is an index-backed search over `<home>/state` and `memory`, not a repo-path read, so widening it is a separate least-privilege decision. That matches what I argued in review — adding it here would not have worked in any case, since the mechanism cannot cover it — and the criterion was amended rather than silently failed.

Still credited from the first round: protected names are enforced at the backend traversal filter and not only on the path argument, so a `grep` rooted at an allowed repo root cannot walk into `.git` or `.env`; and repo **write** was dropped for this principal, so a reviewing turn cannot modify the code under review.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.title: fix(authz): the repo_review profile could not post a PR review

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Summary

The profile expansion and explicit failure fingerprint address the observed review-submission outage, and the positive/negative allowlist cases are useful. I’m requesting one security fix before merge: resolving the review body path during authorization does not confine the file that `gh` later opens.

## Blocking issue

- `mimir/access_control.py` (`_repo_review_body_files_within_scratch`, around the new `candidate.resolve()` check): this is vulnerable to a check/use race. The validator confirms that the path currently resolves beneath `scratch`, then returns an argv that still contains the original pathname. Before `gh` opens that pathname, another service-writable process can replace the accepted file (or a parent component) with a symlink to any readable file, causing the trusted review profile to publish data outside scratch. This is the same structural problem as validating a model-controlled path before handing it to another process: `Path.resolve()` proves only what the pathname meant at check time.

  Please make the authorized artifact independent of a later pathname lookup. One viable shape is for trusted code to open/read the scratch file with descriptor-relative no-follow/beneath confinement and a size bound, then replace `--body-file <path>` in the direct execution argv with `--body <captured contents>`; inserting multiline content into the already-parsed argv is safe because no shell reparses it. Alternatively, use a trusted wrapper that performs equivalent descriptor-safe opening and feeds the captured body to `gh`. Add a regression that swaps an initially accepted file or parent directory to an outside-pointing symlink after authorization but before simulated consumption and proves the outside content cannot be published.

## Validation

Reviewed the three-file patch and its allowlist tests through the GitHub API because the current `repo_review` runtime rejects process-backed `gh` commands—the exact outage this PR repairs. I did not rerun the suite locally.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Summary

The blocking check/use race is resolved at head `7ba9feb9d2a93871de512a4f2795c0a5e4f7afd3`. Authorization now opens the body beneath the resolved scratch root with descriptor-relative `O_NOFOLLOW` on every component, enforces the 65,536-byte bound, decodes it, and replaces `--body-file <path>` with `--body <captured contents>` in the pinned direct argv. The pathname therefore does not survive authorization for `gh` to reopen.

The new regression covers the load-bearing cases: the authorized argv remains unchanged and secret-free after a post-authorization file swap, pre-existing file and parent-component symlink escapes are refused, absent and oversized files fail closed, and multiline contents are preserved as one inert argv element. CI is green on the current head. No remaining blocking findings.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Correct finding, and I should have caught it — I described this exact class of bug (#1134's `openat`/`O_NOFOLLOW` race) in the 0.7.0 changelog earlier today and then wrote the same pattern. Fixed by taking your proposed shape.

**The pathname no longer survives authorization.** `parse_service_shell_argv` reads the body itself — anchored on the fully resolved scratch root, walking every component with `O_NOFOLLOW` (mirroring the #1134 hardening in `tools/registry.py`) — and returns an argv carrying `--body <captured contents>` with no `--body-file` in it. A later swap has nothing to act on.

Your insight about why inlining is safe is what makes this work at all: the control-character rule that rejects newlines applies to the **raw command string before parsing**. Nothing reparses an argv list, so a multiline element is inert. That means the file was never needed as an *execution* artifact — only as a way for the agent to author a long body. I had the constraint backwards.

Also bounded per your note about wedging: a body over 65,536 bytes (GitHub's own review-body limit) is refused rather than truncated, reading one byte past the cap so oversize is detected rather than silently cut.

**The regression you asked for**, `test_repo_review_body_is_captured_not_re_looked_up`, does the swap after authorization and asserts the authorized argv is unchanged and secret-free:

```
--body-file present in argv: False
inlined body: '## Summary\nsecond line\n'
post-swap symlink refused: True
parent-component symlink refused: True
oversize refused: True
```

**One semantic change worth flagging**, since it tightened behaviour beyond the ask: because the body is captured during authorization, the file must already exist and be readable. A not-yet-written body file is now refused rather than admitted on its path alone. That broke my own earlier test, which referenced a body it never created — I updated it to assert the refusal explicitly rather than paper over it.

Suites 6912 passed / 0 failed in both configurations. Re-requesting review.

payload.title: Worklink #1011: authz: system/upgrade principal cannot write its own scratch working directory (scratch + /tmp missing from service write roots)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The authorization logic is careful and correct — better than I asked for in several places. One blocking issue: the test-fixture relocation makes the suite **red on macOS** while staying green in CI, and the cause is the same symlink property the pin check exists to enforce.

## Blocking: `/var/tmp` is a symlink on macOS, so every pin fails closed

The fixture moved from `tmp_path_factory.mktemp(...)` to `tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(dir="/var/tmp")`. On Linux that is a real directory. On macOS `/var` is a symlink to `private/var`:

```
$ ls -ld /var
lrwxr-xr-x  /var -> private/var/

- **The new within-home guard is a tightening**,

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
This is the right shape and every acceptance criterion is met. One blocking item, about durability rather than correctness: the flag is correct today and structurally able to go silently wrong tomorrow.

## Verified

**The invariant I most wanted is actually asserted**, not just the field's presence:

```python
enforced = registry.authorize_tool("saga_feedback", auth, enforce=True)
assert captured[0][1]["would_block"] is (not enforced.allowed)
```

Applied at three sites, covering a service-capability-**allowed** call (`would_block` false), a **denied** call, and the sink path. That is the difference between a `would_block` that is trustworthy and one that is merely present — a hand-computed field agreeing with itself would have proved nothing.

**The redaction test is stronger than the criterion asked for.** Input `HTTPS://Example.INVALID:443/api?token=ghp_secretvalue` is recorded as `https://example.invalid/api?token=[REDACTED]` — so it proves normalization (case, default port) *and* secret scrubbing in one assertion. It also pins `fields["reason"] == enforced.reason` and `fields["trigger"]`, which closes the two remaining ambiguity sources I filed about.

**`service_principal` on the label-blocked branch** — the `missing_ifc_labels` return now passes `service_principal=service`, which was the omission that made 155 events look unattributed in the 2026-07-25 audit.

**Consumers still parse.** `test_compute_stats_accepts_old_and_self_classifying_shadow_events` feeds both an old event and a new one through `compute_stats`, so the ops dashboard survives the schema change and historical events stay readable.

Targeted suites 521 passed; CI green on all six including `pytest-enforced`.

## Blocking: `would_block` is hand-written at 16 sites and defaults to `False`

`ToolAuthorization.would_block: bool = False` (line 3022), and each denial sets `would_block=True` explicitly. So a denial branch that omits it emits `"would_block": false` — asserting that **enforcement would have permitted the call**. That is worse than the ambiguity this leaf removes: today a reader knows the field is unreliable and replays; afterwards they will trust a confidently wrong value.

I checked whether it is correct as written. It is, at 16 of 17 denial-shaped constructions. The exception is `access_control.py:2245` (`reason="not_a_channel_operation"`), which is a misuse guard — `allowed=False` regardless of `enforce`, for calling `authorize_channel_operation` with a non-channel tool — and never reaches the shadow emitter. Fine to leave, ideally with a one-line comment saying why it is exempt.

The ask is a conformance test so this stays true without a reviewer re-deriving it. Here is the check I used, which you can lift directly:

```python
def test_every_denial_sets_would_block():
    """would_block defaults to False, so a denial branch that omits it emits
    "enforcement would have permitted this" — a confident wrong answer, which
    is the failure this event shape exists to prevent."""
    import ast, pathlib
    src = pathlib.Path("mimir/access_control.py").read_text()
    missing = []
    for node in ast.walk(ast.parse(src)):
        if not (isinstance(node, ast.Call)
                and getattr(node.func, "id", None) == "ToolAuthorization"):
            continue
        kw = {k.arg: k.value for k in node.keywords if k.arg}
        allowed = kw.get("allowed")
        if allowed is None:
            continue
        dump = ast.dump(allowed)
        is_denial = ("Not" in dump and "enforce" in dump) or "Constant(value=False)" in dump
        if is_denial and "would_block" not in kw:
            missing.append(node.lineno)
    assert missing == [2245], missing  # 2245: misuse guard, never emitted
```

Pinning the known exemption by line rather than allowing an empty set means adding a new denial branch fails until the author decides deliberately — which is the point.

A derived value would be better still (compute once from the decision instead of res

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The conformance test is in and it works — I mutation-tested it and adding an unguarded denial branch turns it red. One more change, and the flaw is in the snippet **I** handed you, so this is me correcting my own suggestion rather than moving the goalposts.

## The line pin is too brittle to survive

I proposed `assert missing == [2245]`. That pins the exemption to a line number in a 4,700-line file that changes constantly. Inserting a single blank line at line 100 — an edit with nothing to do with authorization — breaks it:

```
-- line-pinned (as submitted):   assert [2246] == [2245]   FAILED
-- reason-keyed:                 passed
```

The failure mode isn't the red build, it's what the red build teaches. The obvious fix is to bump 2245 → 2246, so the assertion gets edited reflexively on unrelated changes. A guard that people routinely edit without reading is the same erosion as an enforcement skip — which is precisely what this class of test exists to prevent.

Keying on the denial's `reason` instead is stable across edits and self-documenting:

```python
        if is_denial and "would_block" not in keywords:
            reason = keywords.get("reason")
            missing.append(
                reason.value if isinstance(reason, ast.Constant) else f"line {node.lineno}"
            )

    assert missing == ["not_a_channel_operation"], missing
```

Verified all three properties with that change:

- baseline passes;
- the blank-line insertion above no longer breaks it;
- a new denial branch that omits `would_block` still fails — and now reports `['mutation_probe', 'not_a_channel_operation']` instead of a line number, so the failure names the offending branch.

That last point is the real gain: the reason string tells the next person *which* denial they forgot, which a line number does not.

## Otherwise confirmed on this head

- The misuse-guard exemption is now documented at the source (`# Misuse guard; never shadow-emitted.`), which was the other half of my note.
- Everything verified on the previous pass still holds: `would_block is (not enforced.allowed)` asserted against real `enforce=True` calls at three sites covering allowed, denied, and sink paths; the redaction test proving both normalization and secret scrubbing (`?token=[REDACTED]`); `reason` and `trigger` pinned; `service_principal` restored on the label-blocked branch; and the ops-dashboard test accepting both old and new event shapes.
- Targeted suites 521 passed; CI green on all six including `pytest-enforced`.

Docs-only, the hard constraint is respected, and every claim I could check against the source is accurate. One blocking item: a shipped snippet that only works on this deployment.

## Blocking: the identities re-verification snippet hardcodes `jason`

`docs/` is force-included into the wheel (`pyproject.toml:152` → `mimir/bundled_docs/docs`), so `docs/authorization.md` is the general operator reference distributed with every install — not a note about this box. The snippet does:

```python
jason = next(person for person in people if person.get("canonical") == "jason")
```

On any install whose admin is not named `jason`, that is an uncaught `StopIteration`. Verified against a fixture whose admin is `alice`:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 6, in <module>
StopIteration
```

An operator following the runbook at flip time — the highest-stakes moment it covers — gets a bare traceback rather than either a pass or a clear failure. It also asserts the wrong property: the precondition is "a deliberate `admin` identity exists", not "jason exists". Please assert that *some* principal carries `admin`, and fail with a message naming what was found. The dated evidence block above it is fine to keep specific, since it is explicitly provenance for this repo's own enablement decision.

Minor, same snippet family: `with sqlite3.connect(path) as connection:` manages the transaction, not the connection — the handle is left unclosed. Harmless for a read-only `PRAGMA`, but in copy-pasteable operator documentation `contextlib.closing` or an explicit `close()` sets a better example.

## Verified against the code, not against the issue text

- **"There is no live provider-compatibility startup exception"** — true. The only remaining mention of `ProviderEnforcementCompatibilityError` anywhere in `mimir/` is a stale comment (see below); the class and its raise are gone with #1213.
- **`tests / pytest-enforced` exists, and leaves the spec unset** — confirmed by parsing the workflow: workflow `name: tests`, job `pytest-enforced`, and its pytest step's env is exactly `{'MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED': '1'}` with no `MIMIR_MODEL_SPEC`. The runbook's "do not pin `MIMIR_MODEL_SPEC` in the enforced CI job" is the right instruction and matches the job.
- **The guard test name resolves** — `tests/test_env_isolation.py:101::test_no_test_is_skipped_because_enforcement_is_on`.
- **The flip is not performed anywhere.** The diff *removes* the old `MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED=true` dotenv block from §3 rather than adding one, and no added line sets the flag in any file. That was the criterion I was most concerned about and it is cleanly met.
- **§7 in `enforcement-enablement.md`** — #922 and #923 are both genuinely closed, so retitling it "closed" and folding the flip-time checks into the runbook is accurate.

The "a green run means nothing failed; it does not prove enforcement-sensitive paths ran" framing, with the skip guard named as what keeps it honest, is exactly the distinction I wanted carried into the docs rather than left in a PR comment.

## Separately — a stale claim this review turned up, and it is mine

While confirming the "no live startup exception" claim I found `mimir/commands/setup.py:1077` still prints, at setup time:

> `↑ cannot be used with MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED=true until #910 lands; choose codex-plus:, anthropic:, or openai: if you plan to enable authorization.`

I added that in #1212. #910 landed two hours later in #1213, and `resolve_access_control_enforcement(True, model_spec="claude-code:claude-sonnet-4-6")` now returns `True` — so the warning is false and steers operators away from a supported configuration. `test_print_setup_report_warns_claude_code_enforcement_incompatible` asserts it, so the suite locks the wrong behavior in. I reviewed #1213 and missed it as well.

**Not for this PR** — your leaf explicitly says to stop and report rather than fix code, which is the right boundary. I am fixing it

**The identities check is now correct for any deployment.** It asserts the required *role* rather than a particular canonical name, and fails with a message naming what it actually found. Verified all three paths:

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The security substance is sound and I verified it rather than reasoning about it. Requesting changes only for a rebase whose resolution has real semantic content, plus one documentation point.

## I withdraw my own initial concern — recording it because it nearly became a false blocker

My first read flagged the config extraction as untested-in-production: `_patched_aquery` reads `kwargs["config"]`/`args[1]` while `_patched_astream` reads `kwargs["_config"]`, and the only things supplying either were the test fakes. That looked like tests validating a path production doesn't take.

It isn't. I installed `langchain-claude-code-mimir` and introspected the real surface:

```
_aquery   (self, prompt, config: RunnableConfig | None = None, run_manager=None, **kwargs)
_astream  (self, messages, stop=None, run_manager=None, **kwargs)
# and in invoke/ainvoke/stream/astream, 4 sites:
kwargs.setdefault("_config", config)
```

So `config` really is `_aquery`'s second positional, and `_config` really is a kwarg the adapter deliberately threads through for exactly this purpose. Both extractions match the production surface precisely, and the asymmetry between them is the adapter's, not yours.

## Verified

- **The four skips are gone**, not relabelled: 0 occurrences of `_CLAUDE_CODE_ENFORCEMENT_SKIP`, and run under `MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED=1` all four **pass** (4 passed, 0 skipped). The enforced full suite reports **16 skipped, down from 20** — that delta being exactly these four is the cleanest possible evidence the criterion was met rather than worked around.
- **Gate lifted**: `resolve_access_control_enforcement(True, model_spec="claude-code:claude-sonnet-4-6")` returns `True` instead of raising.
- **Absent carrier fails closed** by construction, not just by test: `resolve()` returns `None` when `_active_token is None`, which flows to `_check_admin_authorized(tool_name, None, ...)` and denies with `missing_auth_context`.
- **Not session_id, not bare ContextVar-as-authority**: the authority comes from `config["configurable"]["__pregel_runtime"].context` with an `isinstance(AuthContext)` check — the exact frozen server-created object, resolved at dispatch before the hook task forks. Nothing model- or SDK-influenceable participates.
- **Cross-turn confusion**: `test_reused_sdk_hook_task_resolves_each_turns_auth_context` forks the hook task **once** and drives two turns through it, asserting turn 1 allowed and turn 2 denied under a non-admin principal. That is the "forked at connect" case the leaf demanded, and it would fail if the carrier were bound once at connect. The `asyncio.Lock` around each invocation closes the converse hole (a late turn-1 hook resolving turn-2 authority) by preventing overlap.
- **Suites**: enforced **6871 passed, 16 skipped, 0 failed**; unenforced **6871 passed, 16 skipped, 0 failed** (PR head merged with current `main`).

## Blocking: rebase — and neither side of the conflict is correct alone

#1212 landed after you branched, so `docs/authorization.md` and `docs/configuration.md` conflict. Please don't resolve by taking one side; **each side is right about one half**:

- Your line: correct that the Claude Code hook now receives the context, but still names `claude-code:claude-sonnet-4-6` as the **default** — stale, #1212 changed it.
- Main's line: correct that the default is `codex-plus:gpt-5.6-luna`, but still says `claude-code:*` fails the preflight — which your PR makes false.

The merged text needs the codex-plus default value **and** the carrier semantics. Same for the enablement-runbook block near `docs/authorization.md:555`: keep #1212's "the shipped default already passes this preflight", and drop the "only `claude-code:` fails it" sentence your change invalidates. I verified the suites against a local resolution along those lines, so the numbers above hold once it is rebased.

## Non-blocking: say what the token is

`bind()` mints `secrets.token_bytes(32)`, but `resolve()` takes no token and the hoo

payload.body:
Both findings were right, and both were mine — I changed part of the default story and left the rest contradicting it. Fixed at `58af1f40`, rebased onto current `main` (post-#1209).

**Finding 1 — setup selected a different default than its own template documented.** Resolved by making it genuinely one default rather than two that agree by convention:

- `DEFAULT_MODEL_NAME` → `DEFAULT_MODEL_SPEC`, now the fully qualified `codex-plus:gpt-5.6-luna`. `detect_route` passes pre-qualified specs straight through, so `detect_route(None)` — the path `mimir setup` uses — yields the same spec the runtime falls back to.
- `config.py` and `agent.py` now **import that constant** instead of repeating a literal, so the two cannot drift again. `test_setup_default_matches_runtime_fallback` pins them together, which is the regression guard for exactly the contradiction you caught.
- The `.env` template's "Without --model, mimir uses `anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6`" is corrected.

You also correctly implied a consequence I had to make deliberate rather than let happen silently: a bare `--subscription` no longer yields claude-code, because the default spec is already a subscription route. Max OAuth now needs `--model claude-sonnet-4-6 --subscription`. That is pinned by `test_setup_bare_subscription_flag_keeps_default`, and `test_setup_max_oauth_routes_claude_to_claude_code` was updated to pass the explicit model rather than deleted, so the Max opt-in path is still covered.

**Finding 2 — README.** Fixed all three spots, including one you didn't name: the enforcement paragraph (line ~152), the `MIMIR_MODEL_SPEC` list entry still calling `claude-code:` the default (line ~209), and the quickstart extra, now `mimir-agent[codex-plus]` with the matching auth step.

**Also added, per operator decision:** `mimir setup` now warns when the resolved spec is `claude-code:*`, since startup preflight refuses it under enforcement (#910). Keyed on the resolved spec rather than on `--subscription`, so an explicit `--model claude-code:*` is covered too. Two tests: the warning fires for claude-code, and does **not** fire for the default (otherwise it would be noise on every ordinary setup).

## Corrected measurements

My original PR body claimed 189 failures for "enforced + unset spec". **That number is now wrong and I want it on the record rather than quietly updated.** Re-measured on the rebased head:

| configuration | main | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| unenforced full suite | 6868 / 0 failed | **6868 passed, 0 failed** |
| enforced + explicit `anthropic:` | 0 failed (20 skipped) | **6864 passed, 20 skipped, 0 failed** |
| enforced + **unset** spec (the default) | `tests/test_agent.py` alone: **71 failed / 33 passed** | **6864 passed, 20 skipped, 0 failed** |

The 189 collapsed to 0 once #1209 merged, and the reason is worth recording because it is a live defect independent of this PR. `_load_home_dotenv` calls `load_dotenv(..., override=False)`, which **mutates `os.environ`** — and `monkeypatch` cannot undo what it did not set. Before #1209, `test_resolve_model_claude_code_home_dotenv_requires_enforcement` wrote `MIMIR_MODEL_SPEC=claude-code:...` into a temp home and loaded it, leaking that value process-wide; under enforcement every subsequent `Config.from_env()` then hit the provider gate. payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1004: scheduler/worklink: budget+arbiter log scans run on the event loop, diverging from the CR#5 to_thread pattern the scheduler already established

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving at `df3a02c9`. Every criterion met, and the tests are the kind that will still catch a regression in a year.

**The regression tests fail pre-fix.** Main's production code with this PR's test files:

```
FAILED tests/test_scheduler.py::test_fire_poller_budget_checks_do_not_block_loop_and_reuse_snapshot
FAILED tests/test_worklink_autonomy.py::test_worklink_run_arbiter_gate_does_not_block_loop
2 failed in 1.43s
```

They fail for the right structural reason, which is what makes them durable: the loop-progress probe spins `await asyncio.sleep(0)` until the worker signals `entered`, then asserts the blocking call has *not* completed. On-loop, the `while` body can't run at all until the sync call returns, so the assertion is false — it's testing the actual concurrency property, not a timing coincidence, and there's no sleep-based flakiness to rot later.

**Criteria, each checked:**

- `worklink_run` offloads via `await asyncio.to_thread(arbiter.should_fire, priority=priority, event_loop=loop)` — and it passes `event_loop`, which was the subtle requirement. Without it, `_check_quota_pause` would take its `RuntimeError` branch on the worker thread and silently drop the lazy-expiry `quota_recovered` event. `assert passed_loop is loop` pins exactly that.
- The "cheap, in-process" comment is corrected to name the real cost ("`should_fire` may scan turns.jsonl, so keep it off the event loop").
- `_poller_budget_exceeded` stays **synchronous** and the async caller wraps it — no `async def` cascade through the budget helpers, per the standing convention.
- Both budget calls are still made (`len(calls) == 2`), so the #488 post-acquire re-check survives as a genuine second evaluation rather than being memoized away — that was the specific thing I was worried an "optimization" would eat.
- Decisions and events unchanged: `ran == ["p1"]`, `"worklink_run shed" in out`, `dispatched == []`.

**One risk this change introduced that I checked specifically.** `_poller_budget_exceeded` now passes a **turns** snapshot into `aggregate_poller_turn_usage`, which scans *two* files. Had that snapshot also fed the events scan, turn records would be parsed under event logic and external-usage attribution would silently corrupt. It doesn't: line 418 uses `tail_jsonl_records(events_path)` directly and ignores `snapshot` entirely. `getattr(self._arbiter, "turns_snapshot", None)` is also correct for a `None` arbiter.

**Suites:** 329 passed across `test_scheduler` / `test_worklink_autonomy` / `test_poller_budget` / `test_tool_registry`; full suite **6858 passed, 16 skipped in 181s**. CI green on all five.

**Calibration worth recording, since it affects how much this actually buys.** The `to_thread` wrapping is the load-bearing half; the snapshot addition helps less than it appears:

- The live turns snapshot is *saturated* (1,237 records at the 64 MiB cap), so post-#1003 `iter_window_records` correctly detects that and streams the file anyway — the cache is bypassed on exactly the deployment we have.
- The events half of `aggregate_poller_turn_usage` has no snapshot support at all and always streams.

So this removes the stall (which was the point) rather than the IO. That's the right outcome for this leaf, and I'd rather the follow-up conversation start from an accurate picture than from "budget checks are cached now." The remaining IO is off-loop, which is where it belongs.

Merging. Closing chainlink #1004.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #1003: usage/budget: three windowed JSONL scans use the saturation-unaware iterator (#498 completion) — silent fail-open undercount when the cap binds inside the window

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Approving at `15806d94`. Every criterion verified independently, including the one that mattered most.

**The regression tests genuinely fail pre-fix.** I checked out `origin/main`, overwrote only the two test files with this PR's versions (main's production code + your tests), and ran the three new cases:

```
FAILED tests/test_usage_stats.py::test_aggregate_saturated_snapshot_matches_file_window
FAILED tests/test_usage_stats.py::test_cooldown_saturated_snapshot_matches_file_window
FAILED tests/test_budget.py::test_partition_saturated_snapshot_matches_file_window
3 failed in 0.23s
```

And the failure is exactly the defect, not an incidental mismatch: `At index 3 diff: 3000 != 13000` — the 7-day token total reads 3,000 instead of 13,000 once the snapshot saturates inside the window. That is the silent fail-open undercount the leaf described, now pinned by a test. Using `max_records=2` to force saturation *short* of the window, and comparing against the unsnapshotted file scan as the oracle, is the right construction — the assertion can't drift with the fixture data.

**Criterion 4 (no warm-path regression) — proven, not assumed.** Rather than time it, I built an unsaturated snapshot, called `aggregate`, then **deleted the file** and called it again: identical result, 5 turns. The cache path is still served without touching disk, so the common non-saturated path is unchanged by construction.

**Criterion 3 (don't over-convert).** Both legitimately non-windowed callsites are left on `iter_snapshot_or_tail` with the reasoning recorded in-code — `_authorized_records` ("no time cutoff... sibling `_authorized_snapshot` preserves saturated window fallback through `stream_filtered`") and `pending_forget_candidates_count` ("needs only the most recent matching events, which the capped tail preserves by construction"). That is the distinction `iter_window_records`' own docstring draws, and getting it right was the easiest thing to get wrong here.

**Two failure modes I checked for and did not find:**

- *Recursion via the filtered hook.* `iter_window_records` probes `getattr(snapshot, "iter_window_records", None)` on the saturated path, so a plain snapshot carrying that attribute would recurse. `hasattr(JsonlSnapshot, "iter_window_records")` is `False`, and nothing in `mimir/feedback/` feeds its filtered adapter into these three functions, so the hook stays reachable only by the adapters it was built for.
- *Dangling import.* Both modules had their import switched from `iter_snapshot_or_tail` to `iter_window_records`; neither retains any reference to the old name, so there's no `NameError` waiting on a cold path.

**Suites:** 319 passed across `test_usage_stats` / `test_budget` / `test_budget_gate_and_alias` / `test_jsonl_snapshot` / `test_feedback` / `test_poller_budget`; full suite **6859 passed, 16 skipped in 208s**.

**No cap or retention tuning**, which the review criteria specifically forbade as a substitute — the correctness now holds independent of cap values, which was the whole point.

Worth recording for context: on the live deployment this fix is currently a **no-op**, because the saturated turns snapshot happens to reach 17.1 days against a 7-day window. That is precisely why this was filed as latent rather than active — the fix removes a cliff the deployment is presently sitting 2.4x away from, and the margin was shrinking because the cap binds on bytes at ~54 KB/record.

Merging. Closing chainlink #1003.

**The concurrency assertion survived intact**, which was the trap I was most worried about. So the original finding was a test-harness gap, not a product defect. That is good news and it is exactly what the PR should say.

**Three things to add before merge:**

1. **State the root cause for both symptoms.** Criterion 1 asked for this explicitly and the PR body says only "Closes chainlink #999". A reader six months from now needs to be able to tell "the test was wrong" from "we adjusted a test until it went green" — those look identical in a diff, and only the reasoning distinguishes them. Say that the events lacked bridge attribution, that the enforced ingress gate was right to deny them, and whether the non-completion shared that cause (I believe it did — denied events left the file's later cases unable to drain — but you are better placed to confirm than I am to infer).
2. **Re-run validation with enforcement on.** The evidence line reads `env -u MIMIR_MODEL_SPEC uv run pytest -q` → so the suite was validated *without* `MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED=1`, meaning the change was never tested against the condition in the issue title. The suggested command on #999 pins both variables for this reason. My verifying it does not discharge that — next time nobody may check.
3. **Record the cross-suite enforced picture (criterion 6).** I ran it: the **full suite under enforcement is 21 failed, 6835 passed, 16 skipped in 216s** (clean baseline 183s, so no hang anywhere). I captured only the last 5 failure lines and they are all in `tests/test_prohibited_action_guard.py`; I am enumerating the remaining 16 now and will post the full list on #952, since that is where "full suite green under enforcement" lives. Those failures are pre-existing — this PR touches one test file — so they are not a regression here, but #952 inherits them and its criterion (a) is still unmet.

To be clear about the bottom line: the dispatcher is fixed, enforcement no longer breaks turn concurrency, and this is a real step toward enablement. I want the reasoning written down before it lands.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #997: authz round-3 coverage: live-path sink denials, service file policy, and tool-catalogue completeness

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The retry is correct, and one of the assertions is stronger than the criterion asked for.

**The false positive is fixed at its root.** The catalogue assertion now uses `get_operation_catalog()` rather than constructing a fresh `OperationCatalog()`, which is what produced the spurious "UNKNOWN tiers for fetch_channel_history, list_channels, send_message" demotion. All three are and were catalogued (`resource_scoped`/sink, `admin_required`/source, `resource_scoped`/source).

**And the assertion has teeth now that the accessor is right.** I injected a fake UNKNOWN into the predicate (treating `send_message` as uncatalogued) and the test fails, so it would genuinely catch a newly added tool that reaches the model surface without a tier. That was the whole point of the criterion, and it would have been silently useless against an unpopulated catalog.

**The live-path test does what I asked and then some.** It drives the real middleware — `BudgetGateMiddleware().wrap_tool_call(_make_request(...), handler)` — rather than calling `SinkGate` directly, and asserts:

```python
assert decisions[-1].allowed is False
assert decisions[-1].reason == reason
assert result.status == "error"
assert handler_calls == 0
```

`handler_calls == 0` is the assertion I would have added on review: it proves the tainted egress was denied **before execution**, not that an error came back afterwards. For a sink gate that distinction is the entire property.

**Service file policy strengthened exactly where specified** — `wrong_source`, `outside_root` and `tmp` now assert `.allowed is False` rather than only inspecting `.reason`.

Local run: `test_budget_gate_and_alias.py`, `test_information_flow.py`, `test_tool_registry.py` → **307 passed**. CI green on all five checks.

Approving and merging. That completes all four of the #923 subissues (#995, #996, #998, #997), leaving #999 — the enforcement concurrency failure — as the last gate before #952 and #854 can close.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #998: authz round-4 coverage: ownership migration, legacy_admin mutation denial, public-channel visibility, non-enumerating denials

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
All six criteria covered, and two of the three specific review criteria came back stronger than I asked for.

**Non-enumerating denial.** I asked for full-string equality rather than "both denied", and the test does that plus pins the exact text:

```python
assert denials[0] == denials[1]
assert denials[0] == "saga_end_session failed: session write denied"
```

So a future change that denies with a subtly different message for the nonexistent-id case — reintroducing the enumeration oracle — fails here.

**Public-channel extraction.** Asserts a real owner (`owner_principal == "user:alice"`), explicitly excludes the degenerate values (`not in {"", "legacy_admin"}`), asserts `visibility == "public"`, and includes the negative case: alice sees the row, bob gets `[]`. That is exactly the shape the criterion asked for.

**Migration isolation.** All paths are `tmp_path`-based (137 references, no absolute or `/mimir-home` paths), so no live `saga.db` is touched.

**On the source change.** `mimir/commitments/store.py` is +10-6, which the leaf permits only as a narrow fail-closed tightening, so I looked closely. It is a genuine correctness fix and the criterion is what surfaced it: the old code claimed to preserve malformed lines verbatim while `rstrip("\n")` plus `"\n".join(...) + "\n"` normalised every line ending and forced a trailing newline. Reading and writing with `newline=""` and preserving each line's original ending makes the preservation real, and the added `isinstance(event, dict)` guard stops a non-dict JSON line (a bare list or string) raising on `.get()`. Nothing is relaxed.

I verified the fix is actually pinned rather than incidental, and it took two attempts worth mentioning. Reverting only the write side leaves the tests green — `rstrip("\n")` preserves a lone `\r`, so that path round-trips for this fixture. Reverting the read side (dropping `newline=""`, so universal newlines translate CRLF) fails the test:

```
FAILED tests/test_commitments_store.py::test_ownership_migration_is_atomic_preserves_malformed_and_is_idempotent
```

Using `write_bytes` with a real `\r\n` malformed line is the right way to test byte-level preservation — a `write_text` fixture would have passed either way.

Local run: `test_commitments_store.py`, `test_commitment_extraction_wiring.py`, `test_saga_ops_tools.py` → **113 passed**. CI green on all five checks.

Approving and merging. Third of the four #923 subissues; #997 is the last of the coverage set, and #999 remains the gate that actually decides enablement.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #996: authz round-3 coverage: IFC cross-turn guard and MCP fail-closed branches (#917, #918, #920)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
All four criteria covered, test-only with no source changes, and the guards are genuinely pinned.

- `test_classifier_flow_metadata_mismatch_hard_fails_closed` — a classifier that source-declares its direction but returns contradictory `sink_resources` hard-fails closed under enforcement.
- `test_cross_turn_ifc_guards_use_and_update_only_exact_request_carrier` — the symmetric cross-turn guard (#918) exercised directly rather than incidentally.
- `test_mcp_source_taints_after_execution_and_sinks_gate_before_execution` — read-direction results taint labels after execution while write/both-direction calls pass the `EXTERNAL_MCP` gate before it (#918/#920).
- `test_complete_forged_label_cannot_egress_from_service_turn` — a hand-forged complete `SourceLabel` is still denied egress (#917).

The review criteria asked for the guards to be verified by reverting them rather than trusting reachability, so I did that. Neutralising the mismatch branch in `access_control.py` (`reason = "mcp_flow_metadata_mismatch"` → `None`) produces exactly one failure, `TestMCPResourceAdapter::test_classifier_flow_metadata_mismatch_hard_fails_closed`, with the other four still green — so the assertion is reachable, specific, and not passing for incidental reasons.

It also asserts the right thing. My criterion was to assert `.allowed`, not merely a reason string, and the test does both:

```python
assert authorization.allowed is False
assert authorization.reason == "mcp_flow_metadata_mismatch"
```

That is the better form — the `allowed` assertion is the security property and the reason pins which branch produced it, so a future refactor that denies for a different reason gets noticed rather than silently passing.

No source files touched, so nothing was relaxed to make a test pass, and the MCP `result_integrity="untrusted"` default is untouched.

Local run: `test_information_flow.py`, `test_mcp_client.py`, `test_access_control.py` → **570 passed**. CI green on all five checks.

Approving and merging. Second of the four #923 subissues; #997 unblocks once this lands, and #998 remains dispatchable.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #995: authz round-3 coverage: service exec path binds and execs the server-parsed argv (shell=False, model argv dropped)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
All four criteria are met, and the source change is a genuine tightening rather than the relaxation the leaf's constraints forbid.

**The mechanism.** The middleware now binds the server-parsed argv into a ContextVar (`bind_direct_exec_argv`) immediately before `handler(execution_request)`, and the tool reads `bound_direct_exec_argv()` in preference to its own `mimir_direct_argv` kwarg. That closes the channel properly: the kwarg is model-adjacent, the ContextVar is server-set for exactly the duration of the call, so a tampered or rewritten kwarg cannot reach `subprocess`. The `if direct_argv is None: direct_argv = mimir_direct_argv` fallback keeps direct/sync invocations working without the middleware, and since `budget_gate` already pops and re-sets the kwarg server-side, both channels are server-controlled in production.

**No ContextVar leakage.** The reset sits in `finally:` at both call sites (sync 933-937, async 1090-1094), so an exception in the handler cannot leave a previous call's argv bound for a later one. That was my main worry with a ContextVar-based approach and it is handled.

**The tests have teeth — verified by mutation, not by reading.** Both pass as merged. I then flipped the precedence back to trusting the model's kwarg (`direct_argv = mimir_direct_argv`, dropping the bound lookup) in both `extra.py` and `shell_async.py`:

```
FAILED tests/test_shell_exec.py::test_service_shell_exec_graph_executes_server_bound_argv
FAILED tests/test_shell_async_wiring.py::test_service_bash_async_graph_executes_pinned_script_with_interpreter
2 failed
```

So they assert on the executed argv rather than on a return value, which is exactly what the review criteria asked for — a test that merely observed a successful call would have stayed green through that mutation.

They also exercise the merged #991 pinning: the pinned-interpreter test covers a script pin invoked through its interpreter, and both run green on macOS where none of the production pin paths exist, which tells me the autouse pin-table fixture is doing its job and the tests are host-independent.

Local run on this head: `test_shell_exec.py`, `test_shell_async_wiring.py`, `test_shell_env.py`, `test_access_control.py` → **382 passed**. CI green on all five checks.

Approving and merging. This is the first of the four #923 subissues; #996 and #998 are dispatchable now, #997 is queued behind #996.
