payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #994: worklink: budget-continuation mechanism is inert — 0/11 comments posted (wrong cwd + admin gate) and no sidecar consumer

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
All four parts of the issue are addressed, and two of the choices are better than what I specified.

**The cwd fix landed at the source, not just the call site.** `orchestrator._runner_for_home` now reads `command_cwd = home if args[0] == chainlink_bin else cwd`, so the configured chainlink home is authoritative even when a caller supplies a worktree — which is what I asked for, since the previous form (`cwd if cwd is not None else …`) meant any explicit cwd bypassed exactly the rule that existed to make chainlink work. `test_runner_for_home_overrides_explicit_cwd_only_for_chainlink` pins the scoping so non-chainlink argv keeps its caller-supplied cwd, which was my review criterion.

**The admin gate was resolved the right way.** The consumer is "intentionally a deterministic Worklink process, not an agent tool: it has only the fixed Chainlink comment/status operations below and does not grant an admin capability to the service principal whose turn exhausted its budget." That is the non-admin durable channel route, stated explicitly, and it avoids widening a service principal's capability set just to post a comment.

**Terminal-state reads fail closed**, "preventing a stale continuation from re-running already completed work when Chainlink is unavailable." That is the #975 clobber class, and `test_consumer_treats_completed_evidence_as_terminal` plus `test_consumer_resolves_closed_issue_without_reaction` cover it.

**Comments are posted once per sidecar**, not once per occurrence — the early return on `state.get("posted")` with `skipped_reason: "already_posted"` means an `occurrences` count climbing to 15 produces one comment, not fifteen.

I checked what the first run will actually do to the 11 sidecars on the live box, since that was my remaining criterion. Every issue they reference — #870, #676, #740, #896, #934, #922, #909, #879, #882 — is **closed**, and the two remaining sidecars carry no validated target (`no_validated_target`). So the terminal-state path resolves all 11 silently with **zero comments**: no first-run storm, no orphans left behind, and no one-off migration script needed. Handling the backlog by mechanism rather than by a bespoke migration is the better outcome.

Local run: `test_worklink_continuation.py`, `test_worklink_claims.py` → **41 passed**. CI green on all five checks.

One observation, not a change request: the poller now moves entries within `sys.path` ("Move, don't merely add, so script and imported package always come from one checkout") to keep the script and the imported package on the same revision. The reasoning is sound for a standalone poller script, but it is the kind of import-path surgery that gets surprising when a second checkout appears — worth a comment pointing at the failure it fixes if it is not already covered by a test.

Approving and merging.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #993: LLM retry: a 429 whose message mentions tokens is classified non-retryable and fails fast (status must outrank message keywords)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Fixed correctly, and at the right layer: status now outranks message heuristics instead of the keyword scan getting first look. The new `http_status_retryable` reason makes the decision path legible in logs, which matters because the old failure mode was a wrong decision that *looked* right.

Verified against the table from the issue plus four adversarial cases I added to check the fix did not overshoot:

| case | classified | correct |
|---|---|---|
| 429 "Rate limited. Please retry." | retryable | yes |
| 429 "…rate limit of 80000 **max tokens** per minute" | retryable | yes (was the bug) |
| 429 "request queue **too long**, retry shortly" | retryable | yes (was the bug) |
| 529 "Overloaded" / 500 "internal server error" | retryable | yes |
| 400 "bad request: invalid schema" | non-retryable | yes |
| 400 "prompt is too long: 250000 tokens > 200000 maximum context" | non-retryable | yes |
| **400 "unknown field rate_limit"** | non-retryable | yes — status wins, no retry storm on a terminal 400 |
| **403 "forbidden"** | non-retryable | yes |
| **no-status "maximum context exceeded"** | non-retryable | yes — keywords still apply without a status |
| **no-status "rate limit exceeded"** | retryable | yes |

Eleven for eleven. The last four are the ones I cared about most: the review criteria warned that a retry storm on a genuine terminal error would be worse than the current fail-fast, and a 400 whose body happens to contain "rate limit" stays terminal while message heuristics still work when no status is available.

The falsy-zero handling is fixed too — `max_attempts=1` now yields exactly one attempt rather than silently becoming the default 3, and an explicit `base_delay=0` is honoured (observed `delay=0.00s` between retries instead of the 0.5s default).

Approving; merging once CI settles on this head.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #989: Harden trusted direct-exec PATH against writable virtualenv shadowing

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The `direct_exec_env` half of this is exactly right, and `test_direct_exec_env_discards_writable_path_and_does_not_select_decoy` is precisely the decoy regression I asked for. A fixed `_TRUSTED_PATH_DIRS` of root-owned directories is the correct construction for the service path, and it composes properly with #1195: every admitted service command is already bound to an absolute pinned executable, so that path does not need PATH lookup at all and the trusted list only governs what the *child* resolves.

**Blocking — applying the same replacement to `login_shell_command` breaks the unpinned path, and the deleted tests were protecting exactly that.**

`login_shell_command` is not the service path. It is the fallback for every shell_exec that has no pinned argv:

```python
argv = (
    mimir_direct_argv
    if mimir_direct_argv is not None
    else ["bash", "-lc", login_shell_command(command)]
)
```
(`mimir/tools/extra.py:391-395`, `mimir/tools/shell_async.py:320-324`)

Those commands are free-form and depend entirely on PATH lookup. Replacing PATH with the six root-owned directories removes the virtualenv bin, and in the live container that directory holds console scripts that exist nowhere else — I enumerated it: `mimir`, `pytest`, `py.test`, plus ~20 others (`dotenv`, `httpx`, `jsonschema`, `mcp`, `huggingface-cli`, …). The venv `python` also stops being selected, so `python -c "import mimir…"` would resolve the system interpreter without mimir's dependencies.

This is not hypothetical: **shipped prompts invoke the `mimir` CLI** and would get "command not found" —

- `mimir commitments list --status all` (`mimir/prompt_templates/commitments-review.md`)
- `mimir reflection most-retrieved` (`mimir/prompt_templates/reflect.md`)
- `mimir skills install chainlink-orchestrator` (`mimir/optional-skills/chainlink-orchestrator/SKILL.md`)
- `mimir setup`, `mimir verify-creds`

And the PR deletes the two tests that encoded this requirement. `test_login_shell_command_prepends_venv_bin` documented the reason in its own docstring — "prepends the venv bin — where `mimir` and the venv `python` live — via an export that runs after the profile, so `mimir` is reachable regardless of how the server was launched" — and used `mimir reflection introspection-report --days 7` as its example. `test_shell_exec_puts_venv_bin_on_path` was the end-to-end guard. Replacing both with assertions of the opposite inverts a deliberate, documented invariant.

It also buys very little there. #989's threat model is a service principal getting a *validated, allow-listed* argv to execute something it did not name — which requires bare-name PATH resolution, and that only happens on the pinned direct-exec path. On the login path the command is arbitrary text already, so anyone who can reach it can write `/workspace/mimir/.venv/bin/gh` explicitly; removing the directory from PATH prevents nothing while breaking shipped behaviour.

Suggested shape: keep `env["PATH"] = _TRUSTED_PATH` for `direct_exec_env`, and for `login_shell_command` keep the virtualenv bin reachable — appending it *after* the trusted directories rather than prepending would satisfy the spirit of the issue (system tools win; an agent-writable directory can no longer shadow `git` or `gh`) while leaving `mimir` and the venv `python` resolvable. Then restore the two deleted tests alongside the new decoy test; they assert a real requirement, and the decoy test covers the service path where the hardening belongs.

One thing to double-check when you revise: `uv run pytest` under the service profile relies on `uv` discovering the project virtualenv. It should still work, since discovery is by project directory rather than PATH and `uv` is pinned at `/usr/local/bin/uv`, but please add or point me at coverage that proves `uv run` still selects the project venv with the trusted PATH in force.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Resolved exactly as suggested, and the tests are stronger than what I asked for.

`login_shell_command` now joins `(_TRUSTED_PATH, venv_bin)` in that order, so on the live layout the venv bin sits **last** — position 6 of 7 — which satisfies both halves: an agent-writable directory can no longer shadow `git`, `gh`, or any system tool, while `mimir`, `pytest`, and the venv `python` stay resolvable for the unpinned interactive/admin path. Verified directly:

```
export PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin:<venv>/bin
  venv bin position: 6 of 7   (cannot shadow system tools)
direct_exec_env PATH == _TRUSTED_PATH exactly; venv bin absent
```

So the service path keeps the full hardening the issue asked for and the login path keeps its documented capability.

The test set is better than a restoration. payload.title: Worklink #983: Classify Anthropic model_context_window_exceeded turns as errors

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The classification work here is right, and two details are better than what I specified.

All six criteria are met: `model_context_window_exceeded` gets a distinct subtype and `result_is_error=True`; budget exhaustion produces `tool_budget_exhausted` by reading the existing `TurnContext` fields rather than a parallel mechanism; `tool_call_count` lands on both the TurnRecord and the terminal event via `outcome_fields`, which is exactly the instrument #992's measurement needs; and the regressions inject the state instead of requiring a real 200-call turn or a real context overflow. Local run of `test_turn_logger.py`, `test_feedback.py`, `test_agent.py` → **300 passed**.

Two things you got right that I want to call out, because both are easy to get wrong:

- **Requiring an actual denial.** Gating on `tool_call_budget_exhausted` *and* `tool_call_budget_denied_count` means a soft warning alone stays a success, so this cannot double-count against the existing `tool_call_budget_soft_warning` feedback rule — and `test_budget_exhaustion_does_not_duplicate_existing_budget_feedback` pins it.
- **Separating classification from failure side effects.** Routing exhausted turns through the error branch while keeping `_notify_chat_skill_failure` and `_post_deliver_failure` gated on a real `error` is the correct distinction. Treating exhaustion as authoritative over a trailing `end_turn` is also right, and the comment explains why.

**Blocking — one unstated consequence that needs to be a deliberate decision.**

Your test asserts the terminal event becomes `turn_failed`. That is the correct classification, but `turn_failed` is a control signal elsewhere: `mimir/poller_recovery.py` reconciles in-flight poller events against turn outcomes and, per its docstring, `turn_failed` → **re-enqueue the stashed event**, with `recover_failed_turns` defaulting to `True` and `DEFAULT_MAX_RECOVERY_ATTEMPTS = 3`.

So after this merge, a poller turn that exhausts its tool-call budget will be re-fired up to three times before `poller_turn_gave_up`. That is plausibly what we want — budget-starved poller work being retried instead of silently recorded as success is the whole point — but it is a behaviour change the PR does not mention, and two things make it worth deciding explicitly rather than discovering:

1. **These turns exhaust deterministically, not occasionally.** Measured on the live box 2026-07-26: a single-PR remediation turn hit 200/200 at 03:28:54 after `batch_size` was already reduced to 1, and an earlier batched turn hit it at 03:00:06 after 30 minutes. Under this change each such item now consumes up to three full budgets before giving up, which is a real quota and wall-clock cost while #992 (per-trigger budget sizing) is still unfiled work.
2. **A re-fire re-runs partial work.** An exhausted turn stopped midway, so re-enqueueing restarts it from the beginning — the class of hazard #975 was filed for (re-running an attempt that had already pushed). The recovery path's cap and back-pressure bound the blast radius, and I am not claiming a concrete clobber here, but it deserves a look before it is switched on by default.

Please either (a) confirm this is intended and say so in the PR body plus a CHANGELOG line, so the next person reading `poller_turn_gave_up` in the logs knows why it started appearing, or (b) treat `tool_budget_exhausted` as a non-recoverable failure for the recovery path specifically — the item is deterministically starved, so retrying it unchanged is unlikely to help until the budget is sized — and let #992/#994 own resumption instead. Either is fine; what I do not want is for this to land unremarked.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The blocker is resolved, and you took the more conservative of the two routes I offered, which I think is the right call.

`poller_recovery` now special-cases `result_subtype == "tool_budget_exhausted"` and drops the in-flight entry without retry, keeping the failed classification for telemetry. The reasoning is documented in three places — the module docstring, the `recover_failed_turns` docstring, and an inline comment — and it is the correct reasoning: the failure is deterministic under an unchanged budget, so a replay would repeat partial side effects and spend another full budget without changing the limiting condition. Pointing at #992 for sizing and #994 for resumption is the right division of responsibility.

Worth stating explicitly, because it is what makes this safe to merge: the item's *fate* is unchanged from before this PR. A budget-exhausted turn previously emitted `turn_completed`, so recovery already dropped it as "processed OK". What changes is that the drop is now visible and correctly labelled instead of being recorded as a success. So there is no new work loss, no retry storm, and the telemetry gap #983 was filed for is closed.

Verified locally on this head: `test_poller_recovery.py`, `test_turn_logger.py`, `test_feedback.py`, `test_agent.py` → **323 passed**. CI green on all five checks.

Everything from my previous review still holds — the actual-denial gate (so a soft warning stays a success), `tool_call_count` on both the TurnRecord and the terminal events, and failure side effects staying gated on a real exception.

One coordination note, not a change request: your CHANGELOG line landed under `## [Unreleased]`, which is correct against current `main`. I have uncommitted release-prep locally that renames that section to `## [0.7.0]`, so I will fold your entry into the 0.7.0 `Changed` list when I commit rather than asking you to move it. Nothing for you to do.

Approving; merging once this is the head CI ran against.

payload.title: Worklink #991: authz: authorized argv does not determine the executed program — bare argv[0] resolved against an agent-writable PATH in 3 of 4 shell profiles

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
This does the main thing correctly: `parse_service_shell_argv` now ends with `return _maintenance_pinned_execution_argv(argv) if allowed else None`, so all four profiles bind an absolute executable instead of only `maintenance`. The two tests I asked for are both here and are the right shape — `test_every_service_shell_profile_returns_absolute_executables` asserts the invariant per profile across a representative sample of every admitted command (that is what stops a future profile addition from silently reintroducing this), and `test_admitted_service_shell_command_without_pin_fails_closed` proves an admitted-but-unpinned command is denied rather than falling back to PATH.

Adding `.venv` to `_STATIC_SERVICE_PROTECTED_WRITE_NAMES` answers the concern I was about to raise about the `pytest` pin. Pinning `pytest` to `/workspace/mimir/.venv/bin/pytest` — a file owned by the container's `mimir` user, inside the configured RW root — would otherwise have been zero protection, since `resolve(strict=True)` and `is_file()` are both satisfied by a planted regular file. Verified at this head that the write side now denies `<repo-rw-root>/.venv/bin/pytest` and `/.venv/bin/node`, where merged `main` admits both. That closes it.

Also a good companion catch: `_is_pytest_argv` switching to `Path(argv[0]).name` keeps #1186's `PYTEST_ADDOPTS`/`PYTEST_PLUGINS` scrub firing now that argv[0] is an absolute path — without that, the pinning would have silently disabled an existing protection.

**Blocking — the `npm` pin does not pin the program that actually runs.**

`"npm": Path("/usr/lib/node_modules/npm/bin/npm-cli.js")` is not an executable; in the container it is a 54-byte script whose first line is:

```
#!/usr/bin/env node
```

So exec'ing it hands off to `env`, which resolves **`node` via PATH** — and `direct_exec_env` still puts `/workspace/mimir/.venv/bin` first. The effective program for every `npm ci` / `npm test` is therefore PATH-resolved, which is exactly the property this issue exists to remove; it has moved from argv[0] down one level to the interpreter. The `.venv` write denial makes it much harder to exploit today (I confirmed `.venv/bin/node` is denied at this head), but that is a second control compensating for the first being incomplete, and it leaves any non-file-tool write path — `uv sync` recreating `.venv/bin`, an image change, a future root — as the residual.

Fix: invoke npm through its pinned interpreter, `["/usr/bin/node", "/usr/lib/node_modules/npm/bin/npm-cli.js", …]`, with `/usr/bin/node` itself in the pin table (it exists there as a root-owned regular file — I checked). Then no part of the npm invocation is PATH-resolved.

Worth adopting as a general invariant while you are in here, because it would have caught both this and the `pytest` case automatically: **a pin target must resolve outside every configured service-writable root, and a pinned script's interpreter must itself be pinned.** A test asserting the first half over the whole pin table is cheap and would fail loudly the next time someone pins into `.venv`.

One scope note: the `.venv` write-side addition arguably belongs to #989 rather than here. I am not asking you to move it — it is a genuine improvement and it makes the `pytest` pin defensible — but please mention it on #989 so that issue's remaining scope stays accurate.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Both items resolved, and the general invariant I suggested is now enforced in code rather than documented — which is the part I care about most, because it is what stops the next pin from recreating this.

**npm interpreter: closed.** `_MAINTENANCE_PINNED_SCRIPT_INTERPRETERS = {"npm": "node"}` with a `"node": Path("/usr/bin/node")` pin, and `_maintenance_pinned_execution_argv` emits `[interpreter, script, *args]`. Verified the shape directly:

```
npm ci --ignore-scripts  ->  <node> /…/npm/bin/npm-cli.js ci --ignore-scripts
pytest -q tests          ->  <python> -m pytest -q tests
gh pr view 1 --json …    ->  <gh> pr view 1 --json title
ls -la                   ->  <ls> -la
```

The `#!/usr/bin/env node` shebang can no longer select the interpreter, so nothing in the npm invocation is PATH-resolved. Requiring a script pin to *name* its interpreter — and failing closed when it does not (`test_pinned_script_without_pinned_interpreter_fails_closed`) — is better than special-casing npm, since the next script pin cannot forget.

**pytest: fixed, and the reasoning is sound.** Moving off the service-writable `.venv/bin/pytest` entry point to `[Path(sys.executable).resolve(), "-m", "pytest", …]` removes the writable target entirely. I checked the production consequence, since this pin is computed rather than literal: in the live container `/workspace/mimir/.venv/bin/python` resolves to `/usr/local/bin/python3.11` — root-owned, executable, and outside `/workspace/mimir` — so the pin is valid there and the writable-root invariant will not reject it. `npm-cli.js` also carries the exec bit in the image, which the new `os.access(..., os.X_OK)` check requires.

**The invariant is real.** `_maintenance_resolved_pin` rejects a pin that `_maintenance_pin_is_service_writable` reports as inside a configured service-writable root, failing closed with the distinct fingerprint. Tested by pointing the `ls` pin at `<repo-rw-root>/.venv/bin/planted`:

```
maintenance_pinned_executable_missing command=ls expected=…/.venv/bin/planted
  error=pin resolves within a configured service-writable root
```

`test_every_production_service_shell_pin_targets_outside_write_roots` asserts it across the whole table, which is exactly the check that would have caught both the original `pytest` entry and any future one. The added `resolve(strict=True) != expected` symlink rejection and the executable-bit check close the two adjacent ways a pin could point somewhere unintended.

Local suites on this head: `test_access_control.py`, `test_shell_env.py`, `test_information_flow.py`, `test_tool_registry.py` → **562 passed, 0 failed**.

Approving; merging once the pytest jobs finish. Please do mention the `.venv` write-side addition on #989 so that issue's remaining scope stays accurate — it is still the right place for reconstructing the trusted PATH, since pinning now covers the profiles but any non-profile bare-name exec would still resolve against a venv-first PATH.

payload.title: Worklink #984: authz: service principals can write .git metadata (hooks) — deferred code execution on ordinary git operations

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
This is the right size for the problem — two lines in the shared helper, applying to every adapter that reuses it, with no second copy of the logic. Verified against each acceptance criterion rather than reading the tests, driving both the static adapter and a real heartbeat principal's dynamic adapter:

| path | dynamic | static |
|---|---|---|
| `<repo>/.git/hooks/pre-commit` | deny | deny |
| `<repo>/.git/config` | deny | deny |
| `<repo>/.GIT/hooks/x` (casing) | deny | deny |
| `<repo>/.git./hooks/x` (trailing dot) | deny | deny |
| `<home>/state/repo/.git/hooks/post-merge` | deny | deny |
| `<home>/memory/repo/.git/x` | deny | deny |
| `<repo>/.gitignore`, `<repo>/.gitattributes` | ADMIT | ADMIT |
| `<repo>/src/x.py`, `state/reports/x.md`, `memory/issues/x.md` | ADMIT | ADMIT |
| `<home>/memory/core/x.md` | deny | deny |

The `part.rstrip(".") == ".git"` addition covers the trailing-dot variant, and the existing lowercase normalisation in the loop already handled `.GIT` — so both bypasses from the review criteria are closed.

**The symlink case works.** I pointed `<home>/state/sneaky` at `<repo>/.git/hooks`, so the lexical parts contain no `.git` while the resolved path does. Both adapters deny — confirming the denial rides the resolved check, not just the lexical one, which is the property that makes this more than a string filter.

**No legitimate service write is caught.** I checked the one case that worried me: mimir installs a pre-commit secret-scan hook into `<home>/.git/hooks/`, which would be exactly the kind of thing a blanket `.git` denial could break. `mimir/git_bootstrap.py` writes it with plain Python IO (`Path.open`, `os.open`/`os.fdopen`) rather than the authorized `write_file`/`edit_file` tools, so it bypasses the sink adapters entirely and is unaffected. Same for `git clone`/`worktree add` writing their own `.git/config` — that is git's own IO, not a tool call.

Leaving `.gitignore` and `.gitattributes` admitted is the correct call and the docs now say why. `.gitattributes` can *select* a diff or filter driver but cannot *define* one — definitions live in config, which is denied — and #1188's injected `--no-ext-diff --no-textconv` plus per-driver `filter.<driver>.<kind>=` overrides neutralise the drivers anyway. So admitting it costs nothing while keeping ordinary repo work possible.

Local suites: `tests/test_access_control.py tests/test_readonly_backend.py` → **383 passed, 0 failed**.

Approving; merging once the pytest jobs finish.

payload.title: Worklink #987: read policy: symlinked read roots never match (macOS /tmp denied; literal root vs resolved target)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
This fixes the reported behaviour and keeps the containment boundary intact, which was the part I was most concerned about.

The approach is the right one: rather than replacing the roots with their resolved forms — which would have collapsed the lexical and resolved checks into one and weakened the symlink-escape guard — it carries both as `root_pairs`, so lexical root selection still uses the operator's spelling while containment compares resolved-to-resolved. That preserves the security tail from #1174/#977 instead of trading it for portability.

Verified locally on macOS, where the bug reproduces:

- `test_non_admin_read_allows_configured_scopes` → **3 passed**, including the `[tmp]` case that fails on `main`.
- `tests/test_access_control.py tests/test_readonly_backend.py` → **304 passed, 0 failed**. Worth calling out: that clears the pre-existing failure entirely, so a full local run on this platform is now clean rather than permanently one-short.

The three new tests are precisely the cases the review criteria asked for — a child of a symlinked root admitted, an escape out of a symlinked root denied, and a protected path under a symlinked root still denied. That last one is the one that would have caught a lazy fix, so I am glad it is there.

One non-blocking observation. The new loop re-parses `MIMIR_FILE_TOOL_ROOTS` with its own `rpartition(":")` / `{"ro","rw"}` logic alongside the canonical `_parse_file_tool_roots`, which means two parsers for one format. It is safe as written, because a re-parsed entry is only accepted when `root.resolve() in configured_path_set` — so a spelling the canonical parser rejected cannot sneak in a root. But the two can drift if the format grows (a third mode, a quoted path, a Windows-style colon). If you touch this again, having `_parse_file_tool_roots` return the raw spelling alongside the canonical path would leave one parser and delete the loop; not worth a revision on its own.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #986: session boundary: unfinished-work summaries assert stale artifact state (merged PR described as open; turns re-verify finished work)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
This does what the leaf asked and the design choices are the right ones. Verified against tonight's actual stale text rather than only the tests — feeding the real preamble strings through `validate_unfinished_work` with an injected lookup:

- "PR #1187 remains OPEN at head 914c409a… CHANGES_REQUESTED remains current" with #1187 reported `MERGED` → **dropped**. That is the exact false claim that rode along in the 01:54 and 02:04 turns, so the motivating case is closed.
- "PR #1188 remains open awaiting revision" with `OPEN` → kept unchanged.
- Lookup raising → all three items **kept** and marked `[unverified]`, which is the correct fail-open direction.

The parts I checked specifically because they are easy to get wrong, all correct:

- **Offline paths stay offline.** Validation is wired only in `agent.py`, gated by `has_validatable_unfinished_work`, and `test_plain_rendering_does_not_validate_or_call_network` pins `subprocess.run` to an assertion — so `mimir stats` and rendering cannot reach the network.
- **Sync IO stays sync, with the async caller wrapping it.** `await asyncio.to_thread(validate_unfinished_work, boundaries)` is the convention here rather than making the whole path async.
- **Bounded.** `timeout=15` on the batched `gh api graphql`, `timeout=3` on `git remote get-url`, one request for the whole batch, `MAX_UNFINISHED_LOOKUPS = 20` with over-cap items failing open as `[unverified]` rather than being dropped unseen.
- **Query construction is injection-safe**: `json.dumps` for owner/name and `int()` for numbers, so a crafted item text cannot break out of the GraphQL literal.
- **Terminal-only drops.** `_artifact_is_terminal` requires `CLOSED`/`MERGED` for a PR and `CLOSED` for an issue, and the `__typename` guard means a number that resolves to an Issue is not read as a PullRequest state. `None` never counts as resolved, so an ambiguous or failed lookup preserves the item.
- **Extraction covers the bare forms, not just URLs** — `_PR_REF_RE`, `_ISSUE_REF_RE`, `_COMMIT_REF_RE` and `_LOCAL_PUSH_CLAIM_RE` match "PR #1187", "commit 2f778518d", "head 914c409a…" and "locally committed … but not pushed", which is what the real summaries actually contain.

One observation rather than a request: `_item_is_terminal` keys commit/branch evidence on the literal sentinel `"REMOTE"`, and the unit tests inject that string directly, so a future change to `_lookup_github_artifacts`' response mapping could silently stop dropping unpushed claims without any test failing. I checked the current mapping and it is correct (`__typename == "Commit"` → `"REMOTE"`, `ref` present → `"REMOTE"`), so there is nothing to fix now — but if you touch that mapping later, add a case that exercises it end-to-end from a fake `gh` payload instead of from an injected status.

Approving; will merge once the pytest jobs finish.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #985: pollers: changes-requested reminder is emission-based, not outcome-based (completed turn with no commit waits 75 min; batching starved the tool budget)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The attempt-accounting half of this is well built. It reuses `REVIEW_REQUEST_MAX_ATTEMPTS` rather than inventing a second mechanism, the migration guards are careful (legacy bare-sha *and* structured-without-`attempts` both migrate as attempt 1, so a cursor upgrade cannot fan out across every tracked PR), a head change resets the attempt budget and correctly bypasses the stale `last_reminded` so a still-blocked push gets an immediate fresh series, and `batch_size: 1` is canonical so a skill update cannot restore the batching that starved the tool budget. Tests cover the cases I asked for.

Two blocking items, the first of which comes from data I gathered after filing the issue.

**Blocking 1 — attempt accounting is delivery-blind, so a backlogged queue can permanently silence a stuck PR.**

The cap counts *emissions*, not deliveries. Measured on the live box tonight, after the leaf was filed: the 02:30 cycle emitted reminders for #1188/#1189/#1190 and `event_queued` landed at 02:30:14 on `poller:github-activity` — and **20+ minutes later no turn for that channel had started** (its previous turn was 02:11:17, while a discord turn ran 02:44:08–02:44:28 and worklink claimed other work at 02:40:04). The queue holding it is in-memory with no persisted artifact.

Now apply this PR to that timeline. Attempt 1 is recorded at 02:30 for work that never ran. At `eligible_after` the poller emits attempt 2, then attempt 3, then `pr_changes_requested_gave_up`, and parks at `cap + 1` — where the only re-arm is `prior_head != head_sha`, i.e. a push. So three undelivered reminders exhaust the budget and the PR goes **permanently silent until someone pushes to it**, which is precisely the thing nobody will do, because the reminder is what would have prompted it. That is a worse failure than the unbounded-retry behaviour it replaces: the old code was noisy, this one goes quiet on the exact PRs that are most stuck.

The issue's criterion was "a reminder was emitted, **the attempt is no longer in flight**, and `head_sha` is unchanged." The in-flight half is not implemented, and it is the half that makes the cap safe. Two workable routes:

- Count an attempt only with evidence the turn actually ran. The framework already records this: `turn_completed` events carry `source_id` (e.g. `poller:github-activity:<ts>:batch:N`) **and** an `items[]` array whose entries hold `event_type` and `number` — I verified that shape directly in `<home>/logs/events.jsonl` for the 01:54:02 and 02:04:28 turns. So a `pr_changes_requested_stale` item for PR N can be matched to a completed turn without new framework plumbing, and an emission with no matching completed turn should not consume the budget.
- Or keep the emission-based cap but make the parked state re-armable by something other than a push — a new blocking review, or a long backstop interval — so "we gave up" can never be permanent for an unresolved PR.

Either is acceptable; what is not acceptable is a cap whose exhaustion is both silent-forever and reachable without a single reminder having been delivered.

**Blocking 2 — the 15-minute slack turns the hourly cadence into a 45-minute one, and the docstring says otherwise.**

`eligible_after = reminder_interval - CHANGES_REQUESTED_REMINDER_SLACK` = 60m − 15m = **45m**. Cycles fall at +15/+30/+45/+60 relative to the previous reminder, so the first eligible cycle is exactly +45m and reminders now fire every 45 minutes. The comment says "still eligible on the intended hourly cycle" and the line you removed explicitly justified the old value as "without making normal 15-minute polls noisy" — so the code and its stated intent disagree, in the direction of more noise.

A full cron period is more slack than the problem needs. The real defect (see my correction comment on #985 — the "missed by 4 seconds / 75 minutes" example in the issue body is **wrong**, the 02:30 cycle did fire at 60m3s) is that `observed_at` is sampled a few seconds into each run, so the +60m comp

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Both blocking items are resolved, and the second one is fixed at the right layer.

**Cadence (item 2): fixed.** `CHANGES_REQUESTED_REMINDER_SLACK` is now `timedelta(minutes=1)`, sized to the jitter rather than to the poll interval, so `eligible_after` is 59m and the cycle landing at ~+60m ± seconds fires deterministically while the hourly floor is preserved. The boundary tests moved to 58:59 / 59:00 / 59:01 accordingly, which is the right way to pin it.

**Delivery-blind cap (item 1): fixed via the re-armable park.** This takes the second route I offered and implements it carefully:

- On reaching the cap it emits `pr_changes_requested_gave_up` once, bumps to `cap + 1`, and — the detail that makes the backstop meaningful — sets `last_reminded_at = observed_at_iso` so the 24-hour clock starts at give-up rather than at the last reminder.
- While inside `CHANGES_REQUESTED_GAVE_UP_BACKSTOP` the entry parks with attempts preserved.
- Past it, `prior_attempts = 0` and a fresh bounded series begins at attempt 1.

So a series whose turns were all stranded in the in-memory queue can no longer silence an unresolved PR permanently, which was the failure mode I objected to, and the cap still bounds noise. The comment naming the actual cause ("emission is not delivery") is accurate — that is exactly what tonight's three rounds demonstrated.

`SKILL.md` documenting the cursor shape, the hourly floor, the bounded series, and the backstop is a good addition; that contract was previously only inferable from the code.

Verified locally on this head rather than trusting CI alone: `mimir/optional-skills/github-poller/tests` → **56 passed**, including `test_attempt_cap_gives_up_once_then_rearms_after_backstop` and `test_seconds_after_boundary_reemits_on_intended_cycle`.

One observation, explicitly not a request. `pr_changes_requested_gave_up` goes to `events.jsonl` via the signal path without spawning a turn, so a give-up is invisible unless a dashboard or a human reads the log. Worst case is now bounded at 24 hours of silence on a stuck PR instead of forever, and this matches the existing `pr_review_request_gave_up` behaviour, so I would not change it here — but if we ever want a stuck PR to be impossible to lose, surfacing that signal (operator alert or a chainlink comment) is the remaining gap, and it belongs with #983's turn-outcome work rather than in this leaf.

Approving; merging once the pytest jobs finish.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Making these two environment-independent is the right fix — better than the workaround I had been using locally (uninstalling the optional extra to match base CI). Verified the claim directly, running the same `-k` selection three ways with the real adapter distribution installed and removed:

| checkout | adapter | result |
|---|---|---|
| `main` | installed | **2 failed** |
| this PR | installed | 2 passed |
| this PR | absent | 2 passed |

Both tests also keep their teeth: if `_resolve_model` ignored the injected failure conditions it would construct the fake and return `"SHOULD_NOT_CONSTRUCT"` with no exception, and if the hook-installer's `RuntimeError` were swallowed nothing would raise — either way `pytest.raises` fails. That is the property that matters and it survives.

**Blocking — `test_resolve_model_claude_code_fails_closed_without_adapter` no longer exercises the without-adapter path, and nothing else does either.**

Injecting `fake_lcc` into `sys.modules` makes `import langchain_claude_code` *succeed*, so both statements in the `try` at `mimir/agent.py:742-744` now pass and the raise comes from `assert_supported_langchain_claude_code_adapter` instead — the incompatible-adapter branch. The assertion does not notice, because `_langchain_claude_code_patches.py:127-135` and `agent.py:745-756` both put `pip install 'mimir-agent[claude-code]'` in their message, so `"mimir-agent[claude-code]" in msg` is satisfied by either. The test name, the docstring, and the assertion all still read as "adapter absent" while the code under test is "adapter present but unsupported."

The consequence is a real coverage loss, not just a naming problem: after this PR the `except ImportError` branch at `agent.py:745-756` is exercised by **no test in the suite**. In a no-adapter environment the fake module is injected, and in an adapter environment the real module imports — so that branch is unreachable from tests in both. I searched for anything that forces genuine absence (`setitem(sys.modules, ..., None)`, an import blocker, a meta-path finder) and there is nothing, in `tests/test_agent.py` or `tests/test_model_resolution.py`. That branch is the one that fires in the default deployment where the extra is not installed, so it is the one I would least like to leave uncovered.

The fix is smaller than what is here. For the absence scenario, `monkeypatch.setitem(sys.modules, "langchain_claude_code", None)` makes `import langchain_claude_code` raise `ImportError` deterministically in both environments — no fake module needed, and the test name stays true. Then either tighten the assertion to text unique to that branch (`"requires the 'claude-code' extra"`) or split this into two tests: absence hitting `agent.py`'s branch, and incompatible-adapter hitting the compat branch. Note the incompatible-adapter case is already covered by `tests/test_model_resolution.py:276` (`match="stale PyPI adapter"`), so converting this test into a second copy of it is a net loss.

**Non-blocking — `match="PreToolUse"` in the second test asserts a string the test itself raised.** Production calls `ensure_tool_enforcement_hooks_installed` at `agent.py:758` and does not wrap it, so the regex matches the message from your own `_fail_enforcement` stub rather than anything the product emits. The behavior being pinned (the error propagates out of `resolve_model_from_config` instead of being caught and downgraded) is worth a test and this does pin it — but the `match=` gives the impression of checking a product message. Dropping the `match=`, or asserting the propagation directly, would say what you mean.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The core of this is right, and I verified it by building a real heartbeat principal against a temp home and driving the adapter directly rather than reading the tests. All 17 cases behave as the leaf specifies:

| target | result |
|---|---|
| `memory/issues/x.md`, `memory/channels/c1/n.md`, `state/reports/x.md` | ADMITTED |
| `state/triggers/heartbeat/x` (per-trigger root), `<repo>/src/x.py` (repo RW root) | ADMITTED |
| `memory/core/x.md`, `memory/core/sub/x.md` | denied |
| `.env`, `state/config.json`, `state/credentials.json`, `state/x.key`, `.mimir/x`, `prompts/heartbeat.md` | denied |
| `x.md` (home root) | denied |
| `state/../.env`, `memory/../prompts/p.md` (traversal) | denied |

Reusing `_is_static_service_protected_write_path` with `under_memory_root` — rather than re-deriving the carve-outs — is the right call, and applying the protected check on both the lexical relative path and the post-`resolve_within_roots` path is what makes the symlink case hold. `memory/core/**` staying denied means core memory is still proposal-only.

Worth calling out that this **tightens** something I expected to find loose: on `main` the `exact_roots` adapter admits `<repo>/.git/config`, and at this head that is denied, because the shared helper's `config` protected name now applies to the repo RW roots too. Good outcome that I do not think was the stated goal.

**Blocking — the PR leaves `exact_roots` registered with no production users, and it is the weaker of the two adapters.**

`build_trigger_service_principal` was the only caller, and this PR repoints it at `trigger_service_write_roots`. At this head `"exact_roots"` appears exactly twice in the source: the `def` at `mimir/access_control.py:1014` and the registry entry at `:1157`. Nothing else in `mimir/` constructs a policy with it, no poller manifest names it (I checked `/mimir-home/skills/` and `/mimir-home/state/` on the live box — the only hits are worklink transcripts, i.e. logs of this work), and the single remaining test reference builds a `spawn_open_code` policy shape production no longer emits.

That matters beyond tidiness: a registered adapter is reachable by name, and this one is measurably weaker than its replacement — it admits `<repo>/.git/config`, which the new adapter denies. Leaving it in place means any future code path or stale policy that names `exact_roots` silently gets the weaker check, and the difference is exactly the protection this PR just gained. We do not keep shims for pre-release surfaces, so please delete `_target_within_exact_roots` and its registry entry in this PR and retarget the test at `tests/test_access_control.py:2495` to the adapter production actually uses. If you believe there is a live consumer I have missed, say which and I will withdraw this.

**Not blocking, and deliberately out of scope here — `.git/hooks/**` remains writable.** `<repo>/.git/hooks/pre-commit` is ADMITTED at this head, as is `state/<some-repo>/.git/hooks/pre-commit` under the newly widened tree. Git executes hooks on commit/checkout/merge, so a write there is deferred code execution — the same shape as the config-driven execution I raised on #1188, from the write side. I am explicitly **not** asking you to fix it here: the same gap exists on `main` for both adapters, and this leaf's review criteria say not to change the static-principal adapter's behavior, which a shared-helper fix necessarily would. The coherent fix is to add `.git` to `_STATIC_SERVICE_PROTECTED_WRITE_NAMES` so no service principal writes git metadata under any adapter — one word, but it touches static behavior, so it belongs in its own leaf. I am filing that chainlink and will link it here.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #922: authz: purpose-built maintenance shell profile for scheduled/heartbeat principals (scheduler_read_only denies shipped-prompt commands; 181 would-blocks)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The mechanism reuse is right: one parser extended, shared guards untouched (control characters, shlex, leading-tilde, argv-as-execution-artifact), destructive shapes denied (`rm`, `git push --force`, `git config`, `npm ci`, `pip install` all verified denied against this branch), and the principal scoping is exactly as the leaf specifies — the static swap is on `canonical="scheduler", trigger="scheduled_tick"`, the dynamic path adds `maintenance` only for `profile == "heartbeat"`, and `github`→`repo_review` / `custom`→`scheduler_read_only` / `upgrade`→`upgrade_workspace` are untouched. Docs are updated. Two blocking items.

**Blocking 1 — `git -C` takes any absolute path, and the admitted git subcommands execute commands named in git config.**

`git status`, `git diff` and `git log -p` are not inert readers. They run programs named in configuration that the argv allow-list never sees. Verified on this branch, in a scratch repo with `diff.external`, `diff.<driver>.textconv` (selected by a `.gitattributes` line) and `core.fsmonitor` set:

- `git -C <repo> diff` → executed **both** `diff.external` and the `textconv` driver
- `git -C <repo> status` → executed `core.fsmonitor`
- `git -C <repo> log -p` → executed the `textconv` driver

and all three argvs are ADMITTED by `_target_matches_maintenance_shell_command`, with `-C` pointed anywhere on the filesystem — the helper only checks that the path does not start with `-`.

To be clear about severity, since I could not complete the escalation end-to-end: today's write policy blocks the config files I could reach. `_STATIC_SERVICE_PROTECTED_WRITE_NAMES` catches any path part named `config`, so `<repo>/.git/config` is denied; home-root dotfiles (`.gitconfig`, `.gitattributes`) are denied by `_target_within_static_service_write_roots`; and `HOME=/root` on the live box, outside `MIMIR_FILE_TOOL_ROOTS`, so the global-config route is not reachable either. So this is defense-in-depth, not a live exploit, and I am not claiming otherwise.

I still think it must be fixed here, for two reasons. First, the barrier lives in a *different* subsystem and only covers config written *through the file tools* — `git clone` and `git worktree add` write `.git/config` themselves, and there are 8+ such clones under `/mimir-home/scratch/**` on the live box right now, created by mimir's own review tooling. "The write adapter protects `config`" is not a property of those repos. Second, #982/#1189 is widening dynamic-principal write scope concurrently, so the thing holding this closed is moving underneath it. A profile whose safety depends on data the profile does not control is the same shape as the pytest `-p`/`PYTEST_ADDOPTS` problem #1186 just closed, and the fix here is equally mechanical.

Two changes, both cheap:

1. Constrain `-C` to the configured roots (home + `MIMIR_FILE_TOOL_ROOTS`) instead of accepting any path.
2. Neutralize config-driven execution in the argv you return — the returned argv *is* the execution artifact, so this is the payoff of that contract. Verified this combination suppresses all three markers:

```
git -C <root> -c core.fsmonitor= -c diff.external= --no-pager <sub> ... --no-ext-diff --no-textconv
```

Note `--no-ext-diff --no-textconv` alone is **not** sufficient — `core.fsmonitor` still fired from `git status` in my test, so the `-c core.fsmonitor=` injection is required, not optional. Both flags are already in your allow-list as optional; make them injected rather than permitted.

**Blocking 2 — the profile admits ~1% of the maintenance commands this leaf exists to unblock, and the PR does not say so.**

I extracted every shell command issued on `trigger=heartbeat` / `scheduled*` turns from `/mimir-home/logs/turns.jsonl` (9,135 distinct, 10,140 occurrences) and ran each through `parse_service_shell_argv(..., "maintenance")` on this branch:

**69 distinct admitted / 9,066 denied — by occurrence, 100 admitted / 10,040 denied (99% still denied).**

The dominant cause is not a gap

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Re-issuing this change request to re-trigger remediation — no new findings, and nothing here supersedes my earlier review on this PR. Please work from that review's blocking items as written.

Context so the history reads correctly: the poller's stuck-PR reminder fired for this PR at 01:30 and again at 02:30, and both attempts were batched with the other two open PRs into a single turn sharing one 200-call tool budget. Neither round produced commits on any of the three. `batch_size` for the github-activity poller is now 1, so this PR gets its own turn and its own budget. #985 is the structural fix for the reminder logic and #1191 is its PR.

The blocking items on this PR are unchanged — see my review above.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
This is a strong revision and it goes well beyond what I asked on the first item. Confirming what now holds, verified by executing the authorized argv rather than reading it:

- **`-C` is confined.** `git -C /etc status` → denied; `git -C <configured-root> status` → admitted.
- **Config-driven execution is dead.** I re-armed the scratch repo with `diff.external`, a `.gitattributes`-selected `textconv` driver, and `core.fsmonitor`, then executed the argv the profile returns for `diff`, `status` and `log -p`: **no marker files created**. The injected `-c core.fsmonitor= -c core.hooksPath=/dev/null -c diff.external= -c protocol.allow=never --no-pager --no-optional-locks`, plus `--no-ext-diff --no-textconv` on diff-producing subcommands and the per-driver `filter.<driver>.<kind>=` overrides, covers more than the three vectors I demonstrated — `core.hooksPath` and `protocol.allow` were not in my list and both are real.
- **All four cheap gaps closed**, verified with `-C <root>`: `log --oneline -5` (the `-<digits>` shorthand), `branch --show-current`, `chainlink issue ready --json`, and absolute-path executables.
- **Destructive shapes still denied**: `push`, `commit`, `config --global`, `rm -rf`, `npm ci`, `chainlink issue close`.
- **The fail-closed binding in `budget_gate.py` is the right instinct** — substituting `/usr/bin/false` when direct-argv binding fails, instead of falling back to `bash -lc`, means a probe race cannot silently reopen the unvalidated shell surface.
- Rewriting the four prompt templates to the admitted forms is the honest answer to acceptance criterion 6, and the docs quoting the 10,140/100 measurement shows the corpus finding was actually engaged with rather than worked around.

**Blocking — `gh` and the read-only utilities keep a bare `argv[0]`, and the PATH they are resolved against is agent-writable.**

This PR establishes pinning as the standard for exactly this reason (`_MAINTENANCE_GIT_EXECUTABLE = "/usr/bin/git"`, and chainlink pinned to `/usr/local/bin/chainlink` with a strict `resolve(strict=True)` symlink check, above the comment "a model-supplied path must never select an arbitrary executable"). But the returned argv for the other commands is still the bare name:

```
gh pr list --state open   ->  gh pr list --state open
ls -la                    ->  ls -la
grep -n foo /etc/hosts    ->  grep -n foo /etc/hosts
```

Those are exec'd with `shell=False` against `direct_exec_env`, which prepends `os.path.dirname(sys.executable)` to `PATH` (`mimir/tools/_shell_env.py:60`). In the live container that directory is **`/workspace/mimir/.venv/bin`**, which sits inside the configured RW root `/workspace/mimir:rw`. And the write side admits it — checked against the merged #1189 adapter with a real heartbeat principal:

```
<repo-rw-root>/.venv/bin/gh    -> ADMITTED
<repo-rw-root>/.venv/bin/ls    -> ADMITTED
<repo-rw-root>/.venv/bin/grep  -> ADMITTED
```

No path part is protected, so nothing stops the write. That completes a chain: a service principal writes `/workspace/mimir/.venv/bin/gh`, a later maintenance turn runs an admitted `gh pr list …`, PATH resolution picks the planted file ahead of `/usr/bin/gh`, and the profile has executed attacker-chosen code while reporting that it authorized a read-only GitHub query. It is the same defect class the `-C` confinement and the config neutralization just closed, reached through argv[0] instead of through config.

Please pin the remaining executables the same way you pinned git and chainlink — resolve each admitted command to its absolute path (`/usr/bin/gh`, `/bin/ls` or `/usr/bin/ls`, `/usr/bin/grep`, `/usr/bin/wc`, `/bin/pwd`) with the same `resolve(strict=True)` identity check, and return that in the argv. Two notes on doing it well:

payload.body:
**Blocking 1 is resolved.** `pytest (3.11)` and `pytest (3.12)` are both SUCCESS. `tests/test_information_flow.py` and `tests/test_tool_registry.py` are updated, the new `tests/conftest.py` `maintenance_git_home` fixture gives those tests a real Git root, and bare `git` stays denied — I re-verified at this head that `git status --short` and `git log --oneline -5` are refused while `git -C <configured-root> status --short` is admitted, that `-C /etc` and a relative `-C state` are both denied, and that the config-driven exec vectors remain dead (armed `diff.external`, `textconv`, `core.fsmonitor`; executed the returned argv for `diff`/`status`/`log -p`; no markers). payload.title: Account for Claude Opus 5 context window

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting one addition — the value is right, but the ID form Claude Code actually reports still falls through to the 200k default.

**Verified correct:** bare `claude-opus-5` does have a **1M-token context window**, and for Opus 5 that is both the default *and* the maximum — no beta header, no long-context premium, and no 200k variant to opt out of. So `"claude-opus-5": 1_000_000` is the right entry, and the rationale (unknown-model fallback overstating utilization 5×) holds.

**Missing: the `[1m]` variant key.** `[1m]` is not an API model ID — it's a deployment/routing identifier surfaced by the **Claude Code** surface (same class as `-fast`, `-200k`, dated snapshots). This file already keys on that form deliberately — `usage_stats.py:54` carries `"claude-opus-4-7[1m]": 1_000_000` — and `context_window_for` does an exact-match lookup (`_MODEL_CONTEXT_WINDOWS.get(model, _DEFAULT_CONTEXT_WINDOW)`) with no bracket stripping or normalization.

So a `claude-code:*` deployment reporting `claude-opus-5[1m]` — which is exactly what that surface emits — misses the new entry and lands on the 200k default, reproducing the very 5× understatement this PR fixes. The `CONTEXT_1M_BETA` prefix path doesn't rescue it either: that branch requires the `context-1m-2025-08-07` beta header, which Opus 5 doesn't use since 1M is native.

Please either add the bracketed key alongside the bare one:

```python
    # Opus 5.x
    "claude-opus-5": 1_000_000,
    "claude-opus-5[1m]": 1_000_000,
```

…or (preferable, since it fixes the whole class) normalize a trailing `[...]` variant suffix in `context_window_for` before the dict lookup, so any future `<model>[1m]` resolves to its base entry without a second key. Add a regression assertion for the bracketed form either way — the existing `claude-opus-4-7[1m]` entry shows this is a live ID shape, not a hypothetical.

Lower-confidence side note, pre-existing and not introduced here: the retained comment says bare `claude-opus-4-7` is the 200k variant unless the request opts into the 1M beta, but current model documentation lists Opus 4.7 at 1M context natively. Worth re-checking that line against the docs while you're in this file — if it's stale, the `CONTEXT_1M_BETA` special-case may be dead code.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The bracket-normalization fix is right, and it resolves my earlier blocker: `claude-opus-5[1m]` now resolves to 1M, malformed variants (`[1m]]`, `[1m][fast]`) fall back to the default rather than being silently mis-parsed, and the tests cover both. Thank you for the `"[" not in base_model` guard — that is the correct way to reject double-bracket ids.

**Blocking — moving the beta check after the dict lookup regresses currently-shipping models.**

On `main` the `CONTEXT_1M_BETA` + prefix check ran *before* the lookup, so any `claude-opus-4-*` / `claude-sonnet-4-*` id got the 1M cap when the beta was active, whether or not it was an exact dict key. At this head the function returns `_DEFAULT_CONTEXT_WINDOW` on a lookup miss and never reaches the beta check. Measured on this branch versus `main`, both with `betas=[CONTEXT_1M_BETA]`:

| model | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `claude-opus-4-8` | 1,000,000 | **200,000** |
| `claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929` | 1,000,000 | **200,000** |
| `claude-opus-4-7` | 1,000,000 | 1,000,000 |
| `claude-opus-5` | 200,000 | 1,000,000 (the fix) |

Both regressions are reachable today, not hypothetical:

- **`claude-opus-4-8` is a shipping model with a native 1M window and is absent from `_MODEL_CONTEXT_WINDOWS`.** It was covered only by the beta-prefix path, which this change removes.
- **Date-suffixed ids reach this function.** The dict's own `"claude-haiku-4-5-20251001"` entry is the evidence; any date-suffixed 4.x Opus/Sonnet id takes the same miss path.

And this is on the live path, not a dormant helper: `config.context_1m` is documented default-on (`mimir/config.py:910`), and `stats_block.py:124` appends `CONTEXT_1M_BETA` to `betas` from it, so `usage_stats.py:557` calls `context_window_for` with the beta populated on ordinary turns. The user-visible effect is that the usage block reports a 200k cap against a real 1M window, so the "current turn / cap" percentage can read well past 100% and the operator loses the headroom signal — the same class of misreporting this PR set out to fix, just relocated.

The normalization and the beta fallback are independent and both should hold. Suggested shape: normalize first, then let the beta+prefix check run on a lookup miss before returning the default —

```python
    normalized_model = model  # after variant stripping
    context_window = _MODEL_CONTEXT_WINDOWS.get(normalized_model)
    if (
        betas
        and CONTEXT_1M_BETA in betas
        and any(normalized_model.startswith(p) for p in _CONTEXT_1M_MODEL_PREFIXES)
    ):
        return 1_000_000
    return context_window if context_window is not None else _DEFAULT_CONTEXT_WINDOW
```

That keeps every behavior the new tests assert except the one that codifies the regression, so `test_context_window_1m_beta_does_not_promote_unknown_prefixed_model` needs to change with it. If the intent was deliberately to stop the beta from lifting unknown ids, that is a separate decision from adding Opus 5 and needs its own justification — it makes the cap wrong for a shipping model, so I do not think it is the right trade here.

**Second item — the sibling 1M models are still missing.** `claude-sonnet-5` and `claude-fable-5` both have native 1M windows and are absent from the dict, so they report 200k (before and after this PR — pre-existing, not caused by it). They do not match the 4.x prefixes, so nothing else rescues them. Since this PR is exactly "teach the table about the 5-series 1M windows", please add them in the same pass rather than leaving two instances of the bug you are fixing.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Both items addressed, and the beta fallback landed in the right place.

`claude-sonnet-5` and `claude-fable-5` are in the table. The beta+prefix check now runs after normalization but *before* the default fallback, so an id that is not an exact key can still be lifted — which restores the two live cases and keeps the forward-compatibility the old ordering had. The added `"[" not in normalized_model` guard is a good catch that I did not ask for: a malformed id is deliberately left unstripped, so without it the beta could have promoted something the lookup had already rejected.

Verified against this head, `beta=on / beta=off`:

| model | beta on | beta off |
|---|---|---|
| `claude-opus-4-8` | 1M | 200k |
| `claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929` | 1M | 200k |
| `claude-opus-4-7` | 1M | 200k |
| `claude-opus-5` | 1M | 1M |
| `claude-sonnet-5` / `claude-fable-5` | 1M | 1M |
| `claude-opus-5[1m]` | 1M | 1M |
| `claude-sonnet-4-6[fast]` | 1M | 200k |
| `claude-haiku-4-5` | 200k | 200k |
| `some-future-model` | 200k | 200k |
| `claude-opus-5[1m]]`, `claude-opus-4-7[1m][fast]` | 200k | 200k |

Twelve cases, no mismatches: the two regressions are gone, Opus 5 resolves bare and bracketed, malformed ids still fall back, and Haiku is not swept up by the beta.

Inverting `test_context_window_1m_beta_does_not_promote_unknown_prefixed_model` into `test_context_window_1m_beta_promotes_prefixed_model_ids` — asserting `claude-opus-4-8` and `claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929` directly — is the right way to close this out, since those two ids are now the guard against the ordering regressing again.

Approving; merging once the pytest jobs finish.

Requesting changes on two command shapes. The architecture here is excellent — genuinely better than what I specified — and I want to be clear about that before the two items.

**Verified good:**
- **The argv is the execution artifact.** `parse_service_shell_argv` rejects `;|&\`$><{}[]*?` and newlines, `shlex.split`s, rejects leading-tilde expansion (with the right nuance that `HEAD~1` is a revision, not expansion), and its docstring states the invariant explicitly — callers exec it with `shell=False`, which is what `mimir_direct_argv` does. So there is no second expansion layer to bypass the allow-list.
- **Allow-list, not deny-list**, per command *and* per subcommand, with option sets and narrow `option_prefixes`. No `gh api`, no `git push`, no `rm`, no arbitrary `npm run <script>` (only `run test`), no `git checkout -f`.
- **`git fetch` operands restricted to `origin`/`upstream`** with the reasoning recorded — catching that a URL or `ext::` remote can select a helper executable is a sharp catch I did not ask for.
- Profile assignment is correctly narrow (`repo_review` only for `profile == "github"`; research/custom stay `scheduler_read_only`, with a test pinning it), and the write half re-checks protected paths on the **lexical** relatives before resolving, so a symlinked protected component can't launder its name.

**Blocking 1 — `npm ci` must not run lifecycle scripts by default.**
`npm ci` currently permits `--ignore-scripts` but does not require it, so `preinstall`/`install`/`postinstall` from the PR's `package.json` **and from every dependency in its lockfile** execute on the operator's host. The trust chain that admits this shell in the first place is "the turn is untainted," which after #980 means the PR author passed `_github_author_is_trusted` — i.e. holds repo permissions. But repo write permission is not consent to execute arbitrary code on mimirbot: a triage/write collaborator (or a compromised collaborator account) could land a malicious `postinstall` and get host execution through a review turn. Please require `--ignore-scripts` on `npm ci` in this profile. If that genuinely breaks the factory repo's install (native deps), say so with the failing output and we'll narrow it differently (e.g. an operator-declared per-repo exception) rather than leaving scripts on by default.

**Blocking 2 — `pytest` is a blanket allow.**
`if argv[0] == "pytest": return True` (and `uv run pytest` with unvalidated tail) is the one place the per-command discipline lapses. Test files are repo code and running them is the point, so I'm not asking for much — but pytest options themselves select code and behavior: `-p <module>` loads an arbitrary plugin, `-c` / `--rootdir` / `-o addopts=…` redirect configuration, `--pdb` drops into an interactive debugger inside an autonomous turn. Please give `pytest` the same treatment as the others: an option allow-list (`-q`, `-x`, `-k`, `--tb=`, `--maxfail=`, `-m`, path operands, etc.) that at minimum excludes `-p`, `-c`, `-o`, `--rootdir`, `--pdb`, and apply it to the `uv run pytest` tail too.

Note on composition (no action needed): this profile's safety depends on the taint gate keeping shell shut for turns that ingested non-contributor content — i.e. it composes with #980. Since both remain shadow-mode until enforcement is enabled, that ordering is fine, but the two should be evaluated together at the #952 gate rather than independently.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Both blocking items are fully addressed, and the revision closed two bypasses I had not named.

**Blocking 1 — `npm ci` lifecycle scripts: fixed.** `_target_matches_npm_ci_command` now *requires* exactly one `--ignore-scripts`, restricts the rest to a small option set, and admits no operands and no `--` terminator. That is the invariant I asked for, enforced positively rather than by denylist.

**Blocking 2 — `pytest` blanket allow: fixed, and then some.** `_target_matches_pytest_command` is a proper allow-list (flags, value options with bounds-checked consumption, `=`-form prefixes) with default-deny on anything else starting with `-`, so `-p`, `-c`, `-o`, `--rootdir` and `--pdb` are all excluded. The same validator is applied to the `uv run pytest` tail. Two things here go beyond the ask and are the right instincts:

- `@file` response operands are rejected, because pytest expands them *after* authorization — the authorized argv would not be the effective argv.
- Path operands are split on `::` and required to be relative with no `..`, which keeps pytest from being pointed at an unrelated host tree to auto-import a `conftest.py` or plugin. Confining collection to the repo is the substantive half of this defense; the option list alone would not have gotten there.

**Bypasses closed beyond the review.** The argv allow-list is only as good as the environment it execs into, and `PYTEST_ADDOPTS` / `PYTEST_PLUGINS` would have reintroduced `-p`/`--pdb` unconditionally. Scrubbing them for pytest argv only (leaving unrelated commands' env intact, and leaving operator-installed entry-point plugins available) is the correct scope. The async follow-up is the subtler catch: `ShellJobRegistry.spawn` overlays onto its own inherited environment, so absence from the mapping is not removal — `direct_exec_env_overlay` emitting explicit `None` deletion markers is required, and `shell_jobs.py:241-244` does pop on `None`, so it holds end-to-end. Tests assert the markers rather than the absence, which is the assertion that actually distinguishes the two behaviors.

Coverage is present for each of these in `tests/test_access_control.py`, `tests/test_shell_env.py`, and `tests/test_shell_async_wiring.py`. All five checks green.

Approving.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #980: authz/IFC trust derivation: self-authored state tainted as untrusted active ingest blocks autonomous sinks (154 would-blocks); trust contributor PRs + allow-listed fetches

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes. The server-side derivation work here is genuinely strong; two trust classes launder untrusted content through a second hop, and one default fails open.

**Verified good:**
- Contributor identity is resolved from the **GitHub API** by parsing the canonical URL (host, `owner/repo` path, issue/PR number, and an event-type-specific fragment) and calling the matching endpoint — never from poller stdout or payload fields. `test_github_content_author_uses_api_and_ignores_payload_claim` pins exactly that.
- Fetch trust is properly bound: file must sit under `attachments/fetch-cache`, have a sidecar whose `file_path` round-trips to the same resource, a filename prefixed with `sha256(url)[:12]`, and **both** `url` and `final_url` on the approved allow-list — so a redirect can't smuggle a non-approved origin. Returning `("trusted", "active_ingest")` rather than `informational` is the right conservative call.
- `agent.py` correctly discriminates history blocks: only `assistant_message` / `system_note` are self-authored, so inbound user/external history stays untrusted.
- Sink-gate predicates and `has_untrusted_active_ingest` are untouched; docs updated.

**Blocking 1 — `turn_history` is trusted unconditionally, which launders external content.**
`protected_result_source` now returns `trusted/informational` for `domain == "turn_history"`, on the rationale that "turn records are written by Mimir, not supplied by the model/caller." That is true of the *file* but not of its *contents*. `_read_turn_record` (mimir/tools/extra.py:244) strips only `input`, `saga_atom_ids`, `usage` — it deliberately keeps `events` (tool calls **and tool results**: `fetch_url` page bodies, shell output, file reads) and `injected_inputs` (mid-turn folded external messages). So: a turn fetches a non-allow-listed page or folds an external message → that text lives in its record → a later turn calls `mimir_get_turn` → the content returns **trusted/informational** → that turn is no longer taint-gated → shell/spawn/file sinks open. This is prompt-endorsed, not hypothetical: `SAGA_SESSION_END_DEFAULT` explicitly instructs `mimir_get_turn(turn_id=...)` (mimir/templates.py:29, 227).
Fix: derive the record's integrity from the *recorded turn's own* provenance rather than from who wrote the file — e.g. stamp the turn record with whether that turn had untrusted active ingest and propagate it (unknown/absent ⇒ untrusted, fail-closed). Leaving `turn_history` untrusted is also acceptable; blanket-trusting it is not.

**Blocking 2 — framework-written state files that carry external payloads.**
`_filesystem_result_integrity` trusts any path under `<home>/memory` or `<home>/state` by first path component. For *agent*-written files this is sound, because a tainted turn's writes are themselves blocked at the file sink gate (the audit shows that firing: 19 `ifc_label_blocked:file`). But some files under `state/` are written by the **framework**, not the agent, and contain raw external event bodies — notably `state/pollers/<name>/.recovery.json`, which since #974 stashes **every** accepted poller event. Reading that back yields attacker-controlled text labeled `trusted/informational`. Please exclude framework-written payload stores from the self-authored class (an explicit deny-list of such paths, or trust only what the agent's own file tools wrote), and add a test for the recovery-stash case.

**Blocking 3 — fail-open default.** `self_authored: bool = True` (mimir/agent.py) defaults to trusted; in security code the default should be `False` so a future caller that forgets the argument fails closed. The current call site passes it explicitly, so this is a one-word change.

To be clear about scope: the operator's decision (contributor PRs trusted, allow-listed fetches trusted, self-authored state trusted) stands — this is about not extending that trust to *derived reads that embed untrusted content*. Once those three are addressed I expect to approve, though the merge

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Re-review at a53ffd7e — all three blocking items are correctly fixed. One small regression to undo, then this is good.

**Fixed:**
1. `turn_history` blanket trust is removed entirely, so turn records fall back to `untrusted/active_ingest` (the fail-closed option). The `mimir_get_turn` laundering path is closed.
2. The poller recovery stash is excluded by path (`state/pollers/*/.recovery.json` → untrusted), with the rationale recorded in the comment. Good catch keeping the exclusion narrow and fail-closed for that class.
3. `self_authored` now defaults to `False`, with explicit `self_authored=True` only at the framework-authored call sites (usage, upcoming/schedules, …). That's the right shape — opt-in trust per known-safe site rather than a trusted default.

**Blocking (small): restore the parametrize case you dropped.**
`tests/test_budget_gate_and_alias.py` lost `("get_turn", "turn_history", {"turn_id": "t-1"})` from `test_exact_protected_native_result_can_reply_to_triggering_channel`. That removes coverage of the exact provenance surface this PR changes, and it wasn't necessary: I restored the case at this head and ran it — **8 passed**. Same-channel replies aren't taint-gated, so an untrusted `turn_history` source still satisfies the assertion. Please put the case back (no other change needed).

One thing to consider, not blocking: `state/worklink/transcripts/*.json` and `state/worklink/evidence/*.json` are also framework-written payload stores under `state/`. They're internally sourced today (chainlink leaves + repo/test output), so I'm not asking for changes — but if a worklink run ever ingests external content, they'd fall into the same class as the recovery stash. Worth a comment near the exclusion list so the next person sees the boundary.

Once the case is restored I'll approve — the merge itself is the operator's call, since this widens trust.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting one change. The companion-invariant work is exactly right; one capability grant goes beyond what this leaf authorizes.

**Verified good:**
- The invariant is enforced at construction (`build_trigger_service_principal` raises when `shell_exec`/`bash_async` is granted without `bash_jobs_list`+`bash_job_output`) **and** pinned by tests on both populations — shipped manifests (`test_shipped_poller_shell_authorities_have_job_inspection_companions`) and the static principals (`test_static_shell_service_principals_have_job_inspection_companions`) — which is what the leaf asked for.
- `test_github_activity_observed_operations_are_admitted_when_enforced` covers exactly the denial set from the audit.
- No read capabilities added, and no `spawn_*` added anywhere. `task` is declared `SCOPE_CONTAINED` and requested only by a `code-execution`-tier principal, so it stays within tier.

**Blocking: drop `shell_exec` (and its `shell_process` sink) from the `synthesis` principal.**

The PR grants the session-boundary principal (`trigger=saga_session_end`, tier `SCOPED_WITH_PROVENANCE`, `mimir.server._on_session_idle`) `shell_exec` plus `sink_destinations += shell_process` and a `ServiceSinkPolicy("shell_exec", "shell_profile", "scheduler_read_only")`. The only evidence for it is 8 observed attempts in the audit — and this leaf's review criterion is explicit that additions must be justified by an actual shipped prompt or framework code path, **not added speculatively**.

I checked the shipped path: `SAGA_SESSION_END_DEFAULT` (mimir/templates.py:18) directs three things — capture memories under `memory/**` and `state/wiki/**`, score atoms, write skill learnings — and points at `mimir_get_turn` when a turn's detail is needed. There is no shell, bash, git, or command step anywhere in it, and mimirbot has no `prompts/saga_session_end.md` override. So the 8 events are the model reaching for a tool the prompt never asks for, which is precisely the case enforcement should keep denying.

It also matters structurally: synthesis ingests whole-session content (including whatever untrusted external material flowed through the conversation), so granting it shell creates a taint→execution path at the summarization seam — the one place we least want it, and directly ahead of #980 relaxing trust derivation.

Please keep `bash_jobs_list` + `bash_job_output` and the `shell_jobs` readable domain (a session-end turn legitimately inspecting the output of a job an earlier turn in that session started is read-only and provenance-scoped — and the invariant is one-directional, so inspectors without a start capability don't trip it), and remove `shell_exec`, the `shell_process` sink destination, and the shell `sink_policies` entry from `synthesis`. If you believe a shipped path does need shell there, cite it and I'll reconsider.

Everything else in this PR stands as-is.
