payload.author: mimir-carreira
jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The per-command argv allowlist is well-built and fail-closed, the file-root /tmp fix is correct, the vector-deny tests are genuine (reach the real gate + live middleware), and #918's taint path survived the rebase. But there is a **third HIGH bypass (verified RCE), and it's the architecture, not the vector list.**

**BLOCKING (HIGH) — bash brace-expansion defeats the allowlist.** `_target_matches_shell_profile` validates the `shlex.split` token stream, but the command is executed via `bash -lc`, which performs brace/glob/tilde expansion that shlex does NOT. `_SHELL_CONTROL_CHARACTERS` omits `{ } , * ? [ ~`. Verified payload (scheduler/system, reproduced writing a real file):
```
git diff --no-ext-diff --no-textconv {--output=/tmp/OUT,HEAD} {--format=format:ATTACKER_%H,HEAD}
```
The `{…}` tokens look like positionals to the validator (admitted), but bash expands them to `--output=/tmp/OUT --format=format:ATTACKER_%H` → arbitrary-content write to any absolute path → overwrite ~/.bash_profile → RCE on the next login-shell turn. Glob `*?[` and `~` are the same class. This is the third round on the same root cause (\n/\r → git/rg flags → brace-expansion); each fix patched the vector, not the model.

**Fix: stop validating a string that's handed to a shell — exec the resolved argv directly.** Concretely: run service shell as `subprocess`/exec of the parsed argv list with NO shell (no `bash -lc`, no `shell=True`, no login shell), setting the venv-bin PATH via the child's `env` dict instead of a login-shell profile. Then the argv the allowlist validates IS the argv that executes — there is no expansion layer, so brace/glob/tilde/separator injection is structurally impossible. **Keep** the existing per-command exact-option allowlist (`_arguments_match_allowlist`) — it's good; just apply it to the real argv with no shell in between. If a login shell is truly required for PATH, that's the thing to remove for service shell.

**Also add tests** for the class this keeps missing: brace `{...}`, glob `*`/`?`/`[`, and tilde `~` smuggling must all be DENIED; plus the currently-untested `rg` without `--no-config`, and the git `--no-ext-diff`/`--no-textconv` requirement in both directions (deny a `git log` lacking them; allow a valid `git log --no-ext-diff --no-textconv --oneline`). Pin 'any unlisted option on a valid command → deny' as a class so a future allowlist→denylist regression is caught.

Everything else (file-root reconcile, destination policy, capability-matrix guards, #918 composition) is correct. Re-request after the exec-argv-direct change.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
4th-round adversarial review (2 agents: exploit/bypass hunt + tests/masking/regression), plus my own verification. **The #919 shell RCE is genuinely closed — the execution-model change is the right fix and I verified it holds.** Under enforce: the sink gate denies a non-allowlisted service command before the handler runs (handler_calls==0, tested); execution re-derives argv from the SAME parse_service_shell_argv the gate used (no validate-one/exec-another); exec is subprocess.run/Popen(argv, shell=False), so brace-expansion/glob/tilde/newline/command-substitution — all three prior bypass classes — are structurally dead; the allowlist is tight (--output/--ext-diff/--pretty/rg --pre rejected, --no-ext-diff --no-textconv mandatory, argv[0] must be a bare command name); the model-supplied mimir_direct_argv is popped on every reachable shell path (main agent + both subagents — the old #909 no-middleware gap is closed). No masking; the bypass-denied / allowlisted-allowed / model-argv-stripped behaviors are all tested with teeth. H1 (fail-open), H3 (parse/exec divergence), H4 (allowlist completeness) all refuted.

**One required change before merge (defense-in-depth on the exact RCE seam):**

`mimir_direct_argv` is declared as a PLAIN, model-visible tool parameter on both `shell_exec` (mimir/tools/extra.py:312) and `bash_async` (mimir/tools/shell_async.py:217). I confirmed it appears in the tool_call_schema sent to the LLM. It is NOT exploitable today because `_request_for_authorized_execution` (budget_gate.py:313-314) pops a model value on every current path — but that makes the entire no-arbitrary-exec guarantee rest on a single non-structural `args.pop` being present on every shell-tool invocation path, forever. That is precisely the 'one fragile guard' pattern that reopened this hole three times. `subprocess.run(argv, shell=False)` runs `argv` verbatim, so if any future path skips the middleware (as subagents once did per #909), a model-supplied `mimir_direct_argv` is arbitrary RCE with no allowlist, in any mode.

Fix — make the guard structural (the pattern is already in the repo for `config`):
1. Annotate the param on BOTH tools: `mimir_direct_argv: Annotated[list[str] | None, InjectedToolArg] = None` (import `InjectedToolArg` from `langchain_core.tools`, as mimir/tools/registry.py:238/419 already do). This removes it from the model-facing tool_call_schema and makes the tool-binding layer drop any model-supplied value.
2. Keep the middleware server-side injection unchanged — `_request_for_authorized_execution` still sets `args['mimir_direct_argv'] = argv` after authorizing (InjectedToolArg hides the param from the model but does NOT block programmatic injection via the args dict). Keep the unconditional `args.pop` too, as belt-and-suspenders.
3. Verify the existing tests still pass (the model-supplied-argv-stripped test AND the exec-the-authorized-argv test at tests/test_access_control.py:1164-1211 — the server-injected argv must still reach the handler).
4. Add a regression test asserting `mimir_direct_argv` is NOT in the model-facing `tool_call_schema` (i.e. `.tool_call_schema.model_json_schema()['properties']`) for shell_exec and bash_async, so a future re-exposure fails CI.

Keep the change scoped to exactly this — do NOT widen the shell allowlist. Two separate items are being tracked elsewhere and are NOT part of this PR: (a) an enable-time finding that the read-only profile denies commands the shipped autonomous prompts use (filed as its own #854 enablement-blocker leaf), and (b) coverage gaps (exec-path shell=False untested; one file-policy test asserts .reason not .allowed) for the consolidated hardening leaf.

payload.title: Worklink #917: authz/IFC: carry principal, domain, resource, and bridge provenance in source labels

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Two-agent adversarial review (logic + tests/masking), verified against the code. **The core is strong** — the two headline attacks are solidly denied (two principals in one channel; same textual channel-id on two bridge instances → the bridge_instance check, not channel-string equality, is what denies), provenance binding is server-authoritative (never model args/display names), labels are monotonic and propagate through continuation/#891/#1089, no new fail-open, and composition with #1107/#1108/#914 is clean (the #1110 MCP-fast-path concern is orthogonal — channel egress is native, always reaches _get_allowed_sinks). But one blocking regression + AC gaps:

**BLOCKING (enable-time functional regression this PR introduces).** _initialize_ifc_labels (agent.py:227-252) now always attaches an ingress SourceLabel, but for author-less events (poller / scheduled_tick / saga_session_end / system-resumed) principal=None → SourceLabel.is_complete is False → _get_allowed_sinks returns frozenset() → SAME_CHANNEL egress is DENIED. Pre-#917 these turns added no source and matched on source_channels → egress ALLOWED (verified: scheduled_tick same-channel → False on this head, allowed on 24447352). Effect: under MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED a reminder-poller/scheduled reply to its OWN channel silently drops; and because the harness egress boundary (_harness_sink_allowed) runs enforce=True unconditionally, harness auto-deliver / resend-nudge for author-less turns can be blocked even before global enforcement. It's fail-closed (no leak), but #917's purpose is to make enforcement *enable-able* — shipping a new enable-time break is self-defeating, and no test covers service/scheduled same-channel ALLOW. Fix: give author-less trusted-service/system turns a complete, appropriate source label (service principal + intersected ACL) or an explicit trusted-service same-channel allow path, and add a test that a scheduled/poller turn CAN egress to its triggering channel under enforce.

**SHOULD-FIX (AC 4 partially unimplemented).** SourceLabel.derived() (service-derived intersected ACLs) is dead in production — only ingress (agent.py:243) and poller_recovery (poller_recovery.py:176) ever build a SourceLabel; tool-results/subagent/SAGA-derived data get no SourceLabel, so 'service-derived outputs carry intersected ACLs' exists only as a tested-but-unwired primitive. Also poller_recovery's new sources reconstruction is unreachable (poller events stash ifc_labels=None) and wouldn't round-trip if hit (asdict leaves frozensets → default=str stringifies them) — it fails closed, but doesn't actually restore provenance. And the fail-closed test (test_information_flow.py:117) only proves deny for the ENTIRELY-empty-sources case; scope it honestly.

**OUT OF SCOPE — hand off to #918 (do NOT fix here).** Preloaded/injected context (SAGA recall / history / memory / subagent completion) is tainted with a bare with_label("private") and NO SourceLabel (agent.py:2273-2286), so the per-source egress gate doesn't constrain it — cross-principal data recalled via SAGA into principal A's turn can egress to A's channel on the strength of A's ingress source alone. Both reviewers confirm this is PRE-EXISTING (the code comment at agent.py:2274-2277 admits it) and it is exactly what #918 (taint protected/partial results before egress) exists to close. Flagging so #918 explicitly owns source-labeling the preloaded taint; not a #917 blocker, but note the new fail-closed test masks it by injecting a fully-sourced preloaded label unlike production.

Re-request review after the fix — I'll re-run the full pass, focused on service same-channel egress under enforce.

payload.title: Worklink #915: authz/MCP: wire durable policy and argument-aware resource adapters into production

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Two-agent adversarial review (logic/wiring + tests, the latter explicitly hunting for a #1109-style mask). Good news first: **no masked-broken-production path** — the runtime authz seam is genuinely wired (real middleware → config-driven adapter → handler, identity-traced), it's argument-aware not enum-only, the durable policy/immutable-provenance loading is correct, startup wiring in build_app is correct, and composition with #1107/#1108 is clean. But there's a **HIGH, live security regression** that blocks merge, plus two real correctness gaps.

**BLOCKING (HIGH) — the MCP fast-path bypasses the IFC/EXTERNAL_MCP sink gate.** `authorize_tool` (access_control.py:1166-1176) calls `MCPResourceAdapter.authorize_call(...)` WITHOUT `ifc_labels` and `return auth` — *before* the `SinkGate.check_sink_flow` block (~:1178+). `mcp_` maps to `SinkCategory.EXTERNAL_MCP` (:115), so before this PR every MCP call ran through the IFC sink gate; now it's skipped and `ifc_labels` is dropped. Under enforcement, a turn that ingested tainted (untrusted-channel) data can call a same-owner MCP tool to exfiltrate — the #871/#1089 tainted→external-MCP block never fires; the argument adapter checks only owner/resource, not IFC labels. This regresses the exact IFC layer #917/#918 are strengthening. Fix: run the EXTERNAL_MCP sink gate for MCP tools too — either don't early-return (run the adapter AND `check_sink_flow`), or forward `ifc_labels` into `authorize_call` and enforce the sink flow there (the adapter already computes source/sink resources — wire them into the IFC decision instead of discarding them). Add a test: tainted labels + same-owner MCP call → denied under enforce.

**SHOULD-FIX (MEDIUM-HIGH) — wildcard denial misses embedded globs.** `_configured_resource_classifier` (mcp_client.py:905) denies `resource == "*"` or chars in `("?","[","]")`, but `*` is not in that char set — so `secrets/*`, `tenant/*`, `*.txt` slip through (owner==principal passes, the glob expands server-side across un-owned resources). Deny any resource containing `*` (or proper glob detection) + test the embedded-`*` case.

**SHOULD-FIX (MEDIUM) — fail-closed MCP decisions ignore `enforce` (break shadow-first rollout).** In `authorize_call` (access_control.py:865-877), every ADMIN_REQUIRED outcome (unclassified/missing-provenance/missing-adapter/drift/exception) sets `allowed = admin` regardless of `enforce` and `is_shadow_decision=False` — so a non-admin call is HARD-denied even in shadow mode, asymmetric with the RESOURCE_SCOPED path (`allowed = not enforce`) and with the non-MCP ADMIN_REQUIRED branch. An operator enabling an MCP server before authoring policies would hard-block poller/non-admin calls before enforcement is even on. Make it shadow-symmetric (shadow-allow + emit shadow decision when not enforcing).

**Test gaps (from the AC's required matrix):** the fail-closed tests (missing-adapter, adapter-exception) assert only `.reason`, never `.allowed` — since reason is set independently, they'd pass even if fail-closed wrongly returned `allowed=True`; add `.allowed is False`. Production startup wiring (build_app) has no test (logic-verified correct, but uncovered). unclassified/missing-provenance/drift are untested via the shipped `authorize_call` path. And set the `mcp_provenance` attribute fallback (mcp_client.py:791 reads it but it's never written) + one identity test, so the new `id(tool)` keying isn't a silently-fail-closed invariant.

Re-request review after the revision — I'll re-run the full adversarial pass, with specific attention to the IFC sink gate now covering MCP.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #914: authz: owner-isolate commitments across trusted service principals

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Two adversarial reviewers independently confirmed (one with an executable repro against both trees), and I verified against the code — **this has a HIGH, live regression that blocks merge.**

**BLOCKING — the ownership guard breaks reminder delivery for all production commitments.** `_is_authorized` (commitments/store.py:231-238) now requires `actor_principal == record.owner_principal` for non-admins. But production commitments are created **ownerless**: `extractor.build_commitment` sets no `owner_principal` (models.py default `None`, visibility PUBLIC), and the poller — the only automated lifecycle caller, unchanged by this PR — calls `store.deliver(..., actor_principal="service:poller")` and `store.expire(..., actor_principal="service:poller")` (poller.py:196,223). `service:poller` is never the owner, so both now return `False` and the poller silently stops emitting `commitment_due`/`commitment_expired` — reminders never fire or expire. Reproduced: PR head → deliver/expire `False/False`; main → `True/True`.

Critically, **this was masked by the tests**: the diff adds `owner_principal="service:poller"` to all five poller fixtures (tests/test_commitments_poller.py) — an ownership that does not occur on the production path — so the delivery assertions pass while the real flow is broken. Please revert those fixtures to production-realistic ownership (owner=None / user-owned) and add a poller test asserting delivery+expiry still succeed for an **ownerless** commitment; that test must be RED before the fix and GREEN after.

**SHOULD-FIX (MEDIUM) — read isolation is incomplete for the production default.** `_can_view` (store.py:642-661) owner-isolates only SERVICE-visibility records, but grants ANY `service:` actor read of ANY PUBLIC record. Reproduced: poller list sees scheduler's PUBLIC record + every user's ownerless-PUBLIC extracted text.

**What's correct** (keep it): the exact-owner MUTATION predicate for owner-mutations, carrier integrity (#887 — authority solely from the frozen AuthContext, HTTP ingress rejected), admin/missing-carrier handling, and the cross-service mutation matrix tests. The core owner-isolation idea is right; it just over-applied to the poller's legitimate cross-owner lifecycle role and under-applied to PUBLIC reads.

payload.title: Worklink #911: memory/disk follow-ups from the 2026-07-17 leak audit (post-#PR fixes)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Reviewed across four dimensions (worklink compute, SAGA read-path, history/eviction, SSE + scheduler + pollers), verified against the code at 0c8f8b0b.

**The hard/dangerous parts are done well and I confirmed them:** no false-green gate (the pytest gate runs a *separate uncapped* subprocess and decides on exit code, not the capped agent stream); no pipe deadlock (stdout/stderr drained concurrently); **no LIMIT-before-scoring bug** (no LIMIT was added — top-k truncation stays post-scoring); **#1104's authz predicate scoping is fully preserved** (query SQL untouched, no new unscoped read); the FAISS-rebuild job is correctly conditioned (>10% removed), thread-safe, and wired (RecordingSagaClient forwards it, log-and-continue on bad cron); chat_history rotation is crash-safe + atomic (`tmp`+`replace`, 0 corrupt lines under 2000 concurrent appends); active-channel eviction is correctly guarded (can't evict a channel with an in-flight turn / queued events); both poller gitignore seeds are correct + idempotent. Good work on those.

Blocking:

**1. Worklink output caps can kill legitimate runs, and an overflow-kill is invisible.** `compute.py:116-117` sets 16 MiB stdout / **1 MiB stderr**, and either stream hitting its cap fires the shared overflow callback that SIGKILLs the whole run (`compute.py:226,231`) → classified `failed`. Coding CLIs stream progress/reasoning to stderr, so a healthy multi-minute run can blow the 1 MiB stderr cap and be discarded — and the PR's own \"tens-to-hundreds of MB per run\" framing suggests 16 MiB stdout may also be too low. Worse, `output_overflow` is written only to the transcript, not to `RawResult` (`backends/base.py`), so an overflow-kill is indistinguishable from an ordinary failure: no distinct event, no circuit-breaker, and the surfaced error is a truncated partial line → the run silently retries and re-hits the cap. Please (a) size the caps against real opencode/codex stdout+stderr volume (stderr especially), (b) propagate `output_overflow` into `RawResult` + emit a distinct event / gate the retry the way `pollers.py` does, and (c) add an env override so retuning doesn't need a code change.

**2. Idle-channel eviction silently drops cross-channel context from active turns.** `evict_channel` pops `_by_channel` (`history.py:303`), but `cross_author_context` selects messages by iterating that same dict (`history.py:473`). After a channel idles out (~60s) its messages remain in `_all` but become unreachable by the cross-channel assembly, so they vanish from a *different* active channel's \"Recent activity\" prompt (self-heals only on reactivation). Please fall back to `_all` for evicted channels in that path (or exclude eviction from it).

Should-fix:

**3. SubagentInbox eviction is a latent lost-notification bug.** `inbox.evict_channel` unconditionally drops the bucket on worker-idle (`server.py:862-868`), but the inbox holds subagent completions *across* the between-turns gap (drained next turn, `agent.py:2212`). Inert only because `push()` isn't wired in production yet — once it is, a subagent finishing during the 60s idle gap (routine for long tasks) is silently dropped. Please only evict when the bucket is empty, or don't tie inbox lifetime to worker-idle.

**4. SSE fresh backfill under-serves the client's limit.** `FRESH_BACKFILL_MAX_RECORDS=100` (`live_events.py:18`) ignores the request's `?limit`, while the shipped React client defaults `backfillLimit=500` (`frontend/src/api/live-events.ts:69`). A fresh load asking for 500 gets ~100 records' worth when turns are lifecycle-only — a visible reduction in initial panel depth. Size the fresh scan off the request, or align the constant with the frontend default.

Non-blocking (follow-ups/nits): the SAGA fix took the \"score in float32\" half but not \"LIMIT/pre-filter\", so full-corpus row materialization (the main churn) remains — legitimate per the \"and/or\", but note it; a verbose `blocked` run can lose its WORKLINK_BLOCKED classification w

payload.title: Worklink #889: authz: create_auth_context HTTP-ingress extra-key guard reads wrong key (dead defense-in-depth)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Request changes — the fix is functionally correct, but it leaves a drift risk that is the same class of bug #889 is fixing.

What's right: both read sites in `create_auth_context` (the service-grant guard and the `event_ingress`-from-extra fallback) now use `HTTP_EVENT_INGRESS_EXTRA_KEY` = the value the stamping code writes; the guard is genuinely exercised (the two-factor `test_service_authorization_requires_two_factor_validation` in test_tool_registry.py, updated to the canonical key, plus the new `test_http_ingress_extra_key_blocks_service_grant`); CI is green.

The issue: this PR **adds a second, independent definition** of the constant. `mimir/worklink/continuation.py:31` already defines `HTTP_EVENT_INGRESS_EXTRA_KEY = "_mimir_event_ingress"` — that's the canonical one the stamping code writes with. This PR defines *another* one in `mimir/access_control.py` with the same literal. Two same-valued copies in two modules is exactly the key-mismatch drift #889 is about: if continuation.py's value ever changes, access_control.py's copy won't follow and the guard silently goes dead again. #889's review criterion is "the same constant the stamping code writes" — one shared constant, not two copies.

Single source of truth (the layering already supports it): `continuation.py` does `from ..access_control import authorize_action`, so access_control is the lower-level module and continuation can import *from* it (access_control importing continuation would be a cycle — which is presumably why you duplicated). So:
- Keep the definition in `access_control.py` (as you have it).
- In `continuation.py`, delete the line-31 definition and instead `from .access_control import HTTP_EVENT_INGRESS_EXTRA_KEY` (and keep `HTTP_EVENT_INGRESS_EXTRA_VALUE` wherever it belongs).

That yields one definition, correct import direction, no cycle, no drift. Confirm continuation.py still stamps the same key after the consolidation.

```python

    return ("1=1", [])   # platform/maintenance: full internal read; isolation enforced on OUTPUTS (#884 derivation-ACL + #871 egress)
```

This is a **read** view only — it must NOT confer admin authority anywhere else. Keep `is_admin=False` in the scope; writes/mutations stay gated by the service's own capabilities (`can_write_saga` / capability matrix), unchanged. This is exactly the "broad internal read, isolation on outputs" model — platform services see everything the agent stores; tenant isolation lives at derivation-ACL + egress + user-facing reads, never at the maintenance read.

Leave integration services (`readable_domains`) and regular users exactly as they are — that scoping is correct.

Acceptance for the change:
- [ ] Platform-service reads return the admin predicate (`1=1`) — a platform turn reads an `other-owner private` atom (add a test: a `private` atom owned by a non-service principal is visible to a platform-service scope).
- [ ] `is_admin` stays `False` for platform services; no write/tool authority is widened (a test that a platform service is still denied a non-owned mutation / an unauthorized capability).
- [ ] Docstring updated: platform/maintenance services get full internal *read*; isolation on outputs.

Everything else (the distinction, the forged-trigger guard, the integration/user scoping, non-enumeration) is correct and should stay.

payload.title: Worklink #896: reliability: subprocess spawn on the event loop can wedge the whole agent (ops_dashboard chainlink load blocked both agents 2026-07-16)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Review of #896 (event-loop-wedging fix). Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES — one acceptance criterion outstanding.**

The core fix is correct and exactly the right shape: `_load_chainlink_issues` is now a sync `subprocess.run(..., timeout=_CHAINLINK_TIMEOUT_SECONDS)` (fail-soft on `TimeoutExpired`) wrapped in `asyncio.to_thread(...)`, so the blocking `fork_exec` runs in a worker thread rather than on the event loop. That avoids the subtle trap (a naive `wait_for` around `create_subprocess_exec` wouldn't help — the fork blocks synchronously before the await). The regression tests verify the spawn goes through `to_thread` off-loop and that a timeout doesn't propagate onto the loop. AC1 (bounded), AC2 (tests), AC3 (off-loop isolation) are all satisfied, and CI is green. This resolves the specific recurrence.

**Outstanding — AC4 (loop-blocked watchdog / self-heal).** The leaf's fourth criterion is not addressed:

> A watchdog or self-heal signal fires when the loop is blocked beyond a threshold (so the operator is alerted / the process can self-terminate for supervisor restart) instead of silently wedging until manual VM intervention.

This is the part that would have made the 2026-07-16 incident *observable and self-correcting* rather than a silent wedge that required a manual OrbStack VM restart. The ops-dashboard spawn is now fixed, but any *other* loop-resident blocking call (another subprocess/shell-out, a sync FS/DB call, a C-extension) can still wedge the agent the same way — and the failure mode was invisible: health just timed out with no alert.

Please add the watchdog. Design notes so it actually works:
- It must run **off the event loop** (a plain daemon thread), because a loop-resident watchdog is itself blocked when the loop wedges — that's the whole point. The event loop periodically stamps a monotonic "last alive" timestamp; the watchdog thread checks it independently.
- On a stall beyond a threshold (comfortably above the longest legitimate loop-blocking operation), emit a **structured operator alert** (the ntfy / negative-algedonic path the agent already uses for operator signals) with the blocked duration, and — per the AC — optionally trigger a **clean self-terminate** so the s6 supervisor restarts the process instead of it hanging until manual VM intervention. Make the self-terminate opt-in/config-gated if you want to be conservative, but the alert should always fire.
- Add a test that simulates a blocked loop (the "last alive" stamp going stale) and asserts the watchdog fires its alert (and, if enabled, the self-terminate) within the threshold.

Once the watchdog is in with a test, this is complete. The `to_thread` fix itself is good and shouldn't change.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Adversarial review of #872 (authorization compatibility, audit, and adversarial integration gate). Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES.**

First — good judgment on the carried-forward enablement blocker: you read the #872 comment, prototyped a concrete fix on a local branch (163+215 tests), and correctly *did not* ship it as a post-merge hotfix, deferring it to the actual enablement gate. That's the right call; #872's scope explicitly excludes enforcement enablement.

What this PR does well:
- Completes the inbound audit **allow/deny pair**: adds `inbound_event_allowed` (the deny event already existed) and stamps `enforcement_enabled` on both — with `test_allow_event_fields_are_stable_and_redacted` proving stable, secret-free fields. That satisfies AC2's audit half + the redaction review criterion.
- Solid compatibility truth-table tests: HTTP-ingress denies without a server-owned principal, enforcement-on missing/unknown context denies, unknown MCP tool denies. CI green (the full suite passing under default enforcement-off is the AC1 single-operator-preservation baseline).

But two of #872's acceptance criteria aren't met:

### Blocking 1 — the AC2 adversarial matrix is largely not delivered

AC2 requires "an adversarial matrix covering forged fields/session ids, unknown native/built-in/MCP tools, synthetic triggers, legacy records, concurrent turns, preloaded private context, same-scope success, and incompatible egress." Of that enumerated set, this PR adds exactly one as a new integration test (**unknown MCP tool**), plus the truth-table compatibility cases. The other eight — forged fields/**session ids**, unknown **native/built-in** tools, **synthetic triggers**, **legacy records**, **concurrent turns**, **preloaded private context**, **same-scope success**, **incompatible egress** — are neither added here nor mapped to the per-leaf tests that cover them. Several of these are *integration-only* (concurrent turns, preloaded private context, incompatible egress, same-scope success) and can't be assumed covered by unit-level leaf tests. For the final adversarial gate, either add these at the integration level, or include an explicit matrix→test reference table so the gate demonstrably covers each enumerated case (a "gate" that silently omits 8/9 of its own matrix isn't gating them).

### Blocking 2 — AC3 docs/config reconciliation not done

AC3 requires "document any intentionally deferred UI gate without enabling multi-user ingress," and the scope names "docs/config reconciliation" and "final inventory checks." This 2-file PR (dispatcher + one test file) changes no docs/config. Add the deferred-UI-gate note (#855 is out of scope but must be documented as deferred) and the config/docs reconciliation the AC calls for — plus, given this gate is the natural home for it, a pointer to the enforcement-enablement blocker (the service-turn recall issue recorded on this issue) so enabling enforcement stays gated.

The audit pairing and truth-table cases are the right bones; the gap is that the enumerated adversarial matrix (AC2) and the docs/inventory reconciliation (AC3) — the substance of an integration/audit *gate* — are mostly still to do. Either implement them or make the coverage explicit with a matrix→test map.

payload.title: Worklink #885: Authorize SAGA feedback forget and destructive mutations

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Adversarial review of #885 (authorize SAGA feedback / forget / destructive mutations). Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES.**

Good structure: the authorization lives in `SagaStore` core mutation methods (feedback/outcome/forget) — not only the tool wrappers, as the review criterion demands — with owner-match (`owner_principal == principal`), an atomic all-or-nothing fail for feedback (returns `marked:0` before any write when the authorized set ≠ requested set), and a dry-run forget preview that filters to owned IDs so it doesn't reveal unauthorized ones. The tools thread the frozen `AuthContext` via `ToolRuntime` (consistent with #882/#883). CI is green. But two things block and one needs scoping.

### Blocking 1 — the core mutation path fails OPEN on `auth_context=None` / missing principal

Every mutation method uses this shape:
```python
is_authorized = is_admin(auth_context) or is_trusted_service(auth_context)   # None → False
principal = getattr(auth_context, "canonical_principal", None) if auth_context else None  # None → None
authorized_ids = atom_ids
if not is_authorized and principal:          # principal is None → condition False → filter SKIPPED
    authorized_ids = _filter_authorized_atoms(...)
    ...
_feedback(conn, authorized_ids)              # mutates the FULL set
```
When `auth_context` is `None` (or carries no `canonical_principal`), `is_authorized` is False *and* `principal` is None, so the owner-filter is skipped entirely and the method mutates **all** requested atoms. There's no outer deny for the "not authorized, no principal" case. The review criterion makes the **core** the boundary precisely so a direct/internal `SagaStore.feedback/forget` call is safe — and internal callers (consolidation, reflection) invoke these without threading an `auth_context`, so they'd get unrestricted mutation. This is the same fail-open-on-None pattern flagged on #883, and it contradicts AC2. Fail closed: no admin/service authority *and* no matching principal ⇒ deny (mutate nothing); internal system callers should pass an explicit admin/service context rather than relying on `None`.

### Blocking 2 — authorization scenario tests are absent

AC2/AC3 and the review criteria require proof of: other-owner / legacy / service-owned denial, a mixed-authority batch failing atomically with no partial writes, forged-ID non-enumeration, and the dry-run preview not revealing unauthorized IDs — plus that observation/triple evidence-refresh and index removal don't cross an unauthorized boundary as a side effect. The test diff only **adapts existing tests to the new signatures** (threading `auth_context`/`runtime`, updating `forget_calls` assertions). No test exercises a denial, a mixed-authority atomic fail, a forged ID, or the dependent-update side-effect boundary. For a mutation-authorization leaf, those are the acceptance bar.

### Should-fix — trusted-service mutations aren't scoped to readable-domain

`is_authorized = is_admin(...) or is_trusted_service(...)` then skips all filtering, so a trusted service can mutate **any** atom. AC2 says admin *and* trusted services "can act only within their configured capability and **readable-domain scope**." Admin-everything is fine; a trusted service should still be constrained to its readable domains, not granted blanket mutation.

### Note — reconcile the tool gate with the core
The tools gate with `can_write_saga` (admin **or** trusted-service only), which denies regular principals outright — so the core's owner-match branch (regular principal → own atoms) is unreachable through the tools. If admin/service-only mutation is the intended policy for now, that's defensible, but then the core's regular-principal branch is dead code whose only live effect is the fail-open-on-None above. Either wire regular-principal owner-match through (and fix Blocking 1), or drop the branch and make the core explicitly admin/service-only with a fail-closed default.

Fix the fail-open default (1) and add the denial/atomi

payload.title: Worklink #884: Propagate intersected ACLs to SAGA observations and triples

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Adversarial review of #884 (propagate intersected ACLs to observations and triples). Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES.**

The intersection design is genuinely good and mostly fail-closed:
- `_compute_intersected_acl` SELECTs the ownership columns from the `atoms` table via the live `conn` — derived authority comes from **persisted source rows inside the write transaction**, not LLM/caller metadata (exactly the review criterion).
- `_update_triple_acl_on_dedup` re-intersects `existing ⊓ new`, so a content-addressed re-assertion can only **narrow**, never widen — AC2, done right.
- `intersect_acl` collapses to `legacy_admin` on mixed owner, mixed/absent domain, or any missing provenance; empty/no-rows → `Ownership()` (legacy_admin). Applied across consolidate (observations), triples, and world_state, and the v8 `world_state` ownership columns are correctly motivated by AC2 (world-state inherits triple ACLs). CI is green on all five checks.

But two things block and two edges need tightening.

### Blocking 1 — AC3 test coverage is essentially absent

AC3 requires tests over "same-owner, mixed-owner, mixed-domain, legacy-source, dedup/reassertion, supersession, and consolidation paths" that "assert no synthesized observation/triple becomes more readable than any source." The only test changes in the PR are schema-version bumps (`test_detect_schema_version_returns_seven…` → `…eight…`, v7→v8 numbering) in `test_saga_correctness_regressions.py` and `test_search_sessions.py`. There is **no** test that exercises `intersect_acl` / `_compute_intersected_acl` / `_update_triple_acl_on_dedup` with mixed owners, a legacy source, a dedup/reassertion narrowing, or the "no-widening" invariant. The entire substance of the leaf — and its real edge cases (below) — is unverified. Add the enumerated scenario tests plus the readability invariant; that's the acceptance bar.

### Blocking 2 — schema.sql ↔ v8 migration diverge on `world_state.visibility`

Greenfield `schema.sql` declares:
```
visibility TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'legacy_admin',
```
but the v8 migration adds it **with** the enum guard:
```
ALTER TABLE world_state ADD COLUMN visibility TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'legacy_admin'
    CHECK(visibility IN ('public','private','service','legacy_admin'));
```
So a fresh DB (from schema.sql) does **not** enforce the visibility enum on `world_state`, while a migrated DB does — the exact schema/migration parity defect #881's review criterion calls out ("schema.sql and the migration produce equivalent columns/defaults/indexes"). Add the `CHECK` to schema.sql, and add a populated v8-migration test asserting existing `world_state` rows are preserved and default to `legacy_admin` (the #881 pattern).

### Should-fix — two fail-open edges in `intersect_acl`
- `if len(acls) == 1: return acls[0]` returns the single source **verbatim**, bypassing the ambiguity collapse. A lone evidence atom with empty provenance or a legacy owner is returned as-is rather than becoming `legacy_admin` — contradicting the AC ("missing evidence provenance, or legacy/ambiguous inputs become service/admin-only"). Run the single-source case through the same collapse.
- The visibility-rank fold uses `vis_order.index(v) if v in vis_order else 0` — an unknown visibility maps to `0` (**public**, least restrictive). With `max(...)` two unknown-visibility sources yield `public`. The schema constrains the column, but a helper documented as fail-closed should map the unknown case to the **most** restrictive (`legacy_admin`), not the least.

Fix the CHECK parity (2) and the two edges (3), and — most importantly — add the AC3 intersection scenario tests (1). The transaction-scoped derivation and narrow-only dedup are the hard parts and they're right; this is about proving it and closing the fail-open edges.

payload.title: Worklink #883: Enforce SAGA read authorization before ranking and rendering

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Adversarial review of #883 (enforce SAGA read authorization before ranking and rendering). Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES.**

Good foundation: the predicate is threaded via `auth_context` into query/get_atoms/session/recall/triple lanes, `memory_get`/`query` read the frozen carrier from `ToolRuntime[AuthContext]` (consistent with #882), principals/domains are **bound parameters**, and the by-id (`get_atoms`) and session reads apply the predicate in SQL so forged IDs return nothing (non-enumeration holds *there*). But three of the criteria are not met — and they're the security core of the leaf. (Enforcement is default-off and today's reads run admin-scoped, so none of this is live-exploitable yet; but these are exactly the multi-principal properties #883 exists to establish.)

### Blocking 1 — `get_authorization_scope(None)` fails OPEN (admin)

```python
if auth_context is None:
    return AuthorizationScope(is_admin=True)   # "backwards compatibility"
```

A missing/None `auth_context` yields admin scope → predicate `"1=1"` → reads everything, legacy_admin included. Every read helper defaults `auth_context: Any = None`, so any lane that isn't threaded silently reads the whole corpus, with no error. That's the opposite of #882's fail-closed write gate and contradicts AC2 (legacy/admin-only rows invisible to regular principals). "Backwards compatibility for internal calls" is the anti-pattern — it makes the boundary opt-in per caller with no backstop. Fail closed: `None` → a minimal deny/public scope, and have the internal system read paths pass an explicit admin/service context.

### Blocking 2 — the owner-match clause is AND-ed, so it collapses to public-only

For a regular user the conditions are built as `[ "visibility = ?"(public), "(owner_principal = ? OR visibility = ?)"(me, public) ]` and joined with `" AND ".join(...)`:

```
visibility='public' AND (owner_principal='me' OR visibility='public')  ≡  visibility='public'
```

The owner-match is subsumed by the public condition, so a caller can read **only PUBLIC** — never its own `private` atoms. That violates AC ("A caller sees only owned resources plus explicitly visible resources") and the function's own docstring ("Regular users can read: PUBLIC + their own owned atoms"), and it makes the `private`-by-default atoms that #882 writes for users **unreadable by their own owner**. (It also over-restricts a service whenever `scope.principal` is set — the same AND intersects the domain grant down to owned-or-public.) Fix: OR the owner-match into the visibility condition, e.g. `(visibility='public' OR owner_principal=? [OR service-domain terms])`, rather than AND-ing it.

### Blocking 3 — in `recall.py` the predicate is a post-ranking filter, not the boundary

Pass 1 generates candidates via `faiss_search_fn` / `fts_search_fn` / `triple_search_fn` with **no auth scope**, then `reciprocal_rank_fusion(...)` scores the **full** candidate set, and only the final content-fetch (`SELECT ... FROM atoms WHERE id IN (...) AND {auth_where}`) drops unauthorized rows. So unauthorized candidates still enter the pool and **shift the RRF ranks/scores of authorized results** (RRF is rank-position-based) before being filtered. AC1 requires the predicate "before scoring, expansion, access-event writes, or rendering," and AC3 says "unauthorized candidates cannot affect returned ranks/counts ... post-filtering after retrieval is not the security boundary." This is precisely post-filtering after retrieval. Push the predicate down into each candidate-producing lane (the FTS SQL, the triple SQL, and the FAISS id set) so unauthorized atoms never enter the candidate pool, the RRF fusion, or the access-event pass. (By-id fetch is already correct; it's the recall ranking pipeline that leaks.)

### Non-blocking
- The service branch's third disjunct `({table}.visibility = 'service' AND {table}.origin_domain IN (...))` is fully subsumed by the second `({table}.origin_domain IN (...))` — redundant; drop it or n

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Re-review of the fix (`ecdee699`). The three original findings are resolved — but the suite is now red, and it exposes a design question. Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES.**

All three prior findings are genuinely fixed:
1. `get_authorization_scope(None)` now returns `AuthorizationScope()` (public-only) — fail-closed, "omission is never ambient authority," and it accepts a pre-built scope for explicit internal admin reads. ✅
2. `_authorization_predicate` is now a single OR group — `(visibility = ? OR owner_principal = ? OR origin_domain IN (…))` — so a caller reads public **or** its own rows; the AND-collapse is gone (with a comment citing exactly that bug). ✅
3. `recall` collects candidate IDs from all lanes, authorizes them via one SQL predicate, and filters `faiss`/`fts`/`triple` **before the rank maps and RRF** — unauthorized candidates no longer affect ranks/counts/access-events (FAISS filtered against a SQL-materialized allowed set). ✅

### Blocking — pytest (3.11 and 3.12) fail: ~14 recall/session tests now return empty

Because the default is now fail-closed, every reader that doesn't pass an authorized scope gets `visibility = public` only — and atoms stored in these tests are `legacy_admin`/`private`, so recall returns nothing:
- `test_memory_tier1`: `test_recall_returns_stored_atom` (`'…' in []`), `test_recall_fires_retrieval_access_event` (`['store'] == ['store','retrieval']` — filtered before the access event), `test_recall_pinned_atoms_bypass_activation_threshold`, `test_recall_two_tier_splits_observations_and_raws`, the extra-pathway tests (`StopIteration`), …
- `test_memory_tier2` / `test_memory_review_fixes`: `test_recent_session_boundaries_*` (`assert 0 == 2/1`), `test_most_retrieved_filters_contributed_only`.

The production main-recall paths (`saga.query`, `get_atoms`, triple retrieval in `agent.py`) do thread `initial_auth_context`, so those are covered — but these low-level tests weren't updated to pass an authorized scope (or store public atoms), and the suite must be green to merge.

### Design concern this surfaces — autonomous/service turns will recall nothing once enforced

The empty-recall failures are the unit shadow of a real question: with fail-closed reads, a **service-triggered turn** (scheduled_tick / poller / saga_session_end synthesis — *not* admin) gets `public OR owned-by-that-service OR in-its-readable-domains`. In this single-operator deployment the agent's memory is almost all admin/user-owned with `private`/`legacy_admin` visibility, owned by neither the service principal nor in its readable domains — so a service turn would **recall none of the agent's own memory**. Enforcement is default-off today so it isn't live, but #883 shouldn't ship a read model where turning enforcement on blinds the scheduler/poller/synthesis to the agent's memory. Please confirm the intended path (e.g., service principals for a single-tenant agent get broad read over the agent's own memory, or autonomous turns carry an admin-equivalent read scope) and cover a scheduled/poller/synthesis recall in the tests — not just admin and explicit-owner.

Net: findings 1–3 are correctly fixed; green the suite (thread an authorized scope through the failing readers/tests) and resolve the service-turn recall path so enforcement doesn't blind autonomous turns to memory.

payload.title: Worklink #882: Thread server-owned SAGA provenance through runtime writes

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Adversarial review of #882 (thread server-owned SAGA provenance through runtime writes). Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES — architectural.**

The value-object plumbing is fine: `is_admin`/`is_trusted_service`/`can_write_saga`/`get_provenance_from_auth_context` correctly read off the passed `AuthContext`, `SagaStore.store`/`end_session` thread `owner/visibility/provenance` and coerce `None → 'legacy_admin'` (no NULL crash against #881's `NOT NULL`), and the `session_id`-mismatch guard is a good instinct. But the core of the leaf — *where the write's authority comes from* — is implemented as exactly the thing #882's review criterion forbids, and it isn't tested where it matters.

### Blocking 1 — authority is sourced from `resolve_active_ctx`, the named-forbidden fallback

Both `memory_store` and `saga_end_session` obtain their `auth_context` from `resolve_active_ctx()`:

```python
ctx, _resolution = resolve_active_ctx({})
auth_context = getattr(ctx, "auth_context", None)
```

`resolve_active_ctx`'s own docstring is the three-level chain: (1) **model-passed `session_id`**, (2) **`get_only_active_turn()` single-active heuristic** (returns None when ≠1 turn active), (3) **`get_current_turn()` contextvar** ("won't fire under SDK dispatch"). The review criterion says verbatim: *"authority never comes from `resolve_active_ctx` single-active/contextvar fallbacks or model arguments."* This sources it from all three. AC1 requires the ownership be *threaded* from the frozen server-created `AuthContext`/`TurnContext` — and tellingly, none of `mimir/agent.py`, `mimir/session_manager.py`, `mimir/server.py`, or `mimir/models.py` (all in scope precisely because threading touches them) were modified. The fix is the actual leaf: pass the frozen `AuthContext` from `Agent.run_turn` down into the SAGA write path explicitly, rather than re-resolving ambient context at the tool.

### Blocking 2 — the write gate fails open

```python
if ctx is not None and not can_write_saga(auth_context):
    return "...denied..."
```

Guarding on `ctx is not None` means that whenever `ctx` resolves to `None` — i.e. **>1 active turn** (single-active returns None) or **SDK-dispatch** (contextvar doesn't fire) — the denial is skipped and the write proceeds (with `owner=None` → coerced to `legacy_admin`). So AC3 ("shared-memory writes rejected for regular users") is defeated in exactly the concurrent/dispatched conditions that matter. It must fail closed: no resolvable server authority ⇒ deny.

### Blocking 3 — misattribution under concurrency is the default outcome, not an edge case

Because authority comes from single-active/contextvar, two concurrent multi-channel turns resolve to `None` (or, via model `session_id`, potentially the *other* turn), and the write is stored mis-owned (`legacy_admin`) rather than attributed to the real principal. This is precisely what the review criterion's "cross-channel/concurrent-turn tests cannot misattribute a write" is meant to prevent — and there is no such test.

### Blocking 4 — required tests are absent, and the ones added forge what AC2 forbids

The two new tests construct `AuthContext(trigger="user_message")` **directly in the test body** — AC2 says the creation paths must be covered *"without forging AuthContext.trigger in the test body."* And they're tool-level only: `test_agent.py`, `test_session_manager.py`, `test_session_boundaries.py` (named in the leaf's own suggested command) were not touched, so none of the required real creation paths (run_turn user, scheduler, poller, saga-session-idle synthesis, upgrade) nor any concurrency/cross-channel misattribution case is exercised. Given Blockings 1–3 turn on the run_turn→tool boundary and concurrency, these are the tests that actually validate the leaf.

### Non-blocking
- `visibility = "service" if is_service else "private"` writes user atoms as `private`, but per #881 (as merged) `is_user_accessible` admits only `PUBLIC` — so user writes become unreadable even by their owner.

## Verdict: blocking comments

## Summary
The v7 migration is contiguous, preserves the exercised v6 data, fixes the older `SELECT *` migration hazard, and both Worklink/full CI are green (`5872 passed, 19 skipped`). I cannot approve the ownership contract yet because the new schema still permits ambiguous ownership states, and the only new access helper grants regular-user accessibility to service-only rows.

## Blocking issues

1. **`mimir/saga/schema.sql:51` — every ownership field is nullable, so writes can bypass the fail-closed defaults by inserting `NULL`.** `owner_principal`, `visibility`, and `provenance` all omit `NOT NULL`; SQLite defaults apply only when a column is omitted, not when a caller explicitly supplies `NULL`. The same shape exists on sessions, observations metadata, and triples, and migration v7 adds the columns without a post-backfill/constraint rebuild. That leaves rows whose ownership cannot be proven in an ambiguous NULL scope rather than the required `legacy_admin` scope. Make the mandatory ownership fields non-null in greenfield and migrated schemas (rebuild/backfill as needed), then add explicit-NULL rejection tests for all four entity tables.

2. **`mimir/saga/ownership.py:87` — `is_user_accessible()` treats `service` visibility as readable by a regular user.** The authorization spec says service/admin SAGA records remain visible to admin or trusted autonomous maintenance, not regular users. Returning true for `Visibility.SERVICE` would turn a service-owned record into user-readable as soon as a later read adapter reuses this helper. Remove `SERVICE` from the regular-user predicate and add direct truth-table tests before this becomes the policy primitive for #883.

3. **`mimir/saga/ownership.py:78` — `Ownership.to_columns()` does not emit JSON provenance.** `str(dict)` produces Python repr such as `{'source': 'turn'}`, which `_safe_json_load` cannot parse and which violates the schema's documented JSON contract. Use deterministic `json.dumps(...)` (and a JSON-compatible mapping type/default factory), with a round-trip test for non-empty provenance.

## Validation
- Worklink evidence: full suite green, `5872 passed, 19 skipped` in 194.53s.
- GitHub CI: skill-conformance, claude-code smoke, frontend, and pytest 3.11/3.12 all green.
- Local static checks: `git diff --check` clean; PR head `3cffee5ffce2fdfe8975567f6b7302b2101f4fb2`.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Adversarial review of #881 (SAGA ownership schema + fail-closed legacy migration). Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES.**

The core of the leaf is right: the v7 migration uses `ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN … DEFAULT 'legacy_admin'`, which backfills every pre-existing row to the fail-closed `legacy_admin` scope — the central security requirement, done correctly. Schema/migration column + index parity looks good, the `detect_schema_version` v7 marker is sound, and converting the v6 rebuild's `INSERT … SELECT *` to explicit column lists is the right fix for the named regression. But four things block.

Note first: the head (`3cffee5f`) hasn't moved since mimir's own self-review, so the three issues that review flagged are all still live — I confirmed each in the code, and add a fourth.

### Blocking 1 — `is_user_accessible()` is fail-open (`ownership.py`)

```python
return visibility in (Visibility.PUBLIC, Visibility.PRIVATE, Visibility.SERVICE)
```
It returns `True` for `SERVICE` — so a regular user is granted access to service-scoped memory, directly contradicting the module's own docstring ("Regular users cannot read … service-only"). `PRIVATE` is also wrong here: private should be owner-only, not readable by any regular user (this helper can't see the owner, so it can't grant private). Only `PUBLIC` is safely user-accessible from visibility alone. The helper is currently dormant (nothing imports it yet), so this is a *latent* fail-open — but #883 will wire it into the read path, inheriting the bug. Fix it now: `return visibility == Visibility.PUBLIC` (leave owner-scoped PRIVATE/SERVICE to the authorized read path).

### Blocking 2 — `Ownership.to_columns()` serializes provenance as Python `repr`, not JSON

```python
"provenance": str(self.provenance) if self.provenance else "{}",
```
`str({'k': 'v'})` → `{'k': 'v'}` (single quotes) — not valid JSON, so it won't round-trip through `json.loads`, while the column is documented as JSON (`provenance TEXT DEFAULT '{}' -- JSON`). Use `json.dumps(self.provenance)`.

### Blocking 3 — ownership columns permit NULL, so "fail-closed" isn't schema-enforced

Every ownership column is `TEXT DEFAULT 'legacy_admin'` **without `NOT NULL`**, and `CHECK(visibility IN (…))` **passes on NULL** in SQLite. So an explicit `visibility = NULL` write is accepted and produces an un-scoped, ambiguous row — exactly the "legacy NULL/default" the review criterion says must not exist. The `ADD COLUMN` default protects *existing migrated* rows, but the schema doesn't stop future/explicit NULLs (which #882's threading could introduce). Make the four scope columns (`owner_principal`, `visibility` at minimum) `NOT NULL DEFAULT 'legacy_admin'` in both `schema.sql` and the migration so fail-closed is enforced by the schema, not just by a default.

### Blocking 4 — the migration tests don't exercise the path the acceptance criterion targets

AC2 asks for a *populated schema-v6 database* asserted for *exact data preservation* to *prevent the prior SELECT-\* column-count regression*. That regression lives in the **v6 table-rebuild** (`INSERT INTO new_x SELECT …`). But every migration test runs `migrations={7: m.MIGRATIONS[7]}` — **migration 7 alone, on hand-built minimal stub tables**. Migration 7 is pure `ADD COLUMN`, which cannot lose or misalign data, so `test_v7_preserves_existing_data`'s assertions pass trivially and would pass even if v6 were broken. Net: the v6 explicit-column fix is **unguarded by any test**, and no test runs the full `1→7` chain or a realistic v6 schema through the rebuild. Add a test that populates a real (non-stub) v6-shaped DB — including the tables v6 rebuilds — runs the v6→(v7) migration, and asserts row counts + exact column values survive the rebuild. That's what actually protects the named regression.

### Non-blocking nits
- `ownership.py` uses `class Visibility(str, Enum)` rather than `StrEnum` (the house style, e.g. `access_control.OperationDecision`). `(str, Enum)` has the `str(member) == "Vis

payload.body:
## Verdict: blocking comments

## Summary
This moves the static service-principal table toward explicit per-trigger capabilities and the full suite is green (`5881 passed, 19 skipped`). The production enforcement gate is still not implemented, though, and the new tests do not exercise server-owned creation paths, so the two load-bearing acceptance criteria are not yet satisfied.

## Blocking issues

1. **`mimir/access_control.py:1247` — the matrix preflight is dead code, so enforcement can still start with an incomplete matrix.** `check_capability_matrix_complete()` is referenced only by its unit tests; neither config loading, server startup, agent construction, nor the `MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED` path invokes it. An operator can therefore enable enforcement while a required principal is missing or empty, directly violating “fail closed or report enforcement blocked while the principal matrix is incomplete.” Wire this into the actual enablement/startup path and add a regression that enables enforcement with an incomplete matrix and observes startup/config rejection (or an explicit blocked state).

2. **`tests/test_tool_registry.py:418` — the claimed production-path test forges the exact `AuthContext.trigger` it says it must not forge.** `_auth_context(trigger="scheduled_tick", event_ingress=None)` constructs a registry-only context directly and then calls `ToolRegistry.authorize_tool`; it never enters through `Scheduler._fire_job`, `run_poller`, `_on_session_idle`, or the upgrade enqueue path. This cannot prove that server-owned trigger/ingress provenance survives the real path, and it does not meet the issue's explicit review criterion. Add enforced-mode integration tests that construct/enqueue events through those server-owned creation paths and exercise representative tools through the live middleware.

3. **`mimir/access_control.py:1278` — readable/sink metadata is still decorative, not reconciled with executable capabilities.** The preflight merely logs when `readable_domains` or `sink_destinations` is empty; it never validates that a principal granted read operations has the corresponding readable domain, that `send_message`/boundary sinks match `sink_destinations`, or that authorization checks either field. As written, the metadata and executable matrix can disagree silently—the condition this issue is supposed to eliminate. Define and enforce the operation→domain/sink contract (or validate it fail-closed at startup), with mismatched-matrix tests.

## Additional least-authority concern

- **`mimir/access_control.py:1179` — synthesis gains unrestricted `shell_exec` without evidence that it is required by the documented capture workflow.** The production synthesis template names `mimir_get_turn`, file operations, SAGA operations, and `saga_end_session`; shell is not part of that contract. Granting arbitrary shell to synthesis is much broader than the requested narrow capture workflow and undermines the review criterion that synthesis not acquire unrelated authority. Remove it unless a concrete production call site and bounded need are demonstrated.

## Validation
- Worklink evidence: full suite green, `5881 passed, 19 skipped` in 235.39s.
- Review based on PR head `cfc8807bf7f694f53f062da231531bc27a83db97`.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Adversarial review of #879 (service-principal capability matrix + enforcement preflight). Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES.**

The direction is right and resolves the coherence gap I flagged on #1067: scheduler/poller/system now carry explicit read caps (rather than relying on a write/shell⇒read implication), synthesis gains file + SAGA capabilities, and spawn/schedule-mutation/cross-channel are correctly withheld from synthesis. The `check_capability_matrix_complete` + `CapabilityMatrixError` shape is the right idea. But four criteria aren't met.

### Blocking 1 — the enforcement preflight isn't wired (AC5 is a no-op)

`check_capability_matrix_complete()` is **defined and unit-tested but has no production caller** — nothing invokes it at the enforcement-enable path (where `MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED` / `enforcement_enabled` is resolved). AC5 requires a preflight that "fails closed or reports enforcement blocked **while the principal matrix is incomplete**." A check that nothing calls at the gate can't gate anything — flip enforcement on with an incomplete matrix today and this never fires. Wire it into the enforcement-resolution path so enforcement genuinely cannot enable while the matrix is incomplete (and add a test that enabling enforcement with a stripped matrix fails closed). This is the same "mechanism exists but isn't connected to the decision" pattern the other DAG leaves hit.

### Blocking 2 — tests forge `AuthContext` instead of the server-owned creation path

The review criteria are explicit: *"tests enter through server-owned trigger/creation paths rather than forged AuthContext fields or direct registry-only calls."* Every principal test uses `_auth_context()`, which constructs `AuthContext(trigger=…, event_ingress=…)` **directly**. So AC4's "end-to-end tests for each principal's representative production workflow" aren't end-to-end — they never exercise `create_auth_context(event)` mapping a real `event.trigger` → the service principal (with the `event_ingress is None` guard). A regression in that real resolution path would pass these tests. Drive at least one test per principal through `create_auth_context` from a synthetic server-created event (trigger=`saga_session_end`/`scheduled_tick`/… ) and assert the resulting principal + capability decision, plus a forged-`event_ingress` case that must NOT inherit the principal.

### Should-fix 3 — synthesis `shell_exec` looks like an over-grant

#879's own problem statement scopes synthesis to *"file reads/writes plus SAGA memory operations,"* and the review criterion requires synthesis to do its capture workflow **"without unrelated shell, spawn, schedule-mutation, or cross-channel authority."** This PR grants synthesis `shell_exec`. Either justify it from synthesis's actual `saga_session_end` production prompt (AC1 inventory) or remove it — as it stands it exceeds the stated scope and the explicit "without unrelated shell" criterion.

### Should-fix 4 — readable_domains / sink_destinations not reconciled with the new capabilities (AC3 + review criterion 4)

AC3 requires reconciling `readable_domains`/`sink_destinations` with the operation capabilities "so metadata and authorization cannot disagree," and the review criterion says they must be "enforced or validated against the same matrix, not merely documented beside it." The principals gained `read_file`/`ls`/`glob`/… but their `readable_domains` are unchanged (`configured_inputs`/`poller_payload`/`session`/`defaults` — no filesystem domain), and `check_capability_matrix_complete` only **warns on empty** domains — it never validates capabilities against domains. So a read_file capability with no matching readable domain is exactly the unreconciled disagreement this AC targets. Have the preflight validate consistency (a read/file capability implies a corresponding readable_domain; an egress capability implies a sink_destination), not just non-emptiness.

payload.title: Worklink #878: Reconcile feature-factory run transitions and merged-PR cleanup

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Adversarial review of #878 (reconcile feature-factory run transitions + merged-PR cleanup). Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES.**

The observe/dedup side is solid and well-tested: discovery at the repo root **and** nested `.worklink/<issue>-<attempt>` checkouts, observation through #858's canonical `_parse_run_state` (fail-closed on missing/malformed → `invalid`/`stale`), a deterministic fingerprint + cursor/tombstone so repeated observations are silent and only *new* actionable transitions (`blocked|partial|needs-human|invalid|stale`) alert, with routing instructions that tell the agent to escalate to you for operator authority. And the cleanup code has the right *shape*: `cleanup_eligible` requires `status=="completed"` AND `_is_pr_merged`, `_run_factory_cleanup` uses `factory cleanup --all [--dry-run] --json` with **no `--force`** and no direct filesystem/branch deletion, and blocked/partial/needs-human are never auto-cleaned.

But the destructive half isn't verified, and it deviates from the AC.

### Blocking — the destructive cleanup path is entirely untested

The 15 new tests cover cursor persistence, discovery, observation, run-id parsing, and fingerprinting. **None** exercises `_attempt_cleanup`, `_run_factory_cleanup`, `cleanup_eligible`, or `_is_pr_merged` — the actual delete path. So the AC's most safety-critical guarantees are unproven:
- a run whose PR is **not merged** (or unavailable) is NOT cleaned;
- `blocked|partial|needs-human`/invalid/stale runs are NOT cleaned;
- a completed+merged run goes dry-run → execute, and a failed/empty dry-run alerts instead of executing;
- the execute never passes `--force` and never falls back to filesystem deletion.

For a destructive operation on retained worktrees, "the guard exists in code" isn't enough — add tests that drive `_attempt_cleanup`/`_reconcile_factory_runs` with a fake factory runner and assert cleanup is invoked only for completed+merged, refused for unmerged/blocked, dry-run precedes execute, and no `--force`.

### Should-fix — the execute is not bound to the dry-run digest (AC deviation)

AC: *"invoke `factory cleanup --all --dry-run --json`, then execute **only the exact returned evidence-bound digest**."* `_attempt_cleanup` dry-runs only to confirm a non-empty digest, then calls `_run_factory_cleanup(dry_run=False)` = a fresh unbound `factory cleanup --all` — it doesn't pass the digest back, and it doesn't re-verify `completed`+merged immediately before executing. Safety is thus delegated entirely to the factory's own `--all` conservatism, and there's a (small, same-worktree) TOCTOU window where the executed set can differ from the evidenced digest. If the 0.2.1 CLI supports executing a specific digest, use it; if it genuinely only offers `--all`, then re-verify eligibility (status + `_is_pr_merged`) immediately before the unbound execute and note in a comment that final protection is the factory's conservative protocol.

Once the cleanup path has tests proving unmerged/blocked runs are never cleaned and the execute is bound to (or re-verified against) the evidenced state, this is a solid reconciliation pass — and it's a prerequisite for #877, so worth locking down.

payload.title: Worklink #871: Per-turn information-flow labels and sink gate

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Adversarial review of #871 (information-flow labels + egress/sink gate). Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES — two blocking findings on the most security-critical leaf.**

The substrate is real: `InformationFlowLabels` are initialized before the first model call (`agent.py:2152-2153` → `_initialize_ifc_labels` from inbound event + attachments), propagated (`_propagate_ifc_labels`), the tool-call path gates via `budget_gate` → `authorize_tool` → `SinkGate.check_sink_flow` (reads `ctx.ifc_labels`), and there's an audited admin `audit_declassification`. But two gaps make it not yet hold.

### Blocking 1 — harness-emitted egress bypasses the sink gate

`SinkGate.check_sink_flow` is invoked in exactly one place — `access_control.py:953`, on the **model tool-call** path. It is never called in `agent.py`, `channel_registry.py`, `resend_nudge.py`, or the bridges. So the harness-emitted egress paths deliver to channels **without checking `ctx.ifc_labels`**:
- `_maybe_auto_deliver_final_text` sends `clean_text` straight to `self._channels.send(...)` with no label check;
- `_maybe_resend_nudge` (recovery delivery) — same, no gate;
- the `MIMIR_ACTIVITY_PANEL_CHANNELS` posts/edits — same.

This is exactly the #1055 finding recurring in the implementation, and it fails an **explicit #871 review criterion**: *"Verify preloaded private context blocks an incompatible sink **without a preceding read tool call**."* Auto-deliver has no preceding tool call, so the tool-path gate can never fire — preloaded private/protected context (e.g. an injected private-labeled memory or attachment) auto-delivered to the triggering channel flows ungated. AC also requires blocking incompatible destinations across "messaging/directives/... and notifications," which includes these harness sends. **Fix:** invoke `check_sink_flow` at the *final egress boundary* of each harness path (`_maybe_auto_deliver_final_text`, `_maybe_resend_nudge`, activity-panel post/edit) against `ctx.ifc_labels` before `self._channels.send`; ideally centralize the gate at the `channels.send` boundary so every egress — tool and harness — passes it uniformly.

### Blocking 2 — the entire IFC implementation ships with zero tests

The PR's net changes are 4 source files (`access_control.py +217`, `agent.py +69`, `models.py +80`, `budget_gate.py +16`) and **no test file**; `tests/test_information_flow.py` does not exist. A 382-line taint-labels + sink-gate + declassification implementation — the leaf with the most explicit, testable review criteria — has no coverage, so CI is green over both the tool gate and the ungated harness paths. Add `test_information_flow.py` covering: labels initialized before the first model call; propagation into subagents/spawns/continuations/resumed turns; **preloaded private context blocked at an incompatible sink with no preceding tool call** (the harness-egress case above — this test would fail today); same-principal/same-channel passes only when every label is destination-compatible; unknown labels/destinations fail closed; and declassification-does-not-erase on summarization/model-assertion/failure/ordinary-admin.

(This is also the pattern #1069's acceptance gate exists to stop — worth noting that the IFC leaf itself shipped untested and with the sink gate wired to only one of its egress surfaces.)

Once the sink gate binds the harness egress boundary (not just tool calls) and `test_information_flow.py` proves the no-preceding-tool-call case + fail-closed defaults, this is the right IFC core.

payload.title: Worklink #859: Add a React Factory Runs view backed by the canonical 0.2.1 state parser

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Adversarial review of #859 (Factory Runs dashboard + read-only API). Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES — one blocking security finding.**

Most of this is well done and I verified it:
- **One interpretation (crit 1):** both handlers read raw JSON then normalize through #858's canonical parser — `data = json.loads(...)` → `_parse_run_state(data)` → serialize. No shell CLI, no hand-rolled JSON semantics. The detail view surfaces the full 0.2.1 field set (steps/slices/gates/validator+security verdicts/terminal_result/cost/debug).
- **Bounded + off-loop (crit 3):** the list enumerates server-side, caps at `[:1000]`, and runs under `await asyncio.to_thread(_list_factory_runs)`. Malformed/unparseable `run.json` degrades to an explicit `status: "invalid"` diagnostic entry — never rendered as running/completed.
- **Auth-gated (crit 2, partial):** both routes register as `DashboardBackendRoute` alongside `/api/v1/ops` and `/api/v1/chainlink-board`, so they inherit the same gating.

### Blocking — path traversal in `factory_runs_detail_v1`

`GET /api/v1/factory-runs/{run_id}` takes the URL `run_id` (only `.strip()`ed — no validation) and passes it straight to:
```python
def factory_run_dir(repo_path, run_id): return repo_path / FACTORY_DIR / run_id   # no confinement
...
run_dir = factory_run_dir(repo, run_id); run_json = run_dir / "run.json"
data = json.loads(run_json.read_text(...)); state = _parse_run_state(data)
```
There is no rejection of `..`/path separators and no `is_relative_to(factory_root)` check. So `GET /api/v1/factory-runs/..%2F..%2F..%2F..%2F<path>` resolves outside `<repo>/.opencode/factory/` and will read, parse, and return any `run.json`-named file the process can reach — a confinement break and information-disclosure primitive. This directly violates the review criterion: *"The endpoint resolves only beneath the configured Worklink repo/factory root, rejects traversal."* It's also untested — the suite covers happy/not-found/malformed but no traversal case, so CI is green over the hole.

**Fix:** reject `run_id` containing path separators or `..` (or require a strict pattern, e.g. `^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$` / `^chainlink-\d+$`), **and** assert `factory_run_dir(repo, run_id).resolve().is_relative_to((repo / FACTORY_DIR).resolve())` before any read. There's a local precedent to mirror — the React-dist handler at `web_ui.py:1241-1242` already does exactly this `resolve()` + root-containment check. Add a traversal-rejection test (`run_id="../../.."` → 400/404 by *confinement*, asserted against a real file that exists outside the root so the test proves rejection, not a coincidental missing-file 404).

This is the rebuild-trigger leaf, so worth getting right before it ships. Once the detail endpoint confines `run_id` beneath the factory root (with a test that proves rejection), the rest of this is good to go.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #870: MCP provenance, classification, adapters, and drift detection

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Adversarial review of #870 (MCP provenance & classification substrate). Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES — the classification default is inverted to fail-open.**

The provenance substrate itself is reasonable: a versioned provenance record, tombstone-on-drift, and `get_decision` correctly returns `ADMIN_REQUIRED` for **missing** provenance and **tombstoned** (drifted) provenance. Those two fail closed. But the central security property of the leaf is inverted.

### Blocking — valid-but-unclassified MCP tools are classified `OPEN` (allow-for-all), not admin-required

`MCPResourceAdapter.get_decision`:
```python
if provenance is None:        return ADMIN_REQUIRED   # ok
if provenance.is_tombstoned:  return ADMIN_REQUIRED   # ok
return OperationDecision.OPEN                          # <-- any valid-provenance MCP tool
```
and `authorize_tool` treats `OPEN` as `allowed = True` unconditionally (no admin/enforce gate). So **under enforcement a bare regular tier can invoke any provenanced MCP tool with arbitrary arguments** — an MCP github-write, slack-post, filesystem, or shell tool all resolve to `OPEN` merely because they carry a provenance record. That directly violates:
- the review criterion "a bare regular-scoped tier cannot authorize arbitrary MCP arguments," and
- AC "treat missing/**unclassified**/stale provenance as admin-required; **require a registered adapter for resource-scoped classification**."

Having provenance is *necessary but not sufficient*. Provenance only establishes stable identity so a **registered adapter** can classify the tool; a provenanced-but-unclassified tool must fail closed. The docstring even conflates the two ("Returns OPEN for MCP tools with valid provenance (classified)") — valid provenance is not classification.

**Correct default:** valid provenance **with** a registered adapter classification → the adapter's decision (`OPEN`/`RESOURCE_SCOPED`/`ADMIN_REQUIRED`); valid provenance **without** a registered adapter → `ADMIN_REQUIRED` (fail closed). As written, every classified-provenance MCP surface is fail-open.

### Blocking (same root) — the adapter registry is dead code

`_global_mcp_adapter_registry`, `register_mcp_adapter`, and `get_mcp_adapter` are defined but **never consulted** by `get_decision` (or anywhere). So AC "require a registered adapter for resource-scoped classification" is unwired — the mechanism exists but the decision ignores it. `get_decision` must consult the registry: registered adapter → its classification; no adapter for a provenanced tool → `ADMIN_REQUIRED`.

### Tests
Add authorization-decision coverage that would have caught this: a provenanced-but-**unclassified** MCP tool → `ADMIN_REQUIRED` (denied for a regular tier under enforcement), a tool with a **registered adapter** → its resource-scoped/open decision, and an assertion that a bare regular principal cannot call an arbitrary provenanced MCP write tool. The current `test_mcp_client.py` additions are largely config/parsing (env expansion, wrapper shapes, collisions, timeouts); the authz classification path — the point of #870 — isn't exercised at the decision level, so CI stays green over the fail-open default.

Once the default flips to admin-required-unless-a-registered-adapter-classifies-it (and the registry is actually consulted + tested), the missing/tombstoned handling you already have completes the fail-closed model.

The dead stub registry is removed and replaced by the real MCPAdapterRegistration/get_mcp_adapter_info in mcp_client, plus a startup stale-policy check. Tests now encode the correct behavior: provenanced-but-unclassified→admin, adapter-version-mismatch→admin, registered-adapter-supplies-decision, and 'regular principal cannot call an arbitrary provenanced write tool'→admin.
