payload.title: Worklink #867: Commitment ownership schema and authorization adapter

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Adversarial review of #867 (commitments ownership, recipient, visibility + authorization). Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES.**

The store layer is well-built and the hard invariants are right:
- `owner_principal` / `recipient_principal` / `originating_channel` / `visibility` / `service_name` added; `dedupe_key` now includes `owner_principal` and `find_by_dedupe_key` is owner-scoped → **different owners can't dedupe together** ✓.
- `_is_authorized` correctly does **not** consult `recipient_principal` → recipient identity grants no mutation authority ✓; service/private/public rules; legacy (owner `None`) → service-only ✓.
- `_can_view` read filter with correct public/service/private semantics; CLI passes the operator actor and the poller passes `service:poller`; store-level tests are thorough.

### Blocking — the agent-facing tools bypass the entire authorization/visibility layer

The model-facing commitment tools call the store **without `actor_principal`**, so every store guard degrades to its backward-compat "allow/return-all" path:

- `mimir/tools/registry.py:1316` `store.complete(commitment_id, message_id=message_id)` — no actor
- `:1349` `store.snooze(commitment_id, until_unix=…, reason=reason)` — no actor
- `:1369` `store.dismiss(commitment_id, reason=reason)` — no actor
- `:1404` `store.list()` — no `actor_principal`/`owner_principal`

`_is_authorized(actor_principal=None)` returns `True` unconditionally, so on the agent path **complete/snooze/dismiss are unauthorized** — the exact surface #867 exists to constrain (AC: "complete/snooze/dismiss authorize before appending lifecycle events"). And `commitment_list` never passes the requester, so `_can_view` isn't driven by the caller — there's no per-requester scoping and it leans on `None` coincidentally failing the private/service equality checks. That fails AC ("list filters before rendering") and the review criterion ("unauthorized existence/text never enters tool results or audit bodies").

Critically, the store-level tests exercise the guards by calling the store **with** `actor_principal`, so they're green while the live tool path is unauthorized — the same green-tests-over-a-bypassed-path gap seen on #866/#873/#1063.

**Fix:** resolve the turn's actor principal from the server-created `AuthContext` (as `budget_gate` does for channel ops) inside the commitment tools, and pass it to `complete`/`snooze`/`dismiss` and to `list(actor_principal=…, owner_principal=…)`. Add tool-path tests asserting (a) an unauthorized actor's complete/snooze/dismiss is rejected, and (b) another owner's private/service records don't appear in `commitment_list` output.

### Minor / verify
- `_is_authorized` grants only `actor_principal.startswith("service:")` for SERVICE/legacy records — an admin operator principal (e.g. `user:jason`) can't mutate service/legacy commitments, but AC says "admin/service-only." Confirm admin authority is granted somewhere (or add an explicit admin allowance) so the operator can still manage legacy/service records.

Once the tools thread the AuthContext actor into the store (and tool-path tests cover unauthorized mutation + cross-owner list isolation), the ownership model actually holds where it matters.

payload.title: Worklink #866: Channel messaging and history resource adapter

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Adversarial review of #866 (channel messaging/history resource adapter). Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES.**

The adapter shape is right and several hard parts are done well: channel equality is not authority across bridges (`test_same_channel_different_bridge_denies`, `test_cross_bridge_denies`), aliases resolve server-side via the injected `IdentityResolver`, cross-channel/unknown → admin, admin cross-channel allowed, denials are structured/redacted and don't echo model-supplied channel values, and a model-supplied target can't inherit triggering authority (a different target is cross-channel). The adapter-hook wiring and `send_message`/`react`/`fetch_channel_history` → RESOURCE_SCOPED reclassification are correct.

### Blocking — the implicit / reply-to-trigger target is denied under enforcement (and mis-shadowed)

All three tools take `channel_id: Optional[str] = None` and **default to the triggering channel when omitted** (registry.py: "Defaults to current turn's"; `send_message` line 434 `if not explicit_channel:`). That implicit reply-to-the-current-channel is the most common operation and is a same-scope regular op that AC requires to pass. But the authorization denies it:

- `budget_gate._extract_channel_from_args` returns `args.get("channel_id")` → `None` for an implicit send (the model didn't pass one).
- `ToolRegistry.authorize_tool` only delegates to the adapter when `tool_name in _CHANNEL_OPERATIONS and target_channel` — with `target_channel=None` it **skips the adapter** and falls through to the generic `RESOURCE_SCOPED` branch → `enforce → allowed=False, reason="resource_scoped"` (and in shadow mode it's logged as generic `resource_scoped`, not `same_scope`).
- Even if reached, `authorize_channel_operation` denies a missing target outright (`reason="missing_target_channel"`).

So under enforcement, every `send_message`/`react`/`fetch_channel_history` that omits `channel_id` (i.e. replies to the triggering channel) is **denied** — the opposite of AC's "same-scope regular operations pass" and its explicit requirement to "cover implicit targets … and reply-to-trigger behavior." In shadow mode it's allowed but mislabeled, so the shadow audit (the whole point of shadow mode — preview what enforcement would do) would show normal replies as would-be-denied, misinforming the enable decision.

This is baked into the tests: `test_missing_target_channel_denies` and `test_empty_target_channel_denies` assert the deny, and there is **no** test asserting an omitted/implicit target resolves to the triggering channel and is allowed. So CI is green on the wrong behavior.

**Fix:** treat an omitted/empty target as the triggering channel (that's what the tools do), so missing-target → same-scope → allow. Concretely: `budget_gate` should default the implicit target to `auth_context.channel_id` for channel ops when no `channel_id` arg is present (and pass through to the adapter regardless of whether the arg is set), and `authorize_channel_operation` should treat `target_channel is None/""` as the triggering channel rather than a hard deny. Then add a reply-to-trigger test that asserts a regular user with no `channel_id` arg is allowed, plus (given the gate is the real entry point) a test that drives `_check_admin_authorized`/`authorize_tool` for an omitted-channel send and asserts same-scope allow — the current unit tests exercise the adapter directly and miss the gate's `and target_channel` skip.

(Keep `missing_triggering_channel` as a deny — a turn with no server-resolved channel genuinely has no channel scope. The issue is only the missing *target*, which defaults to the trigger.)

Once omitted-channel replies resolve to the triggering channel (same-scope allow) at the gate, and a reply-to-trigger allow test covers it end-to-end, this is the right channel adapter for #871/#872.

payload.title: Worklink #876: Bake the pinned OpenCode feature-factory runtime stack

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Adversarial review of #876 (bake the pinned OpenCode feature-factory runtime stack). Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES.**

The install half is clean: exact pins in the root Dockerfile and both scaffold modes, opt-in gated on `MIMIR_ENABLE_OPENCODE=1`, a tool-pin inventory with an install-literal cross-check, and the sentinel always substituted. But the **configure** half (AC3) — the leaf's other stated job ("installs and configures the consumer") — has two real gaps, and the merge path is untested.

### Blocking

**1. The `opencode.json` bootstrap silently no-ops on an existing config — it never merges.**
`scaffold_docker.py` (~L1195):
```python
if oc_path.is_file():
    existing = oc_path.read_text()
    if "opencode-feature-factory" not in existing:
        result.files_written.append("opencode.json (merge required)")   # label only — nothing written
    else:
        result.files_skipped.append("opencode.json (no changes)")
else:
    oc_path.write_text(oc_text); result.files_written.append("opencode.json (created)")
```
When a config already exists without the plugin, the code appends a **`(merge required)` label to `files_written`** and does nothing else — no parse, no merge, no write. So on any runtime that already has an `opencode.json`, the feature-factory / project-memory plugins are **never registered**. AC3 requires "an idempotent bootstrap that registers the package plugins **while preserving unrelated config and existing factory profile options**"; the review criterion requires preserving unrelated config, retaining existing profile tuples, and avoiding duplicate registrations. This path does none of that — it's a stub, and reporting it under `files_written` (not `files_skipped`/a warning) misleads the operator into thinking it was handled. Implement a real preserving merge (parse JSON → add the two plugins iff absent, keep everything else, dedupe) and add a test with a pre-existing *unrelated* `opencode.json`. No current test hits this branch: `test_scaffold_opencode_config_is_idempotent` re-runs after a fresh create, so it exercises the "already has it" branch, never the merge branch.

**2. The config's location isn't wired to where OpenCode (or the factory) actually resolves it.**
The config is written to `<home>/opencode.json`, but the factory runs OpenCode inside `.worklink/<issue>-<attempt>` worktrees, and AC3 explicitly requires the memory/plugin config to apply "into outer and inner worktrees." OpenCode resolves config from XDG (`~/.config/opencode/`) or a project-local `opencode.json` in the run cwd/repo root — nothing in this PR points OpenCode at `<home>/opencode.json` (no `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, no copy into worktrees, no `--config`). As written, the plugins can be installed yet never loaded where the factory executes. Please verify OpenCode loads this exact file in the factory worktree context, or place/copy it where OpenCode resolves it — and cover it with a test that asserts the resolved location, not just that a file was written under `<home>`.

Related: the config bootstrap only runs in `scaffold()` (the generated-scaffold path), not the **root-image** build that mimirbot (and #877's rebuild) uses — the root Dockerfile npm-installs the packages but never writes/register the config. So #877's plugin-registration doctor check would fail on a root-image rebuild unless the bootstrap is also reachable there (a `mimir`-side setup step, or the operator Dockerfile writing it). Worth resolving here since #876 is the "install and configure the consumer" leaf that #877 depends on.

### Minor
- The install-literal drift cross-check (`test_default_tool_pin_inventory_matches_shipped_install_literals`) covers `opencode-ai` / `opencode-feature-factory` / `opencode-project-memory` but **not** the two auth plugins (`opencode-openai-codex-auth@4.4.0`, `opencode-anthropic-auth@0.0.13`) — their pins can drift between the inventory and the Dockerfile without a failing test. AC2 wants all pins un-driftable; add the two.
- AC4 asks f

The old scaffold no-op is gone; `test_ensure_opencode_config_preserves_existing_options_and_deduplicates` covers it.

payload.title: Worklink #873: Harden Worklink admission against duplicate dispatch of review-state leaves

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Verdict: COMMENTED — blocking changes required

The patch adds useful defense-in-depth for `worklink:review` and durable review-ready evidence, and the full local suite is green (5,662 passed, 19 skipped). However, it does not implement the issue's primary lifecycle admission invariant.

## Blocking finding

`mimir/worklink/claims.py:169-172` only rejects `worklink:review`; it does not require `worklink:ready`. Consequently a leaf with no lifecycle label, or only `worklink:in-progress`, still reaches `locks claim` and can create another attempt. The new test explicitly codifies `worklink:in-progress` as accepted. That contradicts #873's acceptance criterion that core admission refuse unless the leaf currently has `worklink:ready`, and that incompatible states such as `worklink:in-progress` or `worklink:review` be rejected.

Please make the core claim path fail closed unless `worklink:ready` is present and no incompatible lifecycle label is present, then add regression coverage for unlabeled and `worklink:in-progress` leaves proving rejection is non-mutating. If a legitimate reattach path exists, it needs a separate explicit API/guard rather than weakening ordinary dispatch admission.

## Validation

- Worklink evidence: full suite `5,662 passed, 19 skipped`.
- `git diff --check origin/main...87c50bed` passed.


Note: GitHub does not permit CHANGES_REQUESTED because this PR is authored by the reviewing bot identity; this COMMENT is blocking.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Adversarial review of #873 (harden Worklink admission against duplicate dispatch of review-state leaves). Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES.**

The shape is right — the guard lives in `ChainlinkClaims.claim_issue` (the core admission point) and runs *before* the lock claim, so rejection is non-mutating. But two defects mean the fix does not actually close the #864 hole, and both are masked by tests that pass.

**Blocking — the durable-evidence guard is a no-op in production; the test hides it with a hand-rolled evidence schema.**
The guard is:
```python
if evidence is not None and evidence.get("review_ready"):
    pr_url = evidence.get("pr_url")
    if pr_url:
        return ClaimResult(False, reason="review_ready_evidence_exists")
```
But `review_ready` is **never serialized into the evidence file**. The file is written by `_write_evidence` → `_evidence_json` → `asdict(WorklinkEvidence)`, and `WorklinkEvidence` (evidence.py) has no `review_ready` field — it has `status`, `pr_url`, `files_changed`, `tests`, etc. `review_ready` lives only on the separate `EvidenceValidation`. So `evidence.get("review_ready")` is always falsy against a real evidence file, and the durable guard never fires — exactly the "durable review-ready PR/evidence association even if labels have drifted" case (acceptance criterion 2 / the label-drift review criterion) is left open. The passing test `test_claim_issue_refuses_when_review_ready_evidence_exists` writes its own dict with a literal `"review_ready": True`, a shape the production writer never emits, so it proves nothing about the real path. Fix: key off the persisted schema — e.g. `status == "completed"` (optionally recomputing review-readiness the way `evidence.py` does) plus a present `pr_url` — and change the test to write evidence via the real writer / real schema.

**Blocking — the epic dispatch path bypasses the guard entirely.**
`claim_issue` has two callers: `WorklinkRunner.run` (orchestrator.py:391, updated to pass `labels`/`home_path`) and `WorklinkRunner.run_epic` (orchestrator.py:959, **not** updated). `run_epic` already reads `issue` and has `self.home` in scope, but calls `claim_issue(issue.issue_id, issue.comments, max_active_locks=...)` with neither guard param — so a review-state epic leaf can still be redispatched. This directly fails the review criterion "admission is enforced in the deterministic core executor, not only in [one path]." Pass `labels=issue.labels, home_path=str(self.home)` there too.

**Should-fix — the guard is opt-in via optional params and silently no-ops when omitted.**
Both guards are gated on `if label_set:` / `if home_path is not None:`, so any caller that doesn't pass them skips admission — which is precisely how `run_epic` slips through, and how any future caller will. Since `claim_issue` is *the* core admission point and already holds `issue_id` + a chainlink runner, it should resolve the current labels and durable evidence itself and always enforce, rather than trusting each caller. That makes the guard uniform and removes the bypass class entirely (and subsumes the previous finding).

**Should-fix — no end-to-end regression reproduces the #864 sequence.**
Acceptance criterion 4 asks for a regression reproducing the sequence "including a generic `chainlink issue ready` caller attempting to dispatch a review-state leaf." The added tests exercise `claim_issue` in isolation (good building blocks) but none drives `WorklinkRunner.run`/`run_epic` through the poller-then-heartbeat sequence — so nothing here would have caught either blocking defect above. Add an orchestrator-level test that (a) marks a leaf review-state with a real-schema evidence file + PR, then (b) asserts a second `run`/`run_epic` admission is refused with no new attempt/claim/branch/PR.

Once the durable guard reads the real evidence schema, `run_epic` is covered (ideally by moving enforcement inside `claim_issue`), and an end-to-end regression locks the sequence, this closes #864.

payload.body:

- **run_epic bypass fixed:** `labels`/`home_path` are wired at :946/:961, with an end-to-end `test_run_epic_refuses_review_state_before_claim_or_factory_launch`.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES**

Adversarial review of #865 (authorization decision engine, operation catalog, service capabilities). The `OperationCatalog` shape is sound and, importantly, the enforcement-off single-operator default is genuinely preserved — but two of the three acceptance criteria aren't actually delivered at runtime, and the new 414-line surface ships with zero tests. This is the foundation leaf for #866–#871, so it needs to hold.

### What's correct (verified)
- `_ADMIN_REQUIRED_OPERATIONS` is a strict **superset** of the old `_ADMIN_TOOL_NAMES` (adds `set_poller_overrides`, drops nothing); `_ADMIN_BUILTIN_TOOL_NAMES` is identical; the MCP `__name`/`_name` suffix match is preserved. So no previously-admin tool is silently un-gated, and the enforcement-off default is unchanged (existing `test_budget_gate.py`/`test_access_control.py` stay green).
- Routing `budget_gate._is_admin_sensitive_tool` through `catalog.get_decision` is the right integration point, and UNKNOWN→fail-closed-under-enforcement is the correct semantics.

### Blocking

**1. Acceptance criteria 2 and 3 are not met — the machinery is defined but never wired.**
Only `OperationCatalog.get_decision` is actually reachable at runtime (via `budget_gate`). Everything else is dead code:
- `_TRUSTED_SERVICE_PRINCIPALS` is **empty** — there are no `register_service_principal(...)` calls anywhere. Criterion 2 requires *explicit* trusted-autonomous entries, and the #856 policy specifically requires scheduler, poller, synthesis, and system turns to be separate entries. None exist. `_find_service_principal_for_trigger` is only reachable from `authorize_tool`, which itself has no runtime caller.
- `ToolRegistry.register_tool` is **never called** — so the "executable inventory over the *final assembled runtime tool surface*" (criterion 3) is empty in production; it never enumerates the real tools.
- Shadow-decision logging is never enabled or emitted in the live path (`enable_shadow_logging` / `authorize_tool` have no runtime caller). The whole point of shadow mode — observe what enforcement *would* decide while it's off — can't happen. Criterion 3's "shadow-decision audit logging while enforcement is off" is undelivered.
- `get_tool_registry` and `ToolAuthorization` are imported into `budget_gate` but never used.

Either wire these into tool assembly / ingress (populate the inventory from the assembled surface, register the required service principals, emit shadow decisions on the live gate path), or if wiring is genuinely deferred, the acceptance criteria and the issue should say so explicitly — right now #865 claims deliverables that don't exist at runtime.

**2. Zero tests for the new surface.**
The PR changes only `access_control.py` and `budget_gate.py` — no test file is added or modified (the suggested `tests/test_tool_registry.py` doesn't exist; `TestMCPToolRegistry` in `test_mcp_client.py` is unrelated). The existing green tests only exercise the *unchanged* admin-gating and the pre-existing `authorize()`/`create_auth_context`. The new decision engine, RESOURCE_SCOPED/UNKNOWN semantics, enforcement toggling, service principals, inventory, and shadow logging are entirely untested. The review criteria ("new/renamed tools fail closed", "single-operator default unchanged") require explicit coverage — at minimum: UNKNOWN denied under enforcement / allowed-and-shadow-logged when off; a regression test asserting the admin set didn't shrink; MCP-suffix admin gating; and the service-principal/`_find_service_principal_for_trigger` behavior including "unknown synthetic trigger → no privilege."

### Should-fix

**3. `_is_admin_sensitive_tool` fails OPEN for `RESOURCE_SCOPED`.** It returns `True` only for `ADMIN_REQUIRED` and (conditionally) `UNKNOWN`, then falls through to `return False` for `RESOURCE_SCOPED` — so a resource-scoped op is not admin-gated by the one live path *even under enforcement*, while `authorize_tool` denies it. A future `register_operation(..

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
**Re-review of `1a23f20d` ("wire authorization catalog into runtime"). Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES — but close; round-1 blocking items are resolved.**

Solid, responsive update. Verified fixed from round 1:
- Catalog is now actually wired: `budget_gate` gates via `get_tool_registry().authorize_tool(...)`; `register_runtime_tools` populates the inventory from the model-bound surface via `wrap_model_call`/`awrap_model_call`; shadow logging is enabled in compat mode.
- Four service-principal **entries** registered, and their triggers (`scheduled_tick`/`poller`/`saga_session_end`/`upgrade`) match the real event triggers in `scheduler`/`pollers`/session-end/upgrade — so they're functional, not inert.
- `RESOURCE_SCOPED` now gated in the live path (`required_tier==admin`); `ServicePrincipal` is `frozen`; the inverted shadow done-callback is replaced with `_consume_task_exception`; unused imports removed.
- Genuinely good tests, including the exact regressions requested: `admin_catalog_never_shrinks_and_preserves_mcp_suffixes`, `unknown_operation_fails_closed_only_when_enforced`, `resource_scoped_operation_is_gated_by_live_path`, and a forged-HTTP-trigger spoof test. CI green.
- I re-traced the enforcement-off / HTTP-ingress-hard-deny / ctx-None paths: the single-operator default is unchanged (no live regression).

Two enforcement-time soundness issues remain. Neither is a live regression (enforcement is off by default), but both must be fixed before the #855/#856 enablement-ordering gate flips enforcement on, and one is actively masked by a test.

**Blocking — the inventory-membership bound on service-principal admin authority is vacuous in production, and the test hides it.**
`test_service_principal_can_use_only_inventoried_runtime_tools` builds a fresh `ToolRegistry()` with **only `shell_exec`** registered, then asserts `spawn_codex` is denied for a `scheduled_tick` turn. That passes only because the inventory is artificially minimal. In production, `wrap_model_call` calls `register_runtime_tools(request.tools)` and inventories the **entire** assembled surface, so `spawn_codex` — and every other admin tool — is present, `get_tool(tool_name) is not None` is always true, and the `has_capability("admin_required") and get_tool(...) is not None` check reduces to blanket admin. So scheduler/poller/system turns get admin over the whole surface under enforcement, and the test gives false assurance of a bound that won't hold. Scope these principals to explicit allowed operations (as `synthesis` already does with `saga_end_session`/`saga_mark_contributions`) instead of `admin_required` + inventory-membership — and make the test exercise the real (full-surface) inventory so it proves the actual bound. This also reconciles with the #856 policy's "separate entries rather than one blanket admin class."

**Blocking — the tool inventory is a process-global singleton cleared+repopulated on every model call; an authorization decision reads it, so it's unsound under concurrency.**
`_global_tool_registry` is module-global; `wrap_model_call`/`awrap_model_call` do `clear()` then re-register on each call with no scoping or lock. With concurrent turns (subagents, parallel channel/poller turns) sharing it: (a) a turn calling `authorize_tool` during another turn's `clear()` window sees an empty inventory → spurious deny under enforcement; (b) the inventory reflects whichever model call ran last, not the turn being authorized, so a subagent with a narrower surface can be authorized against the main turn's broader inventory → **fail-open** under enforcement. An authz decision must not depend on globally-mutated, non-turn-scoped state. Carry the inventory on the per-turn carrier (AuthContext/RunnableConfig), or drop inventory-membership from the decision entirely (see finding 1).

**Notes (non-blocking):**
- With shadow logging on by default, every admin-sensitive tool call now emits a `shadow_tool_decision` event. That's the intended criterion-3 behavior, but o

## Summary

The current head materially improves the first revision: it wires the catalog into the live budget-gate path, inventories the model-bound tool surface, adds explicit service entries, gates `RESOURCE_SCOPED`, fixes the background-task exception callback, and adds focused tests. The targeted authorization suite passes (`30 passed`), and the interrupted broad suite reached 10% with no failures before exit 143; GitHub's Python matrix is still running.

I am still requesting changes because the new runtime wiring does not yet satisfy the security contract in acceptance criteria 2 and 3. The remaining issues are boundary-level rather than missing polish:

## Blocking issues

1. **Service provenance is inferred from trigger text, not bound to the registered server-owned creation path.** `authorize_tool` promotes any context with a matching trigger and null `event_ingress`; the `creation_path` field is never consulted or represented in `AuthContext`. Stamp and carry an immutable service identity/provenance from each trusted creator, then resolve the principal from that binding.

2. **Capabilities are simultaneously too broad and ineffective.** Scheduler, poller, and system get the wildcard `admin_required`, which grants every current and future inventoried admin operation. Synthesis gets exact capabilities, but the UNKNOWN branch never checks them, so those operations are denied under enforcement. Use explicit operations per principal and test the full allow/deny matrix, including a newly added admin operation.

3. **The executable inventory is a mutable process-global singleton.** Concurrent turns replace one another's inventory before tool execution, so authorization can observe the wrong assembled surface. Scope an immutable inventory to the invocation/turn and add an interleaving concurrency regression.

4. **Shadow decisions are silently dropped without a running asyncio loop.** The supported synchronous `wrap_tool_call` path can reach `_emit_shadow_decision`, but the `RuntimeError` branch only emits a debug log. Criterion 3 requires an audit record while enforcement is off; use a sync-safe event sink/queue and cover both sync and async wrappers.

payload.title: Worklink #864: Frozen authorization context and exact-turn carrier

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Adversarial review of #864 (frozen authorization context + exact-turn carrier). The `AuthContext` frozen dataclass, its creation at ingress in `run_turn`, and the `budget_gate` consumption under enforcement are the right shape. But the core invariant this leaf exists to guarantee is not met, and the tests don't exercise the attack. Blocking.

**Blocking — `resolve_auth_context` derives authority through the exact three vectors the policy (#1055) forbids; its docstring claims the opposite of what it does.**

The function's docstring says authority derives ONLY from the frozen carrier, "NOT from model-passed session_id, ContextVar fallback, or single-active-turn heuristics." The body does all three, in order:

```
sid = args.get("session_id")                 # model-supplied
if sid:
    ctx = get_turn_by_saga_session_id(sid)    # (1) global lookup by model sid
    ...
ctx = get_only_active_turn()                  # (2) single-active-turn heuristic
...
ctx = get_current_turn()                      # (3) ContextVar
```

`_active_turns` is a **process-global dict of every concurrently-active turn** (`_context.py:70`, populated by `set_current_turn` for all turns), and `get_turn_by_saga_session_id` scans `_active_turns.values()` and returns any turn whose `saga_session_id` matches the **model-supplied** arg.

Failure scenario (the multi-user case this policy targets): turns A (alice, `roles=[user]`) and B (bob, `roles=[user,admin]`) run concurrently and are both registered in `_active_turns`. A tool call inside alice's turn passes `session_id = <bob's saga_session_id>`. `resolve_auth_context` → `get_turn_by_saga_session_id(bob_sid)` → bob's turn → **bob's admin `AuthContext`**. Alice's turn just acquired admin authority via a model-supplied selector — precisely "model-provided session_id … cannot select another turn's principal" from #1055. The `single_active`/`contextvar` fallbacks are the other two forbidden vectors (and `get_current_turn`'s ContextVar is inherited across forked tasks — see the chainlink-#23 note in `get_turn_by_saga_session_id`'s own docstring, which #1055 lists as never-authority).

The carrier must be bound to the **exact turn/request** the tool call belongs to (the RunnableConfig/turn binding, or the `ctx` handed to the handler) — never resolved by a model-supplied `session_id` against a global registry, nor by single-active/ContextVar. As written, every downstream adapter (leaves 3–8) inherits a spoofable principal.

**Blocking — the tests pass without testing the attack.**
- `test_auth_context_denies_forged_session_id`: bob's turn is created but **never registered** in `_active_turns` (only alice's `set_current_turn`), so the sid lookup misses and falls back to alice. The test's own comment says "bob's turn is not registered." Register both and assert that `resolve_auth_context({"session_id": bob_sid})` from alice's active turn does NOT return bob's admin context — that test will currently **fail**, which is the point.
- `test_auth_context_denies_concurrent_turn_principal_swap`: same — only alice is registered; the `if swapped_auth is not None` guard makes the assertion vacuous when the lookup misses. It needs both turns concurrently registered.

**Should-fix — leaf #864's stated acceptance ("remove security authority from `resolve_active_ctx` fallbacks") isn't done.** The PR *adds* the carrier alongside the old paths but leaves `_turn_has_internal_admin_authority` (`trigger != "user_message"` OR `source ∈ {web,api,stdin}`) live and evaluated **before** the new `auth_context` check in `_check_admin_authorized`. So under enforcement the old source-name/trigger carve-out still grants admin ahead of the frozen context — the insecure authority #864 was meant to remove still wins.

**Minor — fix the docstrings** on `resolve_auth_context`/`get_auth_context`/`AuthContext` to match the actual guarantee. Right now they assert a security property the code doesn't provide, which is worse than silence in an authz module

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body: Verified: the exact-request-carrier binding replaces the spoofable resolve_auth_context, the model-supplied session_id / single-active / ContextVar vectors are gone, the source-name/trigger admin carve-out is removed, and the two attack tests now register both turns and assert no principal-swap. All four blocking findings addressed; CI green. Approving per Jason's go-ahead.

payload.title: docs: specify requester/resource authorization policy

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Adversarial review of the requester/resource authorization policy (chainlink #856).

This is a strong, unusually rigorous decision artifact — the principal taxonomy, the "labels/source-names/ContextVar are never authority" stance, the decision order, the ownership/legacy fail-closed rules, and the honesty about coarse-IFC limits are all right. I verified the compatibility claims against the current code and they hold: `budget_gate._turn_has_http_event_ingress` already hard-denies admin-sensitive tools for HTTP-event ingress regardless of `MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED`, and the `trigger != "user_message"` / `source ∈ {web,api,stdin}` trust in `_turn_has_internal_admin_authority` only applies under enforcement — so "generic HTTP fail-closed" and "enforcement-off preserves current behavior" are both accurate today. Good.

One blocking gap, plus minor notes.

**Blocking — the read-to-egress sink model only covers model-invoked tool calls, but mimir has HARNESS-emitted egress that bypasses the tool-call layer entirely.** The IFC section (decision order step 7 "before a sink executes"; the sink enumeration at "Sinks include …") is framed around tools the model calls. But three existing framework paths push turn content to a channel WITHOUT a model tool call, so a tool-call-scoped sink gate would never see them:

- `MIMIR_AUTO_DELIVER_FINAL_TEXT_CHANNELS` — when a turn ends with captured final text and the model did *not* call `send_message`, the harness delivers that text to the triggering channel itself (#1046). If the turn read cross-principal/protected content (e.g. an admin cross-channel read) into that final text, auto-deliver egresses it with no `send_message` sink to gate.
- `MIMIR_RESEND_NUDGE_CHANNELS` — same shape (harness re-drives delivery).
- `MIMIR_ACTIVITY_PANEL_CHANNELS` — posts per-step detail to a channel; in `detailed` mode it renders tool-**result previews** (`_activity_panel.py`, `scrub_detail`). Secret/path scrubbing is not IFC label-flow: a protected *read result* preview can surface into a (potentially cross-user) channel.

These target the triggering channel, which the same-channel rule often permits — but the taint they carry can be cross-principal (content read during the turn), which is exactly what the IFC gate exists to stop. Since this doc is "the security contract that implementation slices must preserve," leaf #8 will build a tool-call sink gate and inherit this blind spot. Please enumerate harness-emitted egress (auto-deliver final text, resend-nudge, activity panel — coarse *and* detailed) as sinks subject to the same label check, and state that the IFC gate binds on egress paths, not only on model-invoked sink tools.

**Minor:**
- The compatibility story is safe because the fallback-authority removal (leaf #1) and source-name trust are enforcement-gated. But that safety depends on an ordering the doc only implies. Add an explicit invariant: **enforcement must not be enabled before the trusted-autonomous capability registry (leaf #2) lands**, or internal (poller/scheduler/synthesis) turns lose their access the moment enforcement flips on. Leaf #1 removing `resolve_active_ctx` fallback authority before #2 exists is the specific hazard.
- The "generic HTTP event = transport-only, deny non-open" rule means the operator's own **web-chat UI** (HTTP + `MIMIR_API_KEY`) gets no admin-tool authority until a named-principal credential mapping exists. If that's the intended end-state, fine — but call it out explicitly, since it removes admin-tool use from the primary operator surface (and confirm whether web-chat is even classified as HTTP-event ingress today vs. an interactive principal).
- Nit: file has no trailing newline (line 237).

Everything else holds up. Fix the harness-egress sink coverage — it's the one place the contract is incomplete in a way the implementation would faithfully reproduce — plus the ordering invariant, and this is a solid contract to build the #864-#872 leaves against.

The documentation omissions from the previous review are now covered, and the focused configuration tests pass. One blocking gap remains in the new completeness contract:

- `tests/test_config_docs_complete.py:66-69` only records an env name when the first call argument is a string literal. Core already has indirect reads such as `os.environ.get(_WEBHOOK_ENV, ...)` in `mimir/liveness.py`, `os.environ.get(AUTO_SUBMIT_CLEAN_ENV)` in `mimir/defaults_upgrade.py`, and helper calls whose env-name parameter is resolved inside the helper. Please either resolve module-level string constants/simple helper call sites in the scanner and add regression fixtures proving an undocumented indirect read fails, or narrow the stated completeness guarantee and document how the uncovered class is enforced. payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
The constant-backed gap from my previous review is resolved: the scanner now builds a module-level string-constant table, resolves names used by `os.environ.get`, `os.environ[...]`, and env-named helper calls, and includes regressions for both synthetic and known production cases. The documentation now states the static-analysis boundary rather than implying those dynamic plumbing shapes are enforced.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Fix user-scoped cross-channel context

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Adversarial security review — cross-channel/cross-user context isolation.

**Bottom line: the isolation boundary is correct** — I traced every path and could not construct a cross-user leak from the code alone. Requesting changes on one thing only: the newest and trickiest piece of logic (the adjacent-assistant-reply state machine, which is *the* thing standing between "same-user context" and "another user's content") is **completely unguarded by tests**. For a security-critical isolation fix, that invariant has to be pinned so a future refactor can't silently reintroduce the leak. Plus one stale comment. Details below.

## What I verified holds (the trace)

**Public target** (`include_private=False`):
- `within` = `recent_for_channel(active_channel)` → active channel only, all authors. Legit local continuity (everyone in a public channel is a participant of *that* conversation).
- `cross` = `cross_author_context(author, exclude=active, include_private=False)` → anchors are only the initiating user's *canonical* messages on **public** channels; reply-gathering **skips all `dm-*` channels**. No other user's messages, no DM content. ✓ Closes leak path #1 (unrelated users' public convos).

**DM target** (`include_private=True`):
- `within` = that DM channel only. ✓
- `cross` includes private channels, but another user's DM is still excluded: their messages are never in `anchor_ids` (canonical ≠ target), so `include_replies` never flips true for them, so neither their user messages nor the assistant replies to them are appended. Verified against the group-DM case too (anchor user's message flips replies on; the next user message flips it back off before their reply is reached). ✓ Closes leak path #2 (one user's DM into another's).

**SAGA query rewrite** (`_rewrite_context_from_buffer`) now reads `recent_for_channel` = active channel only. Unrelated recent material can no longer perturb the memory query pre-retrieval. ✓ (This was a real part of the surface, not just cosmetics.)

**Object-identity matching** (`id(msg) in anchor_ids` across `_all` and `_by_channel`): valid — `_append_in_memory` stores the *same* Message object in both containers.

The only residual cross-user vector is operator identity **mis**configuration (`resolve(attacker) == victim`), which is operator-controlled trust and out of scope for this PR. Worth a one-line note in the doc but not a code issue.

## Blocking (1) — pin the adjacent-reply boundary with a negative test

`cross_author_context`'s `include_replies` state machine is the entire mechanism that keeps another user's assistant-reply *out* of your context in a **shared** channel. Concretely, in a channel where user B and the anchor user A both spoke:

```
channel "general":
  B: "what's the prod DB password?"   (user_message)
  assistant: "it's hunter2"           (assistant_message)  <- reply to B, MUST NOT leak
  A: "hi"                             (user_message)        <- A's anchor
  assistant: "hello A"                (assistant_message)   <- reply to A, SHOULD include
```

The code handles this correctly (B's reply is dropped because `include_replies` is False when it's reached; it only flips true *after* A's anchor). But **no test exercises it.** Every added test uses channels where only one user speaks, so the `include_replies=False` reset on a non-anchor `user_message` is never actually exercised. Drop that one line in a future refactor and the assistant's reply to B — which can quote/summarize B's private input — leaks into A's prompt, with the suite still green.

Please add a test that puts a *second* user's message **and its assistant reply** in the same channel as the anchor user's message, and asserts the second user's reply is absent from the assembled activity — for both the public-target and DM-target paths. That's the test that actually guards #1048.

## Should-fix (2) — stale comment now asserts the opposite of the truth

`mimir/tools/registry.py::_resolve_recent_message_id` still s

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Follow-up on the round-1 review. The comment fix is good, and `test_assemble_activity_excludes_other_users_adjacent_replies` (parametrized over public + DM) is a real guard — thank you.

One precise gap remains, and it's the exact line I asked to pin: the `include_replies = False` reset inside the `user_message` branch of `cross_author_context`. The new test places bob **before** alice's anchor, so bob's `reply-to-bob` is excluded by the loop's *initial* `include_replies=False`, not by the reset. That ordering stays green even if the reset line is deleted:

```
ordering in added test (bob BEFORE anchor):  reset removed -> still ['alice-anchor','reply-to-alice']  (green with the bug)
other user AFTER the anchor:                 reset removed -> ['alice-anchor','reply-to-alice','reply-to-bob']  (leaks)
```

So the reset — which stops a *later* different user's assistant reply from being attributed to the anchor user within a shared channel — is currently unpinned. It's scope-tightening rather than the hard cross-membership boundary (that's the canonical-anchor match + per-channel initial `False` + `dm-*` skip, all of which you've now covered), but on a security-critical isolation path it's cheap insurance worth having.

Please add one case (or reorder/extend the existing parametrized test) where the second user speaks **after** the anchor in the same channel, and assert the reply to them is absent — keep it parametrized over the public and DM targets. Concretely:

```python
[
    ("general", "user_message",      "alice-anchor",  "alice", -4),
    ("general", "assistant_message", "reply-to-alice", None,   -3),
    ("general", "user_message",      "bob-secret",    "bob",   -2),
    ("general", "assistant_message", "reply-to-bob",   None,   -1),   # must NOT cross
    (target_channel, "user_message", "alice-current", "alice",  0),
]
# expect: ["alice-anchor", "reply-to-alice", "alice-current"]  (reply-to-bob absent)
```

That's the last item. With it in, this is a clean approve — everything else (the boundary logic, the same-canonical anchoring, the DM cross-user exclusion, the comment) is right.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body: Approved. Boundary traced correct; both #1048 leak paths closed (global public pool + `self._all` DM pool → exact-channel within + same-canonical-user cross). Verified the reset test against real code: passes as-is, fails (reply-to-bob leaks, both public + DM params) when the `include_replies=False` reset is removed — the seam is genuinely pinned. Stale registry comment fixed. CI green. Nice work.

payload.title: Worklink #852: Package and document the dependency-advisory poller for opt-in deployment

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Reviewed. The SKILL.md is well-structured (cadence, cursor behavior, clean-scan silence, failure-observability table, coverage boundary, security), the smoke tests (no-mimir-import, stdlib-only, standalone-run) are good additions, wheel-package-data inclusion is the right mechanism, and pollers.json `priority: low` + `batch_size: 10` are sensible. CI green. But the documented install is wrong in a way that breaks the skill, so — blocking.

**Blocker — the SKILL.md osv-scanner install contradicts the pinned/working version and would install an incompatible binary.** The install section documents:
- `osv-scanner` **v1.9.0**, and
- asset `osv-scanner-linux-amd64` (hyphens), and
- `go install ...@latest`.

But the pinned, working install (shipped by #1044) is **v2.4.0**: `tool_pins.py` pins `v2.4.0`, and `dockerfile.fragment` downloads `osv-scanner_linux_${TARGETARCH}` (underscores) at `v2.4.0`. This matters because the code (scanner.py) invokes `osv-scanner scan --format json --lockfile ...` — the `scan` subcommand only exists in **v2**. osv-scanner **v1.x** uses `osv-scanner --lockfile=...` and has no `scan` command, so following these docs (v1.9.0) makes every run fail (`unknown command "scan"` → wrapper raises → poller exits 2). The asset name is also wrong: v2 releases are `osv-scanner_linux_amd64` (underscores), so the documented hyphenated URL 404s. And `@latest` defeats pinning.

Fix: document **v2.4.0**, the correct underscore asset (`osv-scanner_linux_<arch>`), and pin the go install (`@v2.4.0`) — or, better, point operators at the shipped `dockerfile.fragment` as the canonical pinned install rather than duplicating (and drifting from) it in prose.

**Should-fix — doc accuracy on what it scans.** SKILL.md says "This poller scans **Python lockfiles only**" and lists "`package-lock.json` (npm/pip)". `package-lock.json` is **npm/JavaScript**, not Python or pip, and the poller scans both Python (`uv.lock`) and npm (`package-lock.json`). Reword to "Python (`uv.lock`) and npm (`package-lock.json`) lockfiles."

**Minor — package the canonical installer too.** `test_wheel_package_data.py` adds SKILL.md/poller.py/pollers.json/scanner.py to the wheel, but not `dockerfile.fragment`. So the wheel ships the *wrong* manual install (in SKILL.md) but not the *correct* pinned one (the fragment). gmail-poller ships its fragment; do the same here (add it to the package-data list) so the working installer travels with the skill.

Everything else is good — fix the version/asset mismatch (the important one) + the two smaller doc/packaging items and this is mergeable.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #851: Add advisory deduplication, poller events, and failure-safe cursor semantics

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Reviewed. The cursor logic is genuinely solid and correctly layered on the merged osv-scanner scanner — seed-first (no backlog storm), emit-only-new, silent repeats, resolved-IDs pruned, reappearing-IDs re-emitted, atomic temp+replace write, and failure leaves the cursor unchanged + returns exit 2 (no false-clean). The test suite covers all of those directions. One blocking item on cursor location, plus a small dead-code nit.

**Blocker — the cursor is written to the home ROOT, not the framework's STATE_DIR.** `_cursor_path()` returns `Path($MIMIR_HOME) / "dependency-advisory-cursor.json"`, i.e. `<home>/dependency-advisory-cursor.json`. The poller framework injects a dedicated **`STATE_DIR`** (`<home>/state/pollers/<poller-name>/`, created at discovery time — pollers.py:757-760, :947) precisely as "the poller's persistent cursor/state location … so cursors survive container rebuilds." Every other poller uses it (e.g. gmail-poller's cursor at `<home>/state/pollers/gmail-inbox/cursor.json`).

Writing to the home root is wrong two ways:
1. `<home>` is a **git-synced repo** on the real deployments (mimirbot → jasoncarreira/mimirbot, muninn → muninn-mimir), and the agent auto-commits the home per turn. A cursor file churning at the home root gets swept into those commits — repo pollution + noise on every scan-day.
2. It diverges from the STATE_DIR convention; STATE_DIR is framework-created and guaranteed present in the subprocess (it's in `_POLLER_INJECTED_ENV_KEYS` alongside MIMIR_HOME), so there's no reason to hand-roll a home-root path.

Fix: resolve the cursor under `STATE_DIR` — `Path(os.environ["STATE_DIR"]) / CURSOR_FILE` (STATE_DIR is always injected for a registered poller; no pass_env entry needed). Fall back / no-op only if STATE_DIR is genuinely absent (bare-script invocation). Update the tests to `setenv("STATE_DIR", ...)` accordingly.

**Nit — dead constant + misleading fallback.** The module-level `CURSOR_DIR = os.environ.get("MIMIR_HOME", os.environ.get("CURSOR_DIR", ".mimir"))` is never used — `_cursor_path()` reads `MIMIR_HOME` directly and ignores `CURSOR_DIR`/`.mimir`, so the documented fallback doesn't exist. Drop `CURSOR_DIR` (or wire the real STATE_DIR path through it). `test_missing_mimir_home_uses_fallback` also misnames the no-persistence path as a "fallback" (it just emits-everything when there's no cursor dir) — reword once it's STATE_DIR-based.

Everything else is good — with the cursor moved to STATE_DIR this is mergeable. The logic and tests don't need changes beyond the path.

The cursor logic (seed-first, emit-new-only, dedup, resolved-pruned, reappear-emits, failure-safe non-advance, atomic write) was already correct and well-covered. All 5 checks green. payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Reviewed in depth. The core implementation is excellent — one blocking item on scope/close semantics, no code defects found.

**What's right (verified, not just read):**
- The classification is genuinely server-owned and computed once at turn start: `classify_turn_interactivity` on dispatch inputs, stored on `TurnContext`, carried into the durable `TurnRecord`. `/event` ingress forces NON_INTERACTIVE even with a forged interactive-looking trigger/channel.

The tests even cover **forged tool args** (`interactivity: "interactive"` in the send_message args) and the legacy-var-True override attempt.
- Forgery surface is fully closed: `stamp_http_event_ingress_extra` now strips before stamping (always overwrites), web_chat strips the client-supplied marker (with test), discord/slack extras are server-built. I checked the branch: the legacy `_current_turn_interactive_var` has **zero remaining readers** (write-only compat), and `is_interactive_turn` survives only inside `channel_registry` as the classifier's input. No decision site was left on the old signal.
- Both directions of the poller regression at the channel-mechanics level are covered: NON_INTERACTIVE + explicit channel still sends (`test_non_interactive_explicit_channel_works`), channel-less + no-reply sentinels fail closed.

- the near-empty/placeholder content guard (whitespace-only / single-symbol / trivially-short) is not implemented;

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #850: Build a standalone OSV lockfile scanner with deterministic advisory output

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Reviewed (this is attempt a2, superseding #1043's a1). The uv.lock parse is genuinely improved — it uses `tomllib` now instead of the hand-rolled line parser, deterministic sorting + excluded-dirs + stdlib-only are all good, and CI is green. But there are three blockers, and they trace to the same root cause: **this did not adopt the `osv-scanner` direction approved on #1043** — it hand-rolls the OSV API again, so the same class of bugs recurs.

**Blocker 1 — the poller never registers (won't run at all).** `pollers.json` uses `"entrypoint": "poller.py"` and `"frequency": "daily"`, but the framework requires `command` and `cron` (mimir/pollers.py: `command = entry.get("command"); cron = entry.get("cron"); if not name or not command or not cron: log "poller_missing_fields" + continue`). So this skill is silently dropped every reload — the whole feature is inert. Compare the gmail-poller's `pollers.json`: `"command": "python3 poller.py"`, `"cron": "..."`.

**Blocker 2 — npm inventory finds nothing.** `parse_package_lock` reads `info.get("name")` from each `packages` entry, but in package-lock v2/v3 the entries are keyed by install path (`node_modules/<name>`) and normally omit the `name` field. On this repo's own `package-lock.json` that's **0 of 315** node_modules entries with a `name` field → the scanner inventories **0/315** npm packages and silently reports "clean." This is the exact bug that blocked #1043, and it's masked the same way: the test fixture injects `name` into every entry, which isn't how npm writes lockfiles. Derive the name from the key (strip `node_modules/`, keep `@scope/pkg`).

**Blocker 3 — fail-open on OSV errors + dead/contradictory config.**
- `query_osv` swallows `URLError` per package and `continue`s; `run_scan` then emits nothing and returns 0. So a scanner that cannot reach OSV reports "clean" and exits success — the worst failure mode for a security scanner. SKILL.md claims "exit non-zero: OSV transport/parse failure"; the code contradicts it.
- `OSV_API_URL` is defined (constant + SKILL.md, defaulting to `/v1/querybatch`) but `query_osv` hardcodes `https://api.osv.dev/v1/query` and never reads the env var; scanner.py's own docstring says the default is `/v1/query` while the constant says `/v1/querybatch`. Triple inconsistency, and the per-package single-query loop (315 sequential requests) is what the batch endpoint was meant to avoid.

**Fix: adopt the approved `osv-scanner` wrapper (from the #1043 steer).** `osv-scanner` natively parses both `uv.lock` and `package-lock.json` (robust — kills blocker 2), batches its OSV queries, and exits non-zero on real transport/parse errors (kills blocker 3 and the fail-open). The skill collapses to: pin `osv-scanner` as a tool (tool_pins.py + scaffold install, like codex/mermaid), then a thin `poller.py`/`scanner.py` that runs `osv-scanner --format json` over the lockfiles and normalizes `results[].packages[].vulnerabilities[]` into the existing record shape. Then fix `pollers.json` to `command`/`cron` (blocker 1). Watch the exit-code gotcha: `osv-scanner` returns exit 1 when vulns are *found* (parse+emit on that; treat only higher exit codes as failure). Mock the subprocess in tests — don't hit the network.

Please build it on `osv-scanner` this round rather than re-hardening the hand-rolled parser; the three blockers above are exactly what the tool removes.

Confirmed the runtime bits mocked tests miss: 'osv-scanner scan --lockfile' is valid (scan source is the default subcommand), and a bad invocation fails loud (exit 2) rather than false-clean. osv-scanner pinned v2.4.0 + dockerfile.fragment + realistic mocked-subprocess tests covering exit-1-is-success and fail-loud semantics. payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #850: Build a standalone OSV lockfile scanner with deterministic advisory output

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Reviewed. The design is clean — standalone stdlib-only poller (no `mimir.*` imports), deterministic sorted output, silent healthy paths, structured failure signals. But there's a blocking correctness bug in the npm path.

**Blocker — `_scan_package_lock` misses nearly all npm packages.** It requires a `name` field on each `packages` entry:
```python
name = pkg_data.get("name")
if not name or not isinstance(name, str):
    continue
```
In package-lock v2/v3, entries are keyed by install path (`node_modules/<name>`) and the `name` field is normally **absent** — the name comes from the key. On this repo's own `package-lock.json` that's **1 of 316 entries with a `name` field**, so the scanner would inventory 1 package and silently skip 315. For a security advisory scanner that's the worst failure mode: it reports "clean" without having scanned. Derive the name from the key instead, e.g.:
```python
raw = pkg_key.split("node_modules/")[-1] if pkg_key else ""
name = pkg_data.get("name") or raw
if not name:            # skip the root "" entry
    continue
```
(this also handles scoped names — `node_modules/@scope/pkg` → `@scope/pkg`).

The test masks this: `_write_package_lock` injects a `name` into every entry, which isn't how npm writes lockfiles. Please add a fixture with realistic entries (keyed by `node_modules/x`, no `name` field, plus a root `""` entry) so a regression like this is caught.

**Non-blocking, worth addressing:**
- **Use OSV's batch endpoint.** It currently does one POST per package (316 sequential round-trips on this repo) — `https://api.osv.dev/v1/querybatch` is built for exactly this and avoids the per-poll latency + rate-limit risk.
- **One failure aborts the whole scan.** A single package's `urlopen` error raises out of the loop, failing the entire scan. Consider skipping the failed package (or a bounded retry) so one transient error doesn't lose all results.
- **`test_production_subprocess_no_vulnerabilities` makes a real OSV network call** — flaky (if OSV/CI network is down the poller exits 1 and the test fails). Mock it, or mark it as an opt-in network/integration test.
- Minor: `_events` and `_all_lines` are identical (dedupe one); the `mock_urllib` fixture is defined but unused; `create=True` on the `urlopen` patch is unnecessary (the attribute exists).

Fix the npm inventory + add the realistic lockfile test and this is good to go.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Heartbeat QA found acceptance-blocking semantic gaps despite green CI and the passing focused/full suites:

1. **The real npm lockfile is not inventoried.** Root `package-lock.json` is lockfileVersion 3 with 316 `packages` entries, but only the root entry carries a `name` field. `_scan_package_lock()` requires `pkg_data["name"]`, so it returns only `mimir-frontend` and skips the 315 resolved `node_modules/*` packages. The test fixture synthesizes a `name` on every entry and therefore misses the production shape.
2. **Affected ranges are emitted unbounded.** An OSV interval with `introduced=1.0` and `fixed=2.0` becomes `affected_range=">=1.0"` plus remediation `2.0`; the range itself incorrectly implies fixed/later versions remain affected. Normalize bounded intervals and cover multiple affected entries/ranges.
3. **Editable uv packages are queried as PyPI.** The actual root inventory includes local editable `mimir-agent` and `saga`, because every `source =` entry is classified as PyPI. Restrict PyPI queries to registry sources or intentionally map non-registry sources.
4. Add regression coverage using representative real lockfile-v3 entries and assert the normalized `affected_range`, not only remediation.

I recorded the detailed blocker on Chainlink #850 and moved it from `worklink:review` to `worklink:rework`; #851 should remain blocked until this slice is corrected.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Direction change (supersedes the "fix the hand-rolled parser" path in my review above): **replace the hand-rolled scanner with a thin `osv-scanner` wrapper.** Operator call — the goal isn't to reinvent lockfile parsing.

**Why:** `osv-scanner` (Google's official OSV CLI) natively parses both `uv.lock` and `package-lock.json` (plus ~30 other formats) and queries the **same OSV database** this poller already targets — so it needs no account/token and adds no new data egress. It eliminates the blocking npm name-field bug, the per-package-query concern, and the one-failure-aborts-scan concern from my review all at once, and drops most of the 304 lines.

**Shape:**
1. **Pin `osv-scanner` as a tool** in `mimir/worklink/tool_pins.py` + install it in the scaffold Dockerfile(s), same pattern as the codex/mermaid pins (source: GitHub release `google/osv-scanner`; smoke: `osv-scanner --version`). Pin an explicit version, no `@latest`.
2. **Rewrite `poller.py` as a wrapper:** run `osv-scanner` with JSON output over the repo's `uv.lock` and `package-lock.json` (confirm the exact subcommand/flags for the pinned major version — v1 uses `--lockfile ... --format json`, v2 uses `osv-scanner scan source`/`--format json`), then parse `results[].packages[].vulnerabilities[]` and normalize into the existing `dependency_advisory` event schema.
3. **Keep the good parts:** standalone-subprocess model (still `python3 poller.py`, stdlib-only, shells out to the binary), deterministic sorted output, silent-when-healthy, structured failure signals, and the scoped-dir guard.
4. **Drop:** `_scan_uv_lock`, `_scan_package_lock`, `_query_osv`.

**Key gotcha — exit codes:** `osv-scanner` exits **non-zero (1) when vulnerabilities are *found*** — that's the found signal, not a failure. The wrapper must parse the JSON and emit events on exit 1, and only treat genuine errors (e.g. missing binary / higher exit codes / unparseable output) as a `dependency_advisory_*_failed` signal. Don't let "vulns found" masquerade as a scan failure (or it'll silently swallow every advisory).

**Tests:** mock the `osv-scanner` subprocess with a realistic JSON fixture (don't hit the network); keep the malformed-output and no-lockfiles cases. Drop `test_production_subprocess_no_vulnerabilities`'s live network call.

Net: same coverage (OSV), robust parsing, far less code to own.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Add scheduler logging flush lag details

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Reviewed — one blocking concern on diagnostic accuracy; the rest is good.

`stack_is_apscheduler_logging_flush` matches APScheduler's executor logging flush around **any** coroutine job. The pre/post `Running job` / `Job executed` INFO lines are emitted by `apscheduler.executors.default` for every coroutine job (health probe, minimax poll, reaper, `_fire`, etc.), and during that flush the job body isn't even on the captured stack — the pre-log fires *before* `await job.func(...)` and the post-log *after* it returns. So the stalling job is genuinely undeterminable from this signature.

But `_scheduler_loop_lag_details` hardcodes `candidate_job_ids` to `_fire_poller` jobs and the `diagnosis` states "the poller coroutine body." A non-poller coroutine job hitting the same logging-flush stall will be confidently mislabeled as the poller — which sends the next debugging session down the wrong path, the opposite of what this enrichment is for.

Please either:
- broaden `candidate_job_ids` to all registered coroutine jobs (or drop the job-specific field, since it can't be derived from this stack), and
- reword `diagnosis` to "a coroutine job's body" instead of "the poller coroutine body."

`stall_signature` and `likely_logger` (`apscheduler.executors.default`) are accurate and useful as-is, keeping the classification as `scheduler_loop_lag` is right, and the tests are solid. Just fix the poller-specific attribution and this is good to go.

payload.title: Worklink #844: Auto-close worklink chainlinks when their PR merges (stranded in worklink:review)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes. The leaf-flow logic is sound, but two blocking gaps mean #844's goal isn't actually achieved.

## BLOCKING 1 — the reconcile is never wired in (dead code)
`close_merged_chainlinks_for_home` (mimir/worklink/autonomy.py:407) is defined and unit-tested, but it is **not called anywhere**. The worklink-reaper `_fire` (scheduler.py `add_worklink_reaper_job`) invokes only `reap_stale_claims_for_home` + `prune_stale_attempt_worktrees_for_home` (scheduler.py:2256-2257), and this PR doesn't touch scheduler.py. So the auto-close never runs in production — #844's entire purpose (close chainlinks when their PR merges) does not execute; the passing tests only exercise the function directly.

Fix: call `close_merged_chainlinks_for_home(home)` from the reaper `_fire` (via `asyncio.to_thread`, alongside reap + prune — the pinned trigger), and add a test asserting the `_fire` actually invokes it.

## BLOCKING 2 — the epic flow isn't handled (explicit #844 acceptance criterion)
The scan (`issue_ids_with_label("worklink:review")`) does include completed epics (they carry `worklink:review`), but `get_pr_url_for_review_issue` cannot resolve an epic's PR: the detached adapter records the epic PR as `draft PR opened: <url>` via `_factory_mirror_lines` (orchestrator.py), while `_find_pr_url_from_comments` matches only `pr_url=`, and the epic path posts no `WORKLINK_EVIDENCE(pr_url=)`. So epics are scanned but skipped (`pr_url` resolves to None) → never closed.

Fix (either): parse the `draft PR opened: <url>` mirror line in the PR-URL resolver, OR (preferred, per the issue's epic-scope note) have `_finalize_epic` (orchestrator.py) record a durable `pr_url=` / `WORKLINK_EVIDENCE` for epics. Add an epic-close test: a `worklink:epic` + `worklink:review` chainlink whose PR is recorded via the epic mirror → closed on merge; and epic-with-open-PR → untouched.

## What's good (keep as-is)
The leaf path is correct and well-tested: confirmed-merge via `gh pr view --json state` (state == MERGED), fail-safe skip on unresolvable/not-merged, dry-run support, idempotent (closed issues drop out of the `status=open` scan), and a solid test matrix (`actually_closes`/`dry_run`/`skips_open_pr`/`skips_closed_unmerged` + `_check_pr_merged_via_gh_*`). Once it's wired into the reaper `_fire` and covers epics, this is mergeable.

payload.title: Worklink #841: Retry transient LLM-provider errors with backoff (provider-agnostic)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes (chainlink #841). The retry wrapper is well-structured — the `_astream` `yielded`-guard (retry only before the first chunk → no double-emit) is exactly right, backoff+jitter is bounded and env-configurable, the saga wiring is safe, and the named-case tests are solid. Three changes before merge:

1. **Default classification is fail-OPEN — flip it.** `_is_retryable_error`'s fall-through is `return True, "unknown_default_retry"`, so an unrecognized/terminal error is retried up to `max_attempts`. #841's design is "classify retryable vs terminal so non-transient errors **fail fast**." Change the fall-through to non-retryable (`return False, ...`) so only the explicitly-classified transient set retries and unknown errors fail fast. Add a test asserting an unknown/unclassified exception is NOT retried (0 retries).

2. **Structured-output case not covered.** The retry wraps the model-call seam (codex `_astream`, saga `call_llm`), but `StructuredOutputValidationError` from an empty native-structured-output completion (the `CriticFindings` turn-crash, turn `bfd4121e98e5`) is raised downstream in langgraph's structured-output parse — outside these wrappers — so it still isn't retried. Either extend coverage to that seam or explicitly move it to a follow-up leaf; don't leave the added acceptance criterion silently unmet.

3. **Minor — tighten classification.** Substring matching (`"400"`, `"500"`, `"blocked"` in the message) can incidentally match unrelated content (a token count like "14000", or "blocked" used innocuously). Prefer `status_code` / exception-type checks over string matching where the info is available.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.title: worklink: autonomous --detached feature-factory adapter + alive-aware liveness

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES

Thanks for the update — the direction is right, and the current CI is green (`pytest` 3.11/3.12, skill-conformance, claude-code smoke, frontend). I also ran the Worklink-focused tests locally from the PR checkout:

```
uv run pytest -q tests/test_worklink*.py
# 329 passed, 3 warnings in 54.65s
```

I found two correctness issues that look merge-blocking for the detached factory path:

1. `mimir/worklink/backends/feature_factory.py:428` / `mimir/worklink/orchestrator.py:1007` — the concurrent factory-session guard is effectively pointed at the wrong tree.

   `run_epic()` calls `has_concurrent_factory_session(self.repo)` before launching, but the new adapter creates each factory run in the attempt checkout (`lease.path`, e.g. `repo/.worklink/<issue>-<attempt>`) and `work_spec()` puts the factory control plane under `order.worktree / .opencode/factory`. `has_concurrent_factory_session()` only scans `self.repo / .opencode/factory/*/run.json`, so it won't see the active detached sessions this PR creates under `.worklink/.../.opencode/factory`.

   Impact: the intended “one factory session at a time” guard is bypassed; with the default Worklink concurrency cap of 2, a second epic can launch while the first detached factory is still active.

2. `mimir/worklink/orchestrator.py:1559-1560` — the process-log fallback path contradicts the documented factory layout and appears to skip the actual detached logs.

   The docstring and backend command comment both say detached process logs live at `<worktree>/.opencode/factory/processes/<ts>.log`, i.e. as a sibling of the per-run directory under `.opencode/factory/`. But the implementation uses:

   ```python
   run_dir = factory_run_dir(worktree, run_id)  # <worktree>/.opencode/factory/<run-id>
   processes_dir = run_dir.parent.parent / "processes"
   ```

   That resolves to `<worktree>/.opencode/processes`, not `<worktree>/.opencode/factory/processes`. The tests mirror the implementation, so they don't catch the mismatch.

   Impact: when `_detached_factory_alive()` is unknown or misses the process, a stale-heartbeat-but-still-logging factory can be declared stuck because `_run_dir_recent_activity_s()` never observes the advancing process log. That cuts directly against the alive-aware liveness guarantee this PR is adding.

One additional non-blocking concern: `_attempt_is_active()` treats any non-terminal `run.json` as active forever before checking heartbeat freshness, process liveness, or file activity. That is safe against deleting live work, but it also means a crashed detached factory that leaves `status: running` will never be TTL-pruned. I don't think that has to block this PR if the intended policy is “never reap a non-terminal factory attempt automatically,” but it's worth making that tradeoff explicit or adding a follow-up.

payload.body:
Verdict: APPROVE

Thanks for the fast follow-up. I rechecked the two blockers from my previous review against head `01d737cf`:

- The concurrent-session guard now scans both the repo-root factory control plane and `.worklink/<attempt>/.opencode/factory/*/run.json`, with `exclude_run_id` so a same-epic resume is not self-blocking.
- `_run_dir_recent_activity_s()` now looks at `.opencode/factory/processes/*.log`, matching the detached factory layout instead of `.opencode/processes`.

Validation:

```
uv run pytest -q tests/test_worklink_feature_factory.py -q
# 44 passed
```

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Thanks — both blocking issues were real and are fixed in `01d737cf`; full suite green (5614 passed).

**1. Concurrent-session guard pointed at the wrong tree.** Confirmed: `has_concurrent_factory_session(self.repo)` globbed `self.repo/.opencode/factory/*/run.json`, but `work_spec` puts each detached run under `order.worktree/.opencode/factory/` (the `.worklink/<issue>-<attempt>` checkout), so the guard never saw active sessions. Now it scans the repo-root control plane **and** every `.worklink` attempt checkout. Added `exclude_run_id` and pass the current epic's run id at the call site, so a resume/re-dispatch of the *same* epic isn't counted as concurrent (which the corrected scan would otherwise do). New test covers detection under `.worklink/<attempt>/` + the self-exclusion + terminal-not-counted.

**2. Process-log path off-by-one.** Confirmed: `run_dir.parent.parent/"processes"` resolved to `<worktree>/.opencode/processes`, but logs live at `<worktree>/.opencode/factory/processes/`. Fixed to `run_dir.parent/"processes"`. Good catch that the tests mirrored the impl — the `_process_log_dir` helper had the same off-by-one, so I corrected it **and** added a test that writes the log at the literal documented path (and asserts the old buggy location is unused), so impl and test can't silently drift together again.

**3. `_attempt_is_active` treats any non-terminal run.json as active (non-blocking).** Taking your "make the tradeoff explicit" option rather than changing behavior. This is intentional: a heartbeat-freshness or process-liveness gate here could misfire during a legitimately quiet phase (the pre_pr panel) and reintroduce the exact mid-flight reap this guards against — and false-reaping live work is strictly worse than leaking a rare crashed run. I documented the policy in the docstring: a factory that crashed leaving `status: running` is retired explicitly (`factory cleanup --force` / manual removal), not by the TTL prune. Happy to file a follow-up for a smarter "crashed-but-non-terminal" sweep if you'd prefer one.

Holding the merge for Jason.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
## Review: REQUEST CHANGES

Independent adversarial review; full suite green (5589 passed, 17 skipped). The `/event` trust-boundary hardening (SEC1–SEC4) holds — I could not construct a bypass: the strip→stamp on `/event` is unconditional, forged hints are re-validated against on-disk factory state, forged authors hit `http_event_author_untrusted` before any authz, and the admin-tool denial fires regardless of `MIMIR_ACCESS_CONTROL_ENFORCED`. Idempotency, redaction, and path-safety (sha256 sidecar names, regex + within-checked `run_id`) all check out. Two fixes before merge:

**Blocking**
1. `mimir/worklink/continuation.py:393` — `_default_runner` calls `subprocess.run(...)` with **no `timeout`**. The `asyncio.wait_for(timeout=…)` at `agent.py:2534` abandons the *await* but cannot cancel the `to_thread` worker, so a hung `gh`/`chainlink`/`git` permanently occupies a worker in the shared default `ThreadPoolExecutor` that all mimir `asyncio.to_thread` file-IO uses → process-wide `to_thread` starvation under repeated hangs. Add `timeout=` (e.g. 10–15s) to the `subprocess.run` and treat `TimeoutExpired` as a non-zero result — bound the *work*, not just the wait.

**Should-fix (cheap, zero downside)**
2. `continuation.py:~924` — `_comment_authorization_denial` checks the server-stamped-trigger allowance *before* the http_event denial. Safe today only because the hint-strip removes `poller_name`/`schedule_name`; if a future stamped trigger keys off a non-stripped `extra` field this becomes a forgeable-comment bypass. Reorder: deny on `_event_has_http_event_ingress` first, then the stamped-trigger allowance (genuine poller/scheduled turns never carry the http_event stamp).

**Confirm intent:** SEC4 now denies *all* admin-sensitive tools (write/edit/shell/worklink_run/spawn/schedule) for every turn entering via `POST /event`, even with access control disabled. Please confirm no production automation drives admin work through `/event`.

Nits (non-blocking): tools→worklink import coupling for one string constant (hoist to `models.py`); sidecars never reaped (issue+repo dedupe is lifetime-scoped — consider a TTL); redundant identity re-resolution in `_deny_admin_tool`.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Verified at head 4585641af — both items addressed:
- **Blocking (unbounded subprocess):** `_default_runner` now passes `timeout=_EXTERNAL_COMMAND_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (15s) and catches `TimeoutExpired` → `CompletedProcess(argv, 124, …)`. Bounds the work (not just the await), so a hung gh/git/chainlink can't starve the shared `to_thread` pool.
- **Should-fix (auth ordering):** `_comment_authorization_denial` now checks `_event_has_http_event_ingress` → `http_event_author_untrusted` before the server-stamped-trigger allowance, closing the forgeable-comment path.

Fix commit is tight (continuation.py +22, +60 lines of new tests covering the timeout and the reorder). CI green (pytest 3.11/3.12, skill-conformance, smoke, frontend). Confirm-intent resolved: trusted automation (bridges/pollers/scheduler/continuation) uses in-process `enqueue`, never HTTP `/event`, so SEC4 doesn't affect it.

Non-blocking follow-ups remain (import coupling for one constant, sidecar TTL/reaping, redundant identity re-resolution). LGTM.

payload.title: chainlink #783: chat slash-skill discovery + invocation (default-off)

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES

Thanks for the thorough coverage here. I found two trust-boundary issues that should be fixed before this lands.

Blocking findings:

1. `mimir/agent.py:3321` / `mimir/server.py:278` — chat-skill prompt injection can still be triggered from forged generic `/event` metadata. The web chat bridge strips client-supplied `chat_skill_invocation` and re-adds server-owned metadata, but the generic `/event` endpoint still passes `extra=extra or {}` straight into `AgentEvent`. The new agent path treats any event with `CHAT_SKILL_EXTRA_KEY` as a chat-skill invocation and calls `prompt_block_for_invocation`. That means a client with access to `/event` can manufacture `extra.chat_skill_invocation` and cause skill instructions to be injected outside the web bridge's server-owned parsing path. Please strip the chat-skill keys from generic `/event` input, or add an unforgeable provenance/source check so only `WebChatBridge`-created invocations are honored. Add a regression test posting forged `/event` extra and asserting no skill prompt is injected.

2. `mimir/chat_skills.py:146` — slash-command args are interpolated directly into the privileged skill block. `Arguments: {invocation.args}` lets untrusted user text add newlines/headings/instructions immediately before `Follow these skill instructions for this request:` and the trusted `SKILL.md` body. That weakens the boundary between user arguments and skill instructions. Please render args as explicitly untrusted data (for example JSON-encoded or fenced, with wording that arguments must not override system/developer/skill instructions), and add a regression for newline/instruction-shaped arguments.

Validation I ran locally on the PR head (`3230f1ab`):

- `uv run pytest tests/test_chat_skills.py tests/test_web_chat_bridge.py tests/test_agent.py -q --tb=short --disable-warnings --continue-on-collection-errors --maxfail=1` → 128 passed, 3 warnings

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:

So if the worker passes its internal gate, pushes, and then the controller's fresh sandboxed trusted gate fails, the next attempt still sees only `tests_failed`/exit code with no pytest failure detail. That is still the #815 blind retry loop for the remote gate. Please carry a bounded/redacted tail out of the test-only worker job, preserve it through `_run_remote_test_job()`/`fold_remote_test_evidence()`, and use that same tail in the non-review-ready evidence comment / epic retry feedback.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #784: Harden critic-structured parsing (coerce verdict/severity, tolerate model variance)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body: The prescribed coercion pattern, done well: conservative severity/verdict synonym maps (high/critical→blocker, medium→important, low/minor→nit; unknowns→important), unknown verdict falls back to the most severe normalized finding, extra='ignore' + safe defaults + alternate-key mapping (summary/message→title, file/location→evidence — the observed shape), malformed items degrade instead of failing the parse, and the well-formed round-trip is byte-identical.
