payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.title: worklink/epic: action-based roles (tools + text, no structured outputs)

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Summary

Thanks for pushing this toward action-based role seams. I agree with the direction: removing large structured role outputs and capturing decisions from scoped tool closures is the right response to the #783 live-run failures, and the runner-side fail-closed slice/integration gates are much cleaner. Focused tests passed locally (`uv run pytest -q tests/test_worklink_epic_roles.py tests/test_worklink_epic.py tests/test_worklink_review.py -q`), and the GitHub checks are green.

## Blocking issue

- `mimir/worklink/epic_roles.py:147` / `mimir/worklink/epic.py:549`: the decomposer tools do not enforce the mutually-exclusive “file leaves OR report deficiency” state machine. `comment_on_epic()` can still be called after one or more `file_leaf()` calls, and `file_leaf()` can still be called after `comment_on_epic()` records a deficiency. Then `_decompose()` checks `child_leaves()` before `outcome.deficiency`, so a mixed run proceeds with whatever partial leaves exist instead of halting as deficient. That puts one of the PR’s core safety claims back onto prompt compliance (“file nothing if you use it”), which is exactly what this redesign is trying to avoid. Please make the tool closures enforce the mode transition, e.g. `comment_on_epic` returns an error once `state.filed > 0`, `file_leaf` returns an error once `state.deficiency is not None`, and add a regression covering “leaf then deficiency” / “deficiency then leaf”.

## Non-blocking notes

- `ChainlinkEpicClient.comment()` is currently fire-and-forget, unlike `add_blocker()`’s comment path. That weakens the audit promise for deficiency/fixes/integration-block comments if the Chainlink comment command fails. Not blocking because the in-process decision still drives the runner, but worth tightening.
- Multi-mode slice review still relies on prompt compliance for actually calling every `spawn_reviewer` lens before `approve_slice`. That may be an acceptable MVP tradeoff, but if this path becomes safety-critical we should consider recording spawn calls and rejecting approval when required lenses were skipped.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
## Summary

Approved. The latest two commits address the blocking issue I raised on the previous head: the decomposer action surface is now mutually exclusive in both directions, and `_decompose` correctly treats a fresh deficiency as stronger than any stale leaves left by a prior crashed attempt.

I re-read the updated diff around `build_decompose_tools`, `EpicRunner._decompose`, `build_slice_decision_tools`, and `ChainlinkEpicClient.comment`. The new closure-level gates, deficiency-first ordering, lens-gated approval, fail-closed no-decision behavior, and comment-failure warnings line up with the action-based role design.

## Validation

- Local targeted suite on PR head `0948cd35`: `env -u MIMIR_MODEL_SPEC uv run pytest -q tests/test_worklink_epic_roles.py tests/test_worklink_epic.py tests/test_worklink_review.py tests/test_worklink_epic_e2e.py tests/test_structured_subagents.py tests/test_agent_system_prompt_refresh.py` → `64 passed, 3 warnings`.
- GitHub checks are green: pytest 3.11, pytest 3.12, skill-conformance, claude-code-extra-smoke, and frontend all succeeded.

## Notes

No blocking findings remain. One non-blocking future hardening idea: if "lens-gated" eventually needs to mean "each sub-reviewer produced a substantive report" rather than "each lens was spawned," add a fail-closed check for empty sub-reviewer reports. The current implementation is consistent with the stated closure-level gate, so I would not hold this PR on it.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Addressed the review in the latest commit:

**Blocking (fixed + regressions):** the decompose tools now enforce the mutually-exclusive mode in the closures — `comment_on_epic` errors once `state.filed > 0`, `file_leaf` errors once a deficiency is recorded. Tests cover leaf-then-deficiency and deficiency-then-leaf.

**Non-blocking notes (both taken):** `approve_slice` is now tool-gated on every required lens having been spawned first (`request_fixes` deliberately never gated — rejecting must always be possible), and audit comments go through `_safe_comment` — `ChainlinkEpicClient.comment` raises on failure and decision tools degrade to a WARNING in the tool result without voiding the recorded decision.

Affected suites green (108).

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Revision complete across two commits — thanks for the catch; it was exactly the PR's own principle applied back at it.

**Blocking item — tool-enforced file-XOR-deficiency** (`a52b1a3e` + `0948cd35`):
- `comment_on_epic` now errors once any leaf was filed in the run; `file_leaf` (and `add_dependency`) error once a deficiency was recorded. Regression tests cover both orders.
- `_decompose` now checks `outcome.deficiency` **before** `child_leaves()` — the tool gates make the mixed state impossible within one run, but leaves filed by an earlier crashed attempt can coexist with a fresh deficiency report; that resume-case mix now halts as deficient instead of building a partial plan (regression test included).

**Non-blocking notes, both taken:**
- `ChainlinkEpicClient.comment()` now raises on failure (mirrors `add_blocker`), and the tool closures route it through `_safe_comment` — the decision still stands (it drives the runner in-process) but a failed audit comment surfaces as a WARNING in the tool result instead of vanishing.
- Multi-mode lens fan-out is now tool-gated too: `approve_slice` errors until every required lens has been spawned (`request_fixes` is deliberately never gated — rejecting must always stay open). Tests cover the gate and the reject path.

Focused suites green (53); full suite was green pre-revision and the changes are additive gates.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #778: Epic role-runner bridge (concrete EpicRoleRunner + multi-vote aggregation)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Request changes — one blocker (the aggregation rule), plus two notes. The bridge is otherwise well-built: `run()` and `run_epic` now inject the concrete `EpicSubagentRoleRunner` (so `run-epic` is finally runnable — resolves the original "dead on arrival"), the four roles invoke the S4 structured subagents and parse their validated models, and `_render_slice_review_input` correctly feeds the controller-OBSERVED evidence (changed files, diff stat, `diff_observed`, controller commands, test result) with an explicit "do not use worker prose/summaries/intent" instruction. Good.

**1. (blocking) Aggregation must be verify-dissent, not majority.** `_aggregate_slice_reviews` decides `verdict = "APPROVE" if approvals > len(reviews)/2 else "REJECT"` — a straight majority vote. Replace it with the verify-dissent rule:
- If ALL reviewers APPROVE → APPROVE.
- If ANY reviewer REJECTs (even a lone minority), take that reviewer's specific findings and run a DOUBLE-CHECK pass that judges each dissenting finding against the controller-observed evidence (reuse the per-slice-reviewer, or a focused verifier prompt: "is this specific finding real and grounded in the observed diff/tests?"). If any dissenting finding is confirmed REAL → REJECT with those required_fixes; if none survive verification (all dissents spurious) → APPROVE.
- Do NOT decide by vote count. Rationale: a lone reviewer who finds a real bug must be able to block, but a hallucinated dissent must not — the double-check is the arbiter, not the tally.
Add tests: a single REAL dissent (verified) among approvers → REJECT; a single SPURIOUS dissent (fails verification) → APPROVE; unanimous approve → APPROVE with no verification pass.

**2. (note) Fragile dependency on private DeepAgents internals.** `DeepAgentsTaskSubagentInvoker` uses `deepagents.middleware.subagents._build_task_tool` (underscore-private) and hand-constructs a `ToolRuntime`, then reads `result.update["messages"][0].content`. That will silently break on a DeepAgents upgrade. Please guard it (clear error if the private symbol/shape is missing) and pin the DeepAgents version range, or use a public invocation entrypoint if one exists.

**3. (note) Multi-vote reviewers aren't truly independent** — they're the same subagent with the same prompt+model, differing only by a "Reviewer vote N of M" string, so on a deterministic model they'd tend to return the same verdict. With verify-dissent (item 1) this matters less, since the signal comes from verifying findings rather than tallying votes — but it's worth a comment that the value of N>1 is surfacing *different* findings to verify, not counting agreement.

Note: `_resolve_epic_model` mutates global `os.environ["MIMIR_HOME"]` (restored in finally) — minor; prefer passing home to the config path directly if the API allows.

Sequencing: this is the slice S7 (#989) must rebase onto — land this first.

DeepAgents private-API access is guarded with clear errors and deepagents pinned >=0.6.1,<0.7. Tests cover unanimous/verified-real/spurious. run-epic is runnable (concrete EpicSubagentRoleRunner injected). CI green. LGTM.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #775: Epic-scoped claim + reaper (manifest resume)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Request changes. The claim/reaper design is genuinely good — clean epic-vs-leaf reaper separation (`reap_home` skips `worklink:epic` parents; `reap_epic_home` handles only them), recovery steals just the stale PARENT lock and never relabels the child leaves, the dead-epic-without-manifest path returns the parent to ready (not the children), and the heartbeat design (background loop at `max(30, min(300, timeout_s//4))` + per-phase `heartbeat()` calls) correctly keeps a live long-running epic from being reaped mid-flight even during a single long `compute.wait`. Tests are thorough. Two things block it:

**1. (blocking) Epic recovery runs the full epic INLINE inside the reaper thread.** `reap_stale_claims_for_home` → `recover_epic` → `run_epic(...)` → `asyncio.run(EpicRunner(...).run(...))`. The reaper fires from the scheduler as `await asyncio.to_thread(_reap)`, so this executes a *complete* epic run (waves, builds, merges, PR — minutes to hours) synchronously in that worker thread. Consequences: (a) `reap_epic_home` runs *before* `reap_home` in the same call, so **all leaf reaping is starved** for the entire epic duration; (b) the reaper cron can't make progress / ticks pile up or skip; (c) a pool thread is pinned for the whole run.

Recovery should **re-dispatch a detached `mimir worklink run-epic <id> --home … --repo … --autonomous` subprocess** (mirror the poller's dispatch in `poller.py`) and return immediately — the manifest-resume then happens in the normal detached run-epic path, and the reaper stays fast and non-blocking. Steal the stale parent lock, emit the REAPER comment, spawn the detached run, done.

**2. (blocking, sequencing) This collides with S10 (#778) on epic.py, and depends on it.** S7 edits `epic.py` (run() heartbeat wiring, `move_epic_to_review`, imports, new heartbeat helpers) and S10 (#778, in flight) also rewrites `epic.py` (run_epic wiring + the concrete `EpicRoleRunner`). They were dispatched in the same wave but are NOT file-disjoint, so they'll conflict at merge. More fundamentally, S7's recovery *depends on run-epic actually working*, which is exactly S10's deliverable — so **S10 must land first, then S7 rebases onto it**. Please gate this on #778: rebase onto main after S10 merges (the detached-dispatch fix in item 1 also lines up cleanly with S10's runnable run-epic).

Net: solid reaper logic; make recovery detached, and land it after S10 with a rebase.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body: Revision addresses both blockers. Reaper recovery is now DETACHED: recover_epic calls dispatch_detached_epic_resume (subprocess.Popen, start_new_session=True, mimir worklink run-epic … --autonomous) and returns immediately, so the reaper stays fast and leaf reaping proceeds in the same tick. Rebased onto S10: epic.py carries both the EpicSubagentRoleRunner injection and the heartbeat loop/per-phase heartbeats, correctly reconciled. CI green. LGTM.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #773: Epic orchestrator (EpicRunner: decompose/waves/observe-review-merge/integrate/PR)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Request changes. This got a three-pass adversarial review (the high-risk/multi-vote treatment): my read plus two independent reviewers cross-checking against the real helper code. The **orchestration engine is genuinely well-built** — confirmed correct: serial single-writer merges (flock + no-await critical section + file-disjoint batches), never auto-merges to base (draft-PR only), bounded retries, merge-conflict→needs-human (raised, not swallowed), reject-routes-back-without-merging, wave toposort with cycle detection, no duplicate risk config (consumes S1's `TieredReviewConfig`), and every mimir-module helper signature is correct. The problems are wiring/semantics, and CI is green only because the tests use fakes (`FakeRoles`, `FakeChainlink`) that route around the broken production code.

**SCOPE NOTE:** the missing concrete role runner + multi-vote aggregation has been split into a new slice, **#778 (S10, "Epic role-runner bridge")**, which is blocked by this issue. So **leave `run_epic`/`MissingEpicRoleRunner` and the `reviewer_count` plumbing as-is** — do NOT build the role runner here. This PR stays the orchestration engine; #778 makes it runnable. Everything below is in-scope for this revision.

### Blockers to fix here

1. **Decompose files leaves that fail strict `validate_leaf` (empirically reproduced).** `_leaf_body` emits `Scope:` / `Out of scope:` / `Suggested test command:` without the `Worklink notes:` wrapper and without the required leading `- `. Against the canonical `planning._REQUIRED_SECTIONS`, `missing_leaf_template_parts(_leaf_body(...))` returns `['Worklink notes','- Scope','- Out of scope','- Suggested test command']`. Combined with `_issue_from_payload` never setting `created_at` (→ `uses_strict_leaf_validation(None)` is True), every decomposed leaf raises `LeafValidationError` at `validate_leaf`. Fix: emit the exact `planning.LEAF_TEMPLATE_MARKDOWN` structure; set `created_at` from the chainlink payload; add a test that round-trips `ChainlinkEpicClient.file_leaf` → `child_leaves` → `validate_leaf` and asserts `missing_leaf_template_parts` is empty.

2. **`file_leaf` and `add_blocker` use chainlink CLI flags that don't exist.** `file_leaf` calls `chainlink issue create --parent <id> --title <t> --description <b>`, but the real CLI is `issue create [OPTIONS] <TITLE>` with no `--parent` and no `--title`; subissues are created with `issue subissue <parent> "<title>" -d <body> -l <label>`. `add_blocker` calls `issue block <a> <b> --reason <r>`, but `block` takes only `<ID> <BLOCKER>` (no `--reason`). Both fail at runtime; the fakes hide it. Fix: use `issue subissue …` for filing and `issue block <blocked> <blocker>` (drop `--reason`, or record the reason via a separate `issue comment`). Add a test asserting the exact argv.

3. **Autonomous/remote compute can never observe evidence.** The integration branch is created locally and pushed only at the end (after the per-slice loop), but each slice's remote observation (`observe_remote_evidence`) fetches `origin/<base_ref>` where `base_ref` is the integration branch — which isn't on origin yet → `diff_observed=False` → `review_ready=False` for every slice on the isolated/remote backends autonomous mode mandates → everything blocks. Fix: push the integration branch to origin immediately after `create_integration_branch`, and push each slice branch **before** remote observation (it's currently pushed only after, inside the APPROVE block).

4. **Integrate-phase policy, two bugs.** (a) `if validation.verdict == "NO-GO" and not partial:` — a NO-GO on a *partial* epic falls through and opens the PR anyway; NO-GO should block (or refuse to open) regardless of `partial` — only GO / GO-WITH-NITS should reach `_open_epic_pr`. (b) `_run_epic_tests` runs unconditionally and raises on failure, so a partial epic whose suite exercises a blocked leaf's absent behavior aborts *before* the PR — violating "a partial epic still opens ONE draft PR naming the stuck leaf." In part

payload.title: Worklink #772: Worklink review agents (decomposer, reviewers, validator, risk classifier)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes on the risk-classifier config source; the rest is strong — the four structured schemas are well-modeled, the subagent wiring is clean and read-only, and the per-slice reviewer prompt nails the adversarial "observe-don't-trust" framing (find reasons to REJECT; judge only controller-OBSERVED evidence; don't trust worker prose). **Blocking — the risk classifier duplicates S1's config instead of consuming it, resurrecting the "dead validated knob" problem.**

S1 (#982, merged) shipped `TieredReviewConfig` on `WorklinkDefaults.tiered_review` with `high_risk_scope_prefixes`, `high_risk_labels`, and `multi_vote_reviewer_count` — the operator-tunable high-risk set. This PR instead defines a brand-new private `WorklinkReviewRiskConfig` with its own hardcoded pattern/label lists. Two problems:
1. **Divergent definitions.** S1's high-risk set (e.g. `mimir/worklink/autonomy.py`, `mimir/worklink/claims.py`, `mimir/saga/migrations/`, `uv.lock`, `pyproject.toml`) and this PR's lists (`mimir/worklink/**`, `access_control.py`, `SECURITY.md`, `**/migrations/**`, …) are similar but not equal, so the *same leaf can classify differently* depending on which is authoritative.

payload.title: Worklink #771: Worktree integration-branch ops (create/slice-off-HEAD/merge)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes on the merge-mode contract; the rest of the slice is strong — the integration branch is cut from fresh `origin/<base>` (reusing the #517 fetch/resolve hardening), `create_slice_worktree` correctly branches off the *current* integration HEAD (the test proves a dependency committed after branch creation is present), the `fcntl.flock` serializes merges across processes, the conflict path is non-fatal (aborts, returns `SliceMergeConflict`, preserves the slice worktree, leaves integration HEAD untouched), and nothing mutates the caller's cwd. All additive.

**Blocking — the `strategy` parameter is on the wrong git axis and will break when S5 wires S1's config through.**

`merge_slice_into_integration` does `git merge --no-ff --no-edit` and, when `strategy` is set, appends `-s {strategy}`. But `-s` is git's *merge algorithm* (`ort`/`recursive`/…), whereas S1's `merge_strategy` config is a *mode* with valid set `{no-ff, squash, ff-only}`. So `merge_slice_into_integration(strategy=defaults.merge_strategy)` would run `git merge --no-ff -s no-ff …`, which errors (`no-ff` is not a merge strategy). The function also only actually supports `--no-ff` (the tests assert `HEAD^2`, which only exists for a no-ff merge); `squash`/`ff-only` aren't handled.

Decision (keeping it simple): **integration-branch merges are always `--no-ff`.** Per-slice merge commits give clean traceability and one-command reverts, which is what we want for the epic integration branch.

Please:
- **Drop the `strategy` parameter entirely.** Always `git merge --no-ff --no-edit <slice_branch>`. No `-s`.
- Update the two tests that pass `strategy="ort"` to call without it.

Note (not this PR): S1's `merge_strategy` config field then becomes dead weight — I'll file a small follow-up to narrow it to `no-ff` only (or remove it) so S5 doesn't wire a misleading knob. Nothing for you to do here beyond the above.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #770: Epic run manifest + resumable state (epic_state.py)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes on the crash-recovery contract; the rest of the slice is strong — the manifest schema is complete (nice `version` field), the atomic write is done right (same-dir `mkstemp` → `fsync` → `os.replace`, temp cleaned up on exception), and the tests cover init / round-trip / resume / the chainlink-is-source-of-truth invariant.

**Blocking — a present-but-invalid manifest silently reinitializes, defeating crash recovery.**

`load_epic_state` returns `None` for *both* "file absent" and "file present but unreadable/invalid" (it catches `OSError`, `JSONDecodeError`, **and** `KeyError`/`TypeError`/`ValueError` from `from_json`). `load_or_init_epic_state` then treats `None` as "no run yet" and **initializes a fresh manifest**. So a corrupt/half-recovered manifest silently discards a live epic's integration state — the integration branch and merged-slice records are lost, and on the next run the orchestrator can re-merge already-merged slices or orphan the integration branch. That is exactly the failure the manifest exists to prevent.

The `version` field makes this sharper: it's written but never checked, so a schema bump across a deploy makes existing manifests fail `from_json` → `None` → reinit → data loss for every in-flight epic.

Please distinguish the two cases:
- **Absent** → init a fresh manifest (today's behavior, correct).
- **Present but unreadable / invalid / version-mismatched** → do NOT silently discard. Raise (or return a distinct sentinel) so the orchestrator can halt the run and surface `needs-human` rather than starting over. Handle `version` explicitly (accept known versions; treat unknown as the halt case, not the reinit case).
- Add a test: a present-but-corrupt manifest is not silently reinitialized.

**Smaller — resume contract for terminally-blocked slices.** `resume_epic_run` skips only `merged` slices, so a terminally-`blocked` slice is reported as a `build` resume point. On restart the orchestrator would try to rebuild a slice that has already exhausted its retries (livelock risk). Either skip terminal slices (`merged` *and* `blocked`) when computing remaining build work — advancing to `integrate`/partial when only terminal slices remain — or nail that contract in a docstring and add a blocked-slice resume test so S5 (#773) handles it deliberately.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body: Revision fully addresses the review: load_epic_state now returns None only for an absent file and raises EpicStateError on present-but-unreadable/invalid/unsupported-version (so a corrupt manifest is never silently reinitialized), version is checked explicitly, and resume_epic_run skips terminal (merged+blocked) slices. Tests cover all cases incl. file-preservation. CI green. LGTM.

payload.title: Worklink #769: Epic config knobs + worklink:merged label constant

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Requesting changes on one design-contract item; the rest of the slice is good — the epic knobs, the `WORKLINK_MERGED_LABEL` placement in the wave-1 module, and the `load()` fallback refactor (deriving defaults from a `WorklinkDefaults()` instance so old configs stay compatible) all look right, and the tests are thorough.

**Blocking — collapse the tiered-review config to a single high-risk knob (not two axes).**

The intended model is two tiers: *single adversarial pass by default; multi-vote for high-risk slices*. The current `TieredReviewConfig` splits risk into two independent axes — `high_risk_{scope_prefixes,labels}` **and** a separate `multi_vote_{scope_prefixes,labels}` — where `multi_vote_scope_prefixes` defaults to empty and `multi_vote_labels` is just `("risk:multi-vote",)`. That makes the multi-vote trigger ambiguous, and on the natural reading (multi-vote keys off the `multi_vote_*` lists) it ships "multi-vote for high-risk" **off by default**: a slice touching `autonomy.py` / `migrations/` / `auth` is flagged high-risk but would still get a single reviewer unless someone hand-labels `risk:multi-vote`. That contradicts the intended default.

Please collapse to one knob:
- Keep `high_risk_scope_prefixes` and `high_risk_labels` as THE set that marks a slice high-risk.
- Keep `multi_vote_reviewer_count` (default 3) as the reviewer count applied to high-risk slices.
- Remove `multi_vote_scope_prefixes` and `multi_vote_labels`.
- Contract for S4 (#772): a slice is multi-vote **iff** it matches `high_risk_scope_prefixes` or `high_risk_labels`; otherwise a single adversarial pass. If a genuine need for a third tier / explicit escalation list shows up later, add it then — don't pre-build it.

Update `test_worklink_config_epic_overrides_and_tiered_review_parse` to match.

**Minor (worth fixing while here):** `merge_strategy` is an unvalidated free string — a typo like `"noff"` passes config load and would only surface in S3's merge. Validate it against the known set (`no-ff`, `squash`, `ff-only`) at load time.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Request changes — the feature is clean, well-tested, and CI-green; these are refinements, not structural problems. The design is good: `_build_memory_health` degrades visibly (renders an `error` row instead of crashing the report), `run_doctor` is imported lazily and runs read-only, the `aggregate` signature change is backward-compatible, and the aggregate test exercises the real doctor (so the projection mapping is validated, not mocked).

**1. (fix) The "Full report artifact" line is self-referential and misleading.** `memory_health_artifact` is set to the introspection report's *own* path (`str(out)` in the scheduler, `str(args.output)` in the CLI), so inside `introspection-<date>.md` the section renders `Full report artifact: <that same file>`. The label "Full report artifact" implies a more detailed doctor artifact exists elsewhere — it doesn't; the compact summary is self-contained. Please either persist the full `mimir memory doctor --json` output as a separate artifact and point `artifact` at *that*, or drop the self-referential line entirely. (The `test_render_markdown_includes_memory_health_summary` assertion on "Full report artifact" and the scheduler test's `str(reports[0]) in body` should be updated to match whichever you choose.)

**2. (document) The scheduler change broadens the report beyond memory health.** The scheduled path previously called `aggregate(...)` without `home`; this PR adds `home=home`, which now also enables the **skill-health** section (and anything else gated on `home`) in scheduled reports for the first time — not just Memory Health. That's a welcome improvement, but it's a behavior change the PR body/CHANGELOG doesn't mention. Please note it so it's an intentional, documented change rather than an incidental side effect.

**3. (confirm) Added cost per report run.** Every `mimir introspect` / scheduled report now runs the full memory doctor (read-only SQLite integrity + foreign-key checks, atom/triple/embedding scans, wiki/state drift). That's fine for a periodic report, but please confirm it's acceptable on the largest expected SAGA DB, or gate the memory-health section behind a flag if `introspect` is ever run at higher frequency. A one-line note on expected cost is enough.

Nothing here is architectural — #1 is the only concrete change; #2/#3 are a doc line and a confirmation.

payload.title: Restore Claude Code tool safety enforcement

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Reviewed the guard boundary (not just the tests), as the review criteria ask. This is genuine pre-execution enforcement and meets all six acceptance criteria.

**Mechanism is correct.** `_pre_tool_use_hook` runs `_claude_code_pre_tool_enforcement` (admin -> prohibited-bash -> budget, the same order as `BudgetGateMiddleware`) and returns `hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision: "deny"` on failure — the SDK's real pre-execution block, so a denied call never reaches the tool runtime. Not post-hoc logging.

**Consistent, not reimplemented.** It calls the same `_check_and_increment_or_deny` / `_check_admin_authorized` as the LangGraph middleware (refactored to accept a `ctx`), so budget bookkeeping stays identical across the sync-hook and async-middleware paths.

**Handles a subtle trap.** The SDK hook runs in a separate async task where the turn contextvar isn't propagated, so it falls back to `get_turn_by_session_id(session_id)` — with a dedicated regression test.

**Bypass closed.** `is_bash_tool` now also screens MCP/bridged shell aliases (`mcp__mimir__shell_exec`, normalized `mcp_mimir_shell_exec`, etc.), so shell-via-MCP-name still hits `check_prohibited_bash`.

**Fail-closed.** `ensure_tool_enforcement_hooks_installed` raises (claude-code:* unavailable) when the hook surface cannot be installed, cleanly replacing the `MIMIR_ALLOW_CLAUDE_CODE` #426 deprecation gate.

**Canary is real.** `test_prohibited_bash_canary_denies_before_runtime` calls the actual hook with `git push --force origin main`, asserts `deny` + that a simulated dispatcher would not invoke the runtime + a denial tool-result event is recorded. The budget test also exercises the `session_id` fallback path specifically.

Two non-blocking notes:

1. The end-to-end guarantee rests on the SDK honoring `permissionDecision: "deny"`. The unit tests prove the hook returns deny and records it — they cannot prove the live subprocess actually refuses. That live proof is #739's job (correctly out of scope here). Enforcement is implemented correctly; treat it as fully proven after the #739 soak.
2. Prohibited-bash screening reads the `command` arg — covers built-in Bash and mimir's own shell tools (verified they use `command`); a hypothetical external MCP shell with a differently-named arg would skip that one layer, though budget + admin still gate it. Minor hardening opportunity.

Neither blocks. Strong work — this is the enforcement path #426 was waiting on.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Excellent implementation — all six #724 criteria are met (the Ran-name source fix on tool_result/end + span-id join, the "Skill" relabel + dropped redundant call row, opt-in detail level, in-place transient detail that drops on step completion, and the ~2s auto-delete with the soft-fail + no-delete-on-failure paths), #947's trigger gating is fully preserved (session-boundary turns still get no panel), and 217 tests + all 4 CI checks are green. One blocking item, in the highest-risk area:

**Detailed-mode redaction (`_scrub_detail`) has real gaps in the realistic shapes.** It catches `KEY=value` and absolute/`~` paths, but misses:
- Quoted / JSON / dict-repr secret values — `{"password": "hunter2"}`, `'API_KEY': 'sk-12345'` survive verbatim. Since tool args are dicts rendered via `str()`, this is the common shape, so the scrubber misses the most likely leak.
- Keyword-less high-entropy / known-prefix tokens — `AKIA…`, `ghp_…`, `sk-…`, bare bearer values.
- `Authorization: Bearer <token>` (value is space-separated, not after `:`/`=`).
- Relative and Windows paths — `attachments/secret.png`, `C:\Users\…\secret.txt`. Acceptance criterion #5 requires attachment paths never render; a relative attachment path currently does.

This is non-theoretical for this deployment: detailed mode is exactly what we intend to enable on mimirbot's Discord channel, and its tool args/results routinely carry secrets and paths — so these would leak into the channel once detailed is on. coarse-default stays safe, but the feature isn't shippable-to-use until this is closed.

Please harden it. The durable fix is to NOT `str()`-then-scrub raw args/content but render a bounded, structured shape — e.g. for tool calls show the tool name + arg KEYS (not raw values), and for reasoning a short capped preview — so a secret in any arg value can't leak regardless of format. If you keep value-scrubbing, broaden `_SECRET_PATTERNS` to the quoted/JSON/dict forms + a known-prefix/high-entropy token heuristic + `Bearer`, and widen the path masking to relative + Windows paths. Either way, add tests that feed these exact gap shapes (the current detailed-mode test only feeds cases the regex already catches, so it's green without exercising the gaps) and assert nothing leaks.

Nothing else blocking — the rest is merge-ready. Re-request review once detailed-mode redaction covers the realistic secret/path shapes with tests.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Big improvement — I empirically ran the new _scrub_detail against all the gap shapes and 8/9 now scrub correctly, and rendering tool args as keys-only is exactly the right call (dict/JSON secret VALUES can no longer leak regardless of format). Quoted/JSON/dict-repr values, AWS/GitHub/sk- prefixes, high-entropy blobs, and relative + Windows paths are all handled now.

One case still leaks — a pattern-ordering bug, and it's a flagged one:

  Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJ.payload.sig123ABCdef
  -> '[redacted] eyJhbGciOiJ.payload.sig123ABCdef'   (the JWT survives)

Cause: the key=value/JSON secret pattern runs BEFORE the Bearer pattern and matches `Authorization: Bearer` (its value group `[^,\s}]+` grabs "Bearer" and stops at the space), so the Bearer pattern never sees the token. And JWTs contain dots, so the 40+ high-entropy fallback (which excludes `.`) doesn't catch them either. This affects reasoning text and tool RESULT content that echo an auth header (args are safe now via keys-only, but a curl/HTTP tool result dumping headers is realistic).

Fix is a one-liner: move the Bearer pattern (the `(?i)\b(authorization\s*:\s*)?bearer\s+...` one) BEFORE the key=value/JSON pattern so `Authorization: Bearer <token>` is fully redacted before the key=value rule can partially consume it. Add a test asserting a JWT after `Authorization: Bearer` is fully redacted (the current detailed tests don't include this shape).

That's the only remaining item — everything else (the keys-only args, the broadened patterns, the auto-delete/Ran-name/label fixes, #947 coexistence) is solid. Re-request once the Bearer ordering is fixed + tested.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #720: Activity panel s2: TurnEventBus subscriber + lifecycle/debounce/opt-in + Slack Block Kit renderer

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Excellent, security-conscious implementation — all of the amended #720 criteria check out: the three tightening additions (sanitized turn-start trigger metadata with no inbound body, the folded-input event emitted at the actual `_drain()`/`before_model` fold boundary, and the explicit `outbound_message` signal used for finalization instead of parsing `send_message` args), the typed `MessageUpdate` payload from slice 1, opt-in-off-by-default + non-blocking own-task design, clean scope (no Discord creep), and — the high-risk part — a verified-clean redaction trace (the panel reads only sanitized fields; tests feed secret-looking args / message bodies / attachment paths and assert none reach the rendered panel). 

One blocking item:

**`pytest (3.11)` is FAILING** on the PR's own new test `tests/test_activity_panel.py::test_panel_debounces_span_updates_and_finalizes_from_outbound_signal` (`assert 1 == 2`). It's not infra noise — it's a real, environment-dependent bug, reproducible deterministically.

Root cause in `mimir/bridges/_activity_panel.py` `_schedule_edit` (~line 317): `elapsed = loop.time() - self._last_edit_by_channel.get(channel, 0.0)`, flushing immediately only when `elapsed >= debounce_seconds`. The "never edited" sentinel is `0.0`, but `loop.time()` is monotonic with an UNSPECIFIED base. On a process/loop whose `loop.time()` is `< debounce_seconds` at the first edit (true on the 3.11 CI runner, with the test's debounce), `elapsed < debounce` so the FIRST edit is deferred into a pending task and then coalesced away by finalize — yielding 1 edit instead of 2.

This is also a latent product bug, not just a test issue: on any process whose loop's `loop.time()` base is `< debounce_seconds` (default ~1s), the first panel edit on a channel is delayed by up to the debounce window.

**Fix:** use a real "never edited" sentinel instead of `0.0` — e.g. `self._last_edit_by_channel.get(channel)` returning `None` (or `float("-inf")`) ⇒ always flush the first edit immediately, regardless of the loop's monotonic base. That greens 3.11 and removes the first-edit delay.

Everything else is merge-ready — fix the sentinel (and confirm pytest 3.11 goes green) and I'll merge.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #719: Activity panel s1: bridge edit_message (Slack chat.update + Discord message.edit)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The implementation quality is excellent — soft-fail-never-raises on both bridges, send() returns a populated SendResult.message_id on Slack (ts) + Discord (id), no send/react/typing changes, scope clean, and good test coverage. One blocking item: the PR does not match the **current** #719 chainlink.

After this slice was filed, the #719 chainlink was tightened (its "Tightening note from 2026-06-30 review" + amended acceptance criteria): the edit surface must be a **typed `MessageUpdate` payload**, not a loose method signature with ad-hoc per-platform kwargs. This PR implements the original loose shape:

    edit_message(channel_id, message_id, text, *, blocks=None, embed=None) -> SendResult

The amended chainlink requires instead:

1. A typed `MessageUpdate` (dataclass or TypedDict) in `mimir/bridges/base.py` with at least `text: str | None`, `blocks: list[dict[str, Any]] | None` (Slack Block Kit), `embed: Any | None` (Discord embed) — typed and extensible, **no loose `**kwargs`**.
2. `edit_message(channel_id, message_id, update: MessageUpdate) -> SendResult` — a single structured payload arg, not separate text/blocks/embed kwargs — with the same safe no-op default.
3. `SlackBridge.edit_message` uses `update.text` + `update.blocks`, ignoring unsupported fields (e.g. `update.embed`) — not fatal.
4. `DiscordBridge.edit_message` uses `update.text` + `update.embed`, ignoring unsupported fields (e.g. `update.blocks`) — not fatal.
5. Tests assert the typed payload is used and that each bridge ignores the other's unsupported rich field without erroring.

This matters beyond style: slices 2/3 (the panel renderers) will call `edit_message` through this surface, and the chainlink settled on `MessageUpdate` as that bridge-agnostic contract. Please refactor to the typed `MessageUpdate` payload (the per-bridge `chat.update` / `message.edit` calls and the soft-fail handling can stay as-is — just reshape the signature + the call sites + the tests). Everything else looks merge-ready.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Excellent implementation — operator-skin discovery is fail-open with token-key allow-listing, the bootstrap exposes built-in ids + operator manifests, prefs validation returns a clean 400 for unknown skins (null still clears), the bundle↔server parity test actually parses localSkins and catches drift, token values only ever reach the fixed --mimir-* CSS-var allow-list (no injection sink), and #931/#562 is preserved (identity-scoped write, default-fallback-on-unknown-read). pytest 68 passed, vitest 10 passed. Two items, the first blocking:

**[BLOCKING] frontend CI fails — TS7053 typecheck error.** `frontend/src/skins/SkinProvider.tsx:154` (loadSkin): `SkinId` was relaxed to `string` (types.ts:3), but `localSkins` is declared `satisfies Record<string, SkinManifest>`, which keeps its narrow literal-key type. Indexing it with a plain-`string` `DEFAULT_SKIN_ID` under noImplicitAny is an implicit-any error, so the `frontend` job's 'tsc --noEmit && vite build' step exits 2 (reproduced locally with `npx tsc --noEmit`). vitest passes, but the build gate is red — must be green to merge. Please also confirm the full `tsc --noEmit && vite build` passes locally before re-pushing, since vitest alone doesn't run the typecheck.

**[SMALL] validate the operator-skin `fonts` field.** It's the one operator-supplied value not schema-validated — `_validate_operator_skin_manifest` only checks `fonts` is a list, and `useSkinFonts` builds `url(${s.url}) format("${s.format}")` for FontFace. payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Gate poller fires on per-poller budgets

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Strong implementation — budget gate is correctly placed after the global arbiter pre-check and before the subprocess (plus a post-acquire re-check), suppression is per-poller and independent of the global CLEAR decision, the subprocess skip leaves cursor/state untouched, external poller_usage events are aggregated alongside agent-turn usage with a bounded newest-first scan, it fails open on any aggregation error, and poller_budget_suppressed is observational-only (no AgentEvent). CI green, 319 passed locally. One blocking item:

**Window-label silent no-op.** `parse_poller_budget_config` (#925) accepts any non-empty window label (it validates caps, not labels), but `aggregate_poller_turn_usage` only computes the fixed POLLER_USAGE_WINDOWS (1h, 24h). So a budget configured over an unsupported window — e.g. `max_external_usd` on a `7d` or `6h` window — parses with no warning and then silently does nothing (`usage.windows.get(window_label)` is None → `continue` → the cap never suppresses). It fails safe (the poller keeps firing), but an operator gets a budget cap they believe is enforced when it is silently inert — a real footgun on the enforcement slice.

Please validate the window label against the supported set (POLLER_USAGE_WINDOWS) at parse time in `parse_poller_budget_config`: on an unknown label, emit the existing `poller_budget_invalid` log.warning and drop that cap (consistent with the parser's existing fail-open 'drop on invalid shape' behavior), so an unsupported-window cap is rejected loudly rather than silently no-op'd. Add a test that an unsupported window label warns + is dropped (and that 1h/24h still parse and enforce). Alternatively, support the configured window in the aggregator — but loud-reject is the smaller, safer change.

Everything else looks merge-ready; this is the only change requested.

New test asserts the warn + drop and that 1h/24h survive (mutation-verified). No regression: gate placement, per-poller independence, cursor-untouched-on-skip, observational-only event all intact. payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #707: Fail poller/scheduled send_message whose text matches the skip-list (silence-narration)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Solid structure — word-boundary regex (correctly dodges the "Skipton"/"unfiltered" substring traps), tunable module-level phrase list, correct `{poller, scheduled_tick}` trigger gating, event emitted, and it composes cleanly with #910 on the merged tree. One blocking issue:

**False positives drop real escalations.** The gate matches a skip-phrase appearing *anywhere* in the message (`pattern.search(text)`, registry.py:107), with no anchoring or "narration-dominates" gate — and the seed list includes common bare words (`skip`, `filtered`, `no action` at registry.py:81-83). So these genuine poller escalations are wrongly rejected:
- `"No action needed from you, but heads up: your TLS cert expires tomorrow."` → blocked on `no action`
- `"Recommend we skip this release; CI is red on main."` → blocked on `skip`
- `"The filtered alert queue still has 2 P1s awaiting triage."` → blocked on `filtered`
- `"Reminder: no operator alert is configured for the prod DB pager."` → blocked on `no operator alert`

For a gate that silently drops a poller send, the bias must be toward false-negatives (let some narration slip through) over false-positives (drop a real alert). This is partly my chainlink's fault for seeding bare tokens — please refine the matching:

1. Drop the ambiguous bare/short tokens (`skip`, `filtered`, `no action`); keep the unambiguous narration phrases (`skip bucket`, `end silently`/`end-silent`, `routed to skip`, `batch complete`).
2. AND require the narration to dominate — e.g. only trigger when the stripped message is short (a one-line narration, not a substantive alert), or the phrase is the whole/tail of the message — so a real alert that merely *contains* "no action needed" survives. (Narration sends in the data were short one-liners; real escalations are longer with content/URLs — message length is a strong discriminator.)
3. Add a near-miss regression test: a poller escalation containing a stop-phrase (e.g. "no action needed, but your cert expires tomorrow") must PASS.

Minor (non-blocking): the rejection returns a plain string; #910 established `ToolException(...)` + `handle_tool_error=True` for send_message rejections — align to that idiom so there's one rejection mechanism in the function, not two.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body: Re-reviewed: false-positive fix is solid — dangerous bare tokens (skip/filtered/no action/no reply needed/no operator alert) dropped; remaining jargon phrases gated by narration-dominance (word_count<=8 OR phrase-at-tail). My named blocking example ('No action needed... cert expires tomorrow') is now a passing test, plus an embedded 'skip bucket' escalation test; real narration still rejected; interactive turns exempt. CI green.

payload.title: Worklink #702: social-cli: add a count command so agents query the daily post count reliably (retire the hand-maintained counter)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Right repo and a well-chosen design (thin `social-cli` wrapper delegating to the pinned upstream; `count.py` derives from the ledger). UTC day boundary, `dryRun` exclusion, likes/reposts exclusion, multi-ledger aggregation, and empty/missing-ledger → 0 are all correct and tested.

**Blocking correctness bug:** `POST_CREATING_ACTIONS = {"post", "reply"}` (count.py:21) omits `thread`. At the pinned upstream SHA, a multi-post thread writes exactly ONE ledger entry with `action: "thread"` (dispatch.ts), so threads contribute **0** to the count — undercounting against the very daily post cap this command exists to protect (a thread is the single biggest consumer of the budget). Please count `thread` as well. The ledger stores only `textHash` (not `posts.length`), so `+1` per thread is the realistic floor — document that it under-represents a multi-post thread's true post count. Add a `thread` fixture to the tests (none currently exercise it, which is why this slipped through).

Minor (non-blocking): `--since <explicit-date>` with no `--until` is open-ended, while `--since today` bounds to a single UTC day (count.py:~227) — surprising for ad-hoc historical day queries; worth a doc note or a fix. And `or path.is_file()` (count.py:148) makes the platform-name check dead code (harmless, per-record filtering covers it).

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Redact exact poller secret env values

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Verified the redaction doesn't close the leak #437 describes. `_redact_poller_env_values` builds `secret_values` only from keys matching `_DENY_ENV_SUFFIXES` (`_API_KEY`/`_TOKEN`/`_SECRET`/`_PASSWORD`) or the bare names — so a `pass_env` secret under a non-standard name (`WEBHOOK_HMAC`, `DB_DSN`, `SIGNING_KEY`, `DATABASE_URL`) leaks **verbatim** in poller stderr/diagnostics. That's exactly the "bare DB passwords, shared HMACs" case the function's own docstring says it exists for. Confirmed by example: `{'DB_DSN':'postgres://user:s3cr3t@…'}` passes through unredacted.

Fix: the function already receives the fully-assembled `env`, and the assembly path knows which keys came from `pass_env` / `poller.env` (the operator's explicit "forward this secret" signal). Redact the values of **all** forwarded keys, not a name denylist. That also fixes the `< 6`-char false-positive (a deny-named key holding a short ordinary value currently shreds that substring everywhere).

Add a regression test for a `pass_env` secret under a non-deny-suffixed key (the current tests only use `DATABASE_PASSWORD`, which matches `_PASSWORD`, so they pass while the motivating case leaks). Good parts: subprocess passthrough is preserved (the real value still reaches the child), and write-time redaction in `event_logger` is the right layer.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The core fix is correct: redaction is now VALUE-based, keyed off the operator's forwarded `pass_env`/`poller.env` keys regardless of key name, with a good regression test (`WEBHOOK_HMAC`, no TOKEN/SECRET/KEY in the name). That closes the original name-pattern leak on `poller_stderr` and `poller_invalid_line`.

But `_redact_poller_env_values` is wired into only those 2 sinks (pollers.py:1416, 1478). The **same forwarded-secret value still reaches `events.jsonl` unredacted** (token-shape redaction only) on two other durable sinks:

1. **Signal-routing payload (pollers.py ~1511–1520) — blocking.** `payload = {k: v for k, v in parsed.items() if k not in (...)}` → `log_event(signal_type, poller=…, **payload)`. A poller that echoes a forwarded secret into any signal-payload field leaks it verbatim — same threat model and same durable sink as the two paths you fixed.
2. **`poller_event_rejected.prompt_preview` (pollers.py ~1661):** `content[:POLLER_REJECTION_PREVIEW_CHARS]` → `events.jsonl`, token-shape only.

(The enqueued `AgentEvent.content`/`prompt` → `turns.jsonl` is a third, lower-priority sink — at minimum worth an explicit decision in the PR rather than silent omission.)

The `env` + `explicit_env_redact_keys` set are already in scope at the signal/prompt_preview points, so the fix is mechanical: route the string payload values and `prompt_preview` through `_redact_poller_env_values(...)` before logging. Please also add a regression test that a forwarded secret echoed in a **signal payload** is redacted. The original ask was to redact forwarded-key values on all durable sinks regardless of name; these two still leak.

payload.body: Re-reviewed: signal-payload and prompt_preview now value-redacted (non-string values handled safely), signal-payload regression test added; verified no other log_event sink leaks. payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Worklink #685: loop-lag: capture sub-CPU on-loop blocks reliably + surface chronic host descheduling (#682 follow-up)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Enable session-boundary RRF by default

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The adopt decision looks justified — the config comment cites the 2026-06-26 adoption slice at +4.91pp overall / +6.02pp multi-session, and the implementation is clean: config-driven default, per-call overrides preserved, the boundary pathway is wrapped in try/except (auxiliary recall can't break query), and summaries stay routing-only (not rendered to the reader). But this is on by default in production `SagaStore.query`, so the bar is high, and there's a blocker plus two things to close first.

**1. Blocker — CI is red, and it's a real regression, not a stale test.** `tests/test_saga_query_concurrency.py::test_saga_query_uses_independent_connections_for_concurrent_reads` fails `assert 16 == 8` on both 3.11 and 3.12. Cause: with the lane on by default, every `query()` now calls `_session_boundary_atom_pathway` → `search_sessions()` **before** `_do_with_conn`, and that opens its own connection separate from the recall connection — so each query uses 2 connections, and 8 concurrent reads open 16. Please **don't fix this by bumping the test to 16** — that doubles per-query SQLite connection churn for every agent on every query. Reuse a single connection per query (run the session-boundary search within the same per-query connection scope / thread the conn through) so the one-connection-per-read invariant holds. (Also: the PR's "125 passed" validation was a subset — the full suite has to be green; this is exactly the kind of cross-cutting test a subset misses.)

**2. Report the guardrail categories before defaulting on.** The thread's adopt criteria were Target3/multi-session as the primary readout *with single-session regressions as the guardrail*. The PR cites overall + multi-session gains but not whether `single-session-preference` / `single-session-user` / `single-session-assistant` / `temporal-reasoning` **regressed**. A +4.91pp overall can still hide a single-session regression. Please paste the per-category before/after for the adoption slice (and the run tag / artifact path) so we can confirm no guardrail category went backwards — that's the difference between "net win" and "safe to enable for everyone by default."

**3. Acknowledge the per-query cost.** On by default means every production query now adds a `search_sessions` vector search + atom expansion (and currently the extra connection). The accuracy gain justifies the feature, but worth a line on the latency/connection impact, and confirming it degrades gracefully when the `sessions` table is empty/cold (new homes) — the try/except returns `[]`, which looks right, but a no-boundary home shouldn't pay a vector-search round trip per query if avoidable.

Net: the feature and the data are convincing; fix the connection doubling (the real issue the failing test surfaced), show the guardrail categories didn't regress, and note the cost. Then it's good to default on.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Thanks for the quick turnaround, but `05aa42a6` doesn't address the blocker — it sidesteps it. The change passes `enable_session_boundary_rrf=False` into the concurrency test so it exercises the *old* single-connection path. CI is green again, but:

- **The production default is now untested for this invariant.** Production `query()` defaults to `enable_session_boundary_rrf=True`, and the test now explicitly turns it off — so `test_saga_query_uses_independent_connections_for_concurrent_reads` no longer covers the path that actually ships. That's a false green: the behavior the test exists to protect is exactly the one we stopped testing.
- **The real issue is still there.** With the lane on (i.e. in production), every `query()` still opens a second connection via `_session_boundary_atom_pathway → search_sessions()` before the recall connection — 2 connections per query, 16 under 8 concurrent reads. Disabling the feature in the test doesn't change that; it just hides it.

Please do one of:
1. **(preferred) Reuse the query's connection** — run the session-boundary search/expansion within the same per-query connection scope so default-on stays at one connection per read, then keep the concurrency test on the **default** path (lane enabled). That both fixes the doubling and restores real coverage.
2. If a separate connection is genuinely required, **assert the real default-path behavior** (lane on) with the connection count it actually produces, plus a comment justifying the per-query doubling and a note on the load implication — don't disable the feature to make the count look unchanged.

Still open from the first review (no reply yet):
- **Guardrail categories** — paste the per-category before/after for the adoption slice (single-session-preference / -user / -assistant / temporal). +4.91pp overall can hide a single-session regression; defaulting on for everyone needs the guardrail categories shown flat-or-up, with the run tag/artifact path.
- **Per-query cost** — a line acknowledging the added `search_sessions` vector search on every production query, and confirming cold/empty-`sessions` homes (new agents) don't pay a round-trip for nothing.

The feature + the headline result are still convincing; it's the connection doubling (fixed for real, with the test on the live path) and the guardrail breakdown that gate turning this on by default.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
`65b8ebae` is exactly right — the connection blocker is resolved. Verified:

- `_session_boundary_atom_pathway_with_conn(conn, …)` / `_search_sessions_with_conn(conn, …)` reuse the query's connection, so default-on no longer opens a second connection per query.
- The query embedding is computed once and shared between recall and the boundary search — no extra provider round-trip either.

CI green on 3.11/3.12.

That clears the connection doubling and largely addresses the per-query cost concern (shared conn + embedding; cold/empty-`sessions` homes return `[]` cheaply).

**One thing still gates turning this on by default — the guardrail categories.** This enables session-boundary RRF for every agent on every query, and the only result cited is +4.91pp overall / +6.02pp multi-session. Before merge, please paste the per-category before/after for the adoption slice — specifically `single-session-preference`, `single-session-user`, `single-session-assistant`, and `temporal-reasoning` — plus the run tag / artifact path. The adopt criteria from the design thread were "multi-session as the primary readout, single-session regressions as the guardrail," and a +overall can mask a single-session regression. If those categories are flat-or-up, this is good to merge (no further code change needed). No reply on this from the last two rounds, so flagging it's the sole remaining item.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Re-review — all my technical points are resolved, and with the operator's scoping clarification there's no remaining blocker from me.

Verified on the latest commits:
- **Connection reuse (the blocker):** `65b8eba` moves the boundary search into the per-query connection scope; `7d5a931` proves it on the **default** path — the concurrency test now asserts `len(boundary_connections) == 8` and that the boundary-lane conn ids equal the query conn ids (same connection, not a second). No more doubling, and the production default is genuinely covered. ✓
- **Cold/empty-home cost:** `617159f3` short-circuits with `SELECT 1 FROM sessions LIMIT 1` — new/cold homes skip the session vector search entirely, so the default-on lane adds nothing until there are boundaries to match. ✓

On the guardrail question: understood that the adoption slice was deliberately the two *worst* categories from the prior 500q baseline (single-session-preference 0.267, multi-session 0.647), not the full suite. That's sound design — test where the headroom is. By the arithmetic (n=30 preference / n=133 multi-session; +4.91pp overall vs +6.02pp multi-session), **single-session-preference comes out ≈flat** — the gain is essentially all multi-session, with no regression on the other tested slice. Please drop the exact single-session-preference before/after + run tag in the PR for the record, but I'm satisfied that's not a regression.

Residual to accept (operator call, which you've effectively made): default-on applies the lane to the *untested* categories (single-session-user/-assistant, temporal, knowledge-update) for every agent. That risk is bounded — an independent review of the #880 plumbing confirmed the extra pathway is a secondary, additive, 0.5-weight RRF lane that **cannot bypass** the tombstoned/agent/skill/confidence filters, so it can only re-rank, never inject wrong atoms, and the primary lanes still dominate.

One forward note tied to a code-review finding: recall does **not** de-dup atom ids *within* an extra pathway (RRF sums per occurrence), so make sure `_session_boundary_atom_pathway_with_conn` emits a de-duplicated id list — otherwise an atom appearing in two matched sessions gets double-weighted. I'm filing a chainlink to fix the dedup on the recall side too, but the lane should not rely on that.

Net: blocker fixed, cost addressed, scoping understood — good to merge on your sign-off.

This is the capstone that wires #881 (boundary rows) + #880 (RRF pathway) into the actual experiment, and it's clean. Reviewed end-to-end:

- **Correctly wired:** `search_sessions()` → expand matched sessions to their atoms via `atoms.session_id` (persisted by #881) → feed as `extra_atom_ranked_pathways={"session_boundary": …}` with `rrf_pathway_weights` into `query()` (#880). - **Not silently empty:** I confirmed `search_sessions` returns dicts keyed `session_id` (client.py:135), which is exactly what `_session_boundary_rrf_pathway` reads — so the lane actually promotes atoms rather than no-op'ing.
- **Opt-in / default-preserved:** `--session-boundary-rrf-lane` defaults off; when off, `extra_atom_ranked_pathways`/`rrf_pathway_weights` are None and `query()` is unchanged.
- **Clean hypothesis:** the reader gets the promoted *atoms* through normal RRF, not a rendered summary block — and `test_session_boundary_rrf_lane_keeps_summaries_out_of_reader` asserts the summary text and `session_boundary` key never reach the reader. - Nice observability: per-question debug metrics + `--retrieval-debug-jsonl`, which matches the "dry-run with capture, inspect a few qids" plan before the 500q run.

Notes (non-blocking):
- The pathway unit test stubs `search_sessions`, and the end-to-end test asserts summaries are kept *out* of the reader but doesn't assert the lane actually promoted atoms. Since I verified the real return shape this is fine, but an `assert metrics["session_boundary_atom_candidates"] > 0` in the e2e test would guard against a future `search_sessions` shape regression silently emptying the lane.
- Intra-session atom order in the promoted lane is chronological (`created_at, rowid`), not relevance-ranked. Fine for RRF (the session match did the relevance step), just worth knowing when reading results.
- Writeup framing: this measures episode-routing-then-atom-promotion, not summary-rendering — keep that explicit when comparing to the 0.796 baseline.

Recommend merge. Withholding approval for your sign-off.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
The approach is right and the safety property you cared about holds. I verified `make_async_boundary_synth_fn` is a pure summarizer (calls `call_llm`, returns structured fields or `_empty_boundary()` on failure — no channel-memory / learnings-pending / feedback writes), and `end_session` writes only the per-question SagaStore DB. It's also correctly opt-in (`--session-boundary-treatment none|generated`, default `none`). Three things before this is a runnable experiment:

1. **The reader never consults these boundaries** — the code comment says so. On its own, `generated` pays one boundary LLM synth call per haystack session per question (~48/question) and writes `sessions` rows that nothing reads, so it can't move the score. This is half the experiment; it only becomes testable wired to a retrieve→render path — i.e. `search_sessions()` → expand to atoms via #880's `extra_atom_ranked_pathways` → a reader block. Low risk in the current bench — `query()` is called without `session_id` and recall doesn't filter/score on `atoms.session_id` — but please confirm it doesn't shift a fresh baseline relative to the 0.796 run you just measured, or the treatment-vs-baseline comparison drifts.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Reviewed the diff end-to-end. The experiment design is sound and the comparison is clean:

- **Default behavior is untouched.** Every new path is gated (`populate_sessions=False`, `session_summary_lane=False` defaults; `_read` only takes the session path when `retrieved["session_summaries"]` is truthy). A baseline run is byte-for-byte the prior behavior.
- **No confound in the reader.** I checked saga's `read()` — it's exactly `call_reader(build_prompt(question, question_date, retrieved))` returning the 5-key dict. The lane's `_read` reproduces that and appends only the session block to the last message, returning the same shape. So treatment vs. baseline differs solely by the session-context block, with the reader model/temperature held constant. Good — that's the property that makes the #674 adopt/reject decision trustworthy.
- Smoke test is meaningful: it plants "I prefer concise replies" and asserts it surfaces in the captured reader prompt, plus `n_sessions_indexed`/`n_session_summaries`. CI green.

Two things to address/note before the 500q run:

1. **`_read` duplicates `read()`'s body** (build_prompt → call_reader → the 5-key dict). That's what keeps the comparison faithful *today*, but it will silently drift if saga's `read()` ever grows post-processing or changes the prompt assembly — and the drift would contaminate exactly this experiment. Please either factor the shared path (e.g. have the lane call a saga helper that takes an extra appended-block arg) or add a one-line comment in `_read` pinning it as "mirrors saga.benchmarks…read(); keep in sync." A small change that protects the result's validity.

2. **Interpretation caveat (not a code defect):** the "session summary" here is a capped, role-tagged sketch of the *raw turns* (deliberately non-generative, which the docstring is upfront about). So a positive lane result could reflect "session-grouped raw context retrieved a second way" rather than "summaries help." Worth stating explicitly in the #674 writeup so the adopt decision isn't mis-attributed to summarization before the generated-trace variant exists.

Minor (bench-scoped, non-blocking): `_populate_session_summaries` pokes SagaStore privates (`_ensure_conn`, `_sessions_index_built`, `_sessions_index`) and relies on the positional `emb[0]`/`emb[3]` shape from `_batch_embed_texts`. Fine for a harness that already does this for atom ingest, just fragile to a SagaStore refactor.

Withholding formal approval for operator sign-off; the design is sound and #1 is the only thing I'd want touched.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: fix(file-tools): bound recursive search traversal (#673)

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Traced the full path (composite → route backends → `to_thread(self.grep/glob)` → these overrides; home/`:ro` reach `_RootAwareFilesystemBackend` via `__getattr__`). The bounds are wired correctly across home + rw + ro roots, the `ls` filter is reached through `super().ls()` rather than shadowed, and the Python fallback is now capped — so the original outage can't recur even with rg missing. Nice. One blocking issue and a few notes.

## Blocking — truncation via `GrepResult.error` makes the composite discard good matches

`grep()` signals truncation by returning `GrepResult(error=..., matches=partial)`. But `CompositeBackend.agrep` treats any route error as fatal to the fan-out, and on a route error it returns *that route's* result — **discarding `all_matches` already collected from the default backend and earlier routes**:

```python
# deepagents composite.agrep, path=None/"/" branch
default_result = await self.default.agrep(...)
if default_result.error: return default_result
all_matches.extend(default_result.matches or [])
for route_prefix, backend in self.routes.items():
    grep_result = await backend.agrep(pattern, "/", glob)
    if grep_result.error:
        return grep_result        # <-- drops all_matches (home + earlier routes)
    all_matches.extend(...)
```

Concretely, on mimirbot's live config (`/workspace/mimir:rw,/longmemeval-data:ro,/mimir-results:ro`): an unscoped `grep("foo")` searches the home first, then the routes in order. If `/longmemeval-data` (a multi-GB JSON dataset where a common token trivially exceeds 2,000 matching lines) hits `max_grep_matches`, the composite returns **only that route's matches** and throws away the home + `/workspace/mimir` matches the agent most likely wanted. So the cap that's meant to protect the data mount actively suppresses results from the repo roots.

This is the exact multi-root config that motivated the change, and it's untested — the truncation tests exercise `_RootAwareFilesystemBackend` directly, never through `FileToolRouter`/`CompositeBackend`. Could you:
1. Add a `FileToolRouter`-level test: default + a truncating route, asserting the merged result is what we actually want (not just the truncating route's slice).
2. Reconsider signaling truncation via `error`. Options: cap silently + `log.warning` server-side (the agent already gets a strong signal from 2,000 matches); or carry truncation as a non-`error` field / sentinel match so the composite keeps merging. Whatever keeps a broad grep from losing the home/repo matches when a data mount saturates.

(Aside: `glob` truncation has the mirror-image quirk — in the fan-out branch the composite *doesn't* check `error`, so a glob truncation `error` is silently dropped. Worth making grep + glob consistent.)

## Notes (not blocking, but address or reply)

- **Defense-in-depth framing / drift risk.** This reimplements ~400 lines of deepagents `grep`/`glob`. Since #875 now guarantees rg is installed in every image, the Python-fallback bounding is belt-and-suspenders and the rg-exclude path is the real win on no-`.gitignore` mounts — good, but the reimplementation has to track upstream `GrepResult`/`GlobResult` shape changes. Add a comment pointing at #875 + a note to revisit if deepagents grows native bounds, so a future reader knows why we forked it.
- **Home backend behavior change.** The default (home) backend now also excludes `.git/dist/build/node_modules/...` and caps matches — a change beyond the routes. Almost certainly fine/desirable, but confirm it's intended; and note that excluded dirs are skipped *silently* (an agent grepping for something it knows is under `node_modules` gets zero hits with no explanation — matches rg's `.gitignore` UX, so acceptable, just worth knowing).
- **glob semantics.** Stock uses `search_path.rglob(pattern)`; this walks + `candidate.match(pattern)` on the **absolute** path, which is slightly more lenient (e.g. `**/*.py` matches root-level files because the abs path always has parent seg

Defense-in-depth comment + non-blocking responses all good. 59 passed, CI green. LGTM.

Blocking finding:

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Strict review — requesting changes. The design pivot is right: a separate scheduled `memory-hygiene` job keeps reflection focused instead of growing more mandatory sub-passes, coverage matches #644's intent (channel-memory bloat, stale/resolved `memory/issues/*`, missing descriptions, filing-rule mismatches), the "flag, don't delete" + escalate-first posture is correct, and `0 8 * * 2` is a genuine Tuesday under the now-merged #857 day-of-week fix. Three blockers:

**Blocking**

1. **`memory-hygiene.md` Step 1 — scan uses the wrong home.** `home = Path.home()` is the OS user home (`/home/mimir` in the containers), not mimir's home. mimir's home is `$MIMIR_HOME` (bind-mounted `/mimir-home` on muninn/mimirbot), and every other bundled prompt scans it that way — `issues-audit.md`: `ls -tr "$MIMIR_HOME"/memory/issues/*.md`; `reflect.md`: `wc -l "$MIMIR_HOME/memory/learnings-pending.md"`; config resolves home from `os.environ["MIMIR_HOME"]`. As written the scan targets a tree that doesn't exist and finds nothing. → Base the scan on `os.environ["MIMIR_HOME"]`.

2. **`reflect.md` line 80 — dangling cross-reference.** The change `Promote / drop / keep per §B.4` → `§B.6` points at a section that doesn't exist: reflect.md's passes stop at **§B.4 ("Pending-learnings buffer review")**, which *is* the promote/drop/keep pass. The original `§B.4` was correct (looks like a leftover from the expand-then-revert). → Revert to `§B.4`.

3. **`memory-hygiene.md` Step 3 reintroduces the retired `state/proposed-changes.md`.** #856 (merged) made proposed-changes legacy/migration-only; the current `60-filing-rules.md` routes operator decisions to a Chainlink issue or `state/spec/<…>-decision.md`, and reflect.md no longer references proposed-changes at all. A brand-new prompt shouldn't seed fresh usage of it. → Change the "operator decisions" bullet to Chainlink / `state/spec`; keep the protected-surface `open_proposal`/`submit_proposal` bullet as-is.

**Nit:** the scan does `p.read_text(...).splitlines()[:1]` — reads each whole file just to get line one. Fine for memory files, but bounding it (read only the first line) keeps the scan cheap across a large tree.

CI is green, but none of the three blockers are covered by the template tests (they assert frontmatter + cron + two body phrases, not the scan base, the cross-ref, or the proposed-changes routing) — green ≠ correct here.

**Blocking**

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: fix(github-poller): detect stale reviews after content-free rebase

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Strict review — requesting changes, and I don't think this closes #558 as written.

**Blocking**
1. The content guard uses GitHub's three-dot `compare/{review_sha}...{head_sha}`, whose `files` array is the diff from the **merge-base** to head — not a tree-equality check between the reviewed commit and the new head. A content-free rebase re-applies the PR's own changes on top of a newer base, so `files` is non-empty → `_head_has_file_changes_since` returns `True` → the stale reminder is suppressed: the same behavior #558 describes. Please verify against a *real* content-free-rebase compare payload. A reliable signal is harder than `compare.files` — compare commit **tree SHAs** (`GET /commits/{sha}` → `commit.tree.sha`) or patch-ids; note that a rebase pulling in upstream commits changes the tree too, so be precise about what "content-free" means.
2. The unit tests pass only because they hand-feed a fabricated `{"files": []}` compare response for the "rebase" case (and `{"files":[…]}` for "real fix") — shapes GitHub wouldn't return for those scenarios. They validate an unreachable path, which is why CI is green despite #1. Rewrite the tests against the real signal, ideally with a fixture captured from an actual rebase compare response.

**Nit:** the guard adds a per-poll API round-trip for every blocked PR with a newer head date — once the signal is correct, consider short-circuiting/caching.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body: Re-reviewed — now compares the PR's own patch signature (review-time vs current) to detect a content-free rebase, replacing the broken compare.files heuristic, with realistic three-dot compare-payload tests. Both blockers resolved. Approving.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: Add cluster observation GEPA evaluator

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Strict review — requesting changes. Solid structure (follows the `commitments_extraction` GEPA-adapter idiom; scoring is deterministic and wired to the real parsers), but the live optimization path has a crash bug and is untested.

**Blocking**
1. `evals/cluster_observation/adapter.py` `render_candidate_prompt` calls `.format()` directly on the **GEPA-evolved** candidate prompt. Any candidate containing a literal `{`/`}` (JSON/dict examples, a stray brace) raises `KeyError`/`ValueError`, which propagates through `asyncio.gather` and aborts the whole `evaluate` batch. This is exactly the footgun the sibling `commitments_extraction/adapter.py` documents and avoids (evolve only the system prompt; keep the `.format()` template fixed). GEPA mutates this text freely, so it will fire in normal operation. Render the atoms into a separate fixed template the candidate can't break (or brace-safe `str.replace` on one known token).
2. Missing `{indexed_atoms}` placeholder → source atoms are silently dropped and the model is scored on a contentless prompt, so GEPA optimizes against meaningless scores. Validate the placeholder is present (or always append the atoms) and fail loudly / penalize.
3. No test exercises the live path (`make_saga_synth_fn`, `load_corpus`, `_coerce_example`) or the brace/placeholder behavior — every adapter test injects a brace-free stub, so #1/#2 are invisible to CI. Add tests for a brace-containing candidate and a missing-placeholder candidate.

**Nits:** ASI artifact ordering is non-deterministic across processes (`metrics.py` returns `set`s — sort them, since the reflection LLM reads the ASI); `load_corpus` blank-line rows shift the `idx % 4` holdout split; `make_reflective_dataset` emits `Inputs` as a JSON string where GEPA's contract wants a dict.

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body: Re-reviewed — all blockers + nits resolved: render_candidate_prompt uses str.replace (literal braces safe), missing {indexed_atoms} is gated to a hard-fail (score 0, no synth call) with a dedicated test, ASI artifacts sorted, Inputs is a dict, load_corpus blank-line tested, plus a calibrated prompt-overfit regularizer. CI green. Approving.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.body:
Update from Chainlink #629 adoption gate:

- Added candidate-level prompt overfit scoring to the evaluator (`score_prompt_candidate`) plus adapter score/ASI wiring.
- Focused validation: `uv run pytest tests/test_cluster_observation_eval.py -q` => 10 passed.
- Regularized GEPA rerun artifacts: `state/evals/gepa-cluster-observation/gepa-run-2026-06-22-629-regularized/`.

payload.author: mimir-carreira
payload.title: fix(web): require auth identity for chat

payload.author: jasoncarreira
payload.body:
Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES

The backend is exactly right for #621 — `_chat_identity()` gates POST / `/chat/stream` / history with master→403 and missing-identity→401, and that fires even in dev/open mode (no `auth_identity` → 401), so there's no anonymous chat; the channel is always derived from `identity.canonical` and client channel fields/params are ignored; `ChatPostRequest` is cleaned up. Nicely done.

One blocking issue, in the frontend:

- `frontend/src/ChatRoute.tsx` — the chat-stream effect deps changed from `[channelId]` to `[setMessages, update]`. `setMessages` is a stable zustand action, but **`update` is not stable**: `useRouteState` defines it as a plain inline `function update(...)` (`frontend/src/routeState.ts:97`), so it's a new function reference on every render. ChatRoute re-renders on every streaming token (`setStreamingReply`), so the authoritative chat SSE now tears down (`handle.close()` → abort) and reconnects on **every render** during a reply. That churns the connection and can drop the finalizing `chat.message` during a reconnect gap — so the provisional streaming bubble never gets replaced. It's a regression against the reconnect/stability work in #830 and the silent-death fix in #619. The existing tests don't catch it because nothing triggers a re-render between render and unmount.

Fix (either):
- Memoize `update` in `useRouteState` with `useCallback` (preferred — fixes it for every consumer and is correct), or
- Capture `update` in a ref inside ChatRoute and keep the effect deps `[setMessages]`.

Please also add a test that the chat stream is created once across re-renders (e.g. assert `createChatStream` call count stays 1 after a state-driven re-render), so the regression can't silently come back.

Everything else — channel adoption from the first stream message / history response, `fetchChatHistory()` with no arg, dropping the client-selected channel — is coherent and matches the issue.

payload.author: jasoncarreira

Regression test forces a re-render (channel adoption) and asserts createChatStream stays at 1 call + close not called. Backend already correctly required a per-user identity on all chat endpoints (incl. dev/open → 401), derived the channel from identity, and dropped client channel selection. Approving.
